title: How to Watch a Broadcast Like You Mean It
section: Tells: clues you can see before the snap
text:
Tells: clues you can see before the snap
Players can’t hide everything. A lineman about to fire forward stands a little differently from one about to step back; a running back who needs a running start lines up deeper; a defense that wants an extra man near the line has to put him there before the snap. Any such detail that leaks what’s coming is a tell: a clue that shifts the odds, never a guarantee. Coaches hunt for their opponents’ tells all week, and spend just as long hunting for their own, so they can break them (it’s called self-scouting; see Constraint Theory and Sequencing). That arms race is why every tell in this section comes with a “usually.”
Two words you’ll need first. In the shotgun the quarterback stands about five yards behind the center and the ball is snapped back to him through the air; under center (more here) he crouches right behind the center and takes the ball from his hands. Here are four tells to start your catalogue. The full catalogue, with linebackers, cornerbacks and the tight end, is in Watching Live.


Show the Python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(6.5, 4.75))
for ax in axes.flat:
    blank(ax)


def ppy_of(ax, span):
    fig.canvas.draw_idle()
    return ax.get_window_extent().width / span * 72 / fig.dpi


# ---- A. stance (side view, facing right toward the line of scrimmage)
ax = axes[0, 0]
ax.set_xlim(0, 30); ax.set_ylim(-4.8, 11.6); ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.set_title("A  Stance", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
ax.plot([0.5, 29.5], [2, 2], color=style.BASELINE, lw=1.2)
ax.plot([29.0, 29.0], [2.0, 9.6], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (3, 2)))
ax.text(28.6, 10.6, "line  forward ►", ha="right", va="center", fontsize=6.2, color=style.INK_2)
LW = 2.6
WEIGHT = style.DEFENSE_DARK


def stick(x0, pts, head, col=style.OFFENSE):
    (fb, ff, kb, kf, hip, sh, hand) = pts
    for a, b in ((fb, kb), (kb, hip), (ff, kf), (kf, hip), (hip, sh), (sh, hand)):
        ax.plot([x0 + a[0], x0 + b[0]], [a[1], b[1]], color=col, lw=LW, solid_capstyle="round")
    ax.add_patch(Circle((x0 + head[0], head[1]), 0.85, fc=col, ec="none"))


def weight(x, y):
    """A dot where the weight rests, with a short arrow pressing down on it."""
    ax.add_patch(Circle((x, y), 0.42, fc=WEIGHT, ec="white", lw=0.5, zorder=5))
    ax.annotate("", xy=(x, y + 0.5), xytext=(x, y + 2.3),
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=WEIGHT, lw=1.3), zorder=5)


# two-point: a crouch, feet wide, knees bent, hips near knee height, hands resting on the thighs
stick(4.0, [(-1.2, 2), (1.2, 2), (-0.4, 3.8), (1.8, 3.9), (-0.8, 5.0), (1.0, 6.9), (1.7, 4.3)], (1.8, 7.8))
weight(4.0, 1.75)
# light three-point: hips up and back, the hand barely touching; weight on the back foot
stick(13.5, [(-2.4, 2), (0.0, 2), (-1.6, 4.3), (0.8, 4.2), (-1.9, 6.7), (1.8, 7.5), (2.0, 2.15)], (2.9, 8.3))
weight(13.5 - 2.4, 1.75)
# heavy three-point: shoulders out over the hand, weight forward onto it
stick(23.0, [(-2.3, 2), (0.1, 2), (-1.5, 4.0), (0.8, 3.8), (-1.5, 5.9), (2.6, 5.4), (1.9, 2.15)], (3.5, 5.9))
weight(23.0 + 1.9, 1.75)
for x, t in ((4.5, "two-point:\nno hand down,\nweight even"), (13.3, "three-point,\nlight hand:\nweight back\n→ pass set?"),
             (23.6, "three-point,\nheavy hand:\nweight forward\n→ run block?")):
    ax.text(x, 0.7, t, ha="center", va="top", fontsize=6.3, color=style.INK_2, linespacing=1.1)

# ---- B. where the back lines up
ax = axes[0, 1]
ax.set_xlim(-2.6, 30); ax.set_ylim(-15, 3.5); ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.set_title("B  Where the back lines up", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
ppb = ppy_of(ax, 32.6)
for x0, qb_d, rb, name, rate in ((5, -5.0, (1.5, -5.0), "shotgun", "79% pass"),
                                 (15, -4.0, (0.0, -7.0), "pistol", "29% pass"),
                                 (25, -1.6, (0.0, -7.0), "under center", "31% pass")):
    ax.plot([x0 - 4.3, x0 + 4.3], [0.4, 0.4], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=1.0, alpha=0.7)
    for dx in (-2.6, -1.3, 0.0, 1.3, 2.6):
        draw_marker(ax, x0 + dx, -0.3, "off", "", ppb, r=0.55)
    draw_marker(ax, x0, qb_d, "off", "Q", ppb, r=0.6)
    draw_marker(ax, x0 + rb[0], rb[1], "off", "R", ppb, r=0.6)
    ax.text(x0, -9.4, name, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7.4, color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
    ax.text(x0, -10.9, rate, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7.0, color=style.INK_2)
# a depth ruler: yards behind the line
ax.plot([-1.2, -1.2], [0.4, -7.0], color=style.INK_2, lw=0.8)
for dd in (0, 5, 7):
    ax.plot([-1.6, -0.8], [0.4 - dd if dd == 0 else -dd, 0.4 - dd if dd == 0 else -dd], color=style.INK_2, lw=0.8)
ax.text(-1.9, -5.0, "5", ha="right", va="center", fontsize=5.8, color=style.INK_2)
ax.text(-1.9, -7.0, "7", ha="right", va="center", fontsize=5.8, color=style.INK_2)
ax.text(-1.2, -8.0, "yd", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=5.6, color=style.INK_2)
ax.text(14.0, -13.4, "2025 regular season, all downs. Shotgun runs often send the\nback across the QB's face: "
        "offset right, run usually goes left.", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.0, color=style.INK_2,
        linespacing=1.15)

# ---- C. receiver splits (offense's right side, ball in the middle of the field)
ax = axes[1, 0]
ax.set_xlim(-3.4, 28.5); ax.set_ylim(-9.6, 6); ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.set_title("C  Receiver splits", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
ppc = ppy_of(ax, 31.9)
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((-3.4, -9.6), 31.07, 15.6, fc=style.TURF, ec="none", zorder=0))
ax.plot([26.67, 26.67], [-9.6, 6], color=style.INK_2, lw=1.4)               # sideline
ax.plot([-3.4, 26.67], [0.2, 0.2], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=1.0, alpha=0.7)
ax.text(14.7, 3.8, "30", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=11, color=style.MUTED, alpha=0.6, fontweight="bold")
for yy in (-6, -3, 3):
    ax.plot([2.8, 3.4], [yy, yy], color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.8)
ax.text(3.1, 4.9, "hash", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.0, color=style.INK_2, style="italic")
ax.text(14.7, 5.3, "numbers", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.0, color=style.INK_2, style="italic")
ax.text(25.9, 3.4, "sideline", ha="right", va="center", fontsize=6.0, color=style.INK_2, style="italic")
for dx in (-1.6, 0.0, 1.6):
    draw_marker(ax, dx, -0.5, "off", "", ppc, r=0.55)
ax.text(0.0, -2.2, "line", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.0, color=style.INK_2, style="italic")
for x, lab in ((7.6, "reduced"), (14.7, "normal"), (21.3, "wide")):
    draw_marker(ax, x, -0.5, "off", "Z", ppc, r=0.62)
    ax.text(x, -2.2, lab, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7.0, color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
ax.text(7.6, -4.6, "crack block,\ncrosser or dig,\nor room to\nbreak outside", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=5.9,
        color=style.INK_2, linespacing=1.1)
ax.text(14.7, -4.3, "the default:\ntells little", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=5.9, color=style.INK_2,
        linespacing=1.1)
ax.text(21.3, -4.6, "alone: deep,\nbreaking inside,\nor clearing\nspace", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=5.9,
        color=style.INK_2, linespacing=1.1)
ax.text(12.0, -8.4, "one receiver, three possible spots", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.0,
        color=style.INK, style="italic")

# ---- D. safety depth
ax = axes[1, 1]
ax.set_xlim(-1, 41); ax.set_ylim(-3.5, 18.5); ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.set_title("D  Safety depth", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
ppd = ppy_of(ax, 42)
for x0, saf, name in ((10, [(-6.5, 13.0), (6.5, 13.0)], "two deep\n(two-high)"),
                      (30, [(0.0, 13.0), (5.0, 7.5)], "one deep, one down\n(one-high)")):
    ax.plot([x0 - 9.5, x0 + 9.5], [0, 0], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=1.0, alpha=0.7)
    for dd in (5, 10, 15):
        ax.plot([x0 - 9.5, x0 + 9.5], [dd, dd], color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.5)
    for dx in (-3.6, -1.2, 1.2, 3.6):
        draw_marker(ax, x0 + dx, 1.0, "def", "", ppd, r=0.6)
    for dx in (-2.0, 2.0):
        draw_marker(ax, x0 + dx, 4.5, "def", "", ppd, r=0.6)
    for sx, sd in saf:
        draw_marker(ax, x0 + sx, sd, "def", "S", ppd, r=0.75)
    ax.text(x0, -2.2, name, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK, fontweight="bold",
            linespacing=1.05)
for dd in (5, 10, 15):
    ax.text(-0.6, dd, f"{dd}", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=5.8, color=style.INK_2)
ax.text(-0.6, 17.3, "yards off the ball", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=5.8, color=style.INK_2)
ax.annotate("walked down:\nan extra man\nnear the line", xy=(35.6, 7.9), xytext=(37.6, 13.6), fontsize=5.8,
            color=style.INK_2, ha="center", va="center", linespacing=1.1,
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=style.INK_2, lw=0.8, shrinkB=5))
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=0.6, w_pad=0.8)
plt.show()








Figure 8.5: Tells starter card: four clues to check before the snap. A, stance (side view, the line of scrimmage to the right): the dot and arrow show where a lineman’s weight is, which hints at his first step. B, the backfield: typical depths, and how often offenses passed from each setup in the 2025 regular season (FTN charting via nflverse). C, splits: one receiver in three possible spots, measured against the painted numbers. D, safety depth: two deep, or one deep with the other walked down near the line.






Stance: where the weight is
A player’s stance is how he stands just before the snap. In a two-point stance only his two feet are on the ground: for a lineman that is still a crouch, knees bent and hands resting on his thighs, not standing up straight. In a three-point stance one hand is also down (a four-point stance, both hands down, shows up at the goal line). A hand on the ground lets you start low and drive forward, so interior linemen on both sides (the guards, the center, the defensive tackles) mostly use three-point stances. Elsewhere it varies: in offenses that play mostly from the shotgun, the offensive tackles often stand in a two-point stance on most snaps, because a pass blocker’s first step is backward and an upright start makes it quicker; and many edge rushers stand up too.
The tell is in the hand. A lineman with a heavy hand (also called a heavy stance) has his shoulders out over his down hand and a lot of his weight on it; sometimes you can see his knuckles whiten. He is coiled to go forward, which usually means a run block. A lineman whose hand barely touches the grass, hips back and weight on his heels, is ready to step back into a pass set (Pass Protection). Coaches studying film look for a few refinements of the same idea:

A tackle’s stagger. A tackle whose outside foot is set well back of the inside one is ready to kick backward into his pass set (the kick slide).
A guard tipping a pull. Weight leaning, or eyes peeking, toward one side often means he is about to pull that way to lead a run.
A team that puts its hands down only for runs. If a line stands up on passing plays and crouches into three-point stances for runs, the stance itself is the tell.
The defensive line, in reverse. A defensive lineman sitting back on his heels may be about to loop sideways on a stunt (two rushers swapping lanes) or even drop off the line into coverage, which some defenses do to confuse the blockers (Zone Blitzes).

Why does a professional give this away? Because physics doesn’t negotiate. A 320-pound man can’t explode forward from his heels or backward from his fingertips, and a tenth of a second lost at the snap is a lost block. Good coaches teach a balanced stance that looks the same for run and pass, and the best linemen manage it, but on ordinary downs, when the play could be either, the weight tends to creep to where the job is. On short yardage it goes the other way: everyone is heavy on every snap, run or play-action, so the tell goes quiet just when you might expect it to shout.
Be realistic about seeing it. The broadcast shows a close-up of the line before the snap only now and then, so treat stance as a replay clue first (the end-zone angle is best) and a live clue when you happen to get the shot.


The running back: depth and offset
Where the running back lines up is a clue to both whether the play is a run and which way it goes.13 Three common setups:

Shotgun with the back beside the quarterback, offset to one side. This is mostly a passing look: 79% of shotgun snaps were passes in 2025. When they do run from it, the most common runs send the back across the quarterback’s face, so a back offset to the quarterback’s right usually runs to the left. The reason is the handoff itself: the back takes the ball while moving across in front of the quarterback, so his path already points to the other side. (Zone Running shows the whole play.)
Pistol. The quarterback is about four yards back with the back directly behind him, six or seven yards deep (pistol). The back’s central spot hides the direction of the run, and the depth gives him a running start. Only 29% of pistol snaps were passes.
Under center, with the back usually six to seven yards deep. Also mostly a run look, 31% passes, but this is the alignment the play fake is built for, as the film room below shows.

Depth matters within each. A back who creeps closer than usual may be about to block or run a quick route; one who sets deeper than usual wants room to read the blocks before he picks a hole.


Receiver splits: how far out they stand
A receiver’s split is how far from the ball (or the nearest lineman) he lines up. The painted numbers are a handy ruler: most outside receivers line up near them. Departures from that default carry information, because a receiver chooses his split to make his job easier:

A reduced split (well inside the numbers) puts him close to the formation. That suits a crack block (blocking a linebacker or safety from the outside on a run toward him), a route that cuts across the middle underneath (the trip is shorter), or a route that breaks outside, toward the sideline, and needs room to get there.
A wide split (outside the numbers, near the sideline) isolates him. That suits a deep route, a route that breaks inside and wants space to do it, or a quick throw to him; or it simply means his job is to drag his defender out of the way. A route that breaks toward the sideline is cramped from out there, so a wide split makes one less likely.

Splits are a weaker clue than stance or the backfield, since a reduced split can mean three different things. They mainly tell you where to look after the snap. Remember too that the ball’s position on the hash marks (The Game in Fifteen Minutes) changes what “normal” looks like: on the short side of the field, everything is squeezed.


Safety depth: one high or two
The safeties’ depth is the defense’s biggest tell, because the safeties are the defense’s flexible pieces. Two safeties deep, each 10 to 15 yards off the ball on his own side, is a two-high picture: the deep field is protected on both sides, and there are fewer defenders near the line to stop a run. One safety in the deep middle with the other walked down to seven or eight yards is a one-high picture: the defense has added a man near the line (in the box, the area between and just outside the offensive tackles), which helps against the run and makes extra pass rushers possible. A safety who walks down late, with only a few seconds on the play clock, has either seen something he wants to stop or is trying to fool the quarterback. Defenses disguise this on purpose, and Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage teaches how to see through it.
Here is the catch for a TV viewer: Figure 8.1 showed that both safeties are usually off your screen at the snap. What you can do live is limited but real. Watch the top edge of the picture, because a safety walking down appears there. Count the defenders near the line you can see: one more than a moment ago is often a safety arriving. Listen to the analyst, who has a wider monitor (“they’re rotating a safety down”). And take the occasional wide pre-snap shot, or an alternate stream like Prime Vision, when you get one. Otherwise, for now, safety depth is mostly a replay habit: check it on the skycam replay, every time, and you will get faster at spotting it live.


How strong is each clue?
Stance and safety depth aren’t in public data, but the quarterback’s and back’s alignment is, because charting services record it on every snap. The one used in this book is FTN, a company whose staff chart details like alignment, motion and play-action on every NFL play, published free through the nflverse project. That lets us see how much one clue is worth, team by team:


Show the Python
from gridiron.data import pbp, nfl

PCOLS = ["season_type", "game_id", "play_id", "posteam", "play_type", "down", "ydstogo", "pass",
         "half_seconds_remaining", "score_differential", "qtr"]


def plays_with_alignment(season):
    d = pbp([season], columns=PCOLS)
    d = d[(d.season_type == "REG") & d.play_type.isin(["pass", "run"]) & d.down.notna()].copy()
    f = nfl().load_ftn_charting([season]).to_pandas()
    f = f[["nflverse_game_id", "nflverse_play_id", "qb_location", "n_offense_backfield", "is_play_action"]]
    f = f.rename(columns={"nflverse_game_id": "game_id", "nflverse_play_id": "play_id"})
    f["play_id"] = f.play_id.astype(float)
    return d.merge(f, on=["game_id", "play_id"], how="left")


p25 = plays_with_alignment(2025)
ALIGN = [("U", "Under center"), ("P", "Pistol"), ("S", "Shotgun")]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 2.7))
rng = np.random.default_rng(6)
for i, (code, name) in enumerate(ALIGN):
    sub = p25[p25.qb_location == code]
    team = sub.groupby("posteam")["pass"].agg(["mean", "size"])
    team = team[team["size"] >= 40]
    jitter = rng.uniform(-0.17, 0.17, len(team))
    ax.scatter(team["mean"], i + jitter, s=18, color=style.MUTED, alpha=0.55, lw=0, zorder=2)
    lg = sub["pass"].mean()
    ax.plot([lg, lg], [i - 0.32, i + 0.32], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=2.4, zorder=3)
    ax.text(lg, i + 0.42, f"{lg:.0%}", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=7.5, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK,
            fontweight="bold")
    if code == "U":
        for tm, dy, ha in (("LA", -0.30, "left"), ("WAS", -0.30, "right")):
            v = team.loc[tm, "mean"]
            ax.scatter([v], [i], s=34, color=style.THIRD if tm == "LA" else style.DEFENSE, zorder=4, lw=0)
            ax.text(v + (0.012 if ha == "left" else -0.012), i + dy, "Rams" if tm == "LA" else "Washington",
                    ha=ha, va="center", fontsize=7, color=style.INK)
ax.set_yticks(range(len(ALIGN)), [n for _, n in ALIGN])
ax.set_ylim(-0.6, 2.75)
ax.set_xlim(0, 1)
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}"))
ax.set_xlabel("share of snaps that were dropbacks (pass)")
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.legend(handles=[Line2D([], [], marker="o", ls="", color=style.MUTED, ms=5, label="one team"),
                   Line2D([], [], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=2.4, label="league")],
          loc="lower right", fontsize=7, ncol=2)
plt.show()








Figure 8.6: How often offenses passed from each quarterback alignment, 2025 regular season (each dot is one team; pistol shows teams with 40 or more pistol snaps). The alignment is a strong clue on average, but teams differ a lot: Washington passed on 15% of its under-center snaps, the Rams on 40%. Source: nflverse play-by-play joined to FTN charting; runs and dropbacks only.











NoteFilm room: Rams 2025 — when the tell is the bait



Sean McVay’s Rams lined up under center on 59% of their 2025 snaps, more than any other team, and threw from under center 40% of the time, also the most.14 That is not an accident. Defenses read “under center” as “run”, so the linebackers step up at the snap; the Rams fake the handoff and throw behind them. That is play-action, the pass designed to look like a run, and it is the reason the tell exists and the reason it’s unreliable. League-wide in 2025, about 82% of passes thrown from under center used a play fake, against about 10% from the shotgun. (Matthew Stafford, the Rams’ quarterback, was the league’s MVP that season.15)
What to notice: watch the linebackers’ first step at the fake. If they step forward, they bit, and the skycam replay will show you the receiver running into the space behind them; then look for the safety, who is the last line behind that space. Play-callers often reach for the fake after a good run, but don’t treat that as a law: analysts testing it with play-by-play data found that play-action works about as well whether or not a team has been running well.16 What sells the fake is the look (under center, the same footwork as the real run), not the rushing stats.








CautionCommon misconception



“Under center means run.” On average, yes: only 31% of under-center snaps were passes in 2025. But those passes are the most dangerous ones, because they are built to exploit exactly that belief. Every tell in this chapter works the same way. A clue that is never wrong would be fixed by the coaches within a week; the ones that survive are right usually, and the offense chooses when to make them wrong. So log your guess with a confidence, not a certainty.

title: How to Watch a Broadcast Like You Mean It
text:
The prediction log
You now have a lean from the scorebug and a few clues from the formation. The habit that turns those into a skill is writing them down. A prediction log is your running record of pre-snap calls: for each snap, the situation, your guess, how sure you were, the clue you leaned on, and what happened. You started a rough version in Downs, Distance, and Field Position, guessing run or pass from the down and distance alone and keeping a tally. That tally was your baseline. This is the formal log you’ll keep for the rest of the course.
Why write it down rather than just watch and nod? Three reasons.

Memory flatters you. After the play, the clue that pointed the right way seems obvious, and the guess you got wrong quietly disappears. On paper, it doesn’t.
It tells you which clues work. If you note the clue behind each call, after a few games you can see whether “heavy hands” is making you right or wrong, for you, on the teams you watch.
It makes improvement visible. Reading a game gets better slowly. A number that moves from 62% to 70% over a season is the only reliable way to know it’s happening.

Here is the paper version. A notebook page with these columns is all you need, and the column names match the spreadsheet you’ll type it into later:


Show the Python
COLS = [("snap", 3.6), ("qtr", 3.0), ("clock", 4.8), ("down", 4.0), ("togo", 4.0), ("ball_on", 6.2),
        ("score", 4.4), ("call", 3.6), ("conf", 4.2), ("clue", 5.6), ("note", 15.0), ("result", 4.8), ("✓/✗", 3.6)]
ESSENTIAL = {"down", "togo", "call", "conf", "clue", "result"}
ROWS = [("1", "1", "12:40", "1", "10", "own 25", "0", "R", "55%", "align", "under center, 2 TEs", "R", "✓"),
        ("2", "1", "12:02", "2", "7", "own 28", "0", "P", "70%", "align", "shotgun on 2nd & long", "P", "✓"),
        ("3", "1", "11:20", "3", "2", "own 33", "0", "R", "60%", "stance", "heavy hands, right side", "P", "✗"),
        ("4", "1", "10:41", "1", "10", "own 42", "0", "P", "90%", "align", "empty backfield", "P", "✓"),
        ("5", "1", "9:58", "2", "3", "own 49", "0", "R", "65%", "align", "under center, back at 7", "R", "✓"),
        ("6", "1", "9:20", "1", "10", "opp 44", "0", "R", "50%", "sit", "missed the formation", "P", "✗")]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.4))
blank(ax)
W = sum(w for _, w in COLS)
ax.set_xlim(0, W); ax.set_ylim(0, 14.2)
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((0, 0), W, 14.2, fc="#fbfaf4", ec=style.BASELINE, lw=1.0))
ax.text(1.0, 13.3, "PREDICTION LOG   ·   Game: ____________   ·   Watching: offense of ________",
        fontsize=7.8, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK, va="center")
x = 0
for name, w in COLS:
    fc = style.OFFENSE_TINT if name in ESSENTIAL else "#ecebe4"
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x, 11.2), w, 1.3, fc=fc, ec=style.BASELINE, lw=0.6))
    ax.text(x + w / 2, 11.85, name, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.2, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)
    x += w
for j in range(9):
    y = 11.2 - (j + 1) * 1.15
    x = 0
    for (name, w), k in zip(COLS, range(len(COLS))):
        ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x, y), w, 1.15, fc="white", ec=style.GRID, lw=0.6))
        if j < len(ROWS):
            v = ROWS[j][k]
            col = style.INK
            if name == "✓/✗":
                col = style.THIRD if v == "✓" else style.DEFENSE_DARK
            ax.text(x + w / 2 if name != "note" else x + 0.5, y + 0.58, v,
                    ha="center" if name != "note" else "left", va="center", fontsize=6.1, color=col,
                    style="italic" if name not in ("snap", "✓/✗") else "normal",
                    fontweight="bold" if name == "✓/✗" else "normal")
        x += w
ax.text(1.0, 0.45, "Score so far: 4 of 6 = 67%.   Always pass: 4 of 6.   Down & distance only: ____",
        fontsize=7, color=style.INK, va="center")
plt.show()








Figure 8.7: A paper prediction log, with six snaps filled in as an example. One line per snap. Down and to-go are numbers; ‘Score’ is the offense’s margin (−3 = down by three). ‘Call’ is run (R) or pass (P); ‘Conf.’ is how sure you were (50% is a coin flip). ‘Clue’ is the one thing that decided the call, written as one of four words: sit (the scorebug), align (the backfield), stance, or safety; the ‘Note’ column is free text the code ignores. Fill in ‘Result’ after the play, then tick or cross. The essential columns are shaded; the rest are worth keeping when you have time.





A few rules keep the log honest and quick:

Call it before the snap; write it after. Say the call and the confidence out loud during the pause, then jot the line while the replays run. Abbreviate everything. If you have a pause button, use it; if not, fill in only the shaded columns and catch up at the next timeout.
Log what the quarterback did with the ball. If he dropped back to pass, it’s P, even if he was sacked, scrambled, threw it away or threw a screen; a run-pass option counts as whatever he actually did. If he handed off or ran a designed run (a sneak included), it’s R. Skip kneel-downs, spikes and plays wiped out by a penalty.
Pick one team for the half, ideally the offense you know better; which one doesn’t matter, as long as you don’t switch.
No formation on screen? Call it from the scorebug, write “sit” as the clue, and move on.

And here is the same log in pandas, for when you’ve typed a game’s worth into a spreadsheet and saved it as a CSV whose first line is the header from the sheet:
snap,qtr,clock,down,togo,ball_on,score,call,conf,clue,note,result
(Write conf as a decimal, 0.55, and leave out the tick column; the code works it out.) It answers the three questions above: how often you were right, how that compares with the two simplest guessers, and which clues earned their keep.

import pandas as pd

log = pd.read_csv("prediction_log_game1.csv")      # one row per snap you called
log["hit"] = log["call"] == log["result"]            # True when your call was right

# The down-and-distance-only guesser: run on 1st/2nd/4th down with 3 or fewer yards to go
# and on 1st down with 6 or fewer, pass otherwise (the majority call in 2024; the chart below)
dd_run = ((log.togo <= 3) & (log.down != 3)) | ((log.down == 1) & (log.togo <= 6))
log["dd_hit"] = log["result"] == dd_run.map({True: "R", False: "P"})

print(f"You:                     {log.hit.mean():.0%} right on {len(log)} snaps")
print(f"'Always guess pass':     {(log.result == 'P').mean():.0%}")
print(f"Down and distance only:  {log.dd_hit.mean():.0%}")
print(log.groupby("clue").hit.agg(right="mean", snaps="size").round(2).to_string())

You:                     68% right on 34 snaps
'Always guess pass':     59%
Down and distance only:  62%
        right  snaps
clue                
align    0.83     12
safety   0.50      4
sit      0.62     13
stance   0.60      5


The last table is the one to watch over a season: a clue you lean on often that sits near 50% isn’t earning its place. The two guesser lines are the honest comparison. Guessing “pass” on every snap is right about 60% of the time in today’s NFL, so a 60% log hasn’t shown any reading at all. How much better can you do, and where does the improvement come from? Here is what simple rules would have scored over the 2025 season:


Show the Python
p24 = plays_with_alignment(2024)


def prep(d):
    d = d.copy()
    d["dist"] = pd.cut(d.ydstogo, [0, 3, 6, 99], labels=["1-3", "4-6", "7+"])
    d["late"] = (d.half_seconds_remaining <= 120).astype(int)
    d["score"] = pd.cut(d.score_differential, [-99, -9, -1, 0, 8, 99], labels=["d9+", "d1-8", "tie", "u1-8", "u9+"])
    d["q4"] = (d.qtr >= 4).astype(int)
    return d


train, test = prep(p24), prep(p25)


def accuracy(keys):
    if not keys:
        return float((test["pass"] == 1).mean())
    rule = train.groupby(keys, observed=True)["pass"].mean().rename("p_pass").reset_index()
    m = test.merge(rule, on=keys, how="left")
    guess = (m.p_pass.fillna(train["pass"].mean()) >= 0.5).astype(int)
    return float((guess == m["pass"]).mean())


LADDER = [("Always guess pass", []),
          ("Down & distance only (like your 01-02 tally)", ["down", "dist"]),
          ("+ score, quarter and clock", ["down", "dist", "score", "late", "q4"]),
          ("+ the quarterback's alignment", ["down", "dist", "score", "late", "q4", "qb_location"])]
vals = [accuracy(k) for _, k in LADDER]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 2.5))
ys = np.arange(len(LADDER))[::-1]
cols = [style.MUTED, style.OFFENSE, style.OFFENSE, style.THIRD]
ax.barh(ys, vals, color=cols, height=0.58, zorder=2)
for y, v in zip(ys, vals):
    ax.text(v + 0.006, y, f"{v:.0%}", va="center", ha="left", fontsize=8.5, color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
ax.axvline(0.5, color=style.INK_2, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=3)
ax.text(0.505, ys[0] + 0.45, "coin flip", fontsize=7, color=style.INK_2, ha="left", va="center")
ax.set_yticks(ys, [n for n, _ in LADDER], fontsize=8)
ax.set_xlim(0.4, 0.82)
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}"))
ax.set_xlabel("share of 2025 snaps called correctly (run vs pass)")
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
plt.show()








Figure 8.8: The bar to beat. Accuracy of simple run-or-pass guessers on every 2025 regular-season run and dropback (32,813 snaps). Each rule was learned from the 2024 season (for every combination of its inputs it guesses whichever was more common in 2024) and then scored on 2025, the way your own guesses are made before the fact. The situation on the scorebug gets you from 60% to about 68%; one glance at the quarterback’s alignment adds about seven points more. Source: nflverse play-by-play and FTN charting.





Three lessons hide in that chart.17 First, as the scorebug section warned, down and distance alone barely beat “always pass.” It is decisive on the downs where it’s lopsided, but first-and-10, the most common situation by far, is close to a coin flip (about 50% pass in 2025), so a rule built only on down and distance guesses “pass” there and gets half of them wrong. Second, across a whole game the score and the clock add more than the down does: late in a half, and when a team is behind, the run-pass mix swings hard. Third, one glance at the formation is worth almost as much as everything on the scorebug combined. The coaches know this too; it is why the best offenses work so hard to run and pass from the same looks.
So the targets for your own log are clear. If you are under 60%, you’re doing worse than a guesser who never looks up. Around 65–68%, you’re reading the scorebug well. Above 70%, the formation and the tells are working for you. Don’t be surprised if your first log lands in the low 60s; that is what the scorebug alone is worth before you have practised reading it.






NoteGo deeper: why the confidence column?



“Right or wrong” throws away information. A 55% call that misses and a 90% call that misses are very different mistakes, and a good reader knows the difference before the snap. That’s why the log has a confidence column even though we score only hits and misses for now: it costs one number per snap. Film Study: All-22, Charting a Game, and Scoring Yourself scores the season’s log the way forecasters are scored, by whether your 70% calls come true about 70% of the time. Until then, the only thing to log beyond run or pass is nothing: one prediction per snap, made before the snap, is plenty. As the course goes on, chapters add columns (which side the run goes, which receiver gets the ball, whether the safeties rotate, whether the defense blitzes), and by the end your log is a full pre-snap read.








TipWatch for it on Sunday: prediction log, game 1



For one half of one game, on every offensive snap of one team:

During the pause, read the scorebug in order (down and distance, field position, score, clock, timeouts), glance at the quarterback’s and back’s alignment (and any motion, the movement you counted in The Pre-Snap Phase), and say “run” or “pass” out loud before the snap, with a rough confidence (55%, 70%, 85%).
Write the line during the replays: at least down, to-go, call, confidence, and the clue word (sit, align, stance, safety).
After the play, record what happened, using the rules above (sacks and scrambles are passes; skip kneel-downs, spikes and plays wiped out by penalties).
On the replays, pick one thing (Table 8.2) and check one clue you used: was the hand really heavy? Where did the safety go?
At halftime, score it. Compare it with your down-and-distance tally from Downs, Distance, and Field Position, with the two guessers, and with the bar to beat above. Keep the sheet; the course will come back to it.

title: How to Watch a Broadcast Like You Mean It
text:
Predict the play






TipPredict the play 1: third-and-1





Show the Python
off = offense("i_form_22")
off = [p_.moved(label="R") if p_.key == "RB" else p_ for p_ in off]
dfn = defense("4-3_over", "single_high", off)
adj = {"MIKE": dict(d=3.5), "WILL": dict(d=3.5), "SAM": dict(d=3.0), "SS": dict(d=5.0, w=7.6),
       "WDE": dict(w=-5.7), "LCB": dict(d=4.0, w=-7.4), "RCB": dict(d=6.0), "FS": dict(d=11.0)}
dfn = [p_.moved(**adj[p_.key]) if p_.key in adj else p_ for p_ in dfn]
q1 = Play(off, dfn, los=72, to_go=1)
q1.highlight("RB", color=style.THIRD)
fld = q1.draw(lateral=(-18.5, 18.5), window=(-9.5, 13.5), title=False)
# a bracket behind the five linemen: the label is about the whole line, not one gap
(bx0, by0), (bx1, by1) = [tuple(map(float, fld.xy(*q1.to_abs(-1.75, w_)))) for w_ in (-3.6, 3.6)]
(tx0, ty0), (tx1, ty1) = [tuple(map(float, fld.xy(*q1.to_abs(-1.35, w_)))) for w_ in (-3.6, 3.6)]
fld.ax.plot([tx0, bx0, bx1, tx1], [ty0, by0, by1, ty1], color=style.INK_2, lw=1.1, zorder=9)
pointer(fld, q1, "heavy hands\nall along the line", (-4.2, -10.5), (-1.75, -1.2))
pointer(fld, q1, "tailback at\n7 yards", (-7.4, 6.2), (-7.0, 0.8))
plt.show()








Figure 8.9: Third-and-1 at the opponent’s 38, second quarter, tied 7–7. The offense comes out under center with two tight ends and a fullback (U and Y are the tight ends, F the fullback, R the tailback, seven yards deep). On the close-up before the snap, the linemen’s down hands are heavy. The defense has crowded the line: nine defenders within five yards of the ball, a cornerback on the lone wide receiver and one safety deep (on defense, S is the Sam linebacker and SS the strong safety).





Run or pass? How confident are you, and what is the one thing to watch at the snap?






TipAnswer





Run, about 85%. Third-and-1 is the most run-heavy situation in football: in 2025, teams ran on about three in four third-and-1s, and from under center they ran on about 84%.18 A good share of those runs never reach the tailback: about three in ten of the under-center snaps on third-and-1 were quarterback sneaks (the push-from-behind version, the tush push, is in Red Zone, Goal Line, and Short Yardage). The defense agrees with you, which is why nine defenders are crowded near the line.
Why not higher, when every clue points the same way? Because the clues aren’t independent. Two tight ends, a fullback, under center and a deep tailback travel together: that is simply what a short-yardage formation looks like, and the 84% already counts all of them. Adding them up again would be counting the same evidence three times. The heavy hands add even less here: on short yardage every lineman is heavy on every snap, run or play-action, so in this picture the stance tells you nothing new. Stance earns its keep on ordinary downs.
Your one thing: the line of scrimmage (the short-yardage row of Table 8.2), from the end-zone angle if you get it on the replay. Whose linemen move forward first and farther? On short yardage that yard of push decides the play before the ball carrier arrives.
And the other 15%? This is exactly the picture play-action is built for. With nine defenders charging the line and one safety deep, a fake handoff and a pass to a tight end sneaking out behind the linebackers is the classic counterpunch. A good log line here is “R, 85%, align.” If it turns out to be a play fake, that is not a bad prediction; it is the 15%.











TipPredict the play 2: the safety who walks into the picture





Show the Python
q2 = base_play(to_go=10, los=58.0)
moves = {"SS": ((13.0, 9.5), (8.0, 5.0)), "FS": ((13.0, -9.5), (14.0, -1.5))}
for k_, (_, (d_, w_)) in moves.items():
    q2.players[k_] = q2.players[k_].moved(d=d_, w=w_)      # where they are now
q2.highlight("SS", color=style.THIRD)
fld = q2.draw(lateral=(-20, 20), window=(-8.5, 19.5), title=False)
shade_outside(fld, q2, tv_footprint(1.5, 0.0, *TV_WIDE), alpha=0.55)
for k_, ((gd, gw), (nd, nw)) in moves.items():
    (gx, gy), (nx, ny) = [tuple(map(float, fld.xy(*q2.to_abs(d_, w_)))) for d_, w_ in ((gd, gw), (nd, nw))]
    fld.ax.add_patch(RegularPolygon((gx, gy), 4, radius=0.75 * 1.5, orientation=np.pi / 4, fc=style.SURFACE,
                                    ec=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.4, ls=(0, (2, 1.5)), zorder=14))
    fld.ax.text(gx, gy, k_, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.5, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, zorder=14)
    fld.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((gx, gy), (nx, ny), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=11, color=style.DEFENSE,
                                     lw=1.5, ls=(0, (3, 2)), shrinkA=9, shrinkB=12, zorder=14))
pointer(fld, q2, "showed two deep,\nthen walks down late", (17.0, 14.5), (13.8, 10.2))
label(fld, q2, "▲ top edge of\nyour TV picture", (8.2, -7.6), fs=6.8, color=style.INK_2)
plt.show()








Figure 8.10: First-and-10 near midfield, shotgun with the back beside the quarterback. The grey is what your TV shot leaves out. The defense first showed two deep safeties at 13 yards (the outlined ghosts, both off your screen). With about eight seconds on the play clock, the safety on the offense’s right walks down to eight yards, just outside the right tackle, and into the top of your picture; the other slides over toward the deep middle, still off screen (dashed arrows).





On your TV, what tells you this happened, and how should it change your run-or-pass lean?






TipAnswer





What you’d see: not the walk itself, which starts off screen, but its arrival. A defender appears at the top edge of the picture where nobody stood a moment ago and settles a few yards off the ball. Other on-screen hints: count the defenders near the line, which goes from six to seven; linebackers may shift over to make room; the quarterback may point, shout or change the call (The Pre-Snap Phase); and the analyst, who has a wider monitor, often says it (“they’re rotating a safety down”). The other safety sliding to the middle you won’t see live; that is the skycam replay’s job.
What it means: the defense went from two-high to one-high, and now has seven defenders in the box against six blockers (five linemen and the back). That is the picture from 01-05’s second drill, and the logic is the same: against seven in the box a run has a free defender, so many quarterbacks check out of a run into a pass, and run-pass options throw into the space behind the safety who came down.
Your lean: nudge it toward pass, but only a little. First-and-10 from the shotgun was already a passing look (72% pass in 2025).19 Two things keep you from going much higher. With eight seconds left the quarterback may not have time to check, and the walk-down may be a bluff: some safeties race back to the deep middle at the snap, the disguise game of Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage. Something like “P, 75%, safety” is a good line, and if you never saw the safety arrive, the clue is “align” and the lean stays where the shotgun put it.











TipPredict the play 3: which clue wins?





Show the Python
off = offense("gun_trips")
off = [p_.moved(w=-7.8) if p_.key == "X" else p_ for p_ in off]
dfn = defense("nickel", "two_high", off)
dfn = [p_.moved(d=6.5, w=-8.8) if p_.key == "LCB" else p_ for p_ in dfn]   # slight outside leverage
q3 = Play(off, dfn, los=50, to_go=6)
q3.highlight("X", "RB", color=style.THIRD)
fld = q3.draw(lateral=(-20, 23), window=(-8.5, 16.5), title=False)
pointer(fld, q3, "X: reduced split", (-5.2, -14.0), (-0.7, -8.6))
pointer(fld, q3, "back offset\nto QB's left", (-6.6, -6.6), (-5.0, -2.3))
plt.show()








Figure 8.11: Second-and-6 at the offense’s own 40, third quarter, ahead 14–10. Shotgun with trips to the right, the tight end attached to the line (Y, H and Z), and the back offset to the quarterback’s left. On the left, the lone receiver (X) has a reduced split, about eight yards outside the center instead of out near the numbers, and his cornerback has followed him in. The linemen are in two-point stances. Two safeties deep.





Five clues: second-and-6, shotgun, the back’s offset, X’s reduced split, two deep safeties. Run or pass, and what does each clue tell you?






TipAnswer





Pass, about 70–75%. Weigh the clues in order of strength, broad ones first:

Second-and-6 on its own is a coin flip: about 52% pass in 2025 for second-and-medium.
Shotgun moves it a long way. In 2025, teams passed on 76% of their shotgun snaps on second-and-5 to -7. That is your call. (The two-point stances agree, but standing linemen are common in the shotgun, so they add little.)
Two deep safeties pull you back a notch. Two-high leaves six defenders near the line against six blockers, so a run is a fair fight, and offenses like to run against two-high and throw against one-high. It doesn’t flip the call; it is why this isn’t 80%.
The back’s offset doesn’t change run-or-pass much. It tells you which way a run would likely go (from the left, across the quarterback’s face, to the right, toward the trips) and which side he would protect on a pass.
X’s reduced split tells you about X, not about the whole play. Run through its three meanings. A crack block fits a run toward him, but the back’s offset says a run would go the other way, so that one is unlikely. That leaves a route underneath across the middle (a dig, which runs ten or so yards and cuts flat inside, or a shallow crosser) whose trip the tight split shortens, or a route breaking outside, like a corner route toward the sideline, that wants the room he has given himself. A slant, the quick cut inside, is the least likely: it needs space inside, and he has just given it away.

So: “P, 75%, align.” Then pick your one thing: X and the cornerback over him, from the snap. If X cuts inside underneath or breaks for the sideline and the ball goes there, the reduced split was the tell. If the ball goes elsewhere, check on the replay what X did anyway. That is how small clues become reliable ones: by checking them, snap after snap, in your log.

title: How to Watch a Broadcast Like You Mean It
text:
Takeaways

The broadcast is built for the ball. The main sideline camera keeps the formation tight before the snap and chases the ball after it, so the safeties, the outside receivers and most of the coverage are off your screen when it matters. Replays exist to give them back: the end zone shows the line, the skycam shows the coverage, and the All-22 shows everyone.
Use the pause. Read the scorebug in a fixed order (down and distance, field position, score, clock, timeouts) and turn it into a lean before the snap. Down and distance decides the lopsided downs; on first-and-10 the formation tells you more.
Scan before the snap, then watch one thing, chosen by your lean: the safeties (or the quarterback’s first look) when you expect a pass, a guard when you expect a run, the line on short yardage, a different group on each replay. The safeties are mostly a replay habit for now, because the live shot rarely shows them.
Tells are clues, not promises. Stance, the back’s depth and offset, receiver splits and safety depth all shift the odds, and the quarterback’s alignment shifts them the most. Clues that travel together aren’t separate evidence. The offense knows its tells too, and play-action lives on breaking them.
Keep a prediction log, and score it against the bar: “always pass” gets about 60%, down and distance alone about 62%, the whole scorebug about 68%, the scorebug plus the formation about 75%.

title: Personnel: Who’s on the Field Before Anything Else
text:
Eleven players, but only five that change
Third-and-1 at midfield, early in the fourth quarter. The previous play has barely been whistled dead when the broadcast cuts wide: two wide receivers jog toward their own sideline, and two bigger men, a tight end and a fullback, run the other way to join the huddle. Across the field, the defense reacts within a couple of seconds. A cornerback sprints off, a 245-pound linebacker sprints on, and someone near the defensive bench is shouting a single word. The ball hasn’t been snapped, the offense hasn’t even lined up, and the analyst says “they’ve gone to 22 personnel.” He’s right, and both teams have already made a move. This chapter is about that move: who the offense chooses to put on the field, how the defense answers (and why it swapped only one player when the offense swapped two), who that shouting man is, and how much those two digits tell you about what’s coming.
You’ll be able to…
Start with a puzzle. An offense has eleven players on the field, and the label for who they are has only two digits. How can two digits describe eleven people?
Because six of the eleven almost never change. Every normal offensive snap has a quarterback and five offensive linemen (the center, two guards and two tackles, the big men who block and, by rule, can’t catch a forward pass). Those six are the fixed core. The other five spots are the variables, and they can be filled by three kinds of player that The Twenty-Two introduced as the skill positions:
Every way of filling those five spots is a personnel grouping: the mix of running backs, tight ends and wide receivers on the field for a play. Coaches, scouts, broadcasters and the data all write it the same way, as two digits:
So “one-one,” usually just said “eleven,” means one back and one tight end, which leaves three wide receivers. “Twelve” (one-two) is one back and two tight ends, so two receivers. “Twenty-one” is two backs, one tight end and two receivers. You never need a third digit, because the receivers are whatever is left over. (One grouping, jumbo, bends the arithmetic; it gets its own section below.)
The digits are the shared language of scouting reports, broadcasts and data. Inside a team’s own playbook, groupings often carry word names instead, and the words differ from team to team (one Houston Texans explainer mentions “Pony” and “Rabbit” for kinds of two-back grouping).1 When you hear an unfamiliar word on a sideline microphone, it is probably a team’s private name for one of the groupings below.
Why count only backs and tight ends? Because those are the two body types that change what the offense can do and what the defense must fear. A tight end is a blocker who can run routes; a fullback is a blocker who can carry the ball or catch it out of the backfield. Each one you add makes the offense bigger and better at running the ball, and takes away a wide receiver, the player most dangerous in the open field. The two digits are, in effect, a dial between “big” and “fast.”

title: Personnel: Who’s on the Field Before Anything Else
text:
Running backs. Players who line up behind the line, mostly to carry the ball or block. The tailback (or halfback) is the runner; the fullback is a bigger back who mostly blocks for him. Both count as running backs here.
Tight ends. Big, versatile players, usually 245 to 265 pounds, who often line up right next to a tackle. They block like small linemen and catch passes.
Wide receivers. Usually the lightest and fastest on the offense, lined up wide, mainly to catch passes.



First digit = running backs. Second digit = tight ends. Wide receivers = 5 − backs − tight ends.









CautionCommon misconception



The digits are not jersey numbers, and “11 personnel” does not mean “the eleven players.” It is a count of body types: one running back, one tight end. Say it “eleven” or “one-one,” but read it as two separate digits. Defensive labels count differently: a “4-2-5” means four linemen, two linebackers and five defensive backs. Older names such as “4-3” leave off the defensive backs because four was taken for granted. A First Look at Defense owns those names.









NoteMadden vs. real life



In Madden you pick a formation and the right players appear in it, and the computer’s defense swaps its own players instantly. In the NFL, personnel is a separate decision made before the formation and the play. A coach shouts or signals the grouping (“Twelve! Twelve!”), the players in that package run on, and the defense has to see them, decide, and send its own substitutes. It takes several seconds of the forty-second play clock, in plain view: the first thing you can read.

section: Reading the deck: the eight groupings you’ll meet
text:
Reading the deck: the eight groupings you’ll meet
Here are the eight groupings the chapter asks you to know, each drawn in an ordinary, legal alignment. Don’t worry yet about the names of the alignments. Those are formations, the next chapter’s job. For now, count the rings: an aqua ring is a running back, a gold ring is a tight end, and anyone with no ring (apart from the quarterback and the linemen) is a wide receiver.


Show the Python
card_deck(["11", "12", "21", "13"])
plt.show()








Figure 9.1: The four everyday groupings. Count the rings: aqua = running backs (R is the tailback, F the fullback), gold = tight ends; unringed players outside the line are wide receivers (X, Z, H). In 13 personnel the third tight end stands just outside and behind the right tight end (a ‘wing’) and wears the letter H: the letters name spots in the formation, not body types, which is why the ring, not the letter, tells you what he is. Seven men are on the line in every card: the five linemen (only the center, C, is lettered) plus the two players at the ends.





The letters on the receivers are the names most playbooks use for their spots: X is the receiver usually on the line on one side (the “split end”), Z the receiver off the line on the other side (the “flanker”), Y usually the tight end, and H or F a player the offense moves around, who can be a slot receiver, a second tight end or a fullback depending on the grouping. Look at the 12 card and you’ll see X standing off the line: with a tight end on the line at each end, both receivers have to step back so the tight ends stay the end men, and eligible. Formation Rules and the Language of Alignment explains the letters and that rule properly. In this chapter they’re just name tags; the rings do the counting.
11 personnel (1 RB, 1 TE, 3 WR) is the NFL’s default: it was on the field for about six plays in ten every season from 2016 to 2025. Its appeal is that it can do almost anything. Three wide receivers stretch the defense across the field; the one tight end can stay in to block or run a route; the one back can run, block a blitzer or catch. Because the offense can run or pass from it with almost equal ease, it gives the defense very little to go on. It also forces the defense to answer with a fifth defensive back, which we’ll see is the whole substitution game in miniature.
12 personnel (1 RB, 2 TE, 2 WR) swaps the third receiver for a second tight end. Now the offense can line up with a blocker next to both tackles and run either way, or split one of the tight ends out like a receiver and throw. It is the league’s second most common grouping and, as the data below shows, the closest thing football has to a coin flip.
21 personnel (2 RB, 1 TE, 2 WR) adds a fullback, the old-fashioned lead blocker. This is the grouping of the classic I-formation (fullback directly in front of the tailback) and of the old pro set (two backs side by side behind the quarterback), the standard NFL look of an earlier era. A good fullback gives the offense an extra blocker who starts moving before the defense knows where the play is going.
13 personnel (1 RB, 3 TE, 1 WR) is three tight ends and just one receiver. It is mostly a short-yardage and running grouping, though as you’ll see in the film room, one team in 2025 turned it into a weapon for both.


Show the Python
card_deck(["10", "20", "22", "00"])
plt.show()








Figure 9.2: Four groupings at the edges. 10 and 00 personnel are spread groupings, so the quarterback is in the shotgun (about five yards behind the center) and wide receivers fill the Y and F spots that a tight end or back would fill in other groupings. 20 personnel puts two backs beside the quarterback. 22 personnel is the old power look: fullback, tailback and a tight end on each side, with one receiver.





22 personnel (2 RB, 2 TE, 1 WR) is the heavy end of the everyday menu: a fullback, a tailback and two tight ends, leaving one receiver. The offense is telling the defense, more or less, “we’re going to run, and we’re bringing extra people to block for it.” That’s useful near the goal line, on third-and-1, and late in a game when the offense wants to keep the clock running. It is also, for exactly that reason, a great place to fake a run and throw (more on that trade below).
10 personnel (1 RB, 0 TE, 4 WR) drops the tight end for a fourth receiver. It’s everywhere in college football, where spread offenses grew up, but rare in the NFL (around 1% of plays in recent seasons). NFL offenses want a tight end’s blocking against much bigger pass rushers, and four receivers are easy for a defense to answer: it just sends in a sixth defensive back. A good tight end is harder to match, because no substitute is both big enough to take on his block and fast enough to cover him.
20 personnel (2 RB, 0 TE, 3 WR) puts two backs next to the quarterback in the shotgun with three receivers. It’s a niche look (about 1% of NFL plays or less), but a handy one: either back can take a handoff, block, or slip out for a pass. 00 personnel is five wide receivers and no back at all, an “empty” backfield with nobody beside the quarterback. In the NFL it’s so rare that you may not see it all season.2 (Empty formations, in which the back or tight end lines up wide, are common. That’s a formation, not a personnel grouping, and it’s the subject of Spread Formations.)
There are a handful of other combinations, such as 01, 02, 23 and the occasional 30, but together they make up only a percent or two of plays. If you can read the eight above, you can read practically every NFL snap.

Personnel is who, not where
One more rule before we move on, and it’s the one beginners trip over. Personnel counts who the players are, not where they stand. A tight end who lines up out wide like a receiver is still a tight end, so the grouping is still 12 if there are two of them. A running back who lines up in the slot is still a running back. A wide receiver standing in the backfield is still a receiver.
That’s not pedantry; it’s why personnel matters. The defense chooses its players by who comes on the field, and only then does the offense line up. Send in two tight ends, get bigger defenders; then spread those tight ends out like receivers, and bigger, slower players have to cover them. That gap between personnel and formation is one of the oldest tricks in football, and you can’t see it unless you count first.
The hard case is a player whose body doesn’t match his label. Deebo Samuel was a 49ers wide receiver who, in 2021, also carried the ball 59 times for 365 yards and eight touchdowns.3 With him in the backfield, a grouping that reads “11” on paper played like two backs. The Saints have used Taysom Hill, a quarterback, as a runner, a receiver and a tight end; the data lists him as a quarterback in 2023 and 2025 and as a tight end in 2024, so the same kind of snap gets a different label in different seasons. The Ravens’ Patrick Ricard has played both defensive line and fullback. Offenses use players like these on purpose: the defense picks its substitutes by label, and a player who is two things at once makes every answer partly wrong. Note it in your log whenever you see one.






CautionCommon misconception



“You can tell the position by the jersey number.” Not reliably, not any more. Before 2021, NFL tight ends wore numbers in the 80s (or 40s), and receivers wore 80s or 10–19. Since the league loosened its numbering rules in 2021 and again in 2023, tight ends, receivers and backs can all wear single digits and most of the same ranges4 (The Twenty-Two has the details). On TV, use three other clues. Size: tight ends are usually 245 to 265 pounds, receivers well under that. Stance: a tight end next to the tackle usually sets in a three-point stance, one hand down like a lineman, while receivers stand up. Homework: a glance at the team’s roster before kickoff, plus the analyst, who will often name the grouping for you.




Heavy personnel
You’ll hear broadcasters say an offense “went heavy.” Heavy personnel means any grouping with fewer than three wide receivers: the offense has taken receivers off and put tight ends, backs or linemen on. So 12, 21, 13 and 22 are all heavy (some people keep the word for 13, 22 and jumbo; this course uses the wider meaning, as NFL Next Gen Stats does). Why take a fast player off the field? To block more people, since each tight end or fullback is an extra blocker who can also be a threat; to make the defense get bigger, and so slower in coverage; and to hide the play, because a defense facing players who can run and catch can’t relax against either.

section: Jumbo: when a sixth lineman comes in
text:
Jumbo: when a sixth lineman comes in
Sometimes even three tight ends isn’t big enough. In a jumbo grouping, the offense puts a sixth offensive lineman on the field, usually lined up exactly where a tight end would be, at the end of the line next to a tackle. (Some teams put him inside instead, with two tackles side by side on one end of the line; that unbalanced line is a formation trick for a later chapter.) He’s a lineman, often 300 pounds or more, so he blocks much better than any tight end. That’s the point: on the goal line, on third-and-1, or when killing the clock with a lead, the offense wants raw size.
Jumbo is where the two-digit arithmetic needs one adjustment. The sixth lineman takes one of the five changeable spots, so only four are left for backs, tight ends and receivers: receivers = 4 − backs − tight ends. The jumbo below has one back and two tight ends, so one receiver, not two.


Show the Python
off = line5() + [
    Player("E6", "OL", "off", LINE_D, -TE_W, label="79"),
    P("QB", "QB", UC, 0, "Q"), P("RB", "RB", -6.5, 0, "R"),
    P("Y", "TE", LINE_D, TE_W), P("U", "TE", -1.6, 7.2),      # a legal wing, clear of Y's ring
    P("X", "WR", OFF_BALL, -11.0),
]
gl = [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, -5.9), D("DLT", "DT", 1.0, -2.4), D("NT", "NT", 1.0, 0.0),
      D("DRT", "DT", 1.0, 2.4), D("RE", "DE", 1.0, 5.9),
      D("WILL", "WILL", 3.4, -3.4), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 3.4, 0.6), D("SAM", "SAM", 3.0, 7.4),
      D("LCB", "CB", 1.5, -11.0), D("SS", "SS", 4.6, 10.5), D("FS", "FS", 6.5, -2.0)]
p = Play(off, gl, los=108, to_go=2)
ring_by_body(p)
p.highlight("E6", color=OL_RING)
p.note("6th lineman", at=(-2.7, -5.2))          # directly behind #79
p.draw(lateral=(-15.5, 15.5), window=(-9.5, 9.5), title=False)
hide_yard_numbers(plt.gca())
plt.show()








Figure 9.3: Jumbo on the 2-yard line: six offensive linemen (the sixth, #79, ringed in purple, stands at the left end where a tight end would), two tight ends on the right (gold), one back (aqua) and one receiver (X). Six linemen + 1 back + 2 tight ends + 1 receiver + the quarterback = 11. The defense answers with its own goal-line package: five linemen (E = end, T = tackle, N = nose tackle), three linebackers (S, M, W) and three defensive backs (C = cornerback, SS and FS = safeties). To be allowed to catch a pass, #79 must first report to the referee as eligible.





There is a catch, and it is a rule, not a strategy. Linemen wear numbers in the 50–79 range, and a player wearing one of those numbers is ineligible to catch a forward pass (he can block, but not go out for a ball thrown past the line) unless he reports to the referee before the snap. The referee then announces it, often over the stadium microphone (“Number 79 is reporting as eligible”), so the defense knows. The full rules for eligibility and reporting are in Formation Rules, which owns them; for now it’s enough to know that a jumbo lineman is a blocker by default and a receiver only by announcement.
So is the picture above “12” or “13”? It depends who’s counting. The data used in this chapter labels players by roster position, so it calls this snap “12” (one back, two tight ends) plus an extra lineman, and by the jumbo rule that leaves one receiver. Some charters and staffs count a lineman standing at tight end as a tight end and call it “13”; others write “12 jumbo” or “6 OL.” In the charts below, jumbo plays keep the code their backs and tight ends give them, and are also counted separately as jumbo.
Jumbo is the most predictable grouping in football. In neutral situations from 2023 to 2025, offenses in jumbo threw on fewer than one play in three. That predictability is the cost: when the defense knows a run is coming, it can load up for it. It is also the opportunity, as the Detroit Lions showed, because a defense that is sure of the run is the easiest one to fool with a pass.






NoteFilm room: Detroit Lions 2022–2024



Under offensive coordinator Ben Johnson (2022–2024), the Lions made the eligible lineman a regular part of their offense. Backup tackle Dan Skipper was the usual extra lineman, and he or, on the odd trick play, starting left tackle Taylor Decker could report eligible. In 2022 Detroit used a sixth lineman on about 10% of its snaps, second-most in the league.
The most famous of those snaps didn’t count. On December 30, 2023, at Dallas, Detroit scored a touchdown with 23 seconds left to pull within a point at 20–19 and went for two. Jared Goff threw to Decker, who caught it in the end zone. The officials ruled that it was Skipper, not Decker, who had reported eligible, so Decker was an ineligible receiver. The conversion was wiped out and Detroit had to try again from farther back: the next attempt was intercepted but erased by a Dallas offside penalty, the one after that fell incomplete, and the Cowboys won 20–19.5 The play became a national argument about reporting, and it shows the logic of jumbo: the defense saw six linemen and expected a run; the Lions’ answer was a pass to a lineman.
What to notice: when an offense goes jumbo, watch the referee. If he turns to the press box and announces a number, a lineman has reported eligible, and the defense now has to account for him too.
