title: Personnel: Who’s on the Field Before Anything Else
text:
The defense answers: substitution matching
Personnel is a two-sided game. The offense picks its eleven first, and the defense answers with its own. Defensive groupings are named differently, usually by how many defensive backs (cornerbacks and safeties, the players whose main job is pass coverage) are on the field, because that number is what the defense changes most:

Base: four defensive backs, with seven players up front (four linemen and three linebackers in a “4-3,” or three and four in a “3-4”). Built to stop the run.
Nickel: five defensive backs. The fifth, called the nickel back or slot cornerback, usually replaces a linebacker and covers the receiver lined up in the slot (between the outside receiver and the line).
Dime: six defensive backs, for obvious passing downs.

A First Look at Defense builds these packages properly.
The defense’s choice follows a simple logic: match bodies to bodies. A wide receiver is fast, so he should be covered by a defensive back, who is also fast. A tight end or fullback is big, so a linebacker, who is bigger and better at taking on blocks, is a reasonable match. More receivers, more defensive backs; more tight ends and backs, more linebackers. That reflex is called substitution matching.
It is a direction, not a one-for-one swap, because the defense has a floor of four defensive backs: two cornerbacks and two safeties. Even 22 personnel sends five eligible receivers out on every play, and any of them can run deep, so a defense without two corners and two safeties has nobody left to stop the long pass. Only where there is no room for a long pass, near the goal line or on the shortest yardage, does a defense go below four. That is why the opening play worked the way it did: the offense swapped two receivers for two big men (11 to 22), but the defense, already at five defensive backs, could only come down one, to four. Against 22 in 2025, defenses kept exactly four defensive backs on about three snaps in four, and went to three or fewer only about one in seven, mostly at the goal line or on third- and fourth-and-short.6
Who makes the call? The “single word” from the defensive bench is the name of the package: “Base!” or “Nickel!”, or a team’s own code word for it. Someone on every defensive staff is watching for the offense’s substitutes the moment the whistle blows and calls out the grouping; the defensive play-caller answers with the package, the substitutes run on, and the green dot and sideline signals do the rest. Coordinators talk about wanting to see the offense’s personnel “as early as possible,” and players notice when that relay is slow.7 It is also why the hybrid players above are worth so much to an offense: the caller has to name the grouping in a second or two, and a player who is both a receiver and a back has no right name.
Defenses also substitute by situation, not just by personnel. Most have a third-and-long package (often dime, with a sixth defensive back and extra pass rushers) and a short-yardage or goal-line package (more linemen, fewer defensive backs) that come on at the whistle whatever the offense sends. The offense’s personnel then decides only the fine-tuning.


Show the Python (simulated tracking for the substitution sequence)
# Two groups swap players between plays. gridiron's Play schedules all pre-snap movement to finish at
# the snap, so this sequence is built as BDB-style tracking frames directly (x, y in yards, 10 frames
# per second) and drawn with gridiron's Field and draw_marker (markers a little larger than usual,
# because the whole width of the field has to fit in each small panel).
LOS, BALL_Y = 50.0, FIELD_WIDTH / 2
OFF_BENCH, DEF_BENCH = 25.6, -25.6       # the two benches are on opposite sidelines
HUDDLE_C, HUDDLE_R = (-9.5, 0.0), 2.6

# Offense in 11 personnel (singleback 2x2), then 12 personnel (two tight ends) after the swap.
ALIGN_11 = {"LT": (LINE_D, -3.2), "LG": (LINE_D, -1.6), "C": (LINE_D, 0), "RG": (LINE_D, 1.6),
            "RT": (LINE_D, 3.2), "QB": (UC, 0), "RB": (TB_D, 0), "Y": (LINE_D, TE_W),
            "X": (LINE_D, -15), "H": (OFF_BALL, -9), "Z": (OFF_BALL, 15)}
ALIGN_12 = dict(ALIGN_11, U=(LINE_D, -TE_W), X=(OFF_BALL, -15))
ALIGN_12.pop("H")
OFF_LABEL = {"C": "C", "QB": "Q", "RB": "R", "Y": "Y", "U": "U", "X": "X", "H": "H", "Z": "Z"}
OFF_POS = {"RB": "RB", "Y": "TE", "U": "TE", "X": "WR", "H": "WR", "Z": "WR", "QB": "QB"}

# The defense's nickel (4-2-5) against 11, and its base 4-3 against 12.
NICKEL = {"WDE": (1.0, -4.0), "WDT": (1.0, -0.7), "SDT": (1.0, 2.35), "SDE": (1.0, 5.4),
          "MIKE": (4.5, -1.6), "WILL": (4.5, 2.4), "NB": (5.0, -9.0),
          "LCB": (7.0, -15), "RCB": (7.0, 15), "FS": (12.0, -8.5), "SS": (12.0, 8.5)}
# Base keeps the same four linemen. The new linebacker (S) goes where the nickel back was, onto U,
# the tight end who just came in, so the front sets its strength to the left; M and W stay put.
BASE = {"WDE": (1.0, -4.0), "WDT": (1.0, -0.7), "SDT": (1.0, 2.35), "SDE": (1.0, 5.4),
        "WILL": (4.5, 2.6), "MIKE": (4.5, -1.2), "SAM": (4.0, -6.6),
        "LCB": (7.0, -15), "RCB": (7.0, 15), "FS": (12.5, 1.0), "SS": (8.0, -9.5)}
DEF_LABEL = {"WDE": "E", "SDE": "E", "WDT": "T", "SDT": "T", "WILL": "W", "MIKE": "M", "SAM": "S",
             "NB": "$", "LCB": "C", "RCB": "C", "FS": "FS", "SS": "SS"}

# Huddle: ten players in a ring, the quarterback in the middle facing them.
ring_keys = ["LT", "LG", "H", "C", "RG", "RT", "Y", "Z", "RB", "X"]   # H's spot faces his bench
HUDDLE = {k: (HUDDLE_C[0] + HUDDLE_R * np.cos(a), HUDDLE_C[1] + HUDDLE_R * np.sin(a))
          for k, a in zip(ring_keys, np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 10, endpoint=False) + np.pi / 10)}
HUDDLE["QB"] = HUDDLE_C

# Keyframes: player -> [(t, d, w), ...], t = seconds since the whistle (play clock = 40 - t).
KF = {}
for k in ALIGN_11:                                        # everyone but H: huddle, then break to 12 spots
    if k == "H":
        continue
    KF[k] = [(0, *HUDDLE[k]), (15.5, *HUDDLE[k]), (21.5, *ALIGN_12[k])]
KF["H"] = [(0, *HUDDLE["H"]), (3.0, *HUDDLE["H"]), (8.0, -9.0, OFF_BENCH), (24, -9.0, OFF_BENCH)]
KF["U"] = [(0, -11.5, OFF_BENCH), (3.0, -11.5, OFF_BENCH), (8.2, *HUDDLE["H"]),
           (15.5, *HUDDLE["H"]), (21.5, *ALIGN_12["U"])]
for k, spot in NICKEL.items():                            # defense waits in nickel, then adjusts to 12
    if k == "NB":
        KF[k] = [(0, *spot), (9.0, *spot), (14.0, 3.0, DEF_BENCH), (24, 3.0, DEF_BENCH)]
    else:
        KF[k] = [(0, *spot), (16.0, *spot), (21.5, *BASE[k])]
KF["SAM"] = [(0, 6.0, DEF_BENCH), (9.5, 6.0, DEF_BENCH), (14.5, 4.5, -8.5), (16.0, 4.5, -8.5),
             (21.5, *BASE["SAM"])]
# The umpire stands over the ball while the offense substitutes, then steps back to his spot in the
# offensive backfield (NFL umpires have lined up behind the offense since 2010, except late in halves).
UMP = [(0, -12.5, -5.5), (3.5, -12.5, -5.5), (5.0, -0.6, 0.0), (15.0, -0.6, 0.0), (17.0, -12.0, -5.5)]


def at(kf, t):
    ts = np.array([q[0] for q in kf])
    return (float(np.interp(t, ts, [q[1] for q in kf])), float(np.interp(t, ts, [q[2] for q in kf])))


def sub_tracking(t_end=24.0, dt=0.1):
    """BDB-style tracking frames for the substitution sequence."""
    rows = []
    times = np.round(np.arange(0, t_end + 1e-9, dt), 2)
    for fid, t in enumerate(times, 1):
        for k, kf in KF.items():
            d, w = at(kf, t)
            side = "def" if k in DEF_LABEL else "off"
            lab = DEF_LABEL.get(k) if side == "def" else OFF_LABEL.get(k, "")
            rows.append(dict(frameId=fid, time=float(t), displayName=k, x=LOS + d, y=BALL_Y - w,
                             side=side, label=lab))
        rows.append(dict(frameId=fid, time=float(t), displayName="football", x=LOS, y=BALL_Y,
                         side="ball", label=""))
    df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    df["_id"] = df["displayName"]
    return df


SUBS = {"H": style.MUTED, "U": TE_RING, "NB": style.MUTED, "SAM": style.DEFENSE}
SUB_NOTES = ["Whistle. 11 personnel in the huddle (H too);\nU and S wait on their sidelines",
             "Offense subs: H (a receiver) jogs off,\nU (a tight end) runs on. Umpire over the ball",
             "Defense matches: the nickel back\nruns off, S (a linebacker) runs on",
             "Both set: 12 personnel against\na base 4-3 (four DBs, three LBs)"]
SUB_TIMES = [1.5, 6.0, 12.5, 23.5]


def sub_panel(ax, df, t, small=True):
    tmap = df.groupby("frameId")["time"].first()
    fid = int((tmap - t).abs().idxmin())
    fld = Field(ax=ax, orient="vertical", los=LOS, window=(-14.5, 14.5), to_go=None,
                numbers=False, hashes=True)
    cur = df[df["frameId"] == fid]
    trails = df[(df["frameId"] <= fid) & df["displayName"].isin(list(SUBS)) & (df["time"] <= 15.5)]
    ppy = fld.pts_per_yard()
    for k, g in trails.groupby("displayName"):
        px, py = fld.xy(g["x"].values, g["y"].values)
        ax.plot(px, py, color=style.OFFENSE if k in OFF_LABEL else style.DEFENSE, lw=0.9, alpha=0.45,
                zorder=3)
    for _, row in cur.iterrows():
        x, y = fld.xy(row["x"], row["y"])
        draw_marker(ax, float(x), float(y), row["side"], row["label"], ppy * (1.5 if small else 1.1),
                    r=0.85 if small else 0.75)
    for k, col in SUBS.items():                    # ring the four players who change
        row = cur[cur["displayName"] == k].iloc[0]
        x, y = fld.xy(row["x"], row["y"])
        ax.add_patch(Circle((float(x), float(y)), 1.4, fc="none", ec=col, lw=1.6, zorder=7))
    ud, uw = at(UMP, t)                            # the umpire: striped disc
    x, y = fld.xy(LOS + ud, BALL_Y - uw)
    ax.add_patch(Circle((float(x), float(y)), 0.9, fc="white", ec=style.INK, lw=0.9, hatch="||||",
                        zorder=9))
    ax.text(float(x) + 1.4, float(y), "ump", fontsize=6.0 if small else 7.5, color=style.INK,
            ha="left", va="center", zorder=9, fontweight="bold")
    for wy, txt in [(OFF_BENCH, "offense's bench"), (DEF_BENCH, "defense's bench")]:
        bx, by = fld.xy(LOS + 12.9, BALL_Y - wy)
        ax.text(float(bx), float(by), txt, fontsize=6.5 if small else 8, color=style.INK_2,
                ha="left" if wy < 0 else "right", va="center", style="italic", zorder=6)
    return fld


Watch it happen. Between plays, the offense swaps a receiver for a second tight end, and the defense swaps its nickel back for a linebacker:


Show the Python
SUB_DF = sub_tracking()
if PDF:
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(6.6, 5.0))
    for i, (ax, t) in enumerate(zip(axes.flat, SUB_TIMES)):
        sub_panel(ax, SUB_DF, t)
        ax.set_title(f"{i + 1}.  play clock :{40 - t:.0f}", fontsize=8.5, color=style.INK_2, loc="left")
        ax.text(0.5, -0.02, SUB_NOTES[i], transform=ax.transAxes, ha="center", va="top", fontsize=7.3,
                color=style.INK, linespacing=1.15)
    fig.tight_layout(h_pad=2.4, w_pad=0.8)
    plt.show()
else:
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.9))
    tmap = SUB_DF.groupby("frameId")["time"].first()

    def update(fid):
        ax.clear()
        t = float(tmap[fid])
        sub_panel(ax, SUB_DF, t, small=False)
        note = [n for tt, n in zip([0.0, 4.0, 9.5, 20.5], SUB_NOTES) if tt <= t + 1e-6][-1]
        ax.set_title(f"play clock :{40 - t:.0f}    " + note.replace("\n", " "), fontsize=8.5,
                     color=style.INK, loc="left")
        return []

    frames = sorted(SUB_DF["frameId"].unique())[::2]
    anim = animation.FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=frames, interval=200)
    html_video(anim)





  
  Your browser does not support the video tag.



Figure 9.4: Substitution matching, between two plays (simulated, BDB-format tracking; times are typical, not fixed). In this figure the rings mark only the four players who change: gray = leaving, gold = the tight end coming on, orange = the linebacker coming on. 1: the offense huddles in 11 personnel (H is in the huddle) while the defense waits in nickel ($ = nickel back); the two substitutes, U and S, wait on their own sidelines. 2: U runs on for H; the umpire (‘ump’, striped) stands over the ball so the offense can’t snap yet. 3: the defense answers, its nickel back off and a linebacker (S) on. 4: 12 personnel lines up against a base 4-3, with S on U, the tight end who just arrived. The defense is drawn in its alignment for clarity; until the offense breaks the huddle it really stands loose, watching its sideline. Offense: Q = quarterback, R = running back, X/Z = receivers, Y/U = tight ends. Defense: E = end, T = tackle, M/W/S = linebackers, C = cornerback, FS/SS = safeties.




Notice two things. First, the order: the offense moved first and the defense second, and the defense had no sensible way to go first, because any guess could be answered by the next substitute. Second, the defense only matched bodies. It still has no idea whether the second tight end is there to block or to run a route, and the offense hasn’t chosen its formation. The defense has spent its answer; the offense keeps its next two moves.

The rules that protect the match
You met the rule behind panel 2 in What a Play Really Is: when the offense substitutes, the umpire stands over the ball and the snap waits until the defense has had a reasonable chance to respond, except in the last two minutes of each half; when the offense doesn’t substitute, there is no pause, and a defense that changes players anyway risks twelve men on the field.8 Three details matter for personnel:

Any substitution starts the clock on that protection, even a like-for-like one. Swap a tired receiver for a fresh receiver and the personnel hasn’t changed, but the umpire still holds the ball. That’s why fast-tempo offenses rotate players only at stoppages: one swap and their tempo is gone.
Not substituting is a weapon. If the defense is in base against a 12-personnel offense that is throwing well, the offense can stay in 12, play fast, and keep those linebackers on the field. In-Game Adjustments, Tempo, and the Sideline Battle builds that game out.
Bluffing has a limit. An offense can’t run a player on to bait the defense into a change and then pull him straight back off: a substitute who comes on and talks to his teammates must stay for at least one play, or the team is warned and then penalized.9 The fakes come in the formation, not in the substitution.







ImportantWhy it exists



Substitution matching exists because offenses get to choose first. The offense commits to its bodies first, in plain view, and in exchange keeps the last word on the formation and the play. The defense gets the last word on bodies, and the rules guarantee it time to use it. So the offense picks personnel hoping the defense’s best answer to who is the wrong answer to where and what.




What defenses actually do
Here is how NFL defenses answered each grouping in 2025, counting the defensive backs on the field for every regular-season run and pass:


Show the Python (load ten seasons of play-by-play and participation data)
from gridiron.data import nfl, pbp

SEASONS = list(range(2016, 2026))
part = nfl().load_participation(SEASONS).to_pandas()
COLS = ["season", "season_type", "game_id", "play_id", "posteam", "down", "play_type", "pass",
        "wp", "half_seconds_remaining", "shotgun", "ydstogo"]
plays = pbp(SEASONS, columns=COLS)
plays = plays[(plays.season_type == "REG") & plays.play_type.isin(["pass", "run"]) & plays.down.notna()]
df = plays.merge(part, left_on=["game_id", "play_id"], right_on=["nflverse_game_id", "play_id"])


def count(s, positions):
    """Sum the counts for some positions in a personnel string. Two formats exist:
    2016-2022 (NGS) '1 RB, 2 TE, 2 WR' (linemen listed only when there are six or more), and
    2023-2025 (FTN) '1 C, 2 G, 1 QB, 1 RB, 2 T, 2 TE, 2 WR' (every player by roster position)."""
    if not isinstance(s, str):
        return np.nan
    return sum(int(n) for n, pos in re.findall(r"(\d+)\s+([A-Z]+)", s) if pos in positions)


op = df["offense_personnel"]
df["rb"] = op.map(lambda s: count(s, {"RB", "FB"}))       # fullbacks count as backs
df["te"] = op.map(lambda s: count(s, {"TE"}))
df["wr"] = op.map(lambda s: count(s, {"WR"}))
df["ol"] = op.map(lambda s: count(s, {"OL", "C", "G", "T"}))
df.loc[(df.season <= 2022) & (df.ol == 0), "ol"] = 5      # the NGS strings omit a normal five
df["db"] = df["defense_personnel"].map(lambda s: count(s, {"DB", "CB", "S", "FS", "SS"}))
df = df[df.rb.notna() & df.te.notna()].copy()
df["pers"] = df.rb.astype(int).astype(str) + df.te.astype(int).astype(str)
df["jumbo"] = df.ol >= 6

# "Neutral": 1st and 2nd down, win probability 20-80%, outside the last two minutes of each half.
neutral = df[df.down.isin([1, 2]) & df.wp.between(0.2, 0.8) & (df.half_seconds_remaining > 120)]
print(f"{len(df):,} regular-season runs and passes with personnel, 2016-2025")




Show the Python
s = df[(df.season == 2025) & df.db.between(2, 8)].copy()
s["pkg"] = pd.cut(s.db, [0, 3, 4, 5, 9], labels=["3 or fewer DBs", "4 DBs (base)", "5 DBs (nickel)",
                                                  "6+ DBs (dime)"])
order = ["10", "11", "12", "21", "13", "22"]
ct = (pd.crosstab(s.pers, s.pkg, normalize="index") * 100).reindex(order)
n = s.pers.value_counts().reindex(order)
cols = {"3 or fewer DBs": "#898781", "4 DBs (base)": style.DEFENSE, "5 DBs (nickel)": style.OFFENSE,
        "6+ DBs (dime)": style.THIRD}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 2.6))
ax.set_axisbelow(True)          # gridlines behind the bars, not through the labels
left = np.zeros(len(order))
for c in ["4 DBs (base)", "5 DBs (nickel)", "6+ DBs (dime)", "3 or fewer DBs"]:
    v = ct[c].values
    ax.barh(range(len(order)), v, left=left, color=cols[c], label=c, height=0.66, edgecolor=style.SURFACE)
    for i, (l, val) in enumerate(zip(left, v)):
        if val >= 9:
            ax.text(l + val / 2, i, f"{val:.0f}%", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7.5,
                    color="white" if c != "3 or fewer DBs" else style.INK)
    left += v
ax.set_yticks(range(len(order)), [f"{o}  (n={n[o]:,})" for o in order], fontsize=8)
ax.invert_yaxis()
ax.set_xlim(0, 100)
ax.set_xlabel("share of the offense's plays (%)", fontsize=8)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.set_title("Offensive personnel → the defense's answer, 2025", fontsize=10)
ax.legend(ncol=4, fontsize=7, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.45, -0.27), frameon=False)
plt.show()








Figure 9.5: How defenses matched each offensive grouping in 2025 (regular-season runs and passes; nflverse participation data, charted by FTN, a football-data company). Against three or four receivers (11, 10), defenses played nickel or dime almost every time. Against two tight ends or two backs (12, 21), they went to their base defense about 60% of the time; against the heaviest groupings (13, 22), about 80%, sometimes with only three defensive backs (goal-line packages).





The matching is strong but not mechanical. Against 11 personnel, defenses were in nickel or dime about 93% of the time (the slot-receiver problem from The Twenty-Two). Against 12 and 21, though, about a third of defenses stayed in nickel. Those are defenses making a bet: that their nickel back is good enough against the run to survive a second tight end, and that keeping a fifth defensive back is worth it in case the offense throws. The 2025 league as a whole played base on about 30% of snaps, up from a low of about 20% in 2023. The offenses got bigger, so the defenses got bigger too.10

title: Personnel: Who’s on the Field Before Anything Else
section: Why personnel is the first clue
text:
Why personnel is the first clue
The pre-snap read that this course builds, play by play, runs in a fixed order: situation → personnel → formation → motion → the defense’s box and safeties → prediction. (The checklist is assembled step by step through Part 2, and Motion and Shifts as Weapons puts it on one card.) Personnel comes right after the situation for a simple reason: it is the first clue you can see, and you can see it early.


Show the Python
clues = [("Situation (down, distance, score, clock)", 40, 0, style.MUTED),
         ("Personnel (who runs on and off)", 37, 0, style.OFFENSE),
         ("Defense's personnel answer", 33, 0, "#e87ba4"),
         ("Formation (where they line up)", 17, 0, style.OFFENSE_DARK),
         ("Motion and shifts", 7, 0, style.THIRD),
         ("Defense's box and safeties (often disguised)", 5, 0, style.DEFENSE)]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 2.9))
for i, (name, start, end, col) in enumerate(clues):
    ax.barh(i, start - end, left=end, color=col, height=0.55, alpha=0.9)
ax.set_xlim(41, -0.5)           # the play clock counts down, left to right
ax.set_xticks([40, 30, 20, 15, 10, 5, 0], [":40", ":30", ":20", ":15", ":10", ":05", "snap"], fontsize=8)
ax.set_yticks(range(len(clues)), [c[0] for c in clues], fontsize=8)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=0)
ax.invert_yaxis()
ax.axvline(40, color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.8)
ax.text(40, -0.75, "whistle", ha="center", fontsize=7, color=style.INK_2)
ax.axvline(15, color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.8, ls=(0, (3, 2)))
ax.text(15, -0.75, "radio cuts out", ha="center", fontsize=7, color=style.INK_2)
ax.set_xlabel("play clock", fontsize=8)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.spines["left"].set_visible(False)
plt.show()








Figure 9.6: When each pre-snap clue becomes readable during a typical huddling snap (times vary by team and tempo). The situation is known before the whistle; the offense’s personnel shows as substitutes run on, usually with half a minute or more left on the play clock, and the defense’s answering substitutes follow a few seconds later; the formation appears only when the huddle breaks; motion, the defense’s box and its safeties come last, and the defense works to disguise them.





Personnel does three jobs at once.
It narrows the menu. An offense in 22 can’t throw to four receivers; an offense in 11 can’t line up with a tight end beside each tackle. Every grouping rules out much of the playbook and rules in a few favorites (Classic Formations and Spread Formations pair them up).
It moves the run/pass odds, modestly for the common groupings and a lot for the heavy ones, as the numbers below show.
It sets up the matchups. This is the deepest of the three. Because the defense matches personnel and the offense then picks the formation, every grouping is a bet about what the defense will do with its answer. Twelve personnel shows it best:


Show the Python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.95))


def nudge_sde(players, w=4.4):
    """Move the strong-side end to a 6i (inside shoulder of the tight end spot), clear of the tackle's label."""
    return [q.moved(w=w * (1 if q.w > 0 else -1)) if q.key == "SDE" else q for q in players]


# Left: 12 personnel, tight, against nickel. Seal the nickel back and run around him.
off = line5() + [P("QB", "QB", UC, 0, "Q"), P("RB", "RB", TB_D, 0, "R"), P("Y", "TE", LINE_D, TE_W),
                 P("U", "TE", LINE_D, -TE_W), P("X", "WR", OFF_BALL, -10.5), P("Z", "WR", OFF_BALL, 10.5)]
nick = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -5.6, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "T"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "T"),
        D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 4.4, "E"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.0), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.6),
        D("NB", "NB", 3.4, 5.9, "$"), D("LCB", "CB", 6.5, -10.5), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 11.5),
        D("FS", "FS", 12.0, -6.0), D("SS", "SS", 12.0, 6.0)]
a = Play(off, nick, los=35, to_go=10)
a.block("Y", target="NB")                 # the tight end seals the nickel back inside
a.block("RT", target="SDE")               # the tackle reaches the end
a.block("RG", target="MIKE")              # the guard climbs to the middle linebacker
a.block("Z", target="RCB")                # the receiver blocks the corner, the force player
a.run("RB", [(-3.5, 2.5), (-0.6, 7.4), (2.6, 8.9), (8.5, 10.0)], absolute=True, delay=0.5)
a.highlight("Y", "U", color=TE_RING)
a.highlight("NB", color=style.DEFENSE)
a.note("Y seals\nthe $ inside", at=(6.4, 4.9))
a.draw(ax=axes[0], lateral=(-17, 17), window=(-9.0, 14.5), title=False)
hide_yard_numbers(axes[0])
axes[0].set_title("Defense in nickel: run at it", fontsize=9.5, loc="left", color=style.INK)

# Right: the same 12 personnel spread out against base, single-high. Throw at the linebacker.
off = line5() + [P("QB", "QB", GUN, 0, "Q"), P("RB", "RB", GUN, -2.2, "R"),
                 P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -15), P("U", "TE", OFF_BALL, -8.5),
                 P("Y", "TE", OFF_BALL, 8.5), P("Z", "WR", LINE_D, 15)]
base = nudge_sde(defense("4-3_over", "single_high", off))
fix = {"SAM": dict(d=4.5, w=8.0), "WILL": dict(d=4.5, w=-4.0), "MIKE": dict(d=5.0, w=0.4),
       "LCB": dict(d=6.5), "RCB": dict(d=6.5), "FS": dict(d=13.0, w=0.0), "SS": dict(d=7.5, w=-9.0)}
base = [q.moved(**fix[q.key]) if q.key in fix else q for q in base]
b = Play(off, base, los=35, to_go=10)
b.route("Y", r.seam(10.5))
b.highlight("Y", "U", color=TE_RING)
b.highlight("SAM", color=style.DEFENSE)
b.note("S must run\nwith Y", at=(8.6, 3.6))
b.draw(ax=axes[1], lateral=(-17, 17), window=(-9.0, 14.5), title=False)
hide_yard_numbers(axes[1])
axes[1].set_title("Defense in base: throw at it", fontsize=9.5, loc="left", color=style.INK)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 9.7: The two-tight-end dilemma. Left: the defense answered 12 personnel with nickel, so the offense lines up tight and runs at the smallest defender. The tight end (Y, about 250 pounds) seals the nickel back ($, about 195) inside, Z blocks the cornerback, the right guard climbs to the middle linebacker, and the back runs around the sealed nickel (the backside defenders are left to the backside blockers, not drawn). Right: the defense answered with its base 4-3 and a single deep safety, so the offense splits both tight ends out like receivers; with no safety over the seam, a linebacker (S) has to run with a tight end straight up the field (a ‘seam’ route). Gold rings = tight ends.





That’s the bind. If the defense answers two tight ends with nickel, it has a 195-pound defensive back near the line of scrimmage, and the offense can aim its run at him: a 250-pound tight end walls him off, and the back runs around the spot where a linebacker should have been. If it answers with base, it has three linebackers on the field, and the offense can spread the tight ends out and make a linebacker cover one of them down the field. The better the tight ends are at both jobs, the worse the defense’s choice gets. That’s why great two-way tight ends are so valuable, and it’s a big part of why 12 personnel has grown: an offense with two of them can pick whichever mismatch the defense hands it, after the defense has made its choice.
The same logic runs the other way for the defense. A defense with a safety who can tackle like a linebacker, or a linebacker who can cover like a safety, doesn’t have to choose: it can stay in one grouping against everything and take the matchup game away. That’s the idea behind the big nickel, a nickel whose fifth defensive back is a bigger safety rather than a small slot corner, and behind hybrid defenders in general, the defensive mirror of a Deebo Samuel. The 2025 Seahawks, for example, played 220-pound rookie safety Nick Emmanwori as a nickel defender.11 A First Look at Defense tells that story.

title: Personnel: Who’s on the Field Before Anything Else
section: Personnel and run/pass: what the numbers say
text:
Personnel and run/pass: what the numbers say
So how much does personnel tell you about run or pass? Here is every grouping with at least 300 plays in the three most recent seasons, counting only neutral situations: first and second down, outside the last two minutes of each half, with neither team far ahead or behind (win probability between 20% and 80%). Think of neutral as “not late, not lopsided.” In those situations, the offense’s choice reflects its plan rather than the scoreboard; Tendencies: PROE, Personnel, Motion, and Coverage defines it formally and builds on it.


Show the Python
s = neutral[neutral.season.isin([2023, 2024, 2025])]
g = s.groupby("pers")["pass"].agg(["mean", "size"])
g = g[g["size"] >= 300]
j = s[s.jumbo]["pass"].agg(["mean", "size"])
g.loc["jumbo"] = [j["mean"], j["size"]]
g = g.sort_values("mean")
league = s["pass"].mean()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.2))
ax.set_axisbelow(True)          # gridlines behind the bars
colors = [style.DEFENSE if k == "jumbo" else style.OFFENSE for k in g.index]
ax.barh(range(len(g)), g["mean"] * 100, color=colors, height=0.62)
for i, (k, row) in enumerate(g.iterrows()):      # value labels inside the bar ends, clear of the line
    ax.text(row["mean"] * 100 - 1, i, f"{row['mean'] * 100:.0f}%", va="center", ha="right", fontsize=8,
            color="white", fontweight="bold")
ax.axvline(league * 100, color=style.INK_2, lw=1, ls=(0, (4, 3)), zorder=0.5)
ax.text(league * 100 + 0.8, 0, f"all plays\n{league * 100:.0f}%", fontsize=7.5, color=style.INK_2,
        va="center", ha="left")
ax.set_yticks(range(len(g)), [f"{k}  (n={int(row['size']):,})" for k, row in g.iterrows()], fontsize=8)
ax.set_xlim(0, 75)
ax.set_xlabel("share of plays that were dropbacks (%)", fontsize=8)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.set_title("Pass rate by personnel, neutral situations, 2023–2025", fontsize=10)
plt.show()








Figure 9.8: Pass rate by personnel in neutral situations (1st and 2nd down, win probability 20–80%, outside the last two minutes of each half), 2023–2025 regular seasons, groupings with at least 300 plays. A pass is any dropback, including sacks and scrambles. Jumbo plays (six or more offensive linemen) are also counted in the grouping their backs and tight ends give them. The dashed line is the league rate in the same situations.





Three things jump out.
The common groupings are weak clues. In neutral situations, offenses passed on about 56% of plays from 11 personnel and about 49% from 12. That’s a nudge, not a signal. If you predicted “pass” every time you saw 11 and “run” every time you saw 12, you’d be right about 54% of the time on those plays, barely better than the 53% you’d get by saying “pass” on every one of them. That’s deliberate: the groupings an offense uses most are the ones it has built to do both. A team whose 11 personnel was 80% pass would be giving away the game. Even four receivers (10 personnel) was only about 55% pass: spreading the defense out also thins the number of defenders near the ball, which makes running easier.
The heavy groupings are stronger clues. From 22 personnel, offenses passed only about 36% of the time, and from jumbo about 30%. That is also where the rare pass is most dangerous, because the defense has loaded up for the run: the logic of play-action (faking a handoff before throwing).
Personnel predicts the formation as well as the play. From 11 personnel, offenses lined up in the shotgun on about 70% of plays; from 13, only about 30%. Heavy personnel usually means the quarterback under center, close to the ball. You can use that as a check on your count: if you counted three tight ends and the quarterback is five yards deep in the shotgun, count again, or expect something unusual.

How much does personnel add?
Here is a blunt test. Take every neutral play from 2023 to 2025 and make the simplest guess the situation allows: for each down and distance (first or second down; 1–3, 4–6, 7–10 or 11+ yards to go), say whichever of run or pass is more common there. That guesser is right about 60% of the time. Now let it see the personnel as well. It is still right about 60% of the time. On 11 and 12, which are more than eight snaps in ten, the more common call simply doesn’t change. Let it see one more pre-snap fact, whether the quarterback is in the shotgun, and it jumps to about 66%.


Show the Python (how much does personnel add to a down-and-distance guess?)
def hit_rate(d, keys):
    """Guess the more common call (run or pass) in each cell of `keys`; return the share guessed right."""
    p_pass = d.groupby(keys, observed=True)["pass"].transform("mean")
    return ((p_pass >= 0.5) == (d["pass"] == 1)).mean()


def with_dist(d):
    return d.assign(dist=pd.cut(d.ydstogo, [0, 3, 6, 10, 100], labels=["1-3", "4-6", "7-10", "11+"]))


recent = with_dist(neutral[neutral.season.isin([2023, 2024, 2025])])
every = with_dist(df[df.season.isin([2023, 2024, 2025])])
HIT = {"neutral, down & distance": hit_rate(recent, ["down", "dist"]),
       "neutral, + personnel": hit_rate(recent, ["down", "dist", "pers"]),
       "neutral, + personnel + shotgun": hit_rate(recent, ["down", "dist", "pers", "shotgun"]),
       "all downs, down & distance": hit_rate(every, ["down", "dist"]),
       "all downs, + personnel": hit_rate(every, ["down", "dist", "pers"])}
print({k: round(v, 3) for k, v in HIT.items()})
assert 0.58 < HIT["neutral, down & distance"] < 0.62 and abs(HIT["neutral, + personnel"] - 0.60) < 0.02
assert 0.64 < HIT["neutral, + personnel + shotgun"] < 0.67
assert 0.61 < HIT["all downs, down & distance"] < 0.64 and 0.66 < HIT["all downs, + personnel"] < 0.69
short = every[every.down.isin([3, 4]) & (every.ydstogo <= 1)]
SHORT = short.groupby("pers")["pass"].mean()
assert SHORT["22"] < 0.2 and 0.28 < SHORT["11"] < 0.36


So on ordinary first and second downs, personnel barely changes a simple run/pass guess. Its worth is elsewhere: it tells you which formations are coming (and so where the quarterback will stand), it sets up the matchups in the dilemma above, and in the situations where heavy groupings appear, it means a lot. Count every down, not just neutral ones, and adding personnel lifts the same guesser from about 63% to about 67%. The opening play’s situation is the clearest case: on third- or fourth-and-1 from 2023 to 2025, offenses in 22 personnel threw only about 15% of the time, against about 32% from 11.






CautionCommon misconception



“Heavy personnel means run.” Only the heaviest groupings lean hard. Two tight ends threw on about half of neutral plays, because players who can block and catch hide the offense’s intentions, which is exactly why offenses have moved toward them. The formation, the motion and the defense’s answer tell you more, and the next five chapters add those clues one at a time.

title: Personnel: Who’s on the Field Before Anything Else
section: Personnel by season: the rise of 11, and the 2025 turn
text:
Personnel by season: the rise of 11, and the 2025 turn
Three wide receivers weren’t always normal. Football Outsiders, charting games by hand, counted 11 personnel on about 40% of NFL plays in 2011, 46% in 2012 and 51% in 2013.12 That climb, driven by more passing, by college spread offenses supplying receivers and quarterbacks raised on three-receiver sets, and by defenses answering with more defensive backs, finished just before the data in this chapter begins. Different charters count slightly differently, so those numbers don’t belong on the same axis as the ones below, but the direction is clear. Here’s how the mix moved from 2016 to 2025.


Show the Python
share = (pd.crosstab(df.season, df.pers, normalize="index") * 100)
lines = {"11": style.OFFENSE, "12": style.DEFENSE, "21": style.THIRD, "13": "#eda100"}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.1))
other = 100 - share[list(lines)].sum(axis=1)
ends = {k: share.loc[2025, k] for k in lines}
ends["all other"] = other.loc[2025]
# end-of-line labels, nudged apart so close values (13, 21, other) don't collide
ys = dict(sorted(ends.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1]))
pos, last = {}, -99.0
for k, v in ys.items():
    pos[k] = max(v, last + 3.6)
    last = pos[k]
for k, col in lines.items():
    ax.plot(share.index, share[k], color=col, lw=2.2, marker="o", ms=3.5)
ax.plot(other.index, other, color=style.MUTED, lw=1.4, ls=(0, (3, 2)))
for k, v in ends.items():
    ax.text(2025.3, pos[k], f"{k}: {v:.1f}%", va="center", fontsize=8, fontweight="bold",
            color=lines.get(k, style.INK_2))      # each end label in its line's color
ax.axvline(2022.5, color=style.BASELINE, lw=1, ls=(0, (1, 2)))
ax.text(2022.55, 46, "source change\n(NGS → FTN)", fontsize=7, color=style.INK_2, va="center", ha="left")
ax.set_xlim(2015.6, 2027.6)
ax.set_xticks(range(2016, 2026), [str(y) for y in range(2016, 2026)], fontsize=8)
ax.set_ylim(0, 70)
ax.set_ylabel("share of plays (%)", fontsize=8)
ax.set_title("Personnel share by season", fontsize=10)
plt.show()








Figure 9.9: Share of NFL regular-season runs and passes by offensive personnel, 2016–2025 (course calculation from nflverse participation data). 11 personnel held at roughly 60% for a decade and fell to 58.8% in 2025, its lowest in the period; 12 personnel rose to 24.4%, its highest. The dotted line marks a change of data source (see ‘Where the numbers come from’ below).





For most of the decade the story is stability: 11 personnel on about 60% of plays, 12 on about 20%, 21 on about 8%, everything else sharing the rest. By the late 2010s, three receivers was simply what an offense looked like, and Sean McVay’s Rams were the extreme case of that habit.
Then 2025 moved. Eleven personnel fell to 58.8%, its lowest share of the decade, and 12 rose to 24.4%, its highest. Thirteen personnel jumped from 3.7% to 5.1%. Next Gen Stats, measuring it its own way, found offenses with fewer than three wide receivers on 41.7% of 2025 plays, the first season at or above 38% since it began tracking in 2016, and the share kept climbing as the season went on.13
Why then? No rule change or single coach set it off, and nobody can prove a cause from a chart. The explanation most analysts give is an arms race. Through the late 2010s and early 2020s, defenses got smaller and faster to stop the pass: more nickel and dime, and more looks with two safeties deep (which A First Look at Defense introduces as two-high). A defense like that has fewer big bodies near the line, a “light box,” and it was winning: getting to quarterbacks faster and covering better. Offenses answered by getting bigger, to force defenses into base, where “they generally do not want an undersized extra DB to get steamrolled by a tight end,” as an NFL.com Next Gen Stats analysis put it, and then running at whatever was left, often with the quarterback back under center.14 And as you saw above, defenses answered that by playing more base in 2025. Each side’s move invites the other’s. The Modern Era tells the whole arms race, and Working with nflverse Data in Python shows you how to rebuild these charts yourself.






NoteGo deeper: where the numbers come from



Every chart in this chapter is a course calculation from the nflverse participation data (load_participation()), which lists the personnel on each play, joined to nflverse play-by-play.15 Three cautions if you reproduce them. First, the source changes between 2022 and 2023: Next Gen Stats supplied 2016–2022 and FTN Data supplies 2023 onward, and the personnel strings change format (“1 RB, 2 TE, 2 WR” before, every player by position after), so the code normalizes them before counting; the personnel shares agree across the break. Second, players are counted by roster position, not by role. A snap with a second quarterback or a defensive player in the offense (a string like “2 QB, 1 RB, 1 TE, 2 WR”) is labeled by its backs and tight ends, here “11,” even though only two receivers are out there. That is about 1% of plays, too few to move the charts, and the course keeps the simple backs-then-tight-ends count so its numbers match the course fact sheet. Third, the participation file for a season arrives only after the season ends, so 2026 numbers won’t exist until early 2027. Published series from other providers (Next Gen Stats, Sharp Football, PFF) count slightly differently; never put two providers’ numbers on one axis.

title: Personnel: Who’s on the Field Before Anything Else
text:
Film room
Six teams, six ways of using personnel. Each shows a different idea from this chapter.


Show the Python
teams = [("LA", 2018, "Rams 2018"), ("SF", 2019, "49ers 2019"), ("BAL", 2019, "Ravens 2019"),
         ("PHI", 2024, "Eagles 2024"), ("LA", 2025, "Rams 2025"), ("SEA", 2025, "Seahawks 2025"),
         (None, 2025, "League 2025")]
groups = ["11", "12", "21", "13", "22"]
gcol = {"11": style.OFFENSE, "12": style.DEFENSE, "21": style.THIRD, "13": "#eda100", "22": "#e87ba4",
        "other": "#c3c2b7"}
rows = []
for tm, yr, name in teams:
    t = df[(df.season == yr) & ((df.posteam == tm) if tm else True)]
    vc = t.pers.value_counts(normalize=True) * 100
    row = {k: vc.get(k, 0.0) for k in groups}
    row["other"] = 100 - sum(row.values())
    rows.append((name, row))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.4))
ax.set_axisbelow(True)          # gridlines behind the bars
for i, (name, row) in enumerate(rows):
    left = 0
    for k in groups + ["other"]:
        v = row[k]
        ax.barh(i, v, left=left, color=gcol[k], height=0.66, edgecolor=style.SURFACE,
                label=k if i == 0 else None)
        if v >= 7:
            ax.text(left + v / 2, i, f"{v:.0f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7.5,
                    color="white" if k not in ("other", "13") else style.INK)
        left += v
ax.set_yticks(range(len(rows)), [n for n, _ in rows], fontsize=8)
ax.invert_yaxis()
ax.set_xlim(0, 100)
ax.set_xlabel("share of the team's plays (%)", fontsize=8)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.legend(ncol=6, fontsize=7.5, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.45, -0.2), frameon=False,
          title=None, handlelength=1.2)
ax.set_title("Personnel fingerprints", fontsize=10)
plt.show()








Figure 9.10: Personnel fingerprints: each team’s share of regular-season runs and passes by grouping, with the 2025 league for comparison (course calculation from nflverse participation data). The 2018 Rams lived in 11; the 2019 49ers led the league in 21; the 2019 Ravens used 22 personnel more than five times as often as the league; the 2024 Eagles leaned on 12; the 2025 Rams split their snaps between 11 and 13, and the 2025 Seahawks spread theirs across four groupings.











NoteFilm room: Los Angeles Rams 2017–2019



When the Rams hired Sean McVay in January 2017, he was 30, the youngest head coach in modern NFL history.16 His offense became famous for using one grouping, 11 personnel, almost all the time: about 81% of plays in 2017, 93% in 2018 and 73% in 2019, against a league norm of about 60%.
Why would a coach give up the personnel game entirely? Because he was playing a different one. If the offense never substitutes, the defense never gets a reason to, so it sits in nickel all day: in 2018, defenses had five or more defensive backs on about 94% of the Rams’ plays. That suited McVay twice over. A nickel defense has one fewer big body near the line, so his running game was always aimed at a lighter front. And a grouping that never changes tells the defense nothing: in neutral situations in 2018 the Rams passed on 56% of their 11-personnel plays, almost exactly the league rate. McVay put his variety into formation, motion and play-action instead, and it worked: the 2018 Rams reached Super Bowl LIII.
What to notice: an offense that never substitutes isn’t being lazy. It’s denying the defense the first clue.








NoteFilm room: San Francisco 49ers, 21 personnel and Kyle Juszczyk



Kyle Shanahan’s 49ers have been the league’s leading 21-personnel team for most of his tenure: first in the league in 21 personnel in 2017, 2018, 2019, 2021, 2024 and 2025, and second in the other seasons from 2017 to 2025, typically around a third of their plays, against a league share of about 8%. The player who makes it work is fullback Kyle Juszczyk, who signed in March 2017 on a contract that made him, at the time, the highest-paid fullback in the league.17
Juszczyk can block a linebacker on a run, line up in the slot, or split out wide like a receiver. When he lines up wide, the defense that matched 21 personnel with its base package has to send someone with him: a cornerback, which leaves a linebacker covering a receiver somewhere else, or a linebacker, which takes a defender away from the ball (Drill 2 below draws exactly this). Two backs also give the offense two running threats for every play-action fake.
What to notice: when the 49ers come out with a fullback, find him after the huddle breaks. Where he lines up tells you which matchup they’re hunting.








NoteFilm room: Baltimore Ravens 2019



The 2019 Ravens, with Lamar Jackson at quarterback (that season’s unanimous MVP) and Greg Roman as offensive coordinator, set the NFL record for team rushing yards in a season, 3,296.18 They did it big. Baltimore used 22 personnel on about 16% of its plays, more than five times the league’s 3%, with tight ends Mark Andrews, Hayden Hurst and Nick Boyle and the two-way lineman/fullback Patrick Ricard.
The surprise is in the tendencies. In neutral situations, the Ravens ran on about 64% of their 11-personnel plays (the league passed 56% of the time) and passed on about 63% of their 12-personnel plays (league: 49%). With the most dangerous runner on the field at quarterback, three receivers didn’t mean “pass” and two tight ends didn’t mean “run.”
What to notice: league tendencies are where you start. A good scouting report, like your own prediction log, adjusts them team by team (The Ravens’ Option Run Game has the full case).








NoteFilm room: Philadelphia Eagles 2024



The 2024 Eagles signed Saquon Barkley, who ran for 2,005 yards, the ninth 2,000-yard season in NFL history, and won Super Bowl LIX, 40–22 over Kansas City.19 Their personnel was the vehicle: 12 personnel on about a third of their plays (the league was at 23.5%), with tight end Dallas Goedert and a second tight end next to the best offensive line in football.
What to notice: in neutral situations the Eagles passed on only 32% of their 12-personnel plays, against 48% for the league. Everyone knew 12 meant run, and they ran anyway. Predictability costs less when you’re good enough at the thing you’re predicted to do (The Eagles: Trenches, RPOs, and the Tush Push).








NoteFilm room: the 2025 turn, Rams and Seahawks



Two NFC West teams show two different routes to the 2025 turn. McVay’s Rams, the 11-personnel team of 2018, used 13 personnel on about 31% of their plays, far more than any other team (the next was 13%), and 12 on only about 9%: they were a binary team, three receivers or three tight ends. Matthew Stafford won the MVP.20 Defenses did match: they played base on about three of every four Rams 13 snaps. But matching bought them little, because the big grouping didn’t mean run. In neutral situations the Rams threw on 47% of their 13-personnel plays, the league’s 13 rate, almost always from under center, where a pass looks like a run until the fake. The tell was the light grouping: from 11 they threw 67% of the time, against a league 57%.
The champion Seattle Seahawks, under offensive coordinator Klint Kubiak in 2025, got big the other way: by variety. They used fewer than three wide receivers on about 55% of their snaps, fifth-most in the league, spread across 11, 12, 21 and 22, with a fullback (usually Robbie Ouzts) on the field for about 19% of their plays, on the way to beating New England 29–13 in Super Bowl LX.
What to notice: when the Rams show three tight ends, don’t assume run; when they show three receivers, lean pass. When Seattle subs, the fullback is the tell to watch for.

title: Personnel: Who’s on the Field Before Anything Else
text:
Watch for it on Sunday






TipWatch for it: call the personnel




Between plays, watch the sidelines, not the replay. When the broadcast shows a wide shot, count who jogs off and who runs on. Two receivers off and a tight end and a fullback on is a change from 11 to 22.
Count backs, then tight ends, and say the number out loud. Backs stand behind or beside the quarterback; tight ends are the big players at the end of the line or just behind it, usually with a hand down. Receivers are what’s left: 5 minus the other two (4 minus, if there’s a sixth lineman).
Look for a sixth lineman. A 300-pounder standing where a tight end usually stands means jumbo. Listen for the referee’s “reporting as eligible.”
Then watch the defense. Did a defensive back run off or a linebacker run on? Base, nickel or dime? If the offense substituted and the defense didn’t, the defense is making a bet.
Make your first guess from the numbers (neutral downs, 2023–2025): 11 about 56% pass, 12 about 49%, 13 about 45%, 22 about 36%, jumbo about 30%. Treat 11 and 12 as coin flips with a lean; treat 22 and jumbo, especially on third-and-short, as run unless something says otherwise. Then adjust for down and distance, where the quarterback stands, and what you know about the team.
Write it down. Add a “personnel” column to your prediction log: grouping, your guess, the result. After a half, compare your hit rate on the heavy groupings with your hit rate on 11.

title: Personnel: Who’s on the Field Before Anything Else
text:
Predict the play






TipPredict the play 1: count it



First-and-10 at your own 30. The offense has substituted and is lined up. The broadcast’s roster graphic gives you only sizes, not positions: #87 6-5, 258 lb · #81 6-4, 250 lb · #88 6-6, 262 lb · #26 5-11, 215 lb · #11 6-1, 195 lb. On the close-up, #87 and #88 each have a hand on the ground; #81 and #11 are standing up. (A made-up roster for practice. The quarterback is Q, in the pistol, about three and a half yards behind the center; the linemen are unlabeled.)


Show the Python
off = line5() + [P("QB", "QB", PISTOL, 0, "Q"), P("RB", "RB", TB_D, 0, "26"),
                 P("Y", "TE", LINE_D, TE_W, "87"), P("U", "TE", LINE_D, -15.0, "81"),
                 P("H", "TE", OFF_BALL, -WING_W - 0.4, "88"), P("X", "WR", OFF_BALL, 15.0, "11")]
q = Play(off, None, los=40, to_go=10)
q.draw(lateral=(-19.5, 19.5), window=(-9.5, 3.5), title=False)
hide_yard_numbers(plt.gca())
plt.show()








Figure 9.11: Drill 1: who is on the field? Players are labeled by jersey number, as you’d see them on TV. #81 stands far out on the left, at the end of the line; #88 is a yard off the line just outside the left tackle; #87 is next to the right tackle; #11 is wide on the right; #26 is behind the quarterback, who is in the pistol.





What’s the personnel, which defensive package should you expect, and does the grouping lean run or pass?






TipAnswer





13 personnel. The weights do the work. #87, #81 and #88 are all 250 pounds or more: tight-end bodies, and the two with a hand down are standing where tight ends stand. #26, at 215 and behind the quarterback, is the back. #11, at 195, is the only receiver. One back, three tight ends: 13. It doesn’t matter that #81 is standing out wide where a receiver usually lines up; he is a 250-pound tight end wherever he stands.
The defense: against 13 personnel in 2025, defenses played their base package (four defensive backs) about 80% of the time, and went to nickel only about 13%. Expect linebackers.
Run or pass: on neutral downs, 13 personnel leaned run, with passes on about 45% of plays. Now look at #81. A base defense has two cornerbacks, and one of them will probably go out with him. That corner is fine in coverage, but on a run he is a 195-pound defender being blocked by a 250-pound tight end, and he is the man who is supposed to turn the run back inside. If the defense sends a linebacker or safety instead, it has one fewer player near the ball. Either way the offense has made the defense pay for its answer, the same bind as the two-tight-end dilemma. Personnel gives you the first guess; the formation sharpens it, which is where the next chapters go.











TipPredict the play 2: the fullback goes wide



First-and-10 at midfield. The offense came on with a fullback (F), a tailback (R), one tight end and two receivers. The defense answered with its base 4-3. Then the offense lined up like this:


Show the Python
off = line5() + [P("QB", "QB", GUN, 0, "Q"), P("RB", "RB", GUN, -2.2, "R"), P("Y", "TE", LINE_D, TE_W),
                 P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -15), P("Z", "WR", OFF_BALL, 9.5), P("FB", "FB", OFF_BALL, 15.5, "F")]
dfn = nudge_sde(defense("4-3_over", "two_high", off))
fix = {"SAM": dict(d=4.5, w=9.0), "RCB": dict(d=6.0, w=15.5), "LCB": dict(d=6.5), "SDE": dict(d=1.4),
       "SS": dict(d=11.0, w=9.5), "FS": dict(d=12.0, w=-7.0), "MIKE": dict(d=4.5, w=1.2),
       "WILL": dict(d=4.5, w=-2.6)}
dfn = [q2.moved(**fix[q2.key]) if q2.key in fix else q2 for q2 in dfn]
q = Play(off, dfn, los=60, to_go=10)
ring_by_body(q)
q.draw(lateral=(-19, 19), window=(-7.5, 14), title=False)
hide_yard_numbers(plt.gca())
plt.show()








Figure 9.12: Drill 2: the fullback (F, aqua ring) has split out wide on the right, outside receiver Z. The defense is in its base 4-3: E = end, T = tackle, S/M/W = linebackers, C = cornerback, FS/SS = safeties. Gold ring = tight end.





What’s the personnel? Who has the advantage now, and what is the offense hoping for?






TipAnswer





Still 21 personnel, even with the fullback out wide.
Who has the advantage: the offense. Look where the defense’s players have had to go. A cornerback went out with the fullback, so the Sam linebacker (S) has had to walk out over the slot receiver (Z): a bigger, slower player than a nickel back, now covering a receiver. If the defense swaps those two (corner on Z, linebacker on the fullback), it has a linebacker 15 yards from the ball instead. Either way, a linebacker has left the area near the ball.
What the offense is hoping for: whichever of two good options the defense leaves. With a linebacker on Z, a quick throw to Z. With that linebacker gone from the middle, a run: there are only six defenders near the line (four linemen and the two remaining linebackers) against six blockers (five linemen and the tight end), a fair fight for the tailback.
The defense has one more answer: the strong safety walks down over Z, so the Sam linebacker can stay in the box. That keeps the Sam near the ball for the run but leaves only one safety deep, which is exactly the picture the offense’s play-action is built to beat. Every answer costs something. This is the 49ers’ 21-personnel idea in one picture: the defense answered who, and the offense answered where.











TipPredict the play 3: third-and-7



Third-and-7 at the opponent’s 45. On first and second down the offense ran twice from 12 personnel (two tight ends), and the defense matched with its base 4-3 both times. Second down ends, and fourteen seconds later the ball is snapped from this picture:


Show the Python
off = line5() + [P("QB", "QB", GUN, 0, "Q"), P("RB", "RB", GUN, -2.2, "R"), P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -15),
                 P("Y", "TE", OFF_BALL, 5.6), P("U", "TE", OFF_BALL, 9.8), P("Z", "WR", LINE_D, 15)]
dfn = defense("4-3_over", "two_high", off)
fix = {"SAM": dict(d=4.5, w=7.6), "MIKE": dict(d=5.0, w=2.0), "WILL": dict(d=4.8, w=-3.4),
       "SS": dict(d=10.0, w=10.0), "FS": dict(d=13.0, w=-2.0), "LCB": dict(d=6.5), "RCB": dict(d=6.5)}
dfn = [q2.moved(**fix[q2.key]) if q2.key in fix else q2 for q2 in dfn]
q = Play(off, dfn, los=65, to_go=7)
ring_by_body(q)
q.draw(lateral=(-19, 19), window=(-7.5, 15), title=False)
hide_yard_numbers(plt.gca())
plt.show()








Figure 9.13: Drill 3: third-and-7, fourteen seconds after the last whistle. Gold rings = tight ends; S, M and W are linebackers; E = end, T = tackle, C = cornerback, FS/SS = safeties.





Count both teams’ personnel. What’s wrong for the defense, why didn’t it fix it, and what does the offense probably want?






TipAnswer





What’s wrong: nothing changed. The offense is still in 12 personnel (two gold rings), and the defense is still in base, with three linebackers, on third-and-7, a passing down. Fourteen seconds is a no-huddle snap: the offense didn’t substitute.
Why the defense didn’t fix it: it couldn’t, safely. With no offensive substitution the umpire had no reason to stand over the ball. A defense that starts running a linebacker off and a defensive back on while the offense is set risks twelve men on the field at the snap, five yards on third-and-7.
What the offense wants: a pass, probably to a tight end. The offense spent two plays teaching the defense that this grouping runs, which kept it in base. Now both tight ends stand off the line, split out beside Z, and linebackers have to cover them away from the ball.
If the defense saw this coming, its answer was the situational substitution from earlier in the chapter: send its third-down package on at the whistle, before the offense hurried to the line, and live with the risk of a run against a lighter defense.

title: Personnel: Who’s on the Field Before Anything Else
text:
Takeaways

Personnel is two digits: running backs, then tight ends. Receivers fill the rest of the five changeable spots (5 − backs − tight ends), or four of them in jumbo, where a sixth lineman takes one.
Personnel counts who is on the field, not where they stand, and the gap between personnel and formation is where offenses build mismatches. Hybrid players blur the count on purpose.
The offense commits first, and the defense matches in direction (more receivers, more defensive backs; more tight ends and backs, more linebackers) down to a floor of four defensive backs. The rules give it time whenever the offense substitutes, and none when it doesn’t.
Personnel shifts the odds more than it settles them. On ordinary first and second downs it barely improves a down-and-distance guess; its weight shows in heavy groupings and short yardage, in the formation it predicts, and in the matchups it sets up.
The league’s mix moves with the defense. 11 personnel rose through the early 2010s, held near 60% for a decade, then fell to a decade low in 2025 as offenses went bigger against lighter defenses, and defenses answered with more base.

title: Formation Rules and the Language of Alignment
text:
Seven on the line: the rule underneath every formation
First-and-10, ball on the left hash. In the seconds before the snap, three small things happen that the broadcast barely notices. Out wide on the left, a receiver glances at the official on the sideline, points at his own chest and gets a nod back. On the right, the tight end settles next to the tackle, and a linebacker immediately points at him and shouts “Strong right! Strong right!” And the quarterback stops four yards behind the center, not five, with the running back directly behind him. Each detail answers to something different: the first to the rulebook, the second to the defense’s own language, the third to the offense’s plan. All three are clues. By the end of this chapter you’ll know what the receiver was asking (am I on the line?), what the linebacker was shouting about (the formation’s strong side), and why four yards instead of five changes what the offense is likely to do.
You’ll be able to…
Personnel told you who is on the field. This chapter is about where they stand: the rules every alignment must obey, and the vocabulary coaches use to name it. The next two chapters use both to build actual formations (Classic Formations and Spread Formations).
You met the core of it in The Twenty-Two: at least seven offensive players on the line of scrimmage at the snap; only the two ends of the line and the backs are eligible receivers (the quarterback under center excepted); everyone else is an ineligible receiver. This chapter asks the questions underneath that rule. What does “on the line” mean, to the inch? What happens when a formation breaks the rule? And why would a coach ever want one of his own receivers to be ineligible?

title: Formation Rules and the Language of Alignment
text:
On the line, off the line, and the gap in between
Every offensive player at the snap is in exactly one of two places, and the rulebook defines both.1

On the line means roughly level with the center. The rule’s test is the helmet: a player is on the line if he faces the defense with his shoulders square and his helmet breaks an imaginary vertical wall, parallel to the line, that passes through the center’s waist. Linemen crouch right up against the ball, so they’re obviously on it. A wide receiver thirty yards away has to stand on it, which is harder to judge.
Off the line means in the backfield, at least one yard behind the line of scrimmage. For the offense, the line effectively starts at the back tip of the ball: the ball’s own length, the neutral zone, belongs to neither team, and no offensive player may have any part of his body in it. Every back is off the line: the running back, the fullback, a receiver standing a yard deep, a tight end set as a wing. The single exception is the quarterback under center, who has to be closer than a yard to take the ball from the center’s hands.



Show the Python
S = 2.6   # depth stretch for legibility
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 3.1))
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.axis("off")
x0, x1, y0, y1 = -2.0, 13.8, -4.9, 1.9
WAIST, BACK = -0.55 * S, -1.0 * S
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x0, y0), x1 - x0, y1 - y0, fc=style.TURF, ec=style.BASELINE, lw=0.8, zorder=0))
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x0, WAIST), x1 - x0, -WAIST, fc=ELIG, alpha=0.14, ec="none", zorder=1))
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x0, BACK), x1 - x0, WAIST - BACK, fc=FOUL, alpha=0.13, ec="none", zorder=1))
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x0, y0), x1 - x0, BACK - y0, fc=style.OFFENSE, alpha=0.06, ec="none", zorder=1))
ax.plot([x0, x1], [0, 0], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=1.5, zorder=2)
for yy in (WAIST, BACK):
    ax.plot([x0, x1], [yy, yy], color=style.INK_2, lw=0.8, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=2)
ax.add_patch(Ellipse((0, 0.42), 0.34, 0.84, fc=style.BALL, ec="white", lw=0.6, zorder=9))


def man(x, y, lab, ring=None, rad=0.42):
    ax.add_patch(Circle((x, y), rad, fc=style.OFFENSE, ec="white", lw=0.8, zorder=8))
    if ring:
        ax.add_patch(Circle((x, y), rad * 1.5, fc="none", ec=ring, lw=1.8, zorder=7))
    ax.text(x, y, lab, ha="center", va="center", color="white", fontsize=6.5, fontweight="bold", zorder=9)


for x, lab in [(0, "C"), (1.6, ""), (3.2, ""), (4.8, "Y")]:
    man(x, -0.72, lab)
man(12.6, -0.72, "X", ring=ELIG)
man(9.4, -2.0, "Z", ring=FOUL)
man(7.6, -3.75, "H", ring=ELIG)
man(0, -3.1, "Q")
kw = dict(fontsize=7, va="center", ha="left", zorder=10)
ax.text(x1 + 0.3, 0.0, "the offense's line (the\nback tip of the ball)", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, **kw)
ax.text(x1 + 0.3, WAIST, "the center's waist", color=style.INK_2, **kw)
ax.text(x1 + 0.3, BACK, "1 yard behind the line", color=style.INK_2, **kw)
ax.text(x1 + 0.3, -3.9, "the backfield", color=style.INK_2, **kw)
ax.text(6.4, 1.25, "ON THE LINE: up level with the center", fontsize=7.2, ha="center", color=style.INK,
        fontweight="bold", zorder=10)
ax.text(8.6, -2.0, "NEITHER ON NOR OFF:\nillegal formation", fontsize=6.6, ha="right", va="center", color=FOUL,
        fontweight="bold", zorder=10)
ax.text(8.3, -3.75, "OFF THE LINE: a back,\nat least a yard deep", fontsize=6.8, ha="left", va="center",
        color=style.INK, fontweight="bold", zorder=10)
ax.text(0.65, -3.1, "QB under center: the\none back allowed closer", fontsize=6.3, ha="left", va="center",
        color=style.INK_2, zorder=10)
ax.set_xlim(x0 - 0.1, x1 + 5.6)
ax.set_ylim(y0 - 0.1, y1 + 0.1)
plt.show()








Figure 10.1: On the line, off it, and the illegal strip in between (a close-up of the right half of a formation; depths are stretched so the thin bands show). A player whose helmet reaches the center’s waistline is on the line (green band): here the center (C), the guard, the tackle, the tight end (Y) and the receiver (X). A player at least a yard behind the line is a back (blue band), like H. Z is in neither band: too far back to be on the line and too close to be a back, which is an illegal formation. Aqua rings mark eligible receivers; the red ring marks the problem. (Y has no ring: X is on the line outside him, so Y is ‘covered’, which the next section explains.)





The strip between those two zones is no-man’s land. A player standing half a yard behind the line is neither on it nor in the backfield, and the formation is illegal. On a crowded line nobody gets stuck there by accident. But a receiver thirty yards from the ball, looking in at a center he can barely see, can easily end up half a step off. That’s what the receiver in the opening scene was doing: asking the official on his side of the field, by pointing at himself, whether he was on or off. The wing officials (the line judge and the down judge, one on each sideline) watch the receivers on their side for exactly this, and receivers routinely check with them before the snap. The official usually answers with a word or a wave, but he doesn’t have to: he may be busy counting the offense, and the alignment is the receiver’s responsibility.2
Can you see it from your couch? Sometimes. The standard broadcast camera sits high on the sideline, so compare the receiver’s helmet with the helmets of the linemen nearest him: level means on, a visible step back means off. On a replay from the end-zone camera it’s obvious. But you rarely need to judge it by eye, because the count does the work: find the tight end, and the rule tells you which receiver has to be on the line, as the next sections show.






NoteMadden vs. real life



In Madden you can’t line up illegally. You pick a formation from a menu, and the game puts every player on a legal spot. Real formations are built by eleven people walking to marks they memorised, with the play clock running, a crowd screaming and a receiver who can’t hear the quarterback. Every snap, the officials check the count and the depths, and the defense checks them too, because the alignment tells it who can catch the ball. A one-yard mistake is a flag, and a one-yard choice is a clue.


Why seven? The rule is older than the forward pass as we know it. In the early 1900s, college football’s signature plays were “mass” plays: wedges and pile-drives in which most of the offense lined up behind the ball and crashed into one spot with a running start. Players were being badly hurt and killed, and in 1905 the sport came close to being banned. The rule makers spent the next few years reshaping the game, and by 1910 they required seven men on the line of scrimmage, so that most of the offense had to start from a standstill on the line instead of building momentum behind it.3 The seven-man line was a safety rule. Its modern job is different: it guarantees that the offense always has five big, ineligible blockers in the middle, and it forces the offense to declare its receivers by where they stand.
None of this binds the defense. On a scrimmage play it may line up anyone anywhere on its own side of the neutral zone, in any number, and move around before the snap; its only alignment rule is to stay out of the neutral zone.4 That asymmetry runs through the whole book: the offense has to show its hand by rule, and the defense gets to disguise.


Illegal formation
When an alignment breaks those rules, the officials throw a flag for illegal formation: a five-yard penalty on the offense for lining up wrongly at the snap. The common versions are the ones in the next picture: fewer than seven players on the line, or a player stuck in no-man’s land.


Show the Python
titles = {"legal": "1.  Legal: seven on the line",
          "six": "2.  Illegal formation: only six on the line",
          "covered": "3.  Legal, but the tight end is covered"}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(6.6, 6.3))
for ax, case in zip(axes, ["legal", "six", "covered"]):
    moves = {"six": {"X": dict(d=OFF_D)}, "covered": {"Z": dict(d=LINE_D)}}.get(case, {})
    p = Play(pro_11(**moves), None, los=40, to_go=None)
    for k in {"legal": ["X", "H", "Y", "Z", "RB"], "six": [], "covered": ["X", "H", "Z", "RB"]}[case]:
        p.highlight(k, color=ELIG)
    if case == "six":
        p.highlight("X", color=FOUL)
    if case == "covered":
        p.highlight("Y", color=FOUL)
    fld = p.draw(ax=ax, lateral=(-20.5, 20.5), window=(-8.7, 3.7), title=False)
    hide_yard_numbers(ax)
    depth_guide(fld, p, -19.0, 19.0, label_w=9.4)
    count_line(fld, p, on_line(p))
    ax.set_title(titles[case], loc="left", fontsize=9, color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
    if case == "legal":
        say(fld, p, -5.0, -15.0, "X: the left end, eligible", fs=6.8)
        say(fld, p, -5.2, 15.0, "Y is the right end; Z,\na yard back, is a back", fs=6.8)
        say(fld, p, -5.6, 2.2, "Q under center:\nnot eligible", fs=6.6, ha="left")
    if case == "six":
        say(fld, p, -5.4, -15.0, "X stepped back:\nnow he's a back too", fs=6.8, color=FOUL)
        say(fld, p, -5.4, 13.0, "five men in the backfield:\nillegal formation, 5 yards", fs=6.8)
    if case == "covered":
        say(fld, p, -4.4, 15.0, "Z stepped up: now he\nis the right end", fs=6.8)
        say(fld, p, -6.8, 8.0, "Y: on the line but not\nat the end, so ineligible", fs=6.8, color=FOUL)
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 10.2: Three versions of the same 11-personnel formation (X, H, Z = wide receivers, Y = tight end, R = running back, Q = quarterback under center; the linemen are unlettered apart from the center, C). Players behind the dashed line are a yard off the line (depths stretched so you can see it). The small numbers count the players on the line; aqua rings mark the eligible receivers, red rings the problem. 1: legal. 2: X has stepped back a yard: six on the line, illegal formation. 3: Z has stepped up instead: eight on the line is legal, but Y is now covered.





Notice what panel 3 says about the word “illegal.” Covering your own tight end is not an illegal formation. Eight on the line is fine; the rule says at least seven. The formation is legal, but the tight end can’t catch a forward pass on that play. If the ball is thrown to him anyway, that’s a different foul, an ineligible player touching a pass, and the penalties are in Contact Rules and Penalties.






CautionCommon misconception



“An unusual-looking formation must be illegal.” Almost never. Eight men on the line is legal. Two receivers stacked one behind the other is legal. Two tackles side by side on one side of the center is legal (that’s an unbalanced line, the subject of Spread Formations). A lineman standing at the end of the line and catching a pass is legal, if he reported (below). The legality test is short: seven or more on the line, nobody in no-man’s land, no more than one man moving at the snap (the motion rules from The Pre-Snap Phase), and the right people eligible. Weird is allowed. That’s why offenses get away with so much.

title: Formation Rules and the Language of Alignment
section: Covered receivers, and why X stands on the line
text:
Covered receivers, and why X stands on the line
A covered receiver is a player who is on the line of scrimmage but not at either end of it, because a teammate is also on the line outside him. He’s ineligible on that play, whatever his jersey number and whatever his position. In panel 3 above, the tight end was covered by the Z receiver.
Here’s the elegant part. The covered-receiver rule explains the most basic habit in receiver alignment, one you saw in The Twenty-Two without a reason: the X receiver lines up on the line, and the Z receiver lines up a yard off it.
Look again at panel 1. The formation has a tight end attached to the right side of the line. If the receiver on that side also stood on the line, he would cover the tight end, and the offense’s most versatile player would be a blocker only. So the receiver on the tight end’s side (Z) stands a yard back. That keeps Y as the right end and eligible, and as a bonus it makes Z a back, which means Z is the one who can go in motion (only an off-the-line player may move at the snap). On the other side there’s no tight end, so somebody has to be the left end, and someone has to be the seventh man on the line. That’s X’s job: he stands on the line so the formation has seven and an end on that side. The letters didn’t come first. The rule did, and the letters name the jobs it creates.
The same logic places the slot receiver (H in panel 1). If H stood on the line inside X, X would cover him. So the general rule is: on each side, only the outermost man on the line can catch a pass, and anyone inside him who wants to run a route has to stand a yard back. That’s why slot receivers, wings and backs are all “off the ball”.






ImportantWhy it exists: covering on purpose



Why would an offense choose to cover one of its own eligible receivers, as in panel 3? Three common reasons.

To free someone else to move. Only a back may be in motion at the snap. Putting one receiver on the line (and covering the tight end) can let a different receiver line up a yard back and go in motion.
To build a formation the defense hasn’t seen. A tight end who is covered is a sixth blocker. On a pass play he may not go more than a yard past the line before the ball is thrown (that would be an ineligible man downfield, the same rule that holds every lineman back).5 So he can’t really run a route, and if the defense doesn’t notice, it wastes a defender covering him.
To change who the defense must account for. Every eligible receiver needs a defender. Making one ineligible, and making another eligible, changes the count.

The cost is the obvious one: a covered player can’t catch the ball, and an alert defense that spots it can treat him as a blocker. Covering is a deliberate trade of one threat for another.
