title: Zone Running: Inside Zone, Outside Zone, Split Zone, and the Cutback
text:
Tags: insert, arc and bash
Zone teams rarely change the line’s rules. Instead they add a tag, a word added to the play call that changes one or two players’ jobs (you met tags in 01-04). Three zone tags are worth knowing, because you will see all three on Sundays.


Show the Python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.7))

# insert
off = [q for q in named_line(offense("singleback")) if q.key in (*OL_NAMES, "Y", "QB", "RB")]
off.append(Player("H", "TE", "off", -4.4, -1.8, label="H"))            # offset fullback
p = Play(off, front7(), los=35, to_go=None)
p.block("C", pts=[(1.1, 0.6)]); p.block("RG", pts=[(1.0, -0.7)])      # the double stays on the 1
p.block("RT", pts=[(0.9, 0.6)]); p.block("Y", pts=[(0.6, -0.6), (3.6, 1.5)])
p.block("LT", pts=[(0.9, 0.7)]); p.block("LG", pts=[(0.8, -0.6), (4.3, -0.8)])
go_to(p, "H", (3.7, 1.8), via=[(-2.6, 0.6), (0.3, 2.3)])                 # insert on the Mike
p.run("RB", [(3.0, 1.0), (6.0, 2.7), (10.0, 3.0)], delay=0.25)
p.highlight("H")
f = draw(p, ax=axes[0], lateral=(-7.5, 8.5), window=(-8, 6.5), title=False)
point_to(f, p, (-6.2, -4.6), (-4.4, -1.8), "H: offset\nfullback", fontsize=6.8)
point_to(f, p, (-4.2, 5.4), (0.6, 1.0), "double team\nstays on the 1", fontsize=6.8, color=ZONE_GREEN)
axes[0].set_title("Insert: H leads up on the Mike", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")

# arc
off = [q for q in named_line(offense("gun_2x2")) if q.key in (*OL_NAMES, "QB")]
off += [Player("H", "TE", "off", -1.5, -6.6, label="H"), Player("RB", "RB", "off", -5.0, -1.6, label="R")]
dfn = [q for q in front7() if q.key != "SAM"] + [D("SS", "SS", 5.0, -9.6, "SS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
p.block("C", pts=[(0.9, 0.5)]); p.block("RG", pts=[(0.8, -0.8), (4.3, -0.4)])
p.block("RT", pts=[(0.9, 0.6)])
p.block("LT", pts=[(0.9, 0.7)]); p.block("LG", pts=[(0.8, -0.6), (4.3, -0.8)])
go_to(p, "H", (4.1, -9.3), via=[(0.4, -7.6), (2.6, -9.0)])               # arc past the end to the safety
go_to(p, "RB", (1.0, 2.6), "run", via=[(-4.0, -0.4), (-1.4, 2.3)])       # give: inside zone right
p.read("BE")
p.highlight("H"); p.highlight("BE", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, ax=axes[1], lateral=(-12, 4.0), window=(-8, 6.5), title=False)
branch(f, p, [(-5.0, 0.0), (-4.4, -2.0), (-2.6, -4.4), (-0.4, -5.4), (4.0, -6.2)], label="keep",
       label_at=(5.4, -6.0), fontsize=7, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
point_to(f, p, (-3.4, 2.8), (-1.4, 2.3), "give", fontsize=7, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
point_to(f, p, (-6.6, -9.0), (1.0, -4.0), "read end:\nnot blocked", fontsize=6.8, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
axes[1].set_title("Arc: H runs past the end", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 16.11: Two zone tags, both with inside-zone blocking to the right. Left, insert: the H (here an offset fullback) leads through the play-side B gap onto the Mike, a step ahead of the running back, so the double team on the 1 never has to climb. Right, arc: on the backside, the H (an H-back off the ball on the left) runs past the unblocked end without touching him and blocks the safety outside him. The quarterback reads that end (dashed line): if the end stays home, give; if he chases the back, keep and run behind the arc block.





Insert. On insert (or “zone insert”), a fullback, H-back or tight end leads up through a gap and blocks a linebacker, usually the play-side one (some staffs insert on the backside linebacker instead). That frees the play-side double team from having to climb: it can stay on the defensive lineman longer and move him farther. In effect, insert adds a blocker at the point of attack, which is how a zone team answers a defense that keeps one more defender in the box than the offense has blockers. The cost is the usual one: the inserting player is not available as a receiver, and his alignment (an offset fullback, or a tight end off the ball) can tip the play.
The other two tags borrow an idea from option football, which gets its own chapter: instead of blocking the unblocked backside end, the quarterback reads him (watches what he does after the snap) and decides whether to hand the ball off or keep it. For now, all you need is that idea; 03-04 builds it properly.
Arc. Arc happens on the backside, away from the line’s flow. The line zones right and the back runs inside zone to the right, while on the left a tight end or H-back makes an arc block: he releases outside the unblocked backside end, runs past him without touching him, and blocks the next defender out, the linebacker or safety responsible for the alley between the end and the sideline (the alley player of Part 5). The quarterback reads the end. If the end stays home, the quarterback gives and the back runs inside zone. If the end chases the running back down the line, the quarterback keeps, runs around the end the other way, and finds the arc block already waiting for the next man. Arc is why you sometimes see a tight end run right past a defensive end without touching him: he was never supposed to.
Bash needs one more step of background. On the standard zone read (03-04 draws it), the back runs the inside-zone track and the quarterback, reading the backside end, keeps the ball around that end if the end chases the back. Defenses learned an answer: the end crashes down hard at the back, inviting the keep, while a linebacker loops around behind him to meet the quarterback where he was about to run (a scrape exchange: the end and the linebacker swap jobs).9 The defense’s plan is a bet that the back will be inside and the quarterback outside.


Show the Python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.5))
for ax, bash in [(axes[0], False), (axes[1], True)]:
    off = [q for q in named_line(offense("gun_2x2")) if q.key in (*OL_NAMES, "QB")]
    off += [Player("RB", "RB", "off", -5.0, 1.6 if bash else -1.6, label="R"),
            Player("Y", "TE", "off", -0.7, 4.8, label="Y")]
    p = Play(off, front7(), los=35, to_go=None)
    p.block("C", pts=[(0.9, 0.5)]); p.block("RG", pts=[(0.8, -0.8), (4.3, -0.4)])
    p.block("RT", pts=[(0.9, 0.6)]); p.block("Y", pts=[(0.6, -0.6), (3.6, 1.5)])
    p.block("LT", pts=[(0.9, 0.7)]); p.block("LG", pts=[(0.8, -0.6), (4.3, -0.8)])
    p.read("BE")
    p.highlight("BE", color=style.DEFENSE)
    f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-9.5, 7.0), window=(-8, 7), title=False)
    inside = [(-5.0, 0.0), (-3.6, 1.0), (-1.2, 2.3), (4.6, 2.7)]
    outside = [(-4.6, -1.0), (-3.6, -3.4), (-1.6, -6.2), (3.6, -7.6)]
    if bash:
        branch(f, p, [(-5.0, 1.6), (-4.8, 0.4)] + outside, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK,
               label="give (back)\nif the end squeezes", label_at=(-6.6, -5.6), fontsize=6.6)
        branch(f, p, inside, color=ZONE_GREEN, label="keep (QB) if the end\nwidens with the back",
               label_at=(6.2, 3.0), fontsize=6.6)
        ax.set_title("Bash: back outside, QB inside", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
    else:
        branch(f, p, [(-5.0, -1.6), (-3.8, 0.0)] + inside[2:], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK,
               label="give (back)", label_at=(6.0, 3.2), fontsize=6.6)
        branch(f, p, [(-5.0, 0.0)] + outside, color=ZONE_GREEN, label="keep (QB) if the\nend chases the back",
               label_at=(-6.6, -5.6), fontsize=6.6)
        ax.set_title("Zone read: back inside, QB outside", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK,
                     fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 16.12: The zone read and bash, both with the line zoning right and the quarterback reading the same backside end (dashed line). Left, the zone read: the back takes the inside-zone track, and the quarterback keeps around the end if the end chases the back. Right, bash: the back goes the other way, wide around the end, and the quarterback, if he keeps, runs the inside-zone track. The runners have swapped lanes, so a defense planning for ‘back inside, quarterback outside’ has it backwards.





Bash. Bash is short for “back away”: the running back runs away from the direction the line is zoning, on a wide path around the read end, while the quarterback, if he keeps, runs the inside-zone track behind the line (Figure 16.12). It flips the usual roles: the running back threatens the edge and the quarterback becomes the inside runner. The read is the same end, with the answers reversed: if he squeezes (closes down the line toward the zone flow), the quarterback hands the ball to the back going around him; if he stays wide to take the back, the quarterback keeps and runs inside him.10 Against a scrape exchange, that matters: the end who crashes down to take the inside runner has crashed onto the quarterback’s fake, and the ball is going outside him with the running back. Bash is the offense’s reply to the defense’s reply, and the full back-and-forth belongs to option football.
All three tags share one logic: keep the zone rules for the line, and change one or two players to fix the specific problem the defense is creating. Watch for the extra player (the inserting back, the arcing tight end, the back running the “wrong” way) and you will usually know which tag you are watching.

title: Zone Running: Inside Zone, Outside Zone, Split Zone, and the Cutback
text:
How defenses fight zone
Zone’s rules guarantee that every defender is accounted for. They do not guarantee that every block is won, and defenses attack the places where zone is physically hardest. Figure 16.13 shows the two most common.


Show the Python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.6))
# penetration: the 3-technique lines up on the play side this time (Sam still on the right)
dfn = [D("PE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", 1), "5"), D("PT", "DT", 1.0, technique("3", 1), "3"),
       D("BT", "DT", 1.0, technique("1", -1), "1"), D("BE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", -1), "5"),
       D("SAM", "SAM", 4.0, 6.6, "S"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 0.6, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -3.0, "W")]
off = [q for q in ace_condensed() if q.key not in ("X", "Z")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
for k, st in [("LT", (0.1, 1.3)), ("LG", (0.1, 1.3)), ("C", (0.1, 1.2)), ("U", (0.1, 1.3)), ("Y", (0.2, 0.9))]:
    p.block(k, pts=[st])
p.block("RG", pts=[(-0.1, 1.1)]); p.block("RT", pts=[(0.0, 0.9)])
go_to(p, "PT", (-2.7, 3.0), "path")                       # the play-side 3-technique penetrates
go_to(p, "RB", (-2.8, 3.4), "run", via=[(-4.4, 2.4)])
go_to(p, "QB", (-3.6, 1.8), "path", speed=3.2)
p.highlight("PT", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, ax=axes[0], lateral=(-7.5, 8.5), window=(-8, 6.5), title=False)
x, y = _P(f, p, -2.9, 3.5)
axes[0].plot([x], [y], marker="X", ms=11, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, mec="white", mew=0.8, zorder=12)
say(f, p, -2.4, 6.4, "tackle\nfor loss", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
point_to(f, p, (-5.8, 6.0), (1.0, 2.35), "3-tech knifes upfield\nbefore the reach", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK,
         fontsize=6.8)
axes[0].set_title("Penetration", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")

# cutback player: the Will plays fast into the backside A gap before the LG can climb to him
# (the quarterback is left out of this panel so the bend lane behind the line stays visible)
p = Play([q for q in off if q.key != "QB"], front7(+1), los=35, to_go=None)
for k in ("LT", "C", "RG", "RT", "U", "Y"):
    p.block(k, pts=[(0.15, 1.3)])
go_to(p, "LG", (1.4, -0.3), via=[(-0.3, -0.9)])            # steps play-side to climb: late
go_to(p, "MIKE", (3.6, 4.6), "path"); go_to(p, "SAM", (3.4, 8.0), "path")
go_to(p, "WILL", (1.0, -1.1), "path", speed=4.0)           # downhill into the backside A gap
go_to(p, "RB", (-1.9, 4.8), "run", via=[(-4.4, 2.4)])
p.highlight("WILL", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, ax=axes[1], lateral=(-7.5, 8.5), window=(-8, 6.5), title=False)
branch(f, p, [(-1.9, 4.8), (-2.1, 2.4), (-1.8, 0.2), (-0.6, -0.6), (-0.1, -0.75)], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK,
       label="bend", label_at=(-3.2, 0.6), fontsize=7)
x, y = _P(f, p, 0.25, -0.85)
axes[1].plot([x], [y], marker="X", ms=11, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, mec="white", mew=0.8, zorder=12)
point_to(f, p, (-5.0, -4.6), (1.0, -1.1), "Will plays fast into\nthe backside A gap,\nbefore the LG can climb",
         color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
axes[1].set_title("The cutback player", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 16.13: Two ways defenses kill outside zone right. Left: penetration. This time the 3-technique lines up on the play side; at the snap he knifes upfield through the B gap, before the lateral-stepping guard and tackle can get in front of him, and meets the back on his track. Right: a cutback player. Instead of flowing, the Will comes downhill into the backside A gap at the snap, faster than the left guard can climb to him, so when the back bends, the lane he expected is filled.





Penetration and movement. A defensive lineman who gets upfield at the snap, or slants hard toward the play, can beat a lateral-stepping blocker to the spot. Defenses that want to stop zone often play their linemen this way, attacking a gap instead of reading the man in front of them; how defensive linemen are taught to do either is the subject of 05-01.
The cutback player. Because outside zone’s biggest gains come from the cutback, defenses assign someone to stay home for it: usually the backside linebacker, sometimes a safety rotating down. You saw the deep safety arrive late in Figure 16.9; a defense that gets a defender there early takes away the play’s third answer.
Spill or squeeze. When a blocker comes at a defender, the defense chooses whether that defender fights inside the block to force the ball to bounce wide toward pursuit (spill) or holds the edge and squeezes the play back inside (squeeze). Against zone, either plan can work if all eleven players agree on it, which is the subject of run fits in 05-05.11
And when the defense simply puts more defenders in the box than the offense has blockers, a zone team answers with the tools you have already seen: an extra blocker (insert), a read of the unblocked man (arc, bash, the zone read), or a pass that looks like the run.

title: Zone Running: Inside Zone, Outside Zone, Split Zone, and the Cutback
section: Why wide zone and the bootleg are married
text:
Why wide zone and the bootleg are married
Outside zone’s greatest weapon is not a run at all. It is the pass that looks exactly like it.
Think about what outside zone teaches a defense. Every snap, the line steps hard to one side, the back runs at the tight end, and the linebackers learn that if they do not flow fast and hard, they lose. The backside end learns that if he does not chase, the cutback beats him. After a few of these, the defense is trained to run with the line’s first step.
The bootleg cashes that in. It is a play-action pass (a pass that begins with a fake handoff) in which the quarterback fakes outside zone one way and rolls out the other, away from where the line went, with receivers crossing the field to meet him. In the “naked” version nobody blocks for him at all; in the protected version a lineman or a back is assigned to the backside end. Both are built in 04-05; here, what matters is why they pair with zone.


Show the Python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.3))
for i, ax in enumerate(axes):
    p = Play(ace_condensed(), even_front(+1, cb_w=10.0), los=35, to_go=10)
    for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"):
        p.block(k, pts=[(0.15, 1.4)])                      # identical first steps
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (4.3, 4.4), "path"); go_to(p, "WILL", (4.3, 1.2), "path")
    go_to(p, "SAM", (3.8, 8.2), "path")
    if i == 0:
        go_to(p, "U", (0.4, -3.4), via=[(-0.5, -4.2)])     # cut off the end
        go_to(p, "BE", (1.0, -3.0), "path")
        go_to(p, "Y", (0.3, 5.9))
        go_to(p, "QB", (-3.6, 1.8), "path", speed=3.2)
        go_to(p, "RB", (2.5, 5.0), "run", via=[(-4.3, 2.6), (-1.3, 4.9)])
        p.route("X", [(0, 0), (9, 0)]); go_to(p, "Z", (4.0, 9.8))
        p.highlight("RB")
        f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-13, 12), window=(-9, 17.5), title=False)
        ax.set_title("Outside zone right", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
    else:
        go_to(p, "BE", (-2.2, 2.6), "path", via=[(0.4, -3.6), (-1.75, -2.6), (-2.0, 0.0)])  # chases the fake
        go_to(p, "QB", (-3.4, 1.6), "path", speed=3.2)                  # the same fake ...
        go_to(p, "QB", (-6.0, -7.5), "path", speed=4.5, delay=0.1)      # ... then roll the other way
        go_to(p, "RB", (1.0, 5.6), "path", via=[(-4.3, 2.6), (-1.3, 4.9)])
        p.route("U", [(0, 0), (1.5, 1.0), (4.5, 7.5)], delay=0.6)       # flat, boot side
        p.route("Y", [(0, 0), (1.2, -1.0), (4.5, -4.0), (7.0, -8.0), (7.5, -12.5)])  # inside the 5, then across
        p.route("X", [(0, 0), (14, 0.5)])                               # clear out
        p.route("Z", [(0, 0), (10, -1.0), (15, -10), (16, -17)])         # deep over, all the way across
        p.highlight("QB")
        f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-13, 12), window=(-9, 17.5), title=False)
        say(f, p, 2.4, -10.6, "flat", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
        say(f, p, 8.6, -5.0, "cross", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
        say(f, p, 16.2, -3.0, "over", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
        point_to(f, p, (-7.6, 6.0), (-1.9, 0.6), "end chases\nthe fake", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
        ax.set_title("Naked boot left, same first second", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK,
                     fontweight="bold")
    if i == 0:
        say(f, p, -6.8, -7.6, "first steps and linebacker\nflow: the same in both", color=style.MUTED, fontsize=6.6)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.5)
plt.show()








Figure 16.14: The same first second. Left: outside zone right; the U cuts off the backside end. Right: a naked bootleg left off the same look. The line’s first steps, the back’s track and the linebackers’ flow are identical (grey note). What differs: on the boot, nobody blocks the backside end; if he chases the fake down the line onto the back’s track, he ends up behind a quarterback rolling away from him, who has three receivers at three depths on the boot side: the U in the flat, the Y on a crossing route (releasing inside the play-side end) and the Z on a deep over route.





The two plays look identical for the first second, which is the second that decides how the defense moves. (The “over” route is a deep crossing route: the receiver runs across the field 15 or more yards downfield, over the linebackers.) On a bootleg the backside end’s job is to contain the quarterback: stay outside him and force him back toward the pursuit. An end who chased the run fake (as outside zone has taught him to) is now behind a quarterback rolling away from him, and nobody is there to make the quarterback hurry. The linebackers who flowed with the line are a step or two the wrong way, and the crossing routes (receivers running across the field) come open behind them. The boot gives the quarterback three receivers at three depths on the same side: a short one in the flat, one crossing at linebacker depth, and one deep. That simple read is what makes the play so reliable.
Why the pair works. Each play protects the other. If the defense sits back and refuses to flow, outside zone gets the edge or the crease. If it flows hard, the bootleg punishes the flow. And because the two share the same first step, the defense cannot wait to find out which one it is facing. This is the backbone of the Shanahan-family offenses you will meet in 12-03: a run game and a play-action game built to be indistinguishable for as long as possible.
How to tell them apart after the snap. Three plays send a tight end or H-back at the backside end, and before the snap they can look the same. Watch what he does when he gets there:

He hits the end and drives him out: split zone.
He runs past the end without touching him and blocks the next man out (a linebacker or safety), while the quarterback rides the ball with the back and watches the end: arc.
He runs past the end into the flat and turns to look for the ball, while the quarterback pulls the ball and rolls the other way: bootleg.

The cost. A naked bootleg leaves the quarterback with nobody blocking the backside end. If that end does not bite on the fake (if he stays home), he is waiting for a quarterback who has turned his back to him. That is why the bootleg works only once outside zone has earned the defense’s respect.

title: Zone Running: Inside Zone, Outside Zone, Split Zone, and the Cutback
text:
Where zone came from
Running backs reading blocks is as old as football. Vince Lombardi’s Green Bay Packers of the 1960s ran their famous power sweep with a simple instruction to the ball carrier: run to daylight, wherever the blocks open it, a phrase that became the title of a 1963 book Lombardi wrote with W. C. Heinz.12 That sweep was a gap play with pulling guards, not a zone play, but its runner’s freedom to choose the hole is the same idea zone backs live by.
Who invented zone blocking is disputed, and nobody serious claims a single inventor. The best-documented claims put it in the NFL of the 1980s. Jim McNally, the Cincinnati Bengals’ offensive line coach, was one of the era’s most copied line coaches, and Cincinnati’s run game finished in the league’s top five every year from 1986 to 1990. McNally himself said, “I didn’t invent zone blocking, but we and the Cleveland Browns did it back in the ’80s,” and he described it as an answer to the rise of the 3-4 defense and its penetrating linemen. Cleveland’s line coach in those years was Howard Mudd, the same coach who later made the stretch a Colts signature.13 Coaches who credit older roots point to blocking ideas in earlier college offenses; treat any one-name “inventor” story with suspicion.
What is not in dispute is who made outside zone the identity of an NFL offense. Alex Gibbs, an offensive line coach with a famously blunt teaching style and a reputation as one of the best line coaches of his era, built the Denver Broncos’ running game under head coach Mike Shanahan from 1995.14 Denver had a specific problem to solve. Pittsburgh defensive coordinator Dom Capers had popularized the zone blitz, in which a linebacker blitzes and a lineman drops into coverage in his place, so the defenders a man-blocking line had assigned itself kept changing. “When you’re in a man scheme, you’re getting picked off and you look bad,” Gary Kubiak, then Denver’s offensive coordinator, later remembered.15 (In blocking, “picked off” means a blocker’s path is cut off by a defender he was not assigned, so his own man runs free: exactly the left side of Figure 16.2.) Blocking by area meant that whoever came was blocked.
Gibbs’s system was close to a religion: a small number of runs, repeated until the linemen could execute them against any front; light, quick linemen who could reach and run; backside cut blocks; and backs taught to press the aiming point and make one cut. His clinic tapes on zone running circulated widely among coaches and are still sold as coaching videos, and many of the phrases in this chapter descend from his teaching.16
Denver’s results became the advertisement. The Broncos won back-to-back Super Bowls after the 1997 and 1998 seasons, and running back Terrell Davis, a sixth-round draft pick, ran for 2,008 yards in 1998 and was named the league’s MVP.17 When injuries ended Davis’s peak, Denver kept producing 1,000-yard rushers with a string of other backs, several of them mid- or late-round picks, which convinced the league that the scheme was doing much of the work.18
The system spread through a coaching tree. Gary Kubiak carried it to Houston as head coach and back to Denver, where he won Super Bowl 50 after the 2015 season. Kyle Shanahan, Mike’s son, coached under Kubiak in Houston and under his father in Washington, then became the 49ers’ head coach in 2017. From Kyle Shanahan’s staffs came Sean McVay (Rams), Matt LaFleur (Packers) and others, and Kubiak’s son Klint called plays for the 2025 Seattle Seahawks before becoming the Raiders’ head coach for 2026.19 By late in the 2019 season, ESPN’s charting found zone blocking in use by all 32 teams and on at least half of the runs of most of them; LaFleur’s Packers led the league at 70.3% of runs (same ESPN study). The tree and its offense get a full case study in 12-03.






NoteFilm room: Denver Broncos, Super Bowl XXXII (1997 season)



The game: Super Bowl XXXII, January 25, 1998: Denver 31, Green Bay 24. Terrell Davis carried 30 times for 157 yards and three touchdowns and was named MVP, despite a migraine that blurred his vision and kept him out of part of the second quarter.20 Coaches’ film from the 1990s is hard to find, but Super Bowl broadcasts are the easiest games of the era to track down, and this one is dominated by Gibbs’s zone running (Denver mixed in other runs and play-action too).
What to notice:

The line’s first step. Every lineman moves laterally together; you will seldom see a Denver guard pull.
Davis’s patience. He runs at the tight end’s outside leg for two or three steps and does not cut until the end commits. Then he cuts once, hard, and is going north.
The backside. Watch the defensive linemen away from the play. Many end up on the ground in the first second: that is the backside cut, and it is why Davis’s cutbacks so often had nobody in them.
The bootleg. John Elway faking the stretch and rolling away is the other half of the same system.









NoteFilm room: San Francisco 49ers 2019



The game: the NFC Championship Game after the 2019 season, 49ers vs. Green Bay Packers, January 19, 2020. San Francisco won 37–20 and threw the ball only eight times; running back Raheem Mostert, a former undrafted free agent, ran for 220 yards and four touchdowns.21
What to notice:

How often the 49ers ran the wide-zone family, and how little they disguised it. They were not a pure zone team (the same ESPN charting had them using zone on 55% of their runs that season), so gap runs and tosses came off the same formations. Make it a drill: classify each run with this chapter’s Watch-for-it checklist (does the whole line step together, or does a guard pull?).
The linebackers. As the game goes on, watch them flow harder and harder to the play-side, and watch the cutbacks and the inside creases that opens.
Mostert’s runs: many of his biggest gains come on one cut, at full speed, into a crease that appeared only after the defense flowed.









NoteFilm room: Seattle Seahawks, Super Bowl LX (2025 season)



The game: Super Bowl LX, February 8, 2026: Seattle 29, New England 13, the end of Klint Kubiak’s single season as Seattle’s offensive coordinator (he became the Raiders’ head coach for 2026, so this is one season’s offense, not Seattle’s current one). Running back Kenneth Walker III carried 27 times for 135 yards and was named MVP.22 Kubiak’s offense descends directly from the Gibbs-Shanahan-Kubiak tree, built on outside zone from tight, two-tight-end formations and the bootlegs that pair with it.23
What to do: watch Walker’s 27 carries with this chapter’s checklist. For each one, call it zone or gap (does the whole line step together?), inside or outside (up or across?), and bang, bend or bounce. Then count the bootlegs and play-action passes that started with the same first step. It is the 2019 49ers’ film, a quarter-century after Denver.


One more modern example worth finding: Christian McCaffrey’s 2023 season in San Francisco, when he led the NFL with 1,459 rushing yards and was named Offensive Player of the Year.24 He is not a pure one-cut back (he will press, hop sideways and cut again), which makes him a good contrast with Davis and Mostert: watch how he uses the same aiming points with a different running style.

title: Zone Running: Inside Zone, Outside Zone, Split Zone, and the Cutback
section: Does it work? Reading the numbers
text:
Does it work? Reading the numbers
You might expect a data source to tell us how well zone runs work. It cannot, directly, and the reason is worth understanding before looking at any chart.
The NFL’s play-by-play data (which nflverse packages for free) records where a run went, not what play was called. Each run gets a run location (left, middle or right) and, unless it went up the middle, a run gap (guard, tackle or end). These are charted by the league’s scorers from where the ball carrier crossed the line, and they are coarser than the gap letters of 03-01: roughly, “middle” is between the guards (the A gaps), “guard” is over or just outside a guard (the B gap), “tackle” is over or just outside a tackle (the C gap), and “end” is outside the last man on the line. There is no “zone” flag. So a zone run that cuts back is logged where the back ended up, not where the play was aimed. (Commercial charting services such as PFF, Pro Football Focus, do label run concepts by watching film. In the sample of their labels released with the 2025 Big Data Bowl (2022 season), outside zone was the single most common run concept.25 That is the most recent public count we know of; no league-wide zone share for 2025 has been published that we could check.)
So to study zone we need a proxy: a team we know runs a lot of zone. We use Kyle Shanahan’s 49ers. LaFleur’s Packers ran an even higher share of zone in ESPN’s 2019 count, and would also do; the 49ers are the root of the coaching tree and the subject of the 12-03 case study, and Shanahan was their head coach for every season in the chart. (The Packers’ number appears below too.)
One more thing before the chart: expect negative numbers. Across the league, the average running-back carry loses a little expected value, because a typical run gains less than the down and distance needs to keep the offense’s scoring chances where they were. So “good” on this chart means “less negative than the league,” and a run game is judged by how far above the league line it sits, not by whether it clears zero.
With those caveats, here is the 49ers’ efficiency by run location against the league average from 2019 to 2025. The measures are EPA per rush (how much each run changed the offense’s expected points, on average; above zero is good for the offense) and success rate (the share of runs with positive EPA). Only running back and fullback carries count, so quarterback runs and receivers’ jet sweeps and end-arounds, which are not zone runs, stay out.


Show the Python
from gridiron.data import pbp, nfl

style.apply()
SEASONS = list(range(2019, 2026))
cols = ["season", "season_type", "posteam", "play_type", "run_location", "run_gap", "epa",
        "success", "qb_scramble", "qb_kneel", "down", "rusher_player_id"]
plays = pbp(SEASONS, columns=cols)
rosters = nfl().load_rosters(SEASONS).to_pandas()
back_ids = set(rosters.loc[rosters["position"].isin(["RB", "FB"]), "gsis_id"].dropna())

runs = plays[(plays["season_type"] == "REG") & (plays["play_type"] == "run")
             & (plays["qb_scramble"] == 0) & (plays["qb_kneel"] == 0)
             & plays["epa"].notna() & plays["down"].notna() & plays["run_location"].notna()
             & plays["rusher_player_id"].isin(back_ids)].copy()
runs["lane"] = np.where(runs["run_location"] == "middle", "Middle", runs["run_gap"].str.title())
runs = runs[runs["lane"].isin(["Middle", "Guard", "Tackle", "End"])]
LANES = ["Middle", "Guard", "Tackle", "End"]

def by_lane(df):
    return df.groupby("lane").agg(n=("epa", "size"), epa=("epa", "mean"),
                                  sr=("success", "mean")).reindex(LANES)

lg, sf = by_lane(runs), by_lane(runs[runs["posteam"] == "SF"])
gap = sf["epa"] - lg["epa"]
team = runs.groupby("posteam")["epa"].mean().sort_values(ascending=False)
sf_rank = list(team.index).index("SF") + 1
gb_rank, gb_all = list(team.index).index("GB") + 1, team["GB"]
n_pos = int((team > 0).sum())
lg_all, sf_all = runs["epa"].mean(), runs.loc[runs["posteam"] == "SF", "epa"].mean()
ordinal = lambda n: f"{n}{'th' if 10 <= n % 100 <= 20 else {1: 'st', 2: 'nd', 3: 'rd'}.get(n % 10, 'th')}"
pct = lambda v: f"{100 * v:.0f}%"

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.3))
x = np.arange(len(LANES))
for ax, col, ttl, fmt in [(axes[0], "epa", "EPA per rush", "{:+.2f}"),
                          (axes[1], "sr", "Success rate (axis from 30%)", "{:.0%}")]:
    for frame, name, color in [(sf, "49ers", style.SERIES[0]), (lg, "League", style.SERIES[1])]:
        ax.plot(x, frame[col], color=color, lw=2, marker="o", ms=7, mec=style.SURFACE, mew=1.5,
                label=name, zorder=3)
        ax.annotate(f"{name} {fmt.format(frame[col].iloc[-1])}", (x[-1], frame[col].iloc[-1]),
                    xytext=(7, 0), textcoords="offset points", va="center", fontsize=7.5, color=style.INK_2)
    if col == "epa":
        ax.axhline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=1, zorder=1)
    else:
        ax.set_ylim(0.30, 0.48)
    ax.set_xticks(x, [f"{l}\n{lg.loc[l, 'n'] / 1000:.1f}k" for l in LANES], fontsize=7.5)
    ax.set_xlim(-0.3, 4.1)
    ax.set_title(ttl, fontsize=10)
    ax.tick_params(axis="y", labelsize=7.5)
    ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
axes[1].yaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}"))
axes[0].legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=7.5)
fig.supxlabel("Where the run went, from the middle out (league carries in each lane)", fontsize=8, color=style.INK_2)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 16.15: Rushing efficiency by run location, 49ers vs. the league, 2019-2025 regular seasons (running back and fullback carries only; runs pooled across left and right). Nearly every value is below zero: the average carry loses a little expected value. Runs to the end look best for everyone, partly by selection (explained below). The 49ers beat the league average in every lane, by small margins. Note the success-rate axis starts at 30%, so its gaps look bigger than they are. Data: nflverse play-by-play and rosters via nflreadpy.





Four things to read from Figure 16.15.
Runs that reach the end are the least bad, for everyone. League-wide, running back carries logged at the end averaged -0.022 EPA per rush, against -0.083 up the middle. That does not mean “always run outside.” It means that when a run gets outside, it is usually because the edge was open, and the runs that tried to get outside and failed were often logged somewhere else (or as losses at the tackle). This is a selection effect (backs only go outside when the edge is open, so the runs that get there are the lucky ones), and it is why no coordinator reads this chart as a play-calling instruction.
The 49ers were a little better everywhere, most of all at the two ends of the chart. Their EPA edge over the league was +0.031 per carry at the end and +0.025 up the middle, against +0.015 at guard and +0.011 at tackle. That fits outside zone’s two big answers, the bounce (logged at the end) and the cutback (often logged up the middle), but the gaps are small, a few hundredths of a point per carry, and the chart cannot prove the scheme caused them.
Success rate tells a slightly different story. San Francisco’s success rate beat the league’s by 2.6 points at guard and 2.5 up the middle, but only 0.2 at tackle. Success rate rewards steady, positive gains; EPA also rewards big ones. A team can be consistent inside and explosive outside, and the two panels let you see both.
Overall, good, not magic. Across all seven seasons the 49ers’ running back carries averaged -0.043 EPA per rush against a league average of -0.064, ranking 9th of 32 teams; only one team averaged above zero. LaFleur’s Packers, the other famous zone offense of the period, averaged -0.010 and ranked 2nd. So two of the period’s best-known zone offenses landed in quite different places, both above the league average. That spread is the lesson: zone is one input to a run game, alongside the backs, the linemen, the quarterback and what the passing game makes defenses fear. Part of the 49ers’ edge is surely talent rather than scheme (McCaffrey, the 2023 Offensive Player of the Year, carried for them), and run-location data cannot separate the two; that would take play-level scheme labels and a model of player quality. Teams still run, even though the average carry loses a little expected value, because a run game does things a single carry’s EPA does not capture: it keeps the defense honest, it shortens third downs, and above all it sets up the play-action passes that look like it. You will see that argument tested with data in 13-02.






CautionCommon misconception



“Run location tells you which runs a team called.” It tells you where the ball carrier went. On zone runs especially, those are different things: an outside zone that cuts back is logged up the middle. Treat run-location splits as a picture of outcomes, and be suspicious of anyone who ranks “best run plays” from them.








TipWatch for it



On Sunday: bang, bend, bounce. You cannot watch everything in two seconds, so watch in this order.
Before the snap (you have time here)

Count the tight ends and find the running back. Two tight ends and a back directly behind the quarterback (or in the pistol) is a natural zone look. In the shotgun, an inside-zone back usually runs away from the side he lines up on, crossing the quarterback’s face. (How deep the back stands varies too much by team to be a reliable tell on its own.)
Find the backside end, the defender farthest from where you think the play is going. Remember where he is; you will check on him after the play.

The first half-second: watch the line, nothing else

Do all five linemen step the same way? Zone. Does a guard pull? Gap scheme (03-03). Double teams but no zone steps, and the back aiming straight at a linebacker? Probably duo, also in 03-03.
Are the linemen’s helmets going up (inside zone) or across (outside zone)? The high end-zone replay angle shows this best (01-06); on the live sideline angle, look for the whole line drifting toward one sideline.

Then: watch the back’s feet

Where is he aiming: the guard, or the tight end? Wider than the tight end is stretch.
Watch him press, plant and cut. Call it as it happens: bang (play-side gaps), bend (back against the flow) or bounce (outside the end).

After the play (on the replay)

Did a tight end or H-back go at the backside end? Hit him: split zone. Ran past him to the next man: arc. Slipped into the flat looking for the ball: bootleg. Did someone lead up into the line? Insert.
Where was the backside end when the back made his cut? On the ground (cut), chasing (and how close), or blocked?
If the defense has been flowing hard all game, start watching for the bootleg off the same look.

For your prediction log (01-06): before each zone run write I (inside), O (outside) or S (split) from the alignment; afterwards write which of bang, bend or bounce the back chose.

title: Zone Running: Inside Zone, Outside Zone, Split Zone, and the Cutback
text:
Predict the play






TipPredict the play



Drill 1. First-and-10 from your own 40. The offense is in the shotgun with one back and one tight end (11 personnel); the tight end is in-line on the right and the running back is offset to the quarterback’s left. The defense is in nickel with two deep safeties: six defenders in the box against six blockers. Its linemen are a 5 and a 1 on the left, and a 3 and a 7-technique (on the tight end’s inside shoulder) on the right. The offense calls inside zone. Which way is it most likely going, does the front change that, and why does the defense’s picture make a run attractive here?


Show the Python
off = named_line(offense("gun_2x2"))
off = [q.moved(d=-0.7, w=4.8) if q.key == "Y" else (q.moved(w=-2.0) if q.key == "RB" else
       (q.moved(d=-1.5) if q.key == "Z" else q)) for q in off]          # Z off the ball: 7 on the line
from gridiron import defense
DL_TECH = {"SDE": "7", "SDT": "3", "WDT": "1", "WDE": "5"}
dfn = []
for q in defense("nickel", "two_high", off):
    if q.key == "NB":
        q = q.moved(d=5.0, w=-8.5, label="NB")
    elif q.key in DL_TECH:
        q = q.moved(label=DL_TECH[q.key])
    elif q.pos == "CB":
        q = q.moved(label="CB")
    dfn.append(q)
p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=10, title="Drill 1: 1st and 10, gun, 11 personnel")
f = draw(p, lateral=(-17.5, 17.5), window=(-8, 13))
say(f, p, -6.9, -5.6, "RB offset to\nthe QB's left", fontsize=7)
plt.show()








Figure 16.16: Drill 1: gun, 11 personnel, back offset to the quarterback’s left, tight end in-line on the right; nickel defense (NB is the nickel back) with two deep safeties and six in the box. The 7 is a 7-technique, on the tight end’s inside shoulder.











NoteAnswer





Most likely to the right, toward the tight end. From the shotgun, inside zone usually has the back cross the quarterback’s face: he lines up on one side and runs to the other, which gives him a running start toward the aiming point and a downhill angle at the mesh. With the tight end on the right too, the right side is also where the offense has its extra blocker.
Does the front change it? Not the direction. Run the rules to the right: the RG is covered by the 3 and the RT by the 7, so the RG has no uncovered neighbor to help him and the 3-technique is the hardest block on the play side. That tells you where trouble is likely (a 3 who wins knocks the back off his track, and he bends), not which way the play is called. The back’s alignment is the stronger tell.
Why run here: two deep safeties and six in the box means six blockers for six defenders: “hat on a hat,” a fair fight up front, with both safeties starting 11–12 yards away. That is exactly the look zone teams want to run against, and it is a common look now: two-high shells rose from about a third of snaps in 2018 to 42% in 2025.26
The catch: good defenses know the “cross the face” tendency too, which is why offenses mix in same-side zone and the pistol. If you see a team do that a lot, that is why.











TipPredict the play



Drill 2. Outside zone to the right is called. The play-side end (on the offense’s right) is lined up wide, outside the tight end in a 9-technique, and the Sam linebacker lines up off the ball behind the right tackle. Before the snap, use the rules: who blocks the 9, who blocks the Sam, and where is the crease most likely to be? Which of bounce, bang or bend does that make the favorite?


Show the Python
dfn = even_front(+1, cb_w=10.0)
dfn = [q.moved(w=6.0, label="9") if q.key == "PE" else q for q in dfn]
dfn = [q.moved(d=4.5, w=3.4) if q.key == "SAM" else (q.moved(w=1.0) if q.key == "MIKE" else q) for q in dfn]
p = Play(ace_condensed(), dfn, los=40, to_go=10, title="Drill 2: outside zone right is called")
go_to(p, "RB", (-1.3, 4.9), "run", via=[(-4.3, 2.6)])
f = draw(p, width_in=5.4, lateral=(-12, 12), window=(-8, 12.5))
spot(f, p, -0.2, 5.3)
say(f, p, 2.9, 8.6, "end aligned\nwide (9-tech)", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
plt.show()








Figure 16.17: Drill 2: outside zone right (the back’s track to the aiming point is shown), against a play-side end aligned wide in a 9-technique.











NoteAnswer





Most likely bang, inside the end. Run the rules. The tight end is covered by a man lined up outside him, the edge case with no help: he has to block the 9 alone, and reaching him (getting the tight end’s head across his outside shoulder) is close to impossible, so his job becomes “ride him wider.” The right tackle now has nobody on him and nobody in his play-side gap: uncovered. His backside neighbor, the right guard, is uncovered too (the 1 sits in the center’s play-side gap, so the RG helps the center), so the right tackle has nobody to double and climbs straight to the Sam stacked behind him. The back’s first read is the end: he will not be pinned inside, so bounce is off. But a wide end riding wider stretches the gap inside him, so the crease is likely to appear between the tight end and the tackle, in the Sam’s gap. If the right tackle gets to the Sam, bang.
What would make it bend: that is the second read. If the Sam beats the right tackle into that gap, or the Mike scrapes hard over the top to fill it, the back’s third answer is the cutback. A wide 9-technique is a defense saying “we will not let you have the edge”; outside zone’s answer is to stop trying for it and take what the alignment gives.











TipPredict the play



Drill 3. Third time this drive: the offense lines up in the same two-tight-end set it has run outside zone right from twice already. Both times the backside end (on the offense’s left) beat the U’s cut-off by crashing hard inside him at the snap, then flattened down the line and chased the back from behind (the orange arrow shows what he did; the faint dashed line is the back’s track on those runs). It is second-and-6. What call punishes him?


Show the Python
p = Play(ace_condensed(), even_front(+1, cb_w=10.0), los=40, to_go=6,
         title="Drill 3: the same look, third time this drive")
go_to(p, "BE", (-3.0, 1.4), "path", via=[(0.3, -4.0), (-1.3, -3.9), (-2.5, -1.6)])
f = draw(p, width_in=5.4, lateral=(-12, 12), window=(-8, 12.5))
branch(f, p, [(-7.0, 0.0), (-4.3, 2.6), (-1.3, 4.9), (1.5, 5.6)], color=style.MUTED, lw=1.3, dash=(0, (2, 2.5)))
say(f, p, -3.4, -7.2, "what this end did on\nthe last two zone runs", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
plt.show()








Figure 16.18: Drill 3: the same two-tight-end look for the third time. The orange arrow shows what the backside (left) end did on the last two outside zone runs: crash inside the U at the snap, then flatten behind the line, chasing the back’s track (faint dashes).











NoteAnswer





A bootleg the other way (left), probably naked. An end who crashes hard on every outside-zone fake is the exact defender the bootleg is built to beat: the quarterback fakes outside zone right, the end chases the fake, and the quarterback rolls left behind him with the flat open and a crosser coming across. The end has been beating the U’s cut-off anyway, so the boot turns his speed into a liability: the harder he crashes, the farther behind the quarterback he ends up. Second-and-6 is a comfortable down for it, too: even a short completion in the flat keeps the offense on schedule.
A second good answer: split zone, with a tight end kicking out that end. If the end is going to crash, block him and let the back cut back behind him. Coaches choose between the two by asking whether they want to punish the end (the boot, for a potential big play) or neutralize him (split zone, for a safer run). Either way, his habit has become information, and that is how a zone offense talks to itself across a drive.











TipPredict the play



Drill 4. This one is after the snap. Shotgun, back offset to the quarterback’s left, an H-back off the ball on the left. Figure 16.19 shows the first second: everyone’s first steps and paths. Inside or outside zone? Which tag is this? What is the quarterback looking at, and what does he do if that man chases the back?


Show the Python
off = [q for q in named_line(offense("gun_2x2")) if q.key in (*OL_NAMES, "QB", "Y", "Z", "X")]
off = [q.moved(d=-0.7, w=4.8) if q.key == "Y" else (q.moved(d=-1.5) if q.key == "Z" else q) for q in off]
off += [Player("H", "TE", "off", -1.5, -6.6, label="H"), Player("RB", "RB", "off", -5.0, -1.6, label="R")]
dfn = [q for q in front7() if q.key != "SAM"] + [D("SS", "SS", 5.0, -9.6, "SS"), D("NB", "NB", 4.5, 8.0, "NB")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=10, title="Drill 4: name the play and the tag")
p.block("C", pts=[(0.9, 0.5)]); p.block("RG", pts=[(0.8, -0.8), (4.3, -0.4)])
p.block("RT", pts=[(0.9, 0.6)]); p.block("Y", pts=[(0.6, -0.6), (3.6, 1.5)])
p.block("LT", pts=[(0.9, 0.7)]); p.block("LG", pts=[(0.8, -0.6), (4.3, -0.8)])
go_to(p, "H", (4.1, -9.3), via=[(0.4, -7.6), (2.6, -9.0)])
go_to(p, "RB", (-1.4, 2.3), "run", via=[(-4.0, -0.4)])
p.read("BE")
f = draw(p, width_in=5.6, lateral=(-12.5, 11), window=(-8, 9))
plt.show()








Figure 16.19: Drill 4: the first second after the snap. Lines ending in a bar are blocks (look at the direction of each lineman’s first step); the dashed line from the quarterback shows where his eyes are.











NoteAnswer





Inside zone right, with an arc tag. The linemen’s first steps go up, not across, and the back is crossing the quarterback’s face toward the right B gap: inside zone. The H runs past the backside end without touching him and heads for the safety outside him: that is an arc block, not split zone (he would hit the end) and not a bootleg (he would turn into the flat and look for the ball). The quarterback is reading the unblocked backside end. If the end stays home, he hands off. If the end chases the back down the line, he pulls the ball and runs around the end, behind the H’s block on the safety.

title: Zone Running: Inside Zone, Outside Zone, Split Zone, and the Cutback
text:
Takeaways

Zone blocking assigns blockers by rule, not by name: step play-side; block the man head-up on you or in your play-side gap; if nobody is, help the neighbor on your backside and climb to a linebacker. Because the rules are applied after the snap, slants and blitzes get picked up, and the same call re-pairs itself against every front.
Inside zone attacks the guard-tackle area with double teams that drive defenders backward; outside (wide) zone aims at the tight end’s outside leg and moves the defense sideways with reach-and-overtake blocks; stretch is the widest track, edge first; split zone adds a crossing H to kick the backside end. Tell them apart by the line’s first step (up or across) and the back’s aiming point.
The running back makes the play’s last decision: press the aiming point, then bang, bend or bounce, with one cut. On inside zone the order is bang-bend-bounce; on outside zone it is bounce-bang-bend.
The cutback is designed, not improvised: it works because the defense over-runs the play and the backside cut-off keeps the backside defenders out of the lane (in Gibbs’s Denver, often with a cut block, a legal but controversial low block that the rules have steadily narrowed).
Tags change one or two jobs to fix one problem: insert adds a lead blocker, arc runs past the unblocked end to block the next man while the quarterback reads the end, bash sends the back away and makes the quarterback the inside runner. Defenses fight back with penetration, a cutback player and coordinated run fits.
Outside zone’s biggest payoff is the bootleg that looks identical for the first second. The data shows zone running is efficient for a run game, not magic; its value is in what it sets up.

title: Zone Running: Inside Zone, Outside Zone, Split Zone, and the Cutback
text:
Connections
Builds on: The Language of the Run Game (gaps, techniques, covered and uncovered, the core blocks) and the EPA primer in Downs, Distance, and Field Position.
Sets up:

Gap Schemes: the other blocking family (including duo), and when coaches choose it over zone.
Option Football: reading the unblocked end instead of blocking him, the idea behind arc and bash.
Play-Action, Bootlegs, and Screens: the bootleg and the play-action game built on outside zone.
Even Fronts, Odd and Hybrid Fronts and Run Fits: the fronts drawn generically here, named and explained from the defense’s side, and how defenses fit zone runs.
Contact Rules and Penalties as Strategy: the full rules on cut and chop blocks.

See also (case study): The Shanahan Tree: Wide Zone, Boots, and the Illusion of Complexity.
If you want to go deeper: Chris B. Brown’s The Art of Smart Football and his Smart Football writing on the inside and outside zone; Alex Gibbs’s zone-running clinic tapes, still widely circulated among coaches; and the Super Bowl XXXII broadcast and the 2019 49ers’ All-22, watched with nothing but the line’s first step and the running back’s feet in mind.






NoteGo deeper



Names you will hear. Zone vocabulary is a dialect map. Alex Gibbs called inside zone tight zone, and many coaches still do. Some analysts describe a mid zone between inside and outside zone, in which the play-side tackle pushes the end outward instead of trying to reach him, so the back’s read moves to the defensive tackles; one coach-analyst used the name for Sean McVay’s Rams’ base run.27 Split zone is also called zone slice, and bash is sometimes spelled out as back away. And duo, a two-back or one-back run with double teams that a casual viewer can mistake for inside zone, is not a zone play at all: the linemen do not take zone steps and the back reads a linebacker. It belongs to the gap family in 03-03.








NoteGo deeper



From diagrams to real tracking data. Every animation in this chapter is a gridiron simulation written in NFL Big Data Bowl (BDB) coordinates, the format of the league’s public tracking-data competition, so real tracking data drops into the same drawing code. The 2025 Big Data Bowl release (2022 season, weeks 1–9) includes pre-snap and post-snap frames for every player, and its plays.csv carries a run-concept label from PFF, so you can pull real outside-zone runs and watch the line step together. The data is hosted on Kaggle (a data-science competition site) and needs your own free login, so the code for this (in the web edition of this chapter, under “Show the Python”) is not run when this book is built.


Show the Python (real Big Data Bowl tracking; not run in the build)
import pandas as pd
from gridiron import bdb, show_animation

plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")
oz = plays[plays["pff_runConceptPrimary"].astype(str).str.upper().str.contains("OUTSIDE ZONE")]
print(len(oz), "outside zone runs")
g, pl = oz.iloc[0][["gameId", "playId"]]

trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_*.csv")
one = bdb.prepare(trk, plays, game_id=g, play_id=pl)
show_animation(one, times=[0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.6])   # same call as the simulated plays

title: Gap Schemes: Power, Counter, Duo, Trap, Wham, Iso, and the Draw
text:
What makes a run a “gap” run?
Third-and-1, the offense in a heavy formation with a fullback and a tight end, everyone in the stadium knowing it will run. At the snap the right side of the offensive line fires inward, at an angle, away from where the ball is going. At the same instant the left guard, who should be blocking the man in front of him, turns and sprints sideways behind his own line. The fullback heads for the edge. The running back waits a beat, then follows the guard into a hole just outside the tight end, and the guard turns up into it and meets a linebacker head-on. Four yards, first down. The announcer says the offense “just lined up and ran it right at them.” True, but not the interesting part. Everyone knew where the ball was going, so how did the offense get more blockers to that spot than the defense had defenders? The answer is a family of plays coaches call gap schemes, and the guard who ran sideways is the key to every one of them.
You’ll be able to:
How to read the diagrams. Offense is blue circles, defense orange squares, and the offense moves up the page. Left and right are always the offense’s left and right. LT, LG, C, RG and RT are the five offensive linemen; Q is the quarterback, R the running back (HB a halfback, in the 1960s sweep), F a fullback, and Y and U are tight ends on the right and left. H is the “move” player from Formation Rules: an H-back in some diagrams, a slot receiver in others; each caption says which. Defensive linemen carry their technique number; S, M and W are the Sam, Mike and Will linebackers; FS and SS the safeties; CB a cornerback; NB the nickel back. Lines ending in a short bar are blocks; plain arrows are paths; the thick dark arrow is the ball carrier. A purple ring marks a puller (or another extra blocker), the player this chapter wants you to follow. Most diagrams zoom in on the box, so the wide receivers (who keep the formation legal, with seven men on the line) are often outside the picture.
In Zone Running the offensive line asked one question after the snap: who comes into my area? A gap scheme asks its question before the snap: which man do I block, and from which angle? That is why gap blocking is also called man or power blocking. A gap scheme (also man/power blocking) assigns each blocker a man or a gap in advance, picks those assignments to give blockers good angles, and brings extra blockers to a hole the coach chose before the snap.
That definition is the whole family resemblance, and it is worth reading twice, because it says nothing about pulling. What makes a run a gap run is that every blocker knows his man before the snap, and the hole is chosen in advance. Some gap runs pull two linemen; duo, iso and the draw pull nobody. They are still gap runs because their blockers are assigned to men, not areas.
The classic gap run (power, counter, the sweep) is assembled from three parts you met in 03-01, and the rest of the family drops or swaps one of them:
Down blocks in, kick-out out, puller up through the middle. The hole is fixed and known to everyone on the offense, including the running back, who does not have to find it; he has to follow someone into it. Contrast zone, where the hole is wherever the wall cracks and the back’s read is half the play.
The lineman who leaves his spot is the puller: the guard (or tackle, or both) assigned to pull on this play. He is the most important player on the field for you to find, because a puller runs to the hole. The rest of this chapter is, in a sense, a catalogue of where pullers go.

title: Gap Schemes: Power, Counter, Duo, Trap, Wham, Iso, and the Draw
text:
Down blocks on the play side. The linemen at the point of attack block the defender inside them, hitting him from the side. A down block is the easiest block in football to win, because the blocker has an angle and the defender is looking straight ahead. Down blocks build the inside wall of the hole.
A kick-out on the end man. Somebody (a fullback, an H-back, a pulling guard) hits the end man, the last defender on the line (the kick-out; Option Football gives the full rule for finding him), from the inside and drives him toward the sideline. That builds the outside wall.
A puller through the hole. A lineman from the backside runs behind his own line, turns up between the two walls and blocks the first linebacker to show. He is the extra man.









ImportantWhy it exists



Gap schemes exist to win the numbers at the point of attack. A defense can always put as many men in the box as the offense has blockers, and usually one more (hat math). It cannot be equally strong everywhere, though, and it has to line up before it knows where the ball is going. A gap scheme picks one spot, then moves blockers there from elsewhere (a backside guard, a fullback) faster than the defense can move defenders there. It pays for those men by leaving someone away from the play unblocked, and by being more predictable: a pulling guard is a signpost. Every gap play in this chapter is a different answer to the same two questions: where do the extra blockers come from, and who is left free?

title: Gap Schemes: Power, Counter, Duo, Trap, Wham, Iso, and the Draw
section: Power: the play the whole family is built on
text:
Power: the play the whole family is built on
Power (often called Power O) is the purest gap run, and the one to learn first. Here it is from the I-formation (a fullback behind the quarterback and the tailback behind him) against a 4-3 Over, a four-man front whose 3-technique lines up on the side of the tight end (fronts are named and explained in Even Fronts; here it is just a set of numbers to block). Read it from the right, the play side, to the left. The hole is off-tackle, the old name for “just outside the tackle”: here that is the D gap, outside where the tight end lined up (with no tight end on that side, the same play hits the C gap).
Walk through Figure 17.1 one man at a time, because each assignment exists for a reason.
The play-side wall: down blocks. The tight end blocks down on the 5-technique inside him, and the right tackle blocks down on the 3-technique inside him. Neither has to beat a defender lined up across from him; each hits a man from the side, which is why gap teams love the down block. The right guard joins the tackle on the 3-technique for a moment, a combo block, and then climbs to the backside linebacker, the Will. Coaches teach these linemen one short rule, usually some version of gap, down, backer: if a defender is in your inside gap, block him; if not, block down on the man over the lineman inside you; if nobody is there, go to a linebacker.1 The rule means a play-side lineman never has to reach a man lined up outside him.
The center blocks back. The left guard is about to leave. The defensive lineman who was across from the gap he leaves, here the 1-technique, would walk into the backfield, so the center blocks back on him, away from the play. Because the 1 is shaded on the center’s backside shoulder, it is another easy angle. This is not a coincidence: coaches like to call power toward a 3-technique and away from a 1-technique for exactly these angles.


Show the Python
def power_play():
    p = Play(i_form(), over_front(), los=35, to_go=None, title="Power right vs a 4-3 Over")
    go_to(p, "Y", (0.5, 4.3), via=[(-0.3, 4.75)])                       # down on the 5
    go_to(p, "RT", (0.4, 2.8), via=[(-0.3, 3.05)])                      # down on the 3 ...
    go_to(p, "RG", (3.6, -1.6), via=[(0.05, 2.0)])                      # ... with the RG, who climbs to the Will
    go_to(p, "C", (0.35, -0.3), via=[(-0.45, -0.15)])                   # back block on the 1
    go_to(p, "LT", (-1.9, -3.7), via=[(-1.0, -2.6)])                    # hinge
    go_to(p, "LG", (2.7, 5.5), "pull", via=[(-1.7, -1.3), (-3.4, 0.2), (-3.4, 3.4), (-1.9, 5.7)])
    go_to(p, "FB", (0.35, 6.45), via=[(-3.6, 5.2), (-2.2, 7.4)], speed=5.0)  # kick out the Sam
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (3.5, 4.9), "path", speed=4.0)                     # the Mike scrapes to the hole
    go_to(p, "RB", (5.0, 4.9), "run", via=[(-5.7, 1.2), (-3.0, 4.6), (0.4, 5.2), (2.0, 4.8)])
    return p


p = power_play()
p.highlight("LG", color=PURPLE); p.highlight("WE", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, width_in=5.9, lateral=(-8.8, 11.0), window=(-9.0, 12.0))
pair_oval(f, p, 0.2, 2.35, 3.4, 2.6)
spot(f, p, 1.5, 5.4)
point_to(f, p, (-5.4, -4.6), (-1.7, -1.3), "backside guard\npulls (the puller)", color=PURPLE, fontsize=6.8)
point_to(f, p, (3.4, -5.4), (1.0, -4.0), "unblocked: the LT's\nhinge only gets\nin his way", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK,
         fontsize=6.6)
point_to(f, p, (-3.8, 9.3), (0.35, 6.9), "F kicks out\nthe S", fontsize=6.8)
point_to(f, p, (7.6, 8.2), (2.6, 5.2), "puller leads\nup on the Mike", color=PURPLE, fontsize=6.8)
point_to(f, p, (7.6, 1.6), (1.4, 2.35), "RT + RG double the 3;\nthen the RG climbs to the W", fontsize=6.6, shrink=14)
plt.show()








Figure 17.1: Power right against a 4-3 Over. Three lines leave the backfield and stay separate: the pulling left guard (purple ring) tightest, the fullback widest, kicking out the Sam, and the running back’s thick arrow between them, a step behind the guard. Notice the hole (green X): inside wall from the down blocks, outside wall from the kick-out. The one defender nobody blocks is the backside end (orange ring), the farthest from the ball.





The kick-out. The fullback runs at the end man (here the Sam, standing up on the line outside the tight end in a 9-technique) and hits him from the inside, driving him toward the sideline. The fullback does not need to win big. If the Sam stays outside, the hole is inside him.
The puller. The left guard opens his hips toward the play with a short step back and out (coaches call it a bucket step or a skip pull), sprints flat behind the center and the right side, staying tight to his teammates’ down blocks (“hug the down blocks”), and turns up into the hole, just outside the tight end’s down block and inside the kick-out, with his eyes inside for the first defender who appears. His man is the first linebacker who shows, almost always the play-side linebacker (the Mike here) coming to fill. The running back follows him, aiming his first steps at the tight end’s outside hip and staying a step behind the guard’s back, then cutting off the guard’s block.
The backside. With the guard gone, the left tackle hinges: he steps inside to close the B gap the guard left, then swings back outside like a door closing, to keep the backside end from running straight down the line. He does not try to drive the end anywhere. The end is the one defender power chooses not to block. That is the deal at the heart of the play.

Where power’s extra blockers come from
Count the bodies, as in hat math, and power’s logic becomes arithmetic.


Show the Python
p = Play(i_form(), over_front(safeties=False), los=35, to_go=None, title="Where power's extra blockers come from")
go_to(p, "LG", (-0.6, 5.6), "pull", via=[(-1.7, -1.3), (-3.4, 0.2), (-3.4, 3.4), (-1.9, 5.7)])
go_to(p, "FB", (0.35, 6.45), via=[(-3.6, 5.2), (-2.2, 7.4)], speed=5.0)
p.highlight("LG", color=PURPLE); p.highlight("FB", color=PURPLE); p.highlight("WE", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, width_in=5.6, lateral=(-9.2, 10.2), window=(-9.0, 9.0))
shade(f, p, 0.6, 8.8, d0=-6.0, d1=6.4)
say(f, p, 5.4, 7.0, "play side", color=GREEN, fontsize=7.5, weight="bold")
say(f, p, -4.0, 6.9, "before the snap:\n3 blockers (RG, RT, Y)\nvs 4 defenders (3, 5, S, M)", fontsize=6.6)
say(f, p, 5.6, -5.8, "after the snap:\n+ the puller (LG)\n+ the fullback (F)\n= a hat on all four,\nwith one to spare", color=PURPLE,
    fontsize=6.6)
point_to(f, p, (-3.8, -6.2), (1.0, -4.0), "the price: the\nbackside end is\nleft unblocked", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK,
         fontsize=6.6)
plt.show()








Figure 17.2: Power’s arithmetic, against the same 4-3 Over. Before the snap the play side (shaded) has three blockers for four defenders. The pulling guard and the fullback (purple rings) bring it to five for four. The price is the backside end (orange ring).





Figure 17.2 is the reason gap schemes exist. Before the snap, the side the offense wants to run to has three blockers and four defenders. Run zone that way and somebody has to beat a man he is outnumbered against. Run power and two blockers who started on the other side of the ball arrive at the point of attack within a second. Now count the assignments, because that is where the extra man shows up:

the Y takes the 5, the fullback takes the Sam, the pulling guard takes the Mike;
the right tackle takes the 3, and the right guard helps him: that double team is the spare blocker.

Five blockers for four defenders means one man to spare, and power spends him in two installments: first as half of a double team that drives the 3-technique off the ball, then, once the 3 is moving, as the blocker who climbs off it to the backside linebacker, the Will. The defense cannot match that move, because its players learn where the ball is going only when the snap shows them, while the offense knew before the huddle broke.
Now the whole box. The offense has seven blockers (five linemen, the Y and the fullback) against seven defenders (four linemen and three linebackers). The center takes the 1, the right guard’s climb takes the Will, and the left tackle’s hinge is a hat spent on nobody: he only closes the gap the guard left. So one defender is left over, and power makes sure it is the backside end. Power does not add a blocker to the box. It moves one, and the backside end is the receipt. It is betting that a defender who lines up farthest from the hole, and has to run down the line behind a wall of bodies, will arrive too late. Most of the time he does. When the defense knows that and sends that end screaming down the line at the snap, the offense has answers (a quarterback who keeps the ball and runs where the end left, in Option Football; a bootleg pass behind him, in Play-Action, Boots and Screens).
The rest of the offense has jobs too, small but real. The quarterback opens, hands off and keeps carrying out a fake; on many teams he then sells a bootleg away from the play, which is what keeps the free backside end honest. The wide receivers, out of the picture here, block the men over them (usually a cornerback and a safety) so that the run does not end at the second level. And the defense’s usual answer to power, which Run Fits and Box Math builds in full, is to attack the pullers: an end or linebacker who meets the kick-out or the puller inside, so the ball has to bounce outside to a fast safety, plus that free backside end chasing from behind.






CautionCommon misconception



“Power works because the offensive line is bigger and stronger.” Strength helps, but the play is designed so that nobody has to win a fair fight. The down blocks hit men from the side; the kick-out hits the end man from inside, where he is not looking; the puller arrives as an extra man. What power needs is not the biggest line but a line that can pull: a guard who can run ten yards laterally and still hit a linebacker. That is why gap-scheme teams prize athletic guards as much as heavy ones.


The “O” in Power O is not explained consistently from one coaching tree to the next, so do not read much into it.


The same rules against a different front
The diagrams so far are power against one front, but the line does not memorize a picture; it carries rules. Change the front and the rules redraw the play. Figure 17.3 is power’s call against a defense that puts its 3-technique on the backside, over the guard who was supposed to pull, and it is drawn from the shotgun with an H-back as the kick-out man, the version you will see most on Sunday (only about one NFL snap in ten has a fullback or a second back on the field; see the iso section below).


Show the Python
off = line() + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, -1.8, "R"), O("H", "TE", -5.0, 2.0, "H")]
dfn = [dl("WE", "5", -1), dl("DT", "3", -1), dl("NT", "1", +1), dl("SE", "5", +1), D("SAM", "SAM", 1.0, 7.0, "S"),
       D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.6, 1.6, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.6, -1.6, "W")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None, title="Power's rules vs a backside 3: the tackle pulls (dart)")
go_to(p, "Y", (0.5, 4.3), via=[(-0.3, 4.75)])                       # down on the 5
go_to(p, "RG", (0.35, 1.0), via=[(-0.3, 1.3)])                      # the 1 is in his gap: down on him
go_to(p, "RT", (3.7, -1.2), via=[(0.0, 2.6)])                       # nothing in his gap or over the RG: backer
go_to(p, "LG", (0.35, -2.2), via=[(-0.3, -1.9)])                    # stays home on the backside 3
go_to(p, "C", (0.2, -1.4), via=[(-0.45, -0.6)])                     # helps the LG on the 3
go_to(p, "LT", (2.8, 5.0), "pull", via=[(-1.3, -3.6), (-3.0, -2.2), (-3.1, 3.0), (-1.7, 5.6)])   # pulls for the Mike
go_to(p, "H", (0.4, 6.45), via=[(-3.0, 5.4), (-1.4, 6.6)], speed=5.0)   # kicks out the Sam
go_to(p, "MIKE", (3.6, 4.2), "path", speed=4.0)
go_to(p, "RB", (5.4, 5.2), "run", via=[(-4.0, -0.4), (-3.8, 2.6), (-0.4, 5.5)])
p.highlight("LT", color=PURPLE); p.highlight("WE", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, width_in=5.8, lateral=(-9.4, 11.0), window=(-8.4, 9.4))
point_to(f, p, (5.6, -6.2), (1.0, -2.35), "backside 3: the C\ncan't reach him, so\nthe LG stays home", fontsize=6.6,
         color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
point_to(f, p, (-6.6, -3.6), (-2.2, -3.0), "so the LT pulls\ninstead (dart)", color=PURPLE, fontsize=6.6)
point_to(f, p, (-5.4, 8.4), (0.4, 6.6), "H-back kicks\nout the S", fontsize=6.6)
point_to(f, p, (-2.6, -7.8), (1.0, -4.0), "still free:\nthe backside end", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
plt.show()








Figure 17.3: Power’s rules against a backside 3-technique, from the shotgun. Play side, gap-down-backer still works: the Y blocks down on the 5, the RG blocks down on the 1 in his gap, and the RT, with nobody to block down on, goes to the backside linebacker. But the center cannot block back on a 3-technique lined up over the guard, so the left guard stays home on him and the left tackle pulls instead, a variant many teams call dart. The H-back kicks out the Sam. The free man is still the backside end.





Walk the rules and the play draws itself. On the play side nothing changes in principle: the Y has a man in his inside gap (the 5), so he blocks down; the right guard has the 1 in his gap, so he blocks down on him; the right tackle has nobody in his gap and nobody over the guard beside him, so the third word of the rule sends him to a linebacker, the backside one. The problem is the backside. The center can block back on a 1-technique shaded on him, but a 3-technique sits outside the guard, two gaps away, and a center cannot get there. If the left guard pulled anyway, the 3 would be loose in the backfield, right in the path of the puller and the back. So the offense keeps the guard home and pulls the tackle, a version many coaches call dart or “tackle power.”2 The price is distance: the tackle has farther to run, so dart needs an athletic tackle. Other answers to the same front are to check to a different run or to run power the other way, at the 3.
