title: Option Football: Reading Defenders Instead of Blocking Them
section: The NFL’s on-and-off romance with option
text:
The NFL’s on-and-off romance with option
For most of NFL history, option football was a college thing. Professional quarterbacks were pocket passers, too valuable to be hit, and professional defenders were fast enough to punish a slow read. There were exceptions, like Michael Vick’s Falcons, and there were workarounds, like the 2008 Dolphins’ wildcat, which snapped the ball directly to a running back to get the option’s arithmetic without putting the quarterback at risk. But no NFL team built its run game on the read until 2012.
The 2012 wave. In one season, four young, fast quarterbacks, three of them from college spread-option or pistol offenses, arrived in, or took over, NFL offenses at once: Robert Griffin III in Washington, Russell Wilson in Seattle, Colin Kaepernick in San Francisco and, a year after his own rookie season, Cam Newton in Carolina. Washington’s coaches, Mike Shanahan and his son Kyle, the offensive coordinator, married their outside-zone run game to Griffin’s pistol zone read, and the result was the league’s top rushing attack: the rookie running back Alfred Morris ran for 1,613 yards and Griffin for 815, then a record for a rookie quarterback.15 In the playoffs, Kaepernick ran for 181 yards against Green Bay, a playoff record for a quarterback (the film room below has the details).16 The season is remembered as the read-option wave.
The fade. Then it cooled. Griffin, already playing on a sprained knee, tore the ACL and LCL in his right knee in the wild-card loss to Seattle on January 6, 2013, and never recaptured his rookie form.17 Defenses spent the 2013 offseason studying the read, the scrape exchange and the slow-play became standard, and the league told officials that read quarterbacks could be hit as runners. Most coaches concluded that the read option was a good change-up and a dangerous base offense, and through the mid-2010s it became a few plays a game.
The return. Lamar Jackson changed the conversation. In 2019 Baltimore built an entire offense around his reads, from the pistol and the gun, with zone read, inverted veer, speed option and designed quarterback runs, and set the NFL’s team rushing record while Jackson ran for 1,206 yards, a quarterback record, and won the MVP award unanimously.18 Jalen Hurts’s Eagles leaned on QB power, the read and the sneak; in Super Bowl LVII he ran for 70 yards and three touchdowns, both Super Bowl records for a quarterback.19 Josh Allen made the designed run a weapon for a pocket passer, especially near the goal line, and in 2024 the Commanders’ rookie Jayden Daniels broke Griffin’s rookie rushing record.20 The Ravens era is the subject of its own case study, 12-05.

What the numbers say
Can we see that history in data? Partly. The NFL’s play-by-play does not record the play call, so it cannot tell a zone read from inside zone. But it records who carried the ball, and it separately flags quarterback scrambles, the unplanned runs when a pass play breaks down. A quarterback run that is not a scramble, not a kneel-down and not a botched snap is, almost always, a designed quarterback run: a keep on a read, or a planned quarterback run. We also set aside likely sneaks (up the middle, two yards or less to go), because they are their own play with their own story. What is left is a fair proxy for the quarterback run game this chapter is about.


Show the Python
from gridiron.data import pbp, nfl

style.apply()
SEASONS = list(range(2006, 2026))
cols = ["season", "season_type", "posteam", "play_type", "epa", "success", "qb_scramble", "qb_kneel", "down",
        "ydstogo", "rusher_player_id", "rusher_player_name", "run_location", "game_id", "aborted_play",
        "passer_player_id", "pass_attempt", "yards_gained", "fumble", "play_id"]
plays = pbp(SEASONS, columns=cols)
reg = plays[plays["season_type"] == "REG"]
att = reg[reg["pass_attempt"] == 1].groupby(["season", "passer_player_id"]).size()
passers = set(att[att >= 10].index)
runs = reg[(reg["play_type"] == "run") & (reg["qb_kneel"] == 0) & (reg["aborted_play"] == 0)
           & reg["down"].notna() & reg["epa"].notna()].copy()
runs["qb"] = [(s, i) in passers for s, i in zip(runs["season"], runs["rusher_player_id"])]
runs["sneak"] = runs["qb"] & (runs["ydstogo"] <= 2) & (runs["run_location"] == "middle")
rosters = nfl().load_rosters(SEASONS).to_pandas()
backs = set(rosters.loc[rosters["position"].isin(["RB", "FB"]), "gsis_id"].dropna())
runs["kind"] = np.select([runs["qb"] & (runs["qb_scramble"] == 1), runs["sneak"], runs["qb"],
                          runs["rusher_player_id"].isin(backs)],
                         ["scramble", "sneak", "designed", "rb"], "other")
team_games = runs.groupby("season")["game_id"].nunique() * 2
des = runs[runs["kind"] == "designed"]
rb = runs[runs["kind"] == "rb"]
per_game = des.groupby("season").size() / team_games
epa_des, epa_rb = des.groupby("season")["epa"].mean(), rb.groupby("season")["epa"].mean()

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.8, 3.3))
ax = axes[0]
ax.bar(per_game.index, per_game.values, color=[style.SERIES[0] if s in (2012, 2013) or s >= 2018 else "#9ec5f4"
                                                for s in per_game.index], width=0.75)
n_season = des.groupby("season").size()
ax.set_title("Designed QB runs per team-game", fontsize=9.5)
ax.annotate("2012\nwave", (2012, per_game[2012] + 0.03), xytext=(2009.6, 1.15), fontsize=7.5,
            color=style.INK_2, ha="center", arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=style.MUTED, lw=0.7))
ax.annotate("Lamar Jackson\nstarts (2018)", (2018, per_game[2018] + 0.03), xytext=(2014.8, 1.38), fontsize=7.5,
            color=style.INK_2, ha="center", arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=style.MUTED, lw=0.7))
ax.set_ylim(0, 1.6)
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
ax = axes[1]
ax.axhline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=1, zorder=1)
for ser, name, col in [(epa_des, "Designed QB runs", style.SERIES[0]), (epa_rb, "RB carries", style.SERIES[1])]:
    ax.plot(ser.index, ser.values, color=col, lw=2, marker="o", ms=3.5, label=name)
    ax.annotate(name, (ser.index[-1], ser.values[-1]), xytext=(4, 0), textcoords="offset points",
                fontsize=7.5, color=col, va="center")
ax.set_title("EPA per play", fontsize=9.5)
ax.set_xlim(2005.5, 2031)
ax.set_ylim(-0.2, 0.35)
for a in axes:
    a.tick_params(labelsize=7.5)
    a.set_xticks([2006, 2010, 2014, 2018, 2022, 2025])
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=1.2)
plt.show()

d_all, r_all = des["epa"].mean(), rb["epa"].mean()
d_sr, r_sr = des["success"].mean(), rb["success"].mean()
d_first = des.loc[des["down"] == 1, "epa"].mean(); r_first = rb.loc[rb["down"] == 1, "epa"].mean()
third_share_d = (des["down"] >= 3).mean(); third_share_r = (rb["down"] >= 3).mean()
was12 = des[(des["season"] == 2012) & (des["posteam"] == "WAS")]
lj19 = des[(des["season"] == 2019) & des["rusher_player_name"].eq("L.Jackson")]
bal_rb19 = rb[(rb["season"] == 2019) & (rb["posteam"] == "BAL")]["epa"].mean()
rb19 = rb[rb["season"] == 2019]["epa"].mean()
peak = int(per_game.idxmax())
n_early = (int(n_season.loc[2006:2011].min()), int(n_season.loc[2006:2011].max()))
n_late = int(n_season.loc[2018:2025].min())
by_qb = des.groupby(["season", "rusher_player_name"]).size()
vick06, young06 = int(by_qb.get((2006, "M.Vick"), 0)), int(by_qb.get((2006, "V.Young"), 0))


def per_start(name, season):
    """Designed runs per game in which the quarterback threw a pass."""
    ids = des.loc[des["rusher_player_name"].eq(name), "rusher_player_id"].unique()
    games = reg[(reg["season"] == season) & reg["passer_player_id"].isin(ids)]["game_id"].nunique()
    return int(by_qb.get((season, name), 0)), games


lj24, lj25 = per_start("L.Jackson", 2024), per_start("L.Jackson", 2025)
jh24, jh25 = per_start("J.Hurts", 2024), per_start("J.Hurts", 2025)
jd24, jd25 = per_start("J.Daniels", 2024), per_start("J.Daniels", 2025)
fum_d, fum_r = des["fumble"].mean(), rb["fumble"].mean()
# FTN charting (2022-2025): how many players besides the quarterback stood in the backfield?
ftn = nfl().load_ftn_charting([2022, 2023, 2024, 2025]).to_pandas()
ftn = ftn.rename(columns={"nflverse_game_id": "game_id", "nflverse_play_id": "play_id"})
des_ftn = des[des["season"] >= 2022].merge(ftn[["game_id", "play_id", "n_offense_backfield"]],
                                           on=["game_id", "play_id"], how="inner")
empty_share = (des_ftn["n_offense_backfield"] == 0).mean()








Figure 18.12: Designed quarterback runs in the NFL, regular seasons 2006–2025. Left: how often teams ran them, per team per game; the dark bars mark the two eras of the text (the 2012–2013 read-option wave and the rise from 2018), the light bars the seasons between. Right: efficiency, EPA per play, against running back carries in the same seasons; before 2012 each season has only a couple of hundred designed quarterback runs in the whole league, so its EPA swings widely from year to year. Designed quarterback runs are counted as runs by a player who threw at least 10 passes that season (so a gadget passer such as Taysom Hill counts), excluding scrambles, kneel-downs, aborted snaps and likely sneaks (middle runs with two yards or less to go). Read the right panel with the caveats in the text: the comparison is not like for like. Data: nflverse play-by-play via nflreadpy.





Three things to read from Figure 18.12.
The history is there. Designed quarterback runs nearly doubled from the late 2000s to 2012–2013, settled back, and then rose again, much higher, from 2018, peaking in 2022 at 1.4 per team per game before falling back in 2025. Two bars break the pattern, and both are about a few quarterbacks rather than the league. The high 2006 bar is mostly Michael Vick (66 designed runs, by this chapter’s count, in the season he set the quarterback rushing record) and the rookie Vince Young (30). The 2025 dip comes mostly from the heaviest users: Lamar Jackson went from 75 designed runs in 17 games in 2024 to 28 in 13, Jalen Hurts from 58 to 27, and Jayden Daniels, who played 7 games, from 63 to 14. The data shows who ran less, not why: missed games account for part of it, play-calling for the rest. Notice how small these numbers are: about one designed quarterback run a game for a typical team, even at the peak. (Washington in 2012 had 68 of them, more than four a game; Jackson alone had 113 in 2019.) Most of the option’s effect on a game is invisible in these counts, because the read’s main product is the give, a running back carry that looks like any other in the data. No public source flags a read play either: FTN’s charting marks run-pass options, but not whether a quarterback read an end on a handoff, so how often an NFL “gun handoff” is really a read is invisible in the numbers.
Per play, designed quarterback runs look far better than running back carries. Across the twenty seasons they averaged +0.15 EPA per play against -0.07 for running backs, and a 53% success rate against 38%. On first down, where the situations are most comparable, the gap is smaller but still there (+0.03 against -0.08). Read the early seasons of the right panel loosely: before 2012 the league ran only 191 to 303 designed quarterback runs a season, so one long run moves the average, while every season since 2018 has had at least 412.
But the comparison is not like for like, and the right panel cannot tell you to run your quarterback more. Three reasons:

Selection. On a read play, the quarterback keeps precisely when the defense has taken the back away, that is, when the keep is the open option. The keeps in this data are the reads that came out in the quarterback’s favour; the reads that said “give” are filed under the running back.
Situation. 28% of designed quarterback runs come on third or fourth down, against 10% of running back carries, often against defenses spread out to stop a pass. A run that converts third-and-4 is worth a lot of EPA.
Survivorship. The quarterbacks who run often are the ones who are good at it: Jackson, Allen, Hurts. A team without one cannot buy their numbers by calling the plays.

Some of the costs do show up. Designed quarterback runs end in a fumble far more often: on 3.1% of them across these seasons, against 0.9% of running back carries, roughly 3 times the rate, a number that bundles mesh exchanges, quarterbacks who carry the ball less securely, and the hits they take. The hits themselves are not in the play-by-play, and injuries are recorded by week, not by play, so the injury cost the chapter keeps mentioning cannot be measured cleanly from public data. One more thing the charting does show is how NFL teams build these runs: from 2022 to 2025, 11% of designed quarterback runs came from an empty backfield, with nobody beside the quarterback, the five-receiver version of adding a blocker.
The fairest reading is the one coaches reached on their own: a quarterback who is a real running threat makes the whole run game better, partly through his own carries and partly through the gives and the defenders he occupies. Baltimore’s running backs in 2019 averaged +0.043 EPA per carry, against a league average of -0.088 for running backs that season; this data cannot prove the reads caused that, but it is what the arithmetic predicts.21






NoteFilm room: Washington 2012



Washington’s 2012 offense is the cleanest NFL example of the zone read as a base play, not a gadget. The Shanahans ran their outside-zone system from the pistol, with Griffin about four yards deep and Morris directly behind him, so the back could run zone either way and the quarterback could read either end. The line’s first step looked like outside zone every time; the backside end had to decide whether to chase Morris or stay home for Griffin, and Griffin, a former college hurdler, was one of the fastest quarterbacks in the league.
What to notice on the broadcasts and the All-22 of that season: the backside end’s first step. Ends who chased gave up Griffin keeps around the edge; ends who stayed home left wide cutback lanes for Morris. Watch, too, how often Griffin carried out his fake after a give, running toward the sideline without the ball: that fake kept the end honest on the next play, and it was also where he took hits.








NoteFilm room: San Francisco 49ers, NFC divisional round, January 12, 2013



Kaepernick’s 181 rushing yards against Green Bay, in his eighth NFL start, are the read option’s most famous day in the NFL. San Francisco won 45–31. The 49ers ran their read plays from the pistol and the shotgun, and the Packers’ edge had no answer. In Robert Mays’s account for Grantland, midway through the first quarter, on third-and-2, outside linebacker Erik Walden chased Frank Gore on an option read and Kaepernick kept around the end for 13 yards; two quarters later the 49ers ran the same play, with fullback Bruce Miller sealing Walden (blocking him inside, away from the play), and Kaepernick went 56 yards for a touchdown.22
What to notice: the read key on Kaepernick’s keeps. An end who chases the back takes himself out of the play, an end who is sealed can’t recover, and the free safety is too deep to arrive in time. Then watch how defenses played the read the next season: the crash-and-scrape became standard, and long keeps got rarer. That is the defense learning.








NoteFilm room: Baltimore Ravens 2019



The 2019 Ravens are the read game as a complete offense: zone read, bash, inverted veer, speed option, QB power and the sneak, run from the pistol and the gun with tight ends and fullbacks as extra blockers. Jackson’s 113 designed runs that season (by this chapter’s count) averaged +0.32 EPA per play.
What to notice: how many Ravens runs had two threats in the backfield on every snap, and how often the same unblocked end had to defend a different blocking scheme underneath the read. The power read is this chapter’s inverted veer. A counter read uses 03-03’s counter blocking (two pullers) and reads the backside end: the back follows the pullers, and the quarterback keeps around the end if he crashes. Counter bash swaps the runners: the back runs away from the pullers, around the read end, and the quarterback, if he keeps, follows the pullers. All three leave an end alone, but each sends the runners to different places.23 Defenses fought back with the scrape exchange, with ends who kept outside leverage (staying outside the runner, so the only way past them is inside, toward help) to force the give, and with extra second-level defenders flowing to the ball, as Tennessee did in its January 2020 playoff upset with a 3-3 front (three down linemen and three linebackers, one more defender off the ball than usual);24 the full story, including how the offense changed when Derrick Henry arrived in 2024, is in the Ravens case study.








TipWatch for it



On Sunday: find the read key. Option plays happen fast, so do the work before the snap.
Before the snap

Where is the quarterback, and where is the back? Shotgun or pistol with a back beside or behind the quarterback is the read look, but most NFL snaps from that look are plain handoffs or passes, so treat it as “a read is possible,” not “a read is coming.” The more the quarterback has run this season, the more seriously to take it.
Which end? On the zone read, a back offset to one side usually runs to the other side (crossing the quarterback’s face), which makes the end on the back’s side, the backside end, the read key. The power read flips this: the back still crosses the quarterback’s face, but the read is the play-side end, the one the back is running toward. Look for a guard pulling toward that end to tell them apart. (Which end gets read is part of the play call; on some plays the quarterback can flip it at the line.)
Find the end man on the line of scrimmage on each side. Count from the outside in: who is the last defender standing on the line? Recheck after every shift; a linebacker walking up changes the answer.
Is anyone left unblocked on purpose? You can’t know until the snap, but look for a tight end or H-back lined up to the side away from the line’s likely flow: he may be the arc blocker, which means read.

At the snap

Real read or plain handoff? On a real read nobody touches the end, the quarterback’s head is turned toward him rather than toward the back, and the ball stays in the back’s belly for a long ride. On a plain handoff the quarterback looks at the back and the ball is gone in a step.
Watch the read key’s first step, not the ball. Crash or squeeze inside: predict keep. Sit, widen or rush upfield outside: predict give. Say it out loud before the ball comes out.
If the end crashes, find the linebacker behind him. Is he scraping outside? Then the keep is running into a scrape exchange.

After the play

On the replay, check your call. Did the quarterback do what the read key “told” him? If not, was it a mistake, or was the defender slow-playing?
On designed runs, count the hats: if the running back is blocking and the quarterback carries, the offense added a blocker. Did the defense answer with a safety in the box?

For your prediction log (01-06): on every read look, write the read key’s position and your prediction (G or K) from his first step; afterward, write what happened.

title: Option Football: Reading Defenders Instead of Blocking Them
text:
Predict the play






TipPredict the play



Drill 1: the end who always crashes. Second-and-7 in the second quarter. The offense has run the zone read four times today, the running back aligned on the left and the line zoning right each time. On all four, the defense’s backside end crashed hard down the line at the back. The quarterback read him correctly and kept twice, and both keeps were stopped for two yards near the left sideline, both times by a defender who was not the end. The offense lines up in the same look again. Who has probably been making those tackles, what is the defense doing to put him there, and what should the offense call instead?


Show the Python
p = Play(gun(extra=(O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"),)), front7(), los=35, to_go=7,
         title="Drill 1: 2nd and 7, the same look again")
p.highlight("BE", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-11.0, 9.5), window=(-7.5, 8.0), width_in=5.2)
say(f, p, 3.2, -7.2, "crashed\n4 of 4", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
plt.show()








Figure 18.13: Drill 1: gun, 11 personnel (tight end on the right), the back offset left; an even front with the backside end (ringed) and the Will linebacker 4½ yards deep over the left guard. Two deep safeties out of the picture.













TipAnswer





The Will, on a scrape exchange. The end crashes to take the back and the Will, who lines up inside, scrapes over the top at the snap to the spot where a zone-read keep arrives. The quarterback has been reading correctly; the end’s crash is a lie told to him, and a plain zone read believes it every time. Two clues give it away: the tackler wasn’t the end, and he arrived from the inside, near the sideline, where a linebacker who had read “keep” before the ball came out would be. The left guard, climbing to where the Will used to be, has been blocking air (Figure 18.3).
Better calls use the exchange against itself, as The offense’s replies laid out: bash (the back goes wide around the crashing end, so his crash becomes a squeeze and the ball goes outside him), arc (the tight end runs past the end to block the scraping Will), or read the Will instead (block the end, read the scraper, or throw behind him on an RPO, 04-06).
The general lesson: an option defense that does the same thing every time has stopped being an option defense. A good play-caller counts the crashes, as you just did.









TipPredict the play



Drill 2: name that option. Two plays from the same game, drawn with the line’s blocks and the back’s path; both send the back wide and leave a defensive end unblocked. For each one: name the play, name the read key, and say who gets the ball if that read key squeezes inside.


Show the Python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.6))
dl = [D("PE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", 1) + 1.3, "5"), D("PT", "DT", 1.0, technique("3", 1), "3"),
      D("BT", "DT", 1.0, technique("1", -1), "1"), D("BE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", -1) - 0.6, "5")]
lbs = [D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 2.4, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.2, "W")]
# A: power read to the right
p = Play(gun(), dl + lbs, los=35, to_go=None)
go_to(p, "RT", (0.5, 2.6), via=[(-0.4, 3.0)]); go_to(p, "RG", (3.7, -1.2), via=[(-0.2, 1.9), (0.6, 1.4)])
go_to(p, "C", (0.4, -0.5)); go_to(p, "LT", (0.3, -4.2), via=[(-0.6, -3.8)])
go_to(p, "LG", (3.4, 2.6), "pull", via=[(-1.6, -1.2), (-1.8, 1.4), (0.2, 3.4)])
f = draw(p, ax=axes[0], lateral=(-9.0, 9.5), window=(-7.5, 7.0), title=False)
branch(f, p, [(-5.0, -1.6), (-4.7, 0.6), (-4.2, 4.6), (-2.2, 7.6), (3.6, 8.0)], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
branch(f, p, [(-5.0, 0.0), (-3.6, 0.6), (-1.9, 2.5), (-0.6, 4.6), (4.8, 4.7)], color=GREEN)
axes[0].set_title("Play A", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
# B: bash (zone right, back away to the left)
dl_b = [D("PE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", 1), "5")] + dl[1:]
p = Play(gun(rb_w=1.6), dl_b + lbs, los=35, to_go=None)
go_to(p, "LT", (0.4, -2.3), via=[(-0.4, -2.8)])                  # step inside: zone right
go_to(p, "LG", (3.6, -1.6), via=[(-0.4, -1.2), (0.6, -1.0)])    # climb to the Will
go_to(p, "C", (0.6, -0.3))                                       # on the 1
go_to(p, "RG", (0.6, 2.9), via=[(-0.4, 2.1)])                    # reach the 3
go_to(p, "RT", (0.6, 4.6), via=[(-0.4, 3.7)])                    # reach the end
f = draw(p, ax=axes[1], lateral=(-9.5, 9.0), window=(-7.5, 7.0), title=False)
branch(f, p, [(-5.0, 1.6), (-4.8, 0.3), (-4.0, -3.4), (-1.8, -6.6), (3.6, -7.6)], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
branch(f, p, [(-5.0, 0.0), (-3.6, 0.6), (-1.6, 1.0), (4.4, 1.1)], color=GREEN)
axes[1].set_title("Play B", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 18.14: Drill 2: two read plays from the shotgun. Each shows the line’s blocks (short bars), the back’s path (dashed dark arrow) and the quarterback’s possible keep path (dashed green arrow). Which is which, and who is read?













TipAnswer





Play A is the power read (inverted veer); play B is bash. In both, if the read key squeezes inside, the quarterback gives and the back has the ball outside the end. What differs is which end, and the line tells you.

Play A: the line blocks power. The right tackle blocks down, the right guard climbs, the center blocks back, and the left guard pulls across the center toward the right end. Nobody blocks that end, the one the play is aimed at: he is the read key, the play-side end. The back sweeps right across the quarterback’s face.
Play B: the line zones right, every lineman stepping the same way, with no puller. The back runs the other way, wide around the left end, the backside end, who is the read key. It is a zone read with the runners swapped.

The tell is the puller. A guard crossing the formation toward the unblocked end means power read; a line flowing away from the unblocked end means a zone-based read, and the back’s path tells you whether it is the plain zone read (back inside) or bash (back outside).









TipPredict the play



Drill 3: third-and-2. Third-and-2 at the opponent’s 36, fourth quarter, tie game. The offense lines up in the shotgun with one tight end and the running back beside a quarterback who has run for 600 yards this season. The defense puts seven in the box and plays man coverage on the receivers, with one deep safety. Count the hats: on a handoff, how many blockers against how many box defenders? Which kinds of run would give the offense a hat on every hat, and what is the defense’s likely answer?


Show the Python
p = Play(gun(rb_w=1.6, extra=(O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"),)),
         [D("PE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", 1), "5"), D("PT", "DT", 1.0, technique("3", 1), "3"),
          D("BT", "DT", 1.0, technique("1", -1), "1"), D("BE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", -1), "5"),
          D("SAM", "SAM", 1.0, 6.4, "S"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 3.5, 2.4, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 3.5, -2.4, "W"),
          D("FS", "FS", 12.0, 0.0, "FS")], los=64, to_go=2, title="Drill 3: 3rd and 2, opponent's 36")
f = draw(p, lateral=(-9.5, 10.0), window=(-7.5, 13.5), width_in=5.2)
plt.show()








Figure 18.15: Drill 3: third-and-2, gun 11 personnel with the back to the quarterback’s right, against seven in the box (four linemen, the Sam on the line outside the tight end, Mike and Will 3½ yards deep) and one deep safety; the three receivers and their man-coverage defenders are outside the picture.













TipAnswer





On a handoff, six blockers (five linemen and the tight end) against seven in the box: one defender free, and on third-and-2 one free defender is usually enough.
Two kinds of run get a hat on every hat. A designed quarterback run makes the running back the seventh blocker: on QB power (Figure 18.9) the back kicks out the Sam, the guard pulls for the Mike, and seven blockers meet seven defenders. A read gets there the other way, by leaving one defender unblocked and reading him: a zone read or power read makes it six blockers plus a read against seven. A QB draw is tempting against man coverage too, because defenders turn their backs to chase receivers and the middle empties. (A sneak is the shortest version of the same idea, if the line to gain were a yard or less.)
But man coverage has a catch. In man, one of the box defenders, usually a linebacker, is assigned to the running back. When the back stays in to block, as on QB power or a draw, that defender has nobody to cover, and good defenses tell him to attack the run instead (coaches call him a hug or green dog player: he “hugs” the back, and when the back blocks, he comes). So the count stays an honest seven on seven, but none of the seven is busy with a pass, and on a QB draw the man who had the back is already looking at the quarterback. Power, which blocks him, suits this defense better than the draw.
The defense’s likely answer is to account for the quarterback: put a spy on him (from How defenses answer the option), or bring the deep safety down as an eighth man and live with no help deep. Either choice gives something back to the passing game, which is exactly the trade the quarterback’s legs create.

title: Option Football: Reading Defenders Instead of Blocking Them
text:
Takeaways

An option leaves one defender unblocked on purpose and reads him. Whatever he does, the ball goes to the runner he isn’t playing, so the read does a blocker’s work and the offense gets back the man a handoff leaves free.
The usual read key is the end man on the line of scrimmage; find him before the snap, and predict give or keep from his first step: if he can tackle the back, keep; if he can’t, give.
The families differ by who runs where and who is read: the zone read (back inside, quarterback outside, read the backside end), the inverted veer (back outside, quarterback inside behind a puller, read the play-side end; bash also puts the back outside but reads the backside end behind zone blocking), the speed option (quarterback and pitch man at the edge), the triple option (dive, keep, pitch, with two reads) and the midline (read a defensive tackle).
Designed quarterback runs (power, counter, draw, sweep) don’t read anyone; they turn the running back into a blocker. Their price, like every option’s, is hits on the quarterback.
Defenses answer with assignment football, the scrape exchange and gap exchanges, slow-playing the read, an extra man in the box, and hitting the quarterback; offenses answer back with bash, arc, new read keys and RPOs.
The NFL adopted the read in 2012, cooled on it, and returned to it with Jackson, Hurts and Allen. Designed quarterback runs look efficient per play, but selection and situation inflate that; their real value is what they do to the defense on every other run.

title: Perimeter Runs and Misdirection: Jet Sweeps, Reverses, and the Wing-T’s Children
text:
The edge is a race
Third quarter, second-and-8. For the fourth time today a receiver sprints across the formation in jet motion just as the ball is snapped. The first time he got the ball and ran around the left end for eleven yards. The next two times the quarterback stuck the ball in his belly and pulled it out, and both linebackers took three hard steps toward him anyway, while the running back went the other way. This time both linebackers sprint left again, the safety on that side races up to meet the receiver at the corner, and the quarterback hands the ball to the running back going right, into a hole where a linebacker stood a moment ago. Nobody on the left side of the field touched the ball, and every one of them helped make the play. This chapter is about why the defense keeps chasing a receiver who mostly doesn’t get the ball, and what happens to defenses that stop.
You’ll be able to:
How to read the diagrams. Offense is blue circles, defense orange squares; left and right are always the offense’s. LT, LG, C, RG and RT are the five offensive linemen, Q the quarterback, R the running back, Y the tight end, and X, Z and H receivers (each caption says where they line up). In the Wing-T pictures F is the fullback, H the halfback and WB the wingback. Defensive linemen are labelled by technique number; W and M are the Will and Mike linebackers, S the Sam, NB the nickel back, CB a cornerback, FS and SS the safeties. Lines ending in a short bar are blocks, arrows are paths, the thick dark arrow is the ball carrier, and dashed orange arrows are how the defense reacts.
Everything you have seen in the run game so far has been a fight in a phone booth. On inside zone or power, blockers and defenders start a yard apart, and the run hits before the defense can move very far. Runs to the perimeter, the edge of the formation and the open grass outside it, are a different contest. The ball carrier has 10 or 15 yards of sideways running to do before he can turn upfield, and every defender on the field has time to see where he is going and run there too. An outside run is a race between the ball and the defense’s pursuit, the whole team running to the ball.
The defense organizes that race with two jobs. One defender on each side is the force player (more on him in Run Fits): his job is to get outside the ball and turn it back inside, toward everyone else. Everyone else pursues, each on an angle aimed at where the ball carrier will be, not where he is. If the force player holds and the pursuit is fast, an outside run dies for no gain or a loss, and losing yards behind the line is the outside run’s signature failure.
Who is the force player? The coverage decides, so it changes from snap to snap, but a rule of thumb gets you most of the way: he is usually the outermost defender standing near the line on that side. That is often an outside linebacker or a nickel back lined up outside the tight end or slot. If a safety has walked down to about seven or eight yards deep outside the formation, it’s probably him. If the cornerback is squatting at five yards with a safety deep behind him (the look of Cover 2), the corner is the force. You’ll hear a close cousin, contain. Both mean “nothing gets outside me.” Coaches say force for the defender who meets a run coming at him and turns it in, and contain for the man whose rule is to keep the ball, or a scrambling quarterback, from ever getting outside him. That matters most on the side the play is leaving, as you’ll see.
So the defense wants to pursue fast. And that is the opening for everything else in this chapter. A defense that flows hard to stop the sweep leaves the other side of the field empty and its linebackers a step out of place. The offense can punish that in two ways: run the ball back where the defense came from, or simply make the defense think the ball is going somewhere it isn’t.

        say(fld, p, 9.6, -5.6, "left side:\nnobody home", color=GREEN, fontsize=7.2, weight="bold")
        say(fld, p, -5.6, -8.4, "the end chases\nfrom behind", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
        say(fld, p, -6.4, 9.6, "caught behind\nthe line", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
    else:
        for pts in ([(4.5, -2.4), (4.3, -0.6)], [(4.5, 1.4), (4.2, 3.2)], [(4.5, 4.9), (4.0, 6.6)],
                    [(8.0, 8.0), (7.2, 9.0)], [(12.0, -6.0), (11.7, -4.2)]):
            flow(fld, p, pts)
        say(fld, p, 9.6, 3.0, "linebackers wait\nto be sure", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
        say(fld, p, -6.6, 9.4, "the back\nwins the edge", color=GREEN, fontsize=7, weight="bold")
    ax.set_title("Defense reacts slowly" if not fast else "Defense flies to the ball", fontsize=9, loc="left",
                 color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.5))
dilemma(axes[0], False)
dilemma(axes[1], True)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 19.1: The defense’s dilemma on an outside run to the right (here a toss from under center; the two receivers, X and Z, are split wide). Left: if the defenders read and react slowly, the back gets outside the end before the linebackers and the safety arrive, and the race is lost. Right: if they all sprint to the ball at the snap (dashed orange arrows), the Sam and the safety beat the back to the edge and he is tackled behind the line (red X). But the left side of the field is now empty (green shading) and the linebackers have run themselves out of the middle. Plays that go back that way, or fake one way and go the other, exist to punish the fast defense.
Perimeter runs punish a defense that is slow to the edge. Misdirection, any play design that gets the defense to commit in one direction while the ball goes another, punishes a defense that is fast to it. The two families need each other: misdirection only works if the defense has a reason to run hard, and the only reason it has is that the perimeter run will beat it if it doesn’t.

section: The perimeter blocks: crack and seal
text:
The perimeter blocks: crack and seal
Outside runs need two kinds of block that you haven’t met yet, because inside runs rarely need them.
A crack block is a block thrown by a player lined up outside the play, usually a wide receiver or a wingback, who comes back toward the ball and hits a defender from the side. The usual target is a linebacker or safety who is watching the ball carrier and running to the edge, which is why the block is so effective: the defender’s eyes are on the ball, his momentum is going outside, and the blocker arrives from a direction he isn’t looking. You saw one animated in 02-04, where a condensed split put the receiver close enough to crack in a step or two.
A seal block is any block whose job is to wall a defender off from the ball’s path, rather than to move him. On an outside run that usually means pinning an inside defender inside: the tight end steps down onto an end lined up on his inside shoulder, gets his body between that end and the sideline, and the back runs outside the wall. A seal doesn’t need to drive the defender back a yard; it only needs to stay in the way while the ball goes by. Coaches use the word loosely (a log block by a puller who gets outside a defender and pins him in is a kind of seal), but the idea is always the same: you don’t move him, you shut him off.
The two blocks together make the classic outside run of the modern NFL, the crack-toss. 02-04’s animation showed the crack and the puller. Here are the parts it skipped: the seal, exactly who replaces whom, and (after the figure) the rule that governs the crack and the defense’s answer to it.


Show the Python
off = check_legal(line() + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -6.5, -0.5, "R"),
                            O("Y", "TE", LINE_D, 4.8), O("U", "TE", LINE_D, -4.8),
                            O("Z", "WR", OFF_D, 8.6), O("X", "WR", OFF_D, -9.5)])
dfn = front(pe=("7", 4.2), pt=("3", 2.35), bt=("1", -0.7), be=("5", -4.0),
            lbs=(("WILL", 4.5, -2.6, "W"), ("MIKE", 4.5, 1.4, "M"), ("SAM", 4.2, 7.0, "S")),
            cb=(-11.0, 12.6), safeties=((12.0, -6.5), (11.0, 7.0)))
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=10, title="Crack-toss: the crack, the seal and the replace")
p.pitch("RB", t=0.3)
go_to(p, "QB", (-2.7, 1.0), "path", speed=3.0)
go_to(p, "RB", (12.5, 10.3), "run", via=[(-5.8, 3.0), (-5.2, 6.2), (-4.2, 8.6), (-2.6, 10.1)])
go_to(p, "Z", (3.4, 7.5), via=[(-0.2, 8.2)])                       # the crack, from the side
go_to(p, "Y", (0.2, 4.5), via=[(-0.3, 5.0)])                       # the seal: step down, stay outside him
go_to(p, "RG", (3.8, 12.0), "pull", via=[(-1.9, 2.6), (-2.8, 6.0), (-2.9, 8.6), (-1.4, 11.0)])   # pull and replace
go_to(p, "RT", (0.4, 2.6), via=[(-0.4, 3.0)])                      # pin the 3
go_to(p, "C", (3.2, 1.4), via=[(-0.2, 0.7)])                       # climb to the Mike
go_to(p, "LG", (0.5, -0.1), via=[(-0.4, -0.9)])                    # cut off the 1

go_to(p, "U", (0.4, -3.4), via=[(-0.5, -4.4)])                     # cut off the backside end
go_to(p, "X", (8.0, -10.0), "route")                               # run the corner off
p.highlight("Y", color=PURPLE); p.highlight("RG", color=PURPLE)

fld.ax.add_patch(Circle((float(zx), float(zy)), 0.98, fc="none", ec=GREEN, lw=2.0, zorder=3.5))
flow(fld, p, [(6.5, 12.6), (4.8, 12.5)], lw=1.3)                   # the corner comes up

Figure 19.2: Crack-toss right from a condensed two-tight-end set (12 personnel; Z lines up only about 8½ yards from the ball, a yard off the line). The quarterback tosses to the back (R) heading right. Z (green ring) cracks back inside on the Sam linebacker (S), the force player. The purple rings are the two blockers who make the crack possible: the tight end Y seals the 7-technique end lined up on his inside shoulder, and the right guard pulls behind the line and replaces Z on the cornerback, kicking him out as he comes up. The right tackle blocks down on the 3-technique so the guard can leave (pin-and-pull). The back turns up in the lane between the crack and the kick-out; the safety (SS) is the defender left over. Backside, the linemen and the second tight end (U) cut off pursuit.





Read Figure 19.2 as a list of problems and answers. The Sam linebacker lined up outside the tight end is the defense’s force player: if he gets outside the ball, the toss is dead. Nobody on the line can reach him in time, but Z, lined up just outside him, can hit him from the side before he gets going. The end is lined up on the tight end’s inside shoulder (a 7-technique), so Y only has to keep him there: one step down, body between the end and the sideline, and hold. (If the end were lined up outside Y, in a 9, keeping him inside would take a reach, the hardest block a tight end is asked to make, and offenses usually build a different answer for that look.) The cornerback is now unblocked, so a lineman pulls around both blocks to get him. That’s crack-and-replace: the receiver leaves his usual man to crack inside, and a puller replaces him.
Who pulls varies, and this is why the 02-04 animation pulled the guard. Here the right tackle blocks down on the 3-technique and the right guard pulls behind him, the pin-and-pull logic of 03-03: the tackle has the better angle on the 3, the guard is free to go. Some teams pull the tackle instead, which is a shorter trip, as long as the guard can handle the 3 on his own; some pull both, and the second puller goes after the safety who is left over here. Every block on the play is an angle the defender wasn’t expecting.
The cost is that crack-toss is fragile in two specific ways. If the cracked defender sees it coming, he can duck under the crack and be in the backfield, and the puller has to choose between him and the corner. And the cornerback has an answer of his own: when he sees the receiver go inside, he yells “crack!” and comes up hard to take the force job himself. The puller still has him to block, but he now meets him sooner and tighter than planned, can only kick him out, and the back is forced to cut up inside, back toward the pursuit, instead of getting around the edge.






CautionCommon misconception



“A crack block is a cheap shot.” A legal crack is a hands-first block, from the side and chest-high, aimed at the defender’s near number or armpit on the side he’s facing. Receivers practise it the way linemen practise down blocks. What’s illegal is hitting him low, hitting him in the head or neck, or leading with the shoulder, and if all the blocker can see is the back of the defender’s jersey, it isn’t a crack at all but a block in the back (10 yards), so a well-coached receiver lets that man go and finds another.1
The rules are strict because a defender hit from the side by a player running at him can’t protect himself. The crackback rule (Rule 12, Section 2, Article 6) covers a player who lines up more than two yards outside the tackle, or starts in the backfield and is in motion or moves out that wide, and then blocks back toward the spot of the snap: within five yards of the line of scrimmage he may not hit a defender below the waist, nor in the head or neck (or in any other way banned against a defenseless player). It costs 15 yards.2 Since 2019 a separate rule has also banned any blindside block, a forcible hit with the helmet, forearm or shoulder thrown while the blocker’s path is toward or parallel to his own end line, outside the tight area around the snap,3 and from the 2026 season blindside blocks are one of the five fouls in the league’s three-strike suspension policy (three in a season means a one-game suspension).4 A crack runs parallel to the line, which is why the shoulder shot is gone and the hands-first block is the only kind you’ll see.

title: Perimeter Runs and Misdirection: Jet Sweeps, Reverses, and the Wing-T’s Children
section: The jet sweep: a running start at the edge
text:
The jet sweep: a running start at the edge
The jet sweep is the purest perimeter play: a receiver in jet motion takes the ball from the quarterback without slowing down and races for the edge on the side he’s heading toward. You met the motion and the defense’s three answers to it (travel, bump, spin) in 02-06. This section is about the run itself, and about what it does to the linebackers.
Three things make it work:

The running start. The receiver is already at full speed when the ball is snapped; the defenders start from a standstill. The simple model in 02-06 put the gap at about three yards after one second. On a play that is a race to the corner, three yards is the race.
The angle. He takes the ball roughly in front of the quarterback, and within a stride or two he is past the far guard, already outside the box and heading for the edge. The defense’s force player has to cover more ground than he does.
What it does to everyone else. Linebackers are taught to read keys: usually a guard, the running back, or the backfield as a whole, depending on the defense (05-04 covers which). But no key-reading rule lets a linebacker ignore a man crossing the backfield at full speed who might have the ball, so his first steps tend to go with him. Whether or not the receiver gets the ball, the defense’s whole second level is now moving sideways, which is exactly what the rest of this chapter takes advantage of.

The mechanics vary. In some offenses the quarterback hands the ball off in front of himself; in others (Kansas City’s, for one) he flips it forward a foot or two to a receiver passing in front of him, a “pop” or shovel toss that counts as a forward pass in the record books. The flip has a hidden advantage: if the exchange is botched, the ball on the ground is an incomplete pass, not a fumble.5 (It also means those plays won’t appear in the run data later in this chapter.) Either way, the runner is gone before the defense has finished its first step.
Some offenses go one step further and make the jet an option. The quarterback reads a defender on the jet side, usually the end or whoever is responsible for the edge, exactly as 03-04’s read option reads an end: if that defender widens to take the jet, the quarterback hands the ball inside; if he sits inside, the jet man gets it. The motion man’s job is the same either way, which is why the defense can’t tell from his speed or his path.


Show the Python
def jet_formation():
    """11 personnel from the gun: X on the line far left, H in the left slot (off the line), the tight end
    attached on the right and Z off the line outside him. Seven on the line: the five linemen, X and Y."""
    return check_legal(line() + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, -1.8, "R"),
                                 O("X", "WR", LINE_D, -15.0), O("H", "WR", OFF_D, -8.5),
                                 O("Y", "TE", LINE_D, 4.8), O("Z", "WR", OFF_D, 12.0)])


def nickel(cb_l=-15.0, cb_r=12.5):
    return front(pe=("9", 5.7), pt=("3", 2.35), bt=("1", -0.7), be=("5", -4.0),
                 lbs=(("WILL", 4.5, -2.2, "W"), ("MIKE", 4.5, 1.8, "M")),
                 extra=(("NB", "NB", 5.0, -8.0, "NB"),), cb=(cb_l, cb_r))


def jet_sweep_play():
    p = Play(jet_formation(), nickel(), los=35, to_go=10)
    motion_to(p, "Z", [(-2.8, 7.5)], (-3.0, 2.2), speed=6.5)          # jet motion: ball snapped 2 yd short of Q
    go_to(p, "Z", (13.0, -15.2), "run", speed=9.0,
          via=[(-3.1, -0.5), (-2.6, -6.0), (-0.8, -11.0), (3.0, -13.6), (7.5, -14.6)])
    p.handoff("Z", t=0.3)
    go_to(p, "QB", (-4.4, -0.3), "path", speed=2.5)
    go_to(p, "QB", (-5.6, 1.2), "path", speed=3.0, delay=0.1)          # then carry out a fake
    go_to(p, "RB", (-1.4, 6.6), "path", delay=0.3, speed=5.5, via=[(-4.0, 0.6), (-2.8, 3.8)])  # fake a run right
    # the line steps left (zone steps toward the sweep) and engages the down linemen
    go_to(p, "LT", (0.4, -4.7), via=[(-0.4, -3.9)], speed=2.4)        # reach the 5
    go_to(p, "LG", (1.1, -2.6), via=[(-0.4, -2.0)], speed=2.2)        # step, then climb through the gap
    go_to(p, "C", (0.4, -1.4), via=[(-0.4, -0.8)], speed=2.2)         # reach the 1
    go_to(p, "RG", (0.3, 1.6), speed=1.6)                             # cut off the 3
    go_to(p, "RT", (0.2, 3.5), speed=1.6)
    go_to(p, "Y", (0.3, 5.1), via=[(-0.5, 4.7)], speed=1.6)
    go_to(p, "H", (2.6, -10.4), via=[(-0.6, -9.6)], speed=4.5)        # arc to the nickel
    go_to(p, "X", (4.4, -16.6), speed=4.0, via=[(1.5, -15.4)])         # stalk the corner
    # the defense: the down linemen fight the blocks; the second level flows hard to the jet
    go_to(p, "DE_L", (1.3, -5.3), "path", speed=1.2)
    go_to(p, "DT_L", (1.3, -1.9), "path", speed=1.0)
    go_to(p, "DT_R", (1.2, 1.7), "path", speed=0.8)
    go_to(p, "DE_R", (1.6, 4.4), "path", speed=1.0)
    go_to(p, "WILL", (5.2, -11.2), "path", speed=5.5, via=[(4.0, -5.0), (4.4, -8.6)])
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (5.6, -8.6), "path", speed=5.5, delay=0.05, via=[(4.2, -1.0), (4.6, -5.0)])
    go_to(p, "NB", (3.2, -10.9), "path", speed=4.5, delay=0.15)
    go_to(p, "LCB", (5.6, -16.9), "path", speed=2.8, via=[(7.6, -15.6)])
    go_to(p, "FS", (9.6, -13.4), "path", speed=5.0, delay=0.3, via=[(11.0, -10.0)])
    go_to(p, "SS", (10.4, -5.0), "path", speed=4.0, delay=0.4, via=[(11.5, 0.0)])
    go_to(p, "RCB", (8.5, 8.8), "path", speed=2.5, delay=0.6)
    return p


def jet_empty(ax, fld, t):
    """Last panel: shade the side the running back faked to, now empty of linebackers."""
    if t < 2.0:
        return
    x0, y0 = (float(v) for v in fld.xy(*JET_PLAY.to_abs(5.0, 4.4)))
    ax.add_patch(Ellipse((x0, y0), 9.0, 6.4, fc=GREEN, alpha=0.12, ec=GREEN, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1.5))
    ax.text(x0, y0 + 1.0, "empty", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7.5, color=GREEN, fontweight="bold",
            zorder=12)


JET_PLAY = jet_sweep_play()
JET_T = [-1.0, 0.5, 1.3, 2.6]
JET_NOTES = ["Jet motion: Z sprints across;\nnobody follows him (zone)",
             "Handoff at full speed; both\nlinebackers' first steps go with him",
             "Linebackers and nickel fly to the\njet; H and X block on the edge",
             "Z is around the corner. The right\nside, where R faked, is empty"]
animated(JET_PLAY, JET_T, JET_NOTES, lateral=(-19.5, 14.0), window=(-7.0, 13.5),
         rings=(("Z", style.THIRD), ("MIKE", style.DEFENSE), ("WILL", style.DEFENSE)), decorate=jet_empty)





  
  Your browser does not support the video tag.



Figure 19.3: A jet sweep left against a nickel defense playing zone (simulated, BDB-format tracking; faint lines are each player’s path so far). 1: Z (green ring) sprints across in jet motion; nobody follows him, so the defense is in zone. 2: Z takes the handoff at full speed, and both linebackers (orange rings) are already moving toward him. 3: the linebackers and the nickel back run hard to the jet side; H blocks the nickel and X the cornerback, while the offensive line steps left and engages the defensive linemen. 4: Z is outside and past the linebackers, with the deep safety (FS) coming down as the last man to beat. The shaded area on the right, where the running back (R) faked a run, has no linebacker left in it: that is where the plays later in this chapter attack.




Look at the third and fourth panels of Figure 19.3, not at Z. Five defenders (both linebackers, the nickel back, the cornerback and the free safety) are all running toward the left sideline, and the defense’s right side is down to two defensive linemen held at the line, a cornerback out wide and a safety rotating over the top, around grass nobody is using. That is the jet sweep’s second job. Even when it gains four yards, it teaches the defense that the left sideline is where the danger is, and a defense that has learned that lesson will run there faster next time.
What it gives up. The jet sweep is a high-variance play. When the force player holds the edge, the runner is caught going sideways behind the line, and the loss can be large because he started deep. The exchange happens at full speed between two players moving in different directions, which adds fumble risk (the forward flip is one answer). The risk is real but small: over the ten seasons 2016–2025, receivers lost a fumble on about 0.65% of their carries, against 0.46% for running backs, a difference of roughly one extra lost fumble every 500 carries (course calculation from nflverse play-by-play; the receivers’ figure rests on only 26 lost fumbles). And it uses a receiver as a runner, so every jet sweep is a play on which that receiver isn’t running a route. Coaches accept all of that because of what the motion does to the defense when the ball goes somewhere else, which is the subject of the rest of the chapter.

section: End-arounds and reverses: sending the ball back
text:
End-arounds and reverses: sending the ball back
If the defense is going to run hard one way, the obvious punishment is to give the ball to someone running the other way. There are two classic ways to do it, and broadcasters mix up their names all the time.
An end-around gives the ball to a receiver who comes back behind the line from his spot outside and runs toward the other side of the field. The quarterback hands it to him directly: one exchange. Usually the play starts with a fake the opposite way, so the defense flows toward the fake while the receiver runs away from it. (The name is older than the modern receiver: the “end” in end-around is the end of the line, the position that became the wide receiver and the tight end.)
A reverse has two exchanges. The ball first goes to a player running one way, usually a running back on a sweep, and he hands or pitches it to a teammate running the other way. The ball’s direction reverses behind the line. A double reverse does it again.


Show the Python
def reverse_play(kind):
    off = check_legal(line() + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -6.5, 0.0, "R"),
                                O("X", "WR", LINE_D, -11.0), O("H", "WR", OFF_D, -7.0),
                                O("Y", "TE", LINE_D, 4.8), O("Z", "WR", OFF_D, 9.0)])
    dfn = front(pe=("9", 5.7), be=("5", -4.0), lbs=(("WILL", 4.5, -2.6, "W"), ("MIKE", 4.5, 1.6, "M")),
                extra=(("NB", "NB", 5.0, -8.2, "NB"),), cb=(-11.0, 10.0))
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=10)
    if kind == "end-around":
        go_to(p, "QB", (-3.4, 0.6), "path", speed=2.5)                         # fake to the back ...
        go_to(p, "RB", (-1.0, 5.2), "path", speed=6.0, via=[(-5.0, 2.6)])      # ... who runs the fake right
        go_to(p, "Z", (9.0, -11.8), "run", speed=7.5,
              via=[(-3.2, 6.5), (-4.1, 2.0), (-4.2, -2.5), (-3.4, -6.4), (-0.4, -9.4)])
        p.handoff("Z", t=1.1)
        go_to(p, "QB", (2.8, -5.4), "path", speed=4.5, delay=0.5, via=[(-2.4, -3.2), (0.4, -4.6)])   # then lead
        swaps = [("QB", 1.1)]
    else:
        go_to(p, "QB", (-4.0, 1.0), "path", speed=4.5)
        p.handoff("RB", t=0.4)
        go_to(p, "RB", (-4.8, 4.6), "run", speed=6.0, via=[(-4.6, 1.8)])
        go_to(p, "Z", (8.5, -11.8), "run", speed=7.5,
              via=[(-3.4, 7.0), (-5.0, 5.0), (-5.4, 0.0), (-4.4, -5.8), (-0.4, -9.4)])
        p.handoff("Z", t=0.85)
        go_to(p, "QB", (2.8, -5.4), "path", speed=4.5, delay=0.3, via=[(-2.6, -2.8), (0.4, -4.6)])
        swaps = [("QB", 0.4), ("RB", 0.85)]
    for k, end in (("C", (0.2, 0.8)), ("RG", (0.3, 2.6)), ("RT", (0.3, 4.2)), ("Y", (0.4, 6.0)),
                   ("LG", (0.2, -0.6))):
        go_to(p, k, end)                                                       # the line shows flow right
    go_to(p, "LT", (0.7, -4.6), via=[(-0.6, -3.9)])                            # get outside the end, wall him in
    go_to(p, "X", (5.0, -11.0))                                                # stalk the corner
    go_to(p, "H", (3.8, -8.4))                                                 # block the nickel
    p.highlight("Z")
    return p, swaps


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.9))
for ax, kind, ttl in [(axes[0], "end-around", "End-around: one exchange"),
                      (axes[1], "reverse", "Reverse: two exchanges")]:
    p, swaps = reverse_play(kind)
    f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-14.5, 12.5), window=(-9.6, 12.0), title=False)
    for pts in ([(4.5, -2.6), (3.6, 1.5), (3.0, 4.0)], [(4.5, 1.6), (3.4, 5.4)], [(12.0, -8.0), (9.6, -1.0)],
                [(12.0, 8.0), (8.6, 9.6)]):
        flow(f, p, pts)
    x, y = _P(f, p, 1.0, -4.0)
    ax.add_patch(Circle((float(x), float(y)), 1.25, fc="none", ec=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.8, zorder=7))
    for who, t in swaps:                                                       # mark each exchange point
        bx, by = (float(v) for v in _P(f, p, *p.position(who, t)))
        ax.add_patch(Ellipse((bx, by), 1.2, 0.75, fc=style.BALL, ec="white", lw=0.6, zorder=11))
    if kind == "end-around":
        say(f, p, -6.8, 6.0, "fake", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
        point_to(f, p, (-8.2, -3.6), p.position("QB", 1.1), "Q to Z", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
    else:
        point_to(f, p, (-8.0, -3.6), p.position("QB", 0.4), "1st: Q to R", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
        point_to(f, p, (-8.2, 7.0), p.position("RB", 0.85), "2nd: R to Z", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
    say(f, p, 7.8, 2.2, "defense flows right", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
    ax.set_title(ttl, fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 19.4: Two ways to send the ball back against a defense flowing right (dashed orange arrows). Left, an end-around: the quarterback fakes a handoff to the running back going right, then hands the ball to Z, who came behind the line from his spot on the right and runs left. One exchange (football icon), about four yards deep. Right, a reverse: the quarterback hands off to the back going right, and the back hands the ball to Z coming the other way. Two exchanges, about six yards deep. In both, the play depends on the backside end (ringed). Here he does his job and stays home, so the left tackle has to get outside him and wall him inside, and the quarterback, once the ball is gone, leads up the field for the first defender who turns back.





Both plays bet on the same thing: that the defense will chase the first action hard enough to leave the other side empty. Both are beaten by the same defender, the end on the backside (the side away from the first action). He is the contain player on that side, and his rule in most defenses is not to chase flat down the line after the fake. He shuffles along behind the line at about the depth of the ball, trailing the play, and checks the three things that can come back his way before he commits: a bootleg, a counter, a reverse.6 If he stays home like that, the reverse runs straight into him six yards behind the line of scrimmage. So the offense has to account for him. In Figure 19.4 the left tackle’s job is to get outside him and wall him inside, and the quarterback, once the ball is gone, leads up the field for the first pursuer who turns back. It is one of the few plays on which a quarterback is asked to block at all, and most coaches ask only that he get in the way of somebody.
They are also rare. The NFL’s play-by-play descriptions mention a reverse on only about 60 runs in the ten regular seasons 2016–2025, and on just one each in 2023 and 2024. Scorers don’t always note a reverse, so treat those counts as a floor, but the trend is real enough. Those flagged runs averaged about eight and a half yards (course calculation), which is the pattern this chapter ends on: a play that pays well because it’s called only when the defense has been caught chasing.
When you see one, ask two questions. Which defender was responsible for the backside, and did he chase? And how deep was the exchange? A reverse handed off seven yards behind the line has to gain seven yards just to get back to zero. It’s a play for a defense that has been caught chasing on film, not a play to run every week.

title: Perimeter Runs and Misdirection: Jet Sweeps, Reverses, and the Wing-T’s Children
section: The Wing-T: an order of football
text:
The Wing-T: an order of football
Most of the ideas in this chapter were organized into a system long before the NFL adopted them. The Wing-T, the formation with a wingback just outside and behind the tight end, was built by Dave Nelson at Maine and then the University of Delaware, where he coached from 1951 to 1965. His assistant Harold “Tubby” Raymond succeeded him and ran it for 36 more seasons, until 2001, winning 300 games, a total few coaches have reached at one school.7 Raymond, a Michigan graduate famous for painting a portrait of each of his senior players, and his assistant Ted Kempski wrote the book on it, and the title says what it is about: The Delaware Wing-T: An Order of Football.8
The problem Nelson is usually said to have faced is the one every underdog coach faces: his players were usually not bigger or faster than the other team’s. He couldn’t win by blocking every defender one-on-one, so he built an offense that made defenders block themselves, by running to the wrong place.

The buck sweep
The Wing-T’s signature play is the buck sweep. Its name tells you its two halves: the fullback fakes the buck (an old word for a straight plunge up the middle) and the halfback runs the sweep.
The buck sweep is power football, the same family as the gap schemes of 03-03: down blocks to wall off the inside, pullers to add blockers at the point of attack. It is also a close relative of the most famous run in NFL history, Vince Lombardi’s Packers sweep of the 1960s, which also pulled both guards around a down-blocking line, and an ancestor of today’s pin-and-pull.


Show the Python
def wing_t():
    """The Wing-T: Q under center, F behind him, H behind the left tackle, WB just outside and behind Y,
    X split on the left. Seven on the line: five linemen, X and Y."""
    return check_legal(line() + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("FB", "FB", -4.5, 0.0, "F"),
                                 O("HB", "RB", -4.5, -3.2, "H"), O("Y", "TE", LINE_D, 4.8),
                                 O("WB", "WR", -1.6, 6.5, "WB"), O("X", "WR", LINE_D, -12.0)])


def wing_t_d():
    """Four-man front, three linebackers, two deep: the right corner squats at 5 yards (he is the force)."""
    return front(pe=("9", 5.7), pt=("3", 2.35), bt=("1", -0.7), be=("5", -4.0),
                 lbs=(("WILL", 4.5, -2.6, "W"), ("MIKE", 4.5, 1.3, "M"), ("SAM", 4.3, 4.6, "S")),
                 cb=(-12.0, 10.8), safeties=((13.0, -6.0), (13.0, 7.5)))


p = Play(wing_t(), wing_t_d(), los=35, to_go=10, title="Buck sweep right")
p.players["RCB"] = p.players["RCB"].moved(d=5.0)                                   # squatting corner
go_to(p, "QB", (-2.8, -0.9), "path", speed=3.0)                                  # reverse pivot
go_to(p, "QB", (-5.4, -7.6), "path", speed=4.0, delay=0.25, via=[(-3.0, -1.6), (-3.6, -4.8)])  # fake a boot
p.handoff("HB", t=0.8)
go_to(p, "HB", (12.5, 8.9), "run", via=[(-5.6, -1.0), (-5.8, 3.0), (-5.0, 6.6), (-3.2, 8.8), (1.0, 9.0)])
go_to(p, "FB", (-1.0, 1.0), "path", via=[(-2.6, 0.9)])                           # fake the buck, fill
p.block("WB", target="DE_R"); p.block("Y", target="SAM"); p.block("RT", target="DT_R")
go_to(p, "RG", (3.6, 10.2), "pull", via=[(-1.8, 2.6), (-2.0, 6.0), (-1.2, 9.6)])   # kick out the force
go_to(p, "LG", (3.0, 7.4), "pull", via=[(-2.9, -0.7), (-3.2, 4.6), (-2.2, 7.4)])  # turn up inside
go_to(p, "C", (0.2, -1.0), via=[(-0.4, -0.6)])                                   # block back
go_to(p, "LT", (0.3, -3.4), via=[(-0.6, -3.8)])                                  # cut off
go_to(p, "X", (8.0, -12.0), "route")
p.highlight("HB"); p.highlight("RG", color=PURPLE); p.highlight("LG", color=PURPLE)
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-14.5, 16.0), window=(-10.0, 14.0))
flow(fld, p, [(5.0, 10.8), (4.1, 10.6)], lw=1.3)                                 # the corner comes up
flow(fld, p, [(4.5, 1.3), (5.7, 3.4), (5.6, 6.2), (4.7, 7.3)], lw=1.3)          # the Mike scrapes, behind the Sam
ghost(fld, p, 4.0, 7.9, "M")
point_to(fld, p, (1.0, 13.6), (3.7, 10.3), "kick-out", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
point_to(fld, p, (8.6, 3.2), (3.1, 7.4), "LG turns up\non the Mike", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
point_to(fld, p, (-8.2, 9.4), (-1.9, 5.0), "RG pull", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
point_to(fld, p, (-8.2, 3.6), (-3.2, 2.6), "LG pull", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
say(fld, p, -7.9, -8.0, "Q: fake\nthe boot", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()








Figure 19.5: The Wing-T buck sweep, right (wingback WB just outside and behind the tight end Y; halfback H, green ring, behind the left tackle; fullback F behind the quarterback; split end X on the left). Everything on the play side blocks down: the wingback on the end, Y on the Sam, the right tackle on the 3-technique. Both guards pull (purple rings), the right guard on the shallower path. He kicks out the first defender outside the wingback’s block, here the cornerback, who is the force player because the defense is in a two-deep look with the safety (SS) deep behind him. The left guard follows and turns up inside the kick-out on the Mike, who has scraped outside (dashed outline: where the Mike gets to). The center blocks back into the hole the left guard left, and the fullback fakes the buck into the gap the right guard left. The halfback takes the handoff and follows the guards; the quarterback fakes a bootleg the other way.





What makes it a Wing-T play rather than just a sweep is everything that happens in the backfield before the ball goes outside. The quarterback reverse-pivots: instead of turning toward the sweep, he spins the other way, turning his back to the line of scrimmage, so for a moment nobody on the defense can see the ball. In that first second the defense sees the fullback plunge at the middle, the quarterback’s back, the halfback run across, and both guards pull. Then, a beat later, the quarterback rolls the other way without the ball. A linebacker who reads the fullback steps up; one who reads the guards flies outside; one who reads the quarterback drifts backside. Only one of them is right. That is what the buck sweep punishes: a defense that respects the fullback. Every linebacker who takes a step up to stop the buck is a step late to the edge, where two guards are about to arrive.
You’ll rarely hear “buck sweep” on an NFL broadcast, but you’ll see its shape. From the high sideline camera, look for two offensive linemen leaving the line at the snap and running sideways behind it toward one sideline while everyone in front of them blocks down toward the ball. When the back follows them around the end, that’s the buck sweep’s descendant, usually called a pull sweep or pin-and-pull in the modern game.


Series football: every play is the answer to the last one
That first second is the point. Raymond’s Wing-T was built as series football: groups of plays that begin with the same backfield action and end differently, each one designed to beat the defense’s reaction to another. Chris Brown, writing about Raymond’s influence, put the idea in one line: “each time a team tries to stop one thing, it opens itself up to something else.”9 The buck series is the classic example.


Show the Python
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 3.5))
ax.set_xlim(0, 100); ax.set_ylim(0, 66); ax.axis("off")


def box(x, y, w, h, title, body, ec, fc, title_fs=8.4, gap=6.4):
    ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((x - w / 2, y - h / 2), w, h, boxstyle="round,pad=0.4,rounding_size=1.4",
                                fc=fc, ec=ec, lw=1.3, zorder=2))
    ax.text(x - w / 2 + 2, y + h / 2 - 2.0, title, ha="left", va="top", fontsize=title_fs, fontweight="bold",
            color=style.INK, zorder=3)
    ax.text(x - w / 2 + 2, y + h / 2 - gap, body, ha="left", va="top", fontsize=7.0, color=style.INK_2,
            zorder=3, linespacing=1.2)


box(15, 31, 27, 30, "Buck sweep\n(the base play)", "F fakes up the\nmiddle; both guards\npull; H sweeps\nbehind them; Q\nfakes the boot away",
    style.OFFENSE, style.OFFENSE_TINT, title_fs=8.6, gap=10.0)
rows = [(54.5, "Buck trap", "F keeps it up the middle; a guard traps\nthe lineman left unblocked", "linebackers run\nwith the guards"),
        (39.0, "Waggle", "Q keeps it and boots away behind the\npulling guards: run or throw", "backside end\nchases the sweep"),
        (23.5, "Counter or reverse", "WB comes back the other way,\nagainst the flow", "whole defense\nflows to the sweep"),
        (8.0, "Play-action deep", "same fake; the ends run past the\nsafety who came up to stop it", "a safety flies up\nto force")]
for y, title, body, why in rows:
    box(78, y, 42, 12.5, title, body, GREEN, style.SURFACE)
    ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((29.5, 31 + (y - 31) * 0.35), (56.0, y), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=11,
                                 color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.3, zorder=1))
    ax.text(43.5, 31 + (y - 31) * 0.68 + 2.6, why, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.6,
            color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, style="italic", zorder=3, linespacing=1.15,
            bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none"))
ax.text(43.5, 64, "if the defense...", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
ax.text(78, 64, "...the series answers with", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7, color=GREEN)
plt.show()








Figure 19.6: The buck series as a conversation. Every play starts with the same first second (blue box, left). Each orange arrow is something the defense might do to stop the buck sweep, and the box it leads to is the play in the series that punishes that reaction. The plays are illustrative of the Wing-T’s logic; real playbooks have more members and different names.





Read Figure 19.6 from left to right. If the linebackers learn to fly outside with the pulling guards, the fullback, who faked into the middle on the sweep, keeps the ball this time, and the middle they just vacated is where he runs: the buck trap, a trap in which the defensive lineman left unblocked at the snap gets hit from the side by a pulling guard. If the backside end chases the sweep, the quarterback keeps the ball and rolls out behind him. If the whole defense flows, the wingback comes back the other way on a counter or reverse. If a safety races up to make the tackle on the sweep, the receivers run past him on play-action (a fake handoff followed by a pass).
None of those plays is clever on its own. A trap is a trap. What makes the series work is that each play looks like the others for the first second, and that the defender’s correct reaction to one is his wrong reaction to another.
“Looks like” needs one honest qualification. The backfield is identical on the sweep and the trap, but the guards aren’t. On the sweep both guards pull toward the sweep side. On the buck trap the far guard (the left guard here) still pulls toward that side, only a short distance, to trap the first defensive lineman past the center, while the near guard blocks straight ahead to the linebacker. So a linebacker who reads the backfield, or who reads the far guard, sees the sweep starting and flies outside; one who reads the near guard sees him coming straight at him and knows. That is why the series has more than one answer. The trap beats linebackers who chase the backfield and the pulling guard. The waggle beats the backside end. The counter beats a whole defense that flows: the wingback, who starts toward the sweep side as if to block, turns back and takes the ball going the other way, against the flow. The defense can’t stop all of them by being fast or by being patient; it has to be right, play after play, about a fake it can’t see through. That is what “an order of football” means: plays called in a deliberate order, each one asking the defense a question the previous one made it answer.
The buck series is the most famous, not the only one. The Wing-T’s other base family is the belly series. The fullback, instead of faking up the middle, takes the ball off tackle behind down blocks, often with a guard pulling to kick out the end man (a close cousin of 03-03’s power). When the defense starts collapsing on the fullback, the quarterback fakes to him and keeps it, or runs an option to the outside off the same fake, and there is a waggle off belly action too, for teams that have learned to key the fullback. Buck and belly are two conversations running at once: one starts by threatening the middle and goes outside, the other starts off tackle and goes wider still.10


The waggle
One member of the series reaches straight into the modern NFL. The waggle is the Wing-T’s play-action bootleg: the quarterback fakes the buck sweep (or another run) one way and rolls out the other, behind both guards, who pull to that side to protect him, with receivers spread at three depths on that side. Notice which way the guards go: opposite the backfield’s flow. A linebacker who reads the backs runs one way while the blockers go the other.


Show the Python
p = Play(wing_t(), wing_t_d(), los=35, to_go=10, title="Waggle left")
p.players["RCB"] = p.players["RCB"].moved(d=5.0)
go_to(p, "QB", (-2.8, -0.9), "path", speed=3.0)
go_to(p, "QB", (-4.6, -10.4), "run", speed=5.0, delay=0.35, via=[(-4.0, -1.6), (-5.8, -2.6), (-5.6, -6.0)])
go_to(p, "HB", (-3.0, 7.0), "path", via=[(-5.4, -1.0), (-5.0, 3.2)])            # fake the sweep
go_to(p, "FB", (0.6, -10.8), "route", via=[(-2.6, 0.9), (-2.7, -0.8), (-2.8, -5.0), (-1.6, -8.6)])  # fake the buck, then the flat
go_to(p, "LG", (0.3, -4.1), "pull", via=[(-1.4, -2.4)])                          # kick out the end
go_to(p, "RG", (-0.9, -6.4), "pull", via=[(-1.8, 0.4), (-2.3, -4.4)])  # protect the quarterback
go_to(p, "Y", (13.0, -9.0), "route", via=[(1.6, 3.6), (6.5, 2.4)])               # crosser, released inside the Sam
go_to(p, "X", (18.5, -12.4), "route")                                            # clear out deep
go_to(p, "WB", (2.0, 4.0), via=[(-1.0, 5.8)])
for k, end in (("C", (0.2, 0.8)), ("RT", (0.3, 4.1)), ("LT", (0.2, -2.2))):
    go_to(p, k, end)
p.highlight("QB"); p.highlight("RG", color=PURPLE); p.highlight("LG", color=PURPLE)
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-16.0, 13.0), window=(-11.0, 20.5))
flow(fld, p, [(1.0, -4.0), (0.7, -3.3)], lw=1.3)
x, y = _P(fld, p, 1.0, -4.0)
fld.ax.add_patch(Circle((float(x), float(y)), 1.25, fc="none", ec=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.8, zorder=7))
for pts in ([(4.5, -2.6), (3.8, 0.4)], [(4.5, 1.3), (3.6, 4.6)], [(4.3, 4.6), (3.6, 6.6)]):
    flow(fld, p, pts, lw=1.3)
say(fld, p, -2.6, 9.6, "the sweep fake", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
say(fld, p, 2.8, -10.6, "short:\nflat", color=GREEN, fontsize=7, weight="bold")
say(fld, p, 14.2, -4.2, "medium: crossing route", color=GREEN, fontsize=7, weight="bold")
say(fld, p, 17.4, -8.6, "deep: clear-out", color=GREEN, fontsize=7, weight="bold")
say(fld, p, -9.0, -9.4, "Q: run\nor throw", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()








Figure 19.7: The waggle, from the same Wing-T look and the same first second as the buck sweep. The halfback and fullback carry out their fakes to the right, and the linebackers flow with them (dashed orange). The quarterback keeps the ball and rolls left. Both guards pull left, the opposite way from the backfield’s flow: the left guard kicks out the backside end (ringed), who is the first defender outside the tackle, and the right guard pulls flat behind him as the quarterback’s personal protector, turning up on the first defender who comes for the edge. The quarterback has three receivers on his side at three depths: the fullback slipping into the flat (the area near the sideline just past the line) after his fake, the tight end Y on a crossing route from the other side, and the split end X running deep to clear out, taking the cornerback with him and emptying the space underneath. If nobody comes up to stop him, he runs.





If that picture looks familiar, it should. Replace the Wing-T backfield with a single back running outside zone and you have the bootleg that Mike Shanahan’s and Kyle Shanahan’s offenses, and Sean McVay’s, built on (taught in full in Play-Action, Bootlegs, and Screens, where the version with no pulling guard at all, the naked bootleg, gets its own treatment). The waggle’s idea, fake hard one way and put the quarterback on the edge the other way with three receivers at three depths, survived when the formation that invented it disappeared.

title: Perimeter Runs and Misdirection: Jet Sweeps, Reverses, and the Wing-T’s Children
text:
The Wing-T’s children
You will almost never see a true Wing-T in the NFL. You will see its children every Sunday.
The jet sweep. Wing-T offenses already sent the wingback in motion, and the fly sweep, a handoff to a wingback or slot in full-speed motion behind an under-center quarterback, grew up beside them. Its exact origin is murky: many coaches credit Gene Beck’s Delano High School teams in California in the 1950s. In the 1980s and 1990s coaches such as Mark Speckman built whole offenses around it, with a trap, a bootleg and passes off the same motion, and spread it through high school clinics; Dan Hawkins carried it from small-college Willamette to Boise State, where it helped launch the Broncos’ run of winning offenses in 1999 and 2000.11 So the fly sweep is the Wing-T’s adopted child, not its own: Wing-T coaches, who already had the motion, took the play in, and the two are now usually taught together. Move the quarterback back to the shotgun, call the motion “jet,” and you have the NFL play. Pro Football Focus counted 174 jet sweep runs across the league in 2017 and 309 in 2018, when they averaged 6.1 yards a carry and Sean McVay’s Rams ran 48 of them, playoffs included.12
Gus Malzahn’s Auburn. The clearest line from Delaware to modern football runs through Gus Malzahn. As a young high school coach in Arkansas in the early 1990s, he taught himself offense from Raymond and Kempski’s book; by the late 1990s he had moved to an up-tempo shotgun spread, but kept the Wing-T’s plays and its series logic, and at Auburn he ran the buck sweep from the shotgun with pulling linemen and a receiver faking an end-around the other way.13 His 2013 team averaged more than 300 rushing yards a game, the first SEC team to do it in almost thirty years.
The NFL’s misdirection revival. When the McVay Rams and Kyle Shanahan’s 49ers made jet motion a weekly staple in the late 2010s, they were doing what Raymond did with his backfield: one picture, several plays. Shanahan went a step further with Deebo Samuel, a receiver he lined up in the backfield, put in motion and handed the ball on sweeps, reverses and runs between the tackles, so that “which player is the runner” became one more question the defense had to get right. Andy Reid’s Chiefs used jet and orbit motion to set up flips, shovels and screens back the other way. The formations are modern; the logic is the Wing-T’s.
