title: Perimeter Runs and Misdirection: Jet Sweeps, Reverses, and the Wing-T’s Children
section: Eye candy: half a second is a gap
text:
Eye candy: half a second is a gap
Here is the payoff from Figure 19.3. Once the defense has learned to fly at jet motion, the motion itself becomes a weapon even when the ball goes somewhere else. Coaches call this eye candy: motion and fakes by players who won’t get the ball, designed to pull defenders’ eyes and first steps the wrong way.
How much can a fake buy? Not much, and that’s enough. A linebacker who takes one hard step toward a jet fake and then has to come back has lost about half a second. Linebackers move at something like 5 to 7 yards a second when they’re trying to fill a hole; half a second is three yards. A hole on an inside run is a yard or two wide and stays open for less than a second. A linebacker three yards out of place doesn’t fill it.


Show the Python
def eye_candy_play(jet=True):
    p = Play(jet_formation(), front(pe=("7", 4.0), pt=("1", 0.7), bt=("3", -2.35), be=("5", -4.0),
                                    lbs=(("WILL", 4.5, -2.4, "W"), ("MIKE", 4.5, 1.2, "M")),
                                    extra=(("NB", "NB", 5.0, -8.0, "NB"),), cb=(-15.0, 12.5)),
             los=35, to_go=10)
    if jet:
        motion_to(p, "Z", [(-2.8, 7.5)], (-3.0, 2.2), speed=6.5)
        go_to(p, "Z", (2.0, -15.5), "path", speed=8.0, via=[(-3.1, -0.5), (-2.6, -6.0), (-1.0, -11.0)])
        go_to(p, "QB", (-4.5, -0.6), "path", speed=2.4)                 # ride the fake to Z ...
        go_to(p, "QB", (-4.9, -0.1), "path", speed=2.0)                 # ... then turn to hand off
        go_to(p, "MIKE", (4.4, -1.2), "path", speed=4.4)                # first steps: toward the jet
        go_to(p, "MIKE", (3.6, 1.4), "path", speed=4.6)                 # then back to the run, late
        go_to(p, "WILL", (4.3, -4.6), "path", speed=3.6)
        go_to(p, "WILL", (3.6, -1.0), "path", speed=4.5)
        go_to(p, "DE_L", (1.4, -6.6), "path", speed=2.2)                # widens to respect the jet
        go_to(p, "NB", (3.6, -10.2), "path", speed=3.5)
        go_to(p, "FS", (10.0, -10.5), "path", speed=3.0, delay=0.2)
    else:
        go_to(p, "MIKE", (2.5, 2.4), "path", speed=5.2)                 # no fake: he reads the run and fills
        go_to(p, "WILL", (3.2, -0.5), "path", speed=4.5)
        go_to(p, "DE_L", (-1.8, -0.6), "path", speed=2.4, delay=0.3, via=[(0.4, -3.2)])  # no fake: he chases from behind
    p.handoff("RB", t=0.6)
    go_to(p, "RB", (10.5, 3.8), "run", delay=0.15, speed=6.5,
          via=[(-4.6, -0.4), (-2.6, 1.8), (0.4, 3.0), (5.0, 3.7)])
    # inside zone right: the double teams and the climbs (03-02)
    go_to(p, "C", (0.5, 0.6), speed=2.0); go_to(p, "DT_R", (1.5, 0.3), "path", speed=1.0)
    go_to(p, "RG", (3.0, 1.1), via=[(-0.2, 1.1), (0.3, 1.2)], speed=2.6)
    go_to(p, "RT", (0.6, 3.8), speed=2.0); go_to(p, "DE_R", (1.6, 4.2), "path", speed=0.9)
    go_to(p, "Y", (3.6, 6.2), via=[(-0.2, 4.4), (0.4, 4.6)], speed=2.6)
    go_to(p, "LT", (0.5, -2.6), speed=2.0); go_to(p, "DT_L", (1.4, -2.4), "path", speed=0.9)
    go_to(p, "LG", (3.3, -1.3), via=[(-0.2, -1.9), (0.3, -2.0)], speed=2.6)
    go_to(p, "H", (2.4, -9.8), speed=3.5)
    go_to(p, "X", (10.0, -15.0), "route")
    go_to(p, "SS", (9.0, 4.0), "path", speed=3.5, delay=0.5)
    return p


EYE_T = [-0.9, 0.5, 1.0, 2.2]
EYE_NOTES = ["Jet motion: every defender's\neyes go to Z",
             "Jet fake. The Mike stepped toward Z;\ndashed outline: where he'd be without it",
             "The guard climbs to the Mike,\nwho is only now coming back",
             "R is through the hole. The end (5) widened\nfor the jet; his outline shows where he'd be"]
animated(eye_candy_play(True), EYE_T, EYE_NOTES, lateral=(-11.5, 10.5), window=(-7.0, 10.5),
         rings=(("MIKE", style.DEFENSE), ("RB", style.THIRD)), ghosts=(eye_candy_play(False), ["MIKE", "DE_L"]))





  
  Your browser does not support the video tag.



Figure 19.8: Eye candy: a jet fake left, an inside zone run right (simulated, BDB-format tracking). The dashed outlines are where the Mike linebacker (M) and the backside end (5) would be at the same moment if there had been no jet motion (a second simulation of the same play without the motion). 1: Z in jet motion; every defender’s eyes go to him. 2: at half a second the quarterback has faked to Z and is handing to R (green ring). The Mike (orange ring) stepped toward the jet; without the fake he would already be filling the hole. 3: the right guard climbs to the Mike, who is only now coming back. 4: the back is through the hole. The backside end widened for the jet; his dashed outline, near the ball, shows where he would have been chasing the back from behind.




Two defenders were taken out of Figure 19.8 without being blocked. The Mike linebacker’s first step went the wrong way, so the guard who climbed to him got there in time. And the backside end, who on a normal inside zone run is the unblocked defender who can chase the back down from behind (03-02 spent a whole section on him), widened to protect against the jet sweep, so he was out of the play. One receiver running across the formation did the work of two blockers.
That is the trade eye candy makes. The receiver in motion isn’t blocking anybody, so the offense starts a man short at the point of attack, and the motion has to hold more than one defender for the play to come out ahead. It usually does only when the defense believes the motion. Eye candy is only as good as the last time the ball actually went there. Robert Woods, one of the 2018 Rams’ two main jet-sweep runners, carried the ball only 19 times in the regular season,14 but the Rams faked the jet constantly; the defense had to treat every fake as real because some of them weren’t.
How often is “sometimes”? Nobody publishes a count of jet fakes, so there is no clean ratio, but the shape is clear. In 2018 NFL offenses shifted or motioned before the snap on 43% of their plays, roughly 27 plays a game, while even the Rams, the heaviest jet-sweep team in the league, handed the ball off on a jet sweep about twice a game.15 Not every motion is jet motion, but the proportions tell you the real thing can be rare. It just can’t be absent.
Jet motion is the most common kind of eye candy, not the only one. An orbit motion behind the quarterback, a running back faking a sweep one way while the ball goes the other, a tight end running across the formation as though he’s going to block, the quarterback carrying out a bootleg fake after he hands the ball off: all of them are designed to make a linebacker’s eyes and feet do something for a fraction of a second that they shouldn’t.






CautionCommon misconception



“The jet motion was wasted; the guy didn’t even get the ball.” On most plays with jet motion the ball goes to someone else, by design. Judge the motion by what the defenders near it did. If two linebackers took a step toward the motion man and the run went through the gap one of them left, the motion was the most important “block” on the play.

title: Perimeter Runs and Misdirection: Jet Sweeps, Reverses, and the Wing-T’s Children
text:
How defenses fight back
None of this is free for the offense, because good defenses train against every trick in this chapter.

Keep the backside honest. The backside end and the backside cornerback have rules on outside runs, and the first rule is “don’t chase until the ball has crossed the formation”: check boot, counter, reverse first. That kills reverses and end-arounds and makes bootlegs and waggles harder, at the price of one fewer defender pursuing the play that really does go outside.
Answer the crack. When a receiver cracks inside, the cornerback over him yells “crack!” and steps up to replace the man who was cracked as the force player. The puller still has him to block, but meets him sooner and tighter than planned and can only kick him out, so the back has to cut inside, back toward the pursuit. This is a zone rule: a cornerback playing man coverage on that receiver follows him inside, so in man the defense needs someone else, usually a safety, to take over the force.
Spin to the motion. Rotating a safety down toward the jet side at the snap (the spin of 02-06) puts an extra defender at the edge, so the linebackers don’t have to chase. The offense’s counter is to run the other way, into the side the safety left.
Read your keys, not the motion. This is the hard-line version of the keys idea from the jet sweep section: tell the linebackers to read their guard (or the running back) and to leave the motion man entirely to the safeties and corners. A guard stepping right means the run is going right, whatever the jet man is doing. The problem is that the jet man is going very fast, and if nobody on the second level gives him a thought, the edge belongs to him.

Every one of these answers is Figure 19.1 again from the defense’s side: what stops misdirection makes the defense slower to the perimeter, and the reverse. The full catalog of run fits, including who forces and who spills (makes the ball bounce wider, toward help), is in Run Fits.

section: Constraint plays: why you can’t just run it more
text:
Constraint plays: why you can’t just run it more
Here is a puzzle in the numbers. When an NFL wide receiver carries the ball on a run, almost always on a jet sweep, an end-around or a reverse, the play works much better on average than a running back’s carry. So why do teams hand it to receivers less than once a game?


Show the Python (load 2016-2025 runs and tag the ball carrier’s position)
from gridiron.data import pbp, nfl

YEARS = list(range(2016, 2026))
runs = pbp(YEARS, columns=["season", "season_type", "play_type", "rusher_player_id", "epa", "success",
                           "yards_gained", "qb_kneel", "down", "game_id", "posteam", "fumble_lost", "desc"])
runs = runs[(runs["season_type"] == "REG") & (runs["play_type"] == "run") & (runs["qb_kneel"] == 0)
            & runs["down"].notna()]
rosters = nfl().load_rosters(YEARS).to_pandas()[["season", "gsis_id", "position"]]
rosters = rosters.drop_duplicates(["season", "gsis_id"])
runs = runs.merge(rosters, left_on=["season", "rusher_player_id"], right_on=["season", "gsis_id"], how="left")
rb_wr = runs[runs["position"].isin(["RB", "WR"])]
by_season = rb_wr.groupby(["season", "position"])["epa"].mean().unstack()
team_games = runs.groupby("season")["game_id"].nunique() * 2
wr_per_game = rb_wr[rb_wr["position"] == "WR"].groupby("season").size() / team_games
profile = rb_wr.groupby("position").agg(
    carries=("epa", "size"), epa=("epa", "mean"), success=("success", "mean"),
    lost=("yards_gained", lambda s: (s < 0).mean()), big=("yards_gained", lambda s: (s >= 10).mean()))
fumbles = rb_wr.groupby("position")["fumble_lost"].agg(["mean", "sum"])          # lost fumbles per carry
wr = rb_wr[rb_wr["position"] == "WR"]
wr_se = wr.groupby("season")["epa"].agg(lambda e: e.std() / np.sqrt(len(e)))     # noise in one season's mean
team_wr = wr.groupby(["season", "posteam"])["epa"].agg(["size", "mean"])          # volume vs value, by team-season
vol_r = team_wr["size"].corr(team_wr["mean"])
la18 = runs[(runs["season"] == 2018) & (runs["posteam"] == "LA")]
reverses = runs[runs["desc"].str.contains(r"\breverse\b", case=False, na=False)]  # scorer flagged a reverse




Show the Python
fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.0), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.35, 1]})
WR_C, RB_C = style.OFFENSE, style.MUTED
a1.axhline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.9, zorder=1)
for pos, col, lab in (("WR", WR_C, "Wide receivers"), ("RB", RB_C, "Running backs")):
    a1.plot(by_season.index, by_season[pos], color=col, lw=2, marker="o", ms=4.5, mec=style.SURFACE, mew=1.2)
    a1.text(2025.35, by_season[pos].iloc[-1], lab, color=style.INK_2, fontsize=7.5, va="center", ha="left")
a1.set_xlim(2015.5, 2028.6)
a1.set_xticks([2016, 2018, 2020, 2022, 2024])
a1.set_ylabel("EPA per carry", fontsize=8)
a1.set_title("Value per carry, by season", fontsize=9)
a1.tick_params(labelsize=7.5)
labels = ["Lost yards", "Successful (EPA > 0)", "Gained 10+ yards"]
cols = ["lost", "success", "big"]
yy = np.arange(len(cols))
for off_, pos, col in ((-0.19, "WR", WR_C), (0.19, "RB", RB_C)):
    vals = profile.loc[pos, cols].values * 100
    a2.barh(yy + off_, vals, height=0.36, color=col, edgecolor=style.SURFACE, linewidth=1.5)
    for y_, v in zip(yy + off_, vals):
        a2.text(v + 1.0, y_, f"{v:.0f}%", va="center", fontsize=7.2, color=style.INK_2)
a2.set_yticks(yy, labels, fontsize=7.5)
a2.invert_yaxis()
a2.set_xlim(0, 64)
a2.set_xlabel("share of carries (%)", fontsize=8)
a2.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=7.5)
a2.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
a2.set_title("Outcomes, 2016–2025", fontsize=9)
fig.legend(handles=[Line2D([], [], color=WR_C, lw=6, label="Wide receivers"),
                    Line2D([], [], color=RB_C, lw=6, label="Running backs")],
           loc="lower center", ncol=2, fontsize=7.5, bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.02), frameon=False)
fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0.07, 1, 1), w_pad=1.5)
plt.show()








Figure 19.9: Wide receivers as runners, NFL regular seasons 2016–2025. Left: expected points added (EPA) per carry by the ball carrier’s position. A running back’s average carry loses a little expected value every season; a wide receiver’s is worth more than a running back’s in every season, and is positive in eight of the ten. Right: the shape of the outcomes, all ten seasons pooled. Receiver runs are more often successful and twice as often go for 10 or more yards, but they also lose yards more often. League-wide there were only 0.6 to 0.9 receiver carries per team per game. Runs only (jet flips scored as forward passes are not included); kneel-downs removed; position from nflverse season rosters. Data: nflverse play-by-play via nflreadpy; course calculation.





The numbers in Figure 19.9 are striking. Across ten seasons, a running back’s carry was worth about −0.07 expected points on average and succeeded (gained expected points) 39% of the time. A receiver’s carry was worth about +0.10 and succeeded 51% of the time, and it gained ten or more yards on 22% of carries, more than twice the running backs’ rate. That gap, 0.17 expected points a play, is enormous. In 01-02’s terms, a tenth of a point per play is the difference between a good offense and an average one; the receiver’s edge over the back is nearly twice that.
But notice the other bar: receivers lose yards on 15% of their carries, against 10% for backs. That is the jet sweep and reverse caught behind the line. And notice the volume: well under one receiver carry per team per game, every season. Teams aren’t ignoring free yards. The yards come from the rarity.
Coaches call plays like these constraint plays, plays whose main job is to punish the defense for overplaying the offense’s base plays, the bread-and-butter runs and passes it calls most. The idea is developed fully in Constraint Theory, but the shape is already visible here. A jet sweep gains a lot when the defense isn’t ready for it, and the defense isn’t ready for it because the offense mostly runs something else. Run it twenty times a game and the defense would stop playing the inside run and start sitting on the edge, the jet sweep would turn into a two-yard loss, and the inside run would get worse too, because the linebackers would no longer be taking those hard first steps toward the motion. The value of a misdirection play lives partly in the plays it isn’t.
You may be thinking of the 2018 Rams, who ran the jet sweep twice as often as anyone and still got about +0.44 expected points per receiver carry (more in the Film room). Fair objection, and the data answers part of it. Across the ten seasons, the teams that handed the ball to receivers more often did not do worse with it: the correlation between a team’s receiver carries in a season and their average value is close to zero (about 0.07). But “more often” is relative. The Rams’ 35 receiver carries were 8% of their 437 runs, about two a game, and no team in those ten seasons went much beyond four a game. Nobody has tried twenty, so the data can’t show the collapse. What it shows is that every team, the Rams included, stayed in the range where the play still surprises. Their trick was keeping the motion constant and the carry rare.
The same caution applies when you read the chart. Some of the receivers’ edge is selection: coaches call these plays when the film says the defense is vulnerable to them, and the defense often isn’t expecting a receiver run at all. That is not a flaw in the numbers; it’s the point. A constraint play’s average looks great because it’s called at the right moments. And don’t read much into one season’s wiggle, such as 2024’s dip below zero: with only 300 to 500 receiver carries a season, any single season’s average is uncertain by about a tenth of a point either way.






ImportantWhy it exists



Misdirection exists because pursuit works. A defense that runs to the ball fast and together is the best answer to almost every run in football, so the offense needs plays that make running fast to the ball a mistake: plays that go back the other way (reverses, counters, waggles) and motion that makes the defense run to the wrong place (eye candy). The price is risk and blockers: misdirection plays lose yards more often, take longer to develop, and use players as decoys who could have been blocking. They work only in the right dose, which is why the best offenses build them into series, so the base play and its answers look the same until it’s too late.

title: Perimeter Runs and Misdirection: Jet Sweeps, Reverses, and the Wing-T’s Children
text:
Film room






NoteFilm room: Delaware, 1966-2001 (Tubby Raymond’s Wing-T)



There is no tracking data for Raymond’s Delaware teams, and you don’t need it. If you can find old Blue Hens film, watch the backfield and not the ball for the first second of any play: the fullback plunging, the quarterback spinning with his back to the line, the halfback crossing, both guards pulling. Then watch the linebackers. On the buck sweep they are a step slow to the outside because the fullback’s fake made them look inside first; on the trap and the waggle they are a step out of the middle because the sweep has been killing them. The plays changed little for decades. Delaware kept winning with them because the defense’s problem never went away: a defense has to react to something, and everything it can react to is a fake on most plays.








NoteFilm room: Auburn 2013 (Gus Malzahn)



Malzahn’s 2013 Auburn team, led by quarterback Nick Marshall and running back Tre Mason, ran for more than 300 yards a game and reached the national championship game. What to notice: the buck sweep from the shotgun. The guards pull exactly as in Figure 19.5, but the quarterback is five yards deep and the “halfback” is lined up beside him. A receiver often runs across the backfield the other way, faking the end-around, the Wing-T’s buck fake moved to a different player. And the series is there too: the same look produces the sweep, an inside run and a quarterback keep.16








NoteFilm room: Los Angeles Rams 2018 (Sean McVay)



The 2018 Rams made the jet sweep an NFL staple: PFF counted 48 of them, playoffs included, twice as many as any other team.17 In the nflverse play-by-play, Rams wide receivers carried the ball 35 times in the regular season, and those carries averaged about +0.44 expected points, among the best in the league that year (course calculation). The two counts differ because a charting service tags the play, while play-by-play records who carried the ball, and some jet plays are scored as passes. What to notice: the jet sweep is blocked like outside zone, the whole line stepping toward the sweep, so for the first second it looks exactly like the Rams’ base run going the same direction. Then watch the next play with the same motion: often the ball goes the other way, or the quarterback fakes it and throws.








NoteFilm room: San Francisco 49ers, Super Bowl LIV (2019 season)



Deebo Samuel was a rookie receiver in 2019 who ran the ball 14 times for 159 yards and three touchdowns in the regular season.18 In Super Bowl LIV against Kansas City he carried three times for 53 yards, two of them gains of 32 and 14 yards around the ends, at the time the most rushing yards by a wide receiver in a Super Bowl.19 What to notice: the 49ers didn’t hide that Samuel might get the ball. They moved him around so the defense had to decide, on every snap, whether the receiver crossing the formation was a decoy. When linebackers stayed home to stop the inside run, he got the ball at the edge; when they chased him, the 49ers handed the ball to Raheem Mostert on their zone run going away from the motion. By 2021, as 02-06 showed, Samuel was effectively a second running back.

title: Perimeter Runs and Misdirection: Jet Sweeps, Reverses, and the Wing-T’s Children
text:
Watch for it on Sunday






TipWatch for it



Watch the second level. On every play with jet or orbit motion:
Before the snap

Find the motion man and the side he’s heading to. Does anyone travel with him (man coverage), does everyone slide a spot (zone), or does a safety spin down toward his side?
Find the two linebackers and the backside end. These are the players whose reaction you’ll grade.

At the snap: forget the ball for one second

Watch the linebackers’ eyes and feet. Did they take a step toward the motion? Did they keep going?
Did the backside end chase flat down the line after the motion, or stay home, trailing at the depth of the ball and watching for a boot, counter or reverse?

After the play

Where did the ball go? If it went with the motion: did the force player hold the edge, or did the runner beat him? Was there a crack block on the edge?
If it went away from the motion: were the linebackers late because they chased? That’s eye candy working.
If the defense has been chasing all game, start expecting the play that goes back the other way: a counter, a reverse, a bootleg.

For your prediction log (01-06): on every jet motion, write G (the motion man gets it) or F (fake) before the snap, then C if the linebackers chased, H if they held. Count a forward flip to the motion man as G: to the defense it’s the same play. After a game you’ll have a small table of what this defense does with motion, which is exactly what offensive coordinators study during the week.

title: Perimeter Runs and Misdirection: Jet Sweeps, Reverses, and the Wing-T’s Children
text:
Predict the play






TipPredict the play



Drill 1. First-and-10, ball on the offense’s own 35. The offense has run three jet sweeps to the left today, for 9, 12 and 7 yards, and on all three the defensive end on the right (the 9, ringed) chased the jet flat down the line from the backside. Here Z goes in jet motion again, right to left. This time, as he crosses, the free safety (FS, ringed) comes down hard toward the left edge and the strong safety rotates to the deep middle. The two linebackers (W and M) don’t move. Should the quarterback give Z the jet sweep? If not, what would you run off the same motion, and why?


Show the Python
p = Play(jet_formation(), nickel(), los=35, to_go=10, title="Drill 1: jet motion, safety spins down")
p.players["Z"] = p.players["Z"].moved(d=-3.0, w=2.2)
p.players["FS"] = p.players["FS"].moved(d=7.0, w=-11.0)
p.players["SS"] = p.players["SS"].moved(d=13.5, w=0.5)
p.highlight("Z", color=style.THIRD); p.highlight("FS", color=style.DEFENSE); p.highlight("DE_R", color=style.DEFENSE)
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-19.0, 15.0), window=(-8.0, 16.0))
dashed(fld, p, [(-1.5, 12.0), (-2.8, 7.5), (-3.0, 3.3)])
ghost(fld, p, 12.0, -8.0, "FS"); ghost(fld, p, 12.0, 8.0, "SS")
flow(fld, p, [(11.3, -8.6), (7.7, -10.6)], lw=1.2)
flow(fld, p, [(12.2, 7.0), (13.4, 1.6)], lw=1.2)
flow(fld, p, [(2.0, 5.9), (2.5, 4.2), (2.5, 0.2)], lw=1.2, alpha=0.6)
say(fld, p, -5.4, 9.4, "jet motion", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
say(fld, p, 9.6, -15.2, "free safety\nspins down", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
say(fld, p, 3.2, 9.6, "the 9 chased the\nlast three jets", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()








Figure 19.10: Drill 1, at the snap. Z (green ring) is in jet motion from the right (dashed blue path). The free safety (FS, ringed) has spun down toward the left edge and the strong safety (SS) has rotated to the deep middle; hollow outlines show where they started. The linebackers (W, M) haven’t moved. The right end (the 9, ringed) is the player who chased the last three jets (dashed orange).











TipAnswer





No jet sweep. Fake it, and come back right: a bootleg or a quarterback keep to the right, or an outside run that way. The free safety’s spin has done the job the linebackers usually do: the defense now has an extra player at the left edge before the play starts, so the jet sweep would run into the cornerback, the nickel and a safety coming downhill. Meanwhile the linebackers stayed home, so a fake to the jet won’t move them either.
The space is on the right. The strong safety has left it for the deep middle, and the one defender whose job is to guard that side against plays coming back, the backside end, has chased the jet three times in a row. If he chases the fake again, nobody contains the quarterback: fake the jet left and boot right, with the tight end and the running back releasing to that side (the waggle’s descendant). That is the series idea from the Wing-T section applied to one defender. If the end stays home this time, the outside run right, into the side the strong safety left, is the safer call.
Compare this with the jet drill in 02-06, where the linebackers didn’t move and nobody replaced them at the edge, so the jet was the right answer. Same linebackers, different safety, opposite call. An offense that runs the jet as an option (see the jet sweep section) lets the quarterback make the first half of that decision at the snap.











TipPredict the play



Drill 2. Second-and-4. The offense is in the Wing-T and has run the buck sweep right twice in a row from this look. Both times, at the snap, the Mike and Will linebackers (ringed) ran hard to the right with the pulling guards (their paths from those plays are shown in orange). The offense lines up in the same formation again. What does series football call now, and why?


Show the Python
p = Play(wing_t(), wing_t_d(), los=35, to_go=None, title="Drill 2: same look, third time")
p.players["RCB"] = p.players["RCB"].moved(d=5.0)
p.highlight("MIKE", color=style.DEFENSE); p.highlight("WILL", color=style.DEFENSE)
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-14.5, 14.5), window=(-7.0, 15.5))
flow(fld, p, [(4.5, 1.3), (5.7, 4.4), (5.0, 8.2)], lw=1.4)
flow(fld, p, [(4.5, -2.6), (3.3, 0.2), (3.0, 3.8)], lw=1.4)
say(fld, p, 8.6, 4.6, "last two plays: the\nlinebackers flew to\nthe pulling guards", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK,
    fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()








Figure 19.11: Drill 2: the Wing-T look again (wingback WB outside the tight end on the right, halfback H behind the left tackle, fullback F behind the quarterback). Dashed orange arrows show where the two linebackers (ringed) ran on the last two buck sweeps, as soon as they saw the guards pull.











TipAnswer





The buck trap: the fullback keeps the ball up the middle. The first second will look the same as the sweep: the quarterback reverse-pivots, the halfback runs across, the fullback heads for the middle, and the far (left) guard pulls toward the right exactly as he did on the sweep. But this time the fullback has the ball, and the left guard’s pull is a short one: he traps the first defensive lineman past the center, who was left unblocked at the snap, hitting him from the side. The fullback runs through the gap where that lineman was, straight into the space the two linebackers are about to vacate by chasing the pull. The more the linebackers trust what they saw on the last two plays, the bigger the hole.
Why not something else? The waggle punishes the backside end for chasing, and the drill told you about the linebackers. A reverse or counter punishes the whole defense flowing, and here only the second level is flowing hard. Series football means picking the member of the series that beats the specific reaction you saw. On second-and-4 an inside run that only needs four yards is also exactly the right risk.











TipPredict the play



Drill 3. First-and-10. The offense is in a condensed two-tight-end set, this time with X lined up tight on the left, about eight yards from the ball and inside the cornerback. It has run the crack-toss to the left twice from this look. Both times the cornerback (ringed) read X stepping inside, yelled “crack!” and came flying up to take the force (his paths are shown in orange), and the tosses gained 1 yard and lost 2. Same alignment again. You’re the offensive coordinator. What do you call, and what is X’s job?


Show the Python
off = check_legal(line() + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -6.8, 0.0, "R"),
                            O("Y", "TE", LINE_D, 4.8), O("U", "TE", LINE_D, -4.8),
                            O("X", "WR", OFF_D, -8.6), O("Z", "WR", OFF_D, 10.5)])
dfn = front(pe=("5", 4.0), pt=("1", 0.7), bt=("3", -2.35), be=("7", -4.2),
            lbs=(("WILL", 4.5, 2.6, "W"), ("MIKE", 4.5, -1.4, "M"), ("SAM", 4.2, -7.0, "S")),
            cb=(-12.4, 12.0), safeties=((11.0, -7.0), (12.0, 6.5)))
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=10, title="Drill 3: same look, third time")
p.highlight("X", color=style.THIRD); p.highlight("LCB", color=style.DEFENSE)
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-17.0, 14.0), window=(-8.5, 14.5))
flow(fld, p, [(6.0, -12.4), (2.4, -11.2), (0.8, -9.8)], lw=1.3)
say(fld, p, -3.6, -11.4, "X: inside\nthe corner", color=GREEN, fontsize=7)
say(fld, p, 8.6, -12.6, "last two plays:\ncorner flies up", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()








Figure 19.12: Drill 3: a condensed two-tight-end set to the left. X (green ring) is about 8½ yards from the ball, a yard off the line and inside the cornerback (CB, ringed). The Sam linebacker (S) is between the tight end U and X. Dashed orange: the cornerback’s reaction on the last two crack-tosses, straight up to the line as soon as X stepped inside.











TipAnswer





Fake the crack and throw it over the cornerback, or switch the blocks. The corner has learned that X stepping inside means “crack-toss,” and he is now reacting to that first step before he knows what it is. Use it:

The pass. Run the same toss fake. X takes his crack step inside, the corner flies up, and X turns upfield behind him. The deep safety on that side is the only defender who can help, and he has been watching two tosses too. This is a play-action pass, the family taught in Play-Action, Bootlegs, and Screens.
The run. Keep the toss, but swap jobs. A corner who sprints to the line is the easiest man on the field for X to block, because he is running straight at him, so X blocks the corner and the puller takes the Sam instead.

Either way the offense is doing to one cornerback what the Wing-T does to a whole defense: his correct answer to the last play is his wrong answer to this one. The defense’s counter-counter is to have the corner hold his ground for a count and let a safety take the force, which is why you’ll see crack looks answered differently from week to week.

title: Perimeter Runs and Misdirection: Jet Sweeps, Reverses, and the Wing-T’s Children
text:
Takeaways

Outside runs are a race between the ball and the defense’s pursuit. The defense wins it with a force player (usually the outermost defender near the line) who turns the ball back inside and everyone else pursuing fast. Perimeter plays punish a slow defense; misdirection punishes a fast one, and each family needs the other.
Two blocks make outside runs work: the crack block, a receiver or wing hitting an inside defender from the side (above the waist, by rule), and the seal block, walling a defender off rather than moving him. Together with a puller replacing the cracking receiver, they make the crack-toss.
The jet sweep turns jet motion’s running start into a race the defense starts a step behind, and pulls the linebackers sideways even when the ball goes elsewhere. End-arounds (one exchange) and reverses (two) send the ball back against the flow and live or die on the backside end, whose rule is to stay home and check boot, counter, reverse.
The Wing-T organized all of this as series football: the buck sweep and the plays that look the same for one second and punish each reaction to it (the trap, the waggle, the counter), with the belly series as a second conversation. Its children are the NFL’s jet sweeps, pull sweeps and bootlegs.
Eye candy is motion or a fake that holds defenders without blocking them. Half a second is about three yards, which is a gap. It works only as long as the motion is sometimes real.
Receiver runs are rare (under one per team-game) and, on average, much more valuable than running back carries, with more lost-yardage plays. They are constraint plays: their value comes from the base plays they punish, which is why you can’t simply run them more.

text:
Connections
Builds on: Gap Schemes (pullers, kick-outs, logs, trap, toss and pin-and-pull), Motion and Shifts (jet, fly and orbit motion, and the defense’s travel, bump and spin), Zone Running (outside zone, the backside end, the bootleg), Classic Formations (the Wing-T formation) and Spread and Modern Formations (condensed splits and the first look at the crack).
Sets up:

Play-Action, Bootlegs, and Screens: the waggle’s descendants, the bootleg and the naked bootleg, and the play-action passes that live off jet motion.
Run-Pass Options: jet motion and quick screens attached to inside runs, the modern way to put a defender in a bind on every snap.
Linebackers and the Second Level and Run Fits: keys, flow, force and spill, the defense’s side of everything in this chapter.
Constraint Theory and Sequencing: base plays, constraint plays and why the best offenses call them in a deliberate order.
The College Laboratory: the Wing-T, the wishbone and the spread option, and how college football keeps feeding the NFL ideas.

See also (case studies): The Shanahan Tree (wide zone, boots and jet motion as one system) and Andy Reid’s Chiefs (motion, shovels and the creative run game).
If you want to go deeper: Raymond and Kempski’s The Delaware Wing-T: An Order of Football is still the clearest statement of series football. Chris B. Brown’s The Art of Smart Football and his Grantland piece on Gus Malzahn trace the Wing-T into the modern spread. For the NFL version, watch a 2018 Rams or 2019–2021 49ers game on the All-22 and count the linebackers’ first steps on every jet motion.






NoteGo deeper



From diagrams to real tracking data. The two animations in this chapter are gridiron simulations in Big Data Bowl (BDB) coordinates, so real tracking data drops into the same drawing code. The 2025 Big Data Bowl release (2022 season, weeks 1–9) flags, for every player on every play, whether he was in motion at the snap, and records who carried the ball, so you can pull every run by a wide receiver who was moving at the snap (most of them jet sweeps) and watch the linebackers’ first steps for yourself. The data is hosted on Kaggle and needs a free login, so this code is not run when the book is built.


Show the Python (real Big Data Bowl tracking; not run in the build)
import pandas as pd
from gridiron import bdb, show_animation

plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")
player_play = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/player_play.csv")
players = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/players.csv")

# ball carriers on designed runs, with their roster position
carriers = player_play[player_play["hadRushAttempt"] == 1].merge(players[["nflId", "position"]], on="nflId")
jets = carriers[(carriers["position"] == "WR") & (carriers["inMotionAtBallSnap"] == True)]  # noqa: E712
print(len(jets), "runs by a wide receiver in motion at the snap")

g, pl = jets.iloc[0][["gameId", "playId"]]
trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_*.csv")
one = bdb.prepare(trk, plays, game_id=g, play_id=pl)
show_animation(one, times=[-1.0, 0.0, 0.6, 1.4])   # same call as the simulated plays

title: Passing Game Fundamentals: Routes, Timing, and Reads
text:
The passing problem: a race against the rush
Second-and-8 near midfield. The quarterback takes the snap under center, takes five quick steps backward, plants, hops forward once, and throws toward the sideline, to a patch of grass where nobody is standing. The receiver he is throwing to is still sprinting straight up the field, with the cornerback backpedalling in front of him. A beat later the receiver snaps his head around, cuts hard toward the sideline, and the ball arrives at that patch of grass at the same moment he does, a step ahead of the cornerback. The analyst says “that’s timing.” How did the quarterback know where to throw before the receiver got there? Why five steps and not three or seven? And when the cornerback does get there first, how does he decide to throw somewhere else? This chapter is about the three things that make every pass play work: the routes (where the receivers go), the drop (when the ball comes out), and the read (who gets it).
You’ll be able to…
Reading the diagrams: the conventions of What a Play Really Is (blue circles on offense, orange squares on defense, a green ring on the player to watch), plus a few that are new here. X is the wide receiver on the line, Z the one off it, Y usually the tight end, H the third receiver, and $ the nickel back (the slot cornerback). Blue arrows are routes. Orange arrows are defenders: dashed when he drops into a zone, solid when he runs with a receiver or drives on the ball. A dotted line with an arrowhead is a choice, a path he could take; the thin dotted line behind the quarterback is his footsteps. Grey routes are on the play but not the point of the picture. The small numbers on the left edge give the depth past the line of scrimmage.
A pass play has a clock on it, and the defense controls it: four or more rushers start running at the quarterback at the snap, and his linemen can’t hold them off forever. In the 2025 regular season the median pass left the quarterback’s hand 2.5 seconds after the snap.1 Be careful what that number means. It is not how long the line can hold; plenty of deep throws leave after three seconds, so a good pocket often lasts longer, and Pass Protection measures it. It is how long quarterbacks choose to hold the ball, and they choose short because every extra half-second is a gamble that the rush hasn’t arrived. Two and a half seconds is the working budget: the time for receivers to get somewhere useful, for the quarterback to decide, and for the ball to leave.
Inside that budget the offense solves three problems at once. Where: each receiver needs a path to open grass, or to a spot where his defender is at a disadvantage; that is his route. When: the quarterback must be ready to throw the moment the receiver gets there, not before (the defender is still close) and not after (the defender has recovered, or the rush has arrived); his footwork, the drop, synchronises the two. Who: up to five players can go out, and the quarterback needs a plan for choosing one in a second or two; that plan is the read. Every pass concept in the rest of Part 4 is a particular answer to those three questions.

title: Passing Game Fundamentals: Routes, Timing, and Reads
text:
NoteMadden vs. real life



In the video game a pass play is five fixed lines, and you choose a receiver by pressing his button whenever you like. In a real offense a route is a set of instructions that can change with the coverage and the down and distance, and the quarterback can’t wait until a receiver looks open. By the time a receiver looks open on a television screen, it is usually too late to throw it to him. Real quarterbacks throw to where a receiver is about to be open, on a count their feet keep.

title: Passing Game Fundamentals: Routes, Timing, and Reads
text:
Anatomy of a route
A route has four parts.

The release. His first steps off the line, getting past the man in front of him. Against a press cornerback standing nose to nose with him, who tries to jam him (hit him with both hands and knock him off his path), the release is a fight of its own; The Quick Game covers the release techniques.
The stem. The run upfield before the cut. A good stem looks the same for every route, so the defender can’t tell from it which way the receiver will break.
The break. The cut. Its depth is set by rule (“break at 12 yards”, measured from the line of scrimmage, not from where he lined up), and its direction names the route. Breaks come in two kinds. A speed break is rounded, with no plant, to keep the receiver’s speed; it suits quick routes against defenders guarding areas. A sink-and-plant break drops the hips and stops hard, to shake a defender running with him; deep outs and comebacks use it, and many coaches have the 12-yard out break slightly back toward the quarterback rather than dead flat.
The finish. What happens after the cut: keep running away from the defender, stop and face the quarterback, or settle in a gap between defenders.

The break is the moment that matters. A receiver can’t outrun a defender who is backpedalling in front of him, but he can make that defender guess. At the break the receiver knows where he is going and the defender doesn’t, so for a fraction of a second the receiver is ahead. That gap, a yard or two of separation, closes fast. Everything about timing is about getting the ball there before it does.

section: The route tree: a shared language
text:
The route tree: a shared language
Receivers and quarterbacks need to talk about routes quickly, in a huddle or with a hand signal at the line. Most offenses therefore teach a route tree: a numbered menu of the basic routes, drawn as branches off one straight stem. Here is one common version, for a receiver on the right side of the formation.


Show the Python
W0 = 13.0                                    # the receiver: on the line, just inside the numbers
TREE = [  # number, name, absolute (d, w) waypoints after the start, label spot, label alignment
    (0, "hitch", [(6.3, W0), (4.7, W0 - 1.4)], (5.6, 15.6), "left"),
    (1, "flat", [(1.4, W0 + 1.5), (2.4, W0 + 6.5)], (2.4, 20.4), "left"),
    (2, "slant", [(1.8, W0), (6.6, W0 - 6.2)], (6.6, 6.1), "right"),
    (3, "comeback", [(16.0, W0), (13.6, W0 + 3.0)], (13.6, 16.8), "left"),
    (4, "curl", [(12.0, W0), (9.9, W0 - 2.3)], (9.9, 10.0), "right"),
    (5, "out", [(10.0, W0), (10.0, W0 + 6.5)], (10.0, 20.4), "left"),
    (6, "dig (in)", [(14.0, W0), (14.0, 2.5)], (15.6, 2.4), "left"),
    (7, "corner", [(12.0, W0), (22.0, W0 + 7.0)], (23.8, 19.8), "center"),
    (8, "post", [(12.0, W0), (25.5, W0 - 7.5)], (27.0, 5.5), "center"),
    (9, "go", [(29.5, W0)], (31.0, W0), "center"),
]
off = [Player("C", "C", "off", -0.7, 0.0, label="C"), Player("QB", "QB", "off", -5.0, 0.0, label="Q")]
off += [Player(f"R{n}", "WR", "off", -0.7, W0, label="") for n, *_ in TREE]
off[-1] = off[-1].moved(label="X")          # one labelled marker on top of the stack (X: on the line)
tree = Play(off, [], los=35, to_go=None)
for n, name, pts, *_ in TREE:
    tree.route(f"R{n}", pts, absolute=True)
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(6.5, 4.35))
gs = fig.add_gridspec(1, 2, width_ratios=[1.45, 1.0], wspace=0.04)
ax, axl = fig.add_subplot(gs[0]), fig.add_subplot(gs[1])
fld = tree.draw(ax=ax, lateral=(-6, 26.6), window=(-6.5, 32.5), title=False)
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, tree, top=30)
for n, name, pts, at, ha in TREE:
    tag(fld, tree, f"{n}  {name}", at, ha=ha, ec=ODD if n % 2 else EVEN, bold=True, fs=7.2)
tag(fld, tree, "toward the middle", (-4.6, 7.0), fs=6.6)
tag(fld, tree, "toward the sideline", (-4.6, 19.0), fs=6.6)
# the cheat sheet beside the tree
CHEAT = [(0, "hitch", "5-6", "stop, face QB"), (1, "flat", "0-3", "out"), (2, "slant", "3-6", "in, 45°"),
         (3, "comeback", "15, back to 12", "back, out"), (4, "curl", "10-14", "stop, face QB"), (5, "out", "10-14", "out, ~square"),
         (6, "dig", "10-15", "in, square"), (7, "corner", "10-12", "out, climbs"), (8, "post", "10-14", "in, climbs"),
         (9, "go", "—", "straight")]
axl.axis("off")
axl.set_xlim(0, 1)
axl.set_ylim(0, 1)
axl.text(0.025, 0.96, "#", fontsize=7.2, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK, va="center", family="DejaVu Sans Mono")
axl.text(0.11, 0.96, f"{'Route':<9} {'Break (yd)':<15} Direction", fontsize=7.2, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK,
         va="center", family="DejaVu Sans Mono")
for i, (n, name, dep, dirn) in enumerate(CHEAT):
    y = 0.885 - i * 0.07
    axl.text(0.02, y, f"{n}", fontsize=7.6, fontweight="bold", va="center", color=style.INK,
             bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", fc=style.SURFACE, ec=ODD if n % 2 else EVEN, lw=1.1))
    axl.text(0.11, y, f"{name:<9} {dep:<15} {dirn}", fontsize=7.2, va="center", color=style.INK,
             family="DejaVu Sans Mono")
axl.text(0.02, 0.0, "Box colour: dark blue = odd, breaks toward the\nsideline; green = even, breaks toward the middle.\nDepths in yards past the line; typical, not laws.",
         fontsize=6.8, color=style.INK_2, va="bottom")
plt.show()








Figure 20.1: One common numbered route tree, drawn for a wide receiver on the right of the formation (the ball is at the bottom left, the right sideline at the right edge). Every route starts with the same push straight up the field and splits at a break point. Odd numbers (dark blue tags) break toward the sideline, even numbers (green tags) toward the middle, and the numbers roughly grow with depth. The 0, the hitch, is an addition some systems make. The table beside the tree lists each route’s typical break depth, in yards past the line of scrimmage, and its direction.





Two patterns make the tree easy to remember. Odd numbers break toward the sideline and even numbers break toward the middle, and the numbers roughly grow with depth. A receiver on the left simply mirrors the tree, so “breaks outside” always means “toward his own sideline.” Each branch exists for a reason.

1, the flat route. A quick release to the flat, the strip near the sideline within a few yards of the line. Its job is often to pull a defender down and out with it, opening the space above him.
2, the slant. One to three steps upfield, then a sharp cut inside at about 45 degrees, between the defenders near the line and the ones behind them, with the receiver’s body shielding the ball from a defender outside him. It is one of the quickest routes in football, which makes it a favourite hot route: when the defense sends more rushers than the line can block, the quarterback throws at once to a receiver running into the space a rusher just left (Pass Protection).
3, the comeback. A hard push for about 15 yards to sell a deep route, then a stop and a turn back toward the sideline. The more convincing the push, the further a cornerback afraid of the deep ball retreats, and the more room there is underneath.
0 and 4, the hitch. Push upfield, stop, and turn back to face the quarterback. At 5–6 yards it is a hitch (some trees number it 0, many not at all); at 10–14 yards, turning back slightly toward the middle, it is a curl, the 4. Both attack a defender who is backing up: against a cornerback 7 or 8 yards off, a 5-yard hitch is open almost by definition.
5, the out. Straight up the field, then a cut toward the sideline: a quick out at about 5 yards, the deeper out at 10–14. It attacks the area outside the defenders who guard the middle, and the sideline stops the clock.
6, the dig. Up the field 10–15 yards, then a flat cut toward the middle, behind the linebackers; shallower versions are often called an in route.
7, the corner route. Up 10–12 yards, then an angle toward the sideline and the pylon at the corner of the end zone (hence its other name, the flag), above a cornerback who stays low and outside a safety who stays in the middle.
8, the post. Up the field, then an angle deep toward the goalposts in the middle, between deep defenders or behind a safety who has come forward. One that angles only slightly inside is a skinny post.
9, the go route. A straight sprint, also called a fly or a 9 route, to outrun the man covering him. Even unthrown it does a job: a cornerback running with it is no longer near the short routes. A go that drifts toward the sideline is a fade, and a ball thrown short to his sideline shoulder, so he turns back for it while the defender keeps running, is a back-shoulder throw (Red Zone, Goal Line, Two-Point Plays, and Short Yardage).

Where the ball sits changes the menu. The ball is spotted on or between the hash marks, so one side of the formation is usually wider (the field side) and the other shorter (the boundary side). Outs and comebacks usually go to the boundary, where the throw is shorter. A deep out from the far hash to the wide side travels some 30 yards in the air before the cornerback can come down on it, the classic test of a quarterback’s arm. Receivers also keep a sideline rule, finishing their routes about 5–6 yards inside the sideline so an out, a comeback or a fade has room to land, which is one reason they move their alignment from play to play, out to the numbers or in to a reduced split (Formation Rules and the Language of Alignment).
Read the tree in pairs. A receiver runs one route per play, but his defender has to defend all of them, and many routes are built to look like another for as long as possible. The slant and the sluggo (a slant fake, then up the field) start the same way; so do the hitch and the hitch-and-go, and the post and the post-corner. A cornerback who jumps the first route all afternoon gets the second. Pairs work across a game, as calls; inside one route, as a double move; and across two receivers, as the stretches later in this chapter. The idea is the same: make a defender choose, then throw where he didn’t go.






ImportantWhy it exists



The tree makes calls short and practice efficient. If every route has a number and a fixed depth, one digit tells a receiver where to go, and a quarterback and receiver who have run the 5 a thousand times know, without talking, where the ball will be and when. The cost is rigidity: a number says nothing about how two routes work together, and a fixed depth is easy to study. So modern playbooks name combinations of routes (concepts), and teach many routes with rules that change them against different coverages (Offensive Systems and Play-Calling Languages).



Who numbered the routes, and what a call sounds like
The numbered tree is usually traced to Don Coryell, whose “Air Coryell” San Diego Chargers (1978–1986) built on Sid Gillman’s principle of making a defense cover every yard of the field, and led the NFL in passing yards six straight seasons from 1978 to 1983 and again in 1985. Numbers let a play-caller give three receivers their routes in three digits. In the classic version the digits go to the split end, the tight end and the flanker, in that order, so “896” sends X on an 8, Y on a 9 and Z on a 6: with this chapter’s tree, a post, a go up the seam and a dig.2 It never became a standard; some trees reverse the odd-even rule or swap the 3 and the 5. “A 9 route” almost always means a go; most other numbers depend on who is talking. Offensive Systems and Play-Calling Languages builds the digit system into full calls.
The names travel better, with dialects: a go is also a fly, a streak or a 9; a dig a square-in; a hitch a stop; a corner a flag; a skinny post a glance or a bang-8; an option route a choice; a high-low a hi-lo or “levels”. Some systems split the hitch family into a hook, which turns straight back, and a curl, which rounds inside.






CautionCommon misconception



“The receiver runs the route as drawn.” Routes are drawn as lines but taught as rules, and the depths in the tree are targets, not laws. A 12-yard out on third-and-14 is run at 14 yards, past the line to gain. A receiver who sees a defender sitting on his spot may be taught to adjust, and on some routes the adjustment is the whole point (the option routes below). The quarterback has to know the rule as well as the receiver does.

title: Passing Game Fundamentals: Routes, Timing, and Reads
section: Off the tree: seam, wheel, whip and sluggo
text:
Off the tree: seam, wheel, whip and sluggo
The tree describes what one wide receiver can do from the outside, with the sideline on one side of him and the whole field on the other. A receiver inside, in the slot or at tight end, lives in a different place: he has room to break either way, he is usually covered by a slower linebacker or a nickel back rather than a cornerback, and he is closest to the deep middle. So inside receivers, and backs who start in the backfield, have routes of their own, and so do receivers trying to fool a defender rather than simply get past him. Four come up constantly.


Show the Python
off = offense("gun_2x2")
off = [p.moved(w=-17.0) if p.key == "X" else p.moved(w=-8.0) if p.key == "H"
       else p.moved(w=8.0, label="Y") if p.key == "Y" else p.moved(w=15.0) if p.key == "Z"
       else p.moved(w=2.6) if p.key == "RB" else p for p in off]
ot = Play(off, [], los=35, to_go=None)
ot.route("X", r.path((2.0, 0.0), (4.3, -2.2), (25.0, -2.0)))                 # sluggo: slant fake, then go
ot.route("H", r.path((3.0, -0.6), (4.6, -3.0), (4.2, 3.4)))                  # whip: in, plant, back out
ot.route("Y", r.seam(24))                                                      # seam
ot.route("RB", r.path((0.3, 5.0), (1.8, 11.0), (3.5, 15.0), (6.0, 17.0), (24.0, 17.4)), side=+1)  # wheel
ot.dropback(2.0)
fld = ot.draw(lateral=(-22, 26.6), window=(-7.5, 28.5), title=False)
faded_route(fld, ot, [(-0.7, 15.0), (12.0, 15.0), (24.0, 10.8)])          # Z clears inside for the wheel
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, ot, top=25)
tag(fld, ot, "sluggo (slant-and-go)", (26.8, -15.0), bold=True)
tag(fld, ot, "whip", (1.6, -12.6), bold=True)
tag(fld, ot, "seam", (24.4, 7.6), bold=True)
tag(fld, ot, "wheel", (21.0, 22.6), bold=True)
tag(fld, ot, "Z clears", (26.3, 10.8), fs=6.2, color=style.INK_2)
tag(fld, ot, "hash", (-6.4, -3.1), fs=6.0, color=style.INK_2)
tag(fld, ot, "hash", (-6.4, 3.1), fs=6.0, color=style.INK_2)
plt.show()








Figure 20.2: Four routes that live off the tree, from a 2x2 formation (the other routes are left off). Left: the sluggo (X fakes a slant for two steps, then runs straight up the field) and the whip (H runs at the middle as if on a short in-cut, plants, and snaps back out). Right: the seam (Y runs straight up between the hash and the numbers) and the wheel (the back runs to the flat, then turns up the sideline, outside the numbers). The wheel needs room, so Z clears it out by running inside (grey).






The seam. A go route from the inside, straight up the strip between the hash marks and the painted numbers. In most deep coverages that strip is the seam between the safety in the middle and the deep defender outside, so the route forces the defense to decide who takes it: the slot’s and tight end’s best way to threaten the deep middle.
The wheel. Out toward the flat, then up the sideline, usually by a back or a slot receiver. A defender who sees a back heading for the flat comes forward, and the back turns up the field past him; few linebackers covering a back man-to-man can run with him. It needs the sideline cleared, so the outside receiver on that side runs inside.
The whip. A slot receiver runs at the middle as if on a shallow in-cut, plants, and snaps back toward the sideline: the harder a man-to-man defender drives on the in-cut, the more open the receiver is when he reverses.
The sluggo. “Slant and go”: a two-step slant fake, then straight up the field, aimed at a defender who has been jumping slants all game. It is the best-known double move (a route that shows one break and runs another). Double moves take time, so they need protection and usually a pump fake (the quarterback starts a throwing motion and holds the ball); The Quick Game covers the family.

title: Passing Game Fundamentals: Routes, Timing, and Reads
section: Option routes: the receiver gets a vote
text:
Option routes: the receiver gets a vote
The tree assumes the receiver knows his route before the snap. On an option route (also called a choice route) he doesn’t: he picks the finish after the snap, from what the defense does. The rule is usually something like this: “Push to six yards. If one man is following you, break away from him, out if he’s inside, in if he’s outside. If the defenders are guarding areas, find the hole between them and sit down, facing the quarterback.”


Show the Python
def option_play(man):
    off = [p for p in offense("gun_2x2") if p.key in ("C", "RG", "RT", "QB", "Y", "Z")]
    off = [p.moved(w=8.5, label="Y") if p.key == "Y" else p.moved(w=16.0) if p.key == "Z" else p for p in off]
    dfn = [Player("NB", "NB", "def", 1.6 if man else 3.8, 7.6 if man else 11.2, label="$"),
           Player("MIKE", "MIKE", "def", 4.5, 1.5, label="M"),
           Player("RCB", "CB", "def", 7.0, 16.5, label="CB")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    p.dropback(2.5)
    if man:
        p.route("Y", r.path((7.5, 0.0), (8.0, 5.0)))                       # breaks out at 6 yards
        p.path("NB", [(5.6, 8.0), (6.4, 11.0)], absolute=True, speed=6.0, delay=0.25)  # trails, inside hip
        p.path("RCB", [(13.5, 17.0)], absolute=True, speed=5.5)      # carries Z deep
        p.route("Z", r.go(14.5))
    else:
        p.route("Y", r.path((7.5, 0.0), (7.9, -0.8), (7.0, -1.4)))              # sits and turns back
        p.drop("NB", (7.0, 14.2))
        p.drop("MIKE", (8.0, 3.0))
        p.drop("RCB", (13.5, 15.5))
        p.route("Z", r.go(14.5))
    return p


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 3.6))
for ax, man, ttl in ((axes[0], True, "Against man: break away from him"),
                     (axes[1], False, "Against zone: sit in the hole")):
    p = option_play(man)
    fld = p.draw(ax=ax, lateral=(-3, 21), window=(-7, 16.5), title=False)
    no_numbers(ax)
    y0 = p.players["Y"]
    if man:
        dotted(fld, p, [(5.4, y0.w), (6.8, y0.w - 4.6)], color=style.MUTED)
        tag(fld, p, "$ sits inside:\nY breaks out", (11.6, 4.6), fs=6.4)
    else:
        tag(fld, p, "Y sits in the hole\nbetween M and $,\nturns to face Q", (11.6, 6.0), fs=6.4)
    ax.set_title(ttl, loc="left", fontsize=8.6, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 20.3: One option route, two defenses. The slot receiver (Y) pushes to about 6 yards, then decides. Left, man coverage: the nickel defender ($) lines up on Y’s inside shoulder to take away the middle and runs with him (solid orange), so Y breaks out, away from him, and the defender is left trailing on his inside hip (the dotted line is the in-cut Y would run if the defender were outside). Right, zone: the defenders drop to areas (dashed) and watch the quarterback, so Y settles in the hole between the Mike (M), who guards the short middle, and the nickel ($), who guards the short area outside, and turns back to face the quarterback.





Why give the receiver a choice? Because the right route depends on the coverage, which isn’t settled until after the snap. Against man coverage, a defender on the receiver’s inside shoulder is taking away the middle, so the open break is outside, and vice versa. That position is the defender’s leverage, and the receiver, with the two-way go of Spread Formations, breaks away from it. Against zone coverage, the underneath defenders watch the quarterback and nobody follows the receiver, so running away from someone is pointless; he stops in the space between two of them. One call, right against both. Two refinements are common. Against a man defender lined up straight in front of him, the receiver stems right at him to make him commit to one side, then breaks to the other. And many systems tie the choice to the safeties: with one deep safety in the middle (MOFC, “middle of the field closed”) he breaks away from his defender, and with the middle empty (MOFO, “open”) he sits; Coverage Fundamentals explains why.
The cost is that two people must make the same decision in a split second. If the receiver sees man and breaks out while the quarterback sees zone and throws to where he should have sat down, the ball goes to nobody, or to a defender, so option routes go to the receivers a quarterback trusts most. The Patriots of the Tom Brady era were famous for building their passing game around option routes for slot receivers such as Wes Welker and Julian Edelman.3 Many other routes carry smaller rules of the same kind (“against two deep safeties, bend the seam into the middle”), which Dropback Concepts collects as route conversions.

title: Passing Game Fundamentals: Routes, Timing, and Reads
section: The drop: the quarterback’s feet are a clock
text:
The drop: the quarterback’s feet are a clock
Now the “when.” On a dropback (any called pass play on which the quarterback sets up behind his line to throw, including play-action and the ones that end in a sack or a scramble), his feet follow a prescribed pattern called a drop, counted in steps, and each drop is paired with a depth of route.
From under center, where he takes the snap with his hands under the center and starts about a yard and a half behind the line, the classic menu is:

Three-step drop: about 5 yards deep, finished a little under a second after the snap. It goes with the quick routes that break at 5–6 yards: hitches, slants, quick outs. The ball should leave as his third step lands, with no extra step, more or less as the receiver breaks.
Five-step drop: about 7 yards deep, finished in roughly a second and a half. It goes with the intermediate routes at 10–14 yards: outs, curls, digs. The quarterback usually adds a short step forward at the end of the drop, a hitch step (not to be confused with the hitch route), to gather himself, and throws.
Seven-step drop: about 9 yards deep, finished in about two seconds. It goes with the deep routes at 15–20 yards and beyond: comebacks, posts, corners, deep digs. It is the slowest drop and the one that most needs the line to hold, which is a big reason it is rarer now than in the 1970s and 80s.

From the shotgun, the quarterback starts about five yards deep, so he needs fewer steps to reach the same depths. The pairs become one, three and five steps: a one-step drop (catch the snap, one step back, throw) for the quick game, three steps for intermediate routes and five for deep ones. Catching the snap is not a step; count from his first step back. The pairing of depth and time stays the same.4 On the standard broadcast angle, high behind the quarterback, watch his feet rather than the ball: count the steps back, look for the plant of the last one, and then for the small hop forward, the hitch step.


Show the Python
_tt = reads[(reads.season >= 2023) & reads.air_yards.notna()].dropna(subset=["time_to_throw"])
TTT_MED = {"quick": _tt.loc[_tt.air_yards.between(0, 9), "time_to_throw"].median(),
           "mid": _tt.loc[_tt.air_yards.between(10, 14), "time_to_throw"].median(),
           "deep": _tt.loc[_tt.air_yards >= 15, "time_to_throw"].median()}

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(6.5, 3.3))
gs = fig.add_gridspec(1, 2, width_ratios=[1.0, 2.6], wspace=0.08)
axd, axt = fig.add_subplot(gs[0]), fig.add_subplot(gs[1])

# --- left: drop depths
axd.axhline(0, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=1.4, alpha=0.75)

DEPTHS = {0: [("start", 1.5), ("3-step", 5.0), ("5-step", 7.0), ("7-step", 9.0)],
          2: [("start", 5.0), ("1-step", 6.0), ("3-step", 7.5), ("5-step", 9.0)]}
for x, lst in DEPTHS.items():

    ("quick", "Quick: 3-step\n(gun: 1-step)", 0.95, 0.95, 0.95, 1.0, "routes at 5-6 yd: hitch, slant, quick out"),

h = [Patch(color=style.OFFENSE, label="QB drop"), Patch(fc=style.OFFENSE_TINT, ec=style.OFFENSE, label="hitch step"),
     Patch(color=style.THIRD, alpha=0.75, label="receiver to break"),
     Line2D([], [], marker="o", ls="", color=style.BALL, label="ball out"),
     Line2D([], [], color=style.INK, lw=1.6, label="real median, 2023-25")]

           handlelength=1.4, columnspacing=1.0)
plt.show()








Figure 20.4: Drops and routes are built as pairs. Left: roughly where the quarterback’s last step lands for each drop, measured from the line of scrimmage. Shotgun drops are two steps shorter for the same depth because he starts five yards back. Right: the textbook timing of each pair, in seconds after the snap: the quarterback’s drop (blue), his hitch step if the drop has one (light blue), the receiver’s run to his break (green, diamond = the break), and the moment the ball should leave (brown ball). On the quick game there is no hitch step: the ball leaves as the last step lands. The black tick on each row is the real median time to throw for passes of that depth, 2023-2025, which runs later than the textbook because many throws are not first-read, on-time throws (the chart on progressions shows why). Textbook depths and times are typical values; they vary by team and quarterback.





Why pair them? Because both are clocks, and the offense wants them to ring together. A receiver starting from a standstill, with a defender in his way, reaches 5 yards in about a second and 12 in about two; a quarterback backing up covers his drop on about the same schedule. Matched, the quarterback’s foot lands as the receiver cuts, and the ball leaves without a pause. Mismatched, one of them waits: a seven-step drop for a hitch hands the cornerback two free seconds to close, and a three-step drop for a post leaves the quarterback holding the ball while the rush arrives.
The black ticks are a reality check: in 2023–2025 the median throw 10–14 yards downfield left about 2.7 seconds after the snap, and the median deep throw about 3.0. Real throws run later because the medians include second and third reads, scrambles and backs released late. The textbook is the plan; the progression data below show what happens when the plan doesn’t work.






ImportantWhy it exists



Drops turn a judgment (“is he open yet?”) into a rhythm (“throw on the fifth step”). A quarterback who waits to see a receiver open is late, because a receiver who looks open has usually been open for half a second already, and the ball needs another second to get there. A quarterback whose feet tell him when the receiver will be at his spot can throw before the defender has reacted to the break. The cost is that a rhythm can be disrupted: a pass rusher in his face, a receiver jammed off his path at the line, or a defender sitting on the spot breaks the timing. Then the footwork carries him to his next option: the hitch step that ends the drop is also the moment he moves his eyes to the second receiver (more under Reads, below).


Three complications. The shotgun dominates: in 2025 about 82% of NFL dropbacks started from the shotgun or the pistol,5 where the quarterback sees the defense better and reaches his depth sooner. Play-action changes the footwork: a handoff fake comes first, so the routes are timed to a longer clock (Play-Action, Bootlegs, and Screens). Not every throw comes off a drop: quarterbacks roll out and escape a collapsing pocket, and the routes then follow the scramble rules of Quarterback Play.

Timing routes: throw it before he breaks
Put the pieces together and you get a timing route: a route the quarterback throws to a spot at a set moment, as his drop ends and often before the receiver has made his break. This is the play from the opening paragraph.


Show the Python
def timing_out():
    off = [p for p in offense("singleback") if p.key not in ("H",)]
    off = [p.moved(w=14.0) if p.key == "Z" else p for p in off]       # on the numbers: room for the out
    dfn = defense("nickel", "single_high", off)
    keep = {"SDE", "SDT", "WDT", "WDE", "MIKE", "WILL", "FS", "SS", "RCB", "LCB"}
    dfn = [p for p in dfn if p.key in keep]
    mv = {"RCB": (7.5, 14.5), "SS": (6.5, 8.0), "FS": (13.0, 0.0)}
    dfn = [p.moved(d=mv[p.key][0], w=mv[p.key][1], label="CB" if p.key == "RCB" else None) if p.key in mv
           else p.moved(label="CB") if p.key == "LCB" else p for p in dfn]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=10)
    protect(p)
    p.block("Y", pts=[(-0.4, 0.3)])
    p.block("RB", pts=[(1.5, 2.2)])
    p.dropback(5.5, speed=3.8)                         # five steps from under center, done at ~1.45 s
    p.path("QB", [(0.8, 0.0)], speed=2.0)              # the hitch step: ball out at ~1.85 s
    p.route("Z", r.path((13.5, 0.0), (13.5, 8.0)), speed=6.9)   # breaks at 12 yards, ~1.95 s
    p.route("X", r.go(20))
    p.path("RCB", [(15.5, 15.0)], absolute=True, speed=5.0)            # backs up into the deep third
    p.path("RCB", [(14.2, 19.0)], absolute=True, speed=6.5, delay=0.45)  # drives once Z has broken
    p.drop("SS", (9.0, 11.0))                          # the short-outside defender gets depth
    p.drop("FS", (16.0, 1.0))
    p.drop("MIKE", (8.0, 2.0))
    p.highlight("Z", "RCB")
    p.pass_to("Z", t=1.85)
    return p


def catch_time(play, to, t0, t1=5.0):
    """First moment the ball reaches the receiver (the simulation has no explicit catch event)."""
    for t in np.arange(t0, t1, 0.01):
        if np.linalg.norm(play.ball_position(t) - play.position(to, t)) < 0.05:
            return float(t)
    return t1


tp = timing_out()
with ball_speed(22):
    T_CATCH = round(catch_time(tp, "Z", 1.9), 2)
    _a, _b = tp.pass_target_spot()
    THROW_LEN = float(np.linalg.norm(_b - _a))
TIMES = [0.9, 1.85, 2.45, T_CATCH]
if PDF:
    with ball_speed(22):
        strip(tp, TIMES,
              ["+0.9 s: Z still looks like a go route", "+1.85 s: hitch step, ball out",
               "+2.45 s: Z has broken; the corner drives", f"+{T_CATCH:.1f} s: catch; the corner is a step late"],
              lateral=(-3, 26.6), window=(-9.5, 18.5), rings=("Z", "RCB"), ncols=2, rulers=False, width_in=5.6)
        plt.show()
else:
    with ball_speed(22):
        show_animation(tp, times=TIMES)





  
  Your browser does not support the video tag.



Figure 20.5: A timing route: the 12-yard out from a five-step drop under center. The cornerback lines up 7 to 8 yards off Z and, at the snap, backs up to guard the deepest third of the field on his side (a deep third). The ball leaves the quarterback’s hand on his hitch step, a tenth of a second before Z breaks toward the sideline, and is thrown to a spot, not to the man. The cornerback can only drive on the ball once Z breaks, so he arrives a step after it. Panels are seconds after the snap (simulated play; Z and the cornerback are ringed; the ball is drawn beside the quarterback until he throws it).




Follow the cornerback. At 0.9 seconds he is backing up, watching Z run straight at him: this could still be a go route. At 1.85 seconds the quarterback’s hitch step lands and he throws, to a spot near the sideline 12 yards downfield. Z still hasn’t cut. Only when Z breaks, a tenth of a second later, can the cornerback drive toward the sideline, and by then the ball is on its way. Z catches it at about 3.2 seconds with the cornerback a step behind.
Why doesn’t he break when the ball leaves the quarterback’s hand? Because he isn’t watching the quarterback. A defender guarding a deep zone has one job above all, not to be beaten deep, so his eyes are on the receiver who can beat him, and until Z breaks, an out and a go look the same. (The underneath zone defenders, with no deep job, are the ones who watch the quarterback.) A cornerback who guesses early and jumps the out gets beaten by the go: the route tree’s pair logic again. Against this coverage the out usually comes with a flat route from the next receiver inside, to hold the short-outside defender down; here Y stays in to block, so that defender is free to widen, one more reason the ball must be on time.
The throw is to a spot, and it leaves before the receiver gets there, because it has a long way to go: some 29 yards from the quarterback’s hand to the catch, more than a second in the air even at the firm 22 yards a second this simulation uses. That makes it hard to defend and hard to execute: a receiver who is jammed and arrives late, or rounds his cut and arrives a yard short, turns a completion into an incompletion, or an interception. Coaches have related words: a rhythm throw comes out on the last step of the drop, with no hitch step (The Quick Game), and an anticipation throw is any throw released before the receiver is open (Quarterback Play).


A short history: Walsh and the three-step game
The modern emphasis on timing owes a lot to Bill Walsh. In 1970 he was an assistant on Paul Brown’s Cincinnati Bengals, and his quarterback, Virgil Carter, was mobile and accurate but had no deep arm. Rather than ask Carter to throw deep, Walsh built a passing game of short, precisely timed throws, many off three-step drops, spread across the whole width of the field, so that a pass could do the work of a running play. Carter led the NFL in completion percentage in 1971.6 Walsh took the approach, much refined, to San Francisco as head coach in 1979 and won three Super Bowls with it; its descendants became the West Coast offense (Offensive Systems and Play-Calling Languages; Case Study: Bill Walsh’s 49ers and the West Coast Offense).
