title: Passing Game Fundamentals: Routes, Timing, and Reads
section: Reads: what the quarterback is looking at
text:
Reads: what the quarterback is looking at
The routes put receivers in places and the drop sets the moment; the quarterback still has to choose. He does it with a read, a decision made after the snap by watching something specific, in the form “if this, then that.” Pass plays use two kinds of read.

A progression read asks which receiver is open, looking at receivers one at a time, in order.
A defender read asks what is this defender doing, watching one defender and throwing to the receiver he can’t cover.

Most plays mix them. A typical call starts with a defender read on one side (“watch the defender guarding the short area outside; throw the receiver he leaves”), and if both of those receivers are covered, the quarterback moves on to the next receiver in a progression. One check comes before either. If the defense sends more rushers than the line can block, the first answer is the hot route or a receiver’s sight adjust (cutting his route short because he sees the blitz too), thrown at once, before any progression starts.

Progressions
A progression is the order in which the quarterback looks at his receivers. The play call gives him a first read, usually the route the play was designed around; if that receiver is covered, he moves his eyes to the second, then the third, and finally to the checkdown, the short, safe throw to a back or tight end (the outlet) that keeps the play from losing yards. Coaches tie each read to the footwork: the first is thrown on the last step of the drop, the second on the hitch step, the third after a second hitch, so the progression runs on the drop’s clock.


Show the Python
def prog_play(full):
    off = offense("gun_2x2")
    off = [p.moved(w=-14.0) if p.key == "X" else p.moved(w=-7.5) if p.key == "H" else
           p.moved(w=7.5, label="Y") if p.key == "Y" else p.moved(w=14.0) if p.key == "Z" else
           p.moved(w=2.5) if p.key == "RB" else p for p in off]
    dfn = [] if full else [Player("RCB", "CB", "def", 5.5, 16.8, label="CB")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    faded = []
    if full:
        p.dropback(4.0)
        p.route("X", r.post(12))
        p.route("H", r.dig(12, 9))
        p.route("Y", r.curl(12))
        p.route("RB", r.path((2.0, 3.0), (6.5, 4.5)), side=+1)       # checkdown
        faded = [[(-0.7, 14.0), (22.0, 14.0)]]                          # Z: clear-out go
        order = [("1", (24.6, -9.6)), ("2", (12.6, -3.0)), ("3", (12.4, 9.8)), ("4", (1.6, 9.4))]
        drop = ("5-step drop", (-10.5, 0.0))
    else:
        p.dropback(2.5)
        p.route("Y", r.corner(10))
        p.route("Z", r.hitch(5))
        p.route("RB", [(-3.0, 5.0), (0.5, 8.0), (2.0, 11.0)], absolute=True)   # outlet to the flat
        p.highlight("RCB")
        faded = [[(-0.7, -14.0), (1.3, -14.0), (5.0, -9.8)],              # X slant, faded
                 [(-1.5, -7.5), (4.5, -7.5), (4.5, -6.7)]]                # H stick, faded
        order = [("1", (21.6, 13.0)), ("2", (7.4, 11.6)), ("3", (3.6, 9.4))]
        drop = ("3-step drop", (-9.6, 0.0))
    return p, faded, order, drop


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 3.95))
for ax, full, ttl in ((axes[0], False, "Half-field: one side, 1-2-3"), (axes[1], True, "Full-field: left to right, 1-4")):
    p, faded, order, drop = prog_play(full)
    fld = p.draw(ax=ax, lateral=(-18.5, 18.5), window=(-12.0, 27.0), title=False)
    no_numbers(ax)
    # small panels: enlarge the labelled skill players (marker and letter) so they read in print
    from matplotlib.patches import Circle, RegularPolygon
    for t in ax.texts:
        lab = t.get_text()
        if t.get_fontweight() == "bold" and 1 <= len(lab) <= 2 and lab != "C":
            t.set_fontsize(t.get_fontsize() * 1.4)
            for pa in ax.patches:
                if isinstance(pa, (Circle, RegularPolygon)) and pa.get_zorder() == 8 and \
                        np.allclose(getattr(pa, "center", getattr(pa, "xy", (0, 0))), t.get_position(), atol=0.05):
                    if isinstance(pa, Circle):
                        pa.set_radius(pa.get_radius() * 1.35)
                    else:
                        pa.radius = pa.radius * 1.35
    for pts in faded:
        faded_route(fld, p, pts)
    for n, at in order:
        x, y = fld.xy(*p.to_abs(*at))
        ax.text(float(x), float(y), n, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8.5, fontweight="bold", color="white",
                zorder=13, bbox=dict(boxstyle="circle,pad=0.2", fc=style.THIRD, ec="white", lw=0.8))
    tag(fld, p, drop[0], drop[1], fs=6.6)
    ax.set_title(ttl, loc="left", fontsize=8.6, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.5)
plt.show()








Figure 20.6: Two ways to order the quarterback’s looks; the green numbers are the progression. Left, a half-field read off a short drop: the play is a two-man combination on the right, a corner route over a hitch (the pair called smash), read high to low off the ringed cornerback, so the corner route is 1 and the hitch 2, with the back released to the flat as the outlet, 3. The routes on the left (grey) are only there to occupy defenders. Right, a full-field read off a deeper drop: a shot at the post on the left, then the dig and the curl across the middle, then the back as the checkdown. Z’s go on the right has no number: it is there to clear the cornerback out of the way.





Progressions come in two sizes.

Half-field reads. The quarterback reads only one side of the field, usually two or three routes built to work together there. The other side’s routes keep defenders busy, or are an emergency answer if the defense blitzes. Because he looks at one side only, the read is quick, which is why it fits a short drop. He picks the side before the snap from what he sees: a receiver alone against a cornerback playing well off him, or the side with fewer defenders than receivers. Most of the quick passing game works this way.
Full-field reads. The quarterback starts on one side, often with a deep route, and works across the whole field to the checkdown. A full-field progression gives him more chances to find the one mistake the defense made, but moving his eyes and feet across the field takes a deeper drop and time the rush may not allow.

The trade is speed versus flexibility. A play-caller picks between them partly on the situation and partly on the quarterback: a rookie gets more half-field reads; a veteran with a good line gets the whole field.

What the data says about progressions
Since 2022, the charting company FTN has recorded, for every NFL pass, which read in the progression the ball went to. The nflverse project republishes that charting, so we can see how often quarterbacks really get past their first look, and what each look is worth in EPA, the course’s measure of how much a play changed the offense’s expected points (Downs, Distance, and Field Position): positive EPA left the offense better off than before the snap.


Show the Python
READ_NAMES = {"1": "First read", "2": "A later read", "CHK": "Checkdown", "DES": "Designed throw (screens)",
              "SD": "Scramble drill", "0": "No read (mostly throwaways)"}
rd = (reads[reads.read_thrown.isin(READ_NAMES)]
      .groupby("read_thrown").agg(n=("epa", "size"), epa=("epa", "mean"), ttt=("time_to_throw", "median"),
                                  comp=("complete_pass", "mean")))
rd["share"] = rd.n / rd.n.sum()
rd = rd.loc[["1", "2", "CHK", "DES", "SD", "0"]]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 2.9))
ys = np.arange(len(rd))[::-1]
cols = [style.SERIES[0], style.SERIES[0], style.SERIES[0], style.MUTED, style.MUTED, style.MUTED]
ax.barh(ys, rd.share, color=cols, height=0.62)
for y, (k, row) in zip(ys, rd.iterrows()):
    ax.text(row.share + 0.008, y, f"{row.share:.0%}   EPA {row.epa:+.2f}   median {row.ttt:.1f} s   "
            f"completed {row.comp:.0%}", va="center", fontsize=6.9, color=style.INK)
ax.set_yticks(ys, [READ_NAMES[k] for k in rd.index], fontsize=7.4)
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}"))
ax.set_xlim(0, 1.0)
ax.set_xticks([0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6])
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=7)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.set_xlabel("Share of pass attempts", fontsize=7.4)
ax.set_title("The progression in the data: early reads are quicker and worth more", fontsize=9)
plt.show()








Figure 20.7: Where the ball actually goes in a progression: FTN’s charting of 2022-2025 regular-season pass attempts (sacks excluded) by the read the quarterback threw to. Bar length is the share of attempts; the labels give EPA per attempt and the median time from snap to throw. More than half of all throws go to the first read, and they are both the quickest and the most valuable. Every later look costs time and value; checkdowns are completed most often but are worth about nothing. Designed throws (mostly screens) and scramble-drill throws (made after the play broke down and the quarterback ran around) sit outside the progression. Read codes are interpreted as described in the text.





More than half of all throws go to the first read, and they come out fastest and are worth the most: the first read is the receiver the play was built to get open, thrown on time. Each later look costs about half a second and a good chunk of the value, and the checkdown, completed most often, is worth roughly nothing. That is the case for timing in one chart: the offense is at its best when the plan works the first time.7



Defender reads and the conflict defender
The other kind of read watches one defender instead of a sequence of receivers. The idea is to find a conflict defender, a defender who is responsible for two things at once, and put two receivers in his area. Whatever he does, he is wrong about one of them. You met this idea in What a Play Really Is, where the quarterback on Stick reads the slot defender, and the run game uses it on a defender responsible for both a run gap and a pass zone (Run-Pass Options). Defender reads are fast, because the quarterback looks at one man, not five, and they don’t depend on the receivers beating anyone, only on geometry: a defender can only be in one place. The offense creates the conflict up and down or side to side.

title: Passing Game Fundamentals: Routes, Timing, and Reads
section: The vertical stretch: high and low
text:
The vertical stretch: high and low
A high-low read (also called a vertical stretch) puts two receivers in one defender’s area at two depths, one above him and one below. The animation below shows the most common version, a curl over a flat route, against the defender who guards both in a Cover 3 zone, the curl-flat defender, who guards the short area outside, from the flat up to the depth of a curl. (Cover 3 has three deep defenders, each guarding a deep third of the field’s width, and four underneath; you’ll meet it properly in Cover 3. For now all that matters is the one defender.)


Show the Python
def high_low(sink):
    off = offense("gun_2x2")
    off = [p.moved(w=8.5, label="Y") if p.key == "Y" else p.moved(w=15.5) if p.key == "Z" else p for p in off]
    dfn = defense("nickel", "single_high", off)
    mv = {"RCB": (7.5, 16.0), "NB": (4.5, 10.0), "MIKE": (4.5, 2.0), "FS": (13.0, 0.0), "SS": (5.0, -11.0),
          "LCB": (7.5, -16.0), "WILL": (4.5, -4.0)}
    dfn = [p.moved(d=mv[p.key][0], w=mv[p.key][1]) if p.key in mv else p for p in dfn if p.key != "DB"]
    dfn = [p.moved(label="CB") if p.pos == "CB" else p for p in dfn]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=10)
    protect(p)
    p.dropback(2.5)
    p.path("QB", [(0.5, 0.0)], speed=2.0)
    p.route("Z", r.path((12.5, 0.0), (11.2, -1.3)))                     # curl: high
    p.route("Y", r.path((1.0, 3.0), (2.4, 7.5), (3.2, 12.0)), speed=6.4)  # flat: low
    p.path("NB", [(6.5, 11.5)], absolute=True, speed=3.5)               # first steps: shuffle, read
    if sink:
        p.path("NB", [(10.0, 14.0)], absolute=True, speed=4.5)          # sinks under the curl
        p.pass_to("Y", t=1.3)
    else:
        p.path("NB", [(3.8, 17.0)], absolute=True, speed=6.5)           # jumps the flat
        p.pass_to("Z", t=1.7)
    p.path("RCB", [(16.0, 17.0)], absolute=True, speed=5.2)             # deep third
    p.drop("MIKE", (9.0, 4.0))
    p.route("X", r.go(18))                                              # the left side: just occupying
    p.route("H", r.seam(16))                                            # defenders on the web animation
    p.drop("LCB", (15.0, -16.0))
    p.drop("WILL", (8.5, -4.0))
    p.drop("SS", (7.0, -12.0))
    p.drop("FS", (17.0, 0.5))
    p.highlight("NB")
    return p


HL_SINK, HL_JUMP = high_low(True), high_low(False)
if PDF:
    with ball_speed(22):
        strip([HL_SINK, HL_JUMP], [0.7, 1.3, 2.35, 0.7, 1.7, 2.7],
              ["+0.7 s: $ reads the QB", "+1.3 s: $ sinks; ball to the flat", "+2.35 s: Y catches it",
               "+0.7 s: the same start", "+1.7 s: $ jumps the flat", "+2.7 s: Z catches the curl"],
              lateral=(-2, 26.6), window=(-9.5, 18.5), rings=("NB",), rulers=False,
              notes={1: [("high", (14.3, 11.6)), ("low", (1.8, 23.2))],
                     4: [("high", (14.3, 11.6)), ("low", (1.8, 23.2))]})
        plt.show()
else:
    with ball_speed(22):
        show_videos([HL_SINK, HL_JUMP], ["He sinks: throw the flat", "He jumps the flat: throw the curl"])





  
  Your browser does not support the video tag.

  
  Your browser does not support the video tag.



Figure 20.8: A high-low read of one defender, both branches (simulated play, Cover 3, the right half of the field). Z runs a curl at about 12 yards (high); Y runs to the flat (low). The ringed nickel defender ($) is responsible for both areas, so the quarterback watches only him. Top row: he sinks under the curl, so the ball goes to the flat. Bottom row: he jumps the flat, so the ball goes to the curl, behind him and in front of the deep-third cornerback. Times are seconds after the snap.




The ringed nickel’s zone runs from the sideline in toward the hash and from the line out to about 12 yards: two receivers’ worth of field. If he gets depth to stand under the curl, the flat route is alone in front of him, and the ball goes there for a few easy yards with room to run. If he comes forward to cover the flat route, the curl settles in the hole behind him, in front of the cornerback, who is busy guarding the deep third, and the ball goes there for 10 or 12. The quarterback doesn’t need the whole coverage, only one man.
Why does this work? A zone defender is taught to stay between the ball and the deepest threat in his area, so one who sinks under the curl is doing his job; he is just losing the flat. The defense has three good answers. It can change who covers what: in man coverage, each receiver has his own defender, and there’s no one to put in conflict. That is why offenses want a hint of man or zone before they choose a read, and the defense gives some: the safeties’ shell from A First Look at Defense, and cornerbacks who line up tight, eyes on a receiver, rather than deep and watching the quarterback (Coverage Fundamentals and What Beats What build this out). It can pattern-match: zone defenders pick up a receiver who enters their area and stay with him, so the curl-flat defender takes the flat and a linebacker gets under the curl (Cover 3). Or it can bait: show a soft flat, then drive on it once the ball is in the air.
The high-low idea is everywhere. In Cover 2, two safeties split the deep field in halves and the cornerbacks stay short, guarding the flats; a corner route over a hitch puts that cornerback in the same bind (that is the concept called smash), and three receivers at three depths on one sideline make it a three-level stretch (the flood concept). Both are built in full in Dropback Concepts.

title: Passing Game Fundamentals: Routes, Timing, and Reads
section: The horizontal stretch: inside and outside
text:
The horizontal stretch: inside and outside
A horizontal stretch does the same thing side to side: it puts receivers on both sides of an underneath defender at about the same depth, so he can’t stand in front of both.


Show the Python
off = offense("gun_2x2")
off = [p.moved(w=-16.0) if p.key == "X" else p.moved(w=-8.5) if p.key == "H" else
       p.moved(w=8.5, label="Y") if p.key == "Y" else p.moved(w=15.5) if p.key == "Z" else
       p.moved(w=-2.4) if p.key == "RB" else p for p in off]
dfn = defense("nickel", "single_high", off)
mv = {"LCB": (8.0, -16.5), "RCB": (8.0, 16.0), "FS": (13.0, 0.0), "SS": (5.5, -11.0),
      "WILL": (4.5, -4.0), "MIKE": (4.5, 1.5), "NB": (4.5, 10.0)}
dfn = [p.moved(d=mv[p.key][0], w=mv[p.key][1], label="CB" if p.pos == "CB" else None) if p.key in mv else p
       for p in dfn if p.key != "DB"]
hz = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=8)
protect(hz)
hz.dropback(2.5)
hz.route("X", r.hitch(5))
hz.route("H", r.path((5.5, -0.8), (5.5, -0.2)))
hz.route("RB", [(-1.0, -2.5), (5.5, -2.5)], absolute=True)    # back checks for a blitzer, then sits left of M
hz.route("Y", r.path((5.5, 2.5), (5.5, 3.0)), side=-1)        # Y sits right of M
hz.route("Z", r.hitch(5))
for k, to in (("LCB", (14.0, -16.5)), ("RCB", (14.0, 16.0)), ("FS", (15.5, 0.0)),
              ("SS", (6.5, -12.0)), ("WILL", (7.0, -5.0)), ("MIKE", (7.0, 1.6)), ("NB", (6.5, 11.5))):
    hz.drop(k, to)
hz.highlight("MIKE")
fld = hz.draw(lateral=(-21.5, 21.5), window=(-8, 16.5), title=False)
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, hz, top=15)
dotted(fld, hz, [(7.0, 1.6), (7.4, 4.5)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.9, head=13)
dotted(fld, hz, [(7.0, 1.6), (7.4, -1.0)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.9, head=13)
tag(fld, hz, "M leans to Y:\nthrow to R", (10.6, 6.8), fs=6.6)
tag(fld, hz, "M leans to R:\nthrow to Y", (10.6, -4.0), fs=6.6)
plt.show()








Figure 20.9: A horizontal stretch. Five receivers settle at 4-6 yards, spread across the field, against the four underneath zone defenders of a Cover 3 defense (dashed arrows are their drops; the two cornerbacks and the free safety drop into the three deep zones). Every underneath defender has a receiver on each side of him. The quarterback watches the ringed Mike, who sits between the back (R) on his left and Y on his right: whichever way he leans (dotted), the man on the other side is open.





The arithmetic is the heart of it. Eleven defenders, minus four rushers, minus the deep defenders, leaves the underneath ones: 11 − 4 − 3 = 4 in Cover 3, 11 − 4 − 2 = 5 in Cover 2. Put five receivers across the field at the same depth against four underneath defenders, and at least one receiver has nobody in front of him while every defender has a receiver on each side. The Mike in the figure stands in his hook zone, the area just past the line in the middle, with the back sitting on one side of him and Y on the other. If he leans toward Y, the back is open; if he leans toward the back, Y is.
Horizontal stretches work underneath, in front of the deep defenders, so they are short, reliable and quick: the backbone of the quick game’s spacing and stick concepts (The Quick Game). What they give up is depth; the big gains have to come after the catch. Combine one with a vertical stretch and you get three receivers around one defender, the triangle read of Dropback Concepts.






ImportantWhy it exists



Stretches beat zone coverage without winning a one-on-one race. Zone defenders guard areas, and areas have edges: put two receivers in one defender’s area, above and below him or on either side, and he has to choose. It is Gillman’s principle of making the defense cover the whole field, applied one defender at a time. Against man coverage there is no area to overload, so the answers are different: routes that win one-on-one, double moves, and crossing routes that make defenders run into each other (the man-beaters of Dropback Concepts). That is why “man or zone?” sits behind every read.

title: Passing Game Fundamentals: Routes, Timing, and Reads
section: Measuring a throw: air yards, YAC and aDOT
text:
Measuring a throw: air yards, YAC and aDOT
A completion’s yards come from two places, the ball’s flight and the receiver’s run after the catch. Analytics splits them with three numbers you’ll meet on broadcasts and in almost every article about a quarterback.

Air yards measure how far past the line of scrimmage the ball traveled in the air, to the spot where it was caught, or where the target was when it fell incomplete. Only the distance downfield counts, not the sideways distance. A screen caught 3 yards behind the line has −3 air yards.
YAC, yards after catch, is what the receiver adds from the catch to the end of the play.
aDOT, average depth of target, is the average air yards per pass, for a quarterback (per throw) or a receiver (per target), completed or not. It describes where a quarterback throws or a receiver is used, not how well.

An example. A slant caught 6 yards past the line, and run 14 more: a 20-yard gain, 6 air yards and 14 YAC. An incomplete deep out aimed 14 yards downfield: no gain, but 14 air yards toward the quarterback’s aDOT. Across the NFL in 2025 the average throw traveled about 7.8 yards past the line, and about 47% of all receiving yards came after the catch, so the two halves are close to equal.8


Show the Python
dv = passes.groupby("depth", observed=True).agg(n=("epa", "size"), comp=("complete_pass", "mean"),
                                                epa=("epa", "mean"), succ=("success", "mean"),
                                                intr=("interception", "mean"))
dv["share"] = dv.n / dv.n.sum()
cmp_ = passes[passes.complete_pass == 1]
dv["air"] = cmp_.groupby("depth", observed=True).air_yards.mean()
dv["yac"] = cmp_.groupby("depth", observed=True).yards_after_catch.mean()
xs = np.arange(len(dv))
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(6.5, 4.9), sharex=True)
specs = [(axes[0, 0], "share", "Share of all attempts", lambda v: f"{v:.0%}"),
         (axes[0, 1], "comp", "Completion rate", lambda v: f"{v:.0%}"),
         (axes[1, 0], "epa", "EPA per attempt", lambda v: f"{v:+.2f}")]
for ax, col, ttl, fmt in specs:
    vals = dv[col].values
    cols = [style.SERIES[0] if v >= 0 else style.SERIES[1] for v in vals]
    ax.bar(xs, vals, color=cols, width=0.7)
    for x, v in zip(xs, vals):
        ax.text(x, v + (0.012 if col != "epa" else (0.015 if v >= 0 else -0.015)) * (1 if col != "share" else 0.6),
                fmt(v), ha="center", va="bottom" if v >= 0 else "top", fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK)
    ax.set_title(ttl, fontsize=8.6)
    ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _, c=col: f"{v:.0%}" if c != "epa" else f"{v:+.1f}"))
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)
for x, v, c in zip(xs, dv.intr.values, dv.comp.values):                # interception rate inside the bar
    axes[0, 1].text(x, 0.04, f"INT\n{v:.0%}", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=5.6, color="white",
                    fontweight="bold", linespacing=0.95)
axes[1, 0].axhline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=1)
axes[1, 0].set_ylim(-0.3, 0.55)
axes[0, 1].set_ylim(0, 0.92)
axes[0, 0].set_ylim(0, 0.31)
ax = axes[1, 1]
ax.bar(xs, dv.air, color=style.SERIES[0], width=0.7, label="air yards")
ax.bar(xs, dv.yac, bottom=dv.air.clip(lower=0), color=style.SERIES[2], width=0.7, label="yards after catch")
for x, a, y in zip(xs, dv.air, dv.yac):
    ax.text(x, max(a, 0) + y + 0.8, f"{a + y:.0f}", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK)
ax.axhline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=1)
ax.set_ylim(-6, 48)
ax.set_title("Yards per completion: in the air + after the catch", fontsize=8.6)
ax.legend(fontsize=6.8, loc="upper left")
ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)
for a in axes[1]:
    a.set_xticks(xs, list(dv.index), fontsize=6.8)
    a.set_xlabel("Target depth (air yards)", fontsize=7.2)
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=0.8, w_pad=1.0)
plt.show()








Figure 20.10: What each depth of throw is worth, 2021-2025 regular seasons (all pass attempts with a charted target depth; sacks excluded). Short throws are the most common and the easiest to complete, but a completion behind the line of scrimmage loses expected points on average. Completion rate falls steadily with depth while the interception rate (printed inside each completion bar) climbs, yet EPA per attempt rises through about 15-19 yards and then levels off: the deep ball fails often but pays a lot when it hits. The bottom-right panel splits the yards on a completion into the air yards and the yards after the catch.





The chart is the passing game’s central trade. Short throws are reliable but don’t gain much in the air, so they live on YAC. Throws behind the line of scrimmage, mostly screens and flips to backs, are completed four times in five, and a completed one gains about 6 yards (about three lost in the air, nine gained after the catch). Yet as a group they lose expected points, for two reasons. The one in five that falls incomplete wastes a down, and a six-yard gain is only modest progress: on first-and-10, a four-yard gain averages -0.16 EPA and it takes about five yards to break even (+0.02).9 That is stricter than the old yardage rule of thumb you met in Downs, Distance, and Field Position, which counts four yards (40% of the ten needed) as a success; the EPA version says second-and-6 is, on average, a little worse than first-and-10. Throws of 5–9 yards are the most dependable winners: completed about two times in three, they have the highest success rate of any depth (59%). Deep throws fail most of the time and pay anyway. Throws of 20 yards or more are completed less than half the time and are intercepted on about 6% of attempts, against 2% for everything shorter, yet each attempt is worth about as much as a throw of 10–19 yards, because a completion moves the ball so far. The bottom-right panel shows a surprisingly steady 3–6 yards after the catch on anything thrown past the line.






CautionCommon misconception



“High aDOT good, low aDOT bad.” aDOT describes a style, not a level of play. A quarterback in a quick, horizontal offense built on YAC can have a low aDOT and an excellent season; a quarterback with a high aDOT may be taking shots because his team is always behind. YAC has the same problem. It depends on the play design (screens and crossing routes produce YAC; comebacks and corners rarely do), on the receiver, and on the throw itself, since a ball placed in stride lets a receiver keep running. To judge a passer, the course uses measures built on top of these, such as CPOE (completion percentage over expected, which accounts for depth) in Quarterback Play, and EPA per play.


The same split shows up in receivers. The table lists the 2025 receivers whose targets were deepest and the ones who gained the most after each catch.


Show the Python
p25 = passes[passes.season == 2025]
rec = (p25.groupby(["receiver_player_id", "receiver_player_name"])
       .agg(team=("posteam", "last"), targets=("air_yards", "size"), adot=("air_yards", "mean"),
            catches=("complete_pass", "sum"), yac=("yards_after_catch", "sum"))
       .reset_index())
rec = rec[rec.targets >= 80]
rec["yac_per"] = rec.yac / rec.catches
hi_adot = rec.nlargest(5, "adot")
hi_yac = rec.nlargest(5, "yac_per")
nm = lambda row: f"{row.receiver_player_name.replace('.', '. ', 1)} ({row.team})"  # noqa: E731
lines = ["| Highest aDOT | aDOT | YAC/catch | Most YAC per catch | aDOT | YAC/catch |",
         "|:---|---:|---:|:---|---:|---:|"]
for (_, a), (_, b) in zip(hi_adot.iterrows(), hi_yac.iterrows()):
    lines.append(f"| {nm(a)} | {a.adot:.1f} | {a.yac_per:.1f} | {nm(b)} | {b.adot:.1f} | {b.yac_per:.1f} |")
LG_ADOT, LG_YAC = p25.air_yards.mean(), p25.loc[p25.complete_pass == 1, "yards_after_catch"].mean()
lines.append(f"| *League average* | *{LG_ADOT:.1f}* | *{LG_YAC:.1f}* | | | |")
print("\n".join(lines))
print("\n: Two kinds of pass catcher, 2025 regular season: players at any position with at least 80 targets with a charted "
      "depth. aDOT is the average air yards per target; YAC/catch is the average yards gained after the catch. "
      "{#tbl-adot-yac}\n")

The two columns are different jobs. The deep-aDOT players are mostly outside receivers on posts, gos and comebacks, who gain little after the catch because a ball caught 20 yards downfield usually arrives with a defender close by. The YAC leaders are mostly running backs caught at or behind the line in open field, where they can make a defender miss. A passing game needs both.

title: Passing Game Fundamentals: Routes, Timing, and Reads
text:
Film room






NoteFilm room: 49ers 1988 season, Super Bowl XXIII — a progression to the third option



January 22, 1989, Miami. The Bengals led the 49ers 16–13 with a little over three minutes left, and San Francisco took over at its own 8-yard line. Joe Montana drove them 92 yards in 11 plays, mostly on short and intermediate throws: Walsh’s timing game, under pressure. On the final play, from the Bengals’ 10 with 39 seconds left, the call, “20 Halfback Curl, X-Up,” was designed for the halfback, Roger Craig, with Jerry Rice in motion to clear out the other side. Craig was held up in traffic, so Montana moved on in his progression and found John Taylor in the middle of the end zone for the touchdown with 34 seconds left. San Francisco won 20–16.10
What to notice: the winning throw went to the receiver the play was not designed for. That is what a progression is for: the first read was taken away, and the quarterback had a pre-set order of where to look next and the time to look there. It was Walsh’s last game as head coach, and the best-known demonstration of his offense: short, precise, on time, and with an answer when the first answer was covered.








NoteFilm room: Buccaneers and Chiefs 2022 — rhythm against improvisation



The 2022 season gives the cleanest contrast in modern quarterback timing: Tom Brady’s last season in Tampa Bay and Patrick Mahomes’s second MVP season in Kansas City, two prolific passers on very different clocks.


Show the Python
q22 = reads[reads.season == 2022]
BM = {}
for _qb in ("T.Brady", "P.Mahomes"):
    _z = q22[q22.passer_player_name == _qb]
    _late = _z[_z.time_to_throw >= 3.5]
    BM[_qb] = {"lt25": (_z.time_to_throw < 2.5).mean(), "first": (_z.read_thrown == "1").mean(),
               "late": len(_late) / len(_z), "late_epa": _late.epa.mean(),
               "late_oop": ((_late.is_qb_out_of_pocket == True) | (_late.read_thrown == "SD")).mean()}  # noqa: E712
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 2.9))
edges = np.arange(0.5, 6.01, 0.25)
for lab, sel, col, ls in (("League", q22, style.MUTED, (0, (3, 2))),
                          ("T. Brady (TB)", q22[q22.passer_player_name == "T.Brady"], style.SERIES[1], "-"),
                          ("P. Mahomes (KC)", q22[q22.passer_player_name == "P.Mahomes"], style.SERIES[0], "-")):
    tt = sel.time_to_throw.dropna().clip(upper=5.99)
    ax.hist(tt, bins=edges, weights=np.full(len(tt), 1 / len(tt)), histtype="step", lw=2 if ls == "-" else 1.4,
            color=col, ls=ls, label=f"{lab}: median {tt.median():.2f} s")
ax.axvline(3.5, color=style.BASELINE, lw=1)
ax.text(3.55, ax.get_ylim()[1] * 0.92, "3.5 s", fontsize=7, color=style.INK_2)
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}"))
ax.set_xlabel("Seconds from snap to throw (throws after 6 s piled into the last bin)", fontsize=7.4)
ax.set_ylabel("Share of attempts", fontsize=7.4)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)
ax.set_title("Brady threw in rhythm; Mahomes also won late", fontsize=9)
ax.legend(fontsize=7, loc="center right")
plt.show()








Figure 20.11: Two ways to beat the clock, 2022 regular season (Brady’s last season, Mahomes’s second MVP season). Each line is the share of a quarterback’s pass attempts thrown in each quarter-second after the snap; the dashed grey line is the league. Brady’s throws pile up early, in rhythm. Mahomes throws on time too, but he has a long right-hand tail: about a quarter of his throws left after 3.5 seconds, most of them when the play had moved past its design, and they still produced positive EPA.





Brady was the league’s model of a rhythm passer: 55% of his throws left in under 2.5 seconds, and 60% went to his first read. Mahomes threw on time too, but 26% of his throws came after 3.5 seconds, mostly after he had left the pocket or the play had broken down, and those late throws still averaged +0.31 EPA, better than the league’s average throw.11
What to notice: two answers to the same clock. Brady beat the rush by being done before it arrived. Mahomes beat it by keeping the play alive after the design ran out, throwing on the run, off one foot or sidearm to receivers taught where to go when the play broke down (the scramble drill of Quarterback Play). Watch a replay of either and count: on a Brady throw you can usually match the release to the end of the drop; on many Mahomes throws, the drop is long over.








TipWatch for it on Sunday: be the route caller



Pick one drive and call every pass play three times: before the snap, at the snap, and on the replay.

Before the snap: count and number. How many receivers on each side? Number them from the sideline in: #1, #2, #3 (Spread Formations). Note the splits and the hash: a receiver tight to the formation, or on the wide side, has room to break outside (corners, outs); one near the sideline mostly breaks inside (slants, digs, posts).
At the snap: watch the quarterback’s feet. From under center, count three, five or seven steps; from the shotgun, one, three or five, starting after he catches the snap. Three (or one) means the ball should be out at once to a 5-yard route; five (or three) means a 10–14-yard route; seven (or five), or extra hitch steps, means deep routes or a quarterback working past his first read.
Then his head. If it stays on one side and the ball goes to one of two receivers near the same defender, that was a defender read. If it snaps from receiver to receiver, often with his feet resetting each time, and the ball goes somewhere he wasn’t looking first, he moved through a progression.
On the replay: name every route. Use the wide angle that shows the receivers and the deep defenders. Name and number each route (“Z ran a 9, H a 5 at twelve, Y a flat, X a slant”), then find the stretch: which defender had two receivers in his area, which way did he go, and where did the ball go?
In the stats: lots of yards per catch could mean deep targets or big YAC; the box score can’t tell you which. Advanced stat pages (Pro Football Reference, Next Gen Stats) list aDOT and YAC separately, and many broadcasts show Next Gen Stats graphics (the NFL’s player-tracking numbers) with air yards and time to throw.

title: Passing Game Fundamentals: Routes, Timing, and Reads
text:
Predict the play






TipPredict the play 1: count the steps





Show the Python
off = [p for p in offense("singleback") if p.key not in ("H", "X")]
off = [p.moved(d=-6.5, w=-2.2) if p.key == "RB" else p for p in off]
dfn = [p for p in defense("4-3_over", "single_high", off) if p.key in ("SDE", "SDT", "WDT", "WDE", "SAM", "MIKE", "WILL", "RCB", "FS", "SS")]
dfn = [p.moved(d=8.0, w=15.5, label="CB") if p.key == "RCB" else p for p in dfn]
pr1 = Play(off, dfn, los=45, to_go=10)
pr1.dropback(5.5)
pr1.highlight("Z")
fld = pr1.draw(lateral=(-9, 26.6), window=(-9.5, 27), title=False)
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, pr1, top=25)
z = pr1.players["Z"]
dotted(fld, pr1, [(z.d, z.w), (6.0, z.w), (4.6, z.w - 1.4)])
dotted(fld, pr1, [(z.d, z.w), (12.0, z.w), (12.0, z.w + 6.5)])
dotted(fld, pr1, [(z.d, z.w), (14.0, z.w), (24.0, z.w - 6.5)])
tag(fld, pr1, "A", (5.0, z.w - 2.4), bold=True)
tag(fld, pr1, "B", (13.6, z.w + 6.0), bold=True)
tag(fld, pr1, "C", (24.0, z.w - 8.4), bold=True)
tag(fld, pr1, "5-step drop", (-8.0, 3.2), fs=6.6)
plt.show()








Figure 20.12: Second-and-10. The quarterback takes the snap under center and drops back: his marker shows where he starts, and the dotted line behind it is his drop, five steps, about seven yards. The cornerback across from Z plays 8 yards off. Z’s three possible routes are lettered: A, a hitch at 5 yards; B, an out at 12; C, a post breaking at 14.





You can’t see Z’s route yet, but you can see the quarterback’s feet. Which of Z’s three routes is the ball most likely meant for, and roughly when should it come out?






TipAnswer





B, the out at 12 yards, thrown at about 1.8–2 seconds, around the moment Z breaks. A five-step drop from under center ends about 7 yards deep, and it is the drop paired with routes that break at 10–14 yards: outs, curls, digs. The off cornerback is the trap. Eight yards of cushion (the space he gives the receiver) invites the hitch, but the hitch (A) goes with a three-step drop; by the time the quarterback finishes five steps, a 5-yard hitch has been sitting still for a second and the cornerback has had time to close on it. If the offense wanted the hitch against that cushion, it would have called a three-step drop. The post (C) needs another second to get open deep; today it is usually a later read off this drop or a shot off play-action, not the first throw. The cushion still helps the out: a cornerback backing up leaves room in front of him for a ball thrown to the sideline on time. Footwork is not a guarantee (he can hitch and work to a deeper second read), but the drop tells you where the plan was.











TipPredict the play 2: the cornerback who stopped





Show the Python
off = offense("gun_2x2")
off = [p.moved(w=-16.0) if p.key == "X" else p.moved(w=-9.0) if p.key == "H" else p for p in off]
dfn = defense("nickel", "two_high", off)
mv = {"LCB": (5.0, -17.5), "FS": (12.5, -10.0), "WILL": (4.5, -5.0), "MIKE": (4.5, 1.5), "NB": (4.5, 8.0),
      "RCB": (5.5, 15.0), "SS": (12.5, 10.0)}
dfn = [p.moved(d=mv[p.key][0], w=mv[p.key][1], label="CB" if p.pos == "CB" else None) if p.key in mv else p
       for p in dfn if p.key != "DB"]
pp = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=8)
protect(pp)
pp.dropback(2.5)
pp.route("H", r.path((11.5, 0.0), (20.0, 11.0)))                    # high: a real smash corner
pp.block("RB", pts=[(0.8, -1.5)])
pp.route("X", r.hitch(5))                                           # low
pp.path("LCB", [(3.4, -18.6)], absolute=True, speed=3.0)          # squats on the hitch, outside leverage
pp.drop("FS", (16.0, -11.0))
pp.drop("WILL", (8.5, -6.0))
pp.drop("MIKE", (10.0, 0.0))
pp.highlight("LCB")
snapshot(pp, 1.9, lateral=(-26.6, 6), window=(-9, 23), show_ruler=True)
plt.show()








Figure 20.13: Second-and-8, 1.9 seconds after the snap, against Cover 2 (two deep safeties; the cornerbacks play the short zones near the sideline). On the left, X has run a 5-yard hitch and the slot (H) has pushed to about 10 yards and is breaking toward the sideline on a corner route. The ringed cornerback has stopped about 4 yards deep, just outside X and in front of the hitch, squatting on it; the safety on that side is in the middle of his deep half, 16 yards deep. The ball is drawn beside the quarterback, who still has it.





The quarterback is reading the ringed cornerback. Where should the ball go, and why does it have to go now?






TipAnswer





The corner route, to H, thrown now toward the sideline about 18 yards downfield. This is a high-low read of the cornerback: X’s hitch is the low route, H’s corner route the high one. In Cover 2 the cornerback guards the short area near the sideline, and he has done his job, squatting on the hitch. That leaves the area above him empty until the safety, 16 yards deep in the middle of his half, can run over and back to it, so the window is open only for a moment: the ball has to leave as H breaks, over the cornerback’s head and in front of the safety. Had the cornerback sunk under the corner route, the hitch would have been open, and on second-and-8 a 5-yard hitch is a fine result. This pairing is the smash concept, one of the oldest answers to Cover 2 (Dropback Concepts).











TipPredict the play 3: name the routes





Show the Python
off = offense("gun_trips")
off = [p.moved(d=-1.5, w=6.5) if p.key == "Y" else p.moved(d=-0.7) if p.key == "Z" else p for p in off]
off = [p.moved(w=17.0) if p.key == "Z" else p.moved(w=11.0) if p.key == "H" else
       p.moved(w=-2.4) if p.key == "RB" else p for p in off]
pr3 = Play(off, [], los=30, to_go=10)
pr3.route("Z", r.go(24))
pr3.route("H", r.out(13.5, 9.0))
pr3.route("Y", r.path((2.0, 3.5), (3.5, 13.0)))
pr3.route("X", r.slant(2, 8))
pr3.block("RB", pts=[(0.5, 1.0)])
pr3.dropback(2.5)
fld = pr3.draw(lateral=(-20, 25), window=(-7.5, 25.5), title=False)
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, pr3, top=25)
for key, at in (("Z", (24.0, 19.5)), ("H", (13.8, 22.2)), ("Y", (3.6, 21.8)), ("X", (7.3, -7.0))):
    tag(fld, pr3, "?", at, bold=True)
plt.show()








Figure 20.14: Name the routes. Trips right (Z is #1, H #2 and the tight end Y #3), X alone on the left; the back stays in to block. The defense is not drawn: assume Cover 3.





Name each route and give its number in the tree from this chapter. Assuming the defense is in Cover 3, which defender is the play designed to put in conflict, and how should the quarterback read him?






TipAnswer





Z: a go route (9). H: an out (5) at about 12 yards. Y: a flat route (1). X, on the backside: a slant (2). The three routes on the right are a three-level vertical stretch along one sideline. Z’s go carries the cornerback deep (if he stays, Z is open deep). That leaves the out and the flat as a high-low of the curl-flat defender, often the nickel: he is the conflict defender. If he sinks under the out, the flat is open in front of him; if he comes up for the flat, the out is open behind him. This combination is the flood concept (also called sail). X’s slant is the backside answer: if the defense shifts extra defenders toward the three receivers, or blitzes, X is alone on the other side, and the quick slant goes to the side the defense left.

title: Passing Game Fundamentals: Routes, Timing, and Reads
text:
Takeaways

A route has a stem and a break, and the break is where it wins. The route tree (1 flat, 2 slant, 3 comeback, 4 curl, 5 out, 6 dig, 7 corner, 8 post, 9 go; odd out, even in) is a shared vocabulary whose numbers vary by team; the seam, wheel, whip, sluggo and option route live off it.
The drop is a clock. Three, five and seven steps from under center (one, three and five from the shotgun) end at about 5, 7 and 9 yards and pair with routes at 5–6, 10–14 and 15–20 yards. Matched, the ball leaves as the receiver breaks; a timing route is thrown to a spot before he gets there.
Reads come in two kinds. A progression checks receivers in order, over half the field (fast) or the whole field (flexible, slower); a defender read watches one conflict defender and throws where he isn’t. First reads are the quickest and most valuable throws.
Stretch the defender, up and down or side to side. A high-low puts receivers above and below one defender; a horizontal stretch puts them on either side. Both beat zone by geometry; against man the offense needs different answers.
Short throws live on YAC, deep throws on air yards. Air yards, YAC and aDOT describe where an offense gains its yards, not how good it is. Throws behind the line lose value on average, 5–9-yard throws succeed most often, and deep throws fail more but pay.

title: Pass Protection: Slides, Man Schemes, and Who Blocks the Extra Guy
text:
Protection is counting
Third-and-7, late in the first half. The offense lines up with five receivers spread across the field and nobody beside the quarterback. The defense walks two linebackers right up to the line, one on each side of the center, and a slot cornerback creeps toward the edge. You count seven defenders who might rush; the offense has five blockers. The center points and shouts a number. The quarterback points somewhere else and shouts a different word. Then the ball is snapped, the slot cornerback comes free off the edge, untouched, and the ball is already gone: a quick slant to the slot receiver, caught in the space where the cornerback used to be. Nobody blocked the man who came free, and that was the plan. This chapter is about why.
You’ll be able to:
How to read the diagrams. Offense is blue circles, defense orange squares, and left and right are always the offense’s. The five offensive linemen are labelled LT, LG, C, RG and RT, Q is the quarterback and R the running back; X, Z and H are wide receivers and Y (and U) tight ends. On defense, E is an end, and the two defensive tackles are labelled by technique: 1 for the one shaded on the center, 3 for the one on a guard’s outside shoulder. M, W and S are the Mike, Will and Sam linebackers, NB the slot (nickel) cornerback, C a cornerback, FS and SS the safeties. A line ending in a short bar is a block or a pass set (the spot a blocker moves to at the snap to meet his rusher; more on sets later), an arrow a path, a dotted green line “this blocker is responsible for that defender,” and a shaded green oval a gap a lineman owns. Rushers’ paths are orange; a red dashed arrow is a rusher nobody blocks. A dotted orange line from a defender to a receiver means man coverage, the dotted brown arrow is the ball in the air, and the solid orange line across the field, where one is drawn, is the line to gain.
Start with the arithmetic, because every protection in this chapter is an answer to it.
On a pass, the offense always has five blockers: the five offensive linemen, who are not allowed to go out for passes (they are ineligible) and so have nothing else to do. It may add more. A running back or a tight end can stay in to block, making six, seven or even eight. Every extra blocker is one fewer receiver, and that is the trade at the heart of the whole subject.
The defense, meanwhile, can rush anyone it likes. Most of the time it rushes four: in the 2024 and 2025 regular seasons about two dropbacks in three faced exactly four rushers, about one in five faced five, and fewer than one in ten faced six or more.1 Four is the default for the reason A First Look at Defense gave: four rushers leave seven defenders to cover at most five receivers. A blitz (sending a fifth, sixth or seventh rusher) flips that trade, giving up coverage to try to create a rusher the offense cannot block.
So the offense’s question on every pass is: how many might come, how many can I block, and if the answer is “not enough,” who is left over? Three ideas follow from it, and they organise the rest of the chapter.
1. The protection does not have to win forever, only long enough. A quarterback in today’s NFL gets the ball out in a little under three seconds on average (you will see the numbers at the end of the chapter). A rusher who arrives at 3.5 seconds has not hurt anyone. Protection is a race against a clock, not a wrestling match to the finish.
2. Block inside-out. Rushers from the middle of the line have the shortest path to the quarterback; rushers from the edges have to run around the blockers. So when an offense must choose who to block and who to leave, it blocks the inside man and leaves the widest one, because he has the longest way to go and the ball can be out before he gets there.
3. Someone left unblocked on purpose is the quarterback’s. If six come and the offense has five blockers, one rusher is unblocked by design. That man is called a free rusher: a rusher nobody is assigned to block. The protection does not fail when there is a free rusher; it hands him to the quarterback, who must throw before he arrives. A free rusher who was supposed to be blocked is a different thing: a bust, and you will learn to tell the two apart.

title: Pass Protection: Slides, Man Schemes, and Who Blocks the Extra Guy
text:
ImportantWhy it exists



Pass protection exists because the defense chooses its numbers after the offense has chosen its own. The offense commits its blockers in the huddle; the defense can show four rushers and bring six, or show six and bring three. Every protection scheme is a set of rules that decides, after the snap, which blocker takes which rusher, so that the most dangerous rushers are always blocked and any man left over is one the quarterback can beat with a quick throw.

title: Pass Protection: Slides, Man Schemes, and Who Blocks the Extra Guy
section: The pocket: a cup, not a wall
text:
The pocket: a cup, not a wall
Before we can say who blocks whom, we need the shape of what they are protecting. The pocket is the protected space the blockers form around the quarterback, and the best way to picture it is a cup, not a wall.


Show the Python
p = Play(line() + gun(None, qb_d=-7.5), four_down(lbs=False), los=35, to_go=None,
         title="The pocket is a cup, not a wall")
SETS = {"LT": (-3.6, -4.4), "LG": (-2.0, -1.8), "C": (-1.6, 0.0), "RG": (-2.0, 1.8), "RT": (-3.6, 4.4)}
for k, sp in SETS.items():
    to(p, k, sp)
to(p, "LE", (-6.6, -3.4), "rush", via=[(-1.2, -6.1), (-4.6, -5.9)])
to(p, "RE", (-6.6, 3.4), "rush", via=[(-1.2, 6.1), (-4.6, 5.9)])
to(p, "NT", (-1.0, -1.1), "rush"); to(p, "DT", (-1.1, 2.1), "rush")
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-12, 12), window=(-12, 4.2))
cup = [(-3.6, -4.4), (-2.0, -1.8), (-1.6, 0.0), (-2.0, 1.8), (-3.6, 4.4), (-8.6, 3.0), (-9.6, 0.0), (-8.6, -3.0)]
xy = np.array([_P(fld, p, d, w) for d, w in cup], dtype=float)
fld.ax.add_patch(Polygon(xy, closed=True, fc=GREEN, alpha=0.13, ec=GREEN, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1.5))
(x0, y0), (x1, y1) = _P(fld, p, -6.6, 0.0), _P(fld, p, -5.0, 0.0)
fld.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((x0, y0), (x1, y1), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=11, color=GREEN, lw=1.8,
                                 zorder=9))
say(fld, p, -5.6, 1.9, "step up", color=GREEN, weight="bold")
point_to(fld, p, (-10.3, -4.0), (-7.5, 0.0), "launch point\n(about 7-8 yd deep)")
# path lengths: the end's arc around the tackle vs the 3-technique's straight line to the launch point
arc = [(1.0, -5.0), (-1.2, -6.1), (-4.6, -5.9), (-6.6, -3.4), (-7.5, 0.0)]
edge = sum(np.hypot(b[0] - a[0], b[1] - a[1]) for a, b in zip(arc[:-1], arc[1:]))
inside = np.hypot(1.0 + 7.5, 2.35)
point_to(fld, p, (2.75, -7.6), (1.0, -5.0), f"edge rusher: about {edge:.0f} yd\naround the tackle", shrink=9)
point_to(fld, p, (2.75, 4.6), (1.0, 2.35), f"3-technique: about {inside:.0f} yd\nstraight up the middle", shrink=9)
for side in (-1, 1):
    say(fld, p, -5.0, side * 9.6, "tackles give\nground and push\nthe edge past", fontsize=7, color=GREEN)
say(fld, p, -3.6, 0.0, "interior: hold firm", fontsize=7, color=GREEN)
plt.show()








Figure 21.1: The pocket’s shape, about a second after the snap (the quarterback is drawn at his launch point; backs and receivers are not shown). The interior linemen take short sets, only a yard or so back, and hold firm; the tackles kick back several yards so the ends must run an arc around them. That arc is far longer than the 3-technique’s straight path up the middle, which is why the edge can be pushed past the quarterback while the middle must not give an inch, and why the quarterback steps up into the cup rather than drifting back.





Three facts about the cup explain most of pass protection.
The quarterback throws from a spot, and the linemen know where it is. The launch point is where the quarterback sets his feet to throw at the end of his drop. From the shotgun he starts five yards deep and takes a short drop, so on a typical dropback he throws from about seven or eight yards behind the line; from under center a five-step drop ends at a similar depth and a seven-step drop deeper.2 Linemen set their depth to that spot. The aim is not to stop every rusher at the line; it is to keep every rusher off that spot until the ball is gone. When a play-action pass or a rollout moves the launch point, the whole line’s geometry changes with it, which is why those plays have their own protections (Play-Action, Bootlegs and Screens).
The interior must not give ground. Look at the distances in Figure 21.1. A defensive tackle rushing straight up the middle is about nine yards from the launch point. An end rushing around the tackle has to run an arc of about thirteen. So the guards and center set only a step or two back and then hold, because every yard they give is a yard straight into the quarterback’s face. Pressure up the middle is the most destructive kind: the quarterback cannot step up into it, cannot see over it, and cannot escape it by moving forward.
The tackles give ground on purpose. The tackles retreat several yards, backward and outward, keeping themselves between the end and the quarterback. If the end keeps running his arc, the tackle runs with him and pushes him past the launch point, deeper than the quarterback, where he is no threat. That is why a quarterback with a good pocket steps up: he moves forward into the cup as the edge rushers are pushed behind him. Stepping up is a skill the quarterback chapter builds on; for now, notice that it only works if the interior held. A quarterback who drifts backward instead runs into the ends the tackles were pushing past him.






CautionCommon misconception



“The offensive line should form a wall.” A flat wall at the line of scrimmage would be beaten at both ends in a second, because the edge rushers would simply run around it. The pocket is deliberately bent: firm in the middle, deep at the edges, with the quarterback inside the bend. When you see a tackle five yards behind the line with a defensive end running past him, that is usually the protection working, not failing.

title: Pass Protection: Slides, Man Schemes, and Who Blocks the Extra Guy
section: Two ways to block five: slide and man
text:
Two ways to block five: slide and man
Now the assignments. There are two basic ways to decide which blocker takes which rusher, and every protection in the NFL is one of them or a mix of the two. They are the pass-protection cousins of the two run-blocking philosophies in 03-01: blocking an area and blocking a man.


Show the Python
LAT, WIN = (-7.2, 7.2), (-6.8, 6.4)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.7))
for ax, kind in zip(axes, ("slide", "man")):
    p = Play(line() + gun(-1.5), four_down(), los=35, to_go=None)
    if kind == "slide":
        for k, wg in zip(OL_KEYS, (-2.4, -0.8, 0.8, 2.4, 4.0)):
            to(p, k, (-0.25, wg - 0.15))
        to(p, "RB", (-3.6, -3.9))
    fld = draw(p, ax=ax, title=False, lateral=LAT, window=WIN)
    if kind == "slide":
        for wg in (-2.4, -0.8, 0.8, 2.4, 4.0):
            gap_oval(fld, p, wg)
        assign(fld, p, "RB", "LE")
        panel_title(ax, "Slide right: each lineman owns a gap")
        say(fld, p, 2.6, -0.2, "the gap to my right,\nwhoever comes", color=GREEN)
        say(fld, p, -5.2, -4.6, "back: the end\nleft behind", color=GREEN)
    else:
        for k, m in zip(OL_KEYS + ["RB"], ("LE", "NT", "MIKE", "DT", "RE", "WILL")):
            assign(fld, p, k, m, lw=1.6)
        panel_title(ax, "Man (BOB): each blocker owns a man")
        say(fld, p, -3.6, 4.2, "linemen: the four\nlinemen + the Mike", color=GREEN)
        say(fld, p, -5.4, -4.6, "back: the Will", color=GREEN)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.8)
plt.show()








Figure 21.2: The same six blockers against the same front, two ways (receivers and defensive backs not shown). Left, slide right: each lineman takes the gap to his right (shaded), whoever comes through it, so the 1-technique belongs to the LG, the 3-technique to the RG and the right end to the RT; the Mike or Will, if they blitz, run into the C’s or LT’s gap. The slide leaves the left end behind, so the back takes him. Right, man protection, also called BOB (big-on-big): the linemen take the four defensive linemen and the Mike, and the back takes the Will.





Slide protection. In slide protection every lineman takes his first step the same way and owns the gap on that side, whoever comes through it. In the left panel of Figure 21.2 the line slides right: the left tackle owns the gap between himself and the left guard, the left guard the gap between himself and the center, and so on across to the right tackle, who owns the space outside himself. Notice that nobody on the line has to know in advance which defender will rush where. If the 1-technique rushes, he is in the left guard’s gap; if instead the Will linebacker blitzes and the 1-technique drops into coverage (defenses do this; see Zone Blitzes and Simulated Pressure), the left tackle’s gap gets the Will and the left guard’s gap gets nobody, and the left guard helps a neighbor.
The price of sliding one way is the man on the other end. Five linemen sliding right cover five gaps, from the left B gap to outside the right tackle, and that leaves the left end, outside everyone, uncovered. Someone else has to take him: the running back in the picture, or a tight end. That is the slide’s weak spot. The man it leaves behind is usually a defensive end, often the defense’s best pass rusher, and now a 215-pound back has him.
So the direction of the slide is a decision, and it follows one rule of thumb: the slide goes where the trouble is inside, and never leaves a star alone with a back. Offenses slide toward the most dangerous inside rusher, or toward the side with more possible rushers (an overload). If the defense’s best player is an edge rusher, they slide away from him and block him with the tackle man to man (the half-slide coming up next does exactly this), then add a chip (later in this chapter) on top. Help is always in addition to the tackle, never instead of him.
Man protection. In man protection, each blocker is given a specific defender before the snap. The usual rule is the one in the right panel: the five linemen take the four defensive linemen plus one linebacker, and the back takes the other linebacker. Line coaches call it “big on big” (BOB, or big-on-big), because the big men block the big men, and the back is left with a linebacker, a fairer fight than a defensive end.
Man protection matches strength to strength, and it handles a four-man rush cleanly. Its weakness is movement. If two defenders cross paths after the snap (a stunt, coming up later in this chapter), each man-blocker must chase his man through traffic. If a linebacker the line was counting on drops out and a different one rushes, the assignments are wrong for the rusher who actually came. Slide protection shrugs off both, because a gap does not move. That is the trade, and it is the same one zone and gap blocking make in the run game: man blocking wins the one-on-one matchups it planned for; area blocking survives the ones it did not.

title: Pass Protection: Slides, Man Schemes, and Who Blocks the Extra Guy
section: Half-slide: the NFL’s everyday six-man protection
text:
Half-slide: the NFL’s everyday six-man protection
Most real protections split the difference. In a half-slide the center and the two linemen on one side slide that way and block gaps, the two linemen on the other side block man-to-man, and the running back takes the first extra rusher on the man side. This is the “60” protection from the play call you decoded in What a Play Really Is, and some version of it is the most common six-man protection in football. (Many playbooks number their protections in families, “50s,” “60s,” “90s,” with the number saying which way the slide goes and who blocks; others use words. What each number means differs from team to team.)


Show the Python
p = Play(line() + gun(-1.5), four_down(), los=35, to_go=None,
         title="Half-slide right against a four-man rush")
to(p, "C", (-1.8, -0.75), via=[(-1.8, 0.45)])
for k, wg in zip(["RG", "RT"], (2.4, 4.0)):
    to(p, k, (-0.25, wg - 0.15))
to(p, "LT", (-1.6, -4.3)); to(p, "LG", (-1.2, -1.2))
to(p, "LE", (-1.4, -5.6), "rush", via=[(0.0, -5.6)])
to(p, "RE", (-1.4, 5.6), "rush", via=[(0.0, 5.6)])
to(p, "NT", (0.1, -0.85), "rush"); to(p, "DT", (0.1, 2.3), "rush")
p.drop("MIKE", (9.0, 2.0)); p.drop("WILL", (8.5, -4.5))
to(p, "RB", (-1.0, -6.6), "route", via=[(-3.8, -2.6)])
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-9.5, 9.5), window=(-7.2, 10.4))
for wg in (0.8, 2.4, 4.0):
    gap_oval(fld, p, wg)
for k, m in (("LT", "LE"), ("LG", "NT")):
    assign(fld, p, k, m, lw=1.6)
point_to(fld, p, (-3.7, 3.7), (-1.8, 0.3), "C: no one came into\nhis gap, so he helps", color=GREEN)
say(fld, p, 2.9, 4.4, "slide side", color=GREEN, weight="bold")
say(fld, p, 2.9, -4.4, "man side", color=GREEN, weight="bold")
point_to(fld, p, (-5.8, -6.4), (-3.8, -2.6), "back: checks the Will,\nthen releases", color=GREEN)
say(fld, p, 8.8, -6.9, "Will drops", fontsize=6.8)
say(fld, p, 9.2, 4.4, "Mike drops", fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()








Figure 21.3: Half-slide right against a four-man rush (receivers and defensive backs not shown). The C, RG and RT slide right and own the shaded gaps; the LG and LT block the man in front of them; the back’s job is the Will. Here both linebackers drop into coverage, so nobody comes into the center’s gap and nobody comes for the back: the center helps the left guard on the 1-technique, and the back, having checked the Will, slips out into a route. Six blockers have become five against four, with a spare, plus a sixth receiver.





Walk through Figure 21.3. On the right, the slide side, the center, right guard and right tackle each own a gap, so any combination of the 3-technique, the right end and the Mike linebacker is accounted for. On the left, the man side, the guard has the 1-technique and the tackle has the left end. The back watches the Will. Count it: six blockers for six possible rushers (four linemen, two linebackers), with every gap and every man covered once.
The half-slide is popular because it gives each part of the line the job it is best at. The slide side handles the movement defenses love to run inside (stunts, linebackers looping through gaps). The man side keeps the offense’s tackle on the defensive end, big on big, rather than handing that end to the back. And the back gets the defender with the longest path, an off-the-ball linebacker, whom he can meet in the hole.
Against the four-man rush in the picture, both linebackers dropped. The protection does not care: the center had nobody in his gap, so he “looks for work” and helps a neighbor (here the left guard on the 1-technique), and the back, whose man did not come, runs a route. Six blockers turned into five plus a receiver. That last move is called check-release, and it is one of the most important things a back does; it gets its own section below.
Why would anyone still call a full slide, then? Because it puts all five linemen on gaps, and gaps are the answer to movement. Against a front that loves stunts, or that stacks linebackers to come through the A and B gaps, a full slide toward the pressure means no lineman has to chase anybody; the offense accepts the cost (a back or tight end on the backside end) because the inside threat is the bigger one.
How to tell which one you are watching. On the broadcast, look at the linemen’s first step after the snap. All five step the same way: a slide. The center and the two linemen on one side step together while the other two set straight back at the man in front of them: a half-slide, with the slide toward the center’s step. Each lineman sets to a different defender, some stepping left and some right: man.

title: Pass Protection: Slides, Man Schemes, and Who Blocks the Extra Guy
section: Mike identification: counting from the same man
text:
Mike identification: counting from the same man
Every protection above depends on everyone agreeing which linebacker is which. The half-slide said “the back takes the Will,” and the man protection “the linemen take the four linemen and the Mike.” But the defense does not wear name tags, and linebackers move. So before the snap one player makes the call you heard in The Pre-Snap Phase: “54’s the Mike!” That call is Mike identification, often written MIKE ID. In most offenses the quarterback has the final word, because he sees the whole defense; in others the center, who is closest to the front and runs the line’s communication, makes it.3

How the count works
The “Mike” in the call is a reference point, not necessarily the defense’s real middle linebacker. Every assignment is written relative to him, so naming him turns six separate judgments (“which one is mine?”) into one decision that everyone follows. Systems differ in the details, but one common way to build a six-man protection around the call, the one in Figure 21.4, works like this.

The center works toward the Mike. He and the two linemen on that side slide that way and own the gaps there, so the Mike (call him 0) and anyone on his side belong to the slide.
The other two linemen count outward from the Mike on their side. The guard takes the first defender on the line (1), the tackle the second (2). This is the man side.
The back takes the next threat beyond the line’s count (3), usually the linebacker on the man side. If he rushes, the back blocks him; if he drops, the back releases. In many playbooks the back has two men to check in order, inside first (a dual read), and takes whichever comes.



Show the Python
LAT, WIN = (-7.2, 7.2), (-7.4, 6.8)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.0))
for ax, mike in zip(axes, ("54", "52")):
    dfn = [q.moved(label="54") if q.key == "MIKE" else q.moved(label="52") if q.key == "WILL" else q
           for q in four_down(will=(4.5, -2.6))]
    p = Play(line() + gun(-1.5), dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    if mike == "52":
        to(p, "RB", (-3.4, 1.7), via=[(-4.0, -0.5)])
    fld = draw(p, ax=ax, title=False, lateral=LAT, window=WIN)
    if mike == "54":
        for wg in (0.8, 2.4, 4.0):
            gap_oval(fld, p, wg)
        tag(fld, p, "MIKE", "0"); tag(fld, p, "NT", "1"); tag(fld, p, "LE", "2"); tag(fld, p, "WILL", "3")
        for k, m in (("LG", "NT"), ("LT", "LE")):
            assign(fld, p, k, m, lw=1.6)
        assign(fld, p, "RB", "WILL", lw=1.6, via=[(-2.4, -2.4)])
        panel_title(ax, "1  \"54's the Mike!\"")
        say(fld, p, -2.9, 4.6, "slide side:\n0 and his side,\nby gaps", color=GREEN)
        say(fld, p, -3.2, -4.8, "man side:\nG takes 1, T takes 2", color=GREEN)
        say(fld, p, -6.2, -4.2, "back: 3", color=GREEN, weight="bold")
    else:
        for wg in (-0.8, -2.4, -4.0):
            gap_oval(fld, p, wg)
        tag(fld, p, "WILL", "0"); tag(fld, p, "DT", "1"); tag(fld, p, "RE", "2"); tag(fld, p, "MIKE", "3")
        for k, m in (("RG", "DT"), ("RT", "RE")):
            assign(fld, p, k, m, lw=1.6)
        panel_title(ax, "2  The quarterback names 52")
        say(fld, p, -2.9, -4.6, "slide side:\n0 and his side,\nby gaps", color=GREEN)
        say(fld, p, -6.2, 4.0, "back: 3, across\nthe QB's face", color=GREEN, weight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.8)
plt.show()








Figure 21.4: The count, number by number (receivers and defensive backs not shown; the linebackers are labelled by jersey number). Left: “54’s the Mike.” The center works toward 54, so the C, RG and RT slide right and own the shaded gaps; 54 is 0 and belongs to the slide. On the man side the guard takes the first defender on the line (1), the tackle the second (2), and the back the linebacker beyond them (3). Right: the same defense, but the quarterback names 52 instead. Now the slide goes left, the RG and RT take the 3-technique and the end man to man, and the back’s man is 54, on the other side of the quarterback: he has to block across the quarterback’s face, which takes him longer.





Numbered like that, the call does all the work, and the right panel shows its power: change the name and the slide flips, the guard and tackle on the man side have new men, and the back’s man moves to the other side. So the call is also a tool. A quarterback who sees a threat gathering on one side can name a defender over there, which pulls the slide, and its linemen, toward the threat, so that a lineman rather than the back is responsible for the most dangerous rusher. The cost of all this is time and noise: every call has to be heard by five or six men, on the road, with the play clock running.
The right panel also answers a question about the back. In most half-slides he lines up on the man side, the side he will check, so he has a short trip. When the call puts his man on the other side, he has to block across the quarterback’s face, in front of him to the other side, which takes longer. So the back’s alignment is a clue to the protection, not a guarantee. Watch where he steps at the snap.
That is what happened in the opening scene. The center pointed and called a number: his Mike, one of the two linebackers standing in the A gaps. The quarterback, who has the final word, pointed elsewhere and called a word of his own, a code that set which way the line would work and so which side the unblocked rusher would come from. That also told the slot receiver on that side that he was the answer. (The words are code and change from team to team; some staffs use one word for each direction, others fold the direction into a protection number.)


Show the Python
LAT, WIN = (-7.2, 7.2), (-7.4, 6.6)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.9))
for ax, bust in zip(axes, (False, True)):
    dfn = [q.moved(label="54") if q.key == "MIKE" else q.moved(label="52") if q.key == "WILL" else q
           for q in four_down(will=(4.5, -2.9))]
    p = Play(line() + gun(-1.5), dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    fld = draw(p, ax=ax, title=False, lateral=LAT, window=WIN)
    if not bust:
        for k, m in zip(OL_KEYS, ("LE", "NT", "MIKE", "DT", "RE")):
            assign(fld, p, k, m, lw=1.6)
        assign(fld, p, "RB", "WILL", lw=1.6, via=[(-2.4, -2.5)])
        panel_title(ax, "1  One call: \"54's the Mike!\"")
        say(fld, p, -3.3, 4.3, "line: the four linemen\n+ 54 (the Mike)", color=GREEN)
        say(fld, p, -6.4, -3.9, "back: 52", color=GREEN)
    else:
        for k, m in (("LT", "LE"), ("LG", "NT"), ("RG", "DT"), ("RT", "RE")):
            assign(fld, p, k, m, lw=1.6)
        assign(fld, p, "RB", "WILL", lw=1.6, via=[(-2.4, -2.5)])
        assign(fld, p, "C", "WILL", lw=1.6, color=RED, via=[(0.6, -1.9)])
        free_path(fld, p, [(4.5, 1.2), (0.2, 0.75), (-4.0, 0.3)], label="54: free", label_at=(-2.6, 2.6))
        panel_title(ax, "2  The center thought 52 was the Mike")
        say(fld, p, 2.6, -5.0, "two blockers\non 52", color=RED)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.8)
plt.show()








Figure 21.5: Why one player names the Mike (receivers and defensive backs not shown; the linebackers are labelled by jersey number). Left: the call is “54’s the Mike,” so the linemen take the four defensive linemen plus 54, and the back takes 52; every possible rusher has exactly one blocker. Right: the same defense, but the center counted from 52 instead. He turns to 52, the back also takes 52, and when 54 blitzes the right A gap nobody is responsible for him. The defense rushed no more men than the offense had blockers; the free rusher came from two blockers counting from different men.





Figure 21.5 shows what happens when the count is not shared: the defense rushed only five men against six blockers and still got a man free, because two blockers counted from different starting points. This is the classic bust, and when you see a linebacker run untouched through the middle against a normal-looking rush, it is the first thing to suspect. (Re-declaring the Mike when a defender walks up late, which you met in The Pre-Snap Phase, is the offense’s attempt to keep the count shared after the defense has moved.)
Some quarterbacks make this part of their game. Tom Brady was known for it: his Mike calls are audible on broadcasts, and teammates describe him overruling the line’s identification at the line of scrimmage (“no, he’s the Mike”) to move the protection toward a matchup he did not like, then getting the ball out to the hot receiver before a free rusher arrived.4 The skill is invisible on most broadcasts, and it is part of why analysts treat sack rate as partly a quarterback statistic, not only a line statistic.
Defenses know this, which is why they move after the call. Linebackers walk up into the A gaps at the last second, safeties rotate down, a lineman stands up and drops back. Each move is an attempt to make the offense’s count wrong after it is too late to fix. The two-linebacker version, both standing in the A gaps on either side of the center, is the “double A-gap mug” of Blitz and Man Pressure, and it exists almost entirely to attack the Mike call: with both linebackers threatening the middle, which one is the Mike? Here, in miniature, is why the pre-snap phase looks like the busiest few seconds in sport.






NoteMadden vs. real life



In Madden you can tap a button to “slide protection left” or tell the back to block, and the computer linemen then know exactly who to block. Real linemen have to agree on it, out loud, in a few seconds, in a stadium built to drown them out, while the defense rearranges itself to make their agreement wrong. Most of what makes an NFL offensive line “good” in the eyes of coaches is invisible on a broadcast: not strength, but five players reaching the same answer at the same time, snap after snap.
