title: The Quick Game: Slant-Flat, Stick, Snag, Quick Screens, and Beating Press
text:
Watch for it on Sunday






TipWatch for it: one-two-throw



Before the snap

The corners. Off or pressed? Inside or outside the receiver? A corner seven yards off with outside leverage is inviting a slant or a now screen; a pressed corner is daring the receiver to beat him off the line.
The slot defender. Where is the man between the slot receiver and the box? He is the read on almost every quick concept to that side. If he walks up toward the line, think blitz, and think quick throw.
Count outside the box. Three receivers against two defenders on one side, with the safety far away, is a screen waiting to happen.

At the snap: the stopwatch. Count “one-thousand-one, one-thousand-two” from the snap. If the ball is gone before you finish “two,” you just watched the quick game working as designed. Count a dozen dropbacks in a game and you’ll find that roughly half of them are out before “two-and-a-half.”
At the snap: watch the linemen. Three plays come out in about a second, and the linemen tell them apart. On a quick throw they set to pass-block, short and aggressive, and stay at the line. On a run-pass option they fire forward as if blocking a run. On a now or bubble screen the receivers near the ball turn and block.
After the throw

On the replay, find the one defender between the two receivers on the side the ball went. Did he widen, sink or sit? The ball went to the receiver he didn’t take.
When the defense blitzes, watch where the ball goes. Usually it goes quickly to the area the blitzer came from.

For your prediction log (How to Watch a Broadcast): before each third-and-short-to-medium, write quick or not quick, and the side you expect, based on the corners’ leverage. Then time the throw.

title: The Quick Game: Slant-Flat, Stick, Snag, Quick Screens, and Beating Press
text:
Predict the play






TipPredict the play 1: pick a side





Show the Python
off = spread()
dfn = cover3(nb_side=-1, extra={"RCB": (1.3, 14.2), "SS": (3.5, 12.0), "NB": (5.0, -7.0)})
p = Play(off, dfn, los=45, to_go=6)
protect(p)
p.dropback(1.5)
for k in ("X", "Z"):
    p.route(k, r.slant(stem=3.0, length=9.0))
for k in ("H", "Y"):
    p.route(k, r.path((1.0, 1.8), (3.0, 10.0)))
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-25.0, 25.0), window=(-8.5, 15.5))
plt.show()








Figure 22.15: Second-and-6. The offense has called slant-flat to both sides (outside receiver on a slant, slot receiver to the flat) and left the choice of side to the quarterback.





Which side should the quarterback pick, and which defender does he watch after the snap?






TipAnswer





The left side, reading the slot defender ($). Run through the pre-snap read on each side.
On the right, both routes are in trouble before the snap. The cornerback is pressed with inside leverage, sitting right where Z’s slant wants to go, so Z has to beat a jam and get across the cornerback’s face; and the safety has already widened to the flat, standing where Y’s flat route ends. One defender is in each receiver’s path.
On the left, the cornerback is seven yards off and outside X, which concedes the slant (away from leverage), and the slot defender is inside H, the one man who has to choose between the two routes. That’s the slant-flat picture from earlier in the chapter. After the snap the quarterback watches only the $: if he widens with H, throw the slant; if he sits, throw the flat.
Doesn’t the right side have its own answer? A corner pressing with inside leverage invites an outside release and the fade, and Z might win it. But the fade isn’t in this call, and even when it is, it’s a lower-percentage throw against a corner who is right on top of the receiver. On the left, the play works exactly as designed, with two receivers against one defender and an easy read. The quarterback takes the side where the concept he called is already winning.
This is why offenses call a quick concept to both sides. The defense has to give something away somewhere, and the quarterback’s pre-snap job is to find where.











TipPredict the play 2: six at the line





Show the Python
off = spread()
dfn = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -5.4, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.8, "T"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.4, "T"),
       D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 5.4, "E"), D("WILL", "WILL", 1.9, -2.3, "W"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 1.9, 0.8, "M"),
       D("NB", "NB", 3.0, -8.6, "$"), D("SS", "SS", 3.0, 8.6, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 6.0, 0.6, "FS"),
       D("LCB", "CB", 1.3, -13.8, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 1.3, 13.8, "CB")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=50, to_go=5)
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-25.0, 25.0), window=(-8.5, 12.5))
plt.show()








Figure 22.16: Third-and-5, just before the snap. The offense has five linemen, and a running back who can stay in to block or go out for a pass.





Count the threat. What kind of throw does the offense want, how fast, and where?






TipAnswer





A hot throw, out in about a second and a half, and away from the cornerbacks’ leverage. Count first. Nobody is deeper than about six yards: this is a “zero” look, with no deep safety at all (Cover 0). Zero lets the defense put a man on every receiver and send everyone else. With five receivers out, that is six rushers against five blockers. If the back stays in to block, his defender can come too: seven rushers against six blockers. Either way one rusher is free, and nobody can hold the ball. That is the Cover 0 blitz bet: the defense is wagering that the ball can’t come out in time.
Now look at the cornerbacks. Both are pressed and both are a yard inside their receivers. That is the leverage rule at work: with no safety anywhere, the corner has no help inside, so he protects the middle and uses the sideline as his help. The slant, the quick game’s favorite throw, is the route he is sitting on. So the ball goes away from his leverage, outside. Two answers fit:

The outside receivers’ fade or back-shoulder throw. With no safety behind the corner, a receiver who wins outside off the line is one catch from a touchdown, and the quarterback can throw it as soon as the receiver clears the jam. It’s not a high-percentage throw (a pressed corner is right on the receiver), which is why it isn’t the answer every time.
The hot route into the space a blitzer leaves. Some of the defenders crowding the line will cover and some will rush. The receiver whose nearest defender rushes is hot: he breaks into the space that defender just left, and the ball goes there at once.

Which side? The side the protection call says the free rusher is coming from, because that is where the hot receiver is and where the quarterback has the least time. A now screen is a poor choice: the cornerback is standing a yard away, so there is no cushion to run into.
For a real one, see the Super Bowl LVII touchdown to Skyy Moore in the Chiefs film room above: seven rushers, Cover 0, ball out in 1.7 seconds to the flat.
The defense might be bluffing, of course: show zero, bring four, drop two into the throwing lanes. That is exactly why the throw is a read of where the extra defenders went, not just a reflex (Zone Blitz and Simulated Pressure).











TipPredict the play 3: count them





Show the Python
dfn = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -4.6, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.8, "T"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.4, "T"),
       D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 5.0, "E"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.6, "W"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.0, "M"),
       D("SS", "SS", 5.0, 4.4, "SS"), D("NB", "NB", 7.0, 12.4, "$"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.5, 19.8, "CB"),
       D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -16.0, "CB"), D("FS", "FS", 14.0, -1.0, "FS")]
p = Play(trips_right(), dfn, los=30, to_go=10)
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-25.0, 25.0), window=(-8.5, 17.5))
plt.show()








Figure 22.17: First-and-10. The offense lines up in trips to its right.





The defense has loaded the box to stop the run. What quick throw does that invite, and why?






TipAnswer





A quick screen to the trips side: a bubble to H, or a now screen to Z. Start by counting. The box (roughly the area between the offensive tackles, out to about five yards deep) holds seven defenders: four linemen, two linebackers and a safety. Outside it on the right there are only the cornerback and the $. Then run the three questions:

Numbers: on the right, outside the box, the offense has three players (Y, H and Z) and the defense two. The safety who would usually be the third defender out there is standing beside the linebackers, in the box. That’s the trade the defense made: an extra run defender inside, one fewer pass defender outside.
Leverage: the cornerback and the $ are both off and roughly over their receivers, so the blockers start in the right place: Z can turn the cornerback out toward the sideline, and Y, starting inside the $, can block him from the inside while H runs between them.
Grass: both are about seven yards off, and the nearest help, the deep safety, is fourteen yards away in the middle of the field. A bubble caught at the snap is five yards gained before anyone can touch it.

A run into the middle would face seven defenders with five linemen to block them (six if a receiver comes in to help): the defense has the numbers inside. The quick screen is how the offense “runs” outside the box instead, and it’s why so many offenses attach a bubble to their running plays (Run-Pass Options).

title: The Quick Game: Slant-Flat, Stick, Snag, Quick Screens, and Beating Press
text:
Takeaways

The quick game is the passing game’s fast lane: a short drop, short routes and a rhythm throw, out in about 2.5 seconds or less. It is roughly half of what NFL offenses throw.
It exists for three jobs: beat the rush with the clock, keep the offense on schedule with high-percentage throws, and stretch the run game sideways by getting the ball to fast players in space. It trades depth for certainty and needs yards after the catch and a deep threat to keep the bargain.
Most quick concepts put two receivers on opposite sides of one defender, high and low (slant-flat, hitch-seam, double slants) or inside and outside (stick), or both (snag’s triangle), and the quarterback throws to the one that defender doesn’t take. Spacing stretches the whole underneath coverage; the speed out beats one cornerback’s alignment.
Most of the decision is made before the snap: read the defender’s leverage, cushion and help, and throw away from leverage.
Press is the defense’s answer to the quick game’s timing; the receiver’s answer is the release, stem, stack and break, and the double move punishes a defender who jumps the short route.
Now and bubble screens punish soft and outnumbered alignments (numbers, leverage, grass). Against the blitz, the free rusher is the quarterback’s, and the ball that comes out fast, into the space the blitzer left, is worth the most.

title: The Quick Game: Slant-Flat, Stick, Snag, Quick Screens, and Beating Press
text:
Connections
Builds on: Passing Fundamentals (the routes, drops and stretches every concept here is made of) and Pass Protection (hot routes, sight adjustments and the five-, six- and seven-man protections the quick game leans on), with the defensive basics of A First Look at Defense.
Sets up: Dropback Concepts takes the same stretches deeper, with more time and longer progressions; Run-Pass Options attaches the quick throws and screens to runs; Quarterback Play covers anticipation, footwork and the numbers for judging accuracy. On the defensive side, Coverage Fundamentals teaches press and off coverage from the cornerback’s side, and Blitz and Man Pressure does the blitz math from the defense’s. Concepts Versus Coverages finally pairs each concept with the coverages it beats, and Third Down shows where the quick game earns its keep.
Case studies: Walsh’s 49ers and the West Coast offense and Andy Reid’s Chiefs.






NoteGo deeper




Bill Walsh, with Brian Billick and James A. Peterson, Finding the Winning Edge (1997): the coach’s own account of how he built a passing game around timing and short throws.
Chris B. Brown, The Art of Smart Football (2015) and The Essential Smart Football (2012), and his Smart Football site: clear essays on stick, snag, spacing and why they work.
Tim Layden, Blood, Sweat and Chalk (2010): the chapter on Walsh traces the West Coast offense back to the Cincinnati years.
From diagrams to real tracking data. The two animations above are gridiron simulations in NFL Big Data Bowl coordinates. The 2025 Big Data Bowl release (2022 season, weeks 1–9) records every player ten times a second, and its play and player files include each play’s time to throw and each receiver’s charted route, so you can find real quick throws and watch them. The data needs a free Kaggle login, so this code is not run when the book is built.



Show the Python (real Big Data Bowl tracking; not run in the build)
import pandas as pd
from gridiron import bdb, show_animation

plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")
player_play = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/player_play.csv")
# completed passes out in under 2.5 seconds on which some receiver ran a slant
quick = plays[(plays["timeToThrow"] < 2.5) & (plays["passResult"] == "C")]
slants = player_play.loc[player_play["routeRan"] == "SLANT", ["gameId", "playId"]].drop_duplicates()
cand = quick.merge(slants, on=["gameId", "playId"])
g, pl = cand.iloc[0][["gameId", "playId"]]

trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_*.csv")
one = bdb.prepare(trk, plays, game_id=g, play_id=pl)
show_animation(one, times=[0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.6])   # snap, release, break, catch

text:
Course calculation from nflverse participation data (time_to_throw, FTN-sourced), 2025 regular season: 17,394 pass attempts with a recorded time (sacks, spikes and scrambles excluded). Median 2.5 seconds; 48% of attempts left the quarterback’s hand in under 2.5 seconds and 52% in 2.5 seconds or less. The 2.5-second line is an analysts’ convention, not a rule; PFF, for one, splits time to throw there (PFF, “Signature Stat Snapshot: Time To Throw”: https://www.pff.com/news/signature-stat-snapshot-time-to-throw).↩︎
Course calculation, same data: attempts out in under 2.5 seconds were completed 72.2% of the time (success rate 51.5%), slower attempts 57.1% (success rate 44.9%). Success means positive EPA, the definition in Expected Points, EPA and Success Rate.↩︎
Walsh to Tom FitzGerald of the San Francisco Chronicle: “We couldn’t control the football with the run; [opposing] teams were just too strong. So it had to be the forward pass, and obviously it had to be a high-percentage, short, controlled passing game.” The same profile describes his offense as “passes so short they were effectively extended handoffs.” Both in “Walsh, Bill,” Encyclopedia.com: https://www.encyclopedia.com/people/sports-and-games/sports-biographies/bill-walsh↩︎
Course calculation, same data: on 2025 completions thrown in under 2.5 seconds, 58.7% of receiving yards came after the catch; on slower completions, 38.5%. Screens are included, which pushes the quick figure up: about 23% of throws out in under 2 seconds were screens (FTN is_screen_pass).↩︎
Bill Walsh with Brian Billick and James A. Peterson, Finding the Winning Edge (Sports Publishing, 1997), on building the Bengals’ short passing game around Virgil Carter. “West Coast offense,” Wikipedia: Walsh “was tasked with devising an offensive plan suited to Bengal quarterback Virgil Carter, who had an accurate but relatively weak arm,” and Carter “led the league in passing percentage in 1971”: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Coast_offense . Carter completed 138 of 222 (62.2%), the NFL’s best that season: Pro Football Reference, 1971 NFL leaders, https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1971/leaders.htm . Greg Cook tore the rotator cuff in his throwing shoulder in the third game of 1969, played through the season, then needed surgeries that kept him out of the next three seasons: “Greg Cook,” Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greg_Cook . The Bengals began play in 1968.↩︎
Virgil Carter and Robert E. Machol, “Operations Research on Football,” Operations Research 19, no. 2 (1971): 541–544, which estimated the expected-point value of first-and-10 at each part of the field from 8,373 plays in the first 56 games of the 1969 NFL season: https://ideas.repec.org/a/inm/oropre/v19y1971i2p541-544.html . On Carter’s statistics major at BYU and his MBA at Northwestern, taken while he played for the Bears: ESPN, “Ex-Bengals QB Virgil Carter’s legacy of EPA, other analytics” (2024): https://www.espn.com.au/nfl/story/_/id/40276150/nfl-epa-analytics-virgil-carter-cincinnati-bengals↩︎
Pro Football Hall of Fame, “Bill Walsh” (Class of 1993): head coach of the 49ers 1979–1988, winners of Super Bowls XVI, XIX and XXIII: https://www.profootballhof.com/players/bill-walsh/↩︎
Pro Football Hall of Fame, “Jerry Rice” (Class of 2010), including his 22 touchdown catches in the strike-shortened 12-game 1987 season, then an NFL record (Randy Moss caught 23 in 2007): https://www.profootballhof.com/players/jerry-rice/↩︎
Pro Football Hall of Fame, NFL history, 1978: “Rules changes permitted a defender to maintain contact with a receiver within five yards of the line of scrimmage, but restricted contact beyond that point”: https://www.profootballhof.com/football-history/football-history/1960-1979/1978 ; and 1977: “Defenders were permitted to make contact with eligible receivers only once”: https://www.profootballhof.com/football-history/football-history/1960-1979/1977 . The 1978 change is often called the “Mel Blount rule” (Steelers Depot, “Mel Blount explains play that created Mel Blount rule,” 2024: https://steelersdepot.com/2024/02/mel-blount-explains-play-that-created-mel-blount-rule). The era is the subject of The 1978 Liberation.↩︎
Ralph D. Russo, “Air Raid evolution: Pioneering offense passes test of time,” Associated Press, Aug. 24, 2022, on the offense “birthed from the mind of Hal Mumme” and “inspired by LaVell Edwards’ BYU passing game and Bill Walsh’s West Coast offense,” whose “foundational concepts and plays” it lists as “mesh, Y cross, four verts, the quick game”: https://kvia.com/ap-texas/2022/08/24/air-raid-evolution-pioneering-offense-passes-test-of-time/↩︎
NFL Video Rulebook, “Offensive Pass Interference”: it is offensive pass interference for an offensive player to block more than one yard beyond the line of scrimmage before the pass is thrown, or to initiate contact with a defender in a way that restricts him while the pass is in the air: https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-video-rulebook/offensive-pass-interference . The rule is NFL Rule 8, Section 5 (Pass Interference); see https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/ .↩︎
NFL Rulebook, Rule 8, Section 4 (“Legal and Illegal Contact With Eligible Receivers”), Articles 1–3: within the area five yards beyond the line of scrimmage, a defender may chuck an eligible receiver in front of him; beyond five yards, while the passer is still in the pocket with the ball, he may not initiate contact with a receiver who is trying to evade him (illegal contact: five yards and an automatic first down). Grabbing or restricting a receiver is defensive holding (Rule 12, Section 1): https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/ ; NFL Video Rulebook, “Illegal Contact”: https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-video-rulebook/illegal-contact . After the Patriots’ physical coverage in the 2003 season’s AFC Championship Game, the Competition Committee made illegal contact and defensive holding a point of emphasis for 2004: NBC Sports Boston, “They called it the ‘Ty Law Rule’”: https://www.nbcsportsboston.com/nfl/new-england-patriots/they-called-it-the-ty-law-rule-and-that-was-ok-with-him/393549/↩︎
Course calculation from FTN charting (is_contested_ball) joined to nflverse play-by-play, 2025 regular season: 16,733 pass attempts excluding throwaways and spikes; 13.9% charted as contested. Completion rate 41.9% on contested throws, 71.1% on the rest. Contested throws went farther (12.7 yards in the air on average, against 7.1), which accounts for part of the gap.↩︎
NFL Rulebook, Rule 8, Section 7 (“Backward Pass and Fumble”): players of either team may catch a backward pass, or recover one after it touches the ground, and advance it; the special fourth-down and final-two-minutes limits on advancing apply to fumbles, not backward passes: https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/ ; NFL Video Rulebook, “Backward Pass”: https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-video-rulebook/backward-pass↩︎
Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play and participation data (number_of_pass_rushers, time_to_throw), 2025 regular season dropbacks with a charted rush count. “Quick” = a pass attempt out in under 2.5 seconds; “held” = an attempt out in 2.5 seconds or more, a sack, or a scramble. EPA per dropback: four or fewer rushers, quick +0.118 (n = 5,767) and held −0.014 (n = 8,708); five or more rushers, quick +0.226 (n = 2,532) and held −0.098 (n = 2,763). Five or more rushed on 27% of these dropbacks. Pooled over all outcomes, EPA per dropback was +0.054 against five or more rushers (n = 5,306; sack rate 7.8%) and +0.038 against four or fewer (n = 14,524; sack rate 6.0%); success rates 45.9% and 45.5%. Five or more rushed on 25% of first-down, 25% of second-down, 30% of third-down and 34% of fourth-down dropbacks, so the pooled comparison is not controlled for down and distance.↩︎
Pro Football Reference, Drew Brees career passing (2017: 386 of 536, 72.0%; 2018: 364 of 489, 74.4%), and the NFL record book (single-season completion percentage): https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/B/BreeDr00.htm . Guinness World Records lists 74.4% as the record (and 72.0% in 2017 as the mark it broke): https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/93395-highest-completion-percentage-nfl-season . In nflverse play-by-play no qualified passer from 2019 through 2025 topped 74.4% (the closest was Brees himself, about 74% in 2019). title: Dropback Concepts: Smash, Flood, Mesh, Levels, Dagger, and Four Verticals
text:
What a pass concept is
Third-and-8, late in the first half. The offense lines up with two receivers on each side. Before the snap the camera shows both safeties standing thirteen yards deep and both cornerbacks only five yards off the ball, flat-footed, watching the quarterback. The ball is snapped, the quarterback takes three quick steps back from the shotgun, and the outside receiver on the right runs five yards and turns around. The cornerback in front of him does exactly what he has been coached to do: he squats on that receiver. The ball sails over his head to the inside receiver, who has run ten yards up the field and angled toward the sideline, into the space behind the cornerback and in front of the safety. First down. On the replay the analyst circles the two routes with his telestrator and says one word: smash. Why was the cornerback wrong when he did what he was told? How did the quarterback know, before the snap, where the ball was going? And why does the same two-route pattern, under one name or another, show up in every playbook in the league? This chapter is about those patterns: the dropback concepts that make up most of an offense’s passing game beyond the quick throws.
You’ll be able to…
A pass concept is a set of routes designed to work together on one play, usually by putting one or two defenders in a position where whatever they do leaves a receiver open. You met the idea in The Quick Game, where slant-flat and stick each pinned one defender between two receivers. This chapter takes the same idea deeper down the field, where the routes take longer to develop and the defenders in conflict are cornerbacks, linebackers and safeties instead of a single slot defender.
Why do offenses think in concepts rather than routes? Three reasons, and they explain a lot about how football is coached.
A concept is a sentence; routes are only words. A corner route on its own means nothing. A corner route run over a hitch, against a cornerback who has to choose between them, is a plan. The quarterback doesn’t read five receivers one by one; he reads one or two defenders and lets the concept tell him where the open man will be. That’s why concepts are drawn and taught as units, and why a receiver learns not only his route but his partner’s.
A name is a shortcut. “Smash” tells two receivers their routes in one syllable, from any formation, on either side of the field. Offenses that name concepts this way can teach a playbook faster and call plays faster, which matters in a two-minute drive or a no-huddle attack. Not every system names its plays like this; some spell out each receiver’s route in a long string of words or numbers, and the trade-offs between those styles are the subject of Offensive Systems and Languages, where concept-based terminology gets its full story.
A concept travels. Smash works from a 2x2 formation, from trips, with a tight end as the inside receiver or a running back. Because the conflict is about space (the gap between a cornerback sitting short and a safety playing deep), the same concept can be dressed up in a dozen formations, which makes it hard for a defense to recognize from the alignment alone.

title: Dropback Concepts: Smash, Flood, Mesh, Levels, Dagger, and Four Verticals
text:
CautionCommon misconception



“Every pass play has one intended receiver.” Almost none do. A concept has a first look, the route it was designed around, but it’s built so that whichever choice the key defender makes, somebody else is open. When an announcer says the quarterback “went to his second read,” that isn’t a failure of the play. It is often the play working as drawn.



What changes when the quarterback drops back
The quick game lives on throws that leave the quarterback’s hand in about two seconds, aimed at receivers five or six yards away. Dropback concepts give themselves more time and aim farther, and the numbers show what that buys and what it costs. In the 2025 regular season, throws that traveled zero to nine yards past the line of scrimmage left the quarterback’s hand after a median of 2.3 seconds; throws of 10 to 19 yards, the home of most of the concepts in this chapter, took 2.8 seconds, and throws of 20 yards or more took 3.1 seconds.1 That extra half-second is the price of the deeper drop (five steps from under center, or three from the shotgun, in the matched pairs of Passing Fundamentals) and of routes that need ten or fifteen yards to reach the spot where they break.
What does the half-second buy? Value. Those 10-to-19-yard throws averaged about +0.39 expected points added (EPA) per attempt, the course’s measure of how much a play changed the offense’s scoring chances, against about +0.10 for those zero-to-nine-yard throws. But they were completed only 54% of the time, against 72%, and they were intercepted twice as often (about 3.2% of attempts against 1.6%).






ImportantWhy it exists, and what it costs



Dropback concepts trade time and risk for yards. The offense asks its line to protect for three seconds or more, accepts a lower completion rate and more interceptions, and gets in return the throws that move the ball in big pieces: the 15-yard dig on third-and-8, the corner route that turns a drive into a scoring chance. The quick game keeps an offense on schedule; dropback concepts are how it gets ahead of it. The bill comes in sacks, hits on the quarterback and a pass rush with time to get home, which is why protection (Pass Protection) and dropback concepts are planned together.

section: Four ways to put a defender in a bind
text:
Four ways to put a defender in a bind
Every concept in this chapter does one of four things to the defense. Learn the four and you can name the purpose of a concept you have never seen, which is most of what “reading” a pass play from the couch means.


Show the Python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(6.5, 5.0))
# 1 vertical
p1 = Play([O("A", "WR", 0.0, -2.0, "A"), O("B", "WR", 0.0, 2.0, "B")],
          [D("D1", "LB", 6.5, 0.0, "D")], los=LOS, to_go=None)
route_to(p1, "A", (5.0, -2.0), (11.5, -0.6))
route_to(p1, "B", (1.0, 2.0), (2.2, 0.4))
p1.highlight("D1")
# 2 horizontal
p2 = Play([O("A", "WR", 0.0, -7.0, "A"), O("B", "WR", 0.0, 7.0, "B")],
          [D("D1", "LB", 6.0, 0.0, "D")], los=LOS, to_go=None)
route_to(p2, "A", (5.5, -7.0), (6.0, -4.8))
route_to(p2, "B", (5.5, 7.0), (6.0, 4.8))
p2.highlight("D1")
# 3 triangle
p3 = Play([O("A", "WR", 0.0, 7.5, "A"), O("B", "WR", 0.0, 3.0, "B"), O("C", "RB", -2.0, -2.0, "C")],
          [D("D1", "LB", 5.8, 7.4, "D"), D("D2", "LB", 5.6, 3.6, "D")], los=LOS, to_go=None)
route_to(p3, "A", (11.5, 7.5), (10.5, 6.5))
route_to(p3, "B", (1.5, 5.0), (2.5, 10.5))
route_to(p3, "C", (-1.0, -0.4), (3.5, 1.0))
p3.highlight("D1", "D2")
# 4 man-beater
p4 = Play([O("A", "WR", 0.0, -6.0, "A"), O("B", "WR", 0.0, 6.0, "B")],
          [D("D1", "CB", 1.4, -5.6, "D"), D("D2", "CB", 1.4, 5.6, "D")], los=LOS, to_go=None)
route_to(p4, "A", (5.0, -5.6), (6.5, 6.5))
route_to(p4, "B", (4.0, 5.6), (5.0, -6.5))
for ax, (p, ttl) in zip(axes.flat, ((p1, "1. Vertical stretch (high-low)"), (p2, "2. Horizontal stretch"),
                                    (p3, "3. Triangle"), (p4, "4. Man-beater"))):
    fld = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-11.5, 11.5), window=(-3.5, 14.5), show_ruler=False, width_in=3.2)
    panel_title(ax, ttl, fs=8.5)
    if p is p1:
        opening(fld, p, (11.0, -0.6), (2.2, 3.2))
        opening(fld, p, (2.3, 0.4), (2.0, 3.2))
        say(fld, p, 11.6, 5.4, "high", color=OD)
        say(fld, p, 2.3, 4.6, "low", color=OD)
        say(fld, p, 6.5, -5.4, "one defender,\ntwo depths", color=DD)
    elif p is p2:
        say(fld, p, 9.0, 0.0, "one defender,\ntwo sides", color=DD)
        say(fld, p, 2.4, -4.5, "inside", color=OD)
        say(fld, p, 2.4, 4.5, "outside", color=OD)
    elif p is p3:
        triangle(fld, p, [(10.5, 6.5), (2.5, 10.5), (3.5, 1.0)])
        say(fld, p, 12.4, -3.0, "two defenders,\nthree receivers", color=DD)
    else:
        branch(fld, p, [(1.4, -5.6), (4.0, -4.6), (4.4, -1.6), (2.6, 0.2), (4.0, 2.6), (5.2, 4.4)],
               color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.4, dash=(0, (1, 1.6)))
        say(fld, p, 11.0, 0.0, "B's path is in the way:\nA's defender has to\ngo around (dotted)", color=DD)
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=1.2, w_pad=1.0)
plt.show()








Figure 23.1: The four families of pass concepts, drawn as small abstract pictures (offense moving up the page). 1. Vertical stretch (high-low): two receivers in one defender’s area at two depths; he can stand under the high one or in front of the low one, not both. 2. Horizontal stretch: receivers on both sides of a defender at about the same depth. 3. Triangle: three receivers around two defenders, one high (A’s curl) and two low (B’s flat outside, C’s hook inside), so the quarterback has a high-low and an inside-outside choice at once. 4. Man-beater: against man coverage there is no area to overload, so the routes cross close to each other and the defenders chasing them have to fight through traffic (the dotted orange line is a defender forced to go around).






Vertical stretch (high-low). Two receivers in one defender’s area, one above him and one below. He can sink under the high route or come up on the low one, not both. This is the high-low read of Passing Fundamentals, and it is the most common family by far: smash, flood, levels, drive, shallow cross, dagger, Y-cross and yankee are all built on it. Notice that several of these (drive, shallow cross, Y-cross) use crossing routes: what makes them vertical stretches is that, at the moment of the throw, one route is above the key defender and one below him.
Horizontal stretch. Receivers on both sides of a defender at about the same depth, the horizontal stretch of Passing Fundamentals. Underneath, that’s the quick game’s spacing; deep, it is four verticals, post-wheel and scissors, which stretch the deep defenders side to side: two routes split one deep defender’s area (or two defenders’ leverage) inside and outside.
Triangle. Three receivers arranged around two defenders. A triangle read is a three-receiver read in which the routes form a triangle, one high and two low (or two high and one low), so the quarterback has a high-low and an inside-outside choice at once. Snag, from the quick game, is the classic; curl-flat with a third route inside is the dropback version.
Man-beater. A man-beater is a concept designed to beat man coverage. Stretches beat zone defenders, who guard areas; a man defender follows one receiver wherever he goes, so there is no area to overload. Man-beaters win instead with routes that cross close together (so defenders run into traffic), routes that break away from a defender’s leverage, and mismatches like a running back against a linebacker. Mesh and the angle route are the classics. Crossing alone doesn’t make a man-beater; what makes one is that it wins by making a man defender run through traffic or lose his leverage, not by stretching a zone.

Most real concepts are hybrids (a flood is a vertical stretch that also stretches the flat defender sideways; mesh sits in zone holes when it isn’t running away from man defenders), so the family names describe a concept’s main idea. That idea also tells you what coverage the concept is built to beat, and therefore when an offense will call it. We’ll come back to that matchup at the end of the chapter, and What Beats What builds it into a full table.

How to read the plates
The fourteen concepts below are drawn as plates, the way a playbook draws them, in one consistent style:

The offense is in shotgun with 11 personnel (one back, one tight end, three receivers) unless the caption says otherwise: X and Z are the outside receivers, H a slot receiver, Y a tight end or second slot, R the running back.
Blue routes are the concept. Grey routes are part of the call but outside the read: they are there to hold defenders in place. They aren’t forbidden; if a grey route is plainly open (a backside receiver left alone, say), a quarterback may take it, and many teams let him peek at a one-on-one on the backside before the snap. But he doesn’t read his way to them.
Green numbers are the progression, the order in which the quarterback looks. These are typical teaching orders; every team writes its own, and many change the order by coverage.
The defense is drawn in the coverage the concept is built to beat. Dashed orange arrows are zone drops; the ringed defender is the one in conflict, the man the quarterback reads. In the man-coverage plates, dotted lines join each defender to his man; which linebacker takes the back varies by team and call, and here it is always the Will, with the Mike free to rush or to sit in the middle.
The thick orange line is the line to gain; most plates assume ten yards to go, and the caption says so when it doesn’t.
The label at the top right names the concept’s family.

Two more things the plates simplify. First, receivers run to landmarks, spots on the field rather than bare depths, and you can see them on a broadcast: seam routes about two yards outside the hash marks (wider against one deep safety), go routes on or outside the painted numbers so there are five or six yards left for a back-shoulder throw, the smash corner route toward a spot about six yards from the sideline, and the Y-cross to the far numbers (Coverage Fundamentals teaches the defense’s landmarks). Second, the ball is drawn in the middle of the field to keep the picture symmetric. In a game it usually sits on a hash, and concepts get aimed: flood, Y-cross and post-wheel usually go toward the wide side, where the routes have room to finish; smash is often run into the short side against Cover 2, because the corner route is a shorter throw there.
High to low, or low to high? Each plate’s progression follows one of two rhythms, and knowing which saves you memorizing fourteen orders. Most vertical stretches are read from the top down: look at the deep route first, because if it’s open it’s the bigger gain, then come down to the short one, which will still be there a beat later. Some are read from the bottom up: a shallow crosser against man coverage wins immediately or not at all, so it gets the first look. And on a money down the progression often starts with whichever route reaches the line to gain. Each plate says which rhythm it uses.

title: Dropback Concepts: Smash, Flood, Mesh, Levels, Dagger, and Four Verticals
section: On the sideline: smash, flood and the curl-flat triangle
text:
On the sideline: smash, flood and the curl-flat triangle
The first three concepts attack the area near one sideline. Two of them (smash and flood) are vertical stretches; the third (curl-flat) is the dropback game’s triangle. Coaches like to say the sideline is an extra defender, for the defense, because a receiver can’t run past it and a throw that drifts lands out of bounds. Offenses attack it anyway because of arithmetic: out there a defense has only two or three players guarding a wide strip of grass, against five or more crowded between the hashes.

Smash: the corner over the hitch
Smash pairs two receivers on one side. The outside receiver runs a hitch at five or six yards and turns back to the quarterback. The inside receiver runs a corner route: ten or twelve yards straight up the field, then an angle toward the sideline and the back of the end zone. The defender in conflict is the cornerback on that side, and the read is high to low: the corner route first.


Show the Python
p = Play(spread(), cover2(extra={"RCB": (5.0, 17.2), "LCB": (5.0, -17.2)}), los=LOS, to_go=8)
protect(p)
p.dropback(2.5)
p.route("Z", r.hitch(6.0))
route_to(p, "Y", (10.5, 9.0), (18.0, 20.0))
rb_n = swing(p, -1)
p.drop("RCB", (6.5, 18.6))
p.drop("SS", (18.5, 11.5))
p.drop("NB", (8.5, 8.4))
p.drop("MIKE", (9.0, 1.2))
p.drop("WILL", (8.5, -8.0))
p.drop("FS", (18.5, -11.5))
p.drop("LCB", (6.5, -18.6))
p.highlight("RCB")
fld = plate(p, nums=[(1, (19.6, 22.0)), (2, (7.0, 13.2)), (3, rb_n)],
            ghosts=[[(-0.7, -15.0), (6.3, -15.0), (5.3, -14.4)], [(-1.5, -9.0), (10.5, -9.0), (18.0, -20.0)]],
            stretch="Vertical stretch: the cornerback")
opening(fld, p, (15.5, 18.0), (4.6, 5.6))
point_to(fld, p, (22.0, 3.0), (16.0, 16.0), "corner route lands\nbehind the CB, in front\nof the safety",
         color=READ_GREEN)
say(fld, p, 2.4, 21.8, "CB squats\non the hitch", color=DD)
plt.show()








Figure 23.2: Smash to the offense’s right against Cover 2, third-and-8. Z runs a hitch at about six yards; Y, from the slot, breaks at about ten and angles toward a spot six yards from the sideline, about 18 yards deep. The ringed cornerback squats in the flat, as Cover 2 tells him to; the strong safety (SS) has the deep half behind him but starts thirteen yards deep and well inside: the corner route lands in the gap between them (green). Progression, high to low: (1) the corner route if the cornerback sits on the hitch, (2) the hitch if he sinks, (3) the back as the checkdown. The left side (grey) is a mirror-image smash, so the quarterback can pick a side before the snap.





Why does it work against Cover 2? Cover 2 splits the deep field between two safeties and asks the cornerbacks to stay short, guarding the flats, so that nothing quick gets thrown to the outside. That leaves a seam of open grass along each sideline between the corner’s short zone and the safety’s deep half, roughly 12 to 20 yards deep, and the safety has to cover it from his spot near the hash, ten or fifteen yards away. The corner route aims at that seam. Whatever the cornerback does, one of the two routes is on the wrong side of him, so the quarterback only has to watch one man.
The corner route has to be thrown with care. Too flat and the cornerback can recover under it; too high and the safety arrives. Many teams build a rule into the route (a route conversion, which we’ll get to). Against two deep safeties, whose cornerbacks squat, the receiver takes it to depth, 15 to 20 yards along the sideline, over the cornerback and away from the safety. Against one deep safety, whose cornerback bails into a deep third, a corner route to that depth runs straight into him, so the receiver flattens it at about 12 to 14 yards, underneath the bailing cornerback, and some teams convert it to a post.
On third-and-8 there is one more wrinkle a coach would point out: a six-yard hitch is short of the sticks. It needs yards after the catch, which is one more reason the quarterback wants the corner route, and why some teams push the hitch to the line to gain on long downs.
What smash gives up. Against Cover 3, whose cornerbacks drop into deep thirds instead of squatting, a corner route run to full depth runs into a defender standing right on top of it, so the read flips: the cornerback bails, and the hitch underneath (or the flattened corner route) is the throw. Against man coverage, smash becomes two one-on-one routes, a hitch that has to beat a cornerback and a corner route that has to beat a slot defender, which is fine if the receivers are better than the defenders and not otherwise. Smash is a Cover 2 beater first, a decent answer to Cover 3 second, and only a hope against man.


Flood: three levels on one sideline
Flood (many teams call it sail) puts three receivers at three depths near one sideline: one deep, one in between and one shallow. On the strong side of a Cover 3 defense there are only two defenders in that area, the cornerback, who has the deep third, and the curl-flat defender underneath. Three receivers, two defenders.


Show the Python
p = Play(spread(rb_w=1.5), cover3(nb_side=1), los=LOS, to_go=10)
protect(p)
p.dropback(2.5)
p.route("Z", r.go(23.0))
route_to(p, "Y", (8.5, 9.0), (13.0, 17.8))
route_to(p, "RB", (-3.6, 5.0), (1.0, 11.5), (2.4, 16.5))
p.drop("RCB", (17.0, 16.6))
p.drop("NB", (8.0, 12.5))
p.drop("MIKE", (8.0, 3.0))
p.drop("FS", (17.0, 0.0))
p.drop("WILL", (8.0, -4.0))
p.drop("SS", (7.0, -12.0))
p.drop("LCB", (17.0, -16.6))
p.highlight("NB")
fld = plate(p, nums=[(1, (13.0, 20.3)), (2, (2.4, 19.2))],
            ghosts=[[(-0.7, -15.0), (11.3, -15.0), (10.0, -13.8)], [(-1.5, -9.0), (20.0, -7.6)]],
            stretch="Vertical stretch: three levels")
say(fld, p, 19.5, 10.5, "go: clears\nthe corner", color=OD)
say(fld, p, 9.6, 21.7, "sail", color=OD)
say(fld, p, -1.4, 21.3, "flat", color=OD)
plt.show()








Figure 23.3: Flood to the offense’s right against Cover 3. Z’s go route carries the cornerback deep (the clear-out). Y runs a sail route: ten yards up the field, then an angle toward the sideline that settles at about 13 yards. The back runs to the flat. The ringed nickel ($), the curl-flat defender, is the man in conflict. Read high to low: (1) the sail, (2) the flat. The go route is a bonus only if the cornerback lets Z run past him. On the left, X and H (grey) keep the Will and the free safety from drifting over.





Flood is a vertical stretch with three floors instead of two. The go route occupies the top floor and takes the cornerback with it, because a Cover 3 cornerback is taught never to let anyone get behind him. That leaves the curl-flat defender alone with the sail and the flat: the same high-low as the curl-flat read of Passing Fundamentals and slant-flat in the quick game, but with the high route farther outside and deeper, where he has to run farther to get under it. If he comes up for the flat, the sail settles in the space he left, in front of the cornerback, for 12 or 14 yards. If he sinks, the back catches the ball in the flat with open grass in front of him.
Flood’s cost is the other side of the field. It sends three receivers to one sideline, so the backside routes are usually just there to hold defenders, and a defense that rotates its coverage toward the flood (a safety rolling down to the flat side at the snap) can outnumber it. That is why flood is so often run off a fake run or with the quarterback rolling toward the flood side; the run fake and the bootleg, which move the defenders before the routes even arrive, are in Play-Action, Bootlegs, and Screens.


Curl-flat: the West Coast triangle
Curl-flat is the high-low you met in Passing Fundamentals: a curl at 10 to 12 yards over a flat route underneath, both in the area of the one defender who guards the short outside zone. As a dropback concept it usually comes with a third route, a back or tight end who settles in a hook route just inside the curl at five or six yards. That third route turns a two-man read into a triangle.


Show the Python
p = Play(spread(rb_w=1.5), cover3(nb_side=1, extra={"MIKE": (5.0, 3.6)}), los=LOS, to_go=10)
protect(p)
p.dropback(2.5)
p.route("Z", r.curl(12.0))
route_to(p, "Y", (1.0, 11.5), (2.0, 17.5))
route_to(p, "RB", (-3.5, 1.0), (1.0, 0.8), (4.6, 0.6), delay=0.4)
p.drop("NB", (8.5, 11.0))
p.drop("MIKE", (7.6, 5.6))
p.drop("RCB", (17.0, 16.6))
p.drop("FS", (17.0, 0.0))
p.drop("WILL", (8.0, -4.0))
p.drop("SS", (7.0, -12.0))
p.drop("LCB", (17.0, -16.6))
p.highlight("NB", "MIKE")
fld = plate(p, nums=[(1, (12.8, 12.6)), (2, (4.4, 19.4)), (3, (6.8, -0.2))],
            ghosts=[[(-0.7, -15.0), (11.3, -15.0), (9.8, -13.8)], [(-1.5, -9.0), (20.0, -7.6)]],
            stretch="Triangle: the $ and the Mike")
triangle(fld, p, [(9.8, 13.8), (2.0, 17.5), (4.6, 0.6)])
plt.show()








Figure 23.4: Curl-flat to the offense’s right, with the back’s hook route inside, against Cover 3. Z runs a curl at 12 yards, Y runs to the flat, and the back checks for a blitzer, then settles at five yards over the ball, just inside the Mike. The three routes form a triangle (shaded) with two defenders inside it: the ringed nickel ($), who guards the curl-flat area, and the ringed Mike (M), who guards the hook. Read high to low, then inside: (1) the curl, if the $ widens to the flat; (2) the flat, if he sinks under the curl; (3) the hook, if the Mike widens to help on the curl. The left side runs a mirror-image curl and a seam (grey).





The triangle is what makes the concept durable. The nickel can’t cover the curl and the flat (that’s the high-low), and if he splits the difference, the Mike has to choose between widening to help on the curl and staying home on the hook (that’s the in-out). The quarterback reads it with the same rhythm on almost every snap: eyes to the curl as his back foot lands, then down to the flat, then inside to the hook. The routes are short enough that the ball comes out in under three seconds, which is why curl-flat sits at the border between the quick game and the dropback game.
Curl-flat is a West Coast staple, the family of offenses descended from Bill Walsh’s 49ers, which were built on high-percentage throws with a third receiver underneath as the safety valve. Its weakness is its depth. Every route in the triangle is within 12 yards of the line of scrimmage, so a defense that squeezes the short zones and tackles well can hold it to a five-yard gain; and against two-high coverages, whose cornerbacks often sit short and outside, the curl can find a defender standing right on top of it.

title: Dropback Concepts: Smash, Flood, Mesh, Levels, Dagger, and Four Verticals
section: Vertical stretches in the middle: levels, drive, shallow cross and dagger
text:
Vertical stretches in the middle: levels, drive, shallow cross and dagger
The next four concepts carry the high-low into the middle of the field, where the linebackers live. The middle is harder to throw into (there are more defenders there, and they are closer together) but it’s also the most valuable area on the field, as the chart at the end of this section shows. The defender in conflict in each of these concepts is a linebacker, or a safety standing behind the linebackers, and the routes are mostly in-breakers: digs, shallow crosses and in routes that run across his face.

Levels: two in-breakers, two depths
Levels sends two receivers from the same side across the field on in-breaking routes at two depths: in the most common version the outside receiver runs a short in at about five yards and the inside receiver a dig at about twelve. The defender between those levels is the linebacker guarding the hook area on that side.


Show the Python
p = Play(spread(rb_w=1.5), cover3(nb_side=-1), los=LOS, to_go=10)
protect(p)
p.dropback(2.5)
p.route("H", r.dig(13.0, 12.0))
route_to(p, "X", (3.2, -15.0), (3.6, -5.0))
rb_n = swing(p, 1)
p.drop("WILL", (7.5, -6.5))
p.drop("NB", (7.0, -12.0))
p.drop("MIKE", (7.5, 3.5))
p.drop("SS", (7.0, 11.5))
p.drop("LCB", (17.0, -16.6))
p.drop("RCB", (17.0, 16.6))
p.drop("FS", (17.0, 0.0))
p.highlight("WILL")
fld = plate(p, nums=[(1, (12.4, 5.6)), (2, (1.4, -12.2)), (3, rb_n)],
            ghosts=[[(-1.5, 9.0), (20.0, 7.6)], [(-0.7, 15.0), (21.0, 15.0)]],
            stretch="Vertical stretch: the hook linebacker")
say(fld, p, 14.6, -9.0, "dig (high)", color=OD)
say(fld, p, 2.0, -20.0, "in (low)", color=OD)
plt.show()








Figure 23.5: Levels to the offense’s left against Cover 3. H, from the slot, runs a dig at 12 yards; X, from outside, runs a short in route at about 4 yards underneath him. The ringed Will linebacker (W), who drops to the hook area on that side, is the man in conflict: (1) the dig if he jumps the short in route; (2) the in route if he drops under the dig; (3) the back, who checks for a blitzer, then swings out to the right. On the right, Y’s seam and Z’s go route (grey) keep the free safety in the middle and the cornerback deep.





Why in-breakers? Because the linebacker in the middle is usually watching the quarterback, not the receivers, and he drops backward, which makes him slow to react to a route crossing in front of him or behind him. The short in route arrives first; the dig arrives a beat later, behind him. Coaches teach the quarterback to look high first: if the linebacker comes up on the in route, the dig behind him is the bigger gain. Peyton Manning’s Indianapolis offenses (where the play was called “Dig”) ran levels so often, by Chris Brown’s count, that ten times a game was not unusual, and its logic, two in-breakers on two floors, runs through many of the middle-of-the-field concepts that follow.2


Drive: the shallow and the dig, together
The next two concepts are built on one route, the shallow: a receiver crossing the whole field just past the line of scrimmage, two to five yards deep (some teams call it a drag). Each concept pairs it with a deeper in-breaker; what differs is where the two come from.
Drive is levels stretched across the whole field. One receiver runs a shallow, two to four yards deep, all the way to the far side; a teammate from the same side runs a dig at about twelve yards behind him, following him across. The pair passes through the hook zones of both linebackers, but the quarterback reads the first one they reach, the Mike: the ball comes out as the shallow clears him, long before the routes get to the Will. Unlike levels, drive is usually read low to high, because the shallow is open early or not at all.


Show the Python
p = Play(spread(), cover3(nb_side=1), los=LOS, to_go=10)
protect(p)
p.dropback(2.5)
route_to(p, "Y", (2.0, 8.2), (2.7, 4.5), (2.7, -13.0))
p.route("Z", r.dig(12.0, 24.0))
rb_n = swing(p, -1)
p.drop("MIKE", (7.0, 2.0))
p.drop("WILL", (7.0, -4.5))
p.drop("NB", (7.0, 12.0))
p.drop("SS", (7.0, -12.0))
p.drop("LCB", (17.0, -16.6))
p.drop("RCB", (17.0, 16.6))
p.drop("FS", (17.0, 0.0))
p.highlight("MIKE")
fld = plate(p, nums=[(1, (4.0, -4.7)), (2, (13.6, -4.4)), (3, rb_n)],
            ghosts=[[(-0.7, -15.0), (21.0, -15.0)], [(-1.5, -9.0), (20.0, -7.6)]],
            stretch="Vertical stretch: the Mike")
say(fld, p, 1.4, 21.0, "shallow at 2-4 yd", color=OD)
say(fld, p, 14.0, 20.0, "dig at 12 yd", color=OD)
plt.show()








Figure 23.6: Drive against Cover 3. From the right, Y runs a shallow at about three yards across the formation; Z runs a 12-yard dig behind him on the same path. The ringed Mike (M) can step up to the shallow or sink under the dig, not both. Read low to high, as each route crosses the Mike’s area: (1) the shallow, if he drops; (2) the dig, if he comes up; (3) the back, who checks for a blitzer and swings left. X’s go route and H’s seam (grey) take the left cornerback and the free safety deep, clearing the area where both crossers finish.





The shallow is the engine. A receiver crossing the field at three yards is a nightmare in man coverage, because his defender has to chase him through the traffic of linemen and linebackers and can never get in front of him; against zone, he runs through one hook defender after another, and each one has to decide whether to come up and take him. The moment one does, the dig is open behind. That makes drive one of the most useful concepts in football: a man-beater and a zone-beater in the same call. Drive is in a great many NFL playbooks, often under that name, and it’s a favorite of offenses that like to make the defense tackle a receiver who catches the ball running full speed across the field.


Shallow cross: the Air Raid’s bread and butter
Shallow cross uses the same two routes as drive, a shallow under a deeper in-breaker, but sends them from opposite sides. One receiver runs the shallow at three to five yards; the receiver from the other side runs a dig or a “sit” route at 10 to 12 yards, settling over the ball. (A sit route runs up to a depth and simply stops in the open space between zone defenders, facing the quarterback; against man it keeps running, as a dig.) Like drive, it is read low to high. The two routes cross the middle of the field going in opposite directions, so the middle linebacker has a receiver coming from each side at once.


Show the Python
p = Play(spread(), cover2(), los=LOS, to_go=10)
protect(p)
p.dropback(2.5)
route_to(p, "Z", (2.0, 13.0), (2.8, 9.0), (2.8, -12.0))
route_to(p, "H", (8.0, -9.0), (11.0, -6.5), (11.0, 2.0))
rb_n = swing(p, -1)
p.drop("MIKE", (9.5, 0.0))
p.drop("WILL", (8.5, -8.0))
p.drop("NB", (8.5, 8.4))
p.drop("LCB", (6.0, -17.2))
p.drop("RCB", (6.0, 17.2))
p.drop("FS", (18.5, -11.5))
p.drop("SS", (18.5, 11.5))
p.highlight("MIKE")
fld = plate(p, nums=[(1, (4.6, -11.2)), (2, (12.6, 3.6)), (3, rb_n)],
            ghosts=[[(-0.7, -15.0), (21.0, -15.0)], [(-1.5, 9.0), (21.0, 7.5)]],
            stretch="Vertical stretch: the Mike")
say(fld, p, 1.0, 19.5, "shallow at 3 yd", color=OD)
say(fld, p, 13.0, -14.2, "dig or sit at 11 yd", color=OD)
plt.show()








Figure 23.7: Shallow cross against Cover 2. From the right, Z runs a shallow at about three yards to the left; from the left, H runs a dig that settles at 11 yards over the ball. The ringed Mike (M), dropping into the middle, is the read: (1) the shallow, if he sinks; (2) the dig, if he comes up for the shallow; (3) the back on the left as the checkdown. X and Y (grey) run vertically to hold the two safeties, so nobody sinks under the dig from above. Against man coverage, the shallow simply runs away from his defender, and the two crossing paths add traffic.





The shallow cross is the play most associated with the Air Raid, the pass-first college offense built by Hal Mumme and Mike Leach (its story is below), which ran it with wide line splits and a quarterback taught to throw the shallow the instant the linebacker dropped. It works for the same reason drive does, plus one more: because the two crossers come from opposite sides, a man defender chasing the shallow may have to run around the dig receiver coming the other way. That is the first appearance of an idea we’ll make explicit with mesh, the rub.


Dagger: clear the seam, fill it behind
Dagger is the deep member of the family, and the one built to beat two-high coverages. The inside receiver runs straight up the seam; the outside receiver runs a deep dig, 15 to 18 yards, coming in behind him.


Show the Python
p = Play(spread(), quarters(extra={"SS": (10.0, 5.6), "FS": (10.0, -5.6)}), los=LOS, to_go=10)
protect(p)
p.dropback(3.0)
p.route("Y", r.seam(24.0))
p.route("Z", r.dig(15.5, 19.0))
rb_n = swing(p, -1)
p.drop("SS", (19.0, 9.0))
p.drop("NB", (11.0, 8.6))
p.drop("MIKE", (9.0, 3.0))
p.drop("WILL", (8.5, -7.0))
p.drop("FS", (13.0, -11.0))
p.drop("LCB", (16.0, -16.6))
p.highlight("SS")
fld = plate(p, nums=[(1, (21.0, 10.6)), (2, (13.2, -7.0)), (3, rb_n)],
            ghosts=[[(-0.7, -15.0), (11.3, -15.0), (9.8, -13.8)], [(-1.5, -9.0), (5.0, -9.0), (5.2, -7.0)]],
            stretch="Vertical stretch: safety and linebackers",
            keys=["route", "ghost", "drop", "react", "num", "ring", "ltg"])
branch(fld, p, [(7.5, 16.0), (11.5, 16.4), (15.0, 13.0)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.4)
opening(fld, p, (14.8, -1.0), (4.0, 9.0))
say(fld, p, 22.6, 4.0, "the seam pulls\nthem deep", color=OD)
say(fld, p, 18.6, -1.5, "dig fills in\nbehind them", color=READ_GREEN, weight="bold")
plt.show()








Figure 23.8: Dagger to the offense’s right against Quarters. Y runs straight up the seam; Z runs a dig at about 15 yards, in behind him. The ringed strong safety (SS) reads Y, the inside receiver, so the seam pulls him deep. The nickel runs with the seam for a few steps and the Mike drops to his hook zone, both short of the dig; the cornerback, playing Z from outside, can only trail a route that breaks inside (dashed). The dig settles under the safeties and over the linebackers (green). Read high to low: (1) the seam, if the safety doesn’t carry it; (2) the dig; (3) the back, who checks for a blitzer, then swings left. On the left, X and H (grey) keep the free safety from drifting over.





Why would two-high coverages be vulnerable to this? In Quarters and its relatives, each safety reads the inside receiver on his side: if that receiver goes vertical, the safety takes him deep; if he runs short, the safety is free to help on the outside receiver, usually by jumping an in-cut. That rule is what makes Quarters so good against the run and the quick game, because the safety can come up hard on anything short. The cornerback, meanwhile, plays the outside receiver almost man-to-man, from outside leverage.
Dagger turns both rules against them. The seam takes the safety, the one defender whose job was to rob the dig, out of the picture. The underneath defenders don’t come up on a vertical route, as you might expect; they are taught to run with it for a few steps, because a seam thrown over their heads is the play that beats them. So the nickel carries the seam and the Mike drops to his hook zone, eight or nine yards deep. That leaves the cornerback alone on the dig, and he is on the wrong side of it: playing from outside, he can only trail a receiver who breaks inside. The dig, timed to arrive a beat after the seam, settles in the empty middle between the levels.
Against one-high coverage the read is similar but the threat is different: the seam attacks the single safety, and if he stays in the middle, the dig crosses under him. Dagger needs time, because a 15-yard dig takes a deep drop and three seconds or more, which is why it’s usually called with six-man protection, or with five and the back checking for a blitzer before he releases, as drawn.


Where the value is
Why do offenses work so hard to throw into the middle, where the linebackers are, rather than to the open sideline? The chart answers that with three seasons of throws.


Show the Python
order = ["30+", "20–29", "15–19", "10–14", "5–9", "0–4", "behind"]
bins = [-99, 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 99]
labs = ["behind", "0–4", "5–9", "10–14", "15–19", "20–29", "30+"]
h = ATT.copy()
h["depth"] = pd.cut(h["air_yards"], bins, labels=labs, right=False)
g = h.groupby(["depth", "pass_location"], observed=True)["epa"].agg(["mean", "size"]).reset_index()
M = g.pivot(index="depth", columns="pass_location", values="mean").loc[order, ["left", "middle", "right"]]
N = g.pivot(index="depth", columns="pass_location", values="size").loc[order, ["left", "middle", "right"]]
from matplotlib.colors import LinearSegmentedColormap, TwoSlopeNorm
cmap = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("div", [style.DIVERGING[2], style.DIVERGING[1], style.DIVERGING[0]])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.4, 4.0))
ax.imshow(M.values, cmap=cmap, norm=TwoSlopeNorm(vmin=-0.6, vcenter=0.0, vmax=0.6), aspect="auto")
for i in range(M.shape[0]):
    for j in range(M.shape[1]):
        v = M.values[i, j]
        ax.text(j, i - 0.08, f"{v:+.2f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=9.5,
                color="white" if abs(v) > 0.42 else style.INK, fontweight="bold")
        ax.text(j, i + 0.26, f"n = {int(N.values[i, j]):,}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.6,
                color="white" if abs(v) > 0.42 else style.INK_2)
ax.set_xticks(range(3), ["left third", "middle", "right third"], fontsize=8.5)
ax.set_yticks(range(len(order)), [f"{o} yd" if o != "behind" else "behind LOS" for o in order], fontsize=8.5)
ax.set_xlabel("Where the ball went (offense's view)", fontsize=8.5)
ax.set_ylabel("Air yards", fontsize=8.5)
ax.grid(False)
for sp in ax.spines.values():
    sp.set_visible(False)
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((0.5, 1.5), 1.0, 2.0, fill=False, ec=style.INK, lw=1.6, zorder=5))
ax.set_title("EPA per attempt by depth and direction, 2023–2025", fontsize=9.5, loc="left")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 23.9: Expected points added (EPA) per pass attempt by where the ball was thrown, 2023–2025 regular seasons: rows are depth past the line of scrimmage (air yards), columns are the play-by-play charter’s left, middle and right thirds of the field. Blue cells added value on average, red cells lost it; the small number is the count of attempts. The intermediate middle (10–20 yards between the hashes, where the digs of levels, drive, shallow cross and dagger are thrown) is, with the deep middle, the most valuable area on the field per attempt, worth half a point or more. Deep throws are valuable everywhere but rarer; throws behind the line lose value on average. Sacks and spikes are excluded; interceptions count against the cell they were thrown to.





The boxed cells are the payoff. Over three seasons, a throw of 10 to 19 yards into the middle of the field added about half an expected point on average, more than the same depth toward either sideline and more than any short throw anywhere.3 Two cautions keep the chart honest. First, it shows where the ball went, not where the quarterback wanted it to go: quarterbacks throw into the middle when somebody is open there, so the cells partly measure good decisions. Second, the middle is also where interceptions happen (the defenders are closer together), and those are already folded into the averages. (The worst cell, throws behind the line into the middle, is a small and messy one: about a third are screens, one in nine is a throwaway, and only 60% are completed, against about 80% for throws behind the line toward either sideline; the middle behind the line is crowded with linemen and pass rushers.) Even so, the shape explains a great deal of offensive design: the intermediate middle is worth fighting for, and the concepts in this section are the tools for getting there.

title: Dropback Concepts: Smash, Flood, Mesh, Levels, Dagger, and Four Verticals
section: Y-cross: a flood built from across the field
text:
Y-cross: a flood built from across the field
Y-cross combines the two ideas so far, the three-level flood and the in-breaker through the middle. A receiver from one side (in the Air Raid’s lettering, the Y, the inside receiver) runs a crossing route that climbs to 15 to 18 yards as it goes and finishes at the far numbers. On that far side, the outside receiver runs a go route to clear the cornerback away and another receiver runs to the flat. The result is a flood whose middle level arrives from the other side of the field, at full speed, where no defender on that side was looking for it.


Show the Python
p = Play(spread(rb_w=1.5), cover3(nb_side=1, extra={"FS": (14.5, 0.0)}), los=LOS, to_go=10)
protect(p)
p.dropback(3.0)
route_to(p, "Y", (6.5, 9.2), (10.0, 3.0), (15.5, -12.0))
p.route("X", r.go(23.0))
route_to(p, "H", (0.5, -11.5), (2.0, -17.0))
rb_n = swing(p, 1)
p.drop("SS", (8.0, -12.0))
p.drop("LCB", (17.0, -16.6))
p.drop("FS", (18.0, 0.0))
p.drop("WILL", (8.0, -4.0))
p.drop("MIKE", (8.0, 3.0))
p.drop("NB", (8.0, 12.0))
p.drop("RCB", (17.0, 16.6))
p.highlight("SS")
fld = plate(p, nums=[(1, (17.5, -10.4)), (2, (3.6, -19.6)), (3, rb_n)],
            ghosts=[[(-0.7, 15.0), (11.3, 15.0), (21.0, 8.0)]],
            stretch="Vertical stretch: three levels")
say(fld, p, 23.8, -11.6, "go: clears\nthe corner", color=OD)
say(fld, p, 20.4, -4.0, "the cross climbs\nto about 16", color=OD)
plt.show()








Figure 23.10: Y-cross against Cover 3. Y, from the right slot, pushes up past the nickel, then crosses the field under the free safety, climbing to about 16 yards toward the far numbers. On the left, X’s go route takes the cornerback deep and H runs to the flat underneath. Z’s post (grey) holds the free safety in the middle. The ringed strong safety, the curl-flat defender on the left, faces a high-low, read high to low: (1) the cross if he comes up to the flat; (2) the flat if he sinks under the cross; (3) the back, who checks for a blitzer, then swings right. Teams usually run it toward the wide side of the field, so the crosser has room to finish.





The quarterback reads Y-cross like a flood: eyes on the curl-flat defender on the far side, cross over flat. What makes it special is timing and angle. The crosser is running away from the defenders who started on his side and toward a defender who has to turn and find him, so he arrives in the window with momentum and with no one trailing who can catch up. That also makes it a good answer to man coverage, since a crossing route is the hardest route for a man defender to stay on top of. The price is time: a crosser at 15 to 18 yards needs three seconds or more, so Y-cross asks a lot of the pass protection.






NoteGo deeper: the Air Raid’s small menu



The Air Raid was built at small colleges, not in the NFL. Hal Mumme, a former high school coach and college assistant, and Mike Leach, a law-school graduate who had never played college football, put it together at Iowa Wesleyan around 1989, took it to Valdosta State and then, in 1997, to the University of Kentucky, where quarterback Tim Couch became the first pick of the 1999 NFL draft. Leach went on to run it as a head coach at Texas Tech, Washington State and Mississippi State.4
Their starting point was the passing game of LaVell Edwards’s BYU teams, which they studied in person, and their central idea was subtraction: run a handful of concepts (mesh, shallow cross, Y-cross, four verticals, a few quick-game calls) from a handful of formations, and practice them so many times that the quarterback and receivers react instead of think. Where an NFL playbook might carry hundreds of pass plays, the Air Raid lived on a dozen or so. Its lesson for this chapter is that a concept’s power comes as much from repetition as from design: a quarterback who has read the same curl-flat defender on the same Y-cross ten thousand times throws the ball before the defender has finished deciding. The full story of the Air Raid’s spread through college and then the NFL is told in The College Laboratory.

title: Dropback Concepts: Smash, Flood, Mesh, Levels, Dagger, and Four Verticals
section: Man-beaters: mesh, the rub and the angle route
text:
Man-beaters: mesh, the rub and the angle route
Everything so far is built to beat zone defenders, who guard areas and can be put between two receivers. Man coverage changes the problem. Each defender has one receiver and follows him, so there is no area to overload and no defender in two minds; the defense is betting its players can stay with yours. The most common version in the NFL is Cover 1: a man on every receiver, one safety deep in the middle, and often one more defender free to rush or to sit in the middle as a helper (Man Coverage builds it from the defense’s side). The answer is to make staying with a receiver hard: send receivers across the field, where their defenders have to chase them through traffic; break away from a defender’s leverage; or find a defender who is badly matched against the man he has to cover.

Mesh
Mesh is the purest man-beater in football. Two receivers from opposite sides run shallow crossing routes, five or six yards deep, that pass within a yard or two of each other over the middle of the field. One runs his cross a step higher than the other, and Air Raid coaches tell them to pass close enough to slap hands.


Show the Python
p = Play(spread(rb_w=1.5), cover1(), los=LOS, to_go=3)
protect(p, rushers=("WDE", "WDT", "SDT", "SDE"))
p.rush("MIKE", pts=[(-4.0, 2.6)], speed=4.0)
p.dropback(2.5)
route_to(p, "H", (3.8, -9.0), (6.6, -6.0), (7.0, 9.5))
route_to(p, "Y", (2.6, 8.4), (5.2, 5.0), (5.8, -10.5))
p.route("X", r.corner(10.0))
p.route("Z", r.corner(10.0))
route_to(p, "RB", (-3.4, 5.0), (0.2, 9.5), (1.2, 12.0))
for d_, t_ in (("LCB", "X"), ("RCB", "Z"), ("NB", "H"), ("SS", "Y"), ("WILL", "RB")):
    p.man(d_, t_)
p.highlight("NB", "SS")
fld = plate(p, nums=[(1, (21.6, 21.2)), (2, (8.0, 10.6)), (2, (6.6, -12.4)), (3, (-2.6, 12.0))],
            keys=["route", "man", "num", "ring", "ltg"])
opening(fld, p, (6.3, 0.0), (2.6, 4.2))
say(fld, p, 10.0, -0.2, "the mesh point:\nclose enough to\nslap hands", color=OD)
tag(fld, p, "Man-beater (and zone holes)")
plt.show()








Figure 23.11: Mesh against Cover 1 (man coverage with one deep safety), third-and-3, the version run by the Air Raid. H and Y cross at five to six yards over the ball, H a step above Y, so the defenders chasing them, the nickel ($) and the strong safety (SS), both ringed, have to get around one receiver to stay with the other. X and Z run corner routes and the back runs to the right flat. The progression in the traditional Air Raid order: (1) the corner route on the back’s side, over his flat route; (2) the crossers, whichever comes out of the traffic first; (3) the back. Dotted lines are man assignments: the Will has the back, and the Mike rushes.





Against man coverage the two crossing paths do the work. The nickel chasing H has to get past Y coming the other way, and the safety chasing Y has to get past H. One of them almost always loses a step, and a receiver crossing the field with a one-step lead is nearly impossible to catch from behind. Against zone the same routes simply settle: each crosser finds the space between two underneath defenders and sits down facing the quarterback, so the concept is useful even when the defense guesses right. The corner routes give the quarterback a high-low against the cornerbacks, and keep the safety from crowding the middle.
Why would the Air Raid’s progression start with the corner route in the purest man-beater? Timing and payoff. The crossers need a beat to get through the traffic and come out the other side; the corner route over the back’s flat is ready first, and it is a high-low on whoever has the flat, so if it’s open it’s the biggest gain on the play. By the time the quarterback comes off it, one of the crossers has usually come free. Against a defense he knows is in man, many teams skip straight to the crossers, the low-to-high rhythm of drive.
Mesh came into the Air Raid from BYU, which, as Leach put it, ran the crossing pattern “for two decades” under LaVell Edwards, and it became one of the Air Raid’s signature plays;5 versions of it now appear in nearly every NFL playbook, often as a third-down call, when defenses play the most man coverage.


The rub, and where it becomes a pick
Mesh works because of a specific kind of route. A rub route (also called a pick route) is a route designed to cross close to a teammate’s route, so a defender chasing one receiver has to go around the other. Crossers, stacked receivers who release in opposite directions, and a slot receiver running a quick out under an outside receiver’s slant are all rubs. They are among the most effective plays in football against man coverage, especially near the goal line, where the field is short and defenders play tight.
They are also the most argued-about. The rules allow a receiver to run his route even if a defender runs into him. They don’t allow him to block a defender downfield until the pass is touched. In the NFL, a receiver who deliberately makes contact with a defender more than one yard past the line of scrimmage to get a teammate open, from the snap until the pass is touched, has committed offensive pass interference, a 10-yard penalty; contact within a yard of the line isn’t pass interference.6 That is the line between a rub and an illegal pick.
So is a pick inside that first yard legal? As far as pass interference goes, yes, and offenses use it: stacked and bunched receivers who release into each other right at the line are designed to make the contact happen there, before the one-yard limit. A receiver who grabs or shoves a defender can still be flagged for holding or illegal use of hands, but bumping him at the line on the way into a route is not a pick.


Show the Python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 3.5))
for ax, legal in zip(axes, (True, False)):
    off = [O("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, -3.0), O("Y", "WR", OFF_BALL, 3.0), O("C", "C", LINE_D, 0.0)]
    dfn = [D("SS", "SS", 1.6, 2.4, "SS"), D("NB", "NB", 1.6, -2.4, "$")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=LOS, to_go=None)
    if legal:
        route_to(p, "H", (3.0, -3.0), (5.5, 0.0), (6.0, 6.5))
    else:
        route_to(p, "H", (3.0, -3.0), (4.0, -0.8))
    route_to(p, "Y", (2.5, 3.0), (4.6, 0.6), (5.2, -6.5))
    fld = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-9.5, 9.5), window=(-3.5, 10.5), show_ruler=False, width_in=3.2)

    x1, y1 = _P(fld, p, 1.0, 9.5)

    else:
