        say(fld, p, 8.6, -3.6, "H stops and steps\ninto the SS 4 yards\ndownfield: flag", color=DD, fontsize=6.6)
        panel_title(ax, "Illegal pick (OPI)", fs=8.5)
    say(fld, p, -1.6, 6.4, "first yard:\nnot PI", color=READ_GREEN, fontsize=6.2)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=1.0)
plt.show()








Figure 23.12: The same two routes, legal and illegal. Left: a legal rub. H runs his crossing route without breaking stride; the strong safety chasing Y has to go around him (dotted orange), loses a step, and Y comes free. No one blocked anybody. Right: an illegal pick. H stops his route four yards downfield, turns, and steps into Y’s defender before the pass is touched: that is offensive pass interference. The defenders match the mesh plate: the nickel ($) has H, the strong safety (SS) has Y. The green band is the first yard past the line of scrimmage, where contact between receivers and defenders isn’t pass interference in the NFL.





The trouble is that the difference is often a matter of intent and inches, and officials have to judge it at full speed. Offenses teach receivers to run through the defender’s path rather than at him, and to keep running; defenses teach their players to communicate (“switch” or “banjo,” trading receivers instead of chasing through the traffic, which Man Coverage explains) or to play zone, against which rubs gain nothing. How the officials enforce pass interference, and how often they call it, is in Contact Rules and Penalties.
Here is mesh against man coverage, moving. Watch the strong safety chasing Y (circled in brown).


Show the Python
def mesh_play():
    p = Play(spread(rb_w=1.5), cover1(), los=LOS, to_go=3)
    protect(p)
    p.rush("MIKE", pts=[(-4.0, 2.6)], speed=4.0)
    p.dropback(2.5)
    route_to(p, "H", (3.8, -9.0), (6.6, -6.0), (7.0, 9.5), (7.2, 14.0))
    route_to(p, "Y", (2.6, 8.4), (5.2, 5.0), (5.8, -10.5), (6.0, -16.0))
    p.route("X", r.corner(10.0))
    p.route("Z", r.corner(10.0))
    route_to(p, "RB", (-3.4, 5.0), (0.2, 9.5), (1.2, 12.0))
    p.drop("FS", (15.0, 0.0), speed=2.0)
    p.pass_to("Y", t=2.1)
    set_track(p, "NB", chase(p, "NB", "H", lag=0.1, off=(0.6, -0.8)))
    # the SS trails Y closely, then has to go over the top of H at the mesh point
    set_track(p, "SS", chase(p, "SS", "Y", lag=0.08, off=(-0.5, 0.5), detour=(1.6, 2.4, (8.3, 0.9)),
                             lag_after=0.35))
    set_track(p, "LCB", chase(p, "LCB", "X", lag=0.15, off=(-0.6, 0.6)))
    set_track(p, "RCB", chase(p, "RCB", "Z", lag=0.15, off=(-0.6, -0.6)))
    set_track(p, "WILL", chase(p, "WILL", "RB", lag=0.3, off=(1.6, -0.8), t_start=0.3, t_on=1.3))
    return p


mp = mesh_play()
with ball_speed(24.0):
    mt = catch_time(mp)
notes = ["Man coverage: $ on H, SS on Y, Will on\nthe back, one safety deep, Mike rushes.",
         "The mesh point: H and Y cross; the SS\nhas to go over the top of H.",
         "Ball out at 2.1 s: Y is about three\nyards clear, running away from the SS.",
         "Caught in stride, with open grass\nto the left and no one in front."]
with ball_speed(24.0):
    play_movie(mp, [0.0, 1.9, 2.1, mt], notes=notes, lateral=(-16.0, 14.0), window=(-9.0, 17.0),
               rings=(("SS", style.THIRD), ("Y", style.BALL)), throw_t=2.1)





  
  Your browser does not support the video tag.



Figure 23.13: Mesh against Cover 1, simulated (BDB-format tracking, generated by gridiron rather than recorded). H and Y cross at about six yards over the ball, H a step higher. The nickel ($) trails H on his hip, above the traffic. The strong safety (SS, ringed green), trailing Y (ringed brown) by about a yard, meets H at the mesh point and has to go over the top of him; by the time the ball is out, at 2.1 seconds, Y has about a three-yard lead and is running away from him toward the open left side, before the deep safety can come down. Faint lines are where each player has been; the brown dashes are the ball in flight.






The angle route: a running back against a linebacker
The other classic man-beater uses a mismatch instead of traffic. In man coverage, somebody has to cover the running back, and it is usually a linebacker (in these pictures, the Will): a player chosen for stopping runs, often thirty pounds heavier than the back and a step slower in space. The angle route (many playbooks call it the Texas route) is built for that matchup. The back releases toward the flat as if running a swing, and when the linebacker widens to chase him, he plants and snaps back inside, angling upfield under the middle of the field.


Show the Python
p = Play(spread(rb_w=1.5), cover1(extra={"WILL": (5.0, 0.2), "MIKE": (4.2, -2.6), "SS": (4.5, 7.2), "NB": (1.6, -7.4)}), los=LOS, to_go=7)
protect(p)
p.rush("MIKE", pts=[(-4.0, 3.4)], speed=4.0)
p.dropback(2.5)
route_to(p, "RB", (-3.6, 4.8), (-0.8, 7.5), (0.8, 7.2), (6.2, 3.4))
p.route("Y", r.seam(20.0))
p.route("Z", r.go(21.0))
for d_, t_ in (("LCB", "X"), ("RCB", "Z"), ("NB", "H"), ("SS", "Y"), ("WILL", "RB")):
    p.man(d_, t_)
p.highlight("WILL")
fld = plate(p, nums=[(1, (7.6, 2.0)), (2, (19.8, 10.6))],
            ghosts=[[(-0.7, -15.0), (2.3, -15.0), (6.5, -10.2)], [(-1.5, -9.0), (19.0, -9.0)]],
            keys=["route", "ghost", "man", "react", "num", "ring", "ltg"])
branch(fld, p, [(5.0, 0.2), (3.8, 3.8), (2.9, 6.2)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.4)
say(fld, p, -4.6, 10.0, "release\nwide...", color=OD)
say(fld, p, 9.6, 6.4, "...snap back\ninside", color=OD)
tag(fld, p, "Man-beater: the linebacker")
plt.show()








Figure 23.14: The angle route against Cover 1, on the offense’s right, third-and-7. The back (R) releases wide toward the flat, then plants just past the line and breaks back inside and upfield, into the space the linebacker started in. The ringed Will (W), covering him man-to-man, widens with the release (dashed orange) and is left outside when the back cuts back. Y’s seam and Z’s go carry the strong safety and the cornerback deep, out of the area the angle route breaks into. The progression: (1) the angle route; (2) Y’s seam, one-on-one against the strong safety, if the Will doesn’t bite and stays inside. The Mike rushes. The left side (grey) runs a slant and a go.





The angle route is a cousin of the option route of Passing Fundamentals: the back is breaking away from his defender’s leverage. Against zone it still works if the routes outside clear the area, because the back settles in the hook zone the linebacker has left, though the throw is worth less. It is also why offenses love backs who can run routes: a back who wins on the angle route forces the defense either to cover him with a safety, which takes a defender out of the run fit, or to accept the mismatch.

text:
Deep shots: four verticals, post-wheel, scissors and yankee
The last four concepts go deep. They exist because a defense that never has to worry about the deep ball will crowd every short and intermediate route in this chapter; somebody has to make the deepest defenders defend something. Each of them stretches the deep defenders, the safeties and the cornerbacks who play over the top, rather than the linebackers.

Four verticals
Four verticals is the simplest idea in the passing game: four receivers run straight up the field at once. The two outside receivers stay near the sideline, the two inside receivers run up the seams, a few yards outside the hashes. The defense has only two or three deep defenders, so somebody is one-on-one, or nobody is there at all.


Show the Python
p = Play(spread(rb_w=1.5), cover3(nb_side=1), los=LOS, to_go=10)
protect(p)
p.dropback(3.0)
for k in ("X", "Z"):
    p.route(k, r.path((10.0, 0.4), (24.0, 1.0)))
for k in ("H", "Y"):
    p.route(k, r.path((7.0, -1.4), (24.0, -3.0)))
route_to(p, "RB", (-3.6, 2.8), (4.0, 1.0), delay=0.8)
p.drop("FS", (17.0, 0.0))
p.drop("LCB", (17.0, -16.8))
p.drop("RCB", (17.0, 16.8))
p.drop("NB", (11.0, 9.0))
p.drop("SS", (11.0, -9.0))
p.drop("MIKE", (8.5, 3.0))
p.drop("WILL", (8.5, -4.0))
p.highlight("FS")
fld = plate(p, nums=[(1, (22.4, -8.4)), (1, (22.4, 8.4)), (2, (5.8, 0.0))],
            stretch="Horizontal stretch: the deep defenders")
bracket(fld, p, 20.0, -6.0, 6.0, "", color=DD)
say(fld, p, 18.2, 0.0, "one safety,\ntwo seams", color=DD)
plt.show()








Figure 23.15: Four verticals against Cover 3. X and Z run go routes outside the numbers; H and Y run up the seams just outside the hashes. Three deep defenders face four vertical routes: the cornerbacks have the outside receivers in their deep thirds, so the ringed free safety, alone in the middle third, has two seams to cover. The progression: (1) the seam he doesn’t take, read from his first steps; (2) the back, who checks for a blitzer and then settles over the ball, if the curl-flat defenders sink with the seams. The outside go routes are the first look only against a cornerback who sits short, as in Cover 2.





The arithmetic is the point. Against Cover 3, three deep defenders divide the field into thirds; four vertical routes put two receivers in the middle third, where there is only one defender. If he leans toward one seam, the quarterback throws the other. Against Cover 2, with two deep safeties each guarding a half, the seams split the safeties and the outside receivers attack the gap between the squatting cornerbacks and the safeties along the sideline, the same hole smash attacks. The concept forces the deep defenders to show where they are, and the quarterback reads them, not the underneath ones. The defense’s best answer is to have the curl-flat defenders run with the seams for the first several yards, so the safety only has to help on one of them; how Cover 3 defenses do that is a large part of The Cover 3 Family.


Show the Python
def verts_play():
    p = Play(spread(rb_w=1.5), cover3(nb_side=1), los=LOS, to_go=10)
    protect(p)
    p.dropback(3.0)
    for k in ("X", "Z"):
        p.route(k, r.path((10.0, 0.4), (28.0, 1.2)))
    for k in ("H", "Y"):
        p.route(k, r.path((7.0, -1.4), (28.0, -3.2)))
    route_to(p, "RB", (-3.6, 2.8), (4.0, 1.0), delay=0.8)
    p.drop("LCB", (25.0, -17.0), speed=5.5)
    p.drop("RCB", (25.0, 17.0), speed=5.5)
    p.path("FS", [(1.5, 0.6), (3.5, 4.0), (5.0, 6.4)], speed=4.2, delay=0.2)   # drifts with the QB's eyes
    p.path("FS", [(4.0, -6.5)], speed=6.5, delay=0.15)                         # breaks on the throw
    p.path("NB", [(6.5, -0.2)], speed=4.5)     # carries Y's seam a few steps, then lets him go
    p.path("SS", [(6.0, 0.4)], speed=4.5)      # the same with H
    p.drop("MIKE", (8.0, 3.0))
    p.drop("WILL", (8.0, -4.0))
    p.pass_to("H", t=2.2)
    return p


def qb_eyes(ax, fld, cur, t, play=None, until=2.15, look=(7.0, 6.0)):
    """A green arrow from the quarterback toward where he is looking, before the throw."""
    if play is None or not (0.3 <= t <= until):
        return
    qd, qw = play.position("QB", t)
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = fld.xy(*play.to_abs(qd, qw)), fld.xy(*play.to_abs(qd + look[0], qw + look[1]))
    ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((float(x0), float(y0)), (float(x1), float(y1)), arrowstyle="-|>",
                                 mutation_scale=9, color=READ_GREEN, lw=1.4, ls=(0, (2, 1.5)), zorder=9,
                                 shrinkA=6, shrinkB=0))
    ax.text(float(x1), float(y1), " eyes", color=READ_GREEN, fontsize=6.5, ha="left", va="center",
            fontweight="bold", zorder=12)


vp = verts_play()
with ball_speed(24.0):
    vt = catch_time(vp)
notes = ["Three deep defenders (two CBs, FS)\nagainst four vertical routes.",
         "The CBs bail with X and Z; the seams\nrun past the curl-flat defenders.",
         "The QB has looked right; the FS drifted\nto Y. A beat later, the ball goes to H.",
         "Caught about 25 yards deep, in the\nmiddle third the FS left."]
with ball_speed(24.0):
    play_movie(vp, [0.0, 1.6, 2.1, vt], notes=notes, lateral=(-24.0, 24.0), window=(-10.5, 31.0),
               rings=(("FS", style.THIRD),), throw_t=2.2,
               deco=lambda ax, fld, cur, t: qb_eyes(ax, fld, cur, t, play=vp))





  
  Your browser does not support the video tag.



Figure 23.16: Four verticals against Cover 3, simulated (BDB-format tracking, generated by gridiron). The cornerbacks bail with the outside receivers, staying two or three yards on top of them; the curl-flat defenders run with the seams for a few steps and then let them go; and the free safety (ringed) has to choose. The quarterback looks to his right as he drops (the green arrow is his eyes), and the safety drifts that way, toward Y; the ball goes to H on the left seam, behind the curl-flat defender and in front of the cornerback, about 25 yards downfield. The safety breaks on the throw, too late.




Notice what the quarterback did with his eyes. He looked toward Y as he dropped, and the safety, who reads the quarterback, drifted that way. Moving a defender with your eyes is called a look-off, and it’s an essential skill for any concept that reads a single deep defender (Quarterback Play has more).
Four verticals has no single inventor. Its roots are usually traced to the vertical passing games of Sid Gillman and Don Coryell, to LaVell Edwards’s BYU and to the run-and-shoot offenses of Mouse Davis, all of which built their attacks around receivers running up the field; the Air Raid turned it into a signature call, with receivers taught to stay in their lanes but get open in them.7 In the modern NFL it rarely looks like four straight lines. The seam runners usually carry a read, holding straight against one deep safety and bending inside between two (a route conversion, as below), and offenses with speed outside, like Andy Reid’s Chiefs with Tyreek Hill, use the outside go routes to push the cornerbacks off.


Post-wheel
Post-wheel splits the defenders on one side, inside and out. The outside receiver runs a post, angling toward the middle at about 12 yards; the inside receiver (or a back) runs a wheel, out toward the flat and then straight up the sideline, into the space the post receiver just left. It is read high and outside first: the wheel.


Show the Python
p = Play(spread(), cover3(nb_side=1), los=LOS, to_go=10)
protect(p)
p.dropback(3.0)
route_to(p, "Z", (10.0, 15.0), (19.5, 7.5))
route_to(p, "Y", (-0.8, 11.5), (1.5, 14.5), (5.5, 18.5), (21.0, 19.4))
rb_n = swing(p, -1)
p.drop("NB", (6.0, 13.6))
p.drop("FS", (16.0, 0.0))
p.drop("MIKE", (8.0, 3.0))
p.drop("WILL", (8.0, -4.0))
p.drop("SS", (7.0, -12.0))
p.drop("LCB", (17.0, -16.6))
p.highlight("RCB", "NB")
fld = plate(p, nums=[(1, (21.0, 21.9)), (2, (21.2, 7.0)), (3, rb_n)],
            ghosts=[[(-0.7, -15.0), (11.3, -15.0), (11.3, -5.0)], [(-1.5, -9.0), (20.0, -7.6)]],
            stretch="Horizontal stretch: corner and $",
            keys=["route", "ghost", "drop", "react", "num", "ring", "ltg"])
branch(fld, p, [(7.0, 16.0), (11.5, 15.6), (16.5, 11.0)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.4)
say(fld, p, 13.5, 22.4, "wheel", color=OD)
say(fld, p, 12.4, 9.0, "post", color=OD)
plt.show()








Figure 23.17: Post-wheel to the offense’s right against match Cover 3, a version many NFL defenses now play. Z runs a post; Y, from the slot, runs a wheel, out toward the flat and then up the sideline. The two ringed defenders are the pair in conflict. The cornerback’s rule is to carry the outside receiver when he goes deep, so the post drags him inside (dashed). That hands the wheel to the nickel ($), the curl-flat defender, who widened with Y’s release from five yards deep and can’t turn and run with him up the sideline. Progression: (1) the wheel; (2) the post, if the cornerback passes Z on to the free safety and stays outside; (3) the back on the left. H’s seam (grey) holds the free safety in the middle.





Why does it work? Because each defender on that side has a sensible rule, and the two routes make the rules collide. Many NFL defenses now play match Cover 3: instead of dropping to a spot, each defender picks up a receiver once the routes declare. The cornerback’s rule is to carry the outside receiver if he goes deep, so when Z pushes vertical and bends to the post, the cornerback goes inside with him. The curl-flat defender’s rule is to take the second receiver if he goes to the flat. The wheel starts as exactly that, a harmless flat route, and then turns up the sideline, where a nickel who started five yards deep, facing the quarterback, has to turn and run with a receiver who already has a head of steam. The wheel is behind him and outside the cornerback, and nobody’s rule covers it in time.
If the cornerback refuses to be dragged inside (some teams teach him to pass the post on to the free safety and stay outside for anything up the sideline), the post is the throw: now it’s a one-on-one inside against the free safety, whom the backside seam has held in the middle. We file post-wheel as a horizontal stretch because that is its shape: two deep routes, one breaking inside and one outside, splitting the defenders’ areas side to side. Against man coverage it is better still: the wheel puts a slot receiver or a running back against a nickel or a linebacker who has to turn and run up the sideline with him.


Scissors
Scissors is post-wheel’s two-high cousin. The outside receiver still runs a post, but the inside receiver runs a corner route instead of a wheel, so their paths cross at 10 to 12 yards like the blades of a pair of scissors. It is read inside first: the post.


Show the Python
p = Play(spread(), quarters(extra={"SS": (10.5, 6.6), "FS": (10.5, -6.6)}), los=LOS, to_go=10)
protect(p)
p.dropback(3.0)
route_to(p, "Z", (9.3, 15.0), (19.5, 5.0))
route_to(p, "Y", (8.5, 9.0), (18.5, 18.6))
rb_n = swing(p, -1)
p.drop("NB", (8.5, 10.0))
p.drop("FS", (15.0, -8.0))
p.drop("MIKE", (8.0, 3.0))
p.drop("WILL", (8.0, -5.0))
p.drop("LCB", (15.0, -16.0))
p.highlight("SS", "RCB")
fld = plate(p, nums=[(1, (21.2, 3.4)), (2, (20.0, 20.6)), (3, rb_n)],
            ghosts=[[(-0.7, -15.0), (11.3, -15.0), (11.3, -5.0)], [(-1.5, -9.0), (5.0, -9.0), (5.2, -7.0)]],
            stretch="Horizontal stretch: safety and corner",
            keys=["route", "ghost", "drop", "react", "num", "ring", "ltg"])
branch(fld, p, [(10.5, 6.6), (13.4, 7.8), (16.2, 14.0)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.4)
branch(fld, p, [(7.5, 16.0), (11.0, 16.2), (15.6, 11.0)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.4)
point_to(fld, p, (17.6, -1.0), (12.0, 12.4), "the blades cross\nat about 12 yards", color=OD)
plt.show()








Figure 23.18: Scissors to the offense’s right against Quarters. Z runs a post, Y a corner route; their paths cross at about 12 yards. The two ringed defenders both lose their leverage (dashed): the strong safety, who starts inside Y and carries him when he goes vertical, has to cross the field outside to follow the corner route; the cornerback, who starts outside Z, has to cross inside to follow the post. Their paths cross too, a rub at depth. The progression: (1) the post, inside the cornerback and away from the safety; (2) the corner route, if the safety passes Y on and stays inside; (3) the back, checking down on the left.





Scissors beats Quarters by turning its leverage inside out. In Quarters, as you saw with dagger, the safety reads the inside receiver from inside leverage and carries him if he goes vertical, and the cornerback plays the outside receiver almost man-to-man from outside leverage. Each defender starts on the side of his receiver that the receiver is least likely to break toward. Scissors sends both receivers the other way. Y goes vertical, so the safety carries him, and then Y breaks outside: the safety has to cross the field toward the sideline, through Z’s path, from the wrong side. Z breaks inside on the post: the cornerback has to cross inside, through Y’s path, from the wrong side. Both defenders lose their leverage at once, and the crossing paths add a rub at depth. Against man coverage the same crossing makes it a man-beater, too.


Yankee
Yankee is a two-man deep shot. One receiver runs a post from one side; the other runs a deep over route, a crosser at about 18 to 22 yards, from the other side. Both routes finish in the deep middle, one above the single deep safety and one in front of him. It is usually run off play-action, with a fake handoff to freeze the linebackers, and with max protection, seven or eight blockers, because both routes take three seconds or more to develop.


Show the Python
off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", UNDER, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0.0, "R"),
                 O("Y", "TE", LINE_D, 4.8), O("U", "TE", LINE_D, -4.8, "U"),
                 O("X", "WR", OFF_BALL, -15.0), O("Z", "WR", OFF_BALL, 15.0)]
dfn = dline() + [D("SAM", "SAM", 4.0, 5.8, "S"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 0.6, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -3.4, "W"),
                 D("SS", "SS", 8.0, -7.0, "SS"), D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -16.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 16.0, "CB"),
                 D("FS", "FS", 13.5, 0.0, "FS")]
dfn = [q.moved(w=-6.6) if q.key == "WDE" else q.moved(w=6.6) if q.key == "SDE" else q for q in dfn]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=LOS, to_go=10)
protect(p)
p.block("Y", pts=[(-1.0, 0.0)])
p.path("QB", [(-2.6, 1.2)], speed=4.5)
p.path("QB", [(-6.2, 0.0)], speed=4.0)
p.run("RB", [(1.0, 1.2), (2.0, 1.6)], speed=5.0)
route_to(p, "X", (10.5, -15.0), (25.0, -3.0))
route_to(p, "Z", (6.0, 13.5), (16.0, 4.0), (18.4, -12.0))
route_to(p, "U", (-0.4, -6.0), (1.4, -10.0), delay=1.4)
for k, to in (("SAM", (3.0, 4.6)), ("MIKE", (3.4, 1.2)), ("WILL", (3.4, -2.4))):
    p.path(k, [(to[0] - p.players[k].d, to[1] - p.players[k].w)], speed=3.0)
p.drop("FS", (19.5, -0.5))
p.drop("LCB", (19.5, -17.0))
p.drop("RCB", (17.0, 16.6))
p.drop("SS", (8.0, -11.0))
p.highlight("FS")
fld = plate(p, nums=[(1, (26.4, -1.6)), (2, (16.4, -13.6)), (3, (3.0, -11.8))],
            keys=["route", "run", "drop", "num", "ring", "ltg"], window=(-8.5, 29.0),
            stretch="Vertical stretch: the deep safety")
say(fld, p, 25.8, -11.6, "post over the top", color=OD)
say(fld, p, 13.6, 9.6, "deep over\nunder the FS", color=OD)
say(fld, p, -6.6, 5.0, "run fake", color=OD)
plt.show()








Figure 23.19: Yankee against Cover 3, from an under-center formation with two tight ends (12 personnel). Against two tight ends the defense stays in its base personnel, with a third linebacker, the Sam (S), instead of a nickel. The quarterback fakes a handoff to the back (R), then sets up deep. X runs a post from the left; Z runs a deep over from the right, climbing to about 18 yards and finishing near the far numbers. The ringed free safety, alone in the deep middle, faces a high-low, read high to low: (1) the post if he comes up on the over; (2) the over if he stays deep with the post. The over is thrown in front of the left cornerback, who has to stay deep and outside in his third, and behind the linebackers, who step up toward the run fake (short orange arrows). The five linemen, Y and the back block (seven-man protection); U helps for a moment, then releases late to the flat as the outlet (3).





Why does it work? The run fake does half the job. Linebackers are taught to stop the run first, so they step forward when they see a handoff, and that step takes them out of the path of the deep over, which crosses behind them at a depth no underneath defender can reach. The other half is a high-low on the one man left: the free safety in the middle of the field can sink to take away the post or come forward to take away the over, not both. The post keeps him honest, and the over is thrown where nobody else can reach it: in front of the deep-third cornerback, who can’t leave his deep outside area, and behind linebackers who have just stepped toward a handoff. Sean McVay’s Rams made yankee one of their signature shot plays of the late 2010s (the Rams often ran it from three-receiver sets with jet motion), Kyle Shanahan’s 49ers ran it too, and it now appears in most NFL playbooks that come from the Shanahan and McVay family of offenses.8 The price is the protection: with seven or eight blockers, only two or three receivers go out, so if the safety plays it perfectly the quarterback has very little to throw to. How play-action works, and why the fake works even when the run game doesn’t, belongs to Play-Action, Bootlegs, and Screens.

title: Dropback Concepts: Smash, Flood, Mesh, Levels, Dagger, and Four Verticals
text:
Tags and route conversions
Fourteen concepts sounds like a lot, but a real playbook has many more, and most of the extras aren’t new concepts at all. They are the same concepts with a word added. A tag is a word added to a play call that changes one player’s assignment and leaves everyone else’s alone. “Mesh” tells all five receivers what to do; “Mesh, Z-wheel” keeps mesh intact except for Z, who runs a wheel instead of his corner route. Tags let a play-caller adjust a concept to a defense’s habits (a cornerback who jumps corner routes, a safety who cheats toward the crossers) without teaching a new play.
The second tool is subtler, and it explains how one call can be right against several coverages. A route conversion is a rule built into a route that changes it according to the coverage the receiver sees. The receiver doesn’t wait for the quarterback to tell him; he reads the defense himself, usually the safeties, and the quarterback, reading the same thing, knows where he will be.


Show the Python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 3.7))
for ax, one_high in zip(axes, (True, False)):
    off = [O("Y", "TE", OFF_BALL, 8.0), O("C", "C", LINE_D, 0.0)]
    if one_high:
        dfn = [D("FS", "FS", 13.5, 0.0, "FS")]
    else:
        dfn = [D("FS", "FS", 12.5, -8.5, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 12.5, 8.5, "SS")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=LOS, to_go=None)
    if one_high:
        route_to(p, "Y", (8.0, 7.8), (22.0, 9.0))
        p.drop("FS", (17.0, 0.0))
    else:
        route_to(p, "Y", (11.0, 7.6), (21.0, 1.2))
        p.drop("FS", (16.0, -10.0))
        p.drop("SS", (16.0, 10.0))
    p.highlight(*[q.key for q in dfn])
    fld = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-13.5, 15.5), window=(-3.5, 24.5), show_ruler=False, width_in=3.2)
    if one_high:
        say(fld, p, 22.6, -6.0, "one safety:\nstay on the\nlandmark", color=OD, fontsize=6.8)
        panel_title(ax, "One high (MOFC): stay vertical", fs=8.5)
    else:
        opening(fld, p, (20.0, 1.0), (4.0, 7.0))
        say(fld, p, 9.0, -6.0, "two safeties:\nbend into the\nempty middle", color=OD, fontsize=6.8)
        panel_title(ax, "Two high (MOFO): bend inside", fs=8.5)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=1.0)
plt.show()








Figure 23.20: One route conversion: the seam route in four verticals. The receiver (Y) reads the safeties as he runs. Left, one deep safety (middle of the field closed, MOFC): he stays on his landmark just outside the hash and bends slightly away from the safety, keeping him in conflict with the other seam. Right, two deep safeties (middle of the field open, MOFO): the middle is empty, so at about 12 yards he bends inside, splitting the safeties, into the space between them (green). Same call, same receiver; the coverage picks the route.





You’ve already met the most important conversion. The option route of Passing Fundamentals, which some systems call the choice route, is a conversion with two branches: against man, break away from the defender’s leverage; against zone, sit in the hole. Others are everywhere in this chapter. The smash corner route goes to depth over a squatting Cover 2 cornerback and flattens under a bailing Cover 3 one. The levels and mesh crossers keep running against man and settle against zone. The dagger dig sits down in a window against zone and keeps crossing against man. And the Y-cross, the Air Raid’s most conversion-heavy route, keeps running toward the far sideline against Cover 3 and man, and sits down in the window against two deep safeties or a robber lurking in the middle.
One caution about names while we’re here. Teams name the same concept differently (you’ve already met flood and sail, and levels as the Colts’ “Dig”), and some reuse a name for a different concept. The shape is what to learn; a name only tells you what one team calls it.
The Patriots of the Tom Brady era were the model of an offense built on conversions. Their Erhardt-Perkins system (named for Ron Erhardt and Ray Perkins, who coached together on New England’s staff in the 1970s, and carried forward by Bill Parcells to Bill Belichick and Josh McDaniels) named whole concepts with short words, so a quarterback could call them at the line.9 It also gave its slot receivers wide freedom to read and adjust their routes after the snap: the option routes of Troy Brown, Deion Branch, Wes Welker and Julian Edelman, which broke one way against man and sat down against zone, were a staple of the Brady years.10 That’s why New England’s passing game seemed to have an answer for every defense without a thousand plays: the same few concepts, each with branches. The system’s history and its rivals are in Offensive Systems and Languages.






NoteMadden vs. real life



In a video game, the receiver runs the route drawn on the play art, whatever the defense does, and you press a button for the one you want. In the NFL, a large share of routes are conditional: the receiver converts the route against the coverage, the quarterback has to read the same thing and throw to where the receiver will be, and a mismatch between their reads is one of the commonest causes of an interception that looks, on the broadcast, like the quarterback threw to nobody. When an announcer says a receiver and quarterback “weren’t on the same page,” that’s usually what happened: one of them saw man and the other saw zone.

title: Dropback Concepts: Smash, Flood, Mesh, Levels, Dagger, and Four Verticals
section: The quarterback’s side: one clock for every concept
text:
The quarterback’s side: one clock for every concept
Each plate in this chapter carried a progression, and they all follow the same pattern. That pattern is the real skill of dropback passing, so it is worth spelling out.
Before the snap, the quarterback identifies the shell (one high safety or two), checks the leverage of the defenders over the receivers in the concept, and asks the question every concept poses: who is the defender in conflict, and where is he? If the concept is called to both sides, as smash often is, this is when he picks the side. And if what he sees is wrong for the call (a zone-beater against a defense that is plainly in man, say), many offenses let him change it: the play comes in as a pair of concepts, or with a check-with-me, and he picks at the line (The Pre-Snap Phase). The pre-snap picture is still only a hypothesis; the first step of the safeties after the snap confirms or breaks it (Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage).
If the defense shows a blitz, he checks the protection (Pass Protection). Every dropback concept carries its own pressure answer: if the defense brings one more rusher than the protection can block, the concept’s quickest route becomes the hot route, the throw that has to come out before the free rusher arrives. On drive and mesh that is a shallow crosser, which is open almost at once against a blitz; on smash, flood or dagger it is usually the shortest route (the hitch, the flat) or the back releasing from the backfield.
At the snap, his eyes go to the conflict defender, not to a receiver. His drop is timed so that the first read is ready as his back foot lands: on smash, the corner route breaks as he hits the bottom of his drop; on dagger, the dig arrives a beat later, which is why dagger takes a deeper drop or a hitch step.
After the first look, he moves to the next read with his feet as well as his eyes. Each hitch step, a short step up into the pocket, resets his feet for the next throw. A typical dropback progression gets two or three looks before the rush arrives; the last is the checkdown, the short throw to a back that keeps the play from losing yards. As Passing Fundamentals showed with FTN’s charting, more than half of all throws go to the first read, and those are the quickest and most valuable: the concept is at its best when its first answer is right.
The order of the looks follows the two rhythms from the start of the chapter: high to low on most vertical stretches, low to high when a shallow crosser wins early or not at all, and on a long third down, the route that reaches the line to gain first.
The table gathers the fourteen concepts, the family each belongs to, the defender it puts in a bind and the coverage it’s built to beat. The last column is the subject of What Beats What, which pairs concepts with coverages in detail; how each coverage defends these concepts is in Part 6, beginning with Coverage Fundamentals and, for four verticals, The Cover 3 Family.



Table 23.1: The fourteen dropback concepts at a glance. “Built to beat” is the concept’s best matchup, not its only one.

Two honest limits on this table. First, you usually can’t tell these concepts apart before the snap, and that is by design: smash, flood and post-wheel all start as a slot and an outside receiver on one side, and an offense that tipped which one was coming would be easy to defend. What you can predict before the snap is the family, from the shell (two-high invites smash, dagger and scissors; one-high invites flood, four verticals, post-wheel and yankee; man invites mesh and the angle route) and from the down and distance. The concept itself reveals itself in the first two seconds, when the routes break. Second, nobody publishes how often each concept is called. Public play-by-play records where the ball went, not what was drawn; the Big Data Bowl tracking data at the end of this chapter charts each receiver’s route, which is enough to find concepts by their route combinations if you want to count them yourself.

title: Dropback Concepts: Smash, Flood, Mesh, Levels, Dagger, and Four Verticals
text:
Film room
The concepts above are in almost every NFL playbook. A few teams built an identity on them, and watching those teams is the fastest way to learn to see the concepts at game speed.






NoteFilm room: Texas Tech 2007–2008



Mesh and Y-cross, rep after rep. Mike Leach’s Texas Tech teams were the Air Raid at full volume. In 2007, quarterback Graham Harrell threw for 5,705 yards and redshirt freshman receiver Michael Crabtree caught 134 passes for 1,962 yards and 22 touchdowns; Crabtree won the Biletnikoff Award as the nation’s best receiver that season and again in 2008.11 Nearly all of it came out of the same small menu of concepts drawn in this chapter: mesh, shallow cross, Y-cross and four verticals, from wide 2x2 and trips formations with enormous splits between the offensive linemen.
What to notice on the tape: the mesh point, two crossers passing over the center close enough to touch, and a defender losing a step as he goes around; Harrell’s eyes on the curl-flat defender on Y-cross, and the ball arriving as the crosser came into the window; and how few different plays there were. The defense knew what was coming, and it didn’t matter, because the offense had run each concept thousands of times against every look.
One game to find: Texas Tech’s 39–33 win over No. 1 Texas on November 1, 2008, the school’s first win over a top-ranked team. Trailing 33–32 with 1:29 left, Harrell drove the Red Raiders 62 yards in six plays, and Crabtree caught the winning touchdown at the sideline with one second left.12 The final drive is famous; the rest of the game is the small menu at work.
Leach’s former quarterback Kliff Kingsbury later brought the same concepts to the NFL as the Arizona Cardinals’ head coach (2019–2022), and in 2026 joined Sean McVay’s Rams staff as assistant head coach.13








NoteFilm room: Los Angeles Rams 2018



Yankee and the play-action shot. In Sean McVay’s second season, the Rams went 13–3 and reached Super Bowl LIII, where they lost to New England 13–3. Jared Goff threw for 4,688 yards and 32 touchdowns.14 Their passing game ran on a single foundation: line up in the same formation with three receivers, run outside-zone handoffs out of it, and throw play-action shots from the same look, yankee among them. On throws of 20 yards or more in the air, the Rams averaged about +0.77 EPA per attempt, third-best in the league, against a league average of about +0.37.15
What to notice on the tape: the linebackers’ first step on the run fake, toward the line; the deep over crossing behind them at 18 to 20 yards; and the free safety in the middle, who has to decide between the over in front of him and the post behind him. Goff often had only two routes to choose from, and his decision was made by one defender.
One game to find: the Rams’ 54–51 win over the Chiefs on Monday night, November 19, 2018, in Los Angeles, when Goff threw for 413 yards and four touchdowns and Mahomes for 478 yards and six.16 Both offenses’ play-action and deep shots are on display; it is the companion game for the next film room too.








NoteFilm room: Kansas City Chiefs 2018



Four verticals with a 50-touchdown quarterback. In Patrick Mahomes’s first season as the starter he threw for 5,097 yards and 50 touchdowns and was named the league’s MVP. Andy Reid’s offense threw deep more than almost anyone: 15% of the Chiefs’ attempts traveled 20 yards or more in the air (fifth in the league; the league average was 12%), and those throws were worth about +0.75 EPA each, fourth best.17 With Tyreek Hill’s speed outside and Travis Kelce running up the seam, vertical routes made every deep defender declare early, which is the idea four verticals is built on.
What to notice on the tape: the deep defenders’ first steps. With Hill on the outside, cornerbacks bailed at the snap, which opened everything underneath; with Kelce on a seam, the middle safety had to choose. Watch the seam routes for a conversion, bending or staying straight as the receiver reads the safeties, and Mahomes moving the safety with his eyes before throwing the other way. The November 19 game against the Rams (above) is the place to start: Mahomes threw six touchdowns and three interceptions, a good lesson in what deep shots cost as well as what they pay.

title: Dropback Concepts: Smash, Flood, Mesh, Levels, Dagger, and Four Verticals
text:
Watch for it on Sunday






TipWatch for it: name the concept



Before the snap

Find the shell. One deep safety or two? Smash, dagger and scissors are two-high beaters; flood, post-wheel and yankee feast on one-high; four verticals is built for Cover 3 and still splits Cover 2’s safeties. (Can’t see the safeties on the TV angle? See How to Watch a Broadcast.)
Man or zone? Pressed corners, a defender following a motion man across the formation: think man, and think mesh, rubs and the angle route.
Check the situation. On third-and-long, expect a concept with a route past the line to gain; on third-and-short against man, expect crossers and rubs. You are predicting a family, not a name: from the same formation, smash, flood and post-wheel look identical until the routes break.

On the replay (the end-zone camera or the skycam is best)

Find the defender in conflict first. Who stood between the routes on the side the ball went to? What did he do? The ball usually went to the receiver he didn’t take.
Then name the stretch by where the routes were around him when the ball came out. One above and one below him: a vertical stretch (even if the routes crossed on the way there, as in drive or Y-cross). One on each side: horizontal. Three around two defenders: a triangle. No zone defender to stretch at all, with receivers running away from men chasing them through traffic: a man-beater. Then name the concept.
Count the time. A dropback concept takes about “one-thousand-one, one-thousand-two, one-thousand-three.” If the ball is out before “two,” it was the quick game.

For your prediction log (How to Watch a Broadcast): on each third-and-medium, write the shell you see and the concept family you expect (two-high: smash or dagger; one-high: flood or a deep shot; man: mesh or rubs). Check yourself on the replay.

title: Dropback Concepts: Smash, Flood, Mesh, Levels, Dagger, and Four Verticals
text:
Predict the play






TipPredict the play 1: two high, but which two-high?





Show the Python
p = Play(spread(), quarters(), los=55, to_go=9)
fld = draw(p, lateral="full", window=(-8.5, 17.5))
point_to(fld, p, (14.6, 0.0), (10.0, 7.5), "safeties at 10,\nover the slots", color=DD)
point_to(fld, p, (13.0, -19.0), (7.5, -16.0), "corners off", color=DD)
plt.show()








Figure 23.21: Third-and-9. Both safeties are only about ten yards deep, each lined up over a slot receiver; the cornerbacks are seven or eight yards off, with outside leverage; the nickel and the linebackers are at their usual depths.





The call sheet for this down has smash and dagger, both to the right. Which one should the offense run against this picture, and why not the other?






TipAnswer





Dagger. Two high safeties, yes, but this isn’t the Cover 2 that smash was built for. Cover 2’s safeties sit 12 to 14 yards deep and wide, and its cornerbacks squat at five yards. Here the safeties are low and over the slots and the cornerbacks are off: that’s the Quarters look, where each safety reads the slot receiver in front of him.
Against Quarters, smash runs into trouble on both routes. The corner route is the slot going vertical and then outside, which is exactly what the safety is reading: he carries it from inside, and the cornerback, playing deep and outside over the hitch, is above it, so the corner route is bracketed. The hitch underneath is open against an off cornerback, but it’s five or six yards on third-and-9: short of the sticks, and it needs yards after the catch.
Dagger turns the same safety rule against him. Y’s seam takes the safety deep; the nickel and the Mike sink under it; and the dig comes in behind them against a cornerback playing from outside, at 15 yards, past the line to gain. What would make the quarterback come off it? A safety who doesn’t carry the seam (then throw the seam), or a rotation at the snap to one deep safety (then the seam attacks the middle safety, and the dig crosses under him).











TipPredict the play 2: press man on third down





Show the Python
p = Play(spread(rb_w=1.5), cover1(), los=72, to_go=3)
fld = draw(p, lateral="full", window=(-8.5, 17.5))
for d0, col, dash in ((-2.6, style.OFFENSE, (0, (3, 2))), (2.6, style.DEFENSE, (0, (1, 1.6)))):
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = _P(fld, p, d0, -8.3), _P(fld, p, d0, 2.6)
    fld.ax.annotate("", (float(x1), float(y1)), xytext=(float(x0), float(y0)), zorder=6,
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<|-|>", color=col, lw=1.3, ls=dash, mutation_scale=9))
say(fld, p, -3.6, -14.4, "H's motion:\nacross and back", color=OD, fontsize=6.6)
say(fld, p, 6.8, -12.0, "the $ went\nwith him", color=DD, fontsize=6.6)
say(fld, p, 16.0, 0.0, "one deep safety", color=DD)
plt.show()








Figure 23.22: Third-and-3. Both cornerbacks are pressed on X and Z and the nickel ($) is pressed on H; the strong safety stands five yards off Y; the Will is over the back; one safety is deep in the middle. Before the snap, H went in motion across the formation and back (blue dashes), and the nickel ran across with him and back again (orange dots).





The offense has three concepts on its call sheet for this situation: flood, four verticals and mesh. Which one should it run, and why?






TipAnswer





Mesh. Everything here says man coverage: pressed cornerbacks, a defender over every receiver, a single safety deep, and, the clincher, a nickel who followed H across the formation and back on the motion. Zone defenders don’t travel with a motion man; man defenders do (Motion and Shifts).
Against man, the zone-beaters lose their point. Flood’s three levels stretch a curl-flat defender who doesn’t exist; each receiver just has a defender following him. Four verticals is a better man answer but needs three seconds and a receiver who can beat a pressed cornerback deep, which is a big ask on third-and-3. Mesh is built for this: the two crossers run at five or six yards, past the line to gain, and the defenders on H and Y have to fight through each other’s traffic. One of the crossers usually comes free within about two seconds, running away from his man.
How does the offense act on what it saw? If the play called in the huddle was flood, a quarterback with a check-with-me or a paired call can switch to mesh at the line; that’s exactly what motion is for. What should still worry him? The Mike linebacker. In Cover 1, the defender not assigned to anyone often sits in the middle as a robber, exactly where the crossers meet. The quarterback has to find him before the snap and throw the crosser running away from him.











TipPredict the play 3: a concept you haven’t seen





Show the Python
p = Play(spread(), cover3(nb_side=1), los=40, to_go=10)
protect(p)
p.dropback(3.0)
route_to(p, "Z", (10.0, 15.0), (23.0, 4.0))
route_to(p, "Y", (13.5, 9.0), (14.5, -4.0))
p.drop("FS", (17.0, 0.0))
p.drop("RCB", (17.0, 16.6))
p.drop("LCB", (17.0, -16.6))
p.drop("NB", (8.0, 12.0))
p.drop("SS", (7.0, -12.0))
p.drop("MIKE", (8.5, 3.0))
p.drop("WILL", (8.5, -4.0))
fld = draw(p, lateral="full", window=(-8.5, 27.5))
ghost(fld, p, [(-0.7, -15.0), (22.0, -15.0)])
ghost(fld, p, [(-1.5, -9.0), (11.5, -9.0), (10.3, -7.8)])
plt.show()








Figure 23.23: Second-and-10, against Cover 3. On the right, Z runs a post and Y, from the slot, runs a dig at about 14 yards underneath it. On the left, X and H run a go and a curl (grey). The back checks for a blitzer. This exact combination isn’t drawn anywhere in the chapter.





Which family is it, who is the defender in conflict, what coverage does it want, and in what order should the quarterback read it?






TipAnswer





A vertical stretch (a high-low) of the free safety, built to beat one-high coverage, read high to low: the post, then the dig, then the back. Both routes break toward the middle, which can make it look like a horizontal stretch or a crossing man-beater. Ask where the routes are around the key defender when the ball comes out: the post is above the free safety, heading for the deep middle he guards, and the dig is below him, crossing at 14 yards, above the linebackers. One defender, two depths.
That makes it yankee’s logic from one side of the formation, without the run fake: if the safety sinks for the post, the dig comes open in front of him; if he comes up for the dig, the post is behind him. Against two deep safeties, the middle is open and the post has nobody to stretch, so an offense would rather have this against a one-high shell (or with a conversion that bends the post away from a second safety).

title: Dropback Concepts: Smash, Flood, Mesh, Levels, Dagger, and Four Verticals
text:
Takeaways

A pass concept is a set of routes built to work together, usually by putting one or two defenders in a bind; it has a name so the whole offense can learn and call it as a unit, from any formation.
Concepts come in four families, named by where the routes are around the key defender when the ball comes out: vertical stretches (one above him, one below: smash, flood, levels, drive, shallow cross, dagger, Y-cross, yankee), horizontal stretches (one on each side, deep: four verticals, post-wheel, scissors), triangles (three receivers around two defenders: curl-flat, snag) and man-beaters (traffic and leverage against man defenders: mesh, the angle route).
Each concept is built to beat certain coverages: smash, dagger and scissors attack two-high; flood, post-wheel and yankee attack one-high; four verticals is built for Cover 3 and still splits Cover 2; mesh and the angle route attack man. That is why the quarterback’s pre-snap read starts with the safeties.
The quarterback reads the defender in conflict, not the receivers, usually high to low (low to high when a shallow crosser leads), and his progression runs on his feet: the first read as his back foot lands, the next on a hitch step, the checkdown last.
Rub routes beat man coverage by making defenders run through traffic; a receiver who deliberately blocks a defender more than a yard downfield, until the pass is touched, commits offensive pass interference.
Tags change one route in a concept; route conversions let a route change itself by coverage, so one call can be right against several defenses. The intermediate middle of the field is the most valuable place to throw, and most of these concepts exist to get the ball there.

title: Dropback Concepts: Smash, Flood, Mesh, Levels, Dagger, and Four Verticals
text:
Connections
Builds on: The Quick Game (concepts, leverage, the pre-snap read and the short stretches this chapter takes deeper), Passing Fundamentals (routes, drops, progressions and the two stretches) and Pass Protection (the time these concepts need).
Sets up: Play-Action, Bootlegs, and Screens runs flood and yankee off a run fake; Quarterback Play covers progressions, the pocket and look-offs in depth; Offensive Systems and Languages shows how the West Coast, Erhardt-Perkins, Air Raid and Shanahan systems name and call these concepts. On defense, Coverage Fundamentals, Man Coverage and The Cover 3 Family show the other side of each matchup; What Beats What pairs every concept with the coverages it beats; and Contact Rules and Penalties covers how officials judge rubs and picks.
Case study: Walsh’s 49ers and the West Coast offense, the offense that made curl-flat, the triangle read and the timed dropback game famous.






NoteGo deeper




Chris B. Brown, The Essential Smart Football (2012) and The Art of Smart Football (2015), and his Smart Football site: the clearest writing anywhere on smash, flood, mesh, Y-cross, levels and four verticals, and on why they work.
S. C. Gwynne, The Perfect Pass: American Genius and the Reinvention of Football (2016): the story of Hal Mumme, Mike Leach and the Air Raid’s small menu of concepts.
Bill Walsh, with Brian Billick and James A. Peterson, Finding the Winning Edge (1998): the West Coast passing game, including its triangle reads, in the coach’s own words.
From diagrams to real tracking data. The two animations above are gridiron simulations in NFL Big Data Bowl coordinates. The 2025 Big Data Bowl release (2022 season, weeks 1–9) charts every receiver’s route on every play, so you can find real four-verticals and mesh calls and watch them. The data needs a free Kaggle login, so this code is not run when the book is built.



Show the Python (real Big Data Bowl tracking; not run in the build)
import pandas as pd
from gridiron import bdb, show_animation

plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")
player_play = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/player_play.csv")
routes = player_play.dropna(subset=["routeRan"])

# four verticals: at least four receivers on GO routes on the same play
gos = routes[routes["routeRan"] == "GO"].groupby(["gameId", "playId"]).size()
verts = gos[gos >= 4].reset_index()[["gameId", "playId"]]

# mesh-like: two or more crossing routes on the same play, thrown to a crosser
cross = routes[routes["routeRan"] == "CROSS"].groupby(["gameId", "playId"]).size()
mesh = cross[cross >= 2].reset_index()[["gameId", "playId"]]
mesh = mesh.merge(plays[["gameId", "playId", "passResult", "pff_manZone"]], on=["gameId", "playId"])
mesh_vs_man = mesh[mesh["pff_manZone"] == "Man"]

g, pl = verts.iloc[0][["gameId", "playId"]]
trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_*.csv")
one = bdb.prepare(trk, plays, game_id=g, play_id=pl)
show_animation(one, times=[0.0, 1.2, 2.4, 3.2])   # snap, release, safety's choice, catch
