section: The one-yard rule: why NFL RPOs look different
text:
The one-yard rule: why NFL RPOs look different
In football, only some players may catch a forward pass. The five interior linemen are ineligible receivers (The Twenty-Two), and the rules don’t only stop them catching the ball, they stop them running downfield before it is thrown. Imagine the game without that limit: every pass play could begin with the whole line charging out and blocking linebackers, exactly as on a run. A linebacker could never tell run from pass, so he could never safely drop into coverage, and the receivers behind him would be catching passes in space that had been blocked for them. The rule keeps a pass play looking like a pass play. The foul is called illegal man downfield, or ineligible downfield (the referee’s announcement is often “ineligible man downfield”).
Here is the NFL’s version, as written in the 2026 rulebook:2

On a play on which a legal forward pass is thrown, it is a foul if the entire body of an ineligible player is more than one yard beyond the line of scrimmage before the pass is thrown.
Exception: a lineman who makes contact with a defender within a yard of the line, on his initial charge, may be driven or may drive his man further downfield while still blocking him. If they come apart beyond the yard, he may stay where he is, move sideways or back off until the ball is thrown (some line coaches call it freezing). What he may not do is let go of that defender and keep moving forward, or go past a yard without having touched anyone.
Penalty: five yards from the previous spot. A completed pass is wiped out; there is no loss of down.

Now set that against the run game. On inside zone, linemen double-team a defensive lineman and then one of them climbs: he lets go and runs to a linebacker four or five yards deep. That climb is the heart of zone blocking, and on a pass play it is exactly what the rule forbids: letting go of a defender inside one yard and then advancing.
College football draws the line somewhere else. Under the NCAA rule, no originally ineligible player may be more than three yards beyond the neutral zone (the strip the length of the ball between the two lines) until a legal forward pass that crosses the neutral zone has been thrown, also a five-yard penalty. (College judges any part of the body, the NFL the entire body.)3 Three yards is room for a guard to release toward a linebacker who has stepped up. Actually blocking him that far downfield before a pass that crosses the neutral zone is still offensive pass interference in college, unless the block began on the lineman’s first charge within a yard of the neutral zone. And the “crosses the neutral zone” clause means a pass caught behind the line (a bubble, a now screen) doesn’t trigger either college rule at all.
The NFL rule has no such clause: it applies to any legal forward pass, including one caught behind the line, which is how Play-Action, Bootlegs, and Screens described NFL screens too. The one throw it doesn’t touch is a backward pass. A bubble thrown even slightly backward is a lateral, not a forward pass, so nobody can be “ineligible downfield” on it; the price, as The Quick Game warned, is that a dropped lateral is a live ball.


Show the Python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.8, 3.6))
LAT, WIN = (-17.5, 8.0), (-6.4, 14.2)
for ax, college in zip(axes, (False, True)):
    base = only(trips(), -18, 7)
    common = {"QB": (-5.4, -1.2), "RB": (-3.6, 0.9), "X": (7.2, -13.2), "Y": (0.0, 5.2)}
    dcommon = {"LCB": (11.0, -16.0), "FS": (12.6, -8.2)}
    if college:
        spots = {"LT": (0.6, -3.9), "LG": (0.6, -2.3), "C": (0.6, 0.4), "RG": (2.4, 1.7), "RT": (0.6, 3.6)}
        dspots = {"BE": (1.6, -4.1), "BT": (1.6, -2.3), "PT": (1.6, 0.45), "PE": (1.6, 4.0),
                  "WILL": (3.4, -1.0), "MIKE": (5.0, 2.0)}
    else:
        spots = {"LT": (1.9, -3.9), "LG": (0.3, -2.2), "C": (0.3, -0.4), "RG": (0.3, 1.4), "RT": (0.3, 3.2)}
        dspots = {"BE": (3.1, -3.9), "BT": (1.1, -2.4), "PT": (1.1, 0.5), "PE": (1.1, 4.2),
                  "WILL": (3.4, -0.9), "MIKE": (4.6, 2.4)}
    spots.update(common)
    dspots.update(dcommon)
    players = [q.moved(d=spots[q.key][0], w=spots[q.key][1]) if q.key in spots else q for q in base]
    dfn = [q.moved(d=dspots[q.key][0], w=dspots[q.key][1]) if q.key in dspots else q
           for q in only(nickel("two_high"), -18, 7)]
    p = Play(players, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=LAT, window=WIN)
    lim = 3.3 if college else 1.0
    region(f, p, 0.0, lim, -17.4, 7.9, GREEN, alpha=0.13, lw=0.8)
    say(f, p, lim + 0.8, -11.6, ("3 yards past the\nneutral zone" if college else "1 yard past the line"),
        color=GREEN, fontsize=6.8, weight="bold")
    throw(f, p, (-5.4, -1.2), (11.2, -11.6), rad=-0.1)
    if college:
        point_to(f, p, (7.6, 3.6), (2.4, 1.7), "RG climbing to\nthe Mike: legal", fontsize=6.4, color=GREEN)
    else:
        x, y = _P(f, p, 3.2, 1.2)
        ax.add_patch(Circle((float(x), float(y)), 0.75, fc="none", ec=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.2, ls=(0, (2, 1.5)),
                            zorder=8))
        tackle_x(f, p, 3.2, 1.2, ms=7)
        point_to(f, p, (7.6, 3.6), (3.2, 1.2), "a guard who climbs\nhere: flag", fontsize=6.4, color=RED)
        point_to(f, p, (-2.6, 4.9), (0.5, 0.7), "C + RG still\ndouble the 1", fontsize=6.4)
        point_to(f, p, (6.6, -5.2), (2.3, -4.5), "LT drove his man\nback 2 yards: legal", fontsize=6.4, shrink=2)
    panel_title(ax, "College: 3 yards" if college else "NFL: 1 yard", 9)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 25.7: The same glance RPO at the moment the ball is thrown, under the two rulebooks (the left half of the line; the shaded strip is how far past the line of scrimmage an ineligible lineman may be when the pass leaves the quarterback’s hand). Left, NFL: one yard. The linemen are still on the line, holding their first blocks; the center and right guard are still doubling the 1-technique. A right guard who had already come off that double team and climbed to the Mike (hollow circle) would be three yards downfield: flag. The left tackle, by contrast, engaged the end at the line and has driven him two yards back: legal, because he never let go. Right, college: three yards beyond the neutral zone. The right guard has come off the double team and is climbing toward the Mike, about two and a half yards past the line when the ball leaves: no foul in college (in the NFL it would be). Every defensive lineman is still blocked, and the glance goes over the linebackers. (Had the guard already been blocking the Mike that far downfield, college could call offensive pass interference instead.)





That difference is the single biggest reason an NFL RPO looks different from a college one:

NFL RPO throws are quick, and most are short. The decision is made at the mesh and the ball is out within about a second of the snap, before any lineman has had time to drift past a yard. And a ball that must leave in a second can’t go far, because a receiver can’t get far in a second: running full speed from a standing start, he is only about five yards downfield when it’s thrown. A deep route needs two and a half seconds or more to develop, and by then a run-blocking line is well past a yard. So NFL RPOs throw to routes that are open early: slants, glances and sticks a few yards past the line, and bubbles and now screens that come out at once (the bubble, thrown slightly backward, isn’t a forward pass at all). The data below shows how strong this is.
NFL RPO blocking stays at the line. Instead of climbing, linemen hold their first blocks, or the offense uses blocking that naturally stays on the line (down blocks, double teams that don’t release) and lets the read handle the linebacker. The glance RPO is popular in the NFL for exactly this reason: the read takes care of the man the climbing guard would have blocked.
College RPOs can be “run first, throw later.” With three yards and no limit at all on throws behind the line, college linemen can run-block for longer and drift up to three yards downfield, the quarterback can ride the mesh longer, and the pass can go farther downfield: seams and posts over linebackers who have stepped up to the run.

Why hasn’t college changed? It nearly did. In 2015 the NCAA’s rules committee proposed cutting its limit to one yard, and the oversight panel tabled the proposal; the rule is still three yards for 2026.4 The NFL has never had college’s three-yard cushion: its rulebook still says one yard in 2026. That leaves officials judging a one-yard line at full speed on every RPO, and RPOs put the rule under strain on every snap: an RPO whose throw comes out a beat late is exactly the play on which a run-blocking lineman has drifted too far. You will see in the numbers that RPOs draw far more than their share of the flags.






NoteGo deeper



Receivers who block too early. Receivers are eligible, so the one-yard limit doesn’t bind them, but a cousin rule does: in the NFL, blocking a defender more than a yard past the line “clearly prior” to a pass is offensive pass interference, and pass interference can occur “regardless of whether [the pass] crosses the line.”5 So on a bubble RPO the receiver blocking the cornerback wants his block to land as the ball leaves the quarterback’s hand, one more reason the bubble comes out at once. Judging “clearly prior” at full speed is hard; Bill Belichick, asked about RPOs in 2019, called the downfield-blocking question “a tough call for the officials.”6

title: Run-Pass Options: Plays That Are Two Plays
text:
Three choices on one snap
Nothing stops an offense from putting the zone read and an RPO on the same snap. The quarterback reads two defenders in order, exactly like the triple option of 03-04, with a pass in the pitch man’s role:

At the mesh, read the backside end: if he stays wide, give to the back; if he crashes on the back, pull the ball.
Now moving sideways along the line with the ball, read the overhang defender: if he comes up to tackle the quarterback, throw the bubble to the receiver outside him, before crossing the line (a forward pass thrown from beyond the line of scrimmage is illegal); if he stays with the receiver, tuck the ball and run.

In practice the throw on a triple RPO is almost always a bubble or a flare, a ball thrown sideways or slightly backward, not a slant, for the reason of the previous section: by the time the quarterback has pulled the ball and taken a few steps, a second and a half has gone by, and a run-blocking line is past a yard. College offenses called these triple RPOs or simply packaged plays, and they were common in the shotgun spread offenses of the 2000s and 2010s, where the three-yard rule left more room. They are rarer in the NFL, for two reasons: the quarterback carries the ball into the second level on the keep, where he takes hits, and every extra beat of reading is a beat in which the linemen are run blocking further from the line.

title: Run-Pass Options: Plays That Are Two Plays
text:
Where RPOs came from
Nobody invented the RPO in one moment, and several people say they did. What is not disputed is the ingredients: the option’s habit of reading a defender instead of blocking him, and the spread offense’s habit of giving the quarterback a quick throw to whichever side the defense left light. Put a quick throw on a running play and you have it.

Air Raid tags and the 1990s. Coaches in Hal Mumme and Mike Leach’s Air Raid tradition (a spread, pass-first offense built on a handful of plays repeated endlessly; 04-08 has it), at Kentucky in the late 1990s and Leach’s Oklahoma in 1999, tagged quick screens onto runs so the quarterback could throw if the defense overloaded the box. Rich Rodriguez, whose zone read grew out of a fumbled practice handoff at Glenville State (03-04), built quick slants and bubbles into his zone-read offense at Tulane and Clemson.7
Claims to the invention. Urban Meyer says his Utah teams found it by accident in the early 2000s, when a receiver missed a block and ran a bubble instead;8 Brett Favre says he started doing it on his own, bored with handing off, before he had told his coach.9 Treat both as what they are: stories coaches tell about a thing that was in the air.
The college spread, 2000s–2010s. Spread offenses made packaged plays routine. Chip Kelly’s Oregon ran them fast and often enough that when Kelly took over the Eagles in 2013, Washington’s defensive coordinator Jim Haslett prepared to face Kelly’s new team by watching 23 or 24 Oregon films.10 At Auburn, Gus Malzahn’s “still-emerging RPO game,” in CBS writer Dennis Dodd’s words, helped beat Alabama in the 2013 “Kick Six” game; Dodd credits Malzahn with having “refined and perfected the modern run-pass option.”11 And when Robert Griffin III arrived in Washington in 2012 from Art Briles’s Baylor, Mike Shanahan borrowed Baylor’s packaged plays. After Griffin’s first game, Shanahan put it this way: “we had running plays called and all of a sudden they gave us certain looks to take the running game away, and we threw a couple of bubbles early.”12 The full lineage, from the Wing-T and the wishbone through the spread option, is in The College Laboratory.
The NFL boom, 2016–2018. The tree that made RPOs a fixture of NFL offense is Andy Reid’s. By Pro Football Focus’s charting, the share of NFL plays that were RPOs roughly doubled from about 4% in 2016 to about 8% in 2018; Reid’s Chiefs led the league in RPO usage in 2017 (17.1% of their plays) and 2018 (25.0%), and Doug Pederson, who had been Reid’s offensive coordinator in Kansas City from 2013 to 2015, ranked second with the Eagles in 2017 and won a Super Bowl with them (see the film room). Matt Nagy, Pederson’s successor in Kansas City, took the idea to Chicago, where the Bears went from 2.7% RPOs in 2017 to 19.2% in his first season, 2018.13
Since then. PFF’s league-wide rate kept climbing to a peak of about 10.5% of plays in 2023, then fell to about 9.0% in 2024 and 8.0% in 2025.14 RPOs stopped being a trend and became furniture: almost every NFL offense has a handful in every game plan.







NoteFilm room: Philadelphia Eagles 2017



The 2017 Eagles are the RPO’s breakthrough on the NFL’s biggest stage. Doug Pederson built RPOs into the offense for Carson Wentz, and when Wentz tore his ACL against the Rams in December, he leaned on them even harder for the backup, Nick Foles. The logic was the RPO’s sales pitch in miniature: Foles was a less instinctive improviser than Wentz, so the coaches gave him throws whose answer the defense handed him at the snap. During the playoff bye they went back to film of Foles’s 2013 season under Chip Kelly (27 touchdown passes, two interceptions), with Kelly’s Oregon-bred packaged plays, to find the quick, defined reads that suited him. “It’s centered around accurate throwing, good decision-making and good execution,” offensive coordinator Frank Reich said in January 2018. “When we use it, Nick has shown a great aptitude of doing that very well.” By PFF’s count, Foles completed 93.9% of his RPO throws that season. He completed 26 of 33 passes for 352 yards and three touchdowns in the 38–7 NFC Championship win over Minnesota, and two weeks later, on February 4, 2018, in Minneapolis, he threw for 373 yards and three touchdowns (and caught one) as the Eagles beat New England 41–33 in Super Bowl LII. He was the game’s MVP.15
What to notice on the Eagles’ playoff film: how often the ball came out of Foles’s hand almost at the mesh, on quick slants, glances and bubbles, before the linebackers had finished stepping toward the run fake; and how the line’s first step was identical on the handoffs and the throws. Defenses that sat back to take away the throws got Jay Ajayi, LeGarrette Blount and Corey Clement running against light boxes.








NoteFilm room: Kansas City Chiefs, 2017 to 2025



Andy Reid’s Chiefs have used RPOs more, and for longer, than any other NFL team: first in the league in PFF’s count in 2017 and 2018, and first again in 2025 in FTN’s charting (see the next section). The quarterback changed from Alex Smith to Patrick Mahomes; the idea didn’t. Reid’s RPOs are built for his receivers’ speed, glances and slants behind linebackers, quick screens to the fastest player on the field, and since 2020 Mahomes has thrown more passes on RPOs than any other NFL quarterback.16 The full Reid story is in the Chiefs case study.
What to notice: how short Reid’s RPO throws are. In 2025 FTN charted 150 Chiefs RPOs: 88 handoffs and 62 throws, more than half of them on first down and all but two from the shotgun. The median throw was caught two yards behind the line, and the most frequent targets were Rashee Rice (17) and Xavier Worthy (11). The Chiefs use the RPO to put the ball in their fastest players’ hands in space, with a run already blocked if the defense takes that away.17








NoteFilm room: Jalen Hurts’s Eagles, 2022



The RPO came back to Philadelphia in a different form with Jalen Hurts, whose running made every read harder to defend. In 2022, the season the Eagles reached Super Bowl LVII, FTN’s charting has them using RPOs on a larger share of their plays than any other team. Their offensive coordinator that year, Shane Steichen, became the Colts’ head coach in 2023, and the 2023 Colts used RPOs on a bigger share of their plays than anyone in the four seasons of FTN data: a scheme travelling with its coach.18 The Eagles’ RPOs, the run game and the tush push are the subject of their own case study.
One drive to look up: the Eagles’ opening drive of Super Bowl LVII (Feb. 12, 2023, against Kansas City). On first-and-10 from the Chiefs’ 47 with 12:31 left in the first quarter, Hurts threw to the tight end Dallas Goedert for 13 yards; on the next snap, without a huddle, he hit DeVonta Smith for 23. FTN charted both throws as RPOs. It also charted them as play-action, and it charted Hurts’s 45-yard touchdown to A.J. Brown early in the second quarter as an RPO too, a reminder of how blurry the line between the two families is in charting.19
What to notice: how Hurts’s legs change the read. With a quarterback who can also keep on a zone read, the backside end and the overhang defender both have to respect him, so a single snap can carry a give, a keep and a throw.

title: Run-Pass Options: Plays That Are Two Plays
text:
What the numbers say
The NFL’s play-by-play doesn’t say whether a play was an RPO: a handoff is a handoff and a pass is a pass. But FTN’s charters, who watch every NFL play, flag RPOs, and the flag is in the nflverse data from 2022 on. The numbers come with a caveat that is worth learning once: charting services disagree. PFF’s rates for the same seasons run well above FTN’s (about 8 to 10.5 percent of plays against FTN’s 4 to 6), because deciding from film whether a handoff “was” an RPO (did a receiver run a real route? was the quarterback reading someone?) is a judgment, and charters judge differently. Use one series at a time, and compare teams within it.


Show the Python
from gridiron.data import nfl, pbp

style.apply()
SEASONS = [2022, 2023, 2024, 2025]
ftn = nfl().load_ftn_charting(SEASONS).to_pandas().rename(
    columns={"nflverse_game_id": "game_id", "nflverse_play_id": "play_id"})
ftn["is_rpo"] = ftn["is_rpo"].fillna(False).astype(bool)
cols = ["season", "season_type", "game_id", "play_id", "posteam", "play_type", "epa", "success", "air_yards",
        "down", "penalty_type", "complete_pass", "shotgun"]
allp = pbp(SEASONS, columns=cols)
allp = allp[allp["season_type"] == "REG"]
reg = allp[allp["play_type"].isin(["pass", "run"]) & allp["down"].notna()]
m = reg.merge(ftn[["game_id", "play_id", "is_rpo", "n_defense_box", "is_screen_pass"]],
              on=["game_id", "play_id"], how="inner")
rpo = m[m["is_rpo"]]
rate = m.groupby("season")["is_rpo"].mean()
team25 = m[m["season"] == 2025].groupby("posteam")["is_rpo"].mean().sort_values()
lead = {s: m[m["season"] == s].groupby("posteam")["is_rpo"].mean().sort_values(ascending=False)
        for s in SEASONS}
thrown = rpo[(rpo["play_type"] == "pass") & rpo["air_yards"].notna()]
other = m[(~m["is_rpo"]) & (m["play_type"] == "pass") & m["air_yards"].notna()]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.8, 4.9), gridspec_kw=dict(width_ratios=[1.0, 1.25]))
ax = axes[0]
hi = {"KC"}
ax.barh(range(len(team25)), team25.values * 100,
        color=[style.SERIES[0] if t in hi else "#9ec5f4" for t in team25.index], height=0.72)
ax.set_yticks(range(len(team25)))
ax.set_yticklabels(team25.index, fontsize=6.2)
ax.axvline(rate[2025] * 100, color=style.INK_2, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (3, 2)))
ax.text(rate[2025] * 100 + 0.3, 1.0, f"league\n{rate[2025]:.1%}", fontsize=6.8, color=style.INK_2, va="center")
ax.set_xlabel("% of plays charted as RPO, 2025", fontsize=7.5)
ax.set_title("RPO rate by team, 2025", fontsize=9.5)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=7)
ax.set_ylim(-0.7, len(team25) - 0.3)
ax = axes[1]
bins = np.arange(-8, 31)
for d_, name, col in [(thrown, "RPO throws", style.SERIES[0]), (other, "All other passes", style.SERIES[1])]:
    a = d_["air_yards"].clip(-8, 30)
    share = a.round().value_counts(normalize=True).reindex(bins, fill_value=0) * 100
    ax.step(bins, share.values, where="mid", color=col, lw=1.8, label=name)
ax.axvspan(-8.5, 0.5, color=style.GRID, alpha=0.6, zorder=0)
ax.text(-4.0, 15.6, "at or behind\nthe line", fontsize=7, color=style.INK_2, ha="center")
ax.set_xlim(-8.5, 30.5)
ax.set_ylim(0, 17.5)
ax.set_xlabel("air yards (30 = 30 or more)", fontsize=7.5)
ax.set_ylabel("% of throws", fontsize=7.5)
ax.set_title("How far RPO throws go, 2022–2025", fontsize=9.5)
ax.legend(fontsize=7.2, loc="upper right")
ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=1.4)
plt.show()

behind_r, behind_o = (thrown["air_yards"] <= 0).mean(), (other["air_yards"] <= 0).mean()
deep_r, deep_o = (thrown["air_yards"] > 10).mean(), (other["air_yards"] > 10).mean()
gave25 = (rpo.loc[rpo["season"] == 2025, "play_type"] == "run").mean()
gave_all = (rpo["play_type"] == "run").mean()
epa_pass, epa_run = rpo.loc[rpo["play_type"] == "pass", "epa"].mean(), rpo.loc[rpo["play_type"] == "run", "epa"].mean()
comp_r = thrown["complete_pass"].mean()
epa_rpo, epa_non = rpo["epa"].mean(), m.loc[~m["is_rpo"], "epa"].mean()
sr_rpo, sr_non = rpo["success"].mean(), m.loc[~m["is_rpo"], "success"].mean()
idp = allp[allp["penalty_type"].fillna("").eq("Ineligible Downfield Pass")]
idp = idp.merge(ftn[["game_id", "play_id", "is_rpo"]], on=["game_id", "play_id"], how="inner")
idp_n, idp_rpo = len(idp), idp["is_rpo"].mean()
rpo_share = m["is_rpo"].mean()
box_thrown = {k: (rpo.loc[rpo["n_defense_box"] == k, "play_type"] == "pass").mean() for k in (6, 7)}
box_thrown[8] = (rpo.loc[rpo["n_defense_box"] >= 8, "play_type"] == "pass").mean()
kc25, phi22, ind23 = lead[2025].get("KC"), lead[2022].get("PHI"), lead[2023].get("IND")
top = {s: lead[s].index[0] for s in SEASONS}
non = m[~m["is_rpo"]]
epa_npass, epa_nrun = non.loc[non["play_type"] == "pass", "epa"].mean(), non.loc[non["play_type"] == "run", "epa"].mean()
sd_rpo, sd_non = rpo["epa"].std(), non["epa"].std()
gun_rpo = rpo["shotgun"].mean()
rank25 = {t: i + 1 for i, t in enumerate(lead[2025].index)}








Figure 25.8: RPOs in FTN’s NFL charting. Left: the share of each team’s offensive plays charted as RPOs, 2025 regular season (runs and passes, scrambles included, kneel-downs and spikes excluded). Right: how far past the line RPO throws travel in the air, against all other passes, 2022–2025 regular seasons; air yards at or behind zero (shaded) are thrown to a receiver at or behind the line of scrimmage. RPO throws pile up behind the line, the bubbles and now screens that NFL timing favors; other passes spread far downfield. (The bump at the right edge of the ‘all other passes’ line is the last bin, which holds every throw of 30 or more air yards.) Data: nflverse play-by-play joined to FTN charting (load_ftn_charting) via nflreadpy; FTN’s RPO flag is a charter’s judgment, and other services count more RPOs.





Five things to read from Figure 25.8 and the numbers behind it.
RPOs are a small, steady slice of NFL offense. FTN charted 5.0% of plays as RPOs in 2022, 5.3% in 2023, 3.6% in 2024 and 6.2% in 2025 (the 2024 dip is larger than PFF’s and may partly be charting). The leaders are the teams this chapter has already met: PHI in 2022 (13.5%), IND in 2023 (18.3%), and Kansas City in 2025 (14.4%), more than twice the league rate. At the other end, the RPO is plainly a play-caller’s choice, not a law of modern football. The 49ers and Rams, who run mostly from under center with wide-zone blocking, are the bottom two in 2025 (0.7% and 0.5%): 96% of the league’s charted RPOs came from the shotgun, and an offense that lives under center gets the same “make the linebacker step up, then throw behind him” effect from play-action instead (04-05). Yet the 2025 Packers, whose head coach Matt LaFleur comes from the same Shanahan–McVay tree, ranked 5th. And Baltimore, with Lamar Jackson, one of the league’s most dangerous running quarterbacks, sits mid-table (5.6%): a zone read or a designed quarterback run is an option run, and FTN doesn’t count it as an RPO.
Most RPOs are runs. On 69% of the charted RPOs from 2022 to 2025 the ball was handed off (79% in 2025). That is the “run with a safety valve” idea from the Madden callout, in data. It also means the RPO’s main effect is invisible in a box score: its product is the defender who wasn’t in the run fit.
NFL RPO throws are short, and very often behind the line. 57% of RPO throws were caught (or aimed) at or behind the line of scrimmage, against 21% of other passes; only 11% travelled more than ten yards in the air, against 30% of other passes. That shape is the clock at work: the bubbles and now screens come out about half a second after the snap, before any lineman can drift a yard, and a throw beyond the line has to leave so fast that it can’t be far beyond it.
The rule bites. From 2022 to 2025 the NFL called 246 ineligible-downfield fouls on passes in the regular season. 24% of them came on plays FTN charted as RPOs, though RPOs were only 5.0% of plays: per snap, an RPO is many times more likely to draw the flag than any other play.
Per play, RPOs are about average, and steadier. Split by branch, the numbers look dramatic: RPO throws averaged +0.057 EPA with a 79% completion rate, against +0.001 for all other passes; RPO handoffs averaged -0.053, against -0.015 for all other runs. Don’t read that as “the throws are great and the runs are bad.” It is selection, as with the quarterback keeps of 03-04: the quarterback throws precisely when the throw is open and hands off when it isn’t, so the throws are the good half of the reads by construction. Put the halves back together and RPOs come out close to ordinary plays: -0.019 EPA per play against -0.005, and an EPA success rate of 42.8% against 43.5%. What does differ is the spread. The standard deviation of EPA on RPOs is 1.00, against 1.40 on other plays: fewer disasters and fewer explosions, which is what you’d expect from a play that throws only short and only when it’s open.20
The box count shows up, weakly, too: when FTN counted six defenders in the box, 28% of RPOs were thrown; with seven, 33%; with eight or more, 40%. More defenders near the ball, more throws: the counting logic of the bubble RPO, visible in charting that sees only the alignment at the snap.
PFF’s charting, with its larger RPO count, tells a slightly different story: from 2021 to 2025, NFL RPOs gained fewer yards per play than other plays (4.53 against 5.43) but were “successful” more often (52.3% against 48.1%).21 The two series don’t contradict each other so much as measure different things. PFF uses its own success definition, not the EPA-based one above, and its RPO count is about twice FTN’s, so it includes many snaps FTN called plain runs or passes. What both agree on is the shape: RPOs are not big-play machines. They are a low-variance way to gain modest yardage with a run that is always blocked, and whether they beat an ordinary play on efficiency depends on whose charting you trust.

title: Run-Pass Options: Plays That Are Two Plays
text:
How defenses answer
Defenses have had a decade to study NFL RPOs, and the answers all attack one of the RPO’s three parts: the read, the throw, or the run behind it. This is a preview; the defense’s side gets its full treatment in Run Fits: Gap Integrity, Force, Spill, and Box Math.


Show the Python
LAT, WIN = (-19.0, 6.5), (-7.0, 17.0)
dfn = only(nickel("single_high", LCB=(6.5, -16.4)), -20, 7)
p = Play(only(trips(), -20, 7), dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
for k, end in [("LT", (0.25, -4.2)), ("LG", (0.3, -2.2)), ("C", (0.35, 0.3)), ("RG", (0.35, 1.3)),
               ("RT", (0.3, 3.8)), ("Y", (0.35, 4.6))]:
    go_to(p, k, end)
p.route("X", r.slant(stem=2.0, length=8.0))
go_to(p, "SS", (5.4, -11.0), "path")
go_to(p, "FS", (3.4, -1.4), "path", via=[(9.0, -1.0)])
go_to(p, "RB", (2.0, 0.4), "run", via=[(-4.6, -0.2), (-1.6, 1.4), (0.8, 0.9)])
p.highlight("SS", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, lateral=LAT, window=WIN, width_in=5.9)
read_line(f, p, (-4.6, -0.5), (5.2, -8.6))
tackle_x(f, p, 2.6, -0.2)
say(f, p, 3.7, -14.7, "SS walls the slant:\nQ reads 'give'", color=RED, fontsize=6.8)
point_to(f, p, (11.4, 4.0), (8.0, -1.0), "FS comes down into\nthe box at the snap", fontsize=6.8, color=RED)
say(f, p, 15.2, -0.5, "deep middle: empty after the snap", fontsize=6.8, color=style.INK_2)
point_to(f, p, (9.0, -4.8), (2.6, -0.2), "the give meets\nthe safety", fontsize=6.6, shrink=5)
plt.show()








Figure 25.9: Making the read lie: one answer to the slant RPO of the earlier figure. The overhang safety (ringed) is told to play the slant no matter what, and he walls it at the snap, so the quarterback reads ‘give.’ But the free safety, deep in the middle, has a run job on this call, decided before the snap: he comes downhill the instant the ball is snapped, without waiting to read anything, into the backside of the box, the spot the overhang defender would have filled. The read was right and the run still meets an extra defender (the red X). The price: with the free safety in the box, nobody is left in the deep middle.






Read the line, not the back. The most useful key a linebacker has against an RPO team is the uncovered guard, the one with no defensive lineman in front of him (03-01). If he climbs hard to the second level, it’s a true run: he couldn’t legally do that on a pass. If he stays at the line, sits, or blocks whoever is in front of him without climbing, it may be an RPO, and the linebacker plays his pass job first. The cost: the key is only as good as the offense’s honesty, and offenses answer with true runs whose guards climb, to punish linebackers who wait.
Make the read lie. Give the read defender a rule (always play the pass) and put someone else in his run fit, usually a safety rotating down after the snap (showing deep, then dropping toward the line), as in Figure 25.9. It is the scrape exchange of 03-04 with a safety instead of a linebacker, and it’s built on the post-snap rotations of Disguise and Rotation. It works because the safety’s run job is called: he triggers at the snap without reading anything, so he arrives in time. The cost is the deep defender who left, and a play-action shot over him beats it.
Play two-high and fit the run from depth. Two-high shells, especially the quarters family of 06-05 (a two-deep zone in which the safeties also help against the run), keep the overhang defender honest on the pass and let a safety who starts ten yards deep become the extra run defender once he sees a handoff. Against a pre-snap count, this is a defense that shows six in the box and plays like seven. Its weakness is the run itself. Unlike the rotating safety above, this one reads first (run or pass?) and only then comes down, so he arrives late, often after the back is already past the line.
Take away the conflict with man coverage. In man coverage, the defender over the slot isn’t torn between a gap and an area: he has a man, and he goes with him. Nobody is in conflict, so there’s nothing to read. The price is the one man coverage always pays: defenders with their backs to the ball, and a box whose count the run can attack.
Squeeze the clock. Hold the read defender’s decision as long as possible (a bluff, a slow-play) so the quarterback rides the mesh a beat longer and the linemen, run blocking, drift past a yard. The flag is a defensive weapon too, and a defense that has watched the tape knows which linemen climb early. The cost: a defender who is still deciding is in neither job, so against an offense that just hands off on time, the run gets a defender who arrives a step late.
Hit the quarterback. Every RPO exposes him for a moment with his eyes on one defender and his body turned toward the back. While he still holds the ball at the mesh he can be tackled like any ball carrier, and a rusher who arrives just as he throws may still finish the hit within a step of the release (later than that is roughing the passer).22 Pressure off the edge makes him hurry the read. The cost: the extra rusher comes from somewhere, usually the coverage, and the quick throws an RPO carries go to exactly the space he left.

Offenses answer back, as always: with motion that changes who the conflict defender is just before the snap, with RPOs that read the safety instead of the overhang, and with play-action that looks exactly like the RPO for the first second and then throws deep over the safety who has learned to come down. That conversation, how one play makes the next one work, is the subject of Constraint Theory, where the RPO appears as a constraint play: a play that punishes a defense for overplaying the offense’s base run.






TipWatch for it



On Sunday: “Is he reading you?” Every RPO has a defender being read. Find him before the snap and you’ll see the decision before the replay does.
Before the snap

Shotgun or pistol, back beside the quarterback, receivers spread. That’s the RPO look. Not every snap from it is an RPO, so treat it as “possible.”
Count the box, then count outside. Six or seven in the box? How many defenders are within seven yards of the line over the slot receivers? If the box is heavy and the slots are light, expect a throw (a bubble or now screen) the instant the ball is snapped.
Find the apex. Who stands halfway between the box and a slot receiver? On the single-receiver side, is a safety walked down? That’s the likely read. Say it out loud: “he’s being read.”

At the snap

RPO or play-action? Watch the line for half a second. On an RPO the linemen fire forward, low, and stay on their blocks at the line; nobody climbs. On play-action they make one hard run step, then their helmets pop up and they settle into pass protection, often a step behind the line. And on a true run, the uncovered guard climbs to a linebacker. Forward and staying put means RPO.
Where the quarterback’s head turns. On a plain handoff, he looks at the back. On a zone read, his eyes are on a defensive lineman at the line. On a post-snap RPO they go to the second level or out over a slot: his eyes are on a defender. On the live sideline shot you can usually see his helmet turn; for his actual eyes and the defender he’s watching, wait for the end-zone replay (01-06).
The backside receiver. On a pure run he jogs or blocks his cornerback. On an RPO he runs a full-speed slant or glance, because he might get the ball.
Watch the read defender’s first two steps, not the ball. Forward and inside: predict throw, behind him. Backward, widening, or eyes on a receiver: predict give.
Count to one. If the ball isn’t out of the quarterback’s hand by about a second, it’s probably a handoff. (Play-action’s throw comes later, two and a half seconds or more, after a full fake and a drop.)

After the play

On the replay, freeze the frame when the ball leaves the quarterback’s hand and look at the linemen. Is anyone more than a yard past the line without a defender in his hands? That’s the flag the umpire is looking for. Did one get thrown?
On the next snap, did the read defender do the opposite? Defenses adjust within a drive.

For your prediction log (01-06): on every RPO look, write the defender you think is being read and your call (G or T) from his first steps; afterward, write what happened.

title: Run-Pass Options: Plays That Are Two Plays
text:
Predict the play






TipPredict the play



Drill 1: count both sides. First-and-10 at midfield. The offense is in the shotgun, 11 personnel, trips to the right with the tight end attached, the back offset left. It has thrown the bubble RPO twice already today. This time the defense shows the picture below before the snap. Count the box and count outside the box on the trips side. Hand off or throw the bubble? And is there anything on the left side the quarterback should like?


Show the Python
p = Play(trips(), nickel("single_high", NB=(5.0, 9.6), SS=(6.0, 13.4), FS=(13.5, 0.0)), los=60, to_go=10)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-19.5, 20.0), window=(-7.2, 15.6), width_in=6.0)
panel_title(f.ax, "Drill 1: 1st and 10, the trips side crowded")
plt.show()








Figure 25.10: Drill 1: first-and-10, gun 11 personnel, trips right with the tight end attached. The defense has the nickel back over H and the strong safety walked down outside him, six yards deep; the free safety is alone in the deep middle.













TipAnswer





Hand off, and the left side is the bonus.

The box: four linemen and two linebackers, six defenders against six blockers (five linemen and the tight end). A hat on every hat: the run is fairly blocked.
Outside on the trips side: H and Z against the nickel back, the cornerback and the strong safety, all within seven yards of the line. Two against three: the bubble is dead. The defense has done exactly what two thrown bubbles teach it to do.
The left side: to get that third defender over the trips side and keep six in the box, the defense has left X alone against an off cornerback, with the only safety in the middle of the field. A slant or glance to X is the throw the count favors, if the play has one packaged to that side (many RPOs pair a bubble on one side with a slant or glance on the other, for exactly this picture).

The general lesson: the count is never just one side. A defense that wins the numbers in one place has lost them somewhere else, and a pre-snap RPO is a machine for finding where.









TipPredict the play



Drill 2: freeze frame. Second-and-8. The offense runs the slant RPO of Figure 25.5 to the left, the inside-zone run going right. The picture below is frozen about six tenths of a second after the snap, with the ball in the back’s belly at the mesh. The overhang safety (ringed) has taken two quick steps, and his shoulders have turned square to the backfield. Does the quarterback give or throw? What happens if the cornerback had lined up on X’s inside shoulder instead?


Show the Python
dfn = only(nickel("single_high", LCB=(6.5, -16.4)), -20, 7)
p = Play(only(trips(), -20, 7), dfn, los=35, to_go=8)
for k, end in [("LT", (0.25, -4.2)), ("LG", (0.3, -2.2)), ("C", (0.35, 0.3)), ("RG", (0.35, 1.3)),
               ("RT", (0.3, 3.8)), ("Y", (0.35, 4.6))]:
    go_to(p, k, end)
go_to(p, "X", (1.4, -15.0), "route")
go_to(p, "SS", (3.6, -6.9), "path")
go_to(p, "RB", (-4.6, -0.3), "path")
p.highlight("SS", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-19.0, 6.8), window=(-7.0, 14.6), width_in=5.6)
panel_title(f.ax, "Drill 2: 2nd and 8, frozen at the mesh")
read_line(f, p, (-4.8, -0.4), (3.6, -6.9))
plt.show()








Figure 25.11: Drill 2: the slant RPO, about 0.6 seconds after the snap. Players are drawn where they stood at the snap; the lines show where each has gone by the moment of the read: the line run-blocking right, the back arriving at the mesh, X two steps into his stem, and the overhang safety’s first two steps.













TipAnswer





Throw the slant. In six tenths of a second the safety has come two yards forward and two yards inside: shoulders toward the run, eyes in the backfield. He has chosen the run, and in doing so he has left the slant’s landing spot, five yards past the line where he was standing. The quarterback pulls the ball and throws it on time, before the linemen have had a chance to drift past a yard. The cornerback, seven yards off and outside, can’t get there. (Compare Figure 25.5: this is its upper branch.)
If the cornerback had lined up inside, the slant would have been a bad throw no matter what the safety did: the corner sits on the route’s path. The quarterback would know that before the snap, and on a well-built call he’d have a second answer on that side (a quick out or a bubble) or he’d treat the play as a straight handoff. Leverage picks the live route; the read picks whether to throw it.









TipPredict the play



Drill 3: flag or no flag? A glance RPO goes for 15 yards. On the replay, frozen at the instant the ball left the quarterback’s hand, you see the picture below. The left guard blocked the 3-technique at the line, let go, and is now about two and a half yards past the line on his way to the Will. The right tackle engaged the 7-technique at the line and has driven him two yards backward, still locked on. Is there a foul in an NFL game? In a college game?


Show the Python
base = only(trips(), -18, 7)
spots = {"LT": (0.9, -4.3), "LG": (2.5, -2.9), "C": (0.3, -0.4), "RG": (0.3, 1.3), "RT": (1.8, 4.0),
         "Y": (0.0, 5.8), "QB": (-5.4, -1.2), "RB": (-3.6, 0.9), "X": (7.2, -13.2)}
dspots = {"BE": (1.9, -4.9), "BT": (1.4, -1.3), "PT": (1.9, 0.45), "PE": (2.9, 4.3),
          "WILL": (5.4, -3.8), "MIKE": (3.8, 1.8), "LCB": (11.0, -16.0), "FS": (12.6, -8.2)}
off = [q.moved(d=spots[q.key][0], w=spots[q.key][1]) if q.key in spots else q for q in base]
dfn = [q.moved(d=dspots[q.key][0], w=dspots[q.key][1]) if q.key in dspots else q
       for q in only(nickel("two_high"), -18, 7)]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
p.highlight("LG", "RT", color=style.SERIES[6])
f = draw(p, lateral=(-17.5, 8.5), window=(-6.4, 14.2), width_in=5.6)
region(f, p, 0.0, 1.0, -17.4, 8.4, style.MUTED, alpha=0.10, lw=0.6, ls=(0, (2, 2)))
throw(f, p, (-5.4, -1.2), (11.2, -11.6), rad=-0.1)
point_to(f, p, (7.8, -0.8), (2.5, -2.9), "LG: 2½ yards past,\nhands empty", fontsize=6.6)
point_to(f, p, (7.4, 5.0), (1.8, 4.0), "RT: 2 yards past,\nstill blocking", fontsize=6.6)
say(f, p, 1.5, -12.6, "1 yard", fontsize=6.4, color=style.INK_2)
panel_title(f.ax, "Drill 3: the ball is out")
plt.show()








Figure 25.12: Drill 3: the instant of the throw. The left guard (ringed) is about two and a half yards past the line of scrimmage with no defender in his hands; the right tackle (ringed) is two yards past it, still blocking the defensive end he engaged at the line. The pass is on its way to X.













TipAnswer





NFL: yes, on the left guard; the right tackle is fine. Illegal man downfield, five yards from the previous spot, and the 15-yard completion comes back. The guard engaged the 3-technique within a yard of the line, but he let go and kept moving forward, which the rule forbids once he’s past a yard. The right tackle is legal under the rule’s exception: he made contact at the line on his initial charge and has stayed locked on while driving his man downfield.
College: no foul. The limit is three yards beyond the neutral zone, and the guard, about two and a half yards past the line of scrimmage, is inside it. He hasn’t reached the Will yet, which matters too: had he already been blocking him that far downfield, college could call offensive pass interference instead. The right tackle is legal under either rulebook.
This is the NFL RPO’s whole problem in one frame. The guard did exactly what inside zone teaches: a first block and a climb to the backside linebacker. That’s why NFL coaches either keep the guard on his first block when the play might be a pass, or read the Will instead of climbing to him, which is the glance RPO.

title: Run-Pass Options: Plays That Are Two Plays
text:
Takeaways

An RPO blocks a run and carries a pass on the same snap, and the quarterback picks one. Unlike play-action, the run is real; unlike the option, one branch is a pass. Every RPO is a packaged play.
It attacks a conflict defender with a run job and a pass job, most often the apex or overhang defender, sometimes a linebacker or a safety. If he plays the run, throw behind him; if he plays the pass, hand off. The run is the default.
Pre-snap RPOs (the bubble RPO) are decided by counting the box against the defenders outside; post-snap RPOs (the glance, slant and stick RPOs and the pop pass) are decided by watching one defender at the mesh. The read does a blocker’s job.
The NFL’s illegal man downfield rule (one yard, for any forward pass, with an exception for linemen still engaged with a defender they met at the line) makes NFL RPOs quick and short and keeps NFL linemen near the line; college’s three yards past the neutral zone, only for passes that cross it, lets college RPOs run-block longer and throw farther.
RPOs grew out of Air Raid tags, the zone read and the college spread, and the Reid tree carried them to the NFL (the 2017 Chiefs and Eagles). In FTN’s charting they are a few percent of NFL plays, mostly handoffs, with throws that cluster at or behind the line, and about as efficient per play as anything else, with less variance.
Defenses answer by reading the line instead of the back (a guard who climbs means run), making the read lie (a safety called down into the vacated run fit), playing two-high and fitting from depth, playing man to remove the conflict, stretching the clock to draw flags, and hitting the quarterback. Each one gives something back: a deep defender, a step in the run fit, or a rusher’s worth of coverage.

title: Run-Pass Options: Plays That Are Two Plays
text:
Connections
Builds on: Option Football (the read key, the mesh and give or keep), Play-Action, Bootlegs, and Screens (the fake that an RPO doesn’t need), A First Look at Defense (the box and the apex), Zone Running (inside zone and the climb) and The Quick Game (the bubble, slant and stick).
Sets up:

Run Fits: Gap Integrity, Force, Spill, and Box Math: how a defense fits the run against an RPO without losing the pass.
Constraint Theory: RPOs as constraints, and how RPOs, play-action and the base run sequence off each other.
Contact Rules and Penalties as Strategy: offensive pass interference and the other rules offenses and defenses play against.
The College Laboratory: the Wing-T, the wishbone, the Air Raid and the spread option that produced the RPO.

See also (case studies): Andy Reid and the Kansas City Chiefs and The Eagles: Trenches, RPOs, and the Tush Push.
If you want to go deeper: Chris B. Brown’s The Art of Smart Football and his Smart Football essays on packaged plays and the RPO; the RPO film breakdowns in USA Football’s coaching blog and in college coaching clinics (the glance, bubble and slant RPOs are standard clinic topics); and, for the rules, the NFL’s official playing rules (Rule 8, Sections 3 and 5) next to the NCAA rulebook (Rule 7-3), which make the one-yard and three-yard difference concrete.






NoteGo deeper



From diagrams to tracking data. The animation in this chapter is a gridiron simulation written in NFL Big Data Bowl coordinates (simulated, BDB-format), so real tracking data drops into the same drawing code. The 2025 Big Data Bowl’s plays.csv carries a PFF run-pass-option flag (pff_runPassOption), so finding real RPOs is a filter, not a hunt. With the tracking you can measure what this chapter only describes: how far past the line each lineman is at the frame of the pass_forward event, and how long the quarterback held the mesh. The cell below shows the shape of that code (it is not run, because the course does not download the Big Data Bowl files).


Show the Python (real tracking data; not run)
import pandas as pd
from gridiron import bdb, show_animation

trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_*.csv")
plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")
rpos = plays[plays["pff_runPassOption"] == 1]                    # PFF's RPO flag (BDB 2025)
g, pl = rpos.iloc[0][["gameId", "playId"]]
one = bdb.prepare(trk, plays, game_id=g, play_id=pl)
show_animation(one, times=[0.0, 0.6, 1.0, 1.8])

# How far past the line is each offensive lineman when the ball is thrown?
los = one.loc[(one["frameType"] == "SNAP") & (one["side"] == "ball"), "x"].iloc[0]
throw_f = one.loc[one["event"] == "pass_forward", "frameId"].min()
linemen = one[(one["frameId"] == throw_f) & one["position"].isin(["T", "G", "C"])]
print((linemen["x"] - los).round(1).tolist())                  # yards past the line

title: Quarterback Play: Progressions, the Pocket, and Off-Script Football
text:
The quarterback’s clock
Third-and-8, fourth quarter. The quarterback takes the snap in the shotgun, drops, and looks hard to his left. Then his head snaps to the middle of the field. He bounces once on his back foot, then again. The two defensive ends have run around his tackles and are closing from behind him, so he takes two quick steps forward, into the space they left. Now a defensive tackle shoves a guard backward into his face, and the quarterback spins out to his right and runs toward the sideline. His receivers, who had been running set routes, suddenly do something else: the one who was deep turns and runs back toward him, the one who was short takes off deep, and a receiver from the far side of the field races across. Four and a half seconds after the snap, the ball floats over a cornerback who is still turning around, and the receiver catches it alone near the sideline. The analyst says, “That’s what the great ones do.” What, exactly, did he do? Why did he step up and not back? How did the receivers know where to go? And when none of it works, why is throwing the ball into the seats sometimes the best play he can make? This chapter is about the quarterback’s three to four seconds: what he is doing with his eyes, his feet and his judgment, on schedule and off it.
You’ll be able to…
How to read the diagrams. The conventions of the rest of Part 4, plus a few for this chapter:
The moving pictures add three more: faint lines are where a player has been (solid blue for offense, dashed orange for defense), grey dashes are the routes as they were called, and a dashed brown arrow is the ball in flight.
Every dropback is a race against a clock the defense controls, and the quarterback runs a fixed sequence of jobs against it. Coaches teach the sequence by tying each job to a moment in the drop, so that the quarterback’s feet tell him what his eyes should be doing.
Much of the work is done before the clock starts. Before the snap he has identified the Mike and set the protection (Pass Protection), read the defense’s alignment for which half of the field he expects to work (The Pre-Snap Phase), and checked whether the look calls for a change of play or a shot down the field (a subject of Concepts Versus Coverages). After the snap, here is the order, for an ordinary dropback pass from the shotgun.
Show the Python
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.5))
XMAX, SCHED = 6.0, 3.2
PH = [(0.0, 1.7, "Drop: eyes to read 1", style.SEQUENTIAL_BLUE[2], False),
      (1.7, SCHED, "Last step: read 1;\nhitch steps: 2, 3,\ncheckdown", style.SEQUENTIAL_BLUE[4], True),
      (SCHED, XMAX, "Off schedule: climb, slide, escape;\nscramble drill, throwaway or run", style.SERIES[1], True)]
TOP = 5.25
for a_, b_, lab, col, dark in PH:
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((a_, TOP), b_ - a_ - 0.03, 1.0, fc=col, ec="none", alpha=0.95, zorder=3))
    ax.text((a_ + b_) / 2, TOP + 0.5, lab, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.4,
            color="white" if dark else style.INK, linespacing=1.15, fontweight="bold" if dark else "normal",
            zorder=4)
# counting the rush happens during the first steps of the drop: a thin band on top of the drop bar
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((0.0, TOP + 1.04), 0.62, 0.42, fc=style.SEQUENTIAL_BLUE[0], ec=style.SEQUENTIAL_BLUE[3],
                       lw=0.6, zorder=3))
ax.text(0.68, TOP + 1.25, "count the rush (during the first steps of the drop)", ha="left", va="center",
        fontsize=6.2, color=style.INK_2, zorder=4)
# vertical guides drawn by hand, only in the data area, so they never cross the labels above
for xv in np.arange(0.5, XMAX + 0.01, 0.5):
    ax.plot([xv, xv], [-0.2, 4.6], color=style.GRID, lw=0.6, zorder=0)
ax.plot([SCHED, SCHED], [-0.2, 4.95], color=style.SERIES[1], lw=1.1, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1)
ax.text(SCHED + 0.06, 4.85, "the schedule runs out", fontsize=6.4, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, va="center",
        ha="left")
rows = list(CLOCK.items())
for i, (lab, (q1, med, q3)) in enumerate(rows):
    y = 4.0 - i * 0.98
    ax.plot([q1, q3], [y, y], color=style.SERIES[0], lw=5, alpha=0.35, solid_capstyle="round", zorder=2)
    ax.plot([med], [y], "o", color=style.SERIES[0], ms=7, mec="white", mew=1.0, zorder=3)
    ax.text(med, y + 0.3, f"{med:.1f} s", va="bottom", ha="center", fontsize=6.8, color=style.INK_2, zorder=3)
    ax.text(-0.08, y, lab, va="center", ha="right", fontsize=7.6, color=style.INK)
ax.set_xlim(0, XMAX)
ax.set_ylim(-0.2, 6.85)
ax.set_yticks([])
ax.set_xticks(np.arange(0, XMAX + 0.01, 0.5))
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=7.5)
ax.set_xlabel("seconds after the snap", fontsize=8)
ax.grid(False)
ax.spines["left"].set_visible(False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 26.1: The quarterback’s clock. Top: the jobs of an ordinary dropback, tied to the drop and the hitch steps (typical timings; they vary by play and team). He counts the rush during the first steps of the drop, not before it. Bottom: when each kind of throw actually leaves his hand in the NFL, from FTN charting (FTN Data’s staff chart every play from video, including which read the ball went to) of every regular-season pass from 2022 to 2025 that could be matched to a time to throw. The dot is the median, the bar the middle half of throws. First-read throws come out as the quarterback sets or makes his first hitch step; later reads cost about another half second; checkdowns leave at about the same time as later reads, because many are thrown early; throwaways and scramble-drill throws (throws after the quarterback has left the pocket and the receivers have improvised) live past the dashed line at about three seconds, where the play’s schedule has run out. Data: nflverse play-by-play, FTN charting and participation via nflreadpy.
The bottom half of Figure 26.1 is the part to remember. The first-read throw leaves the quarterback’s hand at a median of 2.3 seconds; a throw to a later read, about 0.6 seconds after that; and the throwaways and scramble-drill throws at the far right of the chart, after three seconds, when the rush has usually arrived. The checkdown is the odd one: it is the last look on paper, yet its median is no later than a second read’s. Two things pull it early. On many quick and half-field plays the back is read 2 or 3, not the last of four or five, so his turn comes fast; and some checkdowns are thrown before the deeper reads had a chance, the “bad checkdown” the checkdown section warns about. About 27% of checkdowns left the quarterback’s hand inside two and a half seconds. Every step down the list costs time, and, as you’ll see, value.

title: Quarterback Play: Progressions, the Pocket, and Off-Script Football
text:
At the snap: the protection check. Before he looks at a single receiver, the quarterback answers one question: did more rushers come than the protection can block? If yes, the ball goes now to the hot receiver or a receiver who sight-adjusted his route, before any progression starts. The protection call has already told him which rusher is his: the one the line leaves unblocked by design if he comes, whom the quarterback must beat with a quick throw. So this check takes a glance, not a study.
The drop: read 1. If the rush is covered, his eyes go to the first read as his feet go back, and the decision comes as the last step of the drop lands: open, and the ball comes out as his back foot plants; covered, and he moves on.
Each hitch step: the next read. If read 1 is covered, he takes a short step forward, the hitch step of Passing Game Fundamentals (a step, not to be confused with the hitch route), which resets his feet so he can throw again, and his eyes move to read 2. Another hitch step, read 3. Each hitch step takes about half a second.
The last read: the checkdown. The final look is to a back or tight end a few yards past the line, the safe throw that keeps the play from becoming a loss.
After that: off schedule. If the ball still isn’t out, the play has left its design. The quarterback now has to manage the pocket (step up, slide, or escape), and decide among a scramble, an improvised throw, a throwaway, or taking the sack.









ImportantWhy it exists



Tying the eyes to the feet solves a problem that sounds trivial and isn’t: in the chaos of a rush, how does a quarterback know when to give up on a receiver? Counting seconds doesn’t work with three hundred pounds of defensive tackle in his face. Feet do. “Last step, read one; hitch step, read two; hitch step, checkdown” turns a judgment into a rhythm he can practice ten thousand times, and it keeps him on the same clock as his receivers, whose routes are timed to the same drop (Passing Game Fundamentals).
What it gives up: freedom. A quarterback who throws on rhythm throws to where the play says, not to where a receiver happens to be open. When the defense takes away the design, a rhythm passer can be stuck; that is where the second half of this chapter, the off-script game, comes in.

title: Quarterback Play: Progressions, the Pocket, and Off-Script Football
text:
The progression, live
Passing Game Fundamentals drew a progression as numbers on a play diagram. Watched in real time it looks different: the numbers light up one at a time, on the beat of the quarterback’s feet, and at each one he is asking a yes-or-no question that one defender answers. The play is dagger, drawn as Dropback Concepts drew it, against the two-high coverage it was built to beat.


Show the Python
LOS, TOGO = 40, 10


def upto(p, key, way, t_stop, kind="drop"):
    """Script a defender along `way` [(t, d, w), ...] but only until t_stop, the moment he reacts to the ball."""
    cut, prev = [], (0.0, *p._cur(key))
    for t, dd, ww in way:
        if t <= t_stop:
            cut.append((t, dd, ww))
            prev = (t, dd, ww)
        else:
            f = (t_stop - prev[0]) / (t - prev[0])
            cut.append((t_stop, prev[1] + f * (dd - prev[1]), prev[2] + f * (ww - prev[2])))
            break
    timed(p, key, cut, kind)


def dagger(throw_t=2.4, react=0.5):
    off = line() + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, 1.6, "R"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -15.0),
                    O("H", "WR", -1.5, -8.5), O("Y", "TE", -1.5, 8.5), O("Z", "WR", -0.7, 15.0)]
    # Quarters from a nickel: two safeties at 12 over the slots, corners off, three underneath plus the nickel
    dfn = four_rush() + [D("MIKE", "MIKE", 5.0, 1.8, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 5.0, -5.0, "W"),
                         D("NB", "NB", 5.0, 7.6, "$"), D("SS", "SS", 12.0, 9.0, "SS"),
                         D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -15.0, "C"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 15.0, "C"),
                         D("FS", "FS", 12.0, -9.0, "FS")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=LOS, to_go=TOGO)
    pass_set(p)
    for k, (d, w) in {"LE": (-1.7, -4.6), "NT": (-0.6, -0.9), "DT": (-0.7, 2.0), "RE": (-1.7, 4.6)}.items():
        timed(p, k, [(0.8, d, w)], "rush")
    # quarterback: five-step drop from the gun to 9 yards, then a hitch step every half second
    timed(p, "QB", [(1.95, -9.0, 0.0), (2.4, -8.4, 0.0), (2.9, -8.0, 0.0)])
    # back: checks for a blitzer, then releases to sit underneath as the checkdown
    timed(p, "RB", [(0.5, -5.2, 2.4), (1.4, -5.2, 2.4), (2.4, 2.5, 3.2), (2.9, 3.2, 2.4)], "route")
    timed(p, "Y", [(3.3, 23.5, 8.2)], "route")                                          # seam
    timed(p, "Z", [(2.35, 15.6, 15.0), (2.55, 16.0, 13.6), (3.7, 16.0, 4.0), (4.4, 16.0, -1.5)], "route")  # dig
    timed(p, "X", [(2.8, 20.0, -15.0)], "route")                                        # go
    timed(p, "H", [(1.6, 10.5, -8.5), (1.9, 9.5, -9.3)], "route")                       # curl
    p.pass_to("Z", t=throw_t)
    _, catch = p.pass_target_spot()
    tr = throw_t + react
    # Quarters: the strong safety reads Y and carries the seam; the nickel sinks under it; the Mike sits at ten
    # yards with his eyes on the quarterback and only later walls off the crosser; the corner stays over Z
    upto(p, "SS", [(0.9, 12.8, 8.9), (1.9, 15.6, 8.6), (2.8, 20.5, 8.4), (3.6, 23.5, 8.3)], tr)
    upto(p, "NB", [(1.2, 8.5, 8.2), (2.2, 11.0, 8.4), (3.0, 12.5, 8.4)], tr)
    upto(p, "MIKE", [(1.3, 8.0, 2.4), (2.3, 9.6, 3.0), (2.8, 10.0, 3.0), (3.4, 12.5, 1.8)], tr)
    upto(p, "RCB", [(1.0, 8.5, 15.2), (2.3, 15.2, 15.4), (2.8, 17.6, 13.8), (3.6, 18.2, 8.5)], tr)
    timed(p, "WILL", [(1.3, 8.0, -5.0), (2.3, 9.0, -4.0)], "drop")
    timed(p, "FS", [(1.0, 12.0, -9.0), (2.2, 12.5, -8.0)], "drop")
    timed(p, "LCB", [(2.8, 18.0, -15.5)], "drop")
    # once the ball is in the air, they break on it (after a reaction time) and stop a step short
    for k, spd in (("MIKE", 4.5), ("SS", 4.0), ("NB", 4.0), ("RCB", 4.5)):
        start = np.array(p.position(k, tr))
        dist = float(np.hypot(*(np.array(catch) - start)))
        stop = start + (np.array(catch) - start) * max(0.0, (dist - 0.9) / dist)
        timed(p, k, [(tr + max(0.05, (dist - 0.9) / spd), *stop)], "drop")
    return p, catch


def catch_time(p, key="Z"):
    for kind, to, te in p.ball_events:
        if kind == "pass":
            start = np.array(p.ball_position(te))
            ta = te + 0.5
            for _ in range(4):
                ta = te + float(np.hypot(*(np.array(p.position(to, ta)) - start))) / gplay.BALL_SPEED
            return ta


PLAN = {"Y": [(-1.5, 8.5), (23.5, 8.2)], "Z": [(-0.7, 15.0), (15.6, 15.0), (16.0, 13.6), (16.0, 3.0)],
        "RB": [(-5.0, 1.6), (-5.2, 2.4), (2.5, 3.2), (3.2, 2.4)], "X": [(-0.7, -15.0), (20.0, -15.0)],
        "H": [(-1.5, -8.5), (10.5, -8.5), (9.5, -9.3)]}
prog, _ = dagger()
T_CATCH = catch_time(prog)
LAT, WIN = (-18.0, 18.0), (-11.5, 26.0)
# each numbered read rides beside its receiver: (receiver, offset in d, offset in w)
BADGES = {1: ("Y", 0.2, -2.4), 2: ("Z", 0.3, -2.4), 3: ("RB", -2.0, 1.6)}
T_SET, T_HITCH = 1.95, 2.4


def draw_prog(ax, t):
    s1 = "wait" if t < 1.0 else ("now" if t < T_SET + 0.2 else "done")
    s2 = "wait" if t < T_SET + 0.2 else "now"
    ring = ({"SS": PURPLE} if 1.0 <= t < T_SET + 0.2 else
            ({"MIKE": PURPLE} if T_SET + 0.2 <= t < T_HITCH + 0.4 else {}))
    fld = moment(ax, prog, t, LAT, WIN, rings=ring, plan=PLAN)
    ppy = fld.pts_per_yard()
    for n, st in ((1, s1), (2, s2), (3, "wait")):
        key, dd, dw = BADGES[n]
        rd, rw = prog.position(key, t)
        badge(ax, *XY(fld, prog, rd + dd, rw + dw), n, st, fs=max(6.0, ppy * 1.0))
    if 1.0 <= t < T_SET + 0.2:
        eyes(fld, prog, t, "SS")
    elif T_SET + 0.2 <= t <= T_HITCH + 0.05:
        eyes(fld, prog, t, "MIKE")


TIMES = [0.0, T_SET, T_HITCH, round(T_CATCH, 1)]
NOTES = ["Snap: four rush, four blocked.\nNo hot throw; eyes go to read 1.",
         "Last step of the drop: read 1, the seam.\nThe safety carries Y deep. No.",
         "Hitch step: read 2. The Mike sits at ten\nyards: the window is open. Ball out.",
         "Caught in the window. Read 3,\nthe checkdown, was never needed."]
play_out(draw_prog, TIMES, NOTES, t_end=T_CATCH + 0.4, aspect=(WIN[1] - WIN[0]) / (LAT[1] - LAT[0]), width_in=6.1)





  
  Your browser does not support the video tag.



Figure 26.2: A progression in real time (simulated play), first-and-10 (the yellow-orange line is the line to gain). The call is dagger to the right, the two-high beater of Dropback Concepts: Y runs up the seam to pull the deep defenders, Z runs a deep dig (an in-breaking route at about 16 yards) behind him, and R is the checkdown. The defense plays Quarters, two safeties deep, and rushes four. The quarterback takes a five-step drop from the shotgun. Panel 1: at the snap he counts the rush (four, all blocked: no hot throw). Panel 2: on the last step of his drop his eyes are on read 1, the seam, and its key, the strong safety (ringed), who carries Y deep, as Quarters tells him to: no. Panel 3: on his hitch step he moves to read 2. Its key is the Mike (ringed), who has sat down at about ten yards with his eyes on the quarterback, so the window behind him will be open; the ball comes out as Z breaks. Panel 4: the ball arrives in that window, under the safety and over the linebackers. Read 3 was never needed. The numbered reads ride beside their receivers; X’s go and H’s curl on the left (grey dashes) are not part of this progression.




Three things are happening in Figure 26.2 that you can’t see in a static play diagram.
Every read has a key defender. Passing Game Fundamentals separated two kinds of read: a progression, which looks at receivers one at a time, and a defender read, which watches one defender. Dagger is a progression, but even on a progression each look is answered by one defender, and good quarterbacks look at him. At read 1 the question is not really “is Y open?” but “what is the safety on Y’s side doing?” In Quarters that safety is taught to carry the inside receiver if he goes deep, so a seam route is open only if he doesn’t, and here he does. At read 2 the question is the Mike linebacker: has he dropped deep enough to take away the dig, or is the window behind him open? Here he sits at ten yards with his eyes on the quarterback, and the safety is gone with Y, so the space at sixteen yards between them is empty. Which defender is the key on which play depends on the coverage, and that is a subject of its own: Concepts Versus Coverages teaches it, once Part 6 has taught the coverages themselves.
The order is a ranking of risk and reward, and a timetable. Read 1 is the biggest gain the play can produce (a seam is a touchdown if the safety guesses wrong); read 2 a solid one; read 3 a small, safe one. A progression runs from the most valuable throw the defense might allow to the least dangerous one, so that the quarterback takes the big play when it is there and the safe one when nothing else is. It is also a schedule: each route is built to come open just as his feet arrive at that read. Z’s dig breaks at about 2.4 seconds because that is when the hitch step lands. Many coaches sum it up as deep to short, but the timetable is the real rule, and on quick concepts the order starts short: stick and slant-flat key one underneath defender and throw whichever of two short routes he leaves (The Quick Game). Dagger is a full-field read in the language of Passing Game Fundamentals; on a half-field read the order is shorter, and what the quarterback saw before the snap can decide which half he starts on.
The ball comes out before the receiver is open. In panel 3 the dig hasn’t broken yet; Z is still running straight up the field. The quarterback throws anyway, because he has seen what he needed: the Mike is in front of the window, not in it, and the safety is committed to the seam. That kind of throw has a name.






NoteMadden vs. real life



In Madden every receiver carries a button icon, the camera sits high behind the quarterback, and you can see the whole field at once and press the button of whoever looks open. A real quarterback sees through a forest of six-and-a-half-foot linemen with helmets bouncing in his face, from eye level, and can usefully look at one area at a time. That is why a progression exists at all: he can’t scan everything, so the play tells him what to look at, in what order, and when to give up on each look. When an analyst says a quarterback “got through his progression,” he means the quarterback looked at the right things, in the right order, on time, which is much harder than pressing the right button.



Anticipation: throwing to a window that isn’t there yet
An anticipation throw is a pass released before the receiver is open, usually before he makes his break, aimed at the spot where the window between defenders will be when the ball gets there. It is the bigger, riskier cousin of the timing route of Passing Game Fundamentals: a timing route is thrown to a fixed spot on a fixed step, while an anticipation throw is a judgment, made on any route, about where defenders will be in a second.
Why throw to a receiver who isn’t open? Because the ball takes time to get there. A firm 20-yard throw is in the air for about a second, and in a second a linebacker can close five yards. A window that is open when the quarterback sees it is often closed by the time the ball arrives. What makes it a judgment rather than a timing route is what he reads in the half second before he lets go. On dagger the timing is in the play; the decision is the Mike. If the Mike is sinking as Z stems upfield, eyes turned to the receivers, he is going to be standing in the window, and the throw dies. If he sits with his eyes on the quarterback, he will be in front of it. The quarterback has to make that call while Z is still running straight upfield.


Show the Python
def sep_at_catch(p):
    tc = catch_time(p)
    z = np.array(p.position("Z", tc))
    dd = {k: float(np.hypot(*(np.array(p.position(k, tc)) - z))) for k in ("MIKE", "SS", "NB", "WILL", "RCB")}
    k = min(dd, key=dd.get)
    return tc, k, dd[k]


early, _ = dagger(2.4)
late, _ = dagger(2.9)
SEP = {}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 4.4))
LAT2, WIN2 = (-7.5, 19.5), (-10.5, 24.0)
for ax, p, ttl, key, lab_off in ((axes[0], early, "Anticipation: out at 2.4 s, as he breaks", "early", (-1.9, 3.6)),
                                 (axes[1], late, "“See it, throw it”: out at 2.9 s", "late", (-0.4, -4.4))):
    tc, k, dist = sep_at_catch(p)
    SEP[key] = (tc, dist)
    fld = moment(ax, p, tc, LAT2, WIN2, rings={k: PURPLE}, plan={"Z": PLAN["Z"]})
    z, dfd = p.position("Z", tc), p.position(k, tc)
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = XY(fld, p, *z), XY(fld, p, *dfd)
    ax.add_patch(Circle((x0, y0), dist, fc=PURPLE, alpha=0.08, ec=PURPLE, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (2, 1.5)), zorder=7))
    ax.plot([x0, x1], [y0, y1], color=PURPLE, lw=1.2, ls=(0, (1, 1.2)), zorder=12)
    dot(ax, x0, y0, "off", "Z", fld.pts_per_yard(), r=0.9, z=13)      # the receiver on top of everyone
    name = {"MIKE": "the Mike", "NB": "the nickel", "SS": "the safety", "RCB": "the corner"}.get(k, k)
    say(fld, p, dfd[0] + lab_off[0], dfd[1] + lab_off[1], name, color=PURPLE, fs=6.8, weight="bold")
    say(fld, p, -7.0, 12.5, f"caught at {tc:.1f} s\nnearest defender {dist:.1f} yd", color=PURPLE, fs=7.2,
        weight="bold")
    ax.set_title(ttl, loc="left", fontsize=8.4, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 26.3: One play, two release times (simulated). Both panels freeze the moment the dig is caught. Left: the anticipation throw, released on the hitch step at 2.4 seconds, as Z breaks. Right: the quarterback waits one more hitch step, until Z looks open, and throws at 2.9 seconds. Everything else is the same, including when the defenders react (they break on the ball only once it is thrown), but the later ball is caught further across the field, where the Mike has had time to work back under the crosser. The ringed defender is the one nearest the receiver at the catch; the dashed circle around Z has that defender’s distance as its radius, so a bigger circle is a bigger window.





In the simulation the early throw is caught with the nearest defender 2.4 yards away; the late one with a defender 0.9 yards away, close enough to knock it down or catch it himself. The difference is half a second, one hitch step.
A simulation only shows what it was told, and this one was told that defenders break on the ball when it is thrown, not when they see the receiver break. So treat it as an illustration of the mechanism, not proof. The proof that windows matter is in tracking data. Next Gen Stats measures, for every target, how far the receiver was from the nearest defender when the ball arrived. Across 885 receiver-seasons with 50 or more targets from 2018 to 2025, each extra yard of average separation went with about 3.7 more percentage points of catch rate, at the same average depth of target.1 An anticipation throw is a way of buying that yard with the clock instead of the receiver’s speed.
The trade is just as plain. An anticipation throw is a bet on the future, made on information about the present: the quarterback is predicting that the receiver will break where and when he is supposed to, and that the defender he is reading will keep doing what he is doing. If the receiver slips, rounds his cut, or is held up, the ball arrives at an empty spot, often into a defender’s hands. And if the defender was disguising his intentions, sitting shallow to bait the throw, the window was never going to open. Anticipation is therefore the skill that most separates veteran quarterbacks from rookies: it takes years of reps with the same receivers to know exactly where they’ll be, and years of film to know what a linebacker’s first two steps mean.
Coaches often say the young quarterback “needs to see it before he throws it.” What they mean is that he is throwing a beat late, waiting for the receiver to look open, which, as Figure 26.3 shows, is too late against good defenses.
