title: Quarterback Play: Progressions, the Pocket, and Off-Script Football
text:
The pocket: climb, slide, escape
The progression assumes a quarterback standing calmly at his launch point. He rarely is. A pocket is a moving thing (the tackles giving ground, the interior bending), and the quarterback has to move inside it without losing his eyes or his feet, so that he can still throw on time from wherever he ends up. Coaches name three moves.


Show the Python
LAT3, WIN3 = (-9.6, 9.6), (-11.8, 2.4)


def still(spots, ax, title, box=False):
    off = [O(k, k, *spots[k], "C" if k == "C" else ("Q" if k == "QB" else "")) for k in OL_KEYS + ["QB"]]
    dfn = [D(k, "DE" if k in ("LE", "RE") else "DT", *spots[k], "E" if k in ("LE", "RE") else "T")
           for k in ("LE", "NT", "DT", "RE")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=LOS, to_go=None)
    fld = p.draw(ax=ax, lateral=LAT3, window=WIN3, title=False)
    clean(ax)
    if box:
        tackle_box(ax, fld, p, -11.8)
    ax.set_title(title, loc="left", fontsize=8.6, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)
    return p, fld


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(6.6, 3.3))
# 1. climb
S = {"LT": (-6.6, -4.7), "LG": (-2.1, -1.8), "C": (-1.9, 0.0), "RG": (-2.1, 1.8), "RT": (-6.6, 4.7),
     "QB": (-8.0, 0.0), "LE": (-8.4, -6.3), "NT": (-0.4, -0.9), "DT": (-0.4, 2.0), "RE": (-8.4, 6.3)}
p, fld = still(S, axes[0], "Climb")
for sg in (-1, 1):
    arrow(fld, p, [(1.0, 5.4 * sg), (-3.0, 7.0 * sg), (-6.4, 7.3 * sg), (-7.6, 6.7 * sg)], color=style.DEFENSE,
          lw=1.2, head=7, z=3, alpha=0.8)
arrow(fld, p, [(-6.9, 0.0), (-4.3, 0.0)], lw=2.2, head=11)
say(fld, p, -5.4, 0.9, "step up", color=GREEN, weight="bold", fs=7.2, ha="left")
say(fld, p, -10.4, 0.0, "ends pushed past him", fs=6.4, color=style.INK_2)
# 2. slide
S2 = dict(S, LT=(-5.8, -4.4), LE=(-6.9, -2.6), RE=(-8.6, 6.4), RT=(-7.0, 5.0))
p, fld = still(S2, axes[1], "Slide")
arrow(fld, p, [(1.0, -5.4), (-2.6, -6.2), (-5.9, -3.2)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.2, head=7, z=3, alpha=0.8)
arrow(fld, p, [(-8.0, 1.0), (-8.0, 3.4)], lw=2.2, head=11)
say(fld, p, -10.2, 2.6, "slide away,\nreset the feet", color=GREEN, weight="bold", fs=6.8)
say(fld, p, -9.6, -4.4, "beaten\ninside", fs=6.4, color=RED)
# 3. escape
S3 = dict(S, C=(-5.6, 0.1), NT=(-4.0, -0.3), LT=(-7.3, -4.7), LE=(-8.6, -3.2), RT=(-8.2, 5.5), RE=(-9.9, 6.4))
p, fld = still(S3, axes[2], "Escape", box=True)
arrow(fld, p, [(1.0, -0.7), (-3.1, -0.4)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.2, head=7, z=3, alpha=0.8)
say(fld, p, -3.6, -5.9, "center driven\nback into him", fs=6.2, color=RED)
arrow(fld, p, [(-8.0, 1.0), (-7.2, 3.4), (-6.0, 5.4), (-4.6, 7.6)], lw=2.2, head=11)
say(fld, p, -3.0, 6.2, "escape lane", color=GREEN, weight="bold", fs=7.0)
say(fld, p, -10.5, -1.2, "tackle box", color=PURPLE, fs=6.4)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.4)
plt.show()








Figure 26.4: Three pocket moves, each the answer to a different rush picture (a frozen moment about two seconds after the snap; receivers not shown). Left, climb: both ends have run their arcs and the tackles have pushed them deeper than the quarterback, while the interior held, so he steps forward into the cup and the rushers finish behind him. Middle, slide: one end has beaten the left tackle inside, so the quarterback shuffles a couple of yards right, away from the pressure, resets his feet and keeps his eyes downfield. Right, escape: a defensive tackle has driven the center straight back into the quarterback’s face, so there is no cup to step up into. The ends decide which way he goes: the left end has come inside, but the right end was pushed past him, so the lane is outside the right tackle. Leaving the tackle box (the shaded area, out to the outside shoulders of the two tackles) also changes the rules for throwing the ball away.





Climb. Climbing the pocket means stepping forward into the pocket, between the interior linemen, as the edge rushers are pushed past. It is the single most important pocket skill, and it follows directly from the geometry of Pass Protection: the tackles give ground on purpose and ride the ends on a wide arc behind the launch point, while the guards and center hold firm in front. A quarterback who stays at his launch point, or worse, drifts backward, walks into the spot where the ends’ arcs finish. One who steps up two yards lets the ends run past behind him, and throws from the cleanest spot on the field. Quarterback coaches drill the idea endlessly: pressure from the outside is answered by moving up, not back.
Slide. When pressure comes from one side (an end who beat the tackle inside, a blitzer through a gap) and the middle is still firm, the quarterback slides a yard or two the other way, keeping his shoulders square to the line of scrimmage and his eyes downfield. A slide buys a half second without ending the play: he is still in the pocket and can still throw to anyone in the progression.
Escape. When the pocket is gone, usually because the interior collapsed and the quarterback has nowhere to step up into, he leaves. The usual escape lane is outside one of the tackles, on the side where an end rushed too far upfield and was pushed past; it opens exactly because the tackle did his job. Escaping changes the play into something else, which is the next section’s subject.
All three moves are made with both hands on the ball. Quarterback coaches drill it as hard as the footwork: a quarterback who carries the ball loose in one hand while he climbs or slides is the one who gets it knocked out from behind by the end he never saw, the strip-sack.
The skill under all three is doing them without looking at the rush. A quarterback who drops his eyes to watch the defensive end has stopped reading the coverage, and a quarterback who has stopped reading the coverage has stopped running the play. Great pocket passers feel the rush (from the color at the edge of their vision, from the sound, from the pressure on a lineman’s back) and move their feet while their eyes stay downfield. Coaches call this pocket presence, and it is one of the few things that clearly separates good quarterbacks from bad ones, as Figure 26.5 shows in motion.


Show the Python
def climb_play():
    p = Play(line() + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q")], four_rush(), los=LOS, to_go=None)
    for k, way in {"LG": [(0.6, -1.8, -1.8), (2.6, -2.1, -1.8)], "C": [(0.6, -1.5, 0.0), (2.6, -1.8, 0.0)],
                   "RG": [(0.6, -1.8, 1.8), (2.6, -2.1, 1.8)]}.items():
        timed(p, k, way, "block")
    for sg, (lt, le) in ((-1, ("LT", "LE")), (1, ("RT", "RE"))):
        timed(p, lt, [(0.7, -2.6, 4.2 * sg), (1.3, -4.6, 5.0 * sg), (2.0, -7.2, 5.1 * sg), (2.6, -9.2, 4.4 * sg)],
              "block")
        timed(p, le, [(0.7, -1.4, 6.2 * sg), (1.3, -4.0, 6.5 * sg), (2.0, -7.2, 6.3 * sg), (2.6, -9.8, 5.3 * sg)],
              "rush")
    timed(p, "NT", [(0.6, -0.5, -1.0), (2.6, -0.9, -1.0)], "rush")
    timed(p, "DT", [(0.6, -0.6, 2.0), (2.6, -1.0, 2.0)], "rush")
    timed(p, "QB", [(0.95, -8.0, 0.0), (1.7, -8.0, 0.0), (2.25, -5.7, 0.2), (2.6, -5.6, 0.2)])
    return p


climb = climb_play()
LAT4, WIN4 = (-11, 11), (-12.4, 3.6)


def draw_climb(ax, t):
    fld = moment(ax, climb, t, LAT4, WIN4, ghosts=[(-8.0, 0.0, "launch\npoint")] if t >= 1.7 else [],
                 trail_keys={"LE", "RE", "LT", "RT", "QB"}, r=0.72)
    if t >= 2.3:
        arrow(fld, climb, [(-4.9, 0.0), (2.8, -0.9)], color=style.BALL, lw=1.3, ls=(0, (2, 1.5)), head=8)
        say(fld, climb, 1.6, -4.6, "ball out", color=style.BALL, weight="bold", fs=7.2)


CT = [0.0, 1.0, 1.8, 2.4]
CN = ["Snap: he will set at his launch\npoint, eight yards deep.",
      "1.0 s: set. The ends run their arcs;\nthe tackles ride them deeper.",
      "1.8 s: the ends are level with him.\nBack is where they are going. Up.",
      "2.4 s: two yards further up, in a clean\ncup, he throws. The ends finish behind."]
play_out(draw_climb, CT, CN, t_end=2.7, aspect=(WIN4[1] - WIN4[0]) / (LAT4[1] - LAT4[0]))





  
  Your browser does not support the video tag.



Figure 26.5: Climbing the pocket, in motion (simulated, the box only). Both ends rush wide around the tackles; the tackles kick back with them and push them deeper than the quarterback’s launch point (the dashed circle), while the guards and center hold their ground against the two tackles. At about 1.8 seconds the ends are level with the quarterback: a drift backward would put him between them. He steps up into the cup instead and throws two yards further upfield, and the ends finish their arcs behind him.










CautionCommon misconception



“A mobile quarterback should get out of the pocket whenever it gets crowded.” Quarterback coaches teach the opposite: don’t leave a pocket that still works. Outside it he has fewer throws (he can see only half the field and has to throw on the run), the rushers who were blocked are now chasing him unblocked, and the sideline is an extra defender. The best scramblers in the league are good at not leaving until the pocket is gone. Then they are devastating, as the next section shows.
Be careful with the obvious statistic here. In FTN’s charting from 2022 to 2025, quarterbacks were sacked on 8.3% of dropbacks once they were out of the pocket, against 6.2% in it,2 which looks like proof that leaving gets you sacked. It isn’t, because quarterbacks mostly leave because the pocket has already failed: from 2023 to 2025, 57% of out-of-pocket dropbacks were charted as pressured, against 24% of the rest. Compare like with like, pressured dropbacks only, and the ones that got outside ended in a sack less often (15% against 26%). Once the pocket has collapsed, escaping is a rescue. What the charting can’t tell you is what leaving a pocket that was still good costs, because nobody charts whether it was still good. That part of the rule rests on coaching judgment, not on this number.

title: Quarterback Play: Progressions, the Pocket, and Off-Script Football
section: Off-script football and the scramble drill
text:
Off-script football and the scramble drill
When the quarterback escapes the pocket, or holds the ball past the play’s last read, the play has gone off script. An off-script play (also called an off-schedule play) is one that has left its design: the called routes have run out, the protection has broken, and what happens next depends on improvisation.
Improvisation sounds like the opposite of coaching. It isn’t. The quarterback improvises, but his receivers follow rules, practiced every week, that tell them what to do when he starts running. Those rules are the scramble drill. Every team has its own version and its own vocabulary, but the core is nearly universal.3


Show the Python
LAT5, WIN5 = (-19, 22), (-10.5, 24.0)
off = line() + [O("QB", "QB", -6.6, 8.6, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -4.6, 2.6, "R"), O("X", "WR", 13.0, -12.0),
                O("H", "WR", 4.0, -1.0), O("Y", "TE", 6.0, 9.0), O("Z", "WR", 18.0, 16.0)]
p = Play(off, [], los=LOS, to_go=None)
fld = p.draw(lateral=LAT5, window=WIN5, title=False)
clean(fld.ax)
called = {"X": [(-0.7, -15.0), (13.0, -15.0), (13.0, -12.0)], "H": [(-1.5, -8.5), (1.0, -7.5), (4.0, -1.0)],
          "Y": [(-1.5, 9.0), (6.5, 9.0), (6.0, 8.6)], "Z": [(-0.7, 15.0), (18.0, 16.0)]}
for k, pts in called.items():
    xy = [XY(fld, p, *q) for q in pts]
    xs, ys = zip(*xy)
    fld.ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.MUTED, lw=1.1, ls=(0, (2, 2)), zorder=2)
    fld.ax.add_patch(Circle(xy[0], 0.55, fc="none", ec=style.MUTED, lw=0.8, zorder=2))
arrow(fld, p, [(-8.0, 0.0), (-7.6, 4.0), (-6.6, 8.6)], color=GREEN, lw=1.4, ls=(0, (3, 2)), head=9)
RULES = {"Y": ([(6.0, 9.0), (11.0, 10.0), (16.5, 11.0)], 1, (16.6, 13.3)),
         "Z": ([(18.0, 16.0), (14.0, 17.4), (10.5, 18.4)], 2, (8.4, 18.8)),
         "H": ([(4.0, -1.0), (4.8, 3.0), (5.2, 6.0)], 3, (2.8, 5.6)),
         "X": ([(13.0, -12.0), (17.0, -6.0), (20.0, 0.5)], 4, (21.6, 2.6)),

for k, (pts, n, at) in RULES.items():
    arrow(fld, p, pts, color=GREEN, lw=2.0, head=11)
    badge(fld.ax, *XY(fld, p, *at), n, "now", fs=8)
say(fld, p, 11.8, -4.6, "1  short goes deep\n2  deep comes back\n3  go where he goes\n4  backside: come across deep\n"
    "5  back: leak out, short", fs=7.4, ha="left", color=style.INK)
say(fld, p, -9.0, 8.6, "he escapes right", color=GREEN, fs=7.0, weight="bold")
plt.show()








Figure 26.6: The scramble drill’s core rules, drawn at the moment the quarterback escapes to his right (offense only; grey dashes are the routes as called, green arrows what each receiver does once the quarterback leaves the pocket). (1) Short goes deep: Y, sitting on a short hitch route, takes off up the field. (2) Deep comes back: Z, who was running deep down the sideline, turns and works back toward the line, along the sideline on the quarterback’s side. (3) Go where he goes: H, on a shallow crossing route, keeps crossing toward the scramble side, underneath. (4) Backside receivers come across deep: X, on the far side, works back across the field behind the coverage. (5) The back, who stayed in to block, leaks out to the scramble side, just past the line, as the last outlet. The result is five receivers at five depths, all on or toward the quarterback’s side and in his line of sight. The linemen stay on their men. Rules differ from team to team; these are the common core.





Each rule has a reason.

Short goes deep, deep comes back. Receivers spread out vertically so the quarterback has a choice of depths, and so that two receivers never end up in the same spot dragging their defenders with them. The deep receiver comes back because a quarterback throwing on the run cannot make a 40-yard throw accurately; the short receiver goes deep because the defenders near him have all turned to chase the quarterback, and the space behind them is empty. “Short” and “deep” are measured against the linebackers: in front of them is short, behind them is deep.
Go where he goes. A quarterback running to his right can throw easily to his right and downfield, and only with difficulty back across his body to the left. (Throwing across your body on the run is one of the most dangerous throws in football, because the ball floats back toward the middle of the field where the defenders are.) So receivers work toward his side.
Backside receivers come across, deep. A receiver on the far side can’t stand still and wait; he runs back across the field behind the coverage, where defenders who have turned to chase the quarterback have left the deep middle.
The back leaks out; the linemen stay home. A back who stayed in to block releases toward the scramble side, a yard or two past the line, as the last, safest throw. The linemen keep blocking whoever they have and do not drift downfield: if the quarterback then throws, a lineman more than a yard beyond the line is ineligible downfield, a foul that wipes out the completion (RPOs).4
Get into his line of sight and keep moving. A receiver the quarterback can’t see is not an option. Receivers find grass on a different level from their teammates and stay in his vision, and if he crosses the line of scrimmage to run, they stop running routes and start blocking. Nobody calls out “scramble”: the cue is the clock. A receiver who reaches the end of his route without the ball turns to find the quarterback, and if he is no longer where the drop put him, the drill is on.

When two rules seem to apply, settle it by side first. A receiver on the far side from the scramble comes across: deep if he was deep, and a crosser keeps crossing at his depth, toward the quarterback. On the scramble side, short goes deep and deep comes back. Teams word this differently, but that order keeps the receivers on different levels, which is the whole point.
Where does the quarterback look? The rules hand him receivers at four or five depths; he can’t look at all of them. The throws he can make while moving come first: the receiver working back toward him along his sideline, and the crosser running with him. Both are short, firm throws toward the side he is running to. The deep receivers are the big play, and he takes that shot when he has room to stop, set his feet and throw; a quarterback running flat out usually can’t throw 30 yards accurately. Escaping to his throwing-hand side makes all of this easier. A right-handed quarterback rolling left has to turn his hips and square his shoulders back to the target before he can throw at all, so for him the come-back routes on that side matter even more.
Throw or run? Once he is out of the pocket he has a third choice, and it is the best-valued ending in the data, as Figure 26.10 will show. The rule of thumb is simple. As long as he is behind the line, his eyes stay downfield and every receiver is still an option. When the receivers are covered and there is open grass in front of him, ideally to the line to gain, he runs. Once he crosses the line of scrimmage the passing play is over, because a forward pass thrown from beyond the line is illegal.5 Running too early gives up the throws; running too late, after the defenders have rallied, gives up the grass.
Why does any of this work? Because the defense was built for the play the offense called, and that play is over. Against man coverage, where each defender follows one receiver, defenders are running with their backs to the quarterback; when a receiver stops and reverses, his defender has to stop, turn and find him, and he is a step behind. Against zone coverage, where each defender guards an area, defenders have dropped to spots that were chosen for the original routes, and they have to leave those spots to chase receivers who are now somewhere else, opening the areas they were guarding.
The defense has rules for this too, and the scramble drill works best against a defense that breaks them. Up front the rushers keep their rush lanes and the ends keep contain, not rushing past the quarterback’s depth, which is exactly the mistake that opens the escape lane in Figure 26.4. Some defenses assign a spy, a defender who mirrors the quarterback and tackles him if he runs. And in zone, once the quarterback leaves the pocket, coverage players are taught to stop guarding grass and lock onto the nearest receiver (coaches call it “plastering”). A defense that does all of this leaves the quarterback little; much of the off-script value in the next chart comes against defenses that don’t.


Show the Python
def scramble_play():
    off = line() + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, 1.6, "R"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -15.0),
                    O("H", "WR", -1.5, -8.5), O("Y", "TE", -1.5, 8.5), O("Z", "WR", -0.7, 15.0)]
    dfn = four_rush() + [D("MIKE", "MIKE", 6.0, 0.5, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -1.5, "W"),
                         D("NB", "NB", 4.5, -8.5, "$"), D("SS", "SS", 5.0, 9.6, "SS"),
                         D("LCB", "CB", 6.0, -15.0, "C"), D("RCB", "CB", 6.0, 15.0, "C"),
                         D("FS", "FS", 13.0, 0.5, "FS")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=LOS, to_go=TOGO)
    pass_set(p, depths=(-2.6, -1.7, -1.4, -1.7, -2.6))
    timed(p, "LT", [(1.4, -4.2, -4.6), (2.2, -5.2, -4.4)], "block")
    timed(p, "LE", [(0.8, -1.7, -5.6), (1.5, -4.6, -5.0), (2.1, -7.4, -2.2), (2.6, -8.6, 0.6), (3.3, -7.6, 5.4),
                    (3.9, -7.0, 8.0)], "rush")
    timed(p, "NT", [(0.8, -0.6, -0.9)], "rush")
    timed(p, "DT", [(0.8, -0.7, 2.0)], "rush")
    timed(p, "RE", [(0.8, -1.7, 4.8), (1.6, -5.8, 5.6), (2.2, -9.6, 5.6), (2.8, -11.0, 4.8), (3.6, -9.6, 8.8)], "rush")
    timed(p, "RT", [(1.6, -5.0, 4.5), (2.2, -8.0, 4.4)], "block")
    timed(p, "RB", [(0.5, -5.2, 2.4), (2.2, -5.2, 2.2), (2.8, -5.2, 2.0), (3.6, -3.4, 5.6), (4.6, -2.6, 7.0)],
          "block")                                     # blocks, then leaks out to the scramble side
    timed(p, "QB", [(0.95, -8.0, 0.0), (1.9, -8.0, 0.0), (2.5, -7.5, 3.8), (3.3, -6.1, 9.4), (3.6, -5.7, 10.6),
                    (4.3, -5.2, 12.2)])
    # routes as called, then the scramble rules from about 2.4 s
    timed(p, "X", [(1.7, 12.0, -15.0), (2.2, 12.2, -12.0), (3.3, 16.0, -6.5), (4.6, 19.5, 2.0)], "route")
    timed(p, "H", [(0.6, 1.0, -7.5), (2.3, 3.6, 1.0), (3.4, 4.6, 6.0), (4.6, 5.2, 9.0)], "route")
    timed(p, "Y", [(1.1, 6.5, 8.5), (1.3, 6.0, 8.1), (2.4, 6.0, 8.1), (3.3, 11.5, 9.6), (4.6, 18.0, 10.8)], "route")
    timed(p, "Z", [(2.5, 18.0, 15.6), (2.75, 17.6, 16.2), (3.4, 14.0, 17.6), (4.6, 10.6, 19.0)], "route")
    p.pass_to("Z", t=3.6)
    # man coverage: each defender trails his receiver; the corner on Z keeps running when Z stops
    timed(p, "LCB", [(1.7, 11.0, -14.4), (2.3, 11.6, -12.6), (3.3, 14.6, -8.0), (4.6, 18.0, 0.0)], "path")
    timed(p, "NB", [(0.7, 3.0, -7.6), (2.3, 3.4, -2.6), (3.4, 3.6, 2.4), (4.6, 4.0, 5.6)], "path")
    timed(p, "SS", [(1.3, 7.2, 10.4), (2.5, 7.2, 10.9), (3.4, 10.4, 11.8), (4.6, 16.0, 12.8)], "path")
    timed(p, "RCB", [(2.5, 16.6, 14.0), (2.95, 19.6, 14.3), (3.4, 18.6, 15.6), (4.6, 13.8, 17.4)], "path")
    timed(p, "MIKE", [(1.2, 8.0, 1.0), (2.6, 8.5, 3.0), (3.6, 8.8, 5.0), (4.6, 9.5, 6.6)], "path")
    timed(p, "WILL", [(1.0, 4.0, 0.6), (2.6, 1.0, 3.6), (3.6, 0.4, 7.2), (4.6, 0.2, 9.6)], "path")   # R stays in: the Will mirrors Q
    timed(p, "FS", [(1.5, 14.0, 2.0), (2.6, 15.5, 4.0), (3.6, 17.5, 6.0), (4.6, 19.0, 6.8)], "path")
    return p


scr = scramble_play()
SCR_CATCH = catch_time(scr)
LAT6, WIN6 = (-17.0, 22.0), (-12.6, 23.0)


def draw_scramble(ax, t):
    ring = {"LE": RED} if 1.2 <= t < 2.4 else ({"Z": GREEN} if t >= 3.5 else {})
    fld = moment(ax, scr, t, LAT6, WIN6, rings=ring, r=1.1,
                 plan={"X": [(-0.7, -15.0), (12.0, -15.0), (12.2, -12.0)], "H": [(-1.5, -8.5), (1.0, -7.5), (3.6, 1.0)],
                       "Y": [(-1.5, 8.5), (6.5, 8.5), (6.0, 8.1)], "Z": [(-0.7, 15.0), (21.0, 15.7)]})
    if t >= 2.4:
        eyes(fld, scr, t, "Z" if t >= 3.3 else "Y")


ST = [1.6, 2.6, 3.6, round(SCR_CATCH, 1)]
SN = ["Called: dig, shallow cross, hitch route,\ngo. The left end beats the left tackle.",
      "He escapes right. Every receiver\nswitches to his scramble rule.",
      "Z comes back, Y goes deep, H keeps\ncrossing, X comes across. Throw.",
      "Z catches it on the sideline; his\ncorner is still turning around."]
play_out(draw_scramble, ST, SN, t_end=SCR_CATCH + 0.4, aspect=(WIN6[1] - WIN6[0]) / (LAT6[1] - LAT6[0]))





  
  Your browser does not support the video tag.



Figure 26.7: The scramble drill in motion (simulated). The call is a dig by X, a shallow cross by H, a hitch route by Y and a go by Z, against man coverage with a free safety deep and a linebacker in the middle; the defense rushes four. The back, R, stays in to block, so the Will, whose man he was, has nobody to cover and mirrors the quarterback instead. Panel 1: the left end beats the left tackle (red ring). Panel 2: the quarterback escapes to his right and the receivers switch to their scramble rules. Panel 3: Z has stopped his go route and is working back down the sideline, Y has turned up the field, H keeps crossing, X comes back across deep; the quarterback throws on the run to the come-back receiver, the easy throw toward the sideline he is running at. Panel 4: Z (green ring) catches it near the sideline. His cornerback, who was running deep with his back to the quarterback, is still turning around.










ImportantWhy it exists



What the scramble drill solves. A pass play is designed to finish in under three seconds. When it doesn’t, eleven offensive players are suddenly without instructions, and without rules each receiver would do something different: some keep running their routes into the sideline, some stop, two drift into the same spot. The scramble drill turns the broken play into a second, pre-planned play, so the quarterback’s improvisation lands on receivers who are where he expects them.
What it gives up. Nothing in the design, but plenty in the result: a play that goes off script is, on average, a worse play. It is a rescue, not a strategy, and the offense would usually rather the first play had worked. The exceptions are a handful of quarterbacks for whom the rescue is a weapon, and you can find them in the data.



Off-script value: who gains by leaving the pocket?
FTN charts whether the quarterback was outside the pocket on each dropback, whether by design (a rollout) or by escape; the flag does not say which. From 2022 to 2025 that happened on 18% of NFL dropbacks. On average those plays were worth +0.011 EPA (expected points added) per play, against +0.049 in the pocket. That average hides a split. About 48% of out-of-pocket dropbacks ended in a quarterback run or a scramble-drill throw, and those were worth a lot; another 22% ended in a throwaway, a sack or an interception, and those cost even more. Off script is a high-variance place: for the league as a whole it nets out slightly worse than the pocket, but for a few quarterbacks it is clearly better.


Show the Python
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.3))
lo, hi = -0.25, 0.36
ax.plot([lo, hi], [lo, hi], color=style.INK_2, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (4, 2)), zorder=1)
ax.text(-0.22, 0.2, "better outside the pocket\n(above the diagonal)", fontsize=7.2, color=style.INK_2, ha="left")
ax.text(0.34, -0.17, "better inside the pocket\n(below the diagonal)", fontsize=7.2, color=style.INK_2, ha="right")

ax.axvline(EPA_IN, color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.8)

ax.scatter(OQ.loc[~up, "epa_in"], OQ.loc[~up, "epa_out"], s=24, color=style.GRID, edgecolor=style.MUTED, lw=0.5,

ax.text(-0.245, EPA_OUT + 0.008, "league, out of pocket", fontsize=6.6, color=style.MUTED)
ax.set_xlim(lo, hi)
ax.set_ylim(lo, hi)
ax.set_xlabel("EPA per dropback in the pocket", fontsize=8.5)
ax.set_ylabel("EPA per dropback out of the pocket", fontsize=8.5)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=7.5)
fig.tight_layout()
# name every quarterback above the diagonal, plus three below it that the text discusses
# (the four in the tight cluster near the origin get hand-placed labels with leader lines)
HAND = {"D.Jones": (-0.075, 0.09, "D. Jones"), "G.Smith": (-0.085, 0.045, "G. Smith"),
        "A.Rodgers": (0.0, -0.045, "Rodgers"), "K.Murray": (0.09, 0.115, "Murray")}
for nm, (tx, ty, lab) in HAND.items():
    r_ = OQ[OQ.name == nm].iloc[0]
    ax.annotate(lab, (r_.epa_in, r_.epa_out), xytext=(tx, ty), textcoords="data", fontsize=7.0, color=style.INK,
                ha="center", va="center", arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=style.MUTED, lw=0.6, shrinkB=3))
lab_rows = OQ[(up | OQ.name.isin(["J.Hurts", "B.Purdy", "J.Goff"])) & ~OQ.name.isin(list(HAND))]
lab_rows = lab_rows.sort_values("epa_out", ascending=False)
place_labels(ax, lab_rows.epa_in.to_numpy(), lab_rows.epa_out.to_numpy(),
             [n.split(".")[-1] for n in lab_rows.name], fs=7.0)
plt.show()








Figure 26.8: In the pocket versus out of it: every quarterback with at least 800 dropbacks and 150 out-of-pocket dropbacks in the 2022-2025 regular seasons. Horizontal: EPA per dropback (sacks and scrambles included) while in the pocket; vertical: EPA per dropback once outside it, by escape or by design. Points above the dashed diagonal were better outside the pocket than in it, which few quarterbacks were; all of them are named (Rodgers and Murray sit almost exactly on the line), along with three notable quarterbacks below it. Josh Allen and Patrick Mahomes sit highest: their off-script plays were worth more than most quarterbacks’ on-script ones. Data: FTN charting and nflverse play-by-play via nflreadpy.





Only 11 of the 32 quarterbacks in Figure 26.8 were better outside the pocket than in it, and two of those were level within a hundredth of a point. At the top are the two players the sport thinks of first when it thinks of off-script football: Josh Allen (+0.31 EPA per dropback outside the pocket, +0.20 in it) and Patrick Mahomes (+0.30 and +0.17). Notice what kind of skill that is. Both can run, but the value isn’t mainly in the running: it is in throwing accurately on the move, to receivers who know the scramble drill, while the defense is scrambling too. And notice who is not above the line. Jalen Hurts, one of the most dangerous running quarterbacks of the era, sits well below it (-0.01 outside, +0.19 in). Much of his running comes on designed runs and sneaks, which are not dropbacks and so are not in this chart; running ability and off-script passing are different skills.
Read the chart with two cautions. First, “out of the pocket” includes designed rollouts and bootlegs (Play-Action, Bootlegs and Screens), which are good plays for everyone, so a quarterback whose offense calls many of them looks better out there for reasons that have nothing to do with improvisation. Second, it is four seasons of a few hundred plays per quarterback: the order in the middle of the pack is mostly noise, and only the ends of the chart are worth arguing about.


A short history: from Tarkenton to Mahomes
The scramble entered the NFL’s vocabulary with Fran Tarkenton, a preacher’s son from Athens, Georgia, who quarterbacked the expansion Minnesota Vikings from their first game in 1961. Behind a thin, new offensive line, he ran around behind it, often for long stretches, until someone came open. Coaches of his era, his own first head coach Norm Van Brocklin among them, thought scrambling undisciplined (the feud with Van Brocklin ended with Tarkenton demanding a trade in 1967); Tarkenton’s answer, preserved on his Hall of Fame page, was that “I scramble because I’m good at it, because I can twist and dodge those big pass rushers better than most guys, and we get a lot of touchdowns that way.” He retired in 1978 holding the career records for completions, passing yards and touchdown passes.6
For decades after that the pocket passer was the ideal: the quarterbacks who won the most, from Joe Montana to Peyton Manning and Tom Brady, did their damage on schedule, and the offenses built around them, timed to the drop, treated a scramble as a play that had failed. But the off-script line never died. John Elway passed for 3,000 yards and ran for 200 in seven straight seasons and built a career on late comebacks; Steve Young retired with 43 rushing touchdowns, then the second-most by any quarterback.7 Teams with quarterbacks like them practiced what to do when the play broke.
What changed in the last decade is scale. College football filled with spread offenses and athletic quarterbacks who had been improvising since high school, and NFL offenses stopped treating the scramble drill as an emergency procedure and started repping it weekly and designing around it. The quarterbacks who came out of that world (Mahomes, Allen, Lamar Jackson, Jalen Hurts) made off-script play part of the plan rather than an emergency.

section: Getting rid of it: the throwaway
text:
Getting rid of it: the throwaway
The last of the quarterback’s options when nothing is open is the least glamorous and among the most valuable. A throwaway is a pass he deliberately throws where nobody can catch it, usually out of bounds or well over a covered receiver’s head, to avoid a sack or an interception. He gives up the down but keeps the yards. NFL quarterbacks threw the ball away on 3.5% of dropbacks from 2022 to 2025.
Why is that a skill and not a surrender? Look at what the alternatives cost. In the same seasons, the average throwaway was worth -0.78 EPA (an incompletion, a lost down), the average sack -1.77 (a lost down and six or seven yards), and the average interception -4.42. A quarterback who turns two sacks a game into throwaways gains about 2 points a game for his team, without completing a pass.
There is a catch, and it is a rule. Intentional grounding is a foul for throwing the ball away to avoid a sack when the pass isn’t in the direction and vicinity of an eligible receiver; it costs a loss of down and ten yards (or loss of down at the spot of the pass, if that is worse), and a safety if the quarterback throws it from his own end zone. The rule changes once the quarterback leaves the tackle box, the area between where the two offensive tackles lined up: outside it, any pass that lands at or beyond the line of scrimmage (including out of bounds past it) is legal, receiver or no receiver.8 Officiating, Replay, and the Rules of the Ball covers the full rule; here is what it means for the quarterback.


Show the Python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 3.5))
# left: inside the box
off = line() + [O("QB", "QB", -7.6, 0.4, "Q"), O("Y", "TE", 6.0, 5.0)]
dfn = [D("LE", "DE", -6.6, -1.6, "E"), D("DT", "DT", -5.8, 1.8, "T"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 6.4, 6.4, "M")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=LOS, to_go=None)
fld = p.draw(ax=axes[0], lateral=(-15.5, 15.5), window=(-12.5, 14.0), title=False)
clean(axes[0])
tackle_box(axes[0], fld, p, -12.5)
arrow(fld, p, [(-7.6, 0.4), (2.0, 4.6), (10.0, 6.4)], color=GREEN, lw=1.6, ls=(0, (3, 2)), head=10)
arrow(fld, p, [(-7.6, 0.4), (0.0, -5.0), (6.0, -9.6)], color=RED, lw=1.6, ls=(0, (3, 2)), head=10)
say(fld, p, 11.6, 4.0, "legal: thrown\nnear Y", color=GREEN, fs=7.0, weight="bold")
say(fld, p, 8.4, -7.6, "grounding:\nnobody there", color=RED, fs=7.0, weight="bold")
say(fld, p, -11.0, 0.0, "tackle box", color=PURPLE, fs=6.6)
axes[0].set_title("Inside the tackle box", loc="left", fontsize=8.6, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)
# right: outside the box, ball on the right hash
off = line() + [O("QB", "QB", -6.0, 11.0, "Q"), O("Z", "WR", 9.0, 19.0)]
dfn = [D("RE", "DE", -7.4, 8.0, "E"), D("RCB", "CB", 9.6, 20.4, "C")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=LOS, ball_y="right", to_go=None)
fld = p.draw(ax=axes[1], lateral=(-4.5, 26.5), window=(-12.5, 14.0), title=False)
clean(axes[1])
tackle_box(axes[1], fld, p, -12.5)
arrow(fld, p, [(-6.0, 11.0), (2.0, 19.0), (5.0, 25.4)], color=GREEN, lw=1.6, ls=(0, (3, 2)), head=10)
arrow(fld, p, [(-6.0, 11.0), (-4.6, 17.0), (-3.4, 22.6)], color=RED, lw=1.6, ls=(0, (3, 2)), head=10)
say(fld, p, 6.4, 11.4, "legal: out of bounds\npast the line", color=GREEN, fs=7.0, weight="bold")
say(fld, p, -9.4, 15.6, "grounding: lands\nshort of the line", color=RED, fs=7.0, weight="bold")
say(fld, p, 2.4, 10.2, "line of scrimmage", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fs=6.4)
say(fld, p, -11.0, 0.0, "tackle box", color=PURPLE, fs=6.6)
xs_, ys_ = XY(fld, p, -4.0, 25.0)
axes[1].text(xs_, ys_, "out of bounds", rotation=90, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.0, color=style.INK_2)
axes[1].set_title("Outside the tackle box", loc="left", fontsize=8.6, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 26.9: Where a throwaway is legal. Left: inside the tackle box (shaded), a quarterback under pressure must throw in the direction and vicinity of an eligible receiver; throwing it over Y’s head, near him, is a legal throwaway (green), while throwing it to an empty part of the field is intentional grounding (red). Right: once he is outside the tackle box, the ball only has to land at or beyond the line of scrimmage, so throwing it out of bounds past the line is legal (green), but a throw that lands short of the line, near nobody, is still grounding (red). The ball is on the right hash, so the right sideline is close.





The rule rewards exactly the skills this chapter has been describing. A quarterback who climbs and slides inside the pocket can always find a covered receiver to throw near; a quarterback who escapes the pocket earns the right to throw it into the stands. The quarterback who gets in trouble is the one who stays in the box with nobody near him, panics, and flings it at the turf, or who, outside the box, tries to throw it away on the run and doesn’t get it back to the line.
The most famous grounding call of recent decades shows how expensive the panic is. On the New England Patriots’ first offensive play of Super Bowl XLVI, against the New York Giants in February 2012, Tom Brady dropped back from his own 6-yard line with Justin Tuck bearing down on him, and threw deep down the middle to nobody. The flag came out; Brady had thrown it from his own end zone, so the grounding penalty was a safety, and the Giants, who had punted on their own opening drive, led 2-0. They won by four.9

section: The checkdown: risk management, not cowardice
text:
The checkdown: risk management, not cowardice
The last read in most progressions is the checkdown: a short, safe throw, usually to a running back or tight end a few yards past the line, underneath all the coverage. It is the quarterback giving up on the big play to take a small, nearly certain one. Fans boo it. Coaches mostly don’t, and the data says why.


Show the Python
E = END.sort_values("epa", ascending=True)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.4))
ys = np.arange(len(E))
cols = [style.SERIES[0] if v >= 0 else style.SERIES[7] for v in E.epa]
cols = [style.MUTED if n.startswith("Designed") else c for n, c in zip(E.index, cols)]
ax.barh(ys, E.epa, color=cols, height=0.62)
for y, (n, r_) in zip(ys, E.iterrows()):
    x = r_.epa
    lab = f"{x:+.2f}   ({r_.share:.1%} of dropbacks)"
    if x < -2.5:      # long bar: label inside it
        ax.text(x + 0.1, y, lab, va="center", ha="left", fontsize=6.9, color="white", fontweight="bold")
    else:
        ax.text(x + (0.06 if x >= 0 else -0.06), y, lab, va="center", ha="left" if x >= 0 else "right",
                fontsize=6.9, color=style.INK)
ax.set_yticks(ys, E.index, fontsize=7.4)
ax.axvline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=1)
ax.set_xlim(-4.7, 2.1)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=7.2)
ax.set_xlabel("EPA per dropback", fontsize=7.8)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 26.10: How dropbacks end, and what each ending is worth: every regular-season dropback from 2022 to 2025, grouped by FTN’s charting of where the ball went (best average outcome at the top, worst at the bottom; labels give the share of all dropbacks). A quarterback scramble tops the list partly by selection: quarterbacks run when the coverage has left open grass, and when it hasn’t, the play lands in the throwaway, sack or interception rows instead. That is why off-script football can look great here and still cost value on average. Among throws, the first read is worth the most and each step down the progression gives up value; the checkdown is worth about nothing on average, which is a great deal better than the three endings below it. A throwaway costs a down, a sack a down and yards, an interception the ball. Interceptions and throwaways are counted on their own, whichever read they were aimed at, so the read rows are completions and incompletions only. Data: FTN charting and nflverse play-by-play via nflreadpy.





Read Figure 26.10 from the middle out. A checkdown is worth, on average, +0.03 EPA: essentially nothing. It is caught 82% of the time, thrown about 0.6 yards past the line, and gains most of what it gains after the catch (6.3 yards on average). That looks like a wasted play only if you compare it to the first read. The real comparison is to what happens to a quarterback who doesn’t check the ball down when the first reads are covered: he holds it, and the next three bars are waiting. The checkdown is the cheapest way to end a play that has failed.
That is what risk management means at quarterback. Each read in the progression has an expected value and a risk of disaster, and the checkdown is the read with the least of both. A quarterback who takes it at the right moment gives up a little upside to cut off the tail of sacks and interceptions, and over a season that tail decides games.
The right moment depends on the situation, and the third-down numbers show how much (2022–2025, share of plays that gained the first down, and EPA):



Third down, and the ball goes…
Converted
EPA per play




7+ yards to go: to the first read
43%
–


7+ yards to go: checked down
24%
-0.20


7+ yards to go: sacked
0%
-1.79


3 or fewer to go: checked down
58%
–



On third-and-long, a checkdown usually means a punt. Even so it beats the sack: when the ball is going to be punted anyway, the yards the back gains after the catch still flip a little field position, while a sack can push a field goal out of range. On third-and-short the same throw is a good bet. Good quarterbacks know the down and distance on every snap and adjust: checkdowns early, when four yards on first down keeps the offense on schedule, patience on third-and-long, when only a throw past the sticks will do.






CautionCommon misconception



“Checking it down is what scared quarterbacks do.” Every great quarterback checks the ball down, often, and good offenses design their checkdowns to gain yards: a back who catches it in space with one linebacker to beat. The difference between a good checkdown and a bad one is when: a checkdown after the deeper reads were honestly covered is a good decision; a checkdown on the first beat of a play, before the deep reads had time to open, is a quarterback who has stopped trusting his protection. Watch where his eyes were before he threw it.

section: Measuring a quarterback: time to throw, aDOT, CPOE and EPA
text:
Measuring a quarterback: time to throw, aDOT, CPOE and EPA
You can now describe a quarterback’s process. The data can describe his style and his results, and four numbers do most of the work.

Time to throw (seconds from the snap to the release) says how long he holds the ball: quick and decisive, or patient and hunting.
aDOT (average depth of target) says how far downfield he aims: underneath and safe, or deep and aggressive.
CPOE says how accurate he is, after allowing for how hard his throws were.
EPA per dropback says what it all adds up to: the points his dropbacks added, sacks, scrambles and turnovers included.

The first two describe style, and neither is good or bad on its own; the last two describe results. All four are public: the Next Gen Stats passing leaderboard (https://nextgenstats.nfl.com/stats/passing) has time to throw, air yards and its own CPOE for every starter, and rbsdm.com (https://rbsdm.com/stats/), built on the same nflverse data as this chapter, has EPA per dropback and CPOE, so you can profile this Sunday’s quarterback before kickoff. The one that needs explaining is CPOE.

CPOE: completion percentage, corrected for difficulty
Completion percentage is the oldest quarterback number and one of the most misleading, because it rewards easy throws. A quarterback who checks the ball down all day completes 75% of his passes; one who throws deep outs and posts completes 60% and may be the better passer. CPOE, or completion percentage over expected, fixes this by comparing each throw with a model’s estimate of how often a throw like it is completed. The nflverse model behind the numbers here knows each throw’s depth, which part of the field it went to, the down and distance, and whether the quarterback was hit as he threw;10 the Next Gen Stats version also knows, from tracking data, how far the receiver was from the nearest defender.11 A deep out to the sideline might have an expected completion rate of 45%; a checkdown to the flat, 85%. Complete the deep out and you gain 55 percentage points over expected; drop the checkdown and you lose 85. Average those differences over a season and you have CPOE.


Show the Python
C = Q.sort_values("cpoe")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 0.17 * len(C) + 0.9))
ys = np.arange(len(C))
for y, (_, r_) in zip(ys, C.iterrows()):
    col = style.SERIES[0] if r_.cpoe >= 0 else style.SERIES[7]
    ax.plot([100 * r_.xcomp, 100 * r_.comp], [y, y], color=col, lw=2.2, alpha=0.7, solid_capstyle="round")
    ax.plot([100 * r_.xcomp], [y], "o", ms=5, mfc=style.SURFACE, mec=style.INK_2, mew=1.0)
    ax.plot([100 * r_.comp], [y], "o", ms=5, color=col, mec="white", mew=0.6)
    ax.text(1.06, y, f"{r_.cpoe:+.1f}", va="center", ha="right", fontsize=6.6, color=col,
            transform=ax.get_yaxis_transform(), clip_on=False)
ax.set_yticks(ys, [f"{r_.label} ({'LAR' if r_.team == 'LA' else r_.team})" for _, r_ in C.iterrows()], fontsize=6.6)
lo_x = 5 * np.floor(100 * min(C.comp.min(), C.xcomp.min()) / 5) - 1
hi_x = 5 * np.ceil(100 * max(C.comp.max(), C.xcomp.max()) / 5) + 1
ax.set_xlim(lo_x, hi_x)
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0f}%"))
ax.set_xlabel("completion % (hollow: expected, filled: actual)", fontsize=7.8)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=7.2)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.text(1.06, len(C) - 0.1, "CPOE", ha="right", va="bottom", fontsize=7, color=style.INK_2, fontweight="bold",
        transform=ax.get_yaxis_transform(), clip_on=False)
ax.set_ylim(-0.8, len(C) + 0.4)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 26.11: Completion percentage and what was expected, 2025 regular season (quarterbacks with at least 300 dropbacks). Each row is a quarterback: the hollow circle is the completion rate the nflverse model expected from his throws, the filled circle is what he actually completed, and the line between them is his CPOE, the number on the right. Rows are sorted by CPOE. Two quarterbacks with the same completion percentage can be far apart once difficulty is counted: find Brock Purdy and Jared Goff, whose filled circles sit at almost the same spot, about 72%, and whose hollow circles do not. Data: nflverse play-by-play (cp and complete_pass) via nflreadpy.





In 2025 the spread was enormous: Drake Maye completed +10.8 percentage points over expectation, and Michael Penix -3.6. Purdy and Goff show why the correction matters: Purdy completed 72.4% of his passes and Goff 72.0%, but Purdy’s throws were expected to be completed only 65% of the time and Goff’s 70%, so Purdy’s CPOE was +7.2 and Goff’s +1.8. Goff threw shorter (an aDOT of 6.5 yards to Purdy’s 7.6).
CPOE is the best single public measure of accuracy, and it is steadier from season to season than completion percentage, but read it with three cautions. It credits the quarterback for everything that is not in the model: a receiver who makes a great catch, or a scheme that gets receivers wide open, raises it. It says nothing about where the ball went, only whether it was caught: a quarterback who throws safely and accurately to covered checkdowns can post a fine CPOE and a poor offense. And check what each version does with throwaways. They count as incompletions in plain completion percentage, which punishes a smart habit, but the nflverse model leaves most of them out, because only 18% of charted throwaways get a completion probability.






CautionCommon misconception



“Completion percentage measures accuracy.” It measures accuracy and the difficulty of the throws a quarterback chooses, mixed together, and difficulty dominates. A conservative passer and an aggressive one can be equally accurate and be ten points apart in completion percentage. If you want accuracy, look at CPOE; if you want to know how aggressive he is, look at aDOT; if you want to know whether it worked, look at EPA.




Whose sack is it?
Sacks are charged to the quarterback’s line in the box score, but a good share of them belong to him. FTN’s charters, who watch every sack on video, marked 40% of the sacks from 2022 to 2025 as the quarterback’s fault: held the ball too long, drifted into the rush, missed the hot throw. A cleaner number separates the line’s share from his: pressure-to-sack rate, the share of the dropbacks on which he was pressured that ended in a sack. The line decides how often he is pressured; what happens next is mostly him. From 2023 to 2025 pressured quarterbacks were sacked 22% of the time, but among those with 200 or more pressured dropbacks the rate ran from 13% (Nix) to 30% (Levis).12 That spread is pocket presence, measured. The Pass Rush takes up why pressure is the steadier number and the sack the noisier one.


The style map
Put time to throw and aDOT on two axes and color each quarterback by his EPA per dropback, and quarterback styles separate into families.


Show the Python
from matplotlib.colors import TwoSlopeNorm, LinearSegmentedColormap

cmap = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("epa", [style.SERIES[7], "#f0efec", style.SERIES[0]])
norm = TwoSlopeNorm(vmin=-0.2, vcenter=0.0, vmax=0.3)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.9))
sc = ax.scatter(Q.avg_time_to_throw, Q.adot, c=Q.epa, cmap=cmap, norm=norm, s=46, edgecolor=style.INK_2, lw=0.5,
                zorder=3)
mx, my = Q.avg_time_to_throw.mean(), Q.adot.mean()
ax.axvline(mx, color=style.BASELINE, lw=1, ls=(0, (4, 2)), zorder=1)
ax.axhline(my, color=style.BASELINE, lw=1, ls=(0, (4, 2)), zorder=1)
x0, x1 = Q.avg_time_to_throw.min() - 0.08, Q.avg_time_to_throw.max() + 0.1
y0, y1 = Q.adot.min() - 0.5, Q.adot.max() + 0.6
ax.set_xlim(x0, x1)
ax.set_ylim(y0, y1)
corner = dict(fontsize=7.6, color=style.MUTED, fontweight="bold")
ax.text(x0 + 0.02, y1 - 0.12, "quick and deep:\nthe rhythm shooter", va="top", ha="left", **corner)
ax.text(x1 - 0.02, y1 - 0.12, "holds it and hunts deep:\nthe aggressive creator", va="top", ha="right", **corner)
ax.text(x0 + 0.02, y0 + 0.12, "quick and short:\nthe distributor", va="bottom", ha="left", **corner)
ax.text(x1 - 0.02, y0 + 0.12, "holds it, throws short:\nthe patient (or stuck) passer", va="bottom", ha="right",
        **corner)
# labels: greedy placement around each point, avoiding earlier labels and the points
fig.canvas.draw()
ren = fig.canvas.get_renderer()
placed = []
pts_disp = ax.transData.transform(np.column_stack([Q.avg_time_to_throw, Q.adot]))
OFFS = [(5, 3), (5, -9), (-5, 3), (-5, -9), (6, -3), (-6, -3), (0, 6), (0, -12), (9, 8), (-9, 8), (9, -13), (-9, -13)]
for i, (_, r_) in enumerate(Q.sort_values("db", ascending=False).iterrows()):
    for dx, dy in OFFS:
        t = ax.annotate(r_.label, (r_.avg_time_to_throw, r_.adot), xytext=(dx, dy), textcoords="offset points",
                        fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK, ha="left" if dx > 0 else ("right" if dx < 0 else "center"),
                        zorder=4)
        bb = t.get_window_extent(ren).expanded(1.04, 1.1)
        hits_pts = any(bb.contains(px, py) for px, py in pts_disp)
        hits_lab = any(bb.overlaps(o) for o in placed)
        inside = ax.get_window_extent(ren).contains(bb.x0, bb.y0) and ax.get_window_extent(ren).contains(bb.x1, bb.y1)
        if not hits_pts and not hits_lab and inside:
            placed.append(bb)
            break
        t.remove()
cb = fig.colorbar(sc, ax=ax, fraction=0.035, pad=0.02)
cb.set_label("EPA per dropback", fontsize=7.6)
cb.ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)
ax.set_xlabel("average time to throw (seconds)", fontsize=8.4)
ax.set_ylabel("aDOT (average air yards per throw)", fontsize=8.4)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=7.6)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 26.12: Quarterback style map, 2025 regular season: every quarterback with at least 300 dropbacks. Horizontal: average time to throw (Next Gen Stats, snap to release, sacks excluded). Vertical: aDOT, the average air yards of his throws. Color: EPA per dropback (sacks, scrambles and turnovers included), blue above zero and red below. The dashed lines are the averages of the quarterbacks shown, splitting the map into four styles. Every red dot is in the bottom half, but so are some of the season’s best quarterbacks: style alone doesn’t decide success. Data: nflverse play-by-play and Next Gen Stats via nflreadpy.





The four corners of Figure 26.12 are four ways to play the position.

The distributor (quick and short) wins with decisions: the ball comes out on rhythm to the first open receiver, and the offense lives on YAC. He rarely takes sacks, and his ceiling depends on how many yards his receivers make after the catch.
The rhythm shooter (quick and deep) is the hardest style to play, because deep routes take time to develop; it takes anticipation and a scheme that gets receivers vertical fast.
The aggressive creator (holds it, throws deep) extends plays to give deep routes time, with a pocket he manages and an off-script game he trusts. His sack rate is higher and his big-play rate too.
The patient or stuck passer (holds it, throws short) is the corner to worry about: the ball comes out late and short, which usually means the first reads were not open and the quarterback ended up checking it down after a long look. Sometimes that is a scheme or a line problem rather than a quarterback problem, but it is rarely a good sign.

In 2025 the league MVP, Matthew Stafford, was a rhythm shooter: top-left corner, an aDOT of 9.3 yards at 2.80 seconds, and +0.24 EPA per dropback. Drake Maye, the runner-up, threw just as deep but held the ball longer, top-right, with the league’s best CPOE and its best EPA per dropback (+0.33). Brock Purdy sits at the far right, just below the average depth line, holding the ball longer than almost anyone, and still posted +0.22: the patient passer, not the stuck one.
In 2025 the top half of the map had no red at all; every quarterback below zero threw short. That fits the argument of Dropback Concepts that value lives downfield. But the bottom half also holds Purdy, Josh Allen and Jared Goff, three of the year’s better seasons. Style tells you how a quarterback plays; the color tells you whether it worked.

title: Quarterback Play: Progressions, the Pocket, and Off-Script Football
text:
Why the quarterback dominates value
One last number explains why everything in this chapter matters so much, and why the quarterback is paid like no one else on the field.
First, he touches the ball on almost every play, and on most of them he decides where it goes: in 2025, 60% of NFL offensive plays were dropbacks.
Second, passing plays swing further than running plays. Play by play, the EPA of a 2025 dropback had a standard deviation of 1.57 points, against 1.00 for a designed run: dropbacks hold the touchdowns and the interceptions. And the player who decides which way they swing differs more from team to team. Among 2025 starters with 300 or more dropbacks, average EPA per dropback had a standard deviation of 0.110; among ball carriers with 150 or more carries, average EPA per carry had one of 0.075. Multiply by a season’s workload (536 dropbacks for the median qualifying quarterback, 232 carries for the median back) and a quarterback one standard deviation above average is worth about 59 points over a season, against about 17 for a back.13
Points become wins at a steady rate: since 2012, each extra win has taken about 35 points of season scoring margin.14 So that quarterback is worth something like 1.7 wins a year over an average starter, and the back about 0.5. Over a replacement, the backup a team could sign off the street, the quarterback’s margin is larger still, because the gap between an average starter and a backup is wider at quarterback than anywhere else (the Purdy and Mac Jones numbers in the film room are one example).
All of these numbers share credit with the blockers, the receivers and the play-caller, and the split is unknowable from the box score. But the gap is too big to be an accident. The quarterback is the player with the most chances to add or lose points, on the plays where the most points are at stake. That is the starting point of Building a Roster, where the salary cap turns this gap into the most important economic fact in the sport.

title: Quarterback Play: Progressions, the Pocket, and Off-Script Football
text:
Film room






NoteFilm room: Tom Brady and Peyton Manning — the pocket as a craft



Peyton Manning, Denver Broncos, 2013. Manning set the single-season records for touchdown passes (55) and passing yards (5,477) in 2013, at 37.15 The number that explains how is a quieter one: he was sacked on 2.7% of his dropbacks, the lowest rate of any regular starter that season (the league rate was 6.4%).16 Manning had famously little interest in running. His pocket skill was making the decision before the rush arrived: an elaborate pre-snap read (The Pre-Snap Phase) that told him which side to work, then a progression run so fast that the ball was usually gone before pressure mattered.
Tom Brady, 2000-2022. Watch any Brady dropback and look at his feet, not his arm. When the edge closed he moved up into the pocket a step or two, rarely more, and kept his eyes downfield; when an interior rusher came he slid a yard and reset. He did it so economically that it looks like nothing happened, which is the point: a quarterback who climbs well never seems to be under pressure at all. He also got rid of the ball. Even at 44 and 45 his average time to throw was among the quickest in the league: 2.50 seconds in 2021 (rank 2 of 30 qualifying passers) and 2.45 in 2022 (rank 1 of 30).17
What to notice: neither man was a scrambler, and both were extraordinarily hard to sack. Pocket skill is mostly decision speed and footwork, not escapability.








NoteFilm room: Chiefs 2018 and Bills 2024 — the off-script pair



Patrick Mahomes’s left hand. Monday night, October 1, 2018, at Denver. The Chiefs trailed 23-20 with 3:14 left and faced third-and-5. Mahomes, in his first season as a starter, was flushed to his left, and Von Miller was dragging him down. On the way to the ground he switched the ball to his left hand and flipped it to Tyreek Hill for six yards and a first down. Kansas City scored the winning touchdown seven plays later. Asked years later for the most impressive play of Mahomes’s career, Andy Reid chose that one: a short throw, made with the wrong hand, with the game on the line.18
Josh Allen’s MVP season. Allen won the 2024 MVP award with a season that mixed both halves of this chapter.19 He is enormous (listed at 6-foot-5 and about 237 pounds), fast, and has one of the strongest arms in the league, which together make the scramble drill unusually dangerous: he can throw 50 yards on the run, so the deep defenders cannot come up to chase him, and he can run through a tackle, so the underneath defenders cannot drop off to cover. His early career was full of off-script plays that went wrong (forced throws across his body, sacks taken while looking for something big). The MVP version still improvises, but the throwaway and the checkdown are in his game too.
What to notice: the two quarterbacks at the top of Figure 26.8 got there in different ways. Mahomes’s off-script value is mostly made of throws like the left-handed flip: short, ugly and converting, from a body going the wrong way. Allen’s is power: a throw nobody else can make on the run, or a run nobody wants to tackle. What they share is the part that took Allen years: off-script talent becomes off-script value only with the judgment to give up on a play.








NoteFilm room: New York Giants 2007 season, Super Bowl XLII — the escape



February 3, 2008. The Giants trailed the unbeaten Patriots 14-10 and faced third-and-5 at their own 44 with 1:15 left. Eli Manning took the snap in the shotgun and the pocket collapsed: Jarvis Green and Richard Seymour got their hands on his jersey and should have had the sack. Manning spun free, backed out of the pile, and threw high down the middle to David Tyree, who had worked back into the middle of the field when his route was disrupted. Tyree caught it against his helmet with Rodney Harrison draped over him, at the Patriots’ 24. The Giants scored four plays later, on Plaxico Burress’s 13-yard touchdown catch, and won 17-14.20
What to notice: escape and scramble drill together. Manning was no runner; he simply refused to go down and kept his eyes downfield while he got loose. Tyree did what the drill tells a receiver to do when the play breaks: get to open grass in the quarterback’s line of sight, on a different level from everyone else.








NoteFilm room: Cincinnati Bengals 2024 — Joe Burrow’s timing



Joe Burrow led the NFL in passing yards (4,918) and touchdown passes (43) in 2024.21 Burrow can extend plays (he is one of the few quarterbacks above the diagonal in Figure 26.8), but that season was built in the pocket, on the gifts of the first half of this chapter: anticipation (throwing outs and digs before the receiver breaks, especially to Ja’Marr Chase, whose timing he has known since they were college teammates at LSU) and subtle movement in the pocket (a step up, a half-slide) that buys the extra beat for the throw.
What to notice: on replays of Bengals completions, freeze the frame at the release and find the receiver. Very often he hasn’t turned around yet.








NoteFilm room: San Francisco 49ers 2023 — Brock Purdy and the system-quarterback debate



Brock Purdy was the last player chosen in the 2022 draft, number 262, the pick nicknamed “Mr. Irrelevant.”22 In 2023, his first full season as the starter, he led the 33 quarterbacks with 250 or more dropbacks in EPA per dropback (+0.32, rank 1) and in the nflverse model’s CPOE (rank 1). The argument about him since has been whether those numbers are his or Kyle Shanahan’s: a scheme famous for motion, play-action and receivers who run after the catch, with Christian McCaffrey, Deebo Samuel, Brandon Aiyuk and George Kittle to throw to. Is he a “system quarterback”?
The data cuts both ways, which is why the argument never ends. Against the “YAC merchant” version of the charge: in 2023, 48% of his receiving yards came after the catch, about the league rate (48%), and his aDOT (8.2) was above the league average (7.8). He was throwing downfield and completing it. For the charge: the two CPOE models disagreed. The nflverse model, which doesn’t know how open the receiver was, ranked him first; Next Gen Stats’ model, which does, ranked him 5th. That is still very good, but the gap between the two rankings is the point: part of what the first model credited to Purdy’s accuracy was receivers being open, which the scheme creates. And in 2025, when a turf-toe injury cost Purdy eight games,23 his backup Mac Jones ran the same offense at +0.15 EPA per dropback, against Purdy’s +0.22: worse, but far better than Jones’s -0.06 across 2022–2024 with New England and Jacksonville.
What to notice: the question “is it the quarterback or the system?” is the right one to ask, and CPOE models that know about separation help answer it. But a quarterback who throws on time to the right read is part of what makes a system work. Watch Purdy’s anticipation on intermediate throws and judge for yourself.

title: Quarterback Play: Progressions, the Pocket, and Off-Script Football
text:
Watch for it on Sunday






TipWatch for it



Watch the eyes. On replays, especially the end-zone camera that looks straight at the quarterback, count how many reads he got through before he threw.

Find his first look. Where do his eyes (and his helmet’s facemask) point as his drop ends? That is usually read 1. Did the ball go there? More than half the time it does.
Count the head turns and hitch steps. Each snap of the head to a new area, usually with a hitch step, is a new read. One look and a throw: a rhythm throw. Two or three: a progression. A long stare at one side: he was waiting for something to open, he was confused, or he was holding a defender with his eyes on purpose, a look-off (Concepts Versus Coverages). His eyes can lie; the ball can’t.
Note the time. Count “one-Mississippi” from the snap. Ball out by about two and a half: quick game or first read. Out after three: off schedule, or a deep shot with max protection.
Watch his feet when the edge closes. Step up (climb)? Slide? Or drift back into the rush? The good ones move forward.
When he leaves the pocket, watch the receivers. Did the deep ones come back and the short ones go deep? Is everyone moving toward his side? That is the scramble drill. Who got open?
Judge the ending. A checkdown on third-and-12 is a punt with a few extra yards; on first-and-10 it is a fine play. A throwaway when nothing is there is a small win. A sack after a long hold in a clean pocket is on the quarterback; a sack that arrives before he could have thrown is on the protection.

For your prediction log: for one quarter, write down for each dropback how many reads the quarterback got through (1, 2, 3, or “off script”), and whether the ball came out on time. By the end you will know which kind of quarterback you are watching.

title: Quarterback Play: Progressions, the Pocket, and Off-Script Football
text:
Predict the play






TipPredict the play 1: the pocket at two seconds





Show the Python
S = {"LT": (-7.0, -4.9), "LG": (-2.0, -1.8), "C": (-1.9, 0.0), "RG": (-3.9, 1.6), "RT": (-7.0, 4.9),
     "QB": (-8.0, 0.0), "LE": (-9.0, -6.2), "NT": (-0.4, -0.9), "DT": (-2.3, 2.1), "RE": (-9.0, 6.2)}
off = [O(k, k, *S[k], "C" if k == "C" else ("Q" if k == "QB" else "")) for k in OL_KEYS + ["QB"]]
dfn = [D(k, "DE" if k in ("LE", "RE") else "DT", *S[k], "E" if k in ("LE", "RE") else "T")
       for k in ("LE", "NT", "DT", "RE")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=LOS, to_go=10)
p.highlight("QB")
fld = p.draw(lateral=(-12, 12), window=(-12.2, 3.6), title=False, width_in=5.8)
clean(fld.ax)
for sg in (-1, 1):
    arrow(fld, p, [(1.0, 5.4 * sg), (-3.0, 7.2 * sg), (-7.0, 7.4 * sg), (-9.0, 6.2 * sg)], color=style.DEFENSE,
          lw=1.2, head=7, z=3, alpha=0.8)
arrow(fld, p, [(1.0, 2.35), (-1.5, 2.15)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.2, head=7, z=3, alpha=0.8)
plt.show()








Figure 26.13: Freeze frame, about two seconds after the snap. Both ends have run their arcs and the tackles have pushed them deep. On the right, the defensive tackle has driven the right guard back about two yards. The left side of the interior is holding. The quarterback (ringed) is at his launch point, eight yards deep.





Where should the quarterback go: back, up, left, right, or out of the pocket?






TipAnswer





Up, and a little to his left: climb into the space behind the left guard and the center. Read the rush picture piece by piece. The ends have been pushed past him, so drifting back walks him into them, and escaping outside means running around a rusher who is already at his depth. The right side of the interior is caving: the tackle has the right guard two yards deep, so stepping straight up, or up and right, takes him into that collision. The left side of the interior is holding firm, and that is where the cup still has room.
So he climbs at an angle, a step or two up and half a step left, which is a climb and a slide at once. He doesn’t have to leave the pocket, his eyes stay downfield, and he is still inside the tackle box, so if nothing is open he can still throw it near a covered receiver or check it down. Escaping would only be right if the left side collapsed too.











TipPredict the play 2: third-and-9 at the 31





Show the Python
off = line() + [O("QB", "QB", -6.5, 10.5, "Q"), O("Y", "TE", 5.0, 8.0), O("Z", "WR", 12.0, 19.5)]
dfn = [D("RE", "DE", -8.0, 7.2, "E"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 5.6, 9.2, "M"), D("RCB", "CB", 13.4, 19.0, "C"),
       D("WILL", "WILL", 1.8, 12.6, "W"), D("FS", "FS", 17.5, 9.0, "FS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=79, ball_y="right", to_go=9)
p.highlight("QB")
fld = p.draw(lateral=(-10, 27), window=(-12.0, 21.0), title=False, width_in=5.8)
clean(fld.ax)
tackle_box(fld.ax, fld, p, -12.0)
arrow(fld, p, [(-8.0, 0.0), (-7.6, 5.0), (-6.5, 10.5)], color=GREEN, lw=1.4, ls=(0, (3, 2)), head=9)
arrow(fld, p, [(-8.4, 4.0), (-8.0, 7.2)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.2, head=7, alpha=0.8)
say(fld, p, -10.6, 0.0, "tackle box", color=PURPLE, fs=6.6)
say(fld, p, 9.0, 2.0, "line to gain", color=style.INK_2, fs=6.6)
say(fld, p, 1.7, -3.4, "ball at the opponent's 31", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fs=6.4)
say(fld, p, 4.0, 25.4, "out of\nbounds", color=style.INK_2, fs=6.2, box=False)
plt.show()








Figure 26.14: Third-and-9 at the opponent’s 31-yard line, so a field goal would be about a 48-yard try. The quarterback has escaped to his right, outside the tackle box (shaded), with the right end chasing him. Z, his only receiver on that side, is running down the sideline with the cornerback on top of him; Y is covered underneath by the Mike. There is no running room to the first-down line: the Will has come up to spy him (to mirror the quarterback and tackle him if he runs).





What should the quarterback do with the ball, and is it legal?






TipAnswer





Throw it away, out of bounds past the line of scrimmage, and kick the field goal. It is legal because he is outside the tackle box. Walk through his options. Z is covered with the cornerback on top, so a throw to him is a contested catch at best and an interception at worst, and an interception here throws away a likely three points. Y is covered by the Mike underneath. Running gets nowhere near the line to gain with the Will spying him (shadowing him, ready to tackle). The sack is the disaster that’s easiest to miss: an eight-yard sack pushes a 48-yard field goal back to about 56 yards, where even good kickers miss often.
So the ball goes out of bounds beyond the line of scrimmage, ideally over Z’s head toward the sideline. From inside the tackle box that throw would have to land near an eligible receiver; from where he is, outside the box, it only has to reach the line. A throwaway costs a down, which on third down he was about to lose anyway, and keeps every yard. That is exactly the bargain in Figure 26.10: a throwaway at about -0.8 EPA against a sack at about -1.8.











TipPredict the play 3: he breaks left





Show the Python
off = line() + [O("QB", "QB", -6.8, -8.6, "Q"), O("X", "WR", 19.0, -15.5), O("H", "WR", 5.0, -8.0),
                O("Y", "TE", 12.0, 2.0), O("Z", "WR", 12.0, 14.5)]
p = Play(off, [], los=LOS, to_go=None)
p.highlight("QB")
fld = p.draw(lateral=(-21, 19), window=(-11.0, 24.5), title=False, width_in=5.8)
clean(fld.ax)
called = {"X": [(-0.7, -15.0), (19.0, -15.5)], "H": [(-1.5, -8.5), (5.6, -8.5), (5.0, -8.0)],
          "Y": [(-1.5, 8.5), (12.0, 8.5), (12.0, 2.0)], "Z": [(-0.7, 15.0), (13.0, 15.0), (12.0, 14.5)]}
for k, pts in called.items():
    xy = [XY(fld, p, *q) for q in pts]
    xs, ys = zip(*xy)
    fld.ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.MUTED, lw=1.1, ls=(0, (2, 2)), zorder=2)
arrow(fld, p, [(-8.0, 0.0), (-7.8, -4.0), (-6.8, -8.6)], color=GREEN, lw=1.4, ls=(0, (3, 2)), head=9)
say(fld, p, -9.3, -3.0, "he breaks left", color=GREEN, fs=7.0, weight="bold")
plt.show()








Figure 26.15: The called play has broken down and the quarterback (ringed) has escaped to his LEFT. The receivers are shown where they are at that moment, with their called routes as grey dashes: X (left outside) was running a go and is 19 yards deep; H (left slot) was on a 5-yard hitch route; Y was running a 12-yard dig from the right that has reached the middle; Z (right outside) was running a 12-yard curl on the far side. The quarterback is right-handed. The defense is not shown.





Using the scramble-drill rules, where should each of X, H, Y and Z go, and where will the quarterback look first?






TipAnswer





X comes back down the left sideline; H takes off deep; Y keeps crossing to the left at his depth; Z works back across the field, deep. The quarterback looks first at the throws he can make on the move, X coming back and Y crossing toward him, and takes the deep shot to H or Z only if he can set his feet.
Settle each receiver by side first, then depth.

X is on the scramble side and deep, so he comes back: he stops his go route and works back toward the line of scrimmage along the left sideline, settling at about 8 to 10 yards, into the space his cornerback (running deep with him) leaves behind.
H is on the scramble side and short, so he goes deep: he turns up the field from his hitch route, behind the defenders who have turned to chase the quarterback.
Y is a crosser, already moving toward the scramble side, so he keeps crossing toward the quarterback, at about 12 yards: a level between X coming back and H going deep.
Z is on the backside. Standing on a curl 30 yards from the quarterback is useless, so he runs back across the field, deep, into the middle the defense has emptied, and into the quarterback’s line of sight.

That gives four receivers at four depths: H deep, Z deep and crossing, Y at about 12, X at 8 to 10, all moving toward the quarterback’s side. Now the look order. He is right-handed and rolling left, so before he can throw at all he has to turn his hips and square his shoulders back toward the target. The short, firm throws toward the sideline he is running at, X coming back and Y crossing, are the ones he can make like that. H and Z are the big play, worth it only if the rush gives him time to stop and set. If all four are covered he has two good options left: run, if there is grass to the line to gain, or throw it out of bounds past the line; he is outside the tackle box. What he must not do is throw back across his body to the right.

title: Quarterback Play: Progressions, the Pocket, and Off-Script Football
text:
Takeaways

The quarterback’s eyes run on his feet’s clock. Protection check at the snap, read 1 on the last step of the drop, a hitch step for each later read, then the checkdown. Each later read costs about half a second, and value.
Each read is answered by a defender, and the ball leaves before the receiver is open. The quarterback looks at the key defender for each read. An anticipation throw, released before the break, beats the defenders’ reaction; a “see it, throw it” ball arrives a hitch step late into a closing window.
Pocket movement is a response to the rush picture. Edges pushed past: climb. Pressure from one side: slide. Interior collapsed: escape, usually outside the tackle on the side the end was run past. Eyes stay downfield throughout.
Off-script football is coached. The scramble drill (short goes deep, deep comes back, go where he goes, backside comes across deep, the back leaks out) turns a broken play into a second play. Off script is high variance: for most quarterbacks it nets out below the pocket; for a few (Allen, Mahomes) it adds value.
Bad endings have a price list. A checkdown is worth about nothing, a throwaway a down, a sack a down and yards, an interception the ball. Throwaways must avoid intentional grounding: near a receiver inside the tackle box, past the line of scrimmage outside it.
Four numbers profile a passer. Time to throw and aDOT describe style; CPOE (completions over expected) and EPA per dropback describe results. Because he decides most plays, and passing varies more than running, the quarterback swings more points than anyone else on the field.

title: Quarterback Play: Progressions, the Pocket, and Off-Script Football
text:
Connections
Builds on: Passing Game Fundamentals (the drop as a clock, progressions, aDOT); Pass Protection (the pocket as a cup, the launch point, time to throw and pressure); The Quick Game (rhythm throws and the pre-snap read); and Dropback Concepts (the numbered reads of each concept).
Sets up: Offensive Systems and Play-Calling Languages, where the progression becomes part of a system’s language; Concepts Versus Coverages, which teaches how the quarterback reads coverage and moves safeties with a look-off (his eyes pointing one way to move a defender before he throws the other); Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage, on defenses built to make the pre-snap read wrong and the post-snap read late; Officiating, Replay, and the Rules of the Ball, for intentional grounding and the tackle box in full; The Pass Rush, on rush lanes and why pressure is a steadier number than sacks; and Building a Roster, on what the quarterback’s value means under a salary cap.
Case study: Andy Reid’s Chiefs, an offense built to make the most of a quarterback who is as dangerous off script as on it.






NoteGo deeper




Ron Jaworski with Greg Cosell and David Plaut, The Games That Changed the Game (2010): seven landmark game plans broken down from the coaches’ film, by a former NFL quarterback and two NFL Films producers who spent careers studying all-22 tape.
Chris B. Brown, The Art of Smart Football (2015) and the Smart Football archive: short essays on progressions, reads and how quarterbacks are taught to see the field.
The all-22 “coaches film” on NFL+ Premium, which shows every player on every snap from above: the only way to check a quarterback’s progression against what was actually open.

title: Offensive Systems and Play-Calling Languages
text:
What an offensive system is
Picture two broadcasts. On one, a microphone catches a 49ers play call coming in, something like the one Kyle Shanahan once recited for reporters: “Y Short to Strong Right Clamp Ace, H2 Y Bingo X Comeback… with Roll Right Z Shallow on Two.” On a replay from the Tom Brady years, the New England quarterback walks to the line without a huddle, points at a linebacker and shouts what sounds like a single word. Both offenses are about to run a pass play with three or four receivers working together, and both will probably gain about the same yardage. So why does one coach need twenty words and the other one? The answer isn’t style. Each offense speaks a language built to solve a particular problem: how to teach a playbook to fifty-odd players, how fast to get the call to the field, and how easily to change one piece of a play in the middle of a game.
You met three of these languages in a paragraph in What a Play Really Is: the long West Coast call, the Erhardt-Perkins concept word “Ghost,” and Air Coryell’s “896.” This chapter puts all seven families side by side, explains what each one buys and costs, shows how a system is taught, and shows how you can tell, from your couch, whose offense you’re watching.
You’ll be able to…
When a broadcaster says a team “runs the West Coast offense,” he means an offensive system: the offense’s whole way of operating, not one play or formation. A system has four layers:
Why a system rather than a big list of plays? An NFL offense runs about 60 plays a game (60.6 runs and passes per team per game in 2025),1 with forty seconds between them, fifteen of which the coach can’t use. A few hundred unrelated plays would be impossible to learn and to call quickly. A system turns the list into a language: a small vocabulary that combines into many plays, so a player learns words once and the coach builds new sentences every week.
This chapter is mostly about the language layer, where the families differ most. Where the systems came from is in 1978 and the Passing Revolution and The College Laboratory.

title: Offensive Systems and Play-Calling Languages
text:
A language. The words for formations, motions, protections, runs and pass routes, and the grammar that strings them into a play call. This is the team’s verbiage.
A core menu. The handful of runs and the couple of dozen pass concepts the offense is built on, the plays it will still be running in December.
Rules. How each play adjusts to what the defense does: which blocker takes which rusher, which routes become other routes against man coverage, whom the quarterback reads.
A teaching method. The order in which all of this is installed, how it’s drilled, and what the players are tested on.








ImportantWhy it exists



A system is how a coach makes a large playbook small. Players don’t memorize three hundred plays; they memorize perhaps a hundred words and a grammar, and the plays fall out of the combinations. The price is that the language has to be learned before anything else works, and a team that changes systems pays that price again.









NoteMadden vs. real life



In Madden, a playbook is a menu: “Gun Trips TE — Flood” is a card you select, and if you want a different play you scroll to a different card. A real playbook is closer to a grammar book. The name is the instruction: each word tells some of the eleven players what to do, so a coach can say a play nobody has ever run (“Flood, but the tight end runs a wheel instead of the flat”) and every player knows his job without a new diagram. That’s why real play calls sound like gibberish on the sideline mic: you’re hearing a sentence in a language you haven’t learned yet.
