section: Reading the front from the broadcast
text:
Reading the front from the broadcast
The diagrams in this book look down from above. The broadcast doesn’t. The main camera sits high on one sideline, near the line of scrimmage, so you see the line from the side, and the one thing a front is made of, which shoulder each lineman is on, runs straight away from you into the screen.


Show the Python
def project(pts, cam, target):
    """Pinhole camera: world points (downfield d, offense's LEFT, height) -> screen (x, y) and depth."""
    C, Tg = np.asarray(cam, float), np.asarray(target, float)
    fwd = (Tg - C) / np.linalg.norm(Tg - C)
    right = np.cross(fwd, [0.0, 0.0, 1.0]); right /= np.linalg.norm(right)
    up = np.cross(right, fwd)
    P = np.atleast_2d(np.asarray(pts, float)) - C
    z = P @ fwd
    return (P @ right) / z, (P @ up) / z, z


def camera_view(ax, players, cam, target, labels, green=(), rings=None, box=(-3, 7, -8, 8), pad=0.08,
                lw=2.0, head=6.4):
    """Upright players seen from a camera. players: (key, side, d, w, label); labels: key -> (dx, dy, text)
    with offsets as fractions of the view's width/height; rings: key -> colour, a ring round the player's head.
    box = (d0, d1, w0, w1) sets the visible region."""
    W = lambda d, w, h=0.0: (d, -w, h)   # noqa: E731  the offense's right is the camera frame's -left
    rings = rings or {}
    dist = np.linalg.norm(np.subtract(target, cam))
    corners = [W(d, w, h) for d in box[:2] for w in box[2:] for h in (0.0, 2.2)]
    cx, cy, _ = project(corners, cam, target)
    x0, x1, y0, y1 = cx.min(), cx.max(), cy.min(), cy.max()
    wpad, hpad = pad * (x1 - x0), pad * (y1 - y0)
    xl, yl = (x0 - wpad, x1 + wpad), (y0 - hpad, y1 + hpad)
    span_x, span_y = xl[1] - xl[0], yl[1] - yl[0]
    for d in range(-15, 26, 5):           # yard lines
        xs, ys, _ = project([W(d, w) for w in np.linspace(-26.6, 26.6, 60)], cam, target)
        ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.9, zorder=1)
    xs, ys, _ = project([W(0, w) for w in np.linspace(-26.6, 26.6, 60)], cam, target)
    ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=1.3, alpha=0.75, zorder=1.5)       # line of scrimmage
    order = sorted(players, key=lambda q: -project([W(q[2], q[3])], cam, target)[2][0])
    for key, side, d, w, lab in order:   # far players first, so near ones are drawn on top
        (xa,), (ya,), (z0,) = project([W(d, w, 0.0)], cam, target)
        (xb,), (yb,), _ = project([W(d, w, 1.5)], cam, target)
        s_ = dist / z0
        col = style.OFFENSE if side == "off" else style.DEFENSE
        z = 3 + 1.0 / z0
        ax.plot([xa, xb], [ya, yb], color=col, lw=lw * s_, solid_capstyle="round", zorder=z, alpha=0.9)
        if side == "off":
            ax.plot([xb], [yb], marker="o", ms=head * s_, mfc=col, mec="white", mew=0.7, zorder=z + 0.001)
        else:
            ax.plot([xb], [yb], marker="s", ms=head * 0.93 * s_, mfc=style.DEFENSE_TINT, mec=col, mew=1.1,
                    zorder=z + 0.001)
        if key in rings:
            ax.plot([xb], [yb], marker="o", ms=head * 2.1 * s_, mfc="none", mec=rings[key], mew=1.5, zorder=19)
        if key in green:   # a dashed ring on the empty spot across from him, where a lineman would be
            (xh,), (yh,), _ = project([W(1.0, w, 0.8)], cam, target)
            ax.add_patch(Ellipse((xh, yh), 0.075 * span_x, 0.075 * span_y * 1.3, fc="none",
                                 ec=GREEN, lw=1.6, ls=(0, (3, 1.5)), zorder=19))
        if key in labels:
            dx, dy, txt = labels[key]
            ax.annotate(txt, (xb, yb), xytext=(xb + dx * span_x, yb + dy * span_y), fontsize=6.6, ha="center",
                        va="center", fontweight="bold", zorder=20,
                        color=GREEN if key in green else (style.OFFENSE_DARK if side == "off" else style.DEFENSE_DARK),
                        arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", lw=0.7, color=style.INK_2, shrinkA=1, shrinkB=4),
                        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.15", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.92))
    ax.set_xlim(*xl); ax.set_ylim(*yl); ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
    for sp in ax.spines.values():
        sp.set_color(style.BASELINE)
    ax.set_facecolor(style.TURF)


def scene(front):
    return ([(q.key, "off", q.d, q.w, q.label) for q in line("full") + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0, "Q")]]
            + [(q.key, "def", q.d, q.w, q.label) for q in front])


SIDE_CAM, SIDE_TGT, SIDE_BOX = (0.0, -62.0, 40.0), (1.0, 0.0, 0.0), (-4.0, 7.0, -7.0, 8.0)
SIDE_RINGS = {"C": style.OFFENSE_DARK, "DT": style.DEFENSE_DARK}
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(6.4, 6.3))
gs = gridspec.GridSpec(2, 2, figure=fig, height_ratios=[1.05, 1])
ax_o, ax_u, ax_e = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 0]), fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 1]), fig.add_subplot(gs[1, :])
camera_view(ax_o, scene(over_front(+1)), SIDE_CAM, SIDE_TGT, box=SIDE_BOX, rings=SIDE_RINGS,
            labels={"Y": (-0.27, -0.10, "tight end\n(near side)"), "C": (-0.30, 0.12, "center"),
                    "DT": (0.22, 0.33, "the 3: near side,\ntoward the TE"),
                    "SAM": (-0.02, -0.13, "Sam off the ball")})
ax_o.set_title("Sideline camera: Over", fontsize=8.6, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
camera_view(ax_u, scene(under_front(+1)), SIDE_CAM, SIDE_TGT, box=SIDE_BOX, rings=SIDE_RINGS,
            labels={"Y": (-0.27, -0.10, "tight end\n(near side)"), "C": (-0.30, 0.12, "center"),
                    "DT": (0.30, 0.10, "the 3: far side,\naway from the TE"),
                    "SAM": (0.27, -0.12, "Sam on the line")})
ax_u.set_title("Sideline camera: Under", fontsize=8.6, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
camera_view(ax_e, scene(under_front(+1)), (-45.0, 0.0, 24.0), (2.0, 0.0, 0.0), box=(-7.0, 6.0, -8.0, 8.0),
            labels={"DT": (-0.12, 0.12, "3: on the LG's outside shoulder"), "NT": (0.02, 0.20, "1: center's right shoulder"),
                    "RG": (0.16, -0.17, "uncovered guard"), "SAM": (0.10, 0.14, "Sam, outside Y")},
            green=("RG",), lw=2.6, head=7.5)
ax_e.set_title("End-zone replay of the Under: behind the offense", fontsize=8.6, loc="left", color=style.INK,
               fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=1.0, w_pad=0.8)
plt.show()








Figure 29.10: Over and Under from the broadcast’s high sideline camera, and the replay that checks the read (players drawn as simple upright figures, offense blue, defense orange; the offense goes left to right with the tight end on the near side, at the bottom of each sideline view). From the side, shoulders line up one behind another, so you can’t measure techniques or see a hole cleanly. What you can see is how far each defensive tackle stands from the center (blue ring). The 1 is almost straight across from him; the 3 (orange ring) stands well off to one side, out over a guard. Top left, an Over: the 3 is on the near side, the tight end’s side, and nobody stands on the line outside the tight end. Top right, an Under: the 3 is on the far side, and the Sam stands on the line outside the tight end. Bottom, the end-zone replay of the Under, looking down the line from behind the offense: now every shoulder is visible, and you can confirm the read (the 3 on the left guard, the 1 on the center’s right shoulder, the right guard uncovered).





From the high sideline shot, you can’t measure a technique, and the bubble is hard to see: the defenders stand one behind another, and the space across from the uncovered guard is only a little wider than the space next to it. What you can find, every snap, are three landmarks.

The tight end. He is the strength, so find him first: the man at the end of the line, a step off the tackle, often with a hand on his knee. If he is on the near side of the screen, the strong side is near; if he is on the far side, it is far.
The 3-technique. Find the center, then the two defensive tackles. One, the 1, is almost straight across from the center. The other, the 3, stands clearly off to one side, out over a guard. If the 3 is on the tight end’s side, it’s an Over; if he is on the other side, it’s an Under. That is the same fact as the bubble, seen from the other direction: the empty guard is always on the side away from the 3.
The edge outside the tight end. A linebacker standing on the line beside the tight end, part of the defensive line, is the Under’s Sam. Nobody there, and a linebacker a few yards off the ball, points to an Over (or to the Tampa-style Under of the dialect box).

Then add the details. Ends lined up so wide they are nearly out of the shot are a wide-9. Three linemen packed across the middle with no tackle off to one side, and extra men stacked on the tight end’s side, is a bear. And the sideline read is a first guess, not a verdict: when the replay comes from the end-zone camera, check it. From behind the offense every shoulder is visible, and after a few weeks of checking, the sideline guess gets fast and mostly right.

title: Even Fronts: 4-3 Over, Under, Wide-9, and the 46 Bear
text:
Film room






NoteFilm room: Chicago Bears, Super Bowl XX (1985 season)



The game: Bears 46, Patriots 10, January 26, 1986, at the Louisiana Superdome. New England gained 7 yards on 11 rushes and 123 yards in all, and had negative total yardage at halftime.19
What to notice:

The 46 was one package in Chicago’s defense, not every snap, and New England trailed early and threw most of the game, so expect more pass rush than run fits on this tape. On the snaps where you count eight defenders in the box, you are looking at the 46.
The interior: a nose on the center and a tackle on each guard. Watch the guards at the snap. Do they ever get to a linebacker?
The outside linebackers. Both on the tight end’s side, one jamming him at the line. Notice how rarely the tight end gets cleanly into a route.
When New England spreads out, watch who has to cover the third receiver. That is where the 46 was always vulnerable, even in its greatest game.









NoteFilm room: Seattle Seahawks, 2013 season



The season: Pete Carroll’s fourth year in Seattle, and the best version of his 4-3 Under: a 323-pound former defensive tackle, Red Bryant, as the strong-side 5-technique end, the Sam on the line outside the tight end, a quick 3-technique on the weak side and a speed rusher at weak-side end (Carroll’s name for the spot is the Leo).20 Seattle led the NFL in scoring defense from 2012 through 2015, the first team of the Super Bowl era to do it four years running, and in Super Bowl XLVIII it beat the Denver Broncos, who had just set the league record for points in a season, 43–8.21 Carroll traces the scheme to 1977, when he was a graduate assistant at Arkansas under the defensive coordinator Monte Kiffin: “It was a one-gap principle defense way back then,” he said. “He taught me everything I know about defense.”22
What to notice: find the tight end, then look for the Sam standing on the line outside him and the big end in the 5 beside him. On runs to that side, watch the two of them meet the blockers at the line and turn the ball back inside, Gus Bradley’s “turn everything back inside to our big guys.” Then look across to the weak side for the 3-technique, alone against a guard.








NoteFilm room: Philadelphia Eagles at Carolina, 2017 (Week 6)



The game: Eagles 28, Panthers 23, Thursday night, October 12, 2017, at Bank of America Stadium in Charlotte. Carolina’s running backs carried 13 times on designed runs and gained 1 yard between them. Their quarterback, Cam Newton, gained 53 yards on 8 designed runs of his own.23
What to notice:

The ends’ alignment on early downs, well outside the tackles (and the tight end), and how often they move in on passing downs.
On the running backs’ carries, Fletcher Cox at the 3-technique and the linebackers behind the ends. Are the off-tackle lanes open when the back arrives, or already filled?
On Newton’s runs, the end the offense didn’t block. A quarterback who can keep the ball turns the wide-9’s free rusher into a defender who has to guess, the zone-read problem from earlier in this chapter.









NoteFilm room: Chicago Bears, 2004–2012 seasons



The coach: Lovie Smith, the Bears’ head coach from 2004 to 2012, who had coached linebackers for Tony Dungy and Monte Kiffin in Tampa Bay and brought their four-man, one-gap front and Cover 2 to Chicago. In his first draft he took the piece the front depends on, Tommie Harris, with the 14th pick, to play the under tackle; Harris made three straight Pro Bowls (2005–2007), and the 2006 Bears went 13–3 and reached Super Bowl XLI.24
What to notice: this is the tape for the front and the coverage together. Find Harris (number 91, a Bear through 2010): on most early downs he is on the guard away from the tight end, though, like every 4-3 team, the Bears mixed their fronts. Then find the middle linebacker, Brian Urlacher, over the strong guard, with the nose’s shade keeping that guard busy, and count how often he reaches the ball untouched. On passing downs, watch him turn and run down the middle of the field at the snap: that is the Tampa 2 behind the front.

title: Even Fronts: 4-3 Over, Under, Wide-9, and the 46 Bear
text:
Watch for it on Sunday






TipWatch for it



Before the snap: over or under?

Find the tight end. That’s the strength for the front.
Find the 3-technique: from the high sideline camera, the defensive tackle standing well off to one side of the center, not the one almost straight across from him. 3-technique toward the tight end (empty guard away): Over. 3-technique away (empty guard toward): Under. Check it on the end-zone replay.
Is a linebacker standing on the line outside the tight end? That’s the Under’s Sam.
How wide are the ends? A couple of yards outside the tight end, or where one would be, in a sprinter’s stance: wide-9.
Center and both guards covered, eight men in the box: a bear front, near the goal line, against two tight ends, or on early downs against a zone-running team.
When the tight end shifts or motions across, watch the defensive tackles. Do they trade places? Is anybody still moving at the snap?

After the play: where did the run go?

At the bubble (the uncovered guard) or away from it? Did that guard reach a linebacker?
Against a wide-9, did the run go off-tackle, and did a linebacker or safety fill the lane in time?

For your prediction log (How to Watch a Broadcast): on early downs, write O or U before the snap and at or away after the play, for whether the run went at the bubble (the uncovered guard’s side) or away from it. After a half, look for a pattern in where each offense runs against each front.

title: Even Fronts: 4-3 Over, Under, Wide-9, and the 46 Bear
text:
Predict the play






TipPredict the play



Drill 1. Name the front, find the bubble. First-and-10. The offense is in a one-back set with its tight end on the left this time. Name the front. Which offensive lineman is free, and if the offense runs inside zone, which side would you expect it to aim for, and which defender has to win?


Show the Python
off = line("full") + [te(-1), O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -6.6, 0, "R")]
p = Play(off, under_front(-1), los=40, to_go=10, title="Drill 1: tight end left. Over or Under?")
f = draw(p, width_in=5.4, lateral=(-9.0, 8.6), window=(-8.6, 7.6))
plt.show()








Figure 29.11: Drill 1: one-back set, tight end (U) on the offense’s left; the receivers are outside the picture.











TipAnswer





A 4-3 Under, with the strength on the left. The tight end is on the left, so the left is strong. The 3-technique is on the right guard, away from the tight end, the nose is shaded toward the tight end, and the Sam is standing on the line outside him. Every landmark says Under.
The free lineman is the left guard, on the tight end’s side: nobody is on him, and the Mike stands over him. That’s the Under’s bubble. Inside zone toward the tight end (to the offense’s left) is aimed right at it: the left guard helps the center move the nose and then climbs to the Mike. The Mike has to win: beat a guard who has a head start, to his gap (the strong B), or the back has a crease. The defense’s counterweight is the edge: the Sam and the 5 on that side should squeeze anything that bounces outside back inside. If the offense instead runs to the right, it runs at the 3-technique, alone against the right guard, which is exactly where the Under wants it.
One more thing to notice: this is the same defensive line an Over makes when the tight end is on the right. Only the tight end’s side, and the Sam standing on the line beside him, tell you which front it is.











TipPredict the play



Drill 2. The base defense meets three receivers. Second-and-6. The defense stayed in its base 4-3 (no nickel back) after an incomplete pass, and the offense has come out in 11 personnel with three receivers to the right. The front is set as an Over to the tight end. What does the Sam do, and what is the offense hoping to see?


Show the Python
off = line("short") + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, -2.0, "R"),
                       O("H", "WR", -1.5, 10.5, "H"), O("Z", "WR", -0.7, 16.5, "Z"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -16.0, "X")]
dfn = over_front(+1) + [D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, 16.5, "CB"), D("SS", "S", 12.0, 8.0, "SS"), D("FS", "S", 12.0, -7.0, "FS"),
                        D("LCB", "CB", 6.5, -16.0, "CB")]   # X and his cornerback: outside the drawn window
p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=6, title="Drill 2: base 4-3 against three receivers")
p.highlight("SAM", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, width_in=5.6, lateral=(-9.4, 18.8), window=(-7.6, 13.6))
say(f, p, 2.6, 10.5, "nobody over him", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
plt.show()








Figure 29.12: Drill 2: 11 personnel, shotgun, tight end and two receivers on the right (H in the slot, Z wide; X wide left, outside the picture). The defense is in its base 4-3, set as an Over to the tight end, with two deep safeties. The Sam (ringed) is still at his base spot outside the tight end; nobody is over the slot receiver.











TipAnswer





The Sam has to choose, and every choice costs something, which is the point of the formation.

If the Sam stays in the box, the defense has seven against the run (four linemen and three linebackers) but nobody near the slot receiver. A quick throw to H, a hitch, a bubble screen or a quick out, gets an easy five or six yards on second-and-6.
If the Sam walks out over the slot (to an apex, halfway between the tight end and H), the throw is covered, at least by a linebacker. But now the box has six defenders (four linemen, the Mike and the Will) against six blockers (five linemen and the tight end), with two safeties twelve yards deep. That’s a light box, and the offense will happily run the ball. Worse, the Over’s bubble is still there: the weak guard is free to climb to the Will.
If the defense rotates instead, the strong safety buzzes down over the slot (or into the box), the Sam stays, and the free safety moves to the middle: a one-high shell, the move Seattle’s defenses made a habit of (see the nickel section). Now the box and the slot are both covered, but one safety guards the whole deep middle against three receivers who can all run vertical routes, so the offense’s answer is four verticals, or a seam route, over the top.

Every answer gives something up. This is why defenses substitute a nickel back against 11 personnel, and why offenses that keep a fullback or a second tight end on the field until the defense commits to base personnel can then spread out without substituting and force exactly this choice. The quarterback’s pre-snap read is simple: count the box, look at the slot, and throw or hand off accordingly, the logic of the RPO.











TipPredict the play



Drill 3. Run against the wide-9. First-and-10, a shotgun one-back set with the tight end on the right. Both defensive ends are in wide-9 alignments, the tackles in a 3 (right) and a 1 (left), with the Sam standing off the ball outside the tight end. Where is the offense’s best run, and which defender decides whether it works?


Show the Python
off = line("full") + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, -2.0, "R")]
dfn = [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, -(4.8 + 2.3), "w9"), D("NT", "DT", 1.0, T("1", -1), "1"),
       D("DT", "DT", 1.0, T("3", 1), "3"), D("RE", "DE", 1.0, T("wide9", 1), "w9"),
       D("WILL", "LB", 4.8, -2.6, "W"), D("MIKE", "LB", 4.8, 0.7, "M"), D("SAM", "LB", 4.6, 6.0, "S")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=10, title="Drill 3: two wide-9 ends")
f = draw(p, width_in=5.4, lateral=(-10.6, 10.6), window=(-7.6, 7.6))
plt.show()








Figure 29.13: Drill 3: both ends in wide-9 alignments, in sprinter’s stances; a 3-technique on the right guard and a 1 on the center’s left shoulder; three linebackers, the Sam off the ball outside the tight end.











TipAnswer





Off tackle, inside either end, and the linebacker on that side decides it. This front has two big lanes, and the drill has more than one good answer.

Toward the tight end, the lane between the 3-technique and the right end spans two gaps, the C and the D, and the wide-9’s whole job on the snap is to go upfield, not to close it. Against this front the right tackle and the tight end are both uncovered, so the blocking is clean: the right guard takes the 3, the right tackle climbs to the Mike, the tight end blocks the Sam, and the end is left alone to run himself out of the play. The Sam is the only defender who owns that lane, so he has to fill it before the back gets there, ideally meeting the tight end at the line so the back has to cut back inside. If he’s late, the next defender is a safety ten yards downfield.
Away from the tight end, the lane between the 1 and the left end is even wider on paper, and it sits on the bubble: the left guard is uncovered. The center and left guard double the 1 and one climbs, the left tackle climbs to the Will, and again the end is left alone. Here the Will decides, with the same two-gap problem and a 300-pound tackle coming at him.

Many coaches would still go strong first, because the tight end gives them an extra blocker on that side and a running back can bounce outside him if the Sam over-fills. Either way, the end can help by squeezing when he reads run, closing down the line behind the play rather than rushing past it, and the defense’s real answer is a safety who arrives in time. That is the trade from Figure 29.5, live: the ends’ rush is a bet that the linebackers and safeties will be on time.
The best modern answer of all uses the end’s alignment against him. A shotgun offense can run inside zone, leave the backside wide-9 unblocked and read him: if he chases the back, the quarterback keeps the ball and runs where the end used to be. That is the zone read of Option Football, and its pass-game cousin, the RPO, punishes the same man the same way.

title: Even Fronts: 4-3 Over, Under, Wide-9, and the 46 Bear
text:
Back to the huddle
The chapter opened with a defensive tackle jogging across the center when the tight end lined up on the right, a linebacker walking up onto the line outside the tight end, and, two plays later, the same defense staying put. Now you can read it. The tackle over the right guard was only standing there while the offense huddled: until the tight end shows his side, the defense doesn’t know where its front goes. On the first play the call was a 4-3 Under: once the tight end set up on the right, the 3-technique went to the weak guard, away from him, and the Sam walked up to make the strong-side edge two men deep at the line. On the second, with the tight end on the left, the call was an Over: the tackle was already on the guard on the tight end’s side, so nobody had to cross, and the Sam stayed off the ball. One word, and the formation, set eleven alignments. And each was a bet about which guard to leave free and where the run would be met.

29  Even Fronts: 4-3 Over, Under, Wide-9, and the 46 Bear

title: Even Fronts: 4-3 Over, Under, Wide-9, and the 46 Bear
text:
Takeaways

An even front sets its linemen in pairs, with nobody head-up on the center. Two tackles can’t cover three interior linemen, so the center or a guard is always free; every even front is a decision about which one, and which linebacker answers for him.
Over and Under are the same players, leaning opposite ways from a strength call. The Over puts the 3-technique and its linemen toward the tight end and leaves the weak guard uncovered for the Will; the Under sends the 3-technique to the weak side to rush one-on-one, puts the Sam on the line to harden the strong-side edge, and leaves the strong guard uncovered under the Mike. Runs aim at the uncovered guard: the bubble.
Strength is relative, so offenses move it. A tight-end shift can make half a front re-set in a second and a half, or the defense can check Over to Under and move only the linebackers, because an Over one way is the same line as an Under the other way. Every answer gives something up.
The wide-9 buys pass rush with run lanes. Unblocked at the snap, the ends reach full speed before the tackle can touch them, and the two-gap lanes inside them become the linebackers’ and safeties’ problem. With a stout interior and fast linebackers (the 2017 Eagles) it can stop the run; without them it gets run through.
The bear front covers the center and both guards, and the 46 built a defense on it. With no uncovered interior lineman, double teams, climbing guards and pullers all become hard. Buddy Ryan’s 1985 Bears smothered two-back offenses with it; three receivers and quick throws made it a situational front, now used near the goal line and against zone-running teams.
Against 11 personnel the line stays and the Sam goes. The four linemen keep their rule; the third linebacker becomes a nickel back, and someone, often a safety, takes his job on the tight end.

title: Odd and Hybrid Fronts: 3-4, Okie, Tite, and Modern Nickel Fronts
text:
Odd and even: who is on the center?
The graphic in the corner of the screen says the defense is in a 3-4. You count. Four players at the line of scrimmage, two of them standing up, two with a hand on the ground. Next snap, after a substitution you barely notice (a huge man jogging on, a linebacker jogging off), there are five across the line, three of them enormous and wedged inside the offensive tackles, with a single linebacker behind them. The offense hands the ball to its running back on an inside run, the kind that worked all afternoon last week, and he runs into a wall two yards deep. No blocker ever touched the linebacker. “That’s their tite front,” says the analyst. “Three big bodies inside, and nobody can get to the second level.” So which is it: a 3-4, a four-man line, a five-man line? And how did a defense with only six men near the ball stop a run aimed at six blockers? This chapter is about the other family of fronts, the odd ones, and about why, in the modern game, the names on the graphic tell you less than the picture on the field.
You’ll be able to:
How to read the diagrams. As in the rest of Part 5: offense is blue circles, defense orange squares, plays go up the page, and left and right are always the offense’s left and right. Defensive linemen are labelled with their technique number (a 0 is a nose head-up on the center, a 4i is on a tackle’s inside shoulder). E is an edge player standing up at the end of the line; M and W are inside linebackers; $ is the nickel back; C a cornerback; FS and SS the safeties. Offensive linemen are LT, LG, C, RG, RT, shortened to T G C G T in the smaller panels; R is the running back and F a fullback. New in this chapter: a dark dot on the front edge of a defender’s square is a hand on the ground. A square with no dot is a player standing up. Counting dots is how you will tell fronts apart, because counting players stopped working a long time ago.
Every front in football starts with one question, and you can answer it from the couch: is anybody lined up head-up on the center?
Show the Python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.2))
OFF = line("short") + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -6.2, 0, "R")]
even = front([("LE", "5", -1), ("L1", "1", -1), ("R3", "3", 1), ("RE", "5", 1)],
             lbs=[("WILL", 4.5, -2.0, "W"), ("MIKE", 4.5, 0.8, "M"), ("SAM", 4.2, 6.2, "S")])
odd = front([("LE", "5", -1), ("NT", "0", 1), ("RE", "5", 1)],
            lbs=[("WILL", 4.6, -2.0, "W"), ("MIKE", 4.6, 2.0, "M")],
            others=[("LOLB", 1.0, -6.2, "E"), ("ROLB", 1.0, 6.2, "E")])
for ax, dfn, ttl, hd, msg in [
        (axes[0], even, "Even: nobody on the center", ("LE", "L1", "R3", "RE"), "nobody head-up:\nat most a shade"),
        (axes[1], odd, "Odd: a nose on the center", ("LE", "NT", "RE"), "the nose is\nhead-up on him")]:
    p = Play(OFF, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-8.2, 8.6), window=(-7.6, 7.0), title=False)
    hands(f, p, hd)
    point_to(f, p, (-3.6, -4.3), (-0.7, 0.0), msg, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8, shrink=6)
    ax.set_title(ttl, fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.7)
plt.show()








Figure 30.1: The one-glance test. Left, an even front (the 4-3 Over of Even Fronts): the two defensive tackles split the center between them, one shaded on his shoulder (the 1) and one outside a guard (the 3), and nobody stands directly over the ball; the ends are in 5s and the Sam (S) is off the ball outside the tight end. Right, an odd front (the 3-4 Okie of this chapter): a nose tackle head-up on the center (the 0), with an end on each offensive tackle and a stand-up edge (E) at each end of the line. Dark dots are hands on the ground: four in the even front, three in the odd one. Both have seven players in the front.
If nobody is head-up on the center, the front is even: the defensive tackles line up on or around the guards, the center is uncovered or only shaded, and you are looking at one of the four-man fronts of Even Fronts. If a big man stands right over the ball, nose to nose with the center, the front is odd: it is balanced around a 0-technique nose tackle. The classic odd fronts have three down linemen (the 3-4, which puts five on the line once you count its two standing outside linebackers) or five (the old 5-2), rather than four.
Why does one alignment decide the family? Because of what it does to the offensive line’s arithmetic. In an even front, nobody is square in front of the center: at most a tackle shaded on one of his shoulders, a man he can work on together with a guard, and often nobody at all, in which case he is free to help or to climb to a linebacker. The defense has eased the center’s job in exchange for putting its tackles where they can attack the guards. In an odd front, the center has a man in his face on every snap, and a nose head-up on him is responsible for both A gaps, one on each side of the center. The center can’t block him alone at a good angle in either direction, so one of the two guards usually has to help. That is the founding idea of every odd front: put a heavy man on the center, make the offense spend two blockers on him, and let somebody else run free. You met that nose in Defensive Line Play. This chapter is about the fronts built around him.
A warning before we start, which the rest of the chapter will keep proving: “odd” and “even” describe where linemen stand, not who is on the roster. A team that calls itself a 3-4 team plays an even front on plenty of snaps, and a 4-3 team can put a nose on the center. Keep your eyes on the center.

title: Odd and Hybrid Fronts: 3-4, Okie, Tite, and Modern Nickel Fronts
text:
The 3-4 Okie
The 3-4 Okie is the classic 3-4, the one drawn in every coaching book: a nose head-up on the center, a defensive end on each offensive tackle, a stand-up edge at each end of the line, and two inside linebackers behind the guards. The name is short for Oklahoma, because the alignment is Bud Wilkinson’s Oklahoma 5-2 of the late 1940s and 1950s with its two outside men standing up (more on that history below).


Show the Python
OFF21 = line("short") + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0, "Q"), O("FB", "FB", -4.5, 0, "F"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0, "R"),
                        O("X", "WR", -0.7, -15.0, "X"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 15.0, "Z")]
OKIE = front([("LE", "5", -1), ("NT", "0", 1), ("RE", "5", 1)],
             lbs=[("WILL", 4.6, -2.1, "W"), ("MIKE", 4.6, 2.1, "M")],
             others=[("LOLB", 1.0, -6.2, "E"), ("ROLB", 1.0, 6.2, "E")]) + secondary(high=12.0, safety_w=8.0)
p = Play(OFF21, OKIE, los=35, to_go=10, title="The 3-4 Okie vs 21 personnel")
f = draw(p, width_in=6.4, lateral=(-18.5, 18.5), window=(-9.5, 15.5))
hands(f, p, ("LE", "NT", "RE"))
point_to(f, p, (-4.6, -7.4), (0.5, -0.1), "nose (0): head-up\non the center", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
point_to(f, p, (-4.6, 8.4), (0.5, 4.0), "ends on the tackles\n(5s here; 4s to two-gap)", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK,
         fontsize=7)
point_to(f, p, (3.7, -11.4), (1.0, -6.7), "stand-up edges (E):\nrush, set the edge, drop", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK,
         fontsize=7)
point_to(f, p, (8.3, 0.0), (5.2, -1.6), "inside LBs behind the guards:\nthe men the front keeps clean",
         color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7, shrink=8)
plt.show()








Figure 30.2: The 3-4 Okie against a two-back, one-tight-end offense (21 personnel, the kind of offense it was built for), all eleven defenders. Three hands on the ground: the nose (0), head-up on the center, and the two ends, here in 5-techniques on the tackles’ outside shoulders (in the two-gap version they line up head-up, in a 4). At each end of the line a stand-up edge (E): on the tight-end side on Y’s outside shoulder (a 9), on the open side a couple of yards outside the tackle. Two inside linebackers (M and W) stand about four and a half yards deep behind the guards, where no lineman blocks them unless a guard leaves to do it. Four defensive backs: two cornerbacks (C) on the wide receivers and two safeties (FS, SS) deep.





Read Figure 30.2 as a list of jobs, the way you learned to in Defensive Line Play.

The nose takes on the center, and very often a guard as well. He is usually the heaviest man on the defense, because his whole value is in not moving.
The ends sit on the offensive tackles. In the classic version they are head-up there, in a 4-technique, and they control the tackle and play the gap on either side of him. Others line up on the tackle’s outside shoulder, a 5. They are long and strong, the 290-to-320-pound bodies built to lock out a tackle at arm’s length.
The outside linebackers are standing up at each end of the line. Against the run they set the edge; against the pass, one or both rush; and on some snaps one drops into coverage. They are the lightest players in the front, edge rushers in all but stance.
The inside linebackers stand behind the guards, and here is the design’s point. Count the offensive linemen who don’t have a defender on or near them before the snap: the two guards. In zone-blocking terms they are uncovered (Zone Running), and an uncovered guard wants to climb straight to a linebacker. The Okie’s whole design is to make that impossible: the nose is too much for the center alone, so one guard has to stay and help; the ends hold the tackles so they can’t climb either. If the front does its job, at most one blocker reaches the second level, and two linebackers are left to make tackles.


One alignment, two ways to play it
What the front does after the snap is a separate choice from where it lines up. A 3-4 can be a two-gap front, in which the three linemen control blockers and read, or a one-gap front, in which every defender attacks a gap at the snap. You learned the difference player by player in Defensive Line Play. Here is what each looks like across the whole front.


Show the Python
GAPS = [(-4.0, "C"), (-2.4, "B"), (-0.8, "A"), (0.8, "A"), (2.4, "B"), (4.0, "C"), (5.95, "D")]


def owners(f, p, groups, d=-3.0):
    """Under the gap letters: a bar spanning the gap(s) each player owns, with his label beneath it."""
    for w0, w1, lab in groups:
        bracket(f, p, d, w0 - 0.35, w1 + 0.35, lw=1.6)
        say(f, p, d - 0.75, (w0 + w1) / 2, lab, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7, weight="bold")


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.0))
SHORT_OFF = line("short") + [te(+1)]
# two-gap 0-4-4
dfn = front([("LE", "4", -1), ("NT", "0", 1), ("RE", "4", 1)],
            lbs=[("WILL", 4.7, -2.0, "W"), ("MIKE", 4.7, 2.0, "M")],
            others=[("LOLB", 1.0, -5.9, "E"), ("ROLB", 1.0, T("9"), "E")])
p = Play(SHORT_OFF, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
f = draw(p, ax=axes[0], lateral=(-8.4, 8.4), window=(-5.4, 7.6), title=False)
hands(f, p, ("LE", "NT", "RE"))
for w, g in GAPS:
    gap_tag(f, p, -2.2, w, g)
owners(f, p, [(-4.0, -2.4, "4"), (-0.8, 0.8, "0"), (2.4, 4.0, "4"), (5.95, 5.95, "E")])
say(f, p, 6.5, 0.0, "M and W: read, then fill", color=GREEN, fontsize=6.9, weight="bold")
say(f, p, 2.6, -6.3, "sets the\nedge", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)

Figure 30.3: Two 3-4s against the same one-tight-end offense, with each defender’s gaps (the bars under the gap letters) and first steps (arrows). Left, two-gap: the nose (0) and the two ends, head-up on the tackles in 4-techniques, each own the two gaps on either side of their blocker; the edge (E) on the tight end owns the D gap; the open-side edge sets the edge outside. Six gaps need only three linemen, so both inside linebackers start with no gap at all: they read and fill wherever the ball goes. Right, one-gap: the same personnel lined up shaded, each man aimed at one gap (arrows). The nose shades to the tight-end side (a 1) and attacks that A gap; the open-side end moves down to a 3 on the guard and takes the B gap; the tight-end-side end takes the C gap from a 5; the edges take the outside gaps, and the linebackers fill the two gaps left over (the Mike the B gap toward the tight end, the Will the other A gap). If you have read Even Fronts, the right-hand picture should look familiar: it is the 4-3 Under with the Sam called an outside linebacker.





The two-gap 3-4 is the old-school version, and its appeal is the math in the left half of Figure 30.3. Three linemen can hold six gaps if each of them can stand up a blocker and play either side of him. That leaves the two inside linebackers gap-free: they don’t have to guess at the snap; they watch the play develop and run to the ball, and the linemen in front of them keep the blockers off them. (Against one back, that is. Against a fullback, like the one in Figure 30.2, the offense has an extra blocker who can lead through a hole, and one inside linebacker has to meet him there while the other fills off the nose; Linebackers has that fight.) Bill Parcells’s New York Giants of the 1980s played it, with Bill Belichick as his defensive coordinator, and Belichick’s New England Patriots of the 2000s played it with linemen like Vince Wilfork, Richard Seymour and Ty Warren, all built like the job: big, long and patient.1
The cost, as Defensive Line Play explained, is that two-gappers are always reacting. They rarely make plays behind the line or sack the quarterback, they need bodies the draft produces only a few of each year, and on passing downs the defense usually has to take the nose off for someone quicker.
The one-gap 3-4 keeps the personnel and changes the job. Line the ends up shaded into gaps, shade the nose, and tell every defender to attack his gap at the snap, and the 3-4 becomes an attacking front. The right half of Figure 30.3 shows the most common way to do it, and it holds a secret: lined up this way, a “3-4” is almost exactly the 4-3 Under of Even Fronts, a nose shaded to the tight end, a 3-technique away from him, a 5 and a 9 to the tight end’s side, with the Sam linebacker called an outside linebacker and standing up. Run this chapter’s one-glance test on it: nobody is head-up on the center any more, so by alignment this “3-4” is an even front.
That is why “3-4” by itself is a weak clue. The number of linemen tells you how many there are; their alignment and first step tell you how they play. A two-gapper’s first step goes into the blocker, hands first, and he stays at the line. A one-gapper’s goes into a gap, and he is across the line before the blocker has finished his first step. Watch the ends for two snaps and you will know which 3-4 you are watching.






ImportantWhy it exists



The 3-4 trades linemen for linebackers, and two-gap play is what makes that trade affordable. Take a defensive lineman off the field and put a linebacker on, and you gain a player who can rush, drop into coverage or fill a run lane, and who keeps the offense guessing which of those he’ll do. You lose one big body at the line. The two-gap 3-4 covers the loss with technique: three linemen hold six gaps, and the linebackers run free. The one-gap 3-4 covers it with movement and speed: every man attacks, and the extra linebacker is just one more fast player who can come from anywhere. Either way, the defense is betting that a fourth linebacker is worth more than a fourth lineman. In an era of spread offenses, three-receiver sets and quarterbacks who throw on first down, that bet has mostly paid.

section: Where the 3-4 came from (and why nobody agrees)
text:
Where the 3-4 came from (and why nobody agrees)
Ask who invented the 3-4 and you will get at least four answers, each true about something. The honest version is a family tree, not a birth certificate.
The ancestors: five men on the line. In 1947 Earle “Greasy” Neale, the Philadelphia Eagles’ head coach, built his defense around a five-man line with two linebackers behind it. It was called the Eagle defense, and the Eagles won NFL championships with it in 1948 and 1949.2 Bud Wilkinson took the five-man line to the University of Oklahoma, where it became the Oklahoma 5-2, the defense behind his Sooners’ 47-game winning streak in the 1950s. (That is where Okie comes from.) Now look at a 5-2 the way a coach of the 1970s did. The two men at the ends of the line were defensive ends, but they were usually smaller and quicker than the three linemen inside them, and their jobs were to set the edge and, on some plays, to drop. Stand them up, call them linebackers, and the same seven players become three linemen and four linebackers. Nobody had to invent the 3-4; it was hiding inside the 5-2.3
The NFL arrivals, early 1970s: several claimants.

Bill Arnsparger, Miami, 1972. The Dolphins’ defensive coordinator under Don Shula had a linebacker, Bob Matheson, who could play with his hand on the ground or standing up. Arnsparger moved him around the front, sometimes as a fourth linebacker, sometimes as a rushing end, and the package was named for his jersey: the 53 defense. The Dolphins went 17–0. Was it a 3-4? On some snaps, yes, and it is often named as the 3-4’s NFL ancestor; the story belongs to The 1978 Liberation.4
Chuck Fairbanks, New England, 1974. Fairbanks had coached the Oklahoma 5-2 as the Sooners’ head coach, and when he took over the Patriots he brought it with him, standing up its ends. His 1974 Patriots are usually named as the first NFL team to use the 3-4 as their regular base defense.5
Bum Phillips, Houston, 1974–75. Phillips, the cowboy-hatted Texan who had devised the technique numbers you have been using since The Language of the Run Game, was the Oilers’ defensive coordinator under Sid Gillman, and had talked Gillman into a 3-4, when they traded for nose tackle Curley Culp in October 1974; he kept the 3-4 when he became head coach in January 1975. Culp, a former NCAA heavyweight wrestling champion at Arizona State, was strong enough to need two blockers, and Phillips gave him the credit: “Curley made [the 3-4 defense] work. He made me look smart.”6

The boom and the bust. Within a few years the 3-4 was everywhere. John Madden’s Raiders switched to it in 1976, after injuries thinned their defensive line, and won the Super Bowl; Arnsparger’s Dolphins went to it full time in 1977; and by the late 1970s and early 1980s it was the league’s most common base defense.7 Then offenses changed again, the one-back passing games of the 1980s and 1990s made four-man fronts with fast defensive ends fashionable, and by the mid-1990s only a handful of teams, most notably Buffalo and Pittsburgh, still lined up in a 3-4. The revival came in the 2000s, led by the Steelers and Belichick’s Patriots, and took a new shape that the rest of this chapter is about: the stand-up edge rusher, the one-gap 3-4, and in the 2020s the five-man tite front. The longer arc, including the 3-4’s role in the rise of the hybrid edge (the stand-up edge below, treated as a position of its own: part end, part linebacker), is in Dynasties and Counterpunches and The Single Wing to the Scoring Drought.
So who invented it? Wilkinson’s 5-2 supplied the alignment, Arnsparger the idea of a hybrid end-linebacker, Fairbanks and Phillips the commitment to it as a base defense, and Madden the Super Bowl that sold it. That is the usual shape of football history: a problem (offenses running more and throwing more on early downs), several smart people solving it in the same few years, and credit that depends on whom you ask.

title: Odd and Hybrid Fronts: 3-4, Okie, Tite, and Modern Nickel Fronts
text:
The stand-up edge
The 3-4’s most important legacy isn’t the nose. It is the player at the end of the line who isn’t sure whether he is a lineman or a linebacker, and doesn’t need to be.
A stand-up edge lines up at the end of the line of scrimmage in a two-point stance, standing, instead of with a hand in the dirt. In a 3-4 he is called an outside linebacker, and the roster lists him that way; on the field, most snaps, he is an edge rusher doing a defensive end’s job. Lawrence Taylor in the 1980s, Kevin Greene and Greg Lloyd in the 1990s, DeMarcus Ware and Von Miller in the 2000s and 2010s, T.J. Watt today: the most feared pass rushers of the 3-4 era stood up.
Why stand? Three reasons, each a trade.

Vision and options. Standing, he sees the whole backfield, and he can move in any direction at the snap: rush, take on a blocker, or turn and drop into coverage. A lineman in a three-point stance, weight forward on his hand, is committed to going forward. The offense can’t rule out a drop from a standing edge, so it can’t be sure who is rushing. That uncertainty is the seed of the simulated pressures of Part 7: four-man rushes in which a lineman drops into coverage and a player the offense didn’t count rushes instead.
Width and a view of the tackle. Standing, he can align wider and watch how the tackle sets before he commits to an inside or outside move. It isn’t a free win: plenty of rushers still prefer a hand down for a faster get-off on obvious passing downs.
Disguise. A front with two standing edges can become a four-man line, a five-man line or a three-man rush without anyone substituting. That is the trick behind the opening of this chapter, and it gets its own animation below.

What it costs. Mostly leverage against the run. A defender in a three-point stance comes out low, and the low man wins at the line; a standing edge has to sink as he takes on a tackle or a tight end, or he gets pushed upfield and the edge goes soft. That is why the stand-up edges who last are the ones who can set the edge as well as rush (in Defensive Line Play’s terms, who keep their outside arm free against a 300-pound tackle), and why many of them put a hand down in short yardage and at the goal line, where leverage is everything. The most common hand-down moment of all is on passing downs in nickel, when the 3-4 outside linebacker becomes, in everything but the roster, a 4-2-5’s defensive end (more on that below). The body type is in between, too: usually 245 to 265 pounds, lighter than a defensive end, heavier than an inside linebacker. Teams that play four-man fronts draft the same players and call them defensive ends. The player is the same; the label follows the scheme.






CautionCommon misconception



“A 3-4 outside linebacker is a linebacker, so he covers people.” Some do, some of the time. Most of the great ones spend the large majority of their passing-down snaps rushing the quarterback. When you see a 3-4 outside linebacker drop into coverage, it is usually a deliberate surprise, designed to put a defender where the quarterback expected an empty space, not his everyday job.

title: Odd and Hybrid Fronts: 3-4, Okie, Tite, and Modern Nickel Fronts
text:
The Phillips branch: the attacking 3-4
The 3-4’s revival in the 2000s split along the line from Figure 30.3. Belichick’s Patriots and the Steelers kept versions that leaned on two-gap play up front. The other branch came from one family, the Phillipses.
Wade Phillips, Bum’s son and his linebackers coach in Houston from 1976 to 1980, spent four decades as a coordinator and head coach running his father’s 3-4, and running it the attacking way, not the two-gap way the Parcells and Belichick branch made famous.8 Phillips’s linemen were shaded into gaps and attacked them; his outside linebackers rushed; the ends were penetrators, not anchors. When he took over the Houston Texans’ defense in 2011, the team’s own preview called it “his one-gap scheme,” and the line coach said it was “not like a two-gap type defense where you need that 350-pound nose man.”9 The proof arrived the following year, when the Texans’ 5-technique end, J.J. Watt, led the league with 20.5 sacks and was Defensive Player of the Year: the end of a 3-4, the position that used to exist to let linebackers make tackles, had become the defense’s best pass rusher.10
Four years later Phillips took the same ideas to Denver, where the 2015 Broncos allowed the fewest yards in the league and won Super Bowl 50 with two stand-up edges, Von Miller and DeMarcus Ware, chasing the quarterback.11 Their film room is below.
A two-gap 3-4 and a one-gap 3-4 use the same eleven bodies and ask opposite things of them. The modern descendants of both branches meet in one front, which is next: it has a two-gap nose like Belichick’s and one-gap linemen beside him like Phillips’s.

section: The tite front: walling off the middle
text:
The tite front: walling off the middle
The tite front is an odd front with five men on the line: a nose on the center, two defensive linemen in 4i-techniques on the inside shoulders of the offensive tackles, and an edge player outside each tackle. Fangio and his coaching tree call it tite; Kirby Smart’s Georgia calls the same picture the mint front; and, as the dialect section below shows, some playbooks call it Eagle.
It is a reduced front on both sides. In a reduced front, the defensive linemen slide a gap inward from their usual spots and an edge player takes the outside gap they left. The 4-3 Under of Even Fronts reduces one side (its backside end moves down toward the guard); the tite takes the Okie and reduces both ends, from the tackles’ outside shoulders (5s) to their inside shoulders (4is). That one move inside is the whole front.
Why move the ends inside? Put a nose on the center and a 4i in each B gap, and the whole interior of the line, from one tackle’s inside shoulder to the other’s, has a big body in it. Now run the covered-or-uncovered test from Zone Running for inside zone to the offense’s right. The center is covered (the nose is on him), the right guard is covered (the 4i is on his play side) and so is the left tackle. The left guard and the right tackle are uncovered, and in an ordinary front those are the two men who would climb to linebackers. Here they can’t, because each stands next to a defender who can’t be blocked one-on-one: the left guard has to help the center with the nose, and the right tackle has to help the right guard with the 4i. The offense can still double-team, but every double team is spent on a lineman, and every blocker who stays on a lineman is a blocker who isn’t on a linebacker.
If that sounds like the bear front of Even Fronts, it should: both fronts decide that no interior blocker will be free. The bear does it by covering the center and both guards (a 0 and two 3s), and the 46 that made it famous put eight men near the ball to fill everything else. The tite sits on the center and the tackles’ inside shoulders, which does the same job against the inside runs with five on the line and two safeties still deep. The price of that choice, as we’ll see, is the space outside the tackles, where the bear had bodies and the tite has only its edges.
Here is the tite doing its job against the most common run in football, inside zone.


Show the Python
def tite_iz():
    off = gun11(y_attached=True)
    dfn = [D("LE", "OLB", 1.0, -5.3, "E"), D("L4", "DL", 1.0, T("4i", -1), "4i"), D("NT", "DL", 1.0, 0.0, "0"),
           D("R4", "DL", 1.0, T("4i", 1), "4i"), D("RE", "OLB", 1.0, 6.1, "E"),
           D("MIKE", "LB", 4.7, 0.8, "M")] + secondary(nickel_w=-6.2, high=11.0, safety_w=7.6)
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=10)
    # doubles: C + LG on the nose, RG + RT on the play-side 4i; they hold, nobody climbs.
    # (blockers stop about 1.25 yd short of their man, centre to centre: contact, with both labels readable)
    go_to(p, "C", (-0.35, 0.3), speed=1.4); go_to(p, "LG", (-0.35, -1.0), speed=1.6, via=[(-0.6, -1.3)])
    go_to(p, "NT", (0.9, -0.05), "path", speed=0.6)
    go_to(p, "RG", (-0.3, 1.95), speed=1.6, via=[(-0.55, 1.75)]); go_to(p, "RT", (-0.3, 3.25), speed=1.6)
    go_to(p, "R4", (0.9, 2.6), "path", speed=0.5)
    # the left tackle cuts off the backside 4i; the backside edge squeezes but stays square (he has the QB)
    go_to(p, "LT", (-0.3, -2.3), speed=1.6); go_to(p, "L4", (0.9, -2.35), "path", speed=0.8)
    go_to(p, "LE", (0.7, -4.0), "path", speed=1.2, delay=0.2)
    # the tight end blocks the play-side edge, who holds the edge
    go_to(p, "Y", (-0.3, 5.0), speed=1.6); go_to(p, "RE", (0.9, 6.1), "path", speed=0.4)
    # the Mike reads and fills the C gap; the strong safety comes down; the nickel holds his slot
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (2.7, 2.3), "path", speed=3.6, delay=0.35)
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (2.1, 4.4), "path", speed=4.6)
    go_to(p, "SS", (4.0, 5.4), "path", speed=5.6, delay=0.45)
    go_to(p, "FS", (9.6, -5.2), "path", speed=2.0, delay=0.5)
    go_to(p, "NB", (4.0, -6.0), "path", speed=0.8, delay=0.3)
    # the QB rides the mesh and carries out a keep fake; the back presses the B gap, bends outside the tackle
    go_to(p, "QB", (-5.1, -0.4), "path", speed=1.5)
    go_to(p, "QB", (-5.6, -3.0), "path", speed=3.0, delay=0.15)
    go_to(p, "RB", (-1.9, 2.15), "run", speed=6.0, via=[(-4.7, -0.2), (-3.8, 1.4)])
    go_to(p, "RB", (0.8, 4.35), "run", speed=5.5)
    p.handoff("RB", t=0.5)
    return p


def tite_marks(fld, play, t, i):
    hands(fld, play, ("L4", "NT", "R4"), t=t, half=0.57)
    if t >= 1.45:
        spot(fld, play, 1.45, 3.4, ms=8)


P_TITE = tite_iz()

                   notes=["five on the line, one LB:\nsix in the box vs six blockers",
                          "both doubles stuck on a\nlineman: nobody climbs",
                          "the B gap is full;\nthe back bends outside",
                          "the unblocked Mike fills\nthe C gap: about a yard"],
                   rings=(("MIKE", style.DEFENSE),), lateral=(-7.8, 8.6), window=(-6.6, 7.2),
                   after=tite_marks, width_in=5.4, enter=("SS",))

Figure 30.4: The tite front against inside zone right (simulated, in Big Data Bowl tracking coordinates; faint lines are each player’s path so far). The offense is a shotgun one-back set with three receivers and an attached tight end (11 personnel), six blockers. The defense is in nickel with a five-man line (dark dots are hands on the ground): a nose (0) and two 4i-techniques with a stand-up edge (E) outside each tackle, one linebacker (M), a nickel back ($) outside the box, and two safeties deep, above the top of the picture until the strong safety (SS) comes down in panel 4. 1: six in the box against six blockers, and the inside linebacker (ringed) has nobody in front of him. 2: the center and left guard double the nose; the right guard and right tackle double the play-side 4i. Neither double moves its man, so neither can send a blocker up to the Mike. The backside edge squeezes down but stays square, keeping the quarterback (who could keep the ball) in front of him. 3: the back presses the play-side B gap, his aiming point, and finds it full; he bends outside the tackle, into the C gap. 4: the Mike, never touched, fills that gap and makes the tackle (X) about a yard past the line, with the strong safety arriving from depth.




Walk through Figure 30.4 with the zone rules from Zone Running in mind. Inside zone wins with double teams: two linemen drive a defensive lineman backward, and when the linebacker behind commits, one of them comes off and blocks him. That requires two things: a lineman the pair can move, and a linebacker within reach. The tite takes away both.

The doubles can’t move their men. The nose plays the center and whichever guard joins the double: what analysts of these light-box fronts call “gap-and-a-half” play, in which a big two-gap nose controls one A gap and leans into the other.12 The 4i sits in the B gap, exactly where inside zone’s aiming point is, so the right guard and the right tackle have to block him together. Neither can come off to climb: the 4i is already in the hole, so the moment one of them leaves, the man who stays is blocking him from the wrong side and the hole closes.
Nobody climbs. With every blocker spent on a lineman, the one inside linebacker is never touched. That doesn’t mean he has no job. He owns a gap like everyone else (the next section counts them), but he can fill it without having to beat a block first, and the wall in front of him has already told the running back where not to go.
The cutback is plugged. Inside zone’s best friend is the bend back to the weak side. In the tite, the backside A and B gaps have the nose and the backside 4i in them, and the backside edge is squeezing down the line behind them. He squeezes square, though, not flat down the line: against a shotgun team the quarterback can pull the ball and run where the edge just left, so the edge closes the gap without giving up the quarterback.

What’s left for the runner is outside the tackle, and here it matters how he gets there. A bounced inside run is late and alone: the back has pressed the B gap, stopped, and turned, and while he did, the Mike, the play-side edge and a safety coming down have had a full second to get there. That is the trade the tite offers on purpose. It turns the inside runs that win against two-high defenses into bounced runs that its linebacker and safeties can chase down. A run designed to go outside is a different matter, because it arrives with its blockers already out there. That is the tite’s weak spot, and we’ll come to it.

Why the tite exists now: six men, seven gaps
The tite has existed in college for a long time, but it took over the NFL conversation in the late 2010s for a reason you have met before: two deep safeties. Defenses facing modern passing offenses want to keep both safeties deep, as long as possible (A First Look at Defense has the numbers: split-safety looks reached a record 42 percent of dropbacks in 2025).13 Two safeties deep and five defensive backs on the field leaves six men in the box. Against an offense with a tight end attached, that is six defenders for six blockers and seven gaps. By the one-man-per-gap accounting of one-gap football, the numbers don’t work.


Show the Python
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.4, 3.9))
TITE = [D("LE", "OLB", 1.0, -5.3, "E"), D("L4", "DL", 1.0, T("4i", -1), "4i"), D("NT", "DL", 1.0, 0.0, "0"),
        D("R4", "DL", 1.0, T("4i", 1), "4i"), D("RE", "OLB", 1.0, T("9"), "E"), D("MIKE", "LB", 4.7, 0.8, "M")]
p = Play(line("short") + [te(+1)], TITE, los=35, to_go=None)
go_to(p, "MIKE", (2.4, 3.9), "path", speed=3.0)
p.highlight("MIKE", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-8.4, 9.6), window=(-5.4, 7.6), title=False)
hands(f, p, ("L4", "NT", "R4"))
for w, g in GAPS:
    gap_tag(f, p, -2.2, w, g)
owners(f, p, [(-4.0, -4.0, "E"), (-2.4, -2.4, "4i"), (-0.8, 0.8, "0"), (2.4, 2.4, "4i"), (4.0, 4.0, "M"),
              (5.95, 5.95, "E")])
lane(f, p, 7.0, 8.4, 0.0, 4.6, color=style.DEFENSE, alpha=0.10)
say(f, p, 5.6, 7.7, "alley:\nsafety\nor $", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
say(f, p, 6.5, -2.6, "M: unblocked, but he owns\nthe C gap toward the TE", color=GREEN, fontsize=6.8, weight="bold")
plt.show()








Figure 30.5: The tite’s gap accounting against a tight end on the right (one common way to assign it; staffs vary). Seven gaps (green letters) and six men in the box. The nose (0) owns both A gaps: he is the one two-gap player. Each 4i owns the B gap he lines up in, one gap apiece, played by locking onto the tackle’s inside half. The open-side edge (E) owns the C gap on his side; the tight-end-side edge, on the tight end’s outside shoulder, owns the D gap. That leaves one gap, the C gap between the right tackle and the tight end, and it belongs to the Mike. He is unblocked, not unassigned. Outside all of them, the alley (the lane between the edge and the sideline where a bounced run goes) belongs to a safety or the nickel, coming from depth.





Figure 30.5 shows how the tite makes the numbers work. One nose who holds both A gaps is the extra defender the box doesn’t have: five men on the line take six of the seven gaps, the Mike takes the last one without a blocker in his way, and the safeties can stay home on the pass and fit the run late, from depth, with the alley outside the edges left to a safety or the nickel. The 4is are one-gap players (each has his B gap), but they play it from an inside shade, by locking onto the tackle rather than darting past him, which is why they need the length and strength of two-gappers.14 The assignments vary by staff and by how many linebackers are on the field. A college tite with two inside linebackers often lets the nose play just one A gap, the one away from the center’s first step, with a linebacker filling the other;15 the NFL’s nickel tite, with one linebacker, leans on the nose to hold both.
The Fangio tree, Vic Fangio himself and the coaches who worked under him, Brandon Staley among them, built their light-box run defense on exactly that bargain. Fangio’s 2018 Chicago Bears, his last season as a coordinator before he became Denver’s head coach, played their 3-4, often in the tite, with big interior linemen (Akiem Hicks and the nose Eddie Goldman) and two stand-up edges (Leonard Floyd and Khalil Mack, acquired in a trade the week before the season), and allowed the fewest points in the league (283) while leading it in takeaways (36).16 The light-box bargain is clearest in Staley’s 2020 Rams, who by one count played a light box on about 78 percent of snaps, the second-highest rate in the league, and allowed the fewest points in the NFL (296).17 Fangio himself is still at it: he is the Eagles’ defensive coordinator in 2026, his third season there.18


What the tite gives up
Every front is a trade. The tite’s costs are specific, and offenses know them.

The pass rush. Three of its five linemen are big interior players built to hold blocks, not beat them; the 4is especially are aligned to take the run away, not to rush. To get four rushers, the tite often has to rush both edges and two interior men, or send an off-ball linebacker. Cody Alexander, one of the most widely read writers on defensive structure, names this as the front’s main drawback: “its inability to get a rush without sending an off-ball defender.”19
The perimeter. With three big bodies inside the tackles, the defense outside them is thin: one edge on each side, a linebacker flowing from the middle, and safeties coming from depth. Runs that are designed to start outside, outside zone, tosses, the jet sweeps of Perimeter and Misdirection, arrive there with blockers in front of them and go straight at that thinness. The next section shows how.
Angles for gap runs. Linemen lined up inside their blockers hand a gap scheme easy down blocks: on power to the right, the right tackle blocks down on the 4i and the right guard down on the nose, both from the side. The tite survives power with technique, not alignment: the 4i squeezes the down block and closes the B gap anyway, the edge meets the pulling guard and spills the ball back inside, and the lone linebacker fits off the spill. If any of the three loses, there is nobody behind them but safeties. (Run Fits and Box Math draws a full fit against power.)
The quick game and the RPO. A light box with a single linebacker leaves big spaces underneath. The RPO was built for exactly this defender: a lone linebacker who must fill the run will leave the space behind him open for a throw.
Rare players, again. Like the two-gap 3-4, the tite needs a nose who can hold two blockers and two 4is with the length to play from an inside shade. The front is only as good as those three men.

Two practical notes before we leave it. First, the tite is balanced, so unlike the Over and Under it has no strength call for its interior: the 0 and the two 4is stay put wherever the tight end lines up, and only the edges and the Mike adjust (the edge on the tight end’s side widens to his outside shoulder, and the Mike’s gap goes with him). Second, when the offense detaches its tight end and goes 2x2 or empty, there are only five blockers and six gaps, and the five-man line covers all six by itself, so the Mike becomes a truly free player. That sounds ideal, but those formations are usually passing formations, and a five-man line that rushes four is exactly the problem in the first bullet above, which is one reason defenses so often meet them with a four-man front instead.

section: Inside zone or outside zone? How a front chooses
text:
Inside zone or outside zone? How a front chooses
The tite is the clearest example of a principle that runs through all of defensive front design, and it is the best way to understand why a defense changes fronts from week to week: every alignment makes some blocks easier and others harder, and a defense picks the alignment that makes the offense’s favourite blocks hard.
Recall the two zone plays from Zone Running:

Inside zone is won by double teams that move a defensive lineman back and then climb to a linebacker. Its aiming point is the play-side B gap.
Outside zone is won by reach blocks: each blocker steps sideways and tries to get his head outside the defender in front of him. Its aiming point is the tight end’s outside leg, and its biggest gains come from the edge being reached (the bounce) or the defense over-running the play (the cutback).

Now ask what kind of alignment makes each one hard.


Show the Python
def zone_panel(ax, outside):
    off = [q for q in gun11(y_attached=True) if q.key not in ("X", "Z", "H")]
    dfn = [D("LE", "OLB", 1.0, -5.3, "E"), D("L4", "DL", 1.0, T("4i", -1), "4i"), D("NT", "DL", 1.0, 0.0, "0"),
           D("R4", "DL", 1.0, T("4i", 1), "4i"), D("RE", "OLB", 1.0, 6.1, "E"),
           D("MIKE", "LB", 4.7, 0.8, "M"), D("SS", "SS", 9.0, 7.4, "SS")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    if not outside:
        for k, end in [("C", (0.0, 0.15)), ("LG", (-0.1, -0.7)), ("RG", (0.0, 1.95)), ("RT", (0.05, 3.1)),
                       ("LT", (-0.1, -2.1)), ("Y", (-0.05, 5.4))]:
            go_to(p, k, end, speed=2.0)
        go_to(p, "RB", (-2.7, 2.1), "run", via=[(-4.7, -0.2), (-3.9, 1.2)])
        p.highlight("MIKE", color=style.DEFENSE)
    else:
        for k, end in [("C", (-0.25, 0.75)), ("LG", (-0.3, -0.35)), ("RG", (-0.35, 2.85)), ("LT", (-0.3, -1.6)),
                       ("Y", (-0.25, 6.0))]:
            go_to(p, k, end, speed=2.0)
        go_to(p, "RT", (2.3, 3.0), via=[(-0.2, 4.6), (0.6, 4.4)], speed=2.0)    # combo on the edge, then climb
        for k, end in [("NT", (0.95, 1.0)), ("R4", (0.95, 3.4)), ("L4", (0.95, -1.6))]:
            go_to(p, k, end, "path", speed=1.0)
        go_to(p, "RB", (-2.6, 6.2), "run", via=[(-5.0, 0.4), (-4.0, 3.6)])
        go_to(p, "MIKE", (3.0, 5.6), "path")
        go_to(p, "SS", (4.0, 8.6), "path")
        p.highlight("RE", color=style.DEFENSE)
    go_to(p, "QB", (-5.2, -0.5), "path", speed=2.0)
    f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-8.0, 11.6), window=(-7.4, 10.6), title=False)
    hands(f, p, ("L4", "NT", "R4"))
    if not outside:
        lane(f, p, 1.75, 3.0, -0.2, 2.8, color=style.OFFENSE, alpha=0.12)
        lane(f, p, -0.5, 0.5, -0.2, 2.8, color=style.OFFENSE, alpha=0.12)
        spot(f, p, -1.85, 2.45, color=GREEN, ms=9)
        say(f, p, -6.8, 6.4, "aims at the\nB gap: a wall", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.7)
        say(f, p, 7.8, 2.2, "nobody climbs:\nthe Mike is unblocked", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.7)
    else:
        lane(f, p, 6.6, 9.4, 0.0, 4.6, color=style.DEFENSE, alpha=0.12)
        spot(f, p, -1.4, 6.6, color=GREEN, ms=9)
        say(f, p, -6.8, 6.6, "aims outside\nthe Y", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.7)
        point_to(f, p, (-3.2, 9.4), (0.2, 6.4), "Y + RT on\none edge", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK,
                 fontsize=6.7, shrink=6)
        point_to(f, p, (6.0, -2.6), (2.4, 2.9), "C gap empty: the\nRT climbs to M", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK,
                 fontsize=6.7, shrink=3)
        say(f, p, -2.6, -4.4, "0 and 4is must\nrun sideways", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.5)
        say(f, p, 2.6, 10.1, "alley", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.5)
    return f


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.4))
zone_panel(axes[0], outside=False)
axes[0].set_title("Inside zone: into the wall", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
zone_panel(axes[1], outside=True)
axes[1].set_title("Outside zone: test the edge", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 30.6: The same tite front against the two zone runs, first steps only (illustrative). Left, inside zone: the run aims at the play-side B gap (green X), right where the 4i stands, and the three interior linemen (dark dots) occupy all five offensive linemen, so the doubles have nobody to climb to and the one linebacker (ringed) is never blocked. The shaded lanes are where the back wanted to go: both full. Right, outside zone: the run aims outside the tight end (green X), and everybody steps to the right. Now the tite’s alignment works against it. The play-side C gap, between the right tackle and the tight end, is empty, so the right tackle is uncovered: he helps the tight end on the edge (ringed, E) and then climbs to the only linebacker. The nose and the 4is, big bodies built to hold their ground, have to run sideways to keep up with the line. And outside the edge there is nobody until the Mike and the strong safety (SS) get there to fill the alley (shaded). The tite takes the middle away and asks one edge to win against two blockers.





The rule of thumb that falls out of Figure 30.6 is simple to state:

To beat the double team, line up on top of or just inside the blockers. A nose on the center and 4is inside the tackles leave the offense’s two uncovered linemen stuck on doubles; the pairs can’t move their men and can’t leave them. That is the tite’s answer to inside zone and duo, the double-team runs. (Gap runs like power, as the last section showed, are a fight it wins with technique, not with alignment.)
To beat the reach, line up outside the blockers, and leave no gap empty on the edge. A reach block is hardest when the defender is already a step to the play side of the blocker: a 3-technique outside the guard, a 5 outside the tackle, a 9 or a wide edge outside the tight end. Against outside zone the tite’s problem isn’t that its linemen are easy to reach; the 4i is actually a hard reach for the guard. It is that the C gap is empty, so the play-side tackle is free to help on the edge or climb to the lone linebacker, and that its biggest men have to run sideways. That is why the classic answer to an outside-zone team is a wider front, with shades outside the blockers, often a four-man even front with a 3-technique who can penetrate before the guard’s reach lands, as in Defensive Line Play’s one-gap animation.

The two answers pull in opposite directions, which is why no front stops everything. A tite that pulls its ends inside to choke inside zone has emptied the gaps outside the tackles that outside zone attacks; a wide four-man front that beats the reach leaves the interior gaps to linebackers who can be climbed to. Defenses solve the dilemma in three ways, and you can watch for all of them:

Change the front by opponent. A defense facing an inside-zone and duo team plays a lot of tite; the same defense facing a wide-zone team widens its edges and plays more four-man fronts. Fangio’s own defenses varied in exactly this way: Alexander notes that in Denver Fangio favoured a four-down front more often than his former assistant Staley, who preferred the five-man front.20
Change the front by down, distance and formation. Tite on first-and-10 against two tight ends, four-man front on second-and-long against three receivers.
Change the front after the offense lines up. Shift from one to the other at the last moment, so the offense’s blocking calls are made against the wrong picture. That is the last section of this chapter.

Who, in either front, makes the tackle on the run that gets through? That is the job of the run fits, the full eleven-man accounting of who owns which gap and who forces the ball back inside, in Run Fits and Box Math.
