title: Linebackers: Keys, Flow, Tackling, and the Hardest Job on the Field
text:
Flow: fast and slow
Keys tell a linebacker what the play is. Flow tells him how to move. In coaches’ language, flow is the direction and speed of the backfield action at the snap: where the backs (and, on zone, the whole line) are going, and how fast. Staffs use different words, but nearly all of them sort it into two kinds.


Show the Python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.3))
LAT, WIN = (-8.6, 10.6), (-8.6, 9.2)
off = line("short") + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0, "R")]
# fast flow: outside zone right
p = Play(off, over_front(+1), los=35, to_go=None)
for k in OL_KEYS + ("Y",):
    q = p.players[k]
    go_to(p, k, (q.d + 0.2, q.w + 1.1), "block", speed=2.0)
go_to(p, "QB", (-2.6, 1.6))
go_to(p, "RB", (-1.6, 6.2), "run", via=[(-5.7, 3.0)])
go_to(p, "MIKE", (2.9, 5.0), via=[(4.0, 2.6)])
go_to(p, "WILL", (5.5, -0.5), via=[(5.0, -1.4)])          # shuffle over the top, deeper than the Mike
go_to(p, "SAM", (1.6, 7.9))
f = draw(p, ax=axes[0], lateral=LAT, window=WIN, title=False)
dashed(f, p, [(-2.8, 4.6), (0.0, 1.6), (3.0, 0.0)], color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.2)
say(f, p, 7.1, 4.6, "run with it,\ninside the ball", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.7)
say(f, p, 7.1, -3.6, "Will: over the top,\nbehind the Mike,\nfor the cutback", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK,
    fontsize=6.6)
say(f, p, 2.6, -3.0, "cutback lane", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.4)
title(axes[0], "Fast flow: outside zone")
# slow flow: inside zone right
p = Play(off, over_front(+1), los=35, to_go=None)
for k in OL_KEYS + ("Y",):
    q = p.players[k]
    go_to(p, k, (q.d + 0.5, q.w + 0.4), "block", speed=2.0)
go_to(p, "QB", (-2.6, 0.9))
go_to(p, "RB", (-1.4, 2.3), "run", via=[(-4.6, 1.2)])
go_to(p, "MIKE", (2.5, 1.5))
go_to(p, "WILL", (2.6, -1.4))
f = draw(p, ax=axes[1], lateral=LAT, window=WIN, title=False)
say(f, p, 7.1, 0.0, "press the gap,\nstay square", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.7)
say(f, p, -4.4, 4.6, "downhill at\nthe B gap", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
title(axes[1], "Slow flow: inside zone")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 31.4: Two kinds of flow against a 4-3 Over (the offensive line, the backfield and the linebackers move; the defensive line is left standing). Left, fast flow: outside zone to the right; the line steps sideways and the back sprints flat for the tight end’s outside leg. The Mike runs with it, just behind his line and a step behind the ball; the Will shuffles over the top, deeper than the Mike and behind the end of the cutback lane (dashed blue), so a back who cuts back runs into him; the Sam stays outside the ball to turn it back in. Right, slow flow: inside zone, the back coming straight downhill at the B gap. Both linebackers press forward into their gaps, square to the line, and wait for the back to commit. Running sideways here would open the gap they just left.





Fast flow is the ball going sideways in a hurry: outside zone, a toss, a sweep, the back sprinting flat for the edge. The linebacker’s job is to run with it, and to run with it correctly. Correctly means inside-out: a yard or so behind his own linemen and a step behind the ball, so that the ball is always a little outside him. (You will see the phrase again; it is the linebacker’s master rule.) If the back keeps going, the linebacker can keep up and fill as soon as he turns upfield. If the back stops and cuts back, which is what outside zone is designed to make him do (see Zone Running), the linebacker is still inside him and can stop. The backside linebacker, the Will in Figure 31.4, shuffles over the top: behind the Mike and a little deeper, ending up behind the spot where a cutback would come through. He is the cutback player: if both linebackers race to the sideline, the back has the whole field behind them.
Slow flow is the ball coming straight at the line, or coming slowly: inside zone, an iso, a draw, a delayed handoff, the counter’s first step. Now the linebacker presses: he steps forward into his gap, square to the line, shoulders parallel to it, and makes the back declare first. The worst thing he can do against slow flow is to run sideways, because every inside run is built around a back who reads the linebackers and cuts into the gap one of them just left.
There is a third case, and coaches have a phrase for it: split flow, the backs going in opposite directions (one back left, the other right, or a back one way and the quarterback the other). Split flow is the offense saying misdirection. A linebacker who sees it plays his gap and does not chase either one until the ball shows.

title: Linebackers: Keys, Flow, Tackling, and the Hardest Job on the Field
section: Fitting the run: fill, plug, scrape and run-through
text:
Fitting the run: fill, plug, scrape and run-through
Once a linebacker knows it’s a run and where it’s going, he has to get into the right gap. The defense’s plan for who takes which gap is the run fit, and its full arithmetic is the subject of Run Fits and Box Math. What a linebacker does to get to his gap has four common names, and you will hear all four on broadcasts and in coaches’ interviews.


Show the Python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(6.6, 6.4))
LAT, WIN = (-7.8, 9.4), (-8.2, 8.8)
ofb = line("short") + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0, "Q"), O("FB", "FB", -4.5, 0, "F"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0, "T")]
one = line("short") + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0, "R")]
# fill vs iso: the hole is the strong A gap, open in the Over because the 1 is shaded the other way
p = Play(ofb, over_front(+1), los=35, to_go=None)
p.highlight("MIKE", color=style.DEFENSE)
go_to(p, "C", (-0.2, -0.45), "block"); go_to(p, "RG", (-0.2, 1.95), "block")
go_to(p, "FB", (0.4, 0.9), "run", speed=5.5)
go_to(p, "RB", (-1.4, 0.9), "run", via=[(-4.6, 0.4)])
go_to(p, "MIKE", (1.7, 0.9))
f = draw(p, ax=axes[0, 0], lateral=LAT, window=WIN, title=False)
say(f, p, 6.6, 4.4, "meet the fullback\nin the hole", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.7)
title(axes[0, 0], "Fill")
# plug: the 3-technique slants inside, the Mike plugs the B gap
p = Play(one, over_front(+1, mike_w=2.4), los=35, to_go=None)
p.highlight("MIKE", color=style.DEFENSE)
go_to(p, "DT", (1.0, 0.95))
go_to(p, "MIKE", (2.0, 2.45))
go_to(p, "RB", (-1.6, 2.3), "run", via=[(-4.6, 1.2)])
f = draw(p, ax=axes[0, 1], lateral=LAT, window=WIN, title=False)
gap_tag(f, p, 0.2, 2.45, "B", fontsize=6.6)
say(f, p, 6.6, 4.4, "straight into the\ngap the 3 left", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.7)
point_to(f, p, (2.8, -2.6), (1.25, 1.5), "the 3 slants\ninside", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.4)
title(axes[0, 1], "Plug")
# scrape: the end squeezes, the Mike scrapes outside him
p = Play(one, over_front(+1), los=35, to_go=None)
p.highlight("MIKE", color=style.DEFENSE)
go_to(p, "SE", (0.6, 2.9))
go_to(p, "RB", (-2.6, 6.1), "run", via=[(-5.8, 2.8)])
go_to(p, "MIKE", (2.0, 4.4), via=[(3.9, 2.6)])
go_to(p, "SAM", (1.8, 6.6))
f = draw(p, ax=axes[1, 0], lateral=LAT, window=WIN, title=False)
say(f, p, 6.6, 2.6, "over the top\nof his linemen", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.7)
point_to(f, p, (2.9, -2.4), (0.75, 2.75), "the end\nsqueezes", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.4)
say(f, p, 3.6, 7.6, "Sam:\nD gap", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.2)
title(axes[1, 0], "Scrape")
# run-through: the Will beats the climbing guard through the A gap
p = Play(one, over_front(+1, will_w=-2.5), los=35, to_go=None)
p.highlight("WILL", color=style.DEFENSE)
go_to(p, "WILL", (-2.0, -2.7))
go_to(p, "RB", (-3.6, -2.2), "run", via=[(-5.6, -0.8)])
f = draw(p, ax=axes[1, 1], lateral=LAT, window=WIN, title=False)
dashed(f, p, [(0.2, -1.4), (2.0, -1.6), (3.2, -1.9)], color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.3)
spot(f, p, -2.75, -2.55, ms=8)
say(f, p, 6.6, 3.0, "through the B gap before\nthe guard gets there", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
title(axes[1, 1], "Run-through")
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=0.8, w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 31.5: Four ways a linebacker fits a run (the ringed linebacker acts in each panel). Fill: on an iso the fullback leads into the strong A gap, open in the Over because the nose is shaded the other way, while the center and right guard block the two tackles; the Mike attacks downhill and meets the fullback in the hole, as close to the line as he can. Plug: the 3-technique slants inside, and the Mike, stacked behind him, steps straight forward into the B gap the 3 left, where the back is aiming. Scrape: on an outside run the end squeezes down inside, and the Mike runs sideways behind his linemen to the C gap outside the end, while the Sam keeps the D gap outside him. Run-through: the Will, over the uncovered left guard (the bubble), attacks through the B gap outside the guard at the snap, before the guard can climb to him (dashed blue: where the guard was heading), and meets the back in the backfield (X).






Fill. To fill is to attack downhill into the gap the run is aimed at and meet whatever comes through it, a lead blocker or the back, as close to the line of scrimmage as possible. It is the general verb: “the Mike filled the hole.” The closer to the line he meets the play, the less room the back has to choose a different hole, so coaches measure fills in yards: a fill at the line of scrimmage is a good play even if the linebacker doesn’t make the tackle, because it forces the back to stop or bounce.
Plug. To plug is to step straight forward into a gap directly in front of you and close it with your body. It is the inside linebacker’s partner to the defensive line’s slant (05-01): when the 3-technique slants into the A gap, the B gap he left behind needs a body, and the linebacker stacked behind him plugs it. Plugs are short and violent, and they usually end in a collision with a lineman.
Scrape. To scrape is to run sideways, behind and close to your own defensive linemen (“over the top” of them), to a gap farther outside. It is how a linebacker gets to an outside gap without getting caught in the traffic at the line, and it is the move you saw in fast flow. Scraping linebackers stay square to the line, shuffling or crossing over, so that they can turn upfield and fill the instant the back commits. The defense’s answer to the zone read, below, is built on it.
Run-through. A run-through is the aggressive version of a fill: the linebacker attacks through his gap at the snap (or on his first key), before the blocker assigned to him can climb, and meets the play in the backfield. “Run-through linebacker” is also a compliment, for the kind of player who does it naturally. It wrecks zone schemes, whose climbing linemen need a fraction of a second to come off their double teams, and it makes tackles for loss. It is also the fit most vulnerable to misdirection: a linebacker who runs through a gap on a counter step or a play-action fake is out of the play, or out of his coverage.

The call and the front decide a lot (a defense whose linemen slant and stunt asks its linebackers to plug and scrape behind them; one that wants plays in the backfield against a zone team asks them to run through), but from the couch you can usually match the fit to what the run looks like:







What the run shows the linebacker
The fit it usually calls for




A fullback or lead blocker coming straight at him (iso, lead)
Fill: meet the lead blocker in the hole, at the line


His own lineman slanting away, leaving the gap in front of him empty
Plug that gap


The ball going outside, or the end in front of him squeezing inside (and the zone read, below)
Scrape over the top to the outside gap


Zone blocking, with linemen who need a moment to climb to him, and a call that says go
Run-through before they arrive



The first step, and the block he can’t avoid. None of these starts with a lunge. A linebacker’s first step is a short read step (some coaches say “pop step”): a few inches, downhill, that keeps him moving without committing him. His second step is the one that tells you what he saw. The cardinal sin is the false step, a first step the wrong way, which is exactly what counters and play-action are built to draw. And sometimes a climbing lineman gets to him anyway. Then he does not run around the block, which would open the gap behind him (unless the call tells him to). He meets the blocker with his hands, a punch to the chest, keeps his gap-side arm free, and gets off the block toward his gap. Which shoulder he takes the blocker on with, keeping the ball inside him (box, or squeeze) or bouncing it outside (spill), is a whole-defense decision, and Run Fits and Box Math builds it.






NoteMadden vs. real life



In Madden, the linebacker you control can run anywhere and the computer fills the gap you left. On a real field, every linebacker’s gap is somebody else’s assumption. If the Mike scrapes outside when the call told him to plug, the gap he was supposed to fill is empty, and the defensive lineman next to it, who slanted away because the Mike would be there, is now on the wrong side of the ball. That is why coaches care more about a linebacker being in the right gap than about him making the tackle, and why “he was out of his gap” is one of the harshest things a linebacker coach says on film.



The scrape against the zone read
The scrape has its most famous use against the zone read. On a zone read the offense leaves the backside end unblocked and the quarterback reads him: if he stays wide, hand off; if he crashes down on the back, keep the ball and run where the end was. The defense’s answer, the scrape exchange from Option Football, has the end crash on the back on purpose and the linebacker behind him scrape around him to the spot where the quarterback will keep. The quarterback reads “keep” correctly and runs into the linebacker.
That chapter showed the trade. Here is the linebacker’s side of it, because the scrape is easy to draw and hard to time.


Show the Python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.4))
LAT, WIN = (-13.2, 6.6), (-7.6, 8.4)
off = line("short") + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, -1.9, "R"),
                       O("H", "WR", -1.5, -10.0, "H")]
dfn = nickel_front(mike=(4.7, 1.4), will=(4.7, -2.2)) + [D("NB", "NB", 4.6, -8.0, "$")]
for ax, good in zip(axes, (True, False)):
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    p.highlight("WILL", color=style.DEFENSE)
    go_to(p, "WE", (-2.3, -2.4))
    go_to(p, "RB", (-3.0, 3.4), "run", via=[(-4.0, -0.4)])
    if good:
        go_to(p, "QB", (1.0, -6.6), "run", via=[(-4.3, -2.6), (-2.0, -5.2)])
        go_to(p, "WILL", (0.9, -5.6), via=[(3.3, -4.6)])
        go_to(p, "NB", (2.4, -8.0))
    else:
        go_to(p, "QB", (2.6, -4.3), "run", via=[(-4.3, -2.6), (-1.6, -5.8), (0.2, -5.3)])
        go_to(p, "WILL", (0.6, -8.4), via=[(3.0, -6.0)])
        go_to(p, "NB", (2.6, -9.2))
    f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=LAT, window=WIN, title=False)
    # the left tackle is uncovered (the end he would block is being read), so he climbs to the Will
    dashed(f, p, [(0.1, -3.2), (2.4, -2.9), (3.9, -2.4)], color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.2)
    if good:
        spot(f, p, 1.25, -6.25, ms=8)
        say(f, p, 6.8, -5.4, "tight over the end,\non the QB's inside hip", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
        title(ax, "On time and inside-out")
    else:
        say(f, p, 6.8, -5.4, "too wide, too fast:\nthe QB cuts inside", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
        title(ax, "Overrun")
    say(f, p, -4.6, -9.4, "end crashes:\nQB keeps", color=style.INK_2, fontsize=6.4)
    say(f, p, 2.6, -0.4, "LT climbs", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.2)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 31.6: The Will’s scrape on a zone read, from the linebacker’s side (the line zones right; the quarterback reads the left end, who crashes down on the back, so the quarterback keeps). Left, a good scrape: the Will runs tight over the top of the end, a step behind him, and arrives on the quarterback’s inside hip with the nickel back ($) outside: the keeper has nowhere to go but toward the help. Right, an overrun: the Will scrapes too wide and too fast, gets outside the quarterback, and the quarterback cuts back inside him, into the space the crashing end left. In both, the left tackle (dashed blue), uncovered because the end he would block is being read, climbs toward the spot the Will left: the scrape has to beat him there.





The scraper has three things to get right. Timing: he has to leave at the snap, before the read, because a quarterback keeps the ball and is past the line in about a second and a half. Path: tight to the crashing end, so that the quarterback can’t run between them and the uncovered left tackle, climbing at the snap, can’t get to him first; coaches tell scrapers to “rub the end’s hip.” Leverage: he has to arrive inside the quarterback, on his inside hip, with a teammate (the nickel back or a safety in Figure 31.6) outside, so that the quarterback’s only way out is toward that teammate. An overrun, on the right, is the scraper’s classic mistake: he gets to the spot so eagerly that he passes it, and an athletic quarterback cuts back underneath him into the hole the end left. Offenses fight back by giving the scraper something else to worry about, like a tight end or H-back who arcs around the end to block him, which is why the scrape exchange is a call the defense mixes in, not something it can do every snap.

title: Linebackers: Keys, Flow, Tackling, and the Hardest Job on the Field
text:
Getting there: pursuit angles
Most runs don’t end in the hole. The back gets through, or bounces outside, and the play becomes a footrace in which several defenders who started in different places converge on one runner. How they converge is the difference between a five-yard gain and a fifty-yard one.
A pursuit angle is the path a defender takes to a ball carrier who is already moving. The instinct, for anyone who has never been coached, is to run at the runner. That is almost always wrong.


Show the Python
def intercept(R0, vR, L0, sL):
    """Earliest time t at which a defender from L0 at speed sL can reach the runner R0 + vR t."""
    d = np.asarray(R0, float) - np.asarray(L0, float)
    a = vR @ vR - sL ** 2
    b = 2 * d @ vR
    c = d @ d
    if abs(a) < 1e-9:
        return -c / b
    disc = b * b - 4 * a * c
    ts = [(-b - np.sqrt(disc)) / (2 * a), (-b + np.sqrt(disc)) / (2 * a)]
    return min(t for t in ts if t > 0)


R0, L0 = np.array([0.5, 6.0]), np.array([2.0, 1.5])
uR = np.array([1.0, 0.45]) / np.hypot(1.0, 0.45)
vR, sL = 7.0 * uR, 7.5
inside = np.array([-0.45, -0.9])                     # meet him a step inside, not on his outside hip
t_meet = intercept(R0 + inside, vR, L0, sL)
MEET = R0 + vR * t_meet + inside
# the chase: always aimed at the runner's current spot
dt, chase = 0.01, [L0.copy()]
for k in range(int(1.9 / dt)):
    tgt = R0 + vR * (k * dt)
    v = tgt - chase[-1]
    chase.append(chase[-1] + sL * dt * v / np.linalg.norm(v))
chase = np.array(chase)
# keep chasing (off the picture) until he is within arm's reach (1 yard): when, and how far downfield?
c_, t_ = chase[-1].copy(), len(chase) * dt
while np.linalg.norm(R0 + vR * t_ - c_) > 1.0:
    v = R0 + vR * t_ - c_
    c_ += sL * dt * v / np.linalg.norm(v)
    t_ += dt
CATCH_T, CATCH_D = t_, (R0 + vR * t_)[0]
GAP = {t: float(np.linalg.norm(R0 + vR * t - chase[int(round(t / dt))])) for t in (0.5, 1.0, 1.5)}
# the overrun: aimed too far ahead, so that he arrives outside the back
over_end = R0 + vR * t_meet + np.array([-0.6, 3.4])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.4, 4.9))
p = Play([O("RB", "RB", R0[0], R0[1], "R")],
         [D("MIKE", "LB", L0[0], L0[1], "M"), D("CB", "CB", 8.0, 15.5, "CB")], los=35, to_go=None)
f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-3.0, 19.0), window=(-2.4, 15.0), title=False)
P = lambda q: _P(f, p, q[0], q[1])  # noqa: E731
rb_end = R0 + vR * 1.8
solid(f, p, [tuple(R0), tuple(rb_end)], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=2.4)
xs, ys = _P(f, p, chase[:, 0], chase[:, 1])
ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.MUTED, lw=1.6, zorder=4)
solid(f, p, [tuple(L0), tuple(MEET)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.8)
dashed(f, p, [tuple(L0), tuple(over_end)], color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, lw=1.3)
cut0 = R0 + vR * (t_meet + 0.05)
dashed(f, p, [tuple(cut0), tuple(cut0 + np.array([3.6, -2.6]))], color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.3)
for k in range(1, 4):                       # half-second ticks
    t = 0.5 * k
    for q, col in ((R0 + vR * t, style.OFFENSE_DARK), (chase[min(int(t / dt), len(chase) - 1)], style.MUTED)):
        x, y = P(q)
        ax.plot([x], [y], marker="o", ms=3.2, color=col, zorder=6)
    if t < t_meet:
        x, y = P(L0 + (MEET - L0) * t / t_meet)
        ax.plot([x], [y], marker="o", ms=3.2, color=style.DEFENSE, zorder=6)
for t in (0.5, 1.0, 1.5):                   # same moment, two men: how far apart the chaser still is
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = P(R0 + vR * t), P(chase[int(round(t / dt))])
    ax.plot([x0, x1], [y0, y1], color=style.INK_2, lw=0.8, ls=(0, (1, 1.2)), zorder=5.5)
    xr, yr = P(R0 + vR * t + np.array([0.0, 0.9]))
    ax.text(xr, yr, f"{t:.1f} s: {GAP[t]:.1f} yd", fontsize=6.0, color=style.INK_2, ha="left", va="center",
            zorder=9, bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.12", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.85))
spot(f, p, MEET[0], MEET[1], ms=9)
solid(f, p, [(8.0, 14.6), (MEET[0] + 1.6, MEET[1] + 2.2)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.4)
point_to(f, p, (2.0, 11.4), tuple(chase[45]), "chase (grey):\naimed at the man", color=style.INK_2, fontsize=6.8)
say(f, p, MEET[0] - 0.4, MEET[1] - 4.6, "angle: aimed where\nhe will be, a step inside", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK,
    fontsize=6.8)
say(f, p, over_end[0] - 1.9, over_end[1] + 1.2, "overrun", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
say(f, p, cut0[0] + 4.4, cut0[1] - 2.8, "cutback", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
say(f, p, 12.7, 15.6, "leverage player:\nstays outside", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
say(f, p, -0.9, 9.4, "the back bounces\noutside", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()








Figure 31.7: Pursuit angles (geometry computed for a back running 7 yards a second as he comes out of his cut and a linebacker running 7.5; dots on each path mark every 0.5 seconds). The back has bounced outside to the right and turned upfield; the Mike starts inside him and a little downfield. Grey, the chase: aimed at where the back is at every instant. The dotted ties join where the two men are at the same moment, labelled with the time and the gap: he is still two yards behind after a second and a half. (The grey path crosses the back’s, but later, after the back has gone.) He doesn’t get within reach until well past 20 yards downfield. Orange, the angle: aimed at where the back will be, a step inside him, he meets him at the X after about a second and a quarter. Dashed orange, the overrun: aimed too flat and too far outside, he gets outside the ball, and the back cuts back inside him (dashed blue) into open field. The cornerback (CB) is the leverage player: he stays outside the back and squeezes him inside, toward the Mike.





Figure 31.7 makes the point with real geometry. A linebacker who runs at the back (the grey path) is always aiming at a spot the back has already left. In this example the linebacker is the faster man, and he is still two yards behind after a second and a half; he gets within arm’s reach only after 3.6 seconds, 23 yards downfield. Against a back who is as fast as he is, or faster, which in the open field is most backs, he never catches him at all. A linebacker who aims at where the back will be (orange) cuts the distance he has to run and meets the back in about a second and a quarter. That is a pursuit angle. The catch is the dashed path: aim too far ahead, and the linebacker gets outside the back, who simply plants his foot and cuts back behind him. Every defender who has been run past has done one of those two things: chased, or overrun.
The rule coaches give for it is inside-out again: take the angle that keeps the ball carrier a step outside you, never inside. If you are inside him, he can only go one way, outside, and outside is where the next defender is.
That next defender is the leverage player: the man on the outside whose job is to keep the ball inside, turning the runner back toward the pursuit. In Figure 31.7 it is the cornerback; on other plays it is the end who set the edge, an outside linebacker, a safety who came down. (The defense names him in advance, as its force player, in Run Fits and Box Math.) Put the two together and you have the shape of good team pursuit: one defender outside the ball, squeezing it in, and everyone else inside-out on it, each a little deeper and farther inside than the man in front, so that whichever way the runner cuts, someone is already there. Coaches drill it constantly, and it is one of the clearest things you can see on the end-zone replay: on a good defense, the arrows all converge.

section: Tackling, and why tackles get missed at the second level
text:
Tackling, and why tackles get missed at the second level
Then the linebacker has to bring the man down. Tackling has changed more in the last decade than in the fifty years before it, for two reasons: safety, and the realization that the old way missed too many tackles.
The old way, the one a lot of fans still picture, was a head-on collision: eyes up, head across the runner’s body (“head across the bow”), drive through him. It produces highlight hits. It also uses the head as the first point of contact, and it fails whenever the runner moves at the last moment, because a tackler who commits his whole body to one spot can’t adjust.
The modern approach is leverage tackling, and its most influential teachers were Pete Carroll’s Seattle Seahawks. In 2014 they made a 20-minute instructional video of their shoulder tackling, borrowed from rugby, and that August the league sent it, with a letter from Carroll, to coaches and parents at every level of the game; a second video in 2015 named its basic tackle the hawk tackle.3 The ideas fit together:

Leverage first. The tackler approaches with the runner on one side of him, usually inside-out, so the runner’s only escape is toward the sideline and the next defender. The pursuit angle in Figure 31.7 is the start of the tackle, not something separate from it.
The near shoulder to the near thigh. The target is the runner’s thighs (“eyes through the thighs,” in Seattle’s coaching points), not his chest; the shoulder makes contact and the head goes to the side, behind the runner on a tackle from an angle, out of the line of contact. The legs are what carry the ball, and they can’t dodge as easily as a torso can.
Wrap and roll. Arms around the thighs, keep the feet moving, and roll the runner to the ground, taking him toward the help rather than trying to drive him backward.
Breakdown in space. Within a couple of yards of the runner, the tackler shortens his steps and lowers his hips, so he can move either way with the runner’s last cut.

The rules have pushed in the same direction. In March 2024 the league banned the hip-drop tackle, in which a tackler grabs a runner from behind and swings his hips and weight down onto the runner’s legs, with a 15-yard penalty; the details are in Contact Rules and Penalties.4 For the 2026 season the league and the players’ union added a three-strike system: a player called for three of five fouls (hip-drop, horse-collar, launching, hits on a defenseless player and blindside blocks) in a season is suspended for a game.5 Most of those fouls are committed by defenders tackling in pursuit, which is the linebacker’s daily life.

Why the second level is where tackles are made, and missed
Where on the field do linebackers actually tackle people? nflverse’s play-by-play records who made the tackle on every play, so we can ask the data. Figure 31.8 sorts every designed run from 2021 to 2025 by how far the runner got before he was brought down, and shows who made the tackle.


Show the Python

ax.axvspan(1.5, 4.5, color=style.GRID, alpha=0.55, lw=0, zorder=0)
order = ["Defensive line", "Outside linebacker (mostly edge)", "Inside linebacker", "Defensive back"]

        "Inside linebacker": style.SERIES[1], "Defensive back": style.SERIES[0]}

           "Outside linebacker (mostly edge)": SHARE["Outside linebacker (mostly edge)"].values[-1] + 1.0,

for g in order:

    ax.text(xs[-1] + 0.15, LABEL_Y.get(g, SHARE[g].values[-1]), g, va="center", fontsize=7.4, color=style.INK_2)
ax.set_xticks(xs, BIN_LABELS)
ax.set_xlabel("Yards gained on the run")
ax.set_ylabel("Share of tackles (%)")

ax.set_ylim(0, 85)
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
ax.text(3.0, 80, "the second level (3-9 yards)", ha="center", fontsize=7.6, color=style.INK_2)
ax.spines["left"].set_visible(False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 31.8: Who makes the tackle, by how far the run got. Every regular-season designed run from 2021 to 2025 that ended in a tackle (no scrambles, touchdowns or penalties), grouped by the yards gained, with the share of tackles made by each position group (the first tackler listed in nflverse play-by-play, matched to the team’s roster position that season). Inside linebackers are those listed ILB, MLB or LB; outside linebackers are those listed OLB, mostly 3-4 edge rushers but also some off-ball 4-3 outside linebackers, so the inside-linebacker line is a floor for off-ball linebackers. The defensive line makes most of the tackles at or near the line. The inside linebackers’ share holds at a fifth to a quarter out to 9 yards and peaks on runs of 5 to 9, as the line’s share collapses. Past 10 yards it is the defensive backs’ tackle.





Read the chart from left to right and you can watch the three levels hand the runner along. Runs stopped at or near the line are the defensive line’s: about two in five of those tackles. The inside linebackers’ share barely moves, a fifth to a quarter of the tackles on every run up to 9 yards, and it peaks, at about a quarter, on runs of 5 to 9 yards, just where the line’s share collapses. They never top the chart, because they share the second level with everyone else who flows to the ball, and because the roster labels undercount them. Past 10 yards the run has beaten them, and it is a defensive back’s tackle. Across all runs, inside linebackers made 22% of the tackles; their median tackle came on a run of 3 yards, against 2 for linemen and 5 for defensive backs.6
One thing in the chart deserves a second look: defensive backs already make 31% of the tackles on runs of only 5 or 6 yards. Those tackles split almost evenly among cornerbacks (39%), free safeties (31%) and strong safeties (30%). The corners are the leverage players on outside runs, turning the ball back in, as in Figure 31.7; the safeties are the eighth man in the box when a single-high defense rotates one down, or the “big nickel” safety playing linebacker. The second level isn’t only linebackers any more, which is where the end of this chapter is heading.
The chart is also a warning about the statistic fans quote most. A linebacker’s tackle total counts every tackle the same, but a tackle five yards downfield is a run that beat the defense first, and the best fill of the game, the one that meets the fullback at the line and makes the back bounce into a teammate, often goes in the box score under someone else’s name. Coaches grade linebackers on whether they were in their gap on time; the tackle is a by-product.
Missed tackles are not in the play-by-play, but Pro Football Reference charts them for every defender, and nflverse carries the numbers. Per hundred tackle attempts from 2021 to 2025 (runs and passes together), defensive linemen missed 7.2, inside linebackers 7.5, outside linebackers 8.4, safeties 8.5 and cornerbacks 9.9.7 The farther from the line a defender usually tackles, the more often he misses. A lineman tackles a back who is still in a crowd, barely moving, with nowhere to go. Past the line the runner is moving at full speed, with room to cut both ways, and the tackler is often coming off a block, from an angle, alone. The runner chooses his cut after seeing the tackler commit; the tackler has to commit first.
Two things stand out. Inside linebackers make their tackles in far more space than linemen do and miss barely more often: that is what leverage tackling, and all the drilling behind it, buys. (Take away one direction with your angle, and you only have to win the other.) And the misses that hurt are the ones past the line, because the cost of a miss grows with the space behind it: a lineman who misses leaves the back a crowd, a linebacker who misses leaves him a safety ten yards away.
For a play-by-play look, the 2024 Big Data Bowl was about tackling, and its data marks every missed tackle on nine weeks of 2022 plays. This chapter’s source includes code (not run here, because the data isn’t downloaded) that counts missed-tackle rates by position from it.


Show the Python (missed tackles by position, Big Data Bowl 2024 data; not run here)

                                   missed=("pff_missedTackle", "sum"))

title: Linebackers: Keys, Flow, Tackling, and the Hardest Job on the Field
text:
Linebackers in coverage
Half the snaps in a game are passes, and on most of them the linebackers are in coverage. Their jobs fall into three families.

Zone: the hook/curl defender
In zone coverage, the linebacker drops to an area. The most common linebacker zone is the one between the offensive tackle and the numbers, about 8 to 12 yards deep, which combines the hook zone over the tackles and the curl zone outside it (both defined in Coverage Fundamentals). A linebacker who drops there is a hook / curl defender.


Show the Python
off = line("short") + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, -1.6, "R"),
                       O("X", "WR", -0.7, -16.0, "X"), O("H", "WR", -1.5, -9.0, "H"),
                       O("Y", "TE", -1.5, 9.0, "Y"), O("Z", "WR", -0.7, 16.0, "Z")]
dfn = nickel_front(mike=(4.6, 1.4), will=(4.6, -1.8)) + [
    D("NB", "NB", 5.0, -7.6, "$"), D("SS", "S", 6.5, 10.6, "SS"), D("FS", "S", 14.0, 0.0, "FS"),
    D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -16.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 16.0, "CB")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
p.dropback(2.0)
p.route("X", r.go(16)); p.route("Z", r.go(16))
go_to(p, "H", (17.0, -8.2), "route", via=[(4.0, -8.9)])        # the seam
go_to(p, "Y", (6.4, 4.4), "route", via=[(2.4, 9.0)])           # the slant
p.drop("WILL", (8.2, -5.8), zone=(6.0, 7.0), label="hook/curl")
p.drop("MIKE", (7.6, 5.0), zone=(6.0, 7.0), label="hook/curl")
p.drop("FS", (17.5, 0.0)); p.drop("LCB", (16.0, -15.0)); p.drop("RCB", (16.0, 15.0))
p.drop("NB", (6.0, -12.0)); p.drop("SS", (6.0, 13.0))
p.highlight("MIKE", "WILL", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, width_in=6.3, lateral=(-19.4, 19.4), window=(-7.4, 20.2), title=False)
dashed(f, p, [(8.4, -6.1), (11.0, -7.0), (13.4, -7.3)], color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, lw=1.4)
say(f, p, 14.4, -4.4, "Will: carry the\nseam to ~12 yd", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
say(f, p, 12.4, 8.4, "Mike: wall the slant,\nthen sink, eyes on the QB", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()








Figure 31.9: Two linebackers as hook/curl defenders in Cover 3 against a 2x2 formation. Cover 3 has three deep defenders, each taking a third of the field (here the two cornerbacks and the free safety, drawn without zones), and four underneath. On the pass read the Mike and the Will drop to their zones (shaded), about 8 to 10 yards deep, from just outside the offensive tackles toward the slot receivers, opening their hips toward the slot on their side and reading the quarterback. The Mike walls Y’s slant: he gets into its path, so the throw has to go around him. The Will’s slot receiver, H, runs straight up the seam, so the Will carries him (dashed) to about 12 yards, until the free safety can take over. Then both sink under the curls, eyes on the quarterback.





The hook/curl defender’s job is a sequence. First, wall: get in the path of the slot receiver’s inside route, so the slant or the dig has to go around him. If the slot runs straight up the seam instead, carry him: run with him, inside and underneath, until a deep defender can take over, about 10 to 12 yards downfield. Four receivers running deep against Cover 3’s three deep thirds is the classic way to beat it, and the hook/curl linebacker’s seam carry is what stops it. Then, sink: as the outside receivers push deep, back up under the curls and comebacks. All the while, eyes on the quarterback, because a zone defender breaks on the throw, not on the receiver. Linebackers in modern NFL defenses rarely drop to a fixed spot and wait; most play some version of pattern matching, zone that turns into man coverage on whichever receiver enters his area. The Cover 3 and Tampa 2 chapters show the most demanding linebacker drops: in Tampa 2, the Mike runs straight down the middle of the field to take away the seam, 15 or 20 yards deep.
The model hook defender of the last decade was Seattle’s Bobby Wagner, the Mike in the 2013 Seahawks’ Cover 3, behind the Under front of Even Fronts and in front of a secondary nicknamed the “Legion of Boom.” Watch his early-down drops in Super Bowl XLVIII, a 43–8 win over Denver in which he made ten tackles: how fast he gets depth, how he walls the crossing routes, and then how his run fills come square and downhill. He went on to six first-team All-Pro selections, more than two thousand career tackles, and the 2025 Walter Payton Man of the Year award, playing for Washington.8


Man: the back and the tight end, and the hole
In man coverage the linebacker is usually assigned the running back or a tight end. This is where a linebacker is most exposed. Running backs are quicker than he is and have the whole width of the field; tight ends are often as fast as he is and bigger. Offenses build plays specifically to get the back in a route against a linebacker in space, like the angle route (a fake to the outside and a break back inside), and to put a fast tight end on a slow linebacker.


Show the Python

                       O("X", "WR", -0.7, -16.0, "X"), O("H", "WR", -1.5, -9.0, "H"),
                       te(+1), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 15.0, "Z")]
dfn = nickel_front(mike=(4.6, 1.2), will=(4.6, -2.0)) + [
    D("NB", "NB", 2.0, -9.0, "$"), D("SS", "S", 6.0, 6.2, "SS"), D("FS", "S", 14.0, 0.0, "FS"),
    D("LCB", "CB", 2.0, -16.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 2.0, 15.0, "CB")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
for d_, rec in (("LCB", "X"), ("NB", "H"), ("SS", "Y"), ("RCB", "Z"), ("WILL", "RB")):
    p.man(d_, rec)
p.drop("MIKE", (10.0, 0.0), zone=(6.0, 9.0), label="hole")
p.highlight("MIKE", "WILL", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, width_in=6.3, lateral=(-19.4, 19.4), window=(-7.4, 17.6), title=False)
say(f, p, 7.4, -7.0, "Will: man\non the back", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
say(f, p, 12.4, 8.8, "Mike: rob the\nmiddle, read the QB", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()








Figure 31.10: Two linebacker jobs in man coverage (Cover 1: one deep safety, everyone else in man). The Will has the running back (dotted line): if the back runs a route, the Will covers him; if the back stays in to block, many defenses let the Will add himself to the rush (a ‘green dog’ or ‘hug’). The Mike has no receiver. He drops to the hole, the middle of the field about 8 to 15 yards deep, reads the quarterback and drives on anything thrown in front of him: the crossing route or the dig that beats man coverage underneath.





The third family is the job in Figure 31.10: the linebacker with nobody to cover. In man coverage with one deep safety, the defense often has a spare man, and it can put him in the hole zone, the middle of the field 8 to 15 yards deep, as a robber (also called the rat). Staffs use the two words loosely, but many say rat for a low hole player, about 5 to 8 yards deep, sitting on crossers, usually a linebacker, and robber for a deeper one, 10 to 12 yards deep, jumping digs and in-cuts, usually a safety. Crossing routes and digs are how offenses beat man coverage, and they arrive right there. A linebacker who reads the quarterback well can make a career out of that spot; Luke Kuechly made a good part of his there.


Play-action, revisited
Play-Action, Boots, and Screens showed play-action from the offense’s side: a fake run that pulls the linebackers forward, and a throw into the space behind them. Now that you know what a linebacker looks at, you can see why it works, and what the good ones do about it.
The fake is aimed at his keys, his run-fit triggers. The linemen fire out low, like a run. The back runs his run path. The quarterback reaches the ball toward him. Every key says run. But one key can’t say it completely, because of a rule: on a pass, an offensive lineman may not be more than a yard downfield when the ball is thrown. So on play-action, the linemen who would climb to the linebackers on the real run can’t. They block at the line and stay there. A linebacker who keys the back sees a run. A linebacker who keys the uncovered guard, the man who should be coming for him on a run, sees a guard who fires out and then doesn’t come. That is the tell.


Show the Python
def pa_play(keys_guard):
    off = line("short") + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0.0, "R")]
    dfn = nickel_front(mike=(4.5, 1.8), will=(4.5, -1.0), wide_ends=False)
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    for k in OL_KEYS:                                         # run-action: low first step, then hold
        q = p.players[k]
        go_to(p, k, (q.d + 0.4, q.w + 0.35), "block", speed=1.8)
    for k, end in (("WE", (1.1, -4.0)), ("DT", (1.1, -2.1)), ("NT", (1.1, 1.0)), ("SE", (1.1, 4.1))):
        go_to(p, k, end, speed=0.8)
    go_to(p, "QB", (-2.7, 1.0), speed=3.0)
    go_to(p, "QB", (-7.0, 0.3), speed=4.6)
    go_to(p, "RB", (-1.2, 3.4), "run", speed=5.5, via=[(-4.2, 2.2)])
    go_to(p, "Y", (12.2, -7.5), "route", speed=7.0, via=[(4.6, 4.7), (11.6, 0.0)])
    go_to(p, "WILL", (9.4, -4.4), delay=0.45, speed=4.8)
    if keys_guard:
        go_to(p, "MIKE", (4.3, 1.9), speed=0.8, delay=0.1)
        go_to(p, "MIKE", (10.0, 0.4), speed=5.0, delay=0.1)
    else:
        go_to(p, "MIKE", (3.0, 2.6), speed=3.2, delay=0.2)
        go_to(p, "MIKE", (5.9, 0.6), speed=4.0, delay=0.3)
    p.pass_to("Y", t=2.0)
    return p


P_PA_BACK, P_PA_GUARD = pa_play(False), pa_play(True)


def pa_marks(fld, play, t, i):
    if t < 0.05:
        key = "RG" if play is P_PA_GUARD else "RB"
        eyes(fld, play, play.position("MIKE", t), play.position(key, t))
    if play is P_PA_GUARD:                    # the key: the right guard, ringed; he never gets past the line
        d, w = play.position("RG", t)
        x, y = _P(fld, play, d, w)
        fld.ax.add_patch(Circle((float(x), float(y)), 0.95, fc="none", ec=GREEN, lw=1.6, zorder=7.5))
        if t > 0.5:
            point_to(fld, play, (2.9, w + 0.6), (d + 0.6, w), "no climb", color=GREEN, fontsize=6.4, shrink=2)
    if t >= 2.0:                              # the throw
        q, y_ = play.position("QB", 2.0), play.position("Y", t + 0.3)
        dashed(fld, play, [tuple(q), tuple(y_)], color=style.BALL, lw=1.2)


animation_or_strip(
    [(P_PA_BACK, 0.0, "keys the back"), (P_PA_BACK, 0.9, ""), (P_PA_BACK, 2.3, ""),
     (P_PA_GUARD, 0.0, "keys the guard"), (P_PA_GUARD, 0.9, ""), (P_PA_GUARD, 2.3, "")],
    notes=["eyes on the back", "the back fakes zone:\nthe Mike steps up", "five yards deep: Y is\nbehind him",
           "eyes on the right guard", "guard fires out, but no\nclimb: not a run", "ten yards deep, in the\ncrosser's path"],
    rings=(("MIKE", style.DEFENSE),), lateral=(-9.0, 7.6), window=(-7.9, 15.4), after=pa_marks,
    ncols=3, width_in=6.2)





  
  Your browser does not support the video tag.



Figure 31.11: Play-action from the linebacker’s side (simulated, BDB-format tracking). The same play twice: an inside-zone fake to the right and a tight end (Y) running a deep crossing route behind the linebackers, against a 4-2-5 whose Mike (ringed) is over the uncovered right guard. Top row: this Mike keys the back. 1: eyes on the back. 2: the back takes the fake, so the Mike steps up to fill. 3: when the ball is thrown he is five or six yards deep, and Y is behind him. Bottom row: this Mike keys the right guard (green ring). 1: eyes on the guard. 2: the guard fires out but stays at the line instead of climbing to him (a lineman may not go downfield on a pass): no climb, so not a run, and the Mike gets depth. 3: he is about ten yards deep, in the crossing route’s path, as the ball is thrown (dashed brown: the throw). The Will drops the same way in both rows; the text says why.




Two things in Figure 31.11 are worth remembering. First, the linebacker who keys the back is not a bad linebacker; he is doing exactly what he is trained to do against the run, and on most snaps it is the right call. That is why, as 04-05 showed, play-action works about as well for teams that run the ball badly as for teams that run it well: the linebacker is reacting to action, not to statistics. Second, the cure is in the keys, and it costs something. A linebacker who waits for the guard to climb is a fraction of a second slower on every real run. Defenses decide, sometimes play by play, which mistake they would rather make: in obvious running situations the linebackers trigger fast, and in play-action situations (first down and second-and-short, the shot zones near midfield, against a team that loves the fake) they read a beat longer.
The Will in Figure 31.11 is drawn the same way in both rows, for a reason: the fake goes away from him, and a backside linebacker’s run job is to shuffle over the top and wait for the cutback, so a fake to the other side moves him less. The test, and the cost, fall on the Mike.

title: Linebackers: Keys, Flow, Tackling, and the Hardest Job on the Field
text:
Linebackers as pressure players
The last job is going forward on a pass play. Linebackers have traditionally been the most common extra rushers, the blitzers, because they start close to the line and in the middle, where a rusher reaches the quarterback fastest (modern defenses send their nickel backs and safeties too). Their pressure roles, all built in Part 7, come in a few recognizable shapes:

The A-gap blitz. Both inside linebackers walk up into the gaps on either side of the center before the snap, the double A-gap mug, threatening the quickest path to the quarterback. The offense has to account for both; the defense may send both, one, or neither and drop them into coverage at the snap (Blitz and Man Pressure).
The green dog (or hug, or add-on). A linebacker assigned to cover the running back who, when the back stays in to block, rushes instead: there is nobody left for him to cover.
The simulated pressure. A linebacker rushes while a defensive lineman drops into coverage, so the offense sees five threats but gets four rushers from unexpected places: simulated pressure, in Zone Blitz and Simulated Pressure.
The spy. Against a quarterback who runs, a linebacker is assigned to mirror him, staying at linebacker depth and following him wherever he goes: a spy, covered in Third Down. Against the fastest quarterbacks, teams often spy with a safety or the nickel back instead, for the same speed reason the Sam lost his job.

Every one of these trades coverage for pressure, or pressure for coverage, and the linebacker is the piece the defense moves to make the trade.

section: The part-time Sam and the safety-sized linebacker
text:
The part-time Sam and the safety-sized linebacker
Put the jobs together, the run fits, the zone drops, the man coverage on backs and tight ends, the blitzes, and you can see the problem the modern NFL created for linebackers. Offenses spread out. The more snaps an offense plays with three wide receivers, the more snaps one of those receivers is in the slot, and the more often the defense has to choose between a linebacker who walks out over him (Figure 31.2) and a defensive back who replaces that linebacker.
For most of the last two decades, defenses chose the defensive back. By Pro Football Focus’s count, base defense (four defensive backs, three linebackers) was on the field for 54% of plays in 2008 and 45% in 2011, and by 2014 defenses had five or more defensive backs out for more than 60% of plays.9 The linebacker they removed was usually the Sam, the strong-side linebacker built to take on tight ends and fullbacks, because the 11-personnel offenses that spread the field had one tight end and no fullback for him to take on. The nickel package, five defensive backs and two linebackers, became the real base defense of the NFL, as A First Look at Defense showed.


Show the Python

    ax.plot(PKG.index, PKG[k], marker="o", ms=3, lw=2.2 if k == "base" else 1.6, color=c)

Figure 31.12: Two trends. Left: how many defensive backs NFL defenses had on the field, as a share of regular-season snaps (nflverse participation data; 2016-2022 from NFL Next Gen Stats personnel labels, 2023-2025 counted from FTN’s position lists, so the dashed line marks a change of source). Base defense, four defensive backs and so three linebackers, fell to about a fifth of snaps by 2023 and came back to about 30% in 2025, as offenses returned to two-tight-end sets. Right: the average NFL Combine weight of off-ball linebackers by draft class (2000-2018: players listed as inside linebackers; 2019 on: players listed as linebackers, with edge rushers listed separately; the 2020 and 2021 classes are left out because their data lumps edge rushers in with linebackers). The labels changed in 2019 too, so read the trend, not the step.





The left half of Figure 31.12 picks the story up in 2016, after that big drop, and its most recent chapter is a partial rebound. In 2016 base defense was on the field for 31% of snaps; by 2023 it was down to 22%. Then it came back: 31% in 2025, close to the 29.7% Next Gen Stats measured, because offenses returned to two-tight-end and fullback sets and defenses answered with bigger personnel.10 The Sam didn’t disappear; he became a part-time player.
The other half of the story is the linebackers who stayed. If two linebackers are going to be on the field for most snaps, and those two have to cover running backs and tight ends in space as well as fill gaps, teams want them faster, and faster usually means lighter. The right half of Figure 31.12 shows the trend at the NFL Combine. Off-ball linebackers in the 2000–2009 draft classes averaged 242 pounds and ran the 40-yard dash in 4.75 seconds; the classes since 2019 have averaged 233 pounds and 4.60 seconds.11 Nine or ten pounds and a tenth and a half of a second doesn’t sound like much. At the second level it is the difference between running with a running back and watching him.
The clearest sign of the shift is where some linebackers come from. In 2015 the Arizona Cardinals moved Deone Bucannon, a safety they had drafted in the first round a year earlier, to inside linebacker, at about 211 pounds. Their depth chart listed him as “$ILB,” and the coaches called him the moneybacker: a safety’s speed and coverage in a linebacker’s spot, playing the run by beating blockers to the hole rather than taking them on.12 Other teams followed with safety-sized linebackers and linebacker-sized safeties, until in some defenses the line between the two positions is mostly a matter of which word is on the depth chart. The big nickel of A First Look at Defense, with a third safety in the box, is the same idea from the other direction.
What the safety-sized linebacker gives up is the thing the Sam was built for: taking on a fullback or a pulling guard in the hole and holding his ground. A 215-pound linebacker who has to stand still and absorb a 315-pound guard loses. So the modern linebacker is coached to not stand still: to beat the blocker to the spot, or run through the gap before he arrives, the fits from earlier in this chapter. The best of today’s linebackers combine both. San Francisco’s Fred Warner, a third-round pick in 2018 and first-team All-Pro in 2020, 2022, 2023 and 2024, is about 6-foot-3 and 230 pounds: the coverage linebacker teams hoped the safety-sized linebacker would be, in a full-sized body. Watch him carry a tight end up the seam in his zone drops, the hook/curl seam carry of Figure 31.9, and then fill against the run.13 And when offenses go heavy, with two tight ends and a fullback, as many did again in 2025, defenses bring back a third linebacker, or a bigger one. The Sam isn’t extinct. He is a specialist who comes in when the offense does.






CautionCommon misconception



“Linebackers are the defense’s run-stoppers; the defensive backs cover.” In the modern NFL the two off-ball linebackers are on the field for most passing snaps and are in coverage on most of them, against running backs, tight ends and slot receivers. A linebacker who cannot cover cannot stay on the field, however well he tackles. That, more than anything, is what has changed about the position.

section: The green dot: the defense’s quarterback
text:
The green dot: the defense’s quarterback
One linebacker usually has one more job, and it starts before anyone moves. Since 2008 NFL rules have allowed one defensive player on the field to have a radio speaker in his helmet, the way quarterbacks have since 1994; the owners approved it by a single vote over the required majority.14 That player wears the green dot sticker you met in What a Play Really Is, and the radio cuts off with 15 seconds on the play clock. On most teams, he is the Mike.


Show the Python
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(6.6, 3.9))
axf = fig.add_axes([0.0, 0.0, 0.56, 1.0])
off = line("short") + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, -1.6, "R"), te(+1),
                       O("H", "WR", -1.5, 10.0, "H"), O("Z", "WR", -0.7, 15.0, "Z"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -15.0, "X")]
dfn = nickel_front(mike=(4.7, 1.4), will=(4.7, -1.8)) + [
    D("NB", "NB", 4.8, 7.8, "$"), D("SS", "S", 8.0, 5.0, "SS"), D("FS", "S", 13.0, -2.0, "FS"),
    D("LCB", "CB", 6.5, -15.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, 15.0, "CB")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
p.highlight("MIKE", color=GREEN)
f = draw(p, ax=axf, width_in=3.7, lateral=(-17.6, 17.6), window=(-7.4, 16.4), title=False)
point_to(f, p, (9.6, -6.0), (5.0, 1.0), "green dot:\n\"Strength right! Under!\"", color=GREEN, fontsize=7.0, shrink=8)
say(f, p, -3.6, 9.6, "TE and trips: strong side", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)

         ("Strength", "\"Strength right!\" Where is the\nTE? The trips? Sets every rule."),

         ("Coverage", "Who has whom: the trips, the\nback, the tight end."),

Figure 31.13: What the green-dot linebacker does before a snap (an illustrative sequence; the words differ from team to team). Against a trips formation with the tight end attached on the right, the Mike (green ring) hears the call in his helmet and relays it, then sets the defense to the formation he sees: the strength, the front, the coverage, then any adjustment to a motion or shift, and the alerts from the week’s film study.





What does he actually do with it?

He relays the call. The defensive coordinator calls the front, the coverage and any pressure into one helmet. The green dot passes it to the other ten, in a huddle or with hand signals, before the radio goes dead.
He sets the strength. Every rule in the call depends on which side is “strong,” and the strength depends on what the offense shows: the tight end, the trips side, the running back, or the wide side of the field. The green dot decides and shouts it, and the front sets off his word, the way Even Fronts showed. The hard part is that many defenses set the front to the tight end (or the back) and the coverage to the receivers. In Figure 31.13 they agree; against trips with the tight end on the other side they don’t, and he has to call both: “Front left, coverage right.”
He adjusts to what the offense does. When the offense shifts or sends a man in motion, the strength may change, and with it the front and the coverage rules. With the radio already off, the green dot is the one who re-sets everyone, in a second or two, with a word. (If the offense substitutes after the radio has cut out, a new call comes from the sideline by hand signal, and he passes it on.)
He makes the alerts. Linebackers study opponents’ tendencies all week. The green dot is the one who sees a formation and yells “Watch the screen!” or “Boot! Boot!” before the snap, from a list built in film study.
He plays a game with the protection. The offense’s center identifies a defender as the “Mike” for its blocking count, the Mike identification of Pass Protection. The defense knows it. Linebackers walk up, back out and swap spots before the snap to make that identification wrong.

It is a lot to ask of one player, and it is why teams prize linebackers who are, in the clichéd but accurate phrase, coaches on the field. It is also why the green dot has started to move. A linebacker who comes off the field in some packages takes the radio with him, and the backup green dot has to take over. More and more teams have given the radio to a safety or another defensive back who never leaves the field: six teams did in 2021, according to one count.15 The Mike’s job doesn’t vanish when he loses the dot; he still sets the front and the run fits in the box, while the safety with the radio runs the coverage.

text:
Film room






NoteFilm room: Baltimore Ravens 2000



The season: Ray Lewis’s Ravens allowed 165 points in 16 games, the fewest in a 16-game season, and 970 rushing yards, also a 16-game record, then beat the Giants 34–7 in Super Bowl XXXV; Lewis was the game’s MVP and the league’s Defensive Player of the Year.16
Where to look: Super Bowl XXXV, against the Giants. What to notice: the two big defensive tackles in front of him, Tony Siragusa and Sam Adams. Their job was to occupy both guards so that nobody could climb to Lewis: watch the guards at the snap, then watch how often Lewis gets to the ball without anyone touching him. This is the protected linebacker at his best (the opposite of the open linebacker over a free guard): two big tackles who keep the guards off him, and a linebacker fast enough to his keys to make that pay.








NoteFilm room: Carolina Panthers 2015



The season: the Panthers went 15–1 and reached Super Bowl 50 with Luke Kuechly at middle linebacker, three seasons after he was the Defensive Rookie of the Year and two after he became the youngest Defensive Player of the Year. In the playoffs that January he returned interceptions for touchdowns in both of Carolina’s NFC games, the first in the opening minutes against Seattle and the second in the 49–15 NFC Championship win over Arizona.17
Where to look: the NFC Championship Game against Arizona. What to notice: Kuechly’s first step. He was famous for moving before the play had declared itself, and on the replay you can usually see why: his eyes are on a guard or the back, and he goes where they tell him. On passing downs, watch him in the hole, reading the quarterback and driving on throws in front of him. He retired in January 2020, at 28.








NoteFilm room: Baltimore Ravens 2022



The trade: On October 31, 2022, Chicago traded Roquan Smith, the eighth pick of the 2018 draft, to Baltimore for a second-round pick, a fifth-round pick and a linebacker; in January 2023 the Ravens signed him to a five-year, $100 million extension, the first for an off-ball linebacker at $20 million a year.18 In the eight games before he arrived, the Ravens allowed 22.9 points a game; in the nine after, 14.7. (Not all of that was Smith: other starters returned from injuries, and the schedule changed. But the timing was hard to miss.)19
Where to look: his first game for Baltimore, a 27–13 win at New Orleans on Monday night, November 7. What to notice: a modern run-through linebacker. Watch Smith’s fills against zone runs: he is through the gap before the climbing lineman gets there, which is how a 235-pound linebacker beats a guard who outweighs him by 80 pounds. Then watch him and Patrick Queen, the other inside linebacker that season, talk before the snap, and how often they swap responsibilities after the offense shifts.

title: Linebackers: Keys, Flow, Tackling, and the Hardest Job on the Field
text:
Watch for it on Sunday






TipWatch for it



Mirror the Mike. For ten snaps, watch only the middle linebacker. Ignore the ball.

Before the snap: Where is he standing: stacked behind a lineman, open over a guard, or walked out over a receiver? Is he pointing and shouting? (That’s the green dot setting the strength.) Does anyone walk up into the A gaps?
At the snap: first steps forward or back? His very first step is a short read step; the second one tells you what he saw. Forward, it’s a run, or he thinks it is. Back, it’s a pass. Sideways means he has read a pull or zone flow; see which way he goes and where the ball goes.
On runs: Did he fill, plug, scrape or run through? Did a guard get to him? Was he inside the ball as he pursued, or did the back cut back behind him?
On passes: Did he drop to a spot, run with a back or a tight end, or rush? On play-action, count his steps forward before he turned around.
On the replay: Watch the guards and the back, his keys. Did they tell the truth?

For your prediction log (How to Watch a Broadcast): write F or B for the Mike’s first real step, then run or pass. After a half, check how often his first step was right, and which plays fooled him.

p.highlight("MIKE", color=style.DEFENSE)
p.read("RB", key="MIKE"); p.read("RG", key="MIKE")
f = draw(p, width_in=5.4, lateral=(-9.0, 9.6), window=(-7.6, 7.6))
plt.show()








Figure 31.14: Drill 1: the first quarter-second. The back steps right (short arrow); the right guard and right tackle step flat to the left behind the line (their pulls); the left side of the line blocks down to the right, and the tight end steps back. The Mike (ringed) is reading the back and the right guard (dotted).











TipAnswer





Go left, with the guard and tackle. It’s counter. The back’s step to the right is the counter step, the lie the play is built on (Gap and Power Runs); the two pullers are the truth, because two linemen can’t run to the left unless the ball is going there. The guard will kick out the end man on the left, and the tackle will wrap through the hole looking for the play-side linebacker, the Will. (On the right, the tight end steps back to wall off the end the pulling tackle left: a hinge.)
You are the backside linebacker. Your guard has just pulled, so you follow him: sideways toward the offense’s left (your right), flat and inside-out, while the center or left guard tries to climb to you, and you fill the hole the tackle leads through. It is the read in Figure 31.3, from the other side. A Mike who believes the back takes a false step toward him, and by the time he recovers the hole has opened behind his back. This is the textbook case for “if your keys disagree, believe the linemen.”











TipPredict the play



Drill 2. The walk-out that gives it away. Third-and-6. The offense is in 11 personnel with the back beside the quarterback. Before the snap the back motions out of the backfield and lines up wide on the left. The Will linebacker walks out with him and stands over him. What did the defense just tell you, and what is the offense likely to do?


Show the Python
off = line("short") + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, -1.6, "R"),
                       O("X", "WR", -0.7, -17.0, "X"), O("H", "WR", -1.5, -8.6, "H"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 15.0, "Z")]
dfn = nickel_front(mike=(4.7, 1.0), will=(4.7, -2.0)) + [
    D("NB", "NB", 3.0, -8.6, "$"), D("SS", "S", 7.6, 6.0, "SS"), D("FS", "S", 13.5, 0.0, "FS"),
    D("LCB", "CB", 3.0, -17.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 3.0, 15.0, "CB")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=6, title="Drill 2: the back goes out, the Will goes with him")
p.motion("RB", to=(-1.5, -12.8))
p.highlight("WILL", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, width_in=6.0, lateral=(-20.4, 18.4), window=(-7.6, 16.4))
dashed(f, p, [(4.6, -2.9), (4.4, -8.0), (4.0, -12.0)], color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, lw=1.3)
ghost(f, p, 4.0, -12.8, "W")
say(f, p, 9.2, -12.8, "the Will\nends up here", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()








Figure 31.15: Drill 2: the back (R) motions out to the left, between the slot receiver (H) and the split end (X); the Will (ringed) walks out of the box and follows him (dashed). One deep safety; the cornerbacks and the nickel back are tight on their receivers.











TipAnswer





The defense told you it is in man coverage, and it told you which matchup the offense now has: a running back against a linebacker, in space, on third down. A zone defense would have let the back go and simply re-set its zones; a defense that sends a specific defender with a man who moves is matching him (the motion-as-indicator idea from Motion and Shifts). With one deep safety, the coverage is probably Cover 1.
The offense will usually go to that matchup: a quick route for the back, a slant, a quick out or an option route, where his quickness against a linebacker who has never covered him from out there is worth six yards. It is the case for linebackers who can cover, and for the safety-sized linebackers who replaced the Sam. Two smaller points: the box has lost a defender, leaving five (four linemen and the Mike) against six blockers, so a quarterback draw is suddenly attractive; and a well-coached defense may answer the motion by swapping assignments (“banjo,” or switching the nickel back onto the back) so that the linebacker never ends up out there at all. A banjo is the general version: two defenders trade who covers whom depending on where the receivers go.











TipPredict the play



Drill 3. Both linebackers flow. First-and-10. Outside zone to the right: the line steps right together, and the back sprints for the tight end’s outside leg. The picture is frozen 0.8 seconds after the snap; compare it with the fast-flow half of Figure 31.4. Both linebackers have flowed hard to the right. Where does the back go, and who made the mistake?


Show the Python
off = line("short") + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0, "R")]
p = Play(off, over_front(+1), los=40, to_go=10)
T_FREEZE = 0.8


def by(key, end, via=(), kind="path"):
    """Move `key` so that he arrives at `end` exactly at T_FREEZE."""
    pts = [tuple(p._cur(key)), *via, end]
    go_to(p, key, end, kind, speed=max(path_len(pts) / T_FREEZE, 0.1), via=via)


for k in OL_KEYS + ("Y",):
    q = p.players[k]
    by(k, (q.d + 0.3, q.w + 1.2), kind="block")
by("QB", (-2.6, 1.6))
by("RB", (-3.6, 4.6), via=[(-5.9, 2.6)], kind="run")
p.handoff("RB", t=0.6)
by("MIKE", (3.6, 5.3), via=[(4.2, 2.8)])
by("WILL", (3.6, 3.3), via=[(4.3, 0.2)])
by("SAM", (2.0, 7.8))
by("NT", (1.2, 0.3)); by("WE", (1.0, -3.4)); by("DT", (1.2, 2.9)); by("SE", (1.2, 4.6))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.4, 4.6))
LAT3, WIN3 = (-8.6, 10.6), (-8.8, 8.2)
fld = panel(ax, p, tracking(p), T_FREEZE, LAT3, WIN3, rings=(("MIKE", style.DEFENSE), ("WILL", style.DEFENSE)))
lane(fld, p, -3.6, 0.4, 1.9, 6.4, color=style.OFFENSE, alpha=0.10)
say(fld, p, 5.0, -1.6, "backside:\nnobody home", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
ax.set_title(f"Drill 3: outside zone, {T_FREEZE:.1f} s after the snap", fontsize=8.6, loc="left", color=style.INK,
             fontweight="bold")
plt.show()








Figure 31.16: Drill 3: outside zone right, 0.8 seconds after the snap (simulated; every player is drawn where he is at that moment, and the faint lines are where he has been). The line has stepped right and is cutting off the backside linemen; the back is pressing the edge; the Mike and the Will (ringed) have both run hard to the right, the Will level with the Mike. The shaded area behind the backside of the line is empty.











TipAnswer





The back cuts back, behind the Will, into the backside A or B gap, and the Will made the mistake. Outside zone is built to make the defense run sideways and then to cut against the flow (Zone Running). The play-side linebacker, the Mike, is right to run with it, inside-out. But the Will is the backside linebacker, and his job against fast flow is to follow a step behind the Mike and a little deeper, over the top, as the cutback player (Figure 31.4). Here he is level with the Mike and nearly as far over as the ball, so the shaded area behind the line’s flow is empty except for linemen who are being cut off. The back plants his foot and goes there, and the next defender is a safety.
A good Will gives up a yard or two to the outside to keep the cutback: if the back keeps going, the Mike and the Sam are there, and the Will arrives late but in the right place. He doesn’t hold the cutback alone; the backside end has to squeeze or chase so the back can’t bend it all the way back. The cutback runs you see go for 20 yards are usually a backside player out of place: a linebacker who ran too fast, an end who got reached or cut, or a safety who flowed too early.

title: Linebackers: Keys, Flow, Tackling, and the Hardest Job on the Field
text:
Back to the huddle
The chapter opened with a middle linebacker who went the “wrong” way, away from the back’s jab step, and stopped the run for no gain, while the analyst circled the left guard. Now you can see what he saw. The guard nearest him fired out (a run), and the left guard opened his hips and ran flat behind the line (a pull, so a gap-scheme run going where he went). The back’s jab step was window dressing. The Mike went with the puller, had the shorter trip, and met him at the line, where the hole was supposed to be. The back never had a chance to choose.

title: Linebackers: Keys, Flow, Tackling, and the Hardest Job on the Field
text:
Takeaways

Where a linebacker stands is a trade. Stacked behind a lineman, he is shielded and hard to read but a step slower to the gaps; open over an uncovered guard, he sees everything and is easy to block; walked out to an apex over a slot receiver, he can cover but he has left the box light and become the offense’s conflict defender.
Linebackers read keys, not the ball. The guards’ first steps (fire out, down block, pull, zone step, pass set) and the near back’s direction tell him run or pass and where, early enough to get there. The offense knows it, which is why counters, traps and play-action are built to make his keys lie.
Flow tells him how to move; the fit tells him where. Fast flow: run with it, inside-out, with the backside linebacker a step behind for the cutback. Slow flow: press the gap and stay square. The fit is a fill, a plug, a scrape or a run-through, and the scrape is also the defense’s answer to the zone read.
The second level is where runs are decided. Pursuit angles aim where the runner will be, a step inside him, with a leverage player outside; leverage tackling takes away one direction and wraps the legs. Inside linebackers make a fifth to a quarter of the tackles on runs up to 9 yards; misses rise with the space around the tackle, and a run that beats the linebackers is a defensive back’s tackle.
On passes, linebackers are hook/curl defenders, man defenders on backs and tight ends, robbers in the hole and blitzers. Play-action targets their keys; the uncovered guard who doesn’t climb is the tell.
The position has shrunk. Spread offenses made the Sam a part-time player, replaced by a nickel back, and made the remaining linebackers lighter and faster, down to safety-sized “moneybackers.” The green-dot linebacker, who sets the strength and adjusts the defense before every snap, is the job that hasn’t changed.

title: Run Fits: Gap Integrity, Force, Spill, and Box Math
text:
What a run fit is
First-and-10, early in the third quarter. The offense runs power to the right: a guard pulls from the left side, the fullback races toward the outermost defender on the line on the right, and for a split second there is a hole outside the tight end that looks big enough to drive a truck through. Then the end man does something that looks like a mistake. Instead of standing up to the fullback, that end man throws himself underneath him, toward the inside, and the two of them go down in a heap right where the hole was supposed to be. The pulling guard has nowhere to go. The running back bounces outside, finds green grass for a stride, and is met by a safety who was twelve yards deep when the ball was snapped. Gain of two. The analyst says, “Great fit by the defense.” Nobody on the defense made a spectacular play. Nobody beat a block. So what, exactly, was great? This chapter is the answer: a run defense is not eleven men chasing the ball, but eleven assignments that add up, and the end who “lost” that collision was the most important part of the sum.
You’ll be able to:
How to read the diagrams. Offense is blue circles, defense orange squares, and left and right always mean the offense’s left and right. On offense, C is the center (the other four linemen are unlettered), Q the quarterback, R the running back, F the fullback, Y the tight end, and X, Z and H receivers. Defensive linemen are labelled by their technique number (5, 3, 1), S, M and W are the Sam, Mike and Will linebackers, $ is the nickel back, CB a cornerback, and FS and SS the free and strong safeties. Blue lines ending in a short bar are blocks; orange arrows are where defenders go; the thick dark-blue arrow is the ball carrier. In the frame strips, faint lines are where each player has been. Rings keep one meaning all chapter: purple is the force (or the plus-one), green the alley player or another free fitter, orange the end man (the spill or box player) or another defender whose technique the figure is about, and gray the offensive player to watch, usually the ball carrier. Where the Sam (S) stands on the line beside a 5-technique (5), he wears the orange ring, so the two never get confused.
Start with the offense, because run defense only makes sense as an answer to it. Every run play in Part 3 is built around one of two ideas. Either it creates a crease the defense did not expect (zone’s moving wall and cutback), or it creates an extra blocker at one spot (power’s pulling guard, the fullback on an iso, the quarterback’s read on the option). Both ideas attack the same weakness: a defender who is not where his teammates think he is.
So the defense’s first answer is not a technique or a tackle. It is a plan. A run fit is the defense’s plan for which defender takes which gap or job against a run, and also the act of carrying it out: each defender getting to his gap after the snap, on the correct side of whoever is blocking him. Coaches use the word both ways. “Our fits were bad” means people went to the wrong places; “he fit it perfectly” means one player arrived in his gap at the right moment, on the right shoulder.
The principle underneath every fit has a name of its own: gap integrity. Every gap the offense can run through has exactly one defender responsible for it, and each defender stays in his gap until the ball shows him where it is going. “Exactly one” cuts both ways. A gap with nobody in it is an obvious problem: that is where the long run goes. A gap with two defenders in it is the same problem in disguise, because the defense only has so many players. If two defenders are in the B gap, some other gap is empty, and a good running back will find it.
You met the counting in Defensive Line Play: against a formation with one tight end there are seven gaps along the line (two A gaps either side of the center, two B gaps, two C gaps, and a D gap outside the tight end), and a one-gap defense puts one defender in charge of each. That count was the static version. Run fits are what happens when the count starts moving, and it moves for three reasons:
A fit is the defense’s way of keeping the count right while all of that happens. Before the snap, each defender knows his gap. After it, each knows how his gap changes when he sees a particular block: if the tackle in front of me blocks down, my gap is outside; if the guard pulls, the linebacker behind me fast-flows and I inherit his. The names you will learn in this chapter (force, spill, box, alley) are the vocabulary of those changes.

32  Run Fits: Gap Integrity, Force, Spill, and Box Math

title: Run Fits: Gap Integrity, Force, Spill, and Box Math
text:
Blockers carry gaps with them. A gap is not a patch of grass; it is the space between two blockers. When the tight end blocks down on the man inside him, the C gap slides inward with him, and a new space opens outside.
Backs add gaps. A fullback who runs to the line, or a guard who pulls, is one more blocker at one spot, and the space beside him is one more gap. Coaches say every back in the backfield can add a gap. Power’s whole point is to create a gap at the point of attack that the defense did not have a man for before the snap.
The defense moves too. Linemen slant, linebackers blitz, safeties rotate. Each of those moves takes a defender out of one gap and puts him in another, so somebody else has to inherit the gap he left.








ImportantWhy it exists



A defense has eleven players and the offense knows where the ball is going; the defense does not. Run fits exist so that the defense does not need to know. If every gap has an owner and every owner knows how his gap moves when the blocking changes, the ball can go anywhere and somebody is waiting. The price is discipline. A fit only works if all eleven players do their job instead of chasing the ball, which means trusting the man next to you. The most talented player on the field can wreck a defense by “making a play” outside his gap and leaving it empty.








NoteMadden vs. real life



In Madden, the move every user learns is to grab the safety, wait for the handoff and sprint at the ball carrier. It works because the computer plays the other ten defenders’ gaps perfectly. In real football, a player who leaves his gap to make a play is the most common reason for a long run, and coaches grade it as a missed assignment even when he makes the tackle. When you see a 60-yard run on a broadcast, rewind to the snap and look for the defender who ran to the wrong side of a block. It is rarely the man who missed the tackle at the end.
