title: Coverage Fundamentals: Zones, Leverage, and Reading the Shell
text:
Predict the play






TipPredict the play 1: off corners, one safety, then the snap





Show the Python
def offman():
    pr = Play(spread(), nickel(FS=(14.5, 0.5), SS=(5.5, 7.4), NB=(5.0, -7.4), LCB=(7.8, -16.3),
                               RCB=(7.8, 16.3), MIKE=(4.5, 1.6), WILL=(4.5, -2.4)), los=40, to_go=11)
    pr.route("X", r.go(20.0))
    pr.route("Z", r.go(20.0))
    pr.route("H", [(0, 0), (2.0, -1.0), (3.0, -18.0)])
    pr.route("Y", r.out(5.0, 5.0))
    pr.block("RB", pts=[(0.6, 1.2)])
    pr.dropback(2.5)
    protect(pr)
    pr.drop("FS", (16.0, 0.5), speed=2.0)
    pr.drop("MIKE", (5.5, 1.2), speed=2.0)
    pr.drop("WILL", (6.8, -1.6), speed=2.5)
    set_track(pr, "LCB", [(0.5, 8.6, -16.0), (0.9, 9.4, -15.5), (1.5, 11.0, -15.4)])
    set_track(pr, "RCB", [(0.5, 8.6, 16.0), (0.9, 9.4, 15.5), (1.5, 11.0, 15.4)])
    # man: the $ follows H across the formation, the SS goes outside with Y
    set_track(pr, "NB", [(0.4, 4.5, -7.6), (0.8, 3.6, -6.0), (1.3, 3.0, -2.4), (2.0, 3.0, 3.0)])
    set_track(pr, "SS", [(0.4, 5.2, 8.0), (0.8, 4.8, 9.2), (1.3, 4.6, 12.4), (2.0, 4.6, 13.0)])
    return pr


pr1 = offman()
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.0))
for ax, t, ttl in zip(axes, (0.0, 1.3), ("Before the snap", "+1.3 s after the snap")):
    fld = moment(ax, pr1, t, (-22.0, 22.0), (-7.5, 18.5), rings=("LCB", "RCB", "NB", "SS"))
    panel_title(ax, ttl, fs=8.2)
    ruler(fld, pr1, fs=5.2, top=15)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.8)
plt.show()








Figure 33.10: Third-and-11, ball in the middle. Left, the pre-snap picture: one safety (FS) deep in the middle; both corners (CB) about 8 yards off with outside leverage; the nickel ($) and the strong safety (SS) about 5 yards deep, just inside the slot receivers. Right, the same play 1.3 seconds after the snap: H is running a shallow cross to the right, Y a short out. The corners and the two slot defenders are ringed.





Before the snap, what does this look like? After it, what is it really, and why would a defense play it this way on third-and-11?






TipAnswer





It looks like Cover 3 and it’s Cover 1, man coverage played from off alignments. Before the snap everything points to Cover 3: middle of the field closed, corners 8 yards off with outside leverage, the slot defenders a few yards inside the slots like curl-flat players. A second later the evidence overrules the hypothesis. The nickel has gone across the formation with H on his shallow cross, and the strong safety has gone outside with Y. Zone defenders don’t do that: a curl-flat defender would let H run out of his area to the hook defender. When a slot defender follows his receiver out of his own area within the first second, it’s man. The corners, square and staying on top of X and Z rather than turning and bailing to a landmark, agree.
Why off-man on third-and-11? Because the first job is to keep everything in front of the defenders and short of the sticks, and a corner pressed on a receiver who only needs to run past 11 yards risks being beaten deep. From off, he can give up the short throw and tackle it. The quarterback’s answer is the crosser: H is dragging his defender through traffic, and a deeper crossing route or a rub would get a receiver past the sticks with a man defender trailing him.











TipPredict the play 2: two safeties, close to the box





Show the Python
pr2 = Play(spread(), nickel(FS=(10.0, -4.5), SS=(10.0, 4.5), NB=(4.5, -6.8), LCB=(7.5, -15.8),
                            RCB=(7.5, 15.8), MIKE=(4.8, 5.6), WILL=(4.5, -0.8)), los=40, to_go=6)
pr2.highlight("FS", "SS")
fld = draw(pr2, lateral=(-22, 22), window=(-7.5, 19.0))
widths(fld, pr2, -6.6)
plt.show()








Figure 33.11: Second-and-6, ball in the middle. Two safeties about 10 yards deep, each just outside a hash and well inside a slot receiver; corners 7 to 8 yards off; the nickel ($) in the apex inside the left slot, the Mike (M) in the apex inside the tight end, the Will (W) over the ball. The safeties are ringed.





Closed or open? What coverage do the safeties’ depth and width suggest, and where is this defense thinnest against the pass?






TipAnswer





Middle of the field open, and the shallow, tight safeties point to quarters (Cover 4). Cover 2 safeties would usually be deeper (12 to 14 yards) and wider (out toward the slot receivers), because each has half the field. These two are at 10 yards, near the hashes and well inside the slots, the alignment of quarters safeties, who guard only the inside quarter deep and read the slot receiver in front of them (#2). If #2 runs vertically, the safety covers him; that is who has Y here. If #2 blocks or the play is a run, the safety comes downhill and becomes an extra run defender. Count them: four linemen, two linebackers and two safeties are eight players who can reach a run between the tackles, with the nickel in the apex as a ninth to the outside. That is why defenses like quarters on early downs: two-high against the pass, with numbers against the run. One caution: a disciplined NFL defense may line up exactly like this and play something else, or play quarters from 13 yards, so the snap still has the last word.
The thin spot is underneath and outside. Four deep leaves three underneath, so short throws to the outside receivers (hitches and quick outs in front of the off corners) and to the flats are open, and a safety reading the run is vulnerable to play-action behind him. What’s hard is the deep ball: four defenders in four narrow lanes. (Quarters shows how its match rules handle the slot routes.)











TipPredict the play 3: third-and-6, everybody tight





Show the Python
pr3 = Play(spread(), nickel(FS=(15.0, 0.0), SS=(4.0, 8.4), NB=(1.6, -8.4), LCB=(1.3, -15.7),
                            RCB=(1.3, 15.7), MIKE=(4.5, 1.2), WILL=(4.5, -2.4)), los=40, to_go=6)
pr3.highlight("FS", "LCB", "RCB")
fld = draw(pr3, lateral=(-22, 22), window=(-7.5, 19.0))
widths(fld, pr3, -6.6)
plt.show()








Figure 33.12: Third-and-6. One safety (FS) 15 yards deep in the middle. Both corners (CB) pressed about a yard off the outside receivers, square to them; the nickel ($) pressed on the left slot; the strong safety (SS) 4 yards off the tight end Y in the right slot; the two linebackers inside. The corners and the free safety are ringed.





Man or zone? What is the defense most likely playing, which routes should the quarterback like, and what does the 5-yard rule have to do with it?






TipAnswer





Most likely man coverage with one deep safety: Cover 1. Middle of the field closed, and every receiver has a defender tight on him: corners pressed and square, the nickel pressed on H, the strong safety close on Y. The linebackers likely “have the back”: one of them covers the running back man to man if he runs a route, and the other, with nobody to cover, sits in the hole as a rat or joins the rush. On third-and-6 that’s a common call: the defense wants every short throw contested.
The quarterback should like routes that beat man: quick slants and outs that win at the break, crossing routes and rubs that drag defenders through traffic (Dropback Concepts‘s mesh), and a back-shoulder throw against a corner in trail. He should not expect receivers to “find a soft spot and sit,” because there are no soft spots in man: sitting down next to your defender just makes the throw harder. And the 5-yard rule is the receiver’s friend: all of the corners’ contact has to happen inside 5 yards. A receiver who wins his release has a defender chasing him with his back to the quarterback, and only the free safety behind them. If the pressed corners bail at the snap, it was a disguised zone and the quarterback has to adjust after the snap.

title: Coverage Fundamentals: Zones, Leverage, and Reading the Shell
text:
Takeaways

Every coverage is a decision about how many defenders to put deep. Thirds (three deep, four under), halves (two deep, five under) and quarters (four deep, three under) each buy something and give something up; with four rushers, every defender added deep is one taken from underneath.
The underneath map is flat, curl, hook and hole. There are always more areas than defenders, so zone players are taught to cover two areas each, and they drop to landmarks so the gaps are the planned size on every play.
How a defender lines up is a message. Press contests timing and needs help deep; off coverage gives a cushion to protect against the deep ball; a press-bail makes zone look like man. Leverage tells you where his help is, and the 5-yard rule means all of press’s contact has to happen in the first 5 yards.
There are three ways to guard a receiver: spot-drop zone (run to a place, watch the quarterback), pattern matching (start as zone, pick up receivers by rule) and man (go with one receiver from the snap). Watch one underneath defender for one second and you can usually tell which.
Read the middle of the field. Closed (one safety in the post) means Cover 1 or Cover 3 most of the time; open means a two-high coverage. Safety depth and width, corner depth and leverage, and slot alignment narrow it down, and the snap confirms or overturns it.
Coverage numbers count deep defenders through Cover 4, then become names. Cover 6, 7, 8 and 9 mean different things in different playbooks, and even charting services disagree.

title: Coverage Fundamentals: Zones, Leverage, and Reading the Shell
text:
Connections
Builds on: A First Look at Defense (man vs zone, one-high vs two-high) and Dropback Concepts (the routes and combinations these zones are built to stop), with leverage and the pre-snap read from The Quick Game.
Sets up: every chapter in Part 6. Man Coverage builds Cover 0 and Cover 1 from press, trail and inside help; Cover 3, Cover 2 and Tampa 2 and Quarters and the Two-High Match Family each take one deep split and make it a full coverage; Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage shows how defenses hide the shell and play Cover 7 and other split-field calls. On the rules side, Contact Rules and Penalties as Strategy covers illegal contact and pass interference, and What Beats What pairs every concept with the coverages here. The Coverage and Pressure Atlas has a card for every coverage number and the full dialect table.
Case study: Fangio’s Two-High Revolution and Macdonald’s Answer follows the middle-of-the-field-open idea through the last decade of NFL defense.






NoteGo deeper




Cody Alexander, Match Quarters and his MatchQuarters newsletter: a coach’s-eye view of zone, match and the modern NFL coverage vocabulary, including the Fangio and Saban numbering systems.
Cameron Soran, “The Complete Guide to Nick Saban Coverages at Alabama,” Throw Deep Publishing (2021): how one famous system names and builds its coverages, numbers included.
Chris B. Brown, The Art of Smart Football (2015) and The Essential Smart Football (2012): short, clear essays on Cover 2, Cover 3 and the history of pattern matching.
Tony Dungy’s Quiet Strength (2007) for the man behind the Tampa 2, and the NFL’s own rulebook (operations.nfl.com) for the exact wording of the contact rules.

title: Coverage Fundamentals: Zones, Leverage, and Reading the Shell
text:

title: Man Coverage: Cover 0, Cover 1, Robbers, and Brackets
text:
What man coverage asks of a defender
Third-and-5 in the red zone. The offense comes out with two receivers on each side, and as the quarterback starts his cadence the broadcast’s camera catches something it rarely shows on first down: both cornerbacks walk up until they are standing a yard from the receivers’ faces, squared up, eyes on the receivers’ belts rather than on the quarterback. The slot receiver motions across the formation, and a defender jogs across with him, mirroring every step. One safety drifts back to the middle of the field, 14 yards deep, all alone. The analyst says, “They’re in man.” The ball is snapped, the quarterback looks to his favourite target running a crossing route, and a linebacker who had been standing in the middle covering nobody steps into the lane and knocks the ball down. Who was that linebacker covering? Nobody, and that was the point. This chapter is about the coverages in which defenders cover people: what each defender is asked to do, the one or two defenders the system deliberately leaves free, and the tricks defenses use when one-on-one isn’t enough.
You’ll be able to…
Every pass defense has to answer one question before the snap: when the receivers start running, how does each defender know what to do? Zone coverage answers with places: you have the deep third, you have the flat, guard it and take whoever comes. Man coverage answers with people: you have number 11, go where he goes. Everything in this chapter grows from that one choice, so it is worth slowing down on what it buys and what it costs.
What it buys is tightness and certainty. A zone defender guards grass, so a receiver can sit down in the soft spot between two zones and catch the ball with nobody within three yards of him. A man defender guards a body. If he is good enough, there is no soft spot, because the soft spot moves with the receiver and so does the defender. There is also no confusion about who takes the receiver who wanders between two areas, which is where zone coverages break down. And man coverage lets a defense choose its matchups: its best cornerback on their best receiver, its fastest linebacker on their running back.
What it costs comes from where the man defender is looking. A zone defender watches the quarterback and can break on the ball the moment it’s thrown. A man defender watches his receiver, usually his hips and belt, because that is where a route’s direction shows first. So he often has his back to the quarterback. He doesn’t see the ball leave the hand; he reacts to the receiver’s hands and eyes going up. He can’t help a teammate, because his own man would be left alone. If the quarterback escapes the pocket and runs, half the defense is running away from him, following receivers downfield. And if a receiver beats his defender, by a quick release, a sharp break, or a route that drags the defender into traffic, there is nobody nearby to fix it.
That last problem is the one man coverages are built around. The pure version, every defender on a receiver and nobody else, is all risk: one lost footrace is a touchdown. So almost every man coverage keeps one or two defenders free, with no receiver of their own, to help the others. Where the free defenders stand, how many there are, and what they do give us the family names: Cover 1, Cover 0, the robber and rat versions, brackets. The free defender is the whole game.

title: Man Coverage: Cover 0, Cover 1, Robbers, and Brackets
text:
ImportantWhy it exists



Man coverage exists because a defender who covers a person never has to decide whose person he is. Against short, precise throws (the slant, the stick, the quick out) a zone defender is often a step too far away, because he started in the middle of an area. A man defender starts on the receiver and stays there, and that tightness is worth most where throws are short and timing is everything: third-and-short, the red zone, any down where the defense is also sending extra rushers. The price is eyes: man defenders watch receivers, not the ball, and need help somewhere behind them.



A little history: the bump-and-run, and the rules that answered it
Man coverage is as old as the forward pass, but the modern, aggressive form grew up in the 1960s American Football League. Willie Brown, a cornerback who had been a linebacker in college, began jamming receivers right at the line in 1963, and with Al Davis’s Raiders he became the face of bump-and-run: line up in the receiver’s face, hit him at the snap, then run with him. (Davis modelled the Raiders’ version on the full-court press of John Wooden’s UCLA basketball teams.) Brown played 12 seasons in Oakland and is in the Hall of Fame.1
The rules answered twice (the 1978 “Mel Blount rule” and the 2004 “Ty Law rule”, both told in Coverage Fundamentals; the Ty Law game is in this chapter’s film room). For man coverage the result is the shape of the modern craft. Inside five yards it is a fight of hands and feet; beyond five yards, until the ball is thrown, the defender may not initiate contact that impedes the receiver, so everything depends on position: being on the right side of the receiver, at the right distance, before he breaks.2 Physical man coverage followed by a rules response is a pattern you’ll see again in Contact Rules and Penalties.

title: Man Coverage: Cover 0, Cover 1, Robbers, and Brackets
text:
Cover 1: man-free
The most common man coverage in football is Cover 1, which coaches also call man-free. The name is the coverage: man coverage on every eligible receiver, plus one free safety who has no man at all and plays the deep middle of the field. The “1” is the one deep defender.


Show the Python
p = Play(spread(), cover1_def(), los=LOS, to_go=7)
for d_, t_ in (("LCB", "X"), ("RCB", "Z"), ("NB", "H"), ("SS", "Y"), ("WILL", "RB")):
    p.man(d_, t_)
p.drop("MIKE", (8.0, -0.5), zone=(3.6, 9.0), label="hole")
p.zone((17.5, 0.0), (6.5, 26.0), label="deep middle")
protect(p)
p.highlight("FS", "MIKE")
fld = draw(p, lateral="full", window=(-8.5, 22.5))
say(fld, p, 14.0, 7.8, "FS: no man.\nHelp for everyone", fontsize=6.8)
say(fld, p, 10.6, -10.0, "the spare defender: sits,\nrushes or spies", fontsize=6.8)
say(fld, p, -3.8, -19.6, "outside shade:\nhelp is inside", fontsize=6.8)
say(fld, p, -3.8, 19.6, "outside shade:\nhelp is inside", fontsize=6.8)
field_legend(fld.ax, ["man", "drop", "area", "ltg"])
plt.show()








Figure 34.1: Cover 1 against a 2x2 formation (11 personnel: one back, one tight end, three wide receivers), third-and-7. Every eligible receiver has a man defender (dotted lines): the cornerbacks (CB) on the outside receivers X and Z, the nickel back ($) on the slot H, the strong safety (SS) on the tight end Y, the Will (W) on the running back. The free safety (FS, ringed) has nobody: he guards the deep middle for all of them. That still leaves one defender over, the Mike (M, ringed), who here drops into the hole, the middle of the field underneath, as a spare helper (a job with its own names, coming up below). The corners line up a step outside their receivers, because their help is inside.





Count the defenders in the picture. Four rush. The offense has five eligible receivers, so five defenders have a man. That is nine. The tenth is the free safety, alone in the middle 13 to 15 yards deep, and the eleventh, here the Mike linebacker, is free too. Cover 1 against five receivers and a four-man rush always leaves that eleventh man over, and the defense gets to decide what to do with him. He can rush, making it a five-man pressure; he can sit in the middle as a helper; or he can mirror a running quarterback (a spy, covered in Third Down). The section on the free defender below is about that choice.
The free safety’s own job sounds impossible at first: one man “helping” on five receivers. He doesn’t try to cover them all. He starts in the middle, 13 to 15 yards deep, reads the quarterback’s eyes and shoulders, and works toward the deepest route breaking inside or straight up the middle, the throws a corner with outside leverage can’t reach. Routes to the sideline are the corners’ problem. Two deep routes into the middle at once (two posts, or a post and a seam) are his nightmare, for the same reason a high-low is the robber’s below: one man, two targets. How common is all this? In the public charting, Cover 1 was the label on roughly a quarter to a third of charted NFL dropbacks in every season from 2018 to 2025, by far the most of any man coverage.3

Who takes whom
A man coverage is only as good as its matching rules, because the offense chooses the formation and the defense has to sort itself out in the 15 or so seconds before the snap. A typical set of rules, which varies by team:

Corners take the widest receiver on each side (#1). They are the best man-to-man athletes on the field and the outside receivers are usually the fastest.
The nickel takes the slot receiver (#2 to his side); in a base defense, with no nickel back, that job goes to a safety or a linebacker.
A safety or linebacker takes the tight end, matched for size.
A linebacker takes the running back, and if the back stays in to block, that linebacker is free to rush the quarterback (a “hug” or “green-dog” rule) or drop into the middle.
The free safety takes nobody and plays the deep middle.

These are starting rules, and the call can rearrange them. If the plan is for the strong safety to come down and rob (the next big section), he can’t also cover the tight end, so a linebacker takes the tight end instead, and the spare defender moves up from the linebacker level to the safety level. The count never changes: five receivers need five men, and whoever is left over is the free defender.
The rules have to cope with whatever the offense shows. When a receiver motions across the formation, his defender either travels with him, the classic tell you met in Motion and Shifts as Weapons, or the defenders exchange, each sliding over a spot and swapping receivers. When the offense shows three receivers to one side, someone from the other side has to be matched across. When the offense lines up in a formation the defense didn’t prepare for, the defense has a short list of simple “checks” to fall back on. Much of what looks like a cornerback getting “beat” on a broadcast is actually two defenders who disagreed about a rule.


The help is inside, so the leverage is outside
Look again at the cornerbacks in the figure: each is a step outside his receiver. That isn’t a style choice; it follows from where the help is. In Cover 1 the free safety lives in the deep middle, and often a second free defender sits underneath in the middle too. That help is inside help: defenders positioned toward the middle of the field from the man defender, who can get to routes that break inside (posts, digs, slants) faster than they can get to the sideline.
So the man defender takes away the side where help can’t reach him. A cornerback with inside help plays outside leverage: he protects the sideline routes (the fade, the out, the comeback) and, in coaches’ language, funnels the receiver inside, toward the help. If the receiver runs a post, the corner chases and the free safety arrives from the middle. If he runs a slant or a dig, the corner trails and the help underneath is waiting. The general rule, which works for every man coverage in this chapter: play away from your help. Where there is help, you can give ground; where there isn’t, you can’t.
That is the starting rule, not a law, and coaches bend it in three common ways:

Split. A receiver who lines up close to the sideline has very little room outside him, so the sideline itself is a kind of help, and his defender often plays inside leverage instead. A receiver with a tight split, near the formation, has room both ways and gets the outside shade.
Down and distance. On third-and-short many Cover 1 teams press head-up or with an inside shade to take away the slant, the fastest way to the sticks, and accept the fade, a slower, harder throw the free safety couldn’t reach anyway.
The slot. A slot receiver has room to break either way (a “two-way go”), and his defender often shades inside: the inside break is the quick throw, while a break outside means a longer throw toward the sideline that gives him time to recover.







ImportantWhy it exists: Cover 1



Cover 1 is the compromise that makes man coverage affordable. Pure man everywhere leaves every defender alone against a deep route. One deep safety turns every one-on-one into a one-on-one with help on the deep, inside throw, and the coverage still has a defender left over to rush or to rob. It keeps the box strong, too. Only one safety lives deep; the other plays close to the line of scrimmage, on the tight end or as the spare, so with the linebackers the defense still has seven or eight players near the line to stop the run. (Against a run, a man defender whose receiver blocks him becomes a run defender; who takes what in the run game is the subject of Run Fits and Box Math.) What it gives up: the middle of the field underneath (unless the extra defender sits there), the receiver who simply wins his matchup to the outside, where there is no help, and the throws that make man defenders run through traffic.

section: Press, off and trail: the man defender’s techniques
text:
Press, off and trail: the man defender’s techniques
“Man coverage” says who; technique says how. The same Cover 1 call can be played with every cornerback in the receivers’ faces or with every cornerback seven yards off, and the difference changes which throws are open. There are three basic ways to cover a man.


Show the Python
LAT_T, WIN_T = (-23.5, -6.5), (-3.5, 20.0)


def tech_panel(ax, kind):
    off = [O("X", "WR", LINE_D, -15.0)]
    dfn = []
    if kind == "press":
        dfn = [D("CB", "CB", 1.0, -14.4, "CB")]
    elif kind == "off":
        dfn = [D("CB", "CB", 7.0, -14.0, "CB")]
    else:
        dfn = [D("CB", "CB", 1.0, -15.8, "CB"), D("FS", "FS", 16.5, -8.6, "FS")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=LOS, to_go=None)
    if kind == "press":
        route_to(p, "X", (18.5, -15.3))
    elif kind == "off":
        route_to(p, "X", (12.6, -15.0), (11.2, -13.7))
    else:
        route_to(p, "X", (9.5, -15.0), (17.0, -10.8))
    p.highlight("CB")
    fld = p.draw(ax=ax, lateral=LAT_T, window=WIN_T, title=False)
    clean(ax)
    ruler(fld, p, fs=5.5)
    if kind == "press":
        hline(fld, p, 5.0, -19.8, -8.0, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
        say(fld, p, 5.9, -10.3, "5 yd: contact\nmust stop", fontsize=6.0)
        branch(fld, p, [(1.0, -14.4), (2.4, -14.5), (5.0, -14.4), (17.0, -14.3)])
        say(fld, p, 2.4, -11.9, "jam", fontsize=6.4, color=DD, weight="bold")
    elif kind == "off":
        # backpedal while X pushes upfield, then drive downhill on the curl from above it
        branch(fld, p, [(7.0, -14.0), (10.8, -14.1), (12.4, -13.3), (11.8, -13.0)])
        vdim(fld, p, -11.0, 0.0, 6.6, "cushion\n~7 yd", fs=6.0)
        say(fld, p, 15.5, -14.0, "sees the break,\narrives late", fontsize=6.0)
    else:
        branch(fld, p, [(1.0, -15.8), (3.0, -15.9), (8.4, -15.9), (14.6, -12.2)])
        say(fld, p, 12.0, -8.9, "help over\nthe top", fontsize=6.0)
        say(fld, p, 12.5, -19.6, "a step behind,\nunderneath", fontsize=6.0)
    return fld


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(6.6, 3.45))
for ax, kind, ttl in zip(axes, ("press", "off", "trail"), ("1. Press-man", "2. Off-man", "3. Trail")):
    tech_panel(ax, kind)
    panel_title(ax, ttl)
fig.legend(handles=[LEGEND["route"], LEGEND["react"], LEGEND["ring"]], loc="upper center",
           bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 0.04), ncol=3, fontsize=7, frameon=False)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.8, rect=(0, 0.05, 1, 1))
plt.show()








Figure 34.2: Three ways to play man on the same receiver (X, on the offense’s left; simulated). Blue is the route, orange dashes the cornerback’s movement. 1. Press-man: the corner starts a yard away, jams X inside the five-yard limit (dashed line), then runs on his hip on a go route. 2. Off-man: the corner starts about seven yards off with a cushion, backpedals while X pushes upfield, and drives on the curl when X stops; he can see the break coming but arrives a step late, conceding the short throw. 3. Trail: the corner presses, then runs a step behind and underneath X on a post, protecting the low throw, because a safety (FS) is over the top to take the high one.





Press-man is the bump-and-run’s descendant. The defender lines up within a yard or two of the receiver, gets his hands on him at the snap (legal inside five yards), and tries to knock him off his path and onto the defender’s terms. If the jam lands, the route is late, and a late route in a timing offense is a dead route: the quarterback’s feet have finished their drop and the receiver isn’t where he’s supposed to be. If the jam misses, the defender has to turn and run with a receiver who now has a step on him. Press-man is the purest test of athletes in football, and the reason teams pay elite cornerbacks: hips that turn fast, long arms, and the recovery speed to survive a miss. You met the receiver’s side of this fight in The Quick Game.
Off-man gives the receiver room. The defender starts 5 to 8 yards away, often with his weight back, and backpedals or shuffles as the receiver comes toward him, keeping that cushion while he reads the route. Off-man trades the jam for vision: he sees the break coming and is rarely beaten deep. The cost is the short throw. A receiver who turns around at six yards against a defender who started at seven is open, and good quarterbacks take that throw all day. Off-man is common against very fast receivers, against receivers in the slot (where a jam is harder because the receiver can release either way), and on long-yardage downs where a six-yard catch doesn’t hurt.
Trail technique is what man defenders do when they have help over the top. The defender runs a step behind the receiver and slightly underneath him, on his hip, taking away anything thrown low or short, and trusts a safety to take the ball thrown high and deep. It is the technique of 2-Man, two deep safeties with man underneath (Cover 2 and Tampa 2), and of any Cover 1 defender whose man runs into the free safety’s area. Trailing looks like losing on a broadcast (the receiver is ahead), but the trailing defender is exactly where he wants to be: under the throw. To tell trailing from being beaten on a replay, look for the safety. If one is arriving over the top, the corner is trailing on purpose; if nobody is coming, he has simply been beaten.
Whatever the technique, everything ends at the catch point, and there the key idea is phase. A defender who is in phase is on the receiver’s hip, stride for stride, close enough to turn his head, find the ball and play it as if he were the receiver. A defender who is out of phase, a step or more behind, can’t afford to turn and look, because he’d lose more ground. So he watches the receiver instead and plays his hands: when the receiver’s eyes widen and his hands come up, the ball is arriving, and the defender rips through the hands as they close. That is what “he reacts to the receiver’s hands” meant earlier. It is also where pass interference lives. Once the ball is thrown, a defender who contacts a receiver more than a yard past the line and significantly hinders his chance to catch it commits pass interference, unless he is playing the ball himself. Not turning around is not a foul in itself, but a defender who isn’t looking for the ball is not “playing the ball”, so any contact before it arrives is likely to draw the flag.4 The details are in Contact Rules and Penalties.
Teams rarely pick one technique for a whole game. They pick per matchup and per call: press on a slow receiver, off on a fast one; press on third-and-2, off on third-and-14. The quarterback’s pre-snap read is partly a read of these techniques, which is why defenses mix them and sometimes show press and bail out at the snap.






CautionCommon misconception



“Press means man, off means zone.” As Coverage Fundamentals warned, alignment alone doesn’t tell you; plenty of man calls are played off, and plenty of zone corners press and bail. The man-coverage tell to add is the defender’s stance and angle before the snap: a man defender is usually squared up to his receiver and slightly turned toward the sideline; a zone corner is usually turned in so he can see the quarterback.

title: Man Coverage: Cover 0, Cover 1, Robbers, and Brackets
section: The free defender: rat, robber and lurk
text:
The free defender: rat, robber and lurk
Back to the eleventh man. In Cover 1 with a four-man rush, one defender has no receiver and no deep responsibility. Defenses can turn him into a fifth rusher (Cover 1 pressure, in Blitzing) or keep him in coverage as a helper. As a helper he has three common names, and coaches don’t use them identically, so learn the jobs rather than the words. On broadcasts you’ll hear the whole call named after him: “Cover 1 Robber,” “Cover 1 Rat,” “Cover 1 Hole.” The figure shows the choices one at a time, and notice that each one changes who covers the tight end and the back.


Show the Python
LAT_F, WIN_F = (-13.5, 13.5), (-7.0, 17.5)


def free_panel(ax, kind):
    extra, keys = {}, [("NB", "H"), ("SS", "Y"), ("WILL", "RB")]
    if kind == "robber":
        extra = {"FS": (13.0, -7.0), "SS": (13.0, 7.0), "MIKE": (4.5, 6.0), "WILL": (4.5, 1.2)}
        keys = [("NB", "H"), ("MIKE", "Y"), ("WILL", "RB")]
    elif kind == "lurk":
        extra = {"WILL": (1.3, -7.6), "MIKE": (4.5, 1.6)}
        keys = [("NB", "H"), ("SS", "Y"), ("MIKE", "RB")]
    p = Play(spread(), cover1_def(extra=extra), los=LOS, to_go=None)
    for d_, t_ in keys:
        p.man(d_, t_)
    free = {"rat": "MIKE", "robber": "SS", "lurk": "WILL", "rush": "MIKE"}[kind]
    p.highlight(free)
    if kind == "rush":
        p.rush("MIKE", pts=[(-3.5, 2.6), (-8.0, 2.4)])
    fld = p.draw(ax=ax, lateral=LAT_F, window=WIN_F, title=False)
    clean(ax)
    ruler(fld, p, fs=5.5)
    if kind == "rat":
        oval(fld, p, (6.6, -0.6), (3.0, 6.5), label="hole", fs=6.0)
        branch(fld, p, [(4.5, -1.8), (6.0, -0.9)], lw=1.3)
        say(fld, p, 10.2, -7.6, "M has no man:\nsits low, eyes on Q", fontsize=6.0)
    elif kind == "robber":
        oval(fld, p, (10.3, 0.4), (3.0, 7.0), fs=6.0)
        branch(fld, p, [(13.0, 7.0), (11.4, 3.6), (10.6, 1.4)], lw=1.3)
        branch(fld, p, [(13.0, -7.0), (14.6, -3.6), (15.2, -0.8)], lw=1.3)
        say(fld, p, 15.4, 7.6, "SS comes\ndown to rob", fontsize=6.0)
        say(fld, p, 15.4, -8.4, "FS spins\nto the middle", fontsize=6.0)
    elif kind == "lurk":
        oval(fld, p, (5.6, -2.6), (3.0, 6.0), fs=6.0)
        branch(fld, p, [(1.3, -7.6), (3.4, -6.2), (5.2, -3.6)], lw=1.3)
        say(fld, p, 9.6, -7.0, "W shows blitz,\ndrops out", fontsize=6.0)
    else:
        say(fld, p, 8.6, -6.2, "M blitzes:\nfive rushers", fontsize=6.0)
    return fld


fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(6.6, 7.2))
ttl = {"rat": "1. Rat (hole player)", "robber": "2. Robber", "lurk": "3. Lurk", "rush": "4. Fifth rusher"}
for ax, kind in zip(axes.flat, ("rat", "robber", "lurk", "rush")):
    free_panel(ax, kind)
    panel_title(ax, ttl[kind])
fig.legend(handles=[LEGEND["man"], LEGEND["drop"], LEGEND["rush"], LEGEND["area"], LEGEND["ring"]],
           loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 0.03), ncol=5, fontsize=6.8, frameon=False)
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=1.4, w_pad=0.8, rect=(0, 0.04, 1, 1))
plt.show()








Figure 34.3: Four ways to use the spare defender in Cover 1, one per panel (a defense picks one per snap; the corners on X and Z, wide of the frame, are the same in all four). 1. Rat: the Mike (M), with no man, drops into the low hole, about 5 to 8 yards deep, under crossing routes. 2. Robber: the safeties start two-high; at the snap the free safety spins to the deep middle and the strong safety (SS) comes down to 8 to 12 yards to drive on digs and deep crossers, so the Mike has to take the tight end Y. 3. Lurk: the Will (W) walks up as if to blitz and drops out at the snap into the shallow middle, where the quarterback’s hot throw is supposed to go; the Mike takes the back. 4. Or the spare man rushes: Cover 1 pressure, with five rushers. Each version changes who covers Y and the back, but the count is the same: five receivers, five men.






The robber is the free defender sitting in the middle of the field, usually 8 to 12 yards deep, driving on in-breaking throws: digs, deep crossers, the slant that gets past its man. He doesn’t just stare at the quarterback. In most teaching he keys a receiver, usually #2 or #3 to the passing strength, and “robs the first in-breaker”, while feeling the quarterback’s eyes to know when to go. Classically he is a safety who lines up deep (often disguised as half of a two-high shell, the subject of Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage) and comes down at the snap. His name says what he is for: he steals the throws man coverage is worst at defending, the ones where receivers run away from their defenders across the field. When the ball goes outside instead, he becomes a pursuit player: the first tackler coming from the inside.
The rat is, in many playbooks, simply another name for the same job. When coaches distinguish them, the rat is lower and usually a linebacker, the man left over when the back he would have covered stays in to block, or the Mike in the figure above, sitting 5 to 8 yards deep, low in the hole. (That is why the hole is sometimes called the rat zone, and the rat a hole player.) His prey is the shallow cross and the quarterback scramble up the middle.
Lurk describes the same idea with disguise built in. The lurker lines up somewhere that says something else, often walked up to the line as if blitzing, sometimes deep as a safety, and drops at the snap into the shallow middle. Pressure defenses love it, because the quarterback who sees a blitz coming throws the quick hot route to the middle, and the lurker is standing in it. Some staffs use “lurk” only for a player who drops into the hole off a pressure look, sometimes even a defensive lineman.

Whatever it’s called, the free underneath defender changes the math of Cover 1. Against pure man, a receiver who wins inside is open. Against Cover 1 with a robber, a receiver who wins inside runs into a second defender who has been watching the quarterback the whole time and is moving before the ball is. Here it is in motion.


Show the Python
p = Play(spread(rb_w=-2.0), cover1_def(extra={"SS": (9.0, 8.0), "MIKE": (4.5, 5.6), "WILL": (4.5, -1.6)}),
         los=LOS, to_go=8)
protect(p)
p.dropback(2.0)
route_to(p, "X", (24.0, -15.4))
route_to(p, "H", (22.0, -8.6))
route_to(p, "Y", (2.6, 10.5), (3.8, 16.5))
route_to(p, "Z", (12.0, 15.0), (12.0, 2.0), (12.4, -4.0))
p.block("RB", pts=[(0.4, -1.6)])          # the back stays in to protect
p.rush("WILL", pts=[(-3.5, -1.0), (-8.5, -1.8)], delay=0.45)   # ... so his linebacker rushes, through the B gap
T_THROW = 2.15
kf, _, _ = p._compile()
# where Z will be when a firm throw arrives, and a spot just in front of him in the lane
qb = np.array(p.position("QB", T_THROW))
t_c = T_THROW + 0.9
for _ in range(4):
    z = p.position("Z", t_c)
    t_c = T_THROW + float(np.linalg.norm(z - qb)) / 18.0
z = p.position("Z", t_c)
lane = z + (qb - z) / np.linalg.norm(qb - z) * 2.7
T_CATCH = round(t_c, 2)
# the Mike carries Y to the flat from a yard above and inside him (never dipping toward the line)
mike = [(t_, max(d_, 3.8), w_) for t_, d_, w_ in chase(p, "MIKE", "Y", off=(0.9, -1.0), lag=0.2, t_on=0.8)]
tracks = {
    "LCB": chase(p, "LCB", "X", off=(-1.0, -0.9)),
    "NB": chase(p, "NB", "H", off=(-1.0, -0.9)),
    "MIKE": mike,
    "RCB": chase(p, "RCB", "Z", off=(-1.2, 1.1), lag=0.3),
    "SS": ease([(0.0, 9.0, 8.0), (0.9, 10.2, 3.4), (T_THROW, 10.6, 2.4), (T_CATCH, *lane), (3.6, *lane)]),
    "FS": ease([(0.0, 14.0, 0.0), (1.2, 16.0, 0.6), (3.6, 16.5, 2.5)]),
}
p.pass_to("SS", t=T_THROW)      # the ball goes where the robber will be: in the lane, in front of Z
set_tracks(p, tracks, t_end=3.6)
RAT_LAT, RAT_WIN = (-11.0, 19.5), (-8.0, 19.0)
notes = ["Cover 1: a man on each receiver, FS deep.\nSS 9 yards deep over Y, as if he had him.",
         "M carries Y to the flat. SS slides to the\nmiddle, eyes on Q. Z's corner trails him.",
         "Z breaks inside on the dig and Q starts\nto throw. SS is already moving.",
         "The robber arrives in the lane in front of Z\nas the ball does: broken up or intercepted."]
if PDF:
    strip_grid(p, [0.0, 1.0, T_THROW, T_CATCH], notes, RAT_LAT, RAT_WIN, rings=[("SS", style.THIRD)],
               deco=lambda i, f, q: ruler(f, q, fs=5.5))
    plt.show()
else:
    video([p], [""], RAT_LAT, RAT_WIN, t_end=T_CATCH + 0.4, rings=[("SS", style.THIRD)], width_in=5.6)





  
  Your browser does not support the video tag.



Figure 34.4: Cover 1 robber against a dig, second-and-8, simulated (BDB-format tracking, generated by gridiron rather than recorded). Z runs a dig, a square break inside at about 12 yards, from the right; his cornerback, playing outside leverage, trails him across the field, as Cover 1 corners do, because the help is inside. The strong safety (SS, ringed) is the robber. Before the snap he stands 9 yards deep over the tight end Y, as if he had him in man; at the snap the Mike (M) takes Y into the flat, and the robber slides to the middle at 10 to 11 yards. Y has gone outside, so the robber looks for the next receiver coming inside: Z. When the quarterback takes his hitch step to throw the dig, the robber drives on it and arrives in the throwing lane, in front of Z, as the ball does. The free safety stays deep; the other receivers are carried by their man defenders, and because the back stays in to block, the Will (W), who had him in man, rushes through the B gap to meet him. X and his cornerback, far to the left, are out of frame. In the web version this is a video.




The animation is simulated. If you download the 2025 Big Data Bowl files, which include the pre-snap frames and a charted coverage for every pass play, you can watch real Cover 1 snaps the same way; the folded code below shows how (the files are not part of this book’s build).


Show the Python (real Cover 1 snaps from the Big Data Bowl 2025 files)
import pandas as pd
from gridiron import bdb, show_animation

plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")                        # BDB 2025: 2022 season, weeks 1-9
trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_*.csv")
# PFF's charted coverage; passResult "IN" = intercepted
cover1_picks = plays[plays["pff_passCoverage"].eq("Cover-1") & plays["passResult"].eq("IN")]
g, pl = cover1_picks.iloc[0][["gameId", "playId"]]
show_animation(bdb.prepare(trk, plays, game_id=g, play_id=pl), times=[-1.0, 0.0, 1.2, 2.4])


What makes the robber work is that the dig is a man-beater by design. The receiver runs straight at his defender, then breaks flat across the field, away from a corner who was protecting the outside. Against pure man that corner is chasing, and a dig thrown on time is a completion with room to run. The robber doesn’t need to cover Z. He only needs to be in the lane when the ball comes, which he can do because he is free to read the whole play (his key receiver and the quarterback) instead of chasing one man. That is the key idea of modern man coverage: man coverage on the receivers, zone eyes on the quarterback from the one defender who can afford them.
The robber has his own weakness, and offenses know it. He is one man in the middle guarding a lane, so put two receivers in his area at different depths, a shallow cross under a dig, and he can only take one. That is a high-low on the robber, exactly the read Dropback Concepts built the drive and shallow-cross concepts around. And a quarterback who looks the robber off, staring at the middle to pull him in before throwing outside, turns the robber’s best habit against him.






NoteMadden vs. real life



In Madden, “Cover 1” is a play on a menu, and the game decides who covers whom. On a real field the call is a family of rules, and the most important ones are about the defender with no man. The same Cover 1 call might have the leftover linebacker rushing if the back stays in to block, sitting in the hole if the back releases, or spying a mobile quarterback; the safety might show two-high and rob, or line up in the middle and stay there. The defensive coordinator also decides technique and leverage player by player and receiver by receiver, often on the sideline between series. Two Cover 1 calls can look nothing alike.

title: Man Coverage: Cover 0, Cover 1, Robbers, and Brackets
text:
Cover 0: everybody’s man, nobody’s deep
Now remove the safety. Cover 0 is man coverage on every eligible receiver with no deep defender at all. The “0” is the number of deep safeties. Do the count again. The two defenders who were free in Cover 1 (the deep safety and the spare man) have no receiver and no deep job, so they become two more rushers. Usually that doesn’t mean the safeties themselves rush: the safeties come down to cover the tight end and the back, and the linebackers who used to cover them rush instead. So Cover 0 usually travels with a big blitz, six or seven rushers. It is the all-out blitz, the “house call,” the coverage behind the moment when the defense decides that the quarterback won’t have time to find the open man. (Not always, though: some zero calls rush only four or five and keep one spare defender sitting low in the middle, a “zero hole” or “zero lurk,” especially near the goal line.)


Show the Python
off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", GUN, 0.0, "Q"), O("X", "WR", LINE_D, -16.0), O("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, -9.5),
                 O("RB", "RB", OFF_BALL, 7.6, "R"), O("Y", "TE", OFF_BALL, 11.5), O("Z", "WR", LINE_D, 16.5)]
dfn = zero_front() + [D("LCB", "CB", 1.2, -15.3, "CB"), D("NB", "NB", 1.5, -8.8, "$"),
                      D("RCB", "CB", 1.2, 15.8, "CB"), D("SS", "SS", 2.5, 10.9, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 3.8, 7.0, "FS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=LOS, to_go=7)
for d_, t_ in (("LCB", "X"), ("NB", "H"), ("RCB", "Z"), ("SS", "Y"), ("FS", "RB")):
    p.man(d_, t_)
for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"):
    p.block(k, pts=[(-1.4, 0.0)])
for k in ("WDE", "MIKE", "WDT", "SDT", "SDE"):
    p.rush(k, pts=[(-1.7, 0.0)], speed=2.0)
p.rush("WILL", pts=[(-4.0, -0.5), (-5.0, -0.8)])
p.highlight("WILL")
fld = draw(p, lateral="full", window=(-9.5, 21.5))
oval(fld, p, (15.5, 0.0), (7.0, 30.0), color=style.MUTED, label="nobody deep", alpha=0.10)
say(fld, p, -7.6, 9.0, "6 rush, 5 block:\none comes free", fontsize=6.8)
say(fld, p, -3.8, -19.6, "inside shade:\nno help anywhere", fontsize=6.8)
field_legend(fld.ax, ["man", "rush", "ring", "ltg"])
plt.show()








Figure 34.5: Cover 0 against an empty formation (five receivers, nobody in the backfield), third-and-7. All five receivers have a man defender, each tight and shaded inside, and no one is deep: the middle of the field is open all the way to the end zone. The other six defenders rush, including both linebackers (M and W) walked up into the A gaps beside the center. Five linemen can block only five of them, so one rusher (ringed) comes free, and the quarterback has to throw before he arrives, usually in about two seconds.





The logic is arithmetic. The offense has five linemen. If the running back and tight end go out on routes, the five linemen are the only blockers, and six rushers beat five blockers: one is free. If the offense keeps a back in to block, his man defender has nobody to cover. In most zero calls he joins the rush (the “hug” rule again), so it’s seven against six, still one free; in some he just sits, as the safety does in the Corn Dog figure in Motion and Shifts as Weapons. Cover 0 is built so that someone comes unblocked, and the quarterback has to get rid of the ball before he arrives. In the charted seasons, Cover 0 was played with five or more rushers about three times in four, and the median throw against it came out about three tenths of a second sooner than against any other coverage.5 Three tenths is roughly the difference between throwing on the last step of the drop and taking one more hitch step to wait for a route to come open.
Because no one is behind them, Cover 0 defenders play inside leverage, the mirror of Cover 1. With the linebackers rushing, nobody is left in the middle of the field, so a slant caught there has open grass in front of it and nobody to tackle the receiver but the man chasing him. So they take the inside throw away and dare the quarterback to throw outside, a longer, slower throw with the sideline as an extra defender. Some teams play it off instead of pressed, five to seven yards deep and inside (“zero off”), so the defenders can see the quick throw, break on it and tackle, without the risk of being beaten clean at the line. The other danger is obvious from the picture: a receiver who beats his man on a deep route has nothing in front of him but grass. That is the bargain.


Show the Python

cols = [style.SERIES[1] if c == "COVER_0" else (style.SERIES[0] if c in ("COVER_1", "2_MAN") else style.MUTED)
        for c in order]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 3.1), sharey=True)
ys = np.arange(len(order))[::-1]
for ax, vals, lab, fmt in ((axes[0], ttt, "Median time to throw (seconds)", "{:.2f} s"),
                           (axes[1], expl, "Dropbacks gaining 20+ yards (%)", "{:.1f}%")):
    ax.barh(ys, vals.values, color=cols, height=0.62)
    for y_, v in zip(ys, vals.values):
        ax.text(v + vals.max() * 0.015, y_, fmt.format(v), va="center", fontsize=7.5, color=style.INK)
    ax.set_xlabel(lab, fontsize=8)
    ax.set_xlim(0, vals.max() * 1.22)
    ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=7.5)

axes[0].set_yticklabels([names[c] for c in order], fontsize=8)
fig.legend(handles=[Patch(color=style.SERIES[1], label="man, no deep help (Cover 0)"),
                    Patch(color=style.SERIES[0], label="other man coverages"), Patch(color=style.MUTED, label="zone")],
           fontsize=7.2, loc="upper center", ncol=3, frameon=False, bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 1.0))
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=1.2, rect=(0, 0, 1, 0.92))
plt.show()








Figure 34.6: The Cover 0 bargain, in charted NFL dropbacks between the 20s (2023–2025 regular seasons, FTN charting). Left: the median time from snap to throw against each coverage; the Cover 0 blitz gets the ball out fastest. Right: the share of dropbacks that gained 20 yards or more; Cover 0 also gives up the most big plays, because nobody is deep. The 2018–2022 seasons (NGS charting) show the same order. Source: nflverse participation data joined to play-by-play; sacks count as dropbacks with no throw, so they are left out of the time-to-throw medians.





The chart puts numbers on the trade. Between the 20-yard lines in 2023–2025, Cover 0 got the ball out fastest (a median of about 2.0 seconds), and it also gave up a gain of 20 yards or more on about one dropback in seven, the highest rate of any coverage and nearly twice the rate of the two-high zones. Cover 1, with its deep safety, sits in between. The defense is trading a higher chance of a quick incompletion or a sack for a higher chance of a long touchdown. That is a good bet when the offense needs a few yards and has to throw quickly anyway; it is a bad bet when one long completion decides the game. (The full blitz menu, and how offenses protect against it, is in Blitzing.)






ImportantWhy it exists: Cover 0



Cover 0 exists to win a race. Every rusher it can spare is sent, so the quarterback must throw now, often before his receivers have finished their routes, and every receiver has a man on him so there is no easy hot throw. It shines where the field is short and the throw has to be quick anyway: third-and-short, fourth down, inside the 10. What it gives up: any help at all. One missed tackle, one blown assignment or one receiver who beats his man deep is a touchdown, and a quarterback who escapes the free rusher finds a field full of defenders with their backs to him.


A handful of modern coordinators have leaned on the call harder than anyone. In nflverse charting the league leader in Cover 0 rate was Wink Martindale’s Baltimore defense in 2019 and his Giants in 2022 and 2023, and Brian Flores’s Miami Dolphins in 2020 and 2021.6 The most famous is Steve Spagnuolo. His 2007 Giants beat the 18–0 Patriots in Super Bowl XLII mostly by rushing four and blitzing only now and then, so his Cover 0 reputation comes from Kansas City, where he has been defensive coordinator since 2019: the Chiefs ranked in the top five in Cover 0 rate in every season from 2019 to 2025, and first in 2025.7 He is known less for how often he calls it than for when: at the moments offenses least expect it, which is part of what makes it work, because a quarterback who knows Cover 0 is coming can call a protection and a route to beat it.

section: Stacks and bunches: banjo and combo coverage
text:
Stacks and bunches: banjo and combo coverage
Man coverage has a structural weak point, and offenses found it long ago: receivers who line up close together. When two receivers stand a yard apart, or one directly behind the other in a stack, their defenders are close together too, and the receivers can release in directions that make the defenders cross. A defender chasing his man has to go around the other receiver, or around his own teammate, and loses a step. That is the rub from Dropback Concepts, and stacks and bunches are formations built to create it. (A rub has to look like an accident. A receiver more than a yard past the line who deliberately blocks a defender before the pass is thrown commits offensive pass interference, so offenses design the two paths to cross close by, not to collide.8)
The defense’s answer is to stop deciding before the snap. In a banjo, two defenders take two receivers together, and decide who has whom by how the routes declare: the outside defender takes the first receiver who breaks outside, the inside defender the first who breaks inside. Nobody has to cross anybody. (Don’t confuse it with the in-out bracket later in this chapter, which puts two defenders on one receiver, or with the exchange on motion from Motion and Shifts as Weapons, which swaps receivers before the snap.)


Show the Python
BJ_LAT, BJ_WIN = (4.0, 28.2), (-4.0, 12.0)


def stack_play():
    off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", GUN, 0.0, "Q"), O("Z", "WR", LINE_D, 13.0), O("H", "WR", -2.6, 13.6)]
    dfn = [D("RCB", "CB", 4.8, 15.8, "CB"), D("NB", "NB", 4.8, 10.4, "$")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=LOS, to_go=None)
    route_to(p, "Z", (2.0, 13.0), (6.0, 8.5), (7.6, 6.4))
    route_to(p, "H", (2.4, 14.1), (4.4, 19.6), (4.7, 21.2))
    return p


lock, banjo = stack_play(), stack_play()
set_tracks(lock, {   # each has to cross the other and H's release: both lose ground in the traffic
    "RCB": ease([(0.0, 4.8, 15.8), (0.6, 3.0, 14.9), (1.0, 3.7, 13.2), (1.45, 5.2, 10.6), (2.0, 6.2, 8.2)]),
    "NB": ease([(0.0, 4.8, 10.4), (0.6, 5.4, 12.4), (1.0, 4.6, 14.4), (1.45, 4.6, 16.6), (2.0, 4.8, 18.6)]),
}, t_end=2.0)
set_tracks(banjo, {  # they wait for the routes to declare, then take the receiver who comes to their side
    "RCB": ease([(0.0, 4.8, 15.8), (0.6, 4.6, 16.0), (1.0, 4.6, 17.4), (1.45, 5.1, 20.3), (2.0, 5.3, 21.6)]),
    "NB": ease([(0.0, 4.8, 10.4), (0.6, 5.1, 9.8), (1.07, 5.8, 7.8), (1.45, 7.8, 6.0), (2.0, 8.0, 5.6)]),
}, t_end=2.0)
BJ_T = [0.0, 0.6, 1.45]
PAIRS = {0: (("RCB", "Z"), ("NB", "H")), 1: (("RCB", "H"), ("NB", "Z"))}


def banjo_deco(i, j, fld, p):
    """Sideline cue in every panel; each receiver's separation from his defender in the last column."""
    say(fld, p, -2.4, 22.6, "outside →", fontsize=6.0)
    if j == len(BJ_T) - 1:
        for dk, rk in PAIRS[i]:
            sep = float(np.linalg.norm(np.array(p.position(dk, BJ_T[j])) - np.array(p.position(rk, BJ_T[j]))))
            rd, rw = p.position(rk, BJ_T[j])
            txt = f"{sep:.0f} yd: open" if sep >= 1.6 else f"{max(sep, 1.0):.0f} yd: covered"
            say(fld, p, rd + 1.9, rw, txt, fontsize=5.8, color=OD if sep >= 1.6 else DD, weight="bold")


if PDF:
    strip_rows([lock, banjo], ["Locked man", "Banjo"], BJ_T,
               [["CB has Z, $ has H.", "They must cross: traffic.", "Both receivers open."],
                ["They wait for the routes.", "Z breaks in, H out.", "CB takes H, $ takes Z."]],
               BJ_LAT, BJ_WIN, deco=banjo_deco)
    plt.show()
else:
    video([lock, banjo], ["Locked man", "Banjo"], BJ_LAT, BJ_WIN, t_end=1.8, width_in=6.4)





  
  Your browser does not support the video tag.



Figure 34.7: The same stack release against two ways of covering it (the offense’s right side, with the sideline at the right edge; simulated). Z is on the line, H directly behind him. Z runs a slant inside, H a quick out. Top row, locked man: the cornerback (CB) has Z and the nickel ($) has H, so they have to cross each other and H’s release; both lose ground in the traffic and both receivers come open (the yards are each receiver’s separation from his defender). Bottom row, banjo: the same two defenders wait for the routes to declare; the cornerback, outside, takes the receiver who breaks out (H) and the nickel, inside, takes the one who breaks in (Z). Nobody crosses, and both receivers are covered. In the web version this is a video.




Notice where the banjo defenders stand: about five yards off, not pressed. They need a moment to see which way each receiver is going, and from the line of scrimmage they would have no time to read before having to commit. The in/out split is the most common; some teams split them low/high instead, so the first receiver to break short goes to one defender and the first to go deep to the other. Every banjo also needs a rule for the release that doesn’t declare neatly, both receivers going the same way or both running straight upfield; usually the defenders fall back on their pre-snap match, or the outside man takes #1.
The banjo solves the rub by trading a little of man coverage’s certainty for zone-like flexibility. It is a small zone rule inside a man call: for the first yard or two, each defender guards a side rather than a person, then locks on to whoever comes to that side. (It runs the opposite way from the pattern matching you met in Coverage Fundamentals, which is a zone call whose defenders become man defenders once the routes declare. A banjo starts from man and borrows a moment of zone.) That makes it the simplest example of a combo coverage, the general name for coverages in which two or more defenders share receivers and decide who takes whom by how the routes declare. Against a three-receiver bunch, a common version is a “point” call: one defender presses the receiver at the point of the bunch (the one nearest the line), and the other two play first-out and first-in on the other two. Bigger combos play man on one side of the formation and zone on the other.
The price is communication and a new weakness. Both defenders must call it, both must read the same release, and both must commit at the same instant. Offenses go after banjos with routes that make the release ambiguous. The clearest is to send both receivers the same way, one a beat after the other.


Show the Python
p = Play(line5() + [O("QB", "QB", GUN, 0.0, "Q"), O("Z", "WR", LINE_D, 13.0), O("H", "WR", -2.6, 13.6)],
         [D("RCB", "CB", 4.8, 15.8, "CB"), D("NB", "NB", 4.8, 10.4, "$")], los=LOS, to_go=None)
route_to(p, "Z", (1.6, 13.0), (4.4, 9.0), (5.0, 7.2))          # first inside: quick slant
route_to(p, "H", (2.4, 14.0), (7.8, 14.3), (8.0, 5.6))         # second inside, a beat later
fld = draw(p, width_in=6.2, lateral=(-4.8, 28.2), window=(-6.8, 12.5))
branch(fld, p, [(4.8, 10.4), (4.7, 9.3), (5.6, 7.9)])                  # $ takes the first in-breaker
branch(fld, p, [(4.8, 15.8), (5.8, 15.7), (7.2, 13.6), (7.4, 11.4)])   # CB chases the second, from behind
say(fld, p, 2.0, 6.0, "1. Z in first:\n$ takes him", fontsize=6.6)
say(fld, p, 10.6, 10.6, "2. H in, a beat later: the CB\nmust chase him across, behind", fontsize=6.6)
say(fld, p, -2.4, 22.6, "outside →", fontsize=6.4)
field_legend(fld.ax, ["route", "react"])
plt.show()








Figure 34.8: How an offense beats a banjo (the same stack and the same two defenders; illustrative). Both receivers break inside, one a beat after the other. Z runs a quick slant (1), the first receiver inside, so the nickel ($), the inside defender, takes him. H pushes upfield and breaks inside a beat later (2) on a short in-cut. Nobody has broken outside, so the cornerback’s man is H, but H is now running away from him across the field with a two-to-three-yard head start, the very traffic problem the banjo was meant to avoid.





Other counters work the same way: a receiver who fakes in and breaks back out after the defenders have committed (the whip from Passing Fundamentals), or a third receiver arriving in the space the two defenders vacated. That is why bunch formations are a red-zone staple, and the red zone, as the numbers later in this chapter show, is where man coverage is most common. Bunches stress whatever rule the defense has.
The charters who label coverages for the NFL’s public data see these mixtures too. From 2023 on, the charting used by nflverse includes a label, COMBO, for plays that don’t fit a single coverage name. The data dictionary lists COMBO without defining it, so it is safest to read it as “a mixture the charter didn’t force into one box”; this chapter’s counts leave those plays out.

title: Man Coverage: Cover 0, Cover 1, Robbers, and Brackets
text:
Brackets: two on one
Sometimes the problem isn’t the formation; it’s one receiver. The offense has a player the defense cannot cover one-on-one, and leaving him in man coverage, even with a deep safety somewhere, is asking for a long afternoon. The answer is a bracket: two defenders on one receiver, one on each side of him, so whichever way he breaks, somebody is already there.


Show the Python
off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", GUN, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", GUN, -2.0, "R"),
                 O("X", "WR", LINE_D, -15.0), O("Y", "TE", OFF_BALL, 7.5),
                 O("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, 12.0), O("Z", "WR", LINE_D, 17.0)]
dfn = dline() + [D("MIKE", "MIKE", 5.0, 6.8, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.4, "W"),
                 D("LCB", "CB", 1.2, -14.4, "CB"), D("FS", "FS", 12.0, -11.0, "FS"),
                 D("NB", "NB", 3.5, 11.3, "$"), D("RCB", "CB", 1.2, 17.6, "CB"),
                 D("SS", "SS", 14.0, 6.0, "SS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=LOS, to_go=8)
for d_, t_ in (("LCB", "X"), ("FS", "X"), ("NB", "H"), ("RCB", "Z"), ("MIKE", "Y"), ("WILL", "RB")):
    p.man(d_, t_)
protect(p)
p.zone((17.5, 9.0), (6.0, 22.0), label="deep, trips side")
p.highlight("X")
fld = draw(p, lateral="full", window=(-8.5, 22.5))
number(fld, p, [("X", "#1"), ("Z", "#1"), ("H", "#2"), ("Y", "#3")])
say(fld, p, 12.0, -7.2, "over: FS", fontsize=6.8, color=DD, weight="bold")
say(fld, p, 2.6, -20.6, "under: CB", fontsize=6.8, color=DD, weight="bold")
oval(fld, p, (9.5, 0.5), (4.0, 8.0), color=style.MUTED, label="empty hole", alpha=0.10)
field_legend(fld.ax, ["man", "area", "ring", "ltg"])
plt.show()








Figure 34.9: A bracket on the isolated receiver in a 3x1 formation. The offense puts its best receiver, X (ringed), alone on the left as #1, with three receivers to the right. The defense brackets him: the left cornerback presses a step inside X and plays underneath, in trail technique, and the free safety (FS) plays over the top, 12 yards deep and only about 4 yards inside X, far from the middle of the field. The trips side is man coverage, with the strong safety (SS) as the single deep defender over it. The cost shows in the middle: the safety who would have been the robber is spent on X, so nobody sits in the hole, and the trips side’s man defenders have only one safety behind them.





Brackets come in two shapes, named for where the two defenders stand.


Show the Python
LAT_B, WIN_B = (-25.0, -3.0), (-3.5, 21.0)
BRACKET2 = style.SERIES[6]   # the second defender in the bracket


def bracket_panel(ax, kind):
    off = [O("X", "WR", LINE_D, -15.0)]
    if kind == "under":
        dfn = [D("CB", "CB", 1.2, -14.4, "CB"), D("FS", "FS", 13.0, -10.5, "FS")]
    else:
        dfn = [D("CB", "CB", 1.2, -16.0, "CB"), D("SS", "SS", 8.0, -7.6, "SS")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=LOS, to_go=None)
    p.highlight("X")
    fld = p.draw(ax=ax, lateral=LAT_B, window=WIN_B, title=False)
    clean(ax)
    ruler(fld, p, fs=5.5)
    opt = dict(color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.2, dash="-", z=3.8)
    if kind == "under":
        oval(fld, p, (7.5, -13.5), (9.0, 8.5))
        say(fld, p, 7.2, -20.4, "CB: under\n(short,\nmiddle)", fontsize=6.0)
        oval(fld, p, (17.2, -12.5), (5.0, 14.0), color=BRACKET2, alpha=0.2)
        say(fld, p, 17.2, -8.8, "FS: over\n(deep)", fontsize=6.0)
        branch(fld, p, [(0.0, -15.0), (8.0, -15.4), (19.5, -17.0)], **opt)    # go / fade: the safety's
        branch(fld, p, [(0.0, -15.0), (9.0, -15.0), (9.0, -9.0)], **opt)      # dig: the corner's
    else:
        oval(fld, p, (8.5, -19.6), (13.0, 5.4), label="CB:\nout", fs=6.0)
        oval(fld, p, (11.5, -10.4), (7.5, 7.5), color=BRACKET2, label="SS: in", fs=6.0, alpha=0.2)
        branch(fld, p, [(0.0, -15.0), (10.0, -15.0), (10.0, -20.5)], **opt)   # out: the corner's
        branch(fld, p, [(0.0, -15.0), (2.0, -15.0), (8.0, -9.5)], **opt)      # slant: the inside man's
    return fld


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.4, 3.9))
for ax, kind, ttl in zip(axes, ("under", "inout"), ("Under-over", "In-out")):
    bracket_panel(ax, kind)
    panel_title(ax, ttl)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=1.2)
plt.show()








Figure 34.10: The two shapes of bracket, on the same isolated receiver (X, offense’s left). Left, under-over: the cornerback, pressed a step inside, takes everything short and intermediate (orange area), trailing underneath, so a dig runs into him; the safety (purple area) takes everything deep, so a go route runs into him. Right, in-out: the cornerback plays outside leverage and takes routes to the sideline (out, comeback, fade), so the out runs into him; a second defender inside, here a safety at 8 yards (a robber or linebacker also works), takes everything that breaks in, so the slant runs into him. Either way X has a defender on both sides of every route he can run. Blue lines are sample routes.






Under-over (top-bottom). The cornerback presses head-up or a step inside and plays underneath, in trail technique, taking away anything short or intermediate (the slant and the dig are his); a safety plays over the top, taking away anything deep, the fade included. The receiver can’t run past the safety and can’t break in front of the corner. It is the classic way to take a deep threat out of a game.
In-out. The cornerback plays outside leverage and owns the sideline; a second defender (a robber, a linebacker, a nickel) sits inside and owns everything that breaks toward the middle. It suits a receiver who wins on slants and digs more than on go routes. (Same “in” and “out” words as a banjo, different job: the banjo is two defenders on two receivers, the bracket two on one.)

In today’s NFL the receiver being bracketed is often a tight end: a linebacker or the nickel underneath him, a safety over the top.
Before the snap, an under-over bracket can look like a two-high shell, two safeties deep, which Coverage Fundamentals taught you to read as Cover 2, quarters or 2-Man. The tell is where the safety stands. A two-high safety has to cover half the field, from the middle to the sideline, so he lines up roughly halfway between them. A bracket safety has one man to cover, so he cheats out over that man: only a few yards inside the receiver, far from the middle, while the other safety sits over the rest of the formation.
Brackets are expensive, and the bill always arrives somewhere else. Eleven defenders minus four rushers leaves seven for five receivers. Spend two on one receiver and the other four have five defenders between them: one is still free, but now he is usually the only deep player, or there is no robber, or one man defender has no help at all. In the 3x1 picture, the bracket on X is paid for by an empty hole in the middle of the field. Bracket the star and the offense’s job becomes simple: throw to the others, especially the receiver now covered by a linebacker.
That is a perfectly good outcome for many defenses. The idea is associated above all with Bill Belichick, whose game plans often started from one question: what does this offense most need to do, and how do we take it away? If the answer was a receiver, the answer was often a bracket, and the offense’s second and third options were invited to beat the Patriots instead. (How that habit became a philosophy is the story of Case Study: Belichick and Game-Plan Football.) A defense can also bracket only on some downs, or only in certain areas of the field, so the quarterback can’t assume where the second defender will be.

title: Man Coverage: Cover 0, Cover 1, Robbers, and Brackets
text:
Shadow corners
There is a cheaper way to deal with a great receiver, if you have the player for it: give him your own great player, everywhere. A shadow corner is a cornerback assigned to one receiver for the whole game. Wherever that receiver lines up (left, right, in the slot, in motion) the corner goes with him.


Show the Python
def shadow_snap(ax, snap):
    if snap == 1:
        off = spread()
        dfn = cover1_def(extra={"LCB": (1.2, -15.9)})
        keys = (("LCB", "X"), ("RCB", "Z"), ("NB", "H"), ("SS", "Y"), ("WILL", "RB"))
        star = "LCB"
    else:
        off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", GUN, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", GUN, -2.0, "R"),
                         O("H", "WR", LINE_D, -15.0), O("Y", "TE", OFF_BALL, 6.5),
                         O("X", "WR", OFF_BALL, 11.0), O("Z", "WR", LINE_D, 16.5)]
        dfn = cover1_def(extra={"LCB": (1.6, 11.6), "NB": (1.6, -15.9), "RCB": (1.2, 17.1),
                                "SS": (5.0, 7.1), "WILL": (4.5, -2.6), "MIKE": (4.5, 2.4)})
        keys = (("LCB", "X"), ("RCB", "Z"), ("NB", "H"), ("SS", "Y"), ("WILL", "RB"))
        star = "LCB"
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=LOS, to_go=None)
    for d_, t_ in keys:
        p.man(d_, t_)
    p.highlight(star)
    fld = p.draw(ax=ax, lateral="full", window=(-7.0, 16.0), title=False)
    clean(ax)
    return fld, p


fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(6.5, 5.6))
fld, p = shadow_snap(axes[0], 1)
panel_title(axes[0], "Snap 1: X wide left. The shadow corner is on him.")
say(fld, p, 1.4, -21.6, "shadow\ncorner", fontsize=6.8, color=style.INK, weight="bold")
fld, p = shadow_snap(axes[1], 2)
panel_title(axes[1], "Snap 2: X moves into the right slot. The shadow corner goes with him.")
say(fld, p, 6.0, 13.6, "same corner,\nnow in the slot", fontsize=6.8, color=style.INK, weight="bold")
say(fld, p, 5.6, -15.8, "the nickel ($)\nslides out to H", fontsize=6.6)
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=1.2)
plt.show()








Figure 34.11: A shadow corner on two snaps. Top: X lines up wide on the left, and the shadow corner (ringed CB) presses him there. Bottom: the offense moves X into the right slot of a 3x1 formation to get him away from that corner, and the corner goes with him into the slot, and the nickel back ($), normally the slot defender, slides out to take whoever is wide on the left (here H). A defense that keeps its corners on fixed sides (left corner, right corner) would let the offense pick the matchup by choosing where X lines up.





The reason most teams don’t do this is that it’s harder than it looks, for the corner and for the defense. A cornerback who has played the left side his whole career has to learn the right side, where his footwork is reversed, and the slot, where a receiver can release in either direction and the help is in different places. The rest of the defense has to adjust every snap around wherever the shadow went. And the corner has to be good enough that the defense can treat one receiver as solved, which is the whole point: a true shadow corner turns a bracket’s two defenders into one, and gives the defense its extra defender back. That is also why even man-heavy defenses with a great corner often don’t travel him every snap: a corner who is superb on the outside may be ordinary in the slot, and keeping him on one side and bracketing when needed is simpler for everyone else.
The modern archetype is Darrelle Revis. With Rex Ryan’s 2009 Jets he followed the opponent’s best receiver week after week, and the list of receivers he held quiet that season reads like an All-Pro team: Randy Moss twice, Andre Johnson, Terrell Owens twice, Reggie Wayne, Chad Ochocinco (no catches at all in their regular-season meeting). The press called it “Revis Island,” the place where receivers went to disappear, and the Jets allowed the fewest points in the NFL that year. Revis went into the Hall of Fame in his first year of eligibility, in 2023.9 More recently, Denver’s Patrick Surtain II, the 2024 Defensive Player of the Year, played the role for Vance Joseph’s defense: in the 2024 opener he lined up across from Seattle’s DK Metcalf on 24 of Metcalf’s 25 routes, by Next Gen Stats’ count.10 By this book’s count from nflverse charting, the Broncos played man coverage on a larger share of dropbacks than any other defense in both 2024 and 2025 (details in the section on when defenses choose man), a reminder that teams play the coverage their best players are built for.
The contrast is instructive. Richard Sherman, one of the best cornerbacks of the 2010s, mostly did not shadow. Seattle’s defense was built on single-high coverage, mostly Cover 3 (a zone) with plenty of Cover 1, and in both Sherman usually lined up on the defense’s left side and stayed there, letting the offense decide who would face him. Seattle sometimes moved him to follow a particular receiver, as against Atlanta’s Julio Jones in October 2016, but it was the exception.11 Revis was a travelling corner in a defense built around his matchup; Sherman was a fixed-side corner in a defense built around its structure. Both were great; the system decided which kind of great it needed.
