title: Man Coverage: Cover 0, Cover 1, Robbers, and Brackets
text:
When defenses choose man
Every defense plays both man and zone, and how often depends on scheme, on personnel and on the situation. You can see the situational part clearly in the public charting data.


Show the Python
dd_order = ["1st down", "2nd down", "3rd/4th & 1–2", "3rd/4th & 3–6", "3rd/4th & 7–10", "3rd/4th & 11+"]
fp_order = ["81–99", "41–80", "21–40", "11–20", "6–10", "1–5"]
eras = ["2018–2022 (NGS charting)", "2023–2025 (FTN charting)"]
ecol = {eras[0]: style.SERIES[0], eras[1]: style.SERIES[1]}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.4))
a = (CV.groupby(["dd", "era"])["man"].mean() * 100).unstack().reindex(dd_order)
b = (CV.groupby(["zone_fp", "era"], observed=True)["c0"].mean() * 100).unstack().reindex(fp_order)
xs = np.arange(len(dd_order))
for e in eras:
    axes[0].plot(xs, a[e].values, marker="o", ms=4.5, color=ecol[e], lw=1.8, label=e)
    axes[1].plot(np.arange(len(fp_order)), b[e].values, marker="o", ms=4.5, color=ecol[e], lw=1.8, label=e)
axes[0].set_xticks(xs)
axes[0].set_xticklabels(["1st", "2nd", "3rd/4th\n& 1–2", "& 3–6", "& 7–10", "& 11+"], fontsize=7)
axes[0].set_ylabel("Man coverage, % of dropbacks", fontsize=8)
axes[0].set_ylim(0, 75)
axes[0].set_title("Man coverage by down and distance", fontsize=9)
axes[1].set_xticks(np.arange(len(fp_order)))
axes[1].set_xticklabels(["81–99", "41–80", "21–40", "11–20", "6–10", "1–5"], fontsize=7)
axes[1].set_xlabel("Yards from the goal line being defended", fontsize=7.5)
axes[1].set_ylabel("Cover 0, % of dropbacks", fontsize=8)
axes[1].set_ylim(0, 70)
axes[1].set_title("Cover 0 by field position", fontsize=9)
for ax in axes:
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)
axes[0].legend(fontsize=6.8, loc="upper left", frameon=False)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=1.5)
plt.show()








Figure 34.12: When NFL defenses play man. Left: share of charted dropbacks played in a man coverage (Cover 0, Cover 1 or 2-Man), by down and distance. Right: share played in Cover 0, by how far the ball is from the goal line the defense is protecting. Each line is one charting source: NGS for 2018–2022 and FTN for 2023–2025. The two sources label man coverage at different rates, so compare the shapes, not the levels: in both, man coverage is most common on third (and fourth) and short or medium, least common on third-and-long, and Cover 0 takes over near the goal line (where ‘Cover 0’ often means nobody deep because there is no deep, not always six rushers). Regular seasons; blown coverages and plays charted as mixed are left out.





Three situations stand out, and each has a reason.
Third down, short and medium. On third-and-3 to third-and-6, defenses played man on about 60% of charted dropbacks in both charting eras, far more than on first down (about 25 to 36%).12 The defense knows where the ball has to go: just past the line to gain. Man coverage contests the throw at the sticks instead of rallying to tackle after a catch short of them. It also pairs naturally with a blitz, and third down invites one: the offense almost has to throw, so the defense can send extra rushers without much fear of a run, and a quick incompletion ends the drive. Notice what happens on third-and-11 or more: man coverage drops to its lowest rate of any situation. With that much to go, the defense is happy to let the receiver catch the ball in front of it and tackle him short, which is a zone’s job. Third-and-long is the zone defense’s down; third-and-medium is man’s. And first down leans zone for the opposite reason: the offense might run, or fake a run and throw, and man defenders with their backs to the backfield are the worst-placed players on the field against both. Zone defenders face the ball and can come up to tackle a runner.
The red zone and the goal line. As the field shrinks, man coverage takes over. Inside the defense’s 5-yard line, charters labelled 78 to 88% of dropbacks as man coverage, and Cover 0 on 41 to 62% of them, depending on the source. Near the goal line the biggest weakness of man coverage nearly disappears. A receiver who beats his man deep runs out of field: the back line of the end zone, the end line, acts like a safety that never misses. Zones, meanwhile, lose their main tool: there is no depth to drop into, so zone defenders end up standing on the end line while quick, sharp-breaking routes are completed in front of them. Man coverage contests the catch itself. So defenses spend their deep defenders on the rush or on more man coverage. Read the goal-line Cover 0 numbers with care, though: near the goal line “Cover 0” often means “nobody deep, because there is no deep,” not necessarily an all-out blitz. Of charted Cover 0 dropbacks inside the 5, only about 60 to 70% had five or more rushers.13 (The red zone gets its own chapter: Red Zone, Goal Line, and Short Yardage.)
Talent. Man coverage is only as good as the worst matchup in it, so teams with great cornerbacks play more of it. In nflverse charting, the Patriots played man on a larger share of dropbacks than any other defense in 2018 and 2019 (about 61% and 68%), the seasons around Stephon Gilmore’s Defensive Player of the Year award; Miami, coached from 2019 to 2021 by Brian Flores, a long-time Belichick assistant, led the league in 2020 and 2021; Denver, with Surtain, led it in 2024 and 2025.14 The reverse is true too. A defense with a weak link in the secondary, or facing a quarterback who punishes defenders with their backs turned by running, leans toward zone, where everyone faces the ball.






CautionCommon misconception



“NFL defenses are playing more and more man coverage.” You may see charts that say so. Be careful. The public coverage labels come from two different charting sources (NGS through 2022, FTN from 2023), and the man share jumps from about 29% of charted dropbacks in 2022 to about 44% in 2023 and 50% in 2024, then falls back to 31% in 2025. Defenses didn’t change that much that fast; the labelling did. Comparisons within a source (one season, or one era, as in the chart above) are safe; trend lines across the 2022/2023 break are not. (The season-by-season figures are in the note to the third-down paragraph above.)

title: Man Coverage: Cover 0, Cover 1, Robbers, and Brackets
section: How offenses attack man, and how the defense answers
text:
How offenses attack man, and how the defense answers
Every offense has a list of plays it calls when it expects man coverage. You met most of them from the offense’s side in Part 4; here they are from the defense’s side, paired with the counter each one provokes. Notice that most of the defense’s counters are things we’ve already met in this chapter: the free defender, the banjo, the bracket.



The offense’s man-beater
Why it works against man
The defense’s counter




Crossers and mesh (Dropback Concepts)
A crossing receiver runs away from a trailing defender, through traffic.
A robber or rat sitting in the middle; defenders who pass crossers on to each other in combos.


Rubs, stacks and bunches
Defenders must go around receivers or teammates (the contact has to look incidental, or it is offensive pass interference).
Banjo and combo rules; pressing the front receiver of a stack to wreck the timing.


The slant (The Quick Game)
Beats an outside-leveraged defender inside, quickly.
Inside help: a rat or lurker under the slant; inside leverage in Cover 0.


Double moves
Punish a man defender who jumps the first break.
A deep safety over the top (Cover 1, a bracket); patient technique.


Motion, especially at the snap (Motion and Shifts as Weapons)
Gives the receiver a running start and forces the defender to chase across the formation; it also reveals man.
Exchanges instead of travelling, so motion reveals less; zone calls disguised to look like man (and man calls disguised as zone).


The running back on a linebacker (the angle route)
The slowest cover man on the field is often matched on a quick back.
Putting a safety or a fast linebacker on the back; a free defender who helps on him.


The scrambling quarterback
Man defenders have their backs to him; nobody is left to tackle.
A spy, or a rat who keeps his eyes on the quarterback; more zone.


The back-shoulder and the fade
Against press, the ball is thrown where only the receiver can reach it.
A safety over the top; a cornerback who plays the receiver’s hands (the out-of-phase technique above).



The Chiefs’ “Corn Dog” touchdowns in Super Bowl LVII, which you met in Motion and Shifts as Weapons, are the textbook case of the motion line in that table: the man defender went with the first move, the receiver came back the other way, and nobody was there. The general lesson is the one you started the chapter with. Man coverage asks each defender to stay with a person, and every man-beater is a way of making that harder: run away, run through traffic, change direction twice, or start already moving.

title: Man Coverage: Cover 0, Cover 1, Robbers, and Brackets
text:
Film room






NoteFilm room: Patriots 2003 and 2019 — Ty Law, Stephon Gilmore and the man-coverage habit



Two Patriots seasons, sixteen years apart, bookend Belichick’s man-coverage defenses. In the 2003 AFC Championship Game against Indianapolis, Ty Law intercepted Peyton Manning three times in a 24–14 win, playing press-man against the Colts’ receivers and, in his words afterward, the simplest game plan imaginable: “Just beat them up.” The rules response that followed, the 2004 crackdown on illegal contact, became known as the “Ty Law Rule.”15
In 2019 the Patriots led the NFL in points allowed (14.1 per game) and total defense, and Stephon Gilmore became the first Patriot to be named Defensive Player of the Year, tying for the league lead with six interceptions and returning two of them for touchdowns.16 That was the season New England led the league in man coverage (the talent paragraph above has the number), and the habit around Gilmore was the Belichick one: man coverage on most of the field, and the spare defenders spent on whatever the opponent most wanted to do, often its best receiver or tight end.
What to notice: on a 2019 Patriots third down, find the free defenders first: usually a safety deep in the middle and a second defender in the hole or bracketing the offense’s best receiver. The pattern repeats from 2003 to 2019 with different players: man coverage on the people the defense trusts, and the free defenders spent on the player or the area it fears.








NoteFilm room: Chiefs, Super Bowl LVIII (February 11, 2024) — Spagnuolo brings the house



Overtime, 49ers ball, third-and-4 at the Kansas City 9. San Francisco called what looked like a well-designed play-action pass for Jauan Jennings, and the replays later showed receivers coming open. It didn’t matter. Steve Spagnuolo sent six rushers in Cover 0, Chris Jones came through untouched, and Brock Purdy had to let the ball go early; it sailed over Jennings’s head. San Francisco settled for a field goal, and Patrick Mahomes answered with the game-winning touchdown drive. “On third down,” linebacker Nick Bolton said afterward, “we brought the house.” “They brought Zero,” Purdy said.17
What to notice: an all-out pressure on a third down inside the 10 is the Cover 0 bargain at its most favourable for the defense. The field is short, so the deep ball that punishes Cover 0 everywhere else barely exists; the throw has to be quick anyway; and one free rusher is enough to end the play. Watch for the same ingredients on any Chiefs third down near the goal line: the safeties walking down, everyone pressed, and a count of rushers that exceeds the count of blockers.








NoteFilm room: Jets at Raiders, December 6, 2020 — the bargain lost



The other side of the bargain. The winless Jets led the Raiders 28–24 with seconds left, and Las Vegas was near midfield. Defensive coordinator Gregg Williams called an all-out blitz with Cover 0 behind it. Derek Carr stood in and threw deep, and Henry Ruggs ran past his rookie cornerback, one-on-one with nobody behind him, for a 46-yard touchdown with 5 seconds left: Raiders 31, Jets 28. The Jets fired Williams the next day.18
What to notice: everything that makes Cover 0 a good bet at the goal line makes it a bad one here. The field was long, so the deep ball existed; the offense needed a big play, not a few yards; and one lost footrace decided the game. Compare it with the Super Bowl LVIII snap above: same call, opposite situation.








NoteFilm room: Jets 2009 — the shadow



Watch any 2009 Jets game against a team with a star receiver and follow Darrelle Revis before the snap. When the star moves from one side to the other, Revis moves with him, and the other Jets defenders reshuffle around that one fixed matchup. (Denver’s 2024 opener at Seattle, with Surtain on Metcalf, shows the same thing in the modern game.)
What to notice: the shadow corner’s matchup frees the rest of the defense. Against Revis’s receiver the Jets often needed no help at all, so the safety who would have bracketed him was available to rob, blitz or double someone else. That is what a shadow corner is really worth: one player doing the job of two.








TipWatch for it on Sunday



Who’s facing the quarterback? It is the fastest man-or-zone test there is.

Before the snap: the corners. Squared up to the receiver, close, weight forward, eyes on the receiver’s belt: lean man. Turned inside, deeper, eyes on the quarterback: lean zone.
Before the snap: motion. Does somebody run across the formation with the man in motion? That is man. Do the defenders shift over and swap? Could be either: watch the next clue.
Before the snap: the safeties. One deep safety in the middle and corners pressed: think Cover 1. Nobody deep and six or seven players on or near the line on third down or near the goal line: think Cover 0 and expect a quick throw.
At the snap: the eyes. One second after the snap, look at the defenders underneath. Backs turned to the quarterback, running with receivers: man. Facing the quarterback, settling into areas: zone. The one defender in the middle facing the quarterback when everyone else is running with someone is the rat or robber. Find him and you’ll know where not to throw.
Close formations. When receivers stack or bunch, watch the two or three defenders over them at the release. Do they cross each other (locked man) or trade (banjo)?
The star. Where is the offense’s best receiver, and who is on him? The same corner every snap, on both sides of the field, is a shadow. A safety 10 to 12 yards deep and only a few yards inside him, far from the middle, is a bracket.

text:
Predict the play






TipPredict the play 1: the man in the middle





Show the Python
off = spread(rb_w=-2.0)
off = [q.moved(w=7.0) if q.key == "H" else q for q in off]
off = [q.moved(w=11.5) if q.key == "Y" else q for q in off]
dfn = cover1_def(extra={"NB": (3.5, 7.6), "SS": (10.6, 3.4), "MIKE": (4.8, 11.0), "WILL": (4.5, -1.6),
                        "LCB": (1.2, -15.9), "RCB": (1.2, 15.9)})
p = Play(off, dfn, los=LOS, to_go=8)
p.highlight("SS")
fld = draw(p, lateral="full", window=(-8.5, 19.0))
branch(fld, p, [(-1.5, -9.0), (-2.8, -6.0), (-2.8, 4.5), (-1.6, 6.0)], color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.3)
branch(fld, p, [(4.0, -9.8), (3.0, -6.0), (3.0, 4.6), (3.4, 6.4)], lw=1.3)
say(fld, p, 6.4, -6.5, "$ followed H across", fontsize=6.6)
number(fld, p, [("Z", "#1"), ("Y", "#2"), ("H", "#3")])
field_legend(fld.ax, ["motion", "react", "ring", "ltg"])
plt.show()








Figure 34.13: Second-and-8, ball in the middle of the field. Before the snap, H motioned from the left slot across to the right (blue dashes) and the nickel ($) ran across with him (orange dashes); both are shown where they finished, so the offense is now 3x1 to the right (Z, the tight end Y, and H, who is now #3). The corners are pressed, a step outside. One safety (FS) is 14 yards deep in the middle; the other (SS, ringed) stands 10 yards deep, just off the middle.





What coverage is this most likely to be, and which throw should the quarterback avoid? What would you call to beat it?






TipAnswer





Cover 1 with a robber. The tells stack up: the nickel travelled with H’s motion all the way across the formation, which is man coverage; the corners are pressed and squared up; and there is exactly one safety deep in the middle, so the middle of the field is closed. Now count. Five receivers need five men: two corners, the nickel on H, the Mike on the tight end, the Will on the back. That leaves the second safety, 10 yards deep near the middle, with nobody to cover. He is the free defender, a robber, and his job is to read the trips side and the quarterback and jump the first route that breaks into the middle.
Avoid the single in-breaking route into his area: a lone dig or crosser at 8 to 12 yards is exactly the throw he is there to steal, as in the robber animation earlier in the chapter. Attack him with a high-low: a shallow crosser underneath and a dig behind it (the drive concept), so he can’t take both, or look him off to the middle and throw outside. You could also attack the corners one-on-one away from the robber with a back-shoulder fade or a double move, since the free safety must cover the whole deep middle, or put the running back on a linebacker with an angle route.











TipPredict the play 2: who has the back?





Show the Python
off = spread(rb_w=2.0)
dfn = zero_front() + [D("LCB", "CB", 1.2, -15.6, "CB"), D("NB", "NB", 1.4, -9.6, "$"),
                      D("RCB", "CB", 1.2, 15.6, "CB"), D("SS", "SS", 4.0, 8.6, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 10.0, 1.2, "FS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=80, to_go=6)
p.highlight("FS")
fld = draw(p, lateral="full", window=(-8.5, 19.0))
branch(fld, p, [(9.2, 1.2), (7.8, 1.2)], lw=1.2)
say(fld, p, 11.6, 7.4, "creeping\nforward", fontsize=6.4)
field_legend(fld.ax, ["react", "ring", "ltg"])
plt.show()








Figure 34.14: Third-and-6 at the defense’s 30. The offense has 11 personnel in a 2x2: four receivers spread out and the running back (R) beside the quarterback. The corners and the nickel are pressed on X, Z and H, and the strong safety is 4 yards off the tight end Y. Six defenders are on the line, including both linebackers in the A gaps beside the center. The only other defender is the free safety (FS, ringed), 10 yards deep in the middle of the field, creeping forward as the quarterback calls the signals.





Count it. If all six defenders on the line rush, who covers the running back? So what coverage is coming, and what should the offense do about it?






TipAnswer





Cover 0, with a six-man rush. Five receivers need five men. Four of them are already standing on their receivers: two corners, the nickel, and the strong safety on Y. The fifth man is the only one left, the free safety, and he is the only possible cover man for the running back. That is why he is at 10 yards and creeping rather than at 13 to 15: he isn’t guarding the deep middle, he is getting closer to his man. So nobody will be deep, and six rush. (Compare Predict the play 1, where there were two players beyond the linebackers and the arithmetic left one free.)
Could it still be Cover 1? Only if one of the six on the line drops out to take the back and the free safety stays deep; a defense can also show this and drop players out at the snap (the “simulated” pressures of Zone Blitzes, Fire Zones, and Simulated Pressure). But a lone safety at 10 yards, creeping, on third down, is the classic picture of zero.
What the offense should do: count the rushers against the blockers. Six rushers against five linemen means one comes free, so the back should stay in to block. That makes it six against six, and if the free safety then joins the rush (“hug”), the quarterback must throw hot, now, to a receiver winning against an inside-shaded defender: a quick out, a fade, or a rub. And because nobody is deep, any receiver who wins a vertical route is a touchdown.











TipPredict the play 3: two on the tight end





Show the Python
off = spread(rb_w=-2.0)
dfn = cover1_def(extra={"MIKE": (4.0, 7.8), "WILL": (4.5, -2.0), "SS": (10.0, 7.5), "FS": (14.0, -1.0),
                        "NB": (1.4, -9.6)})
p = Play(off, dfn, los=LOS, to_go=7)
p.highlight("SS")
fld = draw(p, lateral="full", window=(-8.5, 19.0))
field_legend(fld.ax, ["ring", "ltg"])
plt.show()








Figure 34.15: Third-and-7. The offense’s best receiver is its tight end, Y, in the right slot of a 2x2. The Mike (M) is 4 yards off him, shaded inside. The strong safety (SS, ringed) is 10 yards deep, a step and a half inside Y. The free safety (FS) is 14 yards deep in the middle. The corners and the nickel are pressed on X, Z and H; the Will (W) is over the running back.





What are the two defenders over Y doing, and where should the ball go?






TipAnswer





Cover 1 with a bracket on the tight end. Count: four rushers, and five receivers with a man each (the corners on X and Z, the nickel on H, the Will on the back, the Mike on Y). That leaves two spare defenders. One, the free safety, is deep in the middle: Cover 1. The other, the strong safety, has nobody to cover and yet stands only a step and a half inside Y, 10 yards deep, which no robber would do (a robber sits in the middle). He is the “over” half of an under-over bracket on Y, and the Mike, tight and inside, is the “under” half.
Throw somewhere else. The bracket’s bill is paid in the middle: with the strong safety spent on Y, nobody sits in the hole. A crosser from H or X has room once it clears the Mike’s area, and the running back on the Will (an angle route) is a classic answer. X and Z are one-on-one with only the free safety behind them. Throwing to Y into two defenders on third-and-7 is what the defense is daring the quarterback to do. A defense can disguise this, of course, by standing the safety there and playing something else; and the same lean against a 3x1 formation can also belong to a split-field coverage check (see Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage).

title: Man Coverage: Cover 0, Cover 1, Robbers, and Brackets
text:
Takeaways

Man coverage covers people, not places. It is tight, certain about who covers whom, and lets the defense pick matchups. Its price is that man defenders watch receivers, not the quarterback, and need help somewhere.
The free defenders define the family. Cover 1 keeps one safety deep and usually one more defender to rush, rob or spy; Cover 0 keeps nobody deep and usually sends six or seven. The rat, the robber and the lurker are the same idea: one defender with zone eyes, in the middle, where man coverage is weakest.
Leverage follows the help. With inside help (Cover 1), corners usually play outside and funnel receivers inside (split, down and distance can change it); with no help (Cover 0), they play inside and protect the quick throw. Technique (press, off, trail) is chosen per matchup and per down.
Close formations and great receivers get special rules. Banjo and combo calls stop stacks and bunches from creating rubs; brackets spend two defenders on one star; a shadow corner spends one.
Man coverage is a situational weapon. In the charted NFL seasons it was most common on third and short-to-medium and near the goal line (where Cover 0 is often the most common call), and least common on third-and-long. The public man-rate trend breaks at 2022/2023 because the charting source changed.
Every man-beater makes staying with a receiver harder: crossers and mesh, rubs, slants against leverage, double moves, motion at the snap, a back on a linebacker, a scrambling quarterback. The defense’s counters are the free defender, the banjo and the bracket.

title: Cover 3: Sky, Buzz, Cloud, and Seattle’s Match Version
text:
Cover 3 in one picture: three deep, four under
First-and-10 near midfield. Before the snap the broadcast’s high camera shows one safety, alone, 15 yards deep in the middle of the field. The other safety has walked down to eight yards, just outside the tight end, and stands there like an extra linebacker. The offense hands the ball to its running back, who runs into a wall: eight defenders near the line against seven blockers, and the one nobody blocked makes the tackle for a yard. Two plays later, same formation, same defense. This time it’s a fake handoff, the eight defenders lean forward, and the tight end runs straight up the field past the linebackers. The quarterback drops it in behind them for 28 yards. Same coverage both times, and the analyst says, “That’s the deal with Cover 3.” What deal? Why would a defense take a safety out of the deep part of the field, where the big plays happen, and leave one man in the middle? Why does the same structure stop the run so well and leak a seam route? And why, for more than a decade, was the most feared defense in the NFL built almost entirely on this one plain-looking coverage? This chapter takes Cover 3 apart: what each defender does, the three ways a defense rotates into it, where the holes are, and the version that taught it to close them.
You’ll be able to…
Cover 3 is a zone coverage with three deep defenders, each guarding a third of the field’s width, and four underneath defenders, each guarding an area in front of them. With four rushers, that’s all eleven. The two cornerbacks take the outside thirds, one safety takes the middle third, and the other safety comes down to join three linebackers or nickel backs underneath. That last move, a safety coming down, is what the rest of this chapter is about, and it has a name. Here is the picture with the most common version of it, the sky rotation.
Show the Python
fld, p = two_state(spread(), C3_PRE | {"SS": (11.0, 10.4)}, C3_POST, rings=("SS",))
deep_thirds(fld, p, label_d=24.8)
for s in (-1, 1):
    zone_box(fld, p, 2.0, 13.5, s * 9.4, s * 23.6, "curl-flat", label_d=12.4)
    zone_box(fld, p, 4.5, 13.5, s * 0.6, s * 9.0, "hook", label_d=12.4)
say(fld, p, 4.0, 20.6, "sky: the SS\ncomes down to\nthe curl-flat", fontsize=6.6, color=DD)
say(fld, p, -6.8, 5.5, "four rush", fontsize=6.4)
field_legend(fld.ax, ["ghost", "drop", "zone", "ring"])
plt.show()








Figure 35.1: Cover 3 sky against a 2x2 formation (11 personnel: three receivers, a tight end flexed into the right slot). Dashed outlines show where each defender lined up, dashed arrows where he goes at the snap. Deep: the two cornerbacks (CB) bail to the outside thirds and the free safety (FS) sinks to the middle third, about 17 to 18 yards deep. Underneath: the strong safety (SS, ringed), who lined up about 11 yards deep just outside the tight end (Y), comes down and out to the right curl-flat area (the sky rotation); the nickel ($) widens to the left curl-flat, and the Mike (M) and Will (W) drop to the hooks. Seven defenders cover, four rush. Notice where the SS started: outside the tight end. That is the sky tell.
Read the picture from the top down, because that’s how the coverage is built.
The deep three. Each cornerback has the deep third on his side, from a few yards inside the numbers out to the sideline, and the free safety has the middle third, from hash to hash and a few yards beyond. Their rule is the oldest one in pass defense: nobody gets behind me. A Cover 3 corner lines up 7 to 9 yards off his receiver with outside leverage and, at the snap, opens his hips toward the sideline and runs back, keeping the receiver in front of him and his eyes, as much as he can, on the quarterback. He’ll give up a five-yard hitch all day. He will not give up the deep ball over his head. The free safety starts 13 to 16 yards deep in the middle and drifts back to 17 or 18, reading the quarterback, ready to break toward whichever side the ball is thrown. He is the post safety: the man in the post, where post routes go, and the reason the middle of the field is “closed.”
Why three, and why these three? Because a third of the field, about 18 yards, is ground a deep defender can cover comfortably from a good starting spot while the ball is in the air, and because the corners are the defense’s best pure cover men and the outside thirds are where a single receiver runs a go route along the sideline. Two deep defenders can split the field too (that’s Cover 2), but then each has 27 yards and nobody stands in the deep middle. Three is the fewest that keeps a defender in the post and a defender over each sideline.
The underneath four. That leaves four players for the short and intermediate areas, and there are seven named zones underneath (two flats, two curls, two hooks and the hole). Cover 3 solves the arithmetic the way all zones do, by giving each underneath defender two zones and an order to play them in:
The four rushers don’t cover anything, but they’re part of the deal. Cover 3 is a four-man-rush coverage. If the defense wants to send a fifth rusher and still play three deep, it has to take one of the underneath four away, and then it’s a different call, a three-deep, three-under fire zone, which Zone Blitzes, Fire Zones, and Simulated Pressure builds.

title: Cover 3: Sky, Buzz, Cloud, and Seattle’s Match Version
text:
The two curl-flat defenders, one on each side, take the outside underneath areas. Here they are the strong safety on the right and the nickel on the left. A curl-flat defender drops toward the curl area, about 10 to 12 yards deep under the outside receiver, and breaks to the flat when a receiver or the ball goes there. He’s the busiest man in the coverage, and the next section is about him.
The two hook defenders, the Mike and Will linebackers here, take the inside areas: they drop to 8 to 10 yards around the hashes, wall off anything crossing the middle, and keep an eye on the running back, who may slip out late. Some staffs call them hook-curl players, because when a receiver runs a curl inside the curl-flat defender, the hook defender widens to take it.








ImportantWhy it exists



Cover 3 exists because it is the cheapest way to guard the whole deep field. Three deep defenders, a third each, means nothing goes over the top, and yet one safety is left over to come down and help against the run or underneath. Two-deep coverages (Cover 2, quarters) need two safeties deep; man coverage needs a defender for every receiver. Cover 3 is the middle path: deep security with only three, an extra body near the line, and every underneath defender facing the quarterback, so the ball is always thrown in front of somebody who can see it and tackle (and somebody who sees a quarterback scramble the moment it starts, which man defenders, turned to their receivers, often don’t).
What it gives up. Four underneath defenders for seven underneath zones, so there are always soft spots, and three deep defenders against an offense that can send four receivers deep. Every hole this chapter draws comes from one of those two numbers.

section: The curl-flat defender, and why he became a seam-flat defender
text:
The curl-flat defender, and why he became a seam-flat defender
If you want to understand Cover 3, watch the curl-flat defender. He has the hardest job in the coverage because he has two zones, the curl and the flat, and the offense knows it.
Here is his problem. He lines up a few yards inside the slot receiver, in an apex between the slot and the tackle, because he also has a job against the run. At the snap the outside receiver (#1) is somewhere outside and in front of him, the slot (#2) right in front of him. If #1 runs a curl at 12 yards and #2 runs to the flat at 3 yards, one defender has to cover both: if he sits under the curl, the flat is open; if he jumps the flat, the curl is open behind him. That’s the whole idea of the offense’s curl-flat concept, and of a dozen others (Dropback Concepts and The Quick Game draw them from the quarterback’s side: he reads this one defender and throws away from him).
Coaches handle the problem in two different ways, and the difference is one of the most important in this chapter.
The spot-drop answer: play the quarterback. The classic curl-flat defender drops to his landmark, about 10 to 12 yards deep, a few yards inside the outside receiver, and reads the quarterback’s eyes. If the quarterback looks at the curl, he’s already under it; if the quarterback looks at the flat, he breaks down on it as the ball is thrown, and since he’s facing the throw, a quick receiver in the flat should gain only a few yards before he arrives. The coaching phrase is “sink and drive”: sink under the curl, drive on the flat. It’s simple, it’s fast to teach, and it keeps the defender’s eyes where they can see a scramble or a throw. Its weakness is everything that runs past him. The slot receiver’s seam route, straight up the field between the hash and the numbers, is not his business in spot-drop: he lets it go by, and the deep defenders have to deal with it.
The match answer: play the slot receiver first. The other approach changes the order of his jobs. A seam-flat defender keys the number 2 receiver from the snap. If #2 goes vertical, the defender walls him (gets his body into the receiver’s inside path so #2 has to run around him; any contact has to come within 5 yards of the line) and then carries him up the seam, running with him like a man defender until the deep help is over the top. If #2 goes to the flat, the defender goes with him. If #2 goes inside, the defender passes him to the hook defender and only then settles under the outside receiver’s curl. Seam first, flat second, curl last.

        say(fld, p, 1.7, -21.7, "#2 out:\ngo with him", fontsize=6.2, color=DD)
        say(fld, p, 13.6, -13.6, "#2 in: pass him\nto the hook,\nsink under #1", fontsize=6.2, color=DD)
        panel_title(ax, "Seam-flat (match): a receiver", fs=8.3)
    for k, txt in (("X", "#1"), ("H", "#2")):
        q = p.players[k]

fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.8)
plt.show()








Figure 35.2: Two ways to play the same spot, on the offense’s left. Left: the curl-flat defender of spot-drop Cover 3. Whatever the receivers do, the nickel ($, ringed, drawn where he ends up) widens and sinks to his landmark, about 11 yards deep under the outside receiver’s curl (X), with his eyes on the quarterback. If the ball is thrown to the flat (to a back or a receiver, not drawn), he breaks down on it as it’s thrown (thin arrow). The slot’s seam route (H) runs past him, inside, and becomes someone else’s problem. Right: the seam-flat defender of match Cover 3 reads the slot receiver (#2) first, so he is drawn at the snap with his three possible reactions. If H goes vertical, the nickel walls him off and carries him up the seam; if H breaks out to the flat, he goes with him; if H breaks inside, he passes him to the hook defender and sinks under X. Faint routes are H’s three choices. In both panels the corner (CB) bails to his deep third.





Why would a defense choose one over the other? Because they lose to different things. The curl-flat defender is beaten by routes that go past him (the seam) or that put two receivers on his two zones at once. The seam-flat defender closes the seam, but he is now following a receiver, so he’s beaten by routes that drag him away from his area (a vertical release that pulls him deep while the outside receiver runs a quick out underneath) and by switches, crossing releases in which #1 and #2 trade places at the snap so the defenders’ rules have to trade them back at full speed. The seam-flat label is also what you’ll hear in fire zones (three under, three deep), where the two outside underneath defenders are called seam-flat players for exactly this reason: with only three underneath, nobody else can protect the seams.
Most NFL Cover 3 today is closer to the seam-flat version, at least against vertical releases. Hold that thought: it’s the heart of the four-verticals section below.

section: Why defenses love it: the eighth man
text:
Why defenses love it: the eighth man
Now the payoff. Cover 3 brings one of the two safeties down. Against a passing formation he becomes a curl-flat defender. Against a running formation, he’s something more valuable: an eighth man in the box.


Show the Python
off_i = offense("i_form")
d43 = defense("4-3_over", "single_high", off_i)
moves = {"SS": (8.0, 7.6), "FS": (14.5, 0.0), "LCB": (7.5, -15.8), "RCB": (7.5, 15.8)}
d43 = [q.moved(d=moves[q.key][0], w=moves[q.key][1], label="CB" if q.pos == "CB" else q.label)
       if q.key in moves else q for q in d43]
d43 = [q.moved(label="Sm") if q.key == "SAM" else q for q in d43]
off_i = [q.moved(label="R") if q.key == "RB" else q for q in off_i]
pr = Play(off_i, d43, los=LOS, to_go=None)
pr.highlight("SS", "FS")
fld = draw(pr, lateral=(-22, 22), window=(-9.0, 21.0))
zone_box(fld, pr, 0.2, 9.6, -6.6, 9.8, "", color=style.DEFENSE, alpha=0.10)
say(fld, pr, 11.2, 1.6, "8 defenders in the box", color=DD, fontsize=7.4, weight="bold")
say(fld, pr, -4.6, 6.4, "7 blockers: five linemen,\nthe tight end (Y),\nthe fullback (F)", color=OD, fontsize=6.8, ha="left")
say(fld, pr, 17.0, 0.0, "one deep safety", fontsize=6.8)
for s in (-1, 1):
    path(fld, pr, [(8.9, s * 15.9), (14.6, s * 16.3)], lw=1.0, shrink=0.0)
    say(fld, pr, 16.4, s * 16.3, "to the deep ⅓", fontsize=6.6, color=DD)
plt.show()








Figure 35.3: Why Cover 3 is a run defense: a base 4-3 against 21 personnel (two backs, one tight end) in an I-formation. With the free safety (FS) alone in the deep middle, the strong safety (SS, ringed) can stand 8 yards deep just outside the tight end, where he is a run defender first. The shaded box holds eight defenders (four linemen, the Sam (Sm), Mike (M) and Will (W) linebackers, and the SS) against seven possible blockers (five linemen, the tight end Y and the fullback F): one more defender than the offense can block. The two cornerbacks (CB) line up 7 to 8 yards off but still bail to the deep outside thirds at the snap (short arrows), so the deep field stays covered.





The logic is simple arithmetic, and it’s the arithmetic of every run game in this book (Run Fits and Box Math builds it properly). An offense has at most five linemen plus whatever tight ends and backs stay in to block. If the defense has more men near the line than the offense has blockers, somebody is unblocked, and an unblocked defender usually makes the tackle. That spare man is the plus-one. Two-high coverages keep both safeties 10 to 14 yards deep. They can still fit the run (quarters safeties, in particular, are taught to fill the lane just outside the box as soon as they read run), but they arrive a beat later, from depth, so at the snap the box is seven against seven. Cover 3 puts the eighth man there from the start, and still has three deep.
That down safety also gives the defense a clean answer to the hardest question in run defense: who stops the ball from getting to the outside? In a sky rotation the safety is the force player, the defender whose job is to turn a wide run back inside toward the pursuit. In a buzz rotation he’s the alley player, filling the lane between the force player and the box from the inside out. Behind him the linebackers fit the gaps inside, each knowing that the safety owns the edge or the lane next to it (Run Fits and Box Math draws the full fits). Either way, the coverage and the run fit come from the same call. That’s why Cover 3, and its man-coverage cousin Cover 1, were for decades the default on first-and-10: one call that defends the run with eight and still guards the deep ball with three.
The data shows the pattern. On dropbacks charted from 2018 to 2022, Cover 3 was the call on 38 percent of first downs but only 19 percent of third-and-4-to-6 and 19 percent of snaps in the red zone, against 34 percent elsewhere on the field. Defenses reach for it on early downs, when they have to respect the run, and turn to man coverage when the field is short or the down demands a tight cover: Cover 1 or Cover 0 was the call on about half of those third-and-medium and red-zone dropbacks, against 28 percent elsewhere.1


Show the Python (coverage labels on early-down dropbacks, nflverse, 2018–2022)
from gridiron.data import nfl, pbp

COLS = ["game_id", "play_id", "season_type", "qb_dropback", "defteam", "down", "ydstogo", "yardline_100",
        "complete_pass", "yards_gained"]

def labelled_dropbacks(season):
    """Regular-season dropbacks with a charted coverage label (nflverse pbp + participation)."""
    b = pbp([season], columns=COLS)
    b = b[(b["season_type"] == "REG") & (b["qb_dropback"] == 1)]
    part = nfl().load_participation([season]).to_pandas().rename(columns={"nflverse_game_id": "game_id"})
    m = b.merge(part[["game_id", "play_id", "defense_coverage_type", "defenders_in_box"]],
                on=["game_id", "play_id"])
    m = m[m["defense_coverage_type"].notna()].copy()
    m["season"] = season
    return m

# 2018-2022 only: one charting source (Next Gen Stats); FTN's labels from 2023 split coverages differently
COV = pd.concat([labelled_dropbacks(s) for s in range(2018, 2023)], ignore_index=True)
EARLY = COV[COV["down"].isin([1, 2]) & COV["yardline_100"].between(21, 80)]
NAMES = {"COVER_1": "Cover 1", "COVER_3": "Cover 3", "COVER_2": "Cover 2", "COVER_4": "Quarters"}
TRADE = (EARLY[EARLY["defense_coverage_type"].isin(NAMES)]
         .groupby("defense_coverage_type")
         .agg(box=("defenders_in_box", "mean"), cmp=("complete_pass", "mean"),
              big=("yards_gained", lambda s: (s >= 20).mean()), n=("yards_gained", "size"))
         .rename(index=NAMES).reindex(["Cover 1", "Cover 3", "Cover 2", "Quarters"]))




Show the Python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(6.6, 2.35), sharey=True)
y = np.arange(len(TRADE))[::-1]
cols = [style.DEFENSE if nm == "Cover 3" else style.BASELINE for nm in TRADE.index]
panels = [("box", "box defenders (avg.)", (0.0, 7.0), "{:.1f}"),
          ("cmp", "completion rate", (0.0, 0.8), "{:.0%}"),
          ("big", "plays of 20+ yards", (0.0, 0.14), "{:.1%}")]
for ax, (col, title, lim, fmt) in zip(axes, panels):
    vals = TRADE[col].values
    ax.barh(y, vals, color=cols, height=0.62)
    for yy, v in zip(y, vals):
        ax.text(v + (lim[1] - lim[0]) * 0.02, yy, fmt.format(v), va="center", fontsize=7, color=style.INK_2)
    ax.set_xlim(lim[0], lim[1] + (lim[1] - lim[0]) * 0.22)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=8, loc="left", color=style.INK)
    ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
    ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=6.5)
    ax.axhline(1.5, color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.6, ls=(0, (2, 2)))
for txt, yy in (("one-high ↑", 1.5 + 0.05), ("two-high ↓", 1.5 - 0.05)):
    axes[2].text(0.995, yy, txt, transform=axes[2].get_yaxis_transform(), ha="right",
                 va="bottom" if "one" in txt else "top", fontsize=6.0, color=style.INK_2, style="italic")
axes[0].set_yticks(y, TRADE.index, fontsize=8)
axes[1].xaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}"))
axes[2].xaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}"))
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 35.4: Cover 3’s bargain in numbers: first- and second-down dropbacks between the 20s, 2018–2022 (Next Gen Stats charting via nflverse; about 45,000 plays in these four coverages). Cover 3 (orange) keeps nearly as many defenders in the box as Cover 1 (left) and gives up completions at about the rate of the two-high zones (middle), but more plays of 20 yards or more than either two-high zone (right): the seams and the single safety are the price of the extra man near the line. The dashed line separates the one-high coverages (top two bars) from the two-high ones (bottom two).





Read the chart as a trade. Cover 3 puts as many defenders near the line as Cover 1 does (about 6.3 per dropback, against fewer than 6 for the two-high zones), because one safety is down.
Where’s the eighth man, then? An average of 6.3 isn’t eight, because this chart is all dropbacks, most of them against three-receiver sets, where the down safety is out over a slot as a curl-flat defender rather than in the box. The eighth man shows up against run formations. On the same early downs, when the offense had two or fewer wide receivers on the field, Cover 3 had eight or more defenders in the box on about a quarter of its dropbacks; Cover 2 did on 1 in 20 and quarters almost never.2 The point isn’t that Cover 3 always has eight; it’s that it can, at no cost to its deep coverage, whenever the formation calls for it.
Cover 3 is still a zone with every underneath defender facing the ball, so completions come at about the two-high rate, mostly in front of the defense. Cover 1 allows far fewer completions (about 60 percent) but more 20-yard plays: man coverage contests every catch, but when a defender is beaten there’s nobody behind him except one safety. Cover 3 gives up more 20-yard plays than either two-high zone, about one dropback in ten against fewer than one in eleven for Cover 2 and quarters. Those extra explosive plays are the seams and the single safety, the holes the rest of this chapter is about. (These are observational numbers: defenses choose coverages for situations, so this shows what each coverage looks like when teams call it, not what would happen if they swapped one for another.)






CautionCommon misconception



“Three deep defenders means Cover 3 is safe against the deep ball.” It’s safe against a deep ball along the sideline and down the middle, where the three deep defenders start. It’s thinnest exactly between them, up the seams (hole 1 below). Four receivers going deep against three deep defenders is the oldest Cover 3 problem there is, and the deep defenders can’t solve it alone. The underneath defenders have to help, and how they help is the difference between the 1980s version of the coverage and the modern one.

title: Cover 3: Sky, Buzz, Cloud, and Seattle’s Match Version
section: Sky, buzz and cloud: three ways to get to Cover 3
text:
Sky, buzz and cloud: three ways to get to Cover 3
Very little Cover 3 in the NFL is simply lined up and played. The defense usually arrives at it, because the shell it shows before the snap is part of the plan: it wants the quarterback guessing, and it wants its run fits to match the formation. The three classic ways to arrive have names that describe which defender drops into the extra underneath spot, and they come with a handy memory aid: sky is the safety to the flat, cloud is the corner to the flat, and buzz is the safety to the hook, buzzing around inside.
All three end with the same skeleton, three deep and four under. What changes is who plays which zone, and that matters because players aren’t interchangeable: a safety coming from depth, a linebacker already outside, and a cornerback already pressing a receiver are each good at different things. (Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage shows these rotations launched from a two-high shell at the last instant; here we start each one from the alignment where it is most natural, so you can see what it’s for.)

Sky: the safety takes the flat
The sky rotation is the one in the first figure. The safety on the rotation side comes down and out at the snap to become the curl-flat defender. The corner on that side bails to his deep third as usual, and the free safety goes to the middle.
Which side is the rotation side? Whatever the call’s rule says. The most common rule is “rotate to the strength,” and for a coverage, strength usually means the passing strength, the side with more receivers (Coverage Fundamentals makes the distinction from formation strength, which counts the tight end). In a 2x2 like the first figure the receiver count is even, so the defense needs a tiebreaker, and staffs pick different ones: the tight end’s side (as drawn), the field side or the boundary side, or the side the running back sets to. Some calls rotate away from the strength on purpose (a weak rotation; more on the names in the box below). Because the rule is tied to the formation, motion that changes the formation can change the rotation, and that is how an offense finds out which way it goes.
Why sky? Because it puts a safety, a player who is both a good tackler and fast enough to cover, at the point of the field where the run game and the quick passing game meet. Against a run toward him he’s the force player, coming downhill from outside in. Against a pass he’s the curl-flat defender, reading #2 and #1. Teams with a big, physical strong safety (Kam Chancellor in Seattle is the archetype, below) build their defense around this.
What sky gives up. The safety has a long way to go if he starts deep, so the quick game to his side (a hitch, a bubble screen to the slot, a quick out) can be thrown before he arrives, which is why teams that sky from a deep alignment often “cheat” him down before the snap. That’s a tell. And with the strong safety committed to the flat, the free safety is alone in the middle, with no help on either seam.


Buzz: the safety takes the hook


Show the Python
off_b = [q.moved(w=-q.w) if q.key in ("H", "Y") else q for q in spread()]
BUZZ_PRE = {"MIKE": (4.5, 0.8), "WILL": (5.0, -6.4), "NB": (5.0, 6.8), "LCB": (7.5, -16.3),
            "RCB": (7.5, 16.3), "FS": (15.0, -0.8), "SS": (11.8, 5.4)}
BUZZ_POST = {"MIKE": (9.0, -3.6), "WILL": (9.5, -12.5), "NB": (9.5, 12.5), "LCB": (18.0, -16.8),
             "RCB": (18.0, 16.8), "FS": (17.5, 0.0), "SS": (8.6, 7.4)}
fld, p = two_state(off_b, BUZZ_PRE, BUZZ_POST, rings=("SS",))
deep_thirds(fld, p, label_d=24.8)
zone_box(fld, p, 2.0, 14.4, 9.4, 23.6, "curl-flat ($)", label_d=13.7)
zone_box(fld, p, 4.5, 14.4, 0.6, 9.0, "hook-curl (SS)", label_d=13.7)
zone_box(fld, p, 4.5, 14.4, -9.0, -0.6, "hook (M)", label_d=13.7)
zone_box(fld, p, 2.0, 14.4, -23.6, -9.4, "curl-flat (W)", label_d=13.7)
say(fld, p, 9.6, 3.0, "buzz", fontsize=6.8, color=DD, weight="bold")
field_legend(fld.ax, ["ghost", "drop", "zone", "ring"])
plt.show()








Figure 35.5: Cover 3 buzz to the right, against the same 2x2 with the slots swapped: the tight end (Y) is now the left slot and the receiver H the right one. Before the snap the nickel ($) is in an apex over the receiver in the right slot, the Will (W) over the tight end on the left, and the strong safety (SS, ringed) stands about 12 yards deep over the inside shoulder of the right slot: inside, with a nickel outside him, the buzz tell. At the snap the SS runs downhill to the right hook-curl area, inside the slot’s seam; the $, already outside, widens to the right curl-flat; the Will takes the left curl-flat and the Mike (M) slides to the left hook. What to notice: compared with sky, the safety and the outside defender on the rotation side have traded jobs. The deep three are unchanged: two corners and the free safety (FS).





In the buzz rotation the safety comes down inside, to the hook-curl area, and the player already lined up outside on that side (a nickel or an outside linebacker) takes the curl-flat. Compared with sky, the two defenders on the rotation side trade jobs: the safety goes inside, the outside man goes to the flat. The other side doesn’t change. That’s also why the nickel has moved in the figure. Defenses put the nickel, a defensive back, over the slot receiver and let a linebacker take the tight end; in the first figure the receiver slot was on the left, here it is on the right, and buzz needs that outside defender standing on the rotation side.
Why buzz? Three reasons. First, the flat defender is already standing near the flat, so the quick game to that side is covered from the snap instead of from three seconds later. Second, a safety coming down from depth and inside is perfectly placed to wall the slot receiver’s seam: he arrives on the inside of it, facing it, which makes buzz a good answer to the seam route that haunts Cover 3. Third, against the run he is the alley player, filling inside the force defender rather than outside him, which suits a safety who is a better downhill tackler than a cover man in space.
What buzz gives up. The defender on the edge is now the nickel or linebacker, usually smaller or slower than the safety, so the force against outside runs is weaker on that side. The hook defender who slides across has ground to cover if the offense runs away from the rotation. And the safety’s landing spot, the hook-curl area, is close to where a robber would sit, which makes buzz and Cover 3 robber easy to confuse on a broadcast. The difference: a robber sits in the middle of the field and jumps in-breaking routes, a buzz safety walls the seam on his side and widens to the curl (Man Coverage covers the robber).


Cloud: the corner takes the flat


Show the Python
CLOUD_PRE = {"MIKE": (4.5, 2.4), "WILL": (4.5, -2.2), "NB": (5.0, -7.0), "LCB": (8.0, -16.3),
             "RCB": (5.0, 16.4), "FS": (14.0, -2.0), "SS": (12.5, 11.8)}
CLOUD_POST = {"MIKE": (9.0, 6.0), "WILL": (9.0, -3.6), "NB": (9.5, -12.5), "LCB": (18.0, -16.8),
              "RCB": (7.5, 19.0), "FS": (17.5, 0.0), "SS": (18.0, 16.6)}
fld, p = two_state(spread(), CLOUD_PRE, CLOUD_POST, rings=("RCB", "SS"),
                   via={"RCB": [(3.4, 15.7)], "SS": [(15.5, 14.0)]})
deep_thirds(fld, p, label_d=24.8, labels=("deep ⅓ (CB)", "deep middle ⅓ (FS)", "deep ⅓ (SS)"))
zone_box(fld, p, 1.0, 9.6, 12.2, 24.4, "flat (CB)", label_d=1.9)
zone_box(fld, p, 4.5, 13.5, 0.6, 12.0, "hook-curl (M)", label_d=12.6)
zone_box(fld, p, 4.5, 13.5, -9.0, -0.6, "hook (W)", label_d=12.6)
zone_box(fld, p, 2.0, 13.5, -23.6, -9.4, "curl-flat ($)", label_d=12.6)
say(fld, p, 11.6, 21.3, "cloud corner:\nre-route #1,\nsit in the flat", fontsize=6.4, color=DD)
field_legend(fld.ax, ["ghost", "drop", "zone", "ring"])
plt.show()








Figure 35.6: Cover 3 cloud to the right. Before the snap the defense looks two-high: both safeties about 12 to 14 yards deep, and on the right a cornerback (ringed) squatting about 5 yards off Z with outside leverage, the Cover 2 look on that side. The left corner is off, 8 yards deep. The free safety (FS) is shaded toward the ball, inside the left hash, rather than out on his own side. At the snap the right corner re-routes Z (gets in his way as he releases) and sits in the flat; the strong safety (SS, ringed) runs to the deep right third behind him, and the free safety rotates to the deep middle, a short trip from where he started. The left corner bails to his third, the nickel ($) takes the left curl-flat, the Mike (M) the right hook-curl and the Will (W) the left hook.





The cloud rotation, also called a corner rotation, flips the roles of the corner and the safety on one side. The corner stays shallow and plays the flat; the safety on that side takes the deep outside third. On the other side it’s ordinary Cover 3, and the other safety still goes to the middle.
Why cloud? Look at the picture before the snap: a corner squatting at 5 yards with a safety deep behind him is exactly what a Cover 2 side looks like, so a cloud rotation is a natural disguise, a two-high shell that becomes three-deep. It also puts the defense’s best cover man, already near the receiver, on the quick throws to that side: he can re-route #1 (from 5 yards off he gets in the receiver’s path rather than jamming him; teams that want a real jam press the cloud corner at a yard or two) and sit on the hitch, the quick out and the flat. And it makes him the force player against outside runs, so a defense can cloud to the side where it expects the offense to throw quick or run wide. Defenses like it to the boundary (the short side of the field), where the deep third is a shorter run for a safety. Every diagram in this chapter puts the ball in the middle; with the ball on an NFL hash, the boundary is about 23.6 yards from the ball to the sideline against 29.8 on the field side, so a deep third measured from the ball is about 3 yards narrower on the boundary. That’s a modest gift in the NFL, whose hashes sit only 3 yards off the middle, and a large one in college and high school, whose hashes are much wider (The Game in Fifteen Minutes draws the difference).
What cloud gives up. The deep outside third now belongs to a safety, who is usually not as fast or as practised at running with a wide receiver as the corner. A go route by a fast #1 against a safety who started 12 yards deep and several yards inside him is the classic cloud beater, and the smash corner route (a route that breaks toward the sideline behind a squatting corner) attacks exactly the spot between the cloud corner and the safety, just as it does against Cover 2.






ImportantWhy it exists: three rotations for one coverage



A defense wants to play Cover 3 against many formations without telling the quarterback which defender is the extra underneath player, and it wants that player to be the right kind of player for the job. Each rotation moves a defender who is good at one thing into a job he’s merely adequate at, and each leaks a hint before the snap.

Buzz
Cloud

Safety, to the hook-curl

A safety cheated down, outside the slot or tight end

What hurts it
Quick throws before he arrives; both seams on the post safety
Outside runs at a smaller edge defender
A fast #1 against the safety in the deep third; smash











NoteMadden vs. real life



In Madden, “Cover 3 Sky,” “Cover 3 Buzz” and “Cover 3 Cloud” are separate plays on the menu, and you pick one. Real defenses rarely call them that way. The call is usually “three” plus a rule for the rotation (“rotate to the strength,” “cloud the boundary,” “buzz to the tight end”), and the players work out the rest from the formation: which side is strong, which is the boundary, where the motion went. That’s why the same call can be sky on one snap and buzz on the next, and why a defensive back’s first job before every play is to say out loud which way the rotation goes. In Nick Saban’s system the rotating safety’s declaration is literally a word: “Rip” or “Liz,” for the side he is coming down to.3
The names are dialects, too. “Sky” and “cloud” are also used for the two sides of split-field coverages (the “cloud side” of a Cover 6, a coverage that plays quarters on one half of the field and Cover 2 on the other, is the side where the corner sits in the flat), and a Cover 3 whose rotation goes away from the strength, a weak rotation, is Saban’s “6” and some NFL staffs’ Cover 9, as Coverage Fundamentals explained. When you hear a coverage name, ask which rule it describes, not which picture.

title: Cover 3: Sky, Buzz, Cloud, and Seattle’s Match Version
section: The holes: where Cover 3 can be hit
text:
The holes: where Cover 3 can be hit
Every coverage has soft spots, and Cover 3’s are well known, because it’s been the most common zone in football for decades and offensive coaches have been designing against it the whole time. Most of the concepts in The Quick Game and Dropback Concepts were drawn against a Cover 3 look for exactly that reason. Here are the four places they aim.


Show the Python
hp = Play(spread(rb_w=1.5), nickel(C3_POST), los=LOS, to_go=None)
fld = draw(hp, lateral="full", window=(-8.5, 30.0))
for s in (-1, 1):
    hole(fld, hp, 20.5, s * THIRD_W, 6.6, 9.5, "1")
say(fld, hp, 27.2, 0.0, "(1) the seams: where the thirds meet", color=GREEN_TEXT, fontsize=6.8)
# (2) the curl-flat stretch, on the left: X's curl behind the $, H's flat route in front of him
route_line(fld, hp, [(-0.7, -15.0), (12.6, -15.3), (10.9, -14.1)], alpha=0.45, lw=1.3)
route_line(fld, hp, [(-1.5, -9.0), (1.2, -10.8), (2.6, -19.2)], alpha=0.45, lw=1.3)
hole(fld, hp, 13.2, -15.6, 4.6, 3.6, "2")
hole(fld, hp, 2.8, -20.6, 4.6, 3.4, "2")
(x0, y0), (x1, y1) = P(fld, hp, 11.4, -16.6), P(fld, hp, 4.5, -19.8)
fld.ax.annotate("", (float(x1), float(y1)), xytext=(float(x0), float(y0)),
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color=GREEN_TEXT, lw=1.0, shrinkA=2, shrinkB=2), zorder=6)
say(fld, hp, 7.8, -22.9, "(2) curl or\nflat: one\ndefender", color=GREEN_TEXT, fontsize=6.4)
# (3) the flood, on the right: the go takes the corner deep, the sail and flat stretch the SS
route_line(fld, hp, [(-0.7, 15.0), (8.0, 15.8), (27.0, 17.0)], alpha=0.45, lw=1.3)
route_line(fld, hp, [(-1.5, 9.0), (12.5, 9.6), (14.6, 20.2)], alpha=0.45, lw=1.3)
route_line(fld, hp, [(-5.0, 1.5), (-4.4, 7.0), (-1.0, 11.5), (1.5, 14.0), (2.8, 19.4)], alpha=0.45, lw=1.3)
hole(fld, hp, 14.6, 20.6, 4.6, 3.4, "3")
hole(fld, hp, 2.8, 20.8, 4.6, 3.4, "3")
say(fld, hp, 17.2, 22.8, "sail", color=GREEN_TEXT, fontsize=6.2)
say(fld, hp, 5.4, 23.4, "flat", color=GREEN_TEXT, fontsize=6.2)
point_to(fld, hp, (25.6, 22.2), (22.5, 17.1), "go takes\nthe CB deep", color=GREEN_TEXT, fontsize=6.2)
say(fld, hp, 9.0, 21.8, "(3) flood", color=GREEN_TEXT, fontsize=6.4)
field_legend(fld.ax, ["hole"])
plt.show()








Figure 35.7: Where Cover 3 can be hit: the defenders at their spot-drop landmarks about a second and a half after the snap (sky rotation, as in the first figure), three classic soft spots in green, and, faintly, the routes that attack them. (1) The seams, about 9 yards either side of the middle at 15 to 25 yards, where one deep third meets the next: four verticals puts receivers here. (2) The curl-flat stretch, on the left: X’s curl behind the nickel ($) and H’s flat route in front of him, one defender for two zones. (3) The flood, on the right: Z’s go route takes the corner deep, Y’s sail (up, then bending to the sideline) lands at 12 to 15 yards behind the strong safety (SS), and the back’s (R) flat route runs under him: three receivers, two defenders. The fourth hole, the hitch in front of a corner, is about timing, so it gets its own picture next.





1. The seams. The boundaries between the thirds sit about 9 yards either side of the middle of the field, between the hashes and the numbers, which is precisely where a slot receiver or a tight end runs a seam route. A seam thrown 18 to 25 yards downfield lands between a corner who is guarding the sideline and a free safety who is guarding the middle, and if both receivers run seams, the free safety can take only one. This is four verticals’ target, and the next section draws it. Against match: mostly closed, because the seam-flat defenders carry the seams; the cost moves underneath, to the flat they leave.
2. The curl-flat stretch. The curl-flat defender guards two zones, so two receivers, one in each, force him to choose: the curl-flat concept, slant-flat, stick, snag. The quarterback reads him and throws to the receiver he didn’t take. The hook defenders help on the curl only if they’re not needed elsewhere, which is why offenses add a third route that holds them inside (a check-down by the back or a crossing route). Against match: smaller. The seam-flat defender goes with #2 to the flat by rule, and the corner, seeing #1 break short, sinks and then drives on the curl from above, so both routes have a defender; the curl is still the softer of the two, because the corner arrives from depth.
3. The flood. Put three receivers on one side at three depths (a go route that takes the corner deep, a sail at 12 to 15 yards, a flat route) and there are two defenders to cover them, the corner and the curl-flat defender. One is always open. The sail, landing behind the curl-flat defender and in front of the bailing corner, is the money throw against spot-drop Cover 3, and some version of flood is in every NFL playbook. Against match: still open. Matching changes who is stretched, not how many defenders are on that side (the third drill at the end of the chapter works through it).
4. In front of the corners. A Cover 3 corner’s first rule is to stay deeper than the deepest receiver in his third, so he bails at the snap. A hitch at 5 or 6 yards, or a quick out, is caught in front of him. The curl-flat defender is the nearest help, and in the first figure his zone seems to cover the spot, so why is it open? Timing. Look at the next figure.


Show the Python
def hitch_play():
    p = Play(spread(), nickel(C3_PRE | {"SS": (11.0, 10.4)}), los=LOS, to_go=None)
    protect(p)
    p.dropback(1.5)
    p.route("X", [(-0.7, -15.0), (6.2, -15.3), (5.4, -14.7)], absolute=True)
    p.route("H", [(-1.5, -9.0), (6.0, -7.9), (24.0, -6.6)], absolute=True)
    p.drop("WILL", (9.0, -4.2), speed=4.0)
    p.drop("MIKE", (9.0, 4.2), speed=4.0)
    p.drop("FS", (17.5, 0.0), speed=3.0)
    p.pass_to("X", t=0.9)
    t_c = arrival(p, "X", 0.9)
    xc = p.position("X", t_c)
    set_track(p, "NB", [(0.9, 8.0, -10.6), (1.05, 8.4, -11.0), (t_c, xc[0] + 1.6, xc[1] + 1.6)])
    set_track(p, "LCB", [(0.9, 11.2, -16.5), (1.05, 11.7, -16.5), (t_c, xc[0] + 3.4, xc[1] - 0.8)])
    return p, t_c

hplay, T_HC = hitch_play()

def hitch_notes(fld, i, t):
    if i == 0:
        say(fld, hplay, 15.0, -10.6, "$ still sinking,\neyes on the QB", fontsize=6.0, color=DD)
        say(fld, hplay, 15.2, -21.4, "CB still\nbailing", fontsize=6.0, color=DD)
    else:
        say(fld, hplay, 13.4, -16.0, "both plant and drive;\nthey arrive as he turns", fontsize=6.0, color=DD)

strip(hplay, [0.9, T_HC], ["+0.9 s · the throw", f"+{T_HC:.1f} s · the catch"],
      ["", "Caught at 6 yd:\nconceded, then tackled"], (-25.5, 1.5), (-7.5, 19.5), rings=("NB",),
      throw_t=0.9, width_in=6.6, extra=hitch_notes, tag_loc="bl")
plt.show()








Figure 35.8: Why the hitch is there (simulated, BDB-format tracking). X runs a 6-yard hitch against the sky Cover 3 of the first figure, and the quarterback throws it on time from a quick drop. Left, the throw (+0.9 s): the corner (CB) is still bailing, 11 yards deep, and the nickel ($, ringed), the curl-flat defender, is still sinking toward his landmark, moving up and away from X with his eyes on the quarterback. Right, the catch: both have planted and driven on the ball, but they arrive as X turns with it. The defense gives up 6 yards and tackles: the trade it chose.





The hitch is thrown before the receiver turns around, at a spot, while the curl-flat defender is still doing his first job: sinking toward the curl with his eyes on the quarterback. He can’t stop, turn and close 5 yards in the time the ball is in the air, so the best he and the corner can do is arrive with the catch and tackle. It’s not a big play, but it’s a completion every time the defense lets it be, which is why offenses throw it to “keep the defense honest” and why a corner who cheats up to stop it opens the deep ball. A corner can drive on a hitch once the receiver stops and the quarterback’s arm commits, never earlier, because the hitch-and-go (Man Coverage drew the double move) is waiting for the corner who guesses. This is the trade the coverage makes on purpose: five yards in front of the corner rather than fifty behind him. Against match: the same. The corner’s rule is still to stay on top, so match concedes the hitch too.
There’s a fifth, quieter soft spot you’ll hear analysts mention: the window between the hook defender and the curl-flat defender at 10 to 14 yards, where a dig sits down. And there’s the run game’s answer: a play-action fake that pulls the eight-man front forward and throws behind it, as in this chapter’s opening. Cover 3 brought a safety down to stop the run, and play-action punishes exactly that.

text:
Four verticals: the stress test
Of all these, the seams are the one that shaped the coverage’s history, because four verticals is both simple and brutal against a spot-drop Cover 3. The quarterback doesn’t need to read the underneath defenders at all; he reads the free safety. Watch it from the defense’s side.


Show the Python
def verts(kind):
    off = spread(rb_w=1.5)
    p = Play(off, nickel(C3_PRE), los=LOS, to_go=10)
    protect(p)
    p.dropback(3.0)
    for k, s in (("X", -1), ("Z", 1)):
        p.route(k, [(-0.7, s * 15.0), (8.0, s * 15.8), (34.0, s * 17.2)], absolute=True)
    for k, s in (("H", -1), ("Y", 1)):
        p.route(k, [(-1.5, s * 9.0), (6.0, s * 7.9), (34.0, s * 6.0)], absolute=True)
    for k, s in (("LCB", -1), ("RCB", 1)):
        p.drop(k, (30.0, s * 17.4), speed=6.4)
    if kind == "spot":
        p.route("RB", [(-4.6, 2.6)], absolute=True, speed=2.0)
        p.drop("NB", (11.5, -12.8), speed=4.6)
        p.drop("SS", (11.5, 12.8), speed=4.6)
        p.drop("WILL", (9.5, -4.6), speed=4.0)
        p.drop("MIKE", (9.5, 4.4), speed=4.0)
        p.pass_to("H", t=T_THROW)
        set_track(p, "FS", [(0.5, 15.6, 0.4), (1.6, 17.6, 3.0), (2.35, 19.2, 4.6), (2.6, 19.6, 4.2),
                            (3.6, 21.6, -0.6)])
    else:
        p.route("RB", [(-4.6, 2.6), (-2.0, 7.5), (1.5, 13.0)], absolute=True, speed=5.5, delay=0.9)
        p.drop("WILL", (12.0, -2.6), speed=3.6)
        p.pass_to("RB", t=2.6)
        set_track(p, "FS", [(0.5, 15.8, 0.0), (1.6, 19.6, 0.6), (2.4, 22.2, -0.4), (3.6, 25.4, 0.2)])
        set_track(p, "NB", [(0.3, 6.0, -7.4)] + shadow(p, "NB", "H", off=(-1.3, 1.0), lag=0.12, t_from=0.3,
                                                        t_on=1.1, start=(6.0, -7.4), t_end=3.6))
        set_track(p, "SS", [(0.3, 6.4, 7.3)] + shadow(p, "SS", "Y", off=(-1.3, -1.0), lag=0.12, t_from=0.3,
                                                       t_on=1.1, start=(6.4, 7.3), t_end=3.6))

    return p

           "$ and SS run to curl\nspots; seams go inside",

Figure 35.9: Four verticals against spot-drop Cover 3 (simulated, BDB-format tracking generated by gridiron). The two cornerbacks bail and stay on top of X and Z. The two curl-flat defenders, the nickel ($) and the strong safety (SS), drop to their curl landmarks, wide and about 11 yards deep, so the seam routes by H and Y run past them on the inside. The free safety (FS, ringed) reads the quarterback, who looks at Y on the right seam as he drops (dotted arrow); the safety leans 4 to 5 yards that way. Just as H clears the nickel, about 15 yards downfield, the ball goes to him on the left seam, and he catches it between the corner and the safety, who is still several yards away. Every defender did his job; the coverage is one deep defender short. On the web this is a video.




Look at what went wrong, because nothing did. The corners stayed on top of the outside receivers. The curl-flat defenders got to their landmarks. The hook defenders got to theirs. The free safety read the quarterback, as he’s coached to, and drifted toward the side the quarterback was looking at. The ball went to the other seam. Spot-drop Cover 3 against four verticals is a math problem the defense loses: four receivers past 15 yards, three defenders back there, and the one in the middle can be moved by the quarterback’s eyes. Offensive coaches knew this by the 1980s; the “run-and-shoot” and the BYU passing game of LaVell Edwards made four verticals a staple, and every spread offense since has carried it4 (Dropback Concepts tells that history from the offense’s side).
There are three ways for the defense to stop it, and each has a price. The safety can guess right (he can’t do it every time). The curl-flat defenders can sink deeper and narrower, giving the seams a defender underneath for a few steps longer (which opens the flat and the curl in front of them). Or the coverage can stop being a spot-drop zone and start matching the routes.

title: Cover 3: Sky, Buzz, Cloud, and Seattle’s Match Version
text:
Cover 3 match: carrying the seams
Cover 3 match keeps the Cover 3 shell, three deep and four under, but gives every defender a rule about which receiver to take once the routes declare. It is the pattern-matching idea from Coverage Fundamentals applied to Cover 3, and it’s the version most NFL teams play today. Nick Saban, building it with Bill Belichick in Cleveland in the early 1990s, is the coach most often credited with turning Cover 3 into a match coverage, and his later college defenses spread the idea; like most origin stories it’s disputed, and other staffs built similar rules.5 The rules differ from staff to staff, but the core of most versions fits in a table.








Defender
Reads
Rule (simplified)




Cornerbacks
#1
#1 goes vertical: carry him, on top, like man. #1 breaks short: sink, look for #2 coming outside, then drive on #1.


Seam-flat defenders ($, SS)
#2, then #1
#2 vertical: wall him, carry him up the seam until the post safety is over the top. #2 out: take him in the flat. #2 in: pass him inside, sink under #1.


Hook defenders (M, W)
#3 (the back), then the crossers
The back releases: take him. No release: wall the crossers and sink into the hole.


Free safety
the #2 away from the rotation (in many versions), or both #2s; the quarterback
Stay in the middle third; play over the top of the seam he’s assigned or the quarterback looks at, or the deepest route in the middle.



The key line is the seam-flat defender’s: #2 vertical, carry him. That single rule turns four verticals from a math problem into a matchup. Staffs split on the far seam, though. Some carry both #2s, as drawn below. Many, Seattle among them, carry only the seam on the rotation side and give the other one to the post safety, who leans toward it before the ball is snapped. That keeps the other curl-flat defender home for the flat and the curl, at the price of asking more of the free safety.






ImportantWhy it exists: Cover 3 match



The problem it solves. Spot-drop Cover 3 had a structural problem that no amount of effort fixed: four verticals, and more generally any concept that puts two receivers into one deep defender’s area. Matching the routes gives every vertical receiver a defender, without giving up what makes Cover 3 attractive: three deep, the extra man near the line before the snap, and defenders who start out facing the quarterback.
What it gives up. Simplicity, and the empty spaces the carries leave behind. A seam-flat defender running up the field with #2 is not in the flat, so a quick out by #1, or the back releasing to the flat, is open underneath him. And any route combination that makes two defenders’ rules collide becomes a target: post-wheel (the corner carries the post inside while the wheel goes up the sideline behind the seam-flat defender), switch releases that cross #1 and #2 at the snap, and motion that changes who is #2 at the last moment. The match coverage’s rules close the seams; offensive coaches now design plays to open the gaps between the rules.




Show the Python
match = verts("match")
MATCH_T = [0.0, 1.0, 2.1, arrival(match, "RB", 2.6)]
if PDF:
    strip(match, MATCH_T,
          ["Snap · same shell", "+1.0 s · the walls", "+2.1 s · the carries", f"+{MATCH_T[3]:.1f} s · the check-down"],
          ["Same picture: 3 deep,\n4 under",
           "#2s go vertical: $ and\nSS wall them and run",
           "Each seam: a defender\nunder it, the FS over it",
           "Nothing deep: ball to R in\nthe flat; M runs him down"],
          LAT_V, WIN_V, rings=("NB", "SS"), throw_t=2.6)
    plt.show()
else:
    show_animation(match, times=MATCH_T)





  
  Your browser does not support the video tag.



Figure 35.10: The same four verticals against Cover 3 match (simulated, BDB-format tracking). Now the nickel ($) and the strong safety (SS), the seam-flat defenders (ringed), read the slot receivers: both go vertical, so each walls his man and carries him up the seam, running underneath and inside him. The corners carry X and Z as before. The free safety (FS) no longer has two seams to himself; he sits in the middle over both carries, ready to help on either. Four vertical routes now face four defenders deep, plus a safety. The quarterback holds the ball and checks down to the back (R), who has released to the flat that the carries emptied; the Mike (M), matched to the back, has to run him down from the hook, about 5 yards away when the ball arrives, for a gain of four or five. On the web this is a video.




Compare the second panels of the two plays. In spot-drop, the nickel and the strong safety ran away from the slot receivers toward their curl landmarks. In match, they ran with them. That’s the whole difference, and it’s visible on a broadcast replay if you watch the slot defender for one second. Now each seam has a defender underneath it and the free safety above, a two-on-one in the defense’s favour on both sides, and the quarterback who expected one safety and two seams finds nobody open. He checks the ball down to the back in the flat, the space the two carries emptied, and the Mike has to run him down from the hook. Four or five yards: the price of carrying both seams, and one the defense will pay every time instead of a 25-yard seam.

What offenses attack instead
Match rules are a set of if-then statements, and an offense that knows them can write a route combination in which every defender obeys his rule and the rules still leave a hole. The cleanest example is the post-wheel.
