route_line(fld, pw, [(-0.7, -15.0), (11.5, -15.6), (25.0, -9.8)], lw=1.7)
route_line(fld, pw, [(-1.5, -9.0), (1.4, -12.6), (3.6, -18.4), (8.6, -21.6), (25.5, -22.4)], lw=1.7)
for k in PW_PRE:
    ghost(fld, pw, *PW_PRE[k], LAB[k][1])
path(fld, pw, [PW_PRE["LCB"], (13.5, -16.4), PW_POST["LCB"]])
path(fld, pw, [PW_PRE["NB"], (3.6, -14.6), PW_POST["NB"]])
path(fld, pw, [PW_PRE["FS"], PW_POST["FS"]])
path(fld, pw, [PW_PRE["WILL"], PW_POST["WILL"]])
hole(fld, pw, 21.5, -22.0, 4.6, 6.0, "")
say(fld, pw, 26.8, -19.5, "wheel: open up\nthe sideline", color=GREEN_TEXT, fontsize=6.4)
say(fld, pw, 15.4, -7.6, "#1 post: the CB\ncarries him inside", fontsize=6.2, color=DD)
say(fld, pw, 6.6, -23.2, "#2 to the\nflat: $ goes\nwith him", fontsize=6.2, color=DD)
for k, txt in (("X", "#1"), ("H", "#2")):
    q = pw.players[k]
    say(fld, pw, q.d - 2.4, q.w, txt, fontsize=6.2)
plt.show()








Figure 35.11: Post-wheel against Cover 3 match, on the offense’s left. X (#1) starts vertical and breaks to the post at about 12 yards; by rule the corner (CB, ringed) carries a vertical #1 on top, so he goes inside with him. H (#2) runs toward the flat, so by rule the nickel ($, ringed) goes with him, underneath; then H turns up the sideline (the wheel). The corner is inside, the nickel is trailing from below, and the free safety (FS) is in the middle: the sideline behind them (green) is empty. Every defender obeyed his rule; together the rules left the hole.





Two other answers don’t need a picture once you see this one. A switch release crosses #1 and #2 at the snap, the outside receiver running inside and the slot running outside, so the corner and the seam-flat defender, each reading “his” number, have to decide in the first step who is now #1 and who is #2; if they hesitate or both take the same man, the other one is free. And motion changes the count late: a slot who motions across the formation turns a 2x2 into trips, so the defense’s numbering, its rotation side and possibly its trips check all have to change in the seconds before the snap. The defense’s counter is communication, which is why match defenses talk so much before every snap.


The trips problem
Match rules work cleanly against 2x2, two receivers each side. Against 3x1 (trips: three receivers to one side), Cover 3 has a counting problem: four underneath defenders, but three receivers on one side whose routes can all go vertical. If #3, the innermost trips receiver, runs straight up the middle, who carries him? In spot-drop it’s the free safety, and he can’t be on #3 and over #2’s seam at the same time, so the trips side’s seam falls to the corner and the curl-flat defender, who are guarding other things. Match teams answer with a trips check, a pre-planned adjustment (the two-high versions are the 3x1 checks of Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage). The check doesn’t add a defender; it moves one. In one common version the backside corner takes the lone receiver on the other side by himself, man to man wherever he goes (Saban’s playbook calls this MEG, “man everywhere he goes”). That frees the defenders who would have helped on the backside to slide toward the trips, where the trips-side corner and the free safety stay the deep players and one of the freed underneath defenders (which one varies by staff) takes #3 if he goes vertical, so the free safety can stay over #2. Saban’s system names its trips checks (one is “Mable,” in which the safety comes down toward the trips), and every NFL staff has its own.6 The tell for a viewer: against trips, look at the backside corner. If he’s pressing the single receiver, alone, with no safety leaning his way, the defense has probably checked its Cover 3 to put its help on the trips side. (Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage covers the two-high answers to trips, including rotating to Cover 3 match.)

title: Cover 3: Sky, Buzz, Cloud, and Seattle’s Match Version
section: Seattle’s version: Cover 3 as an identity
text:
Seattle’s version: Cover 3 as an identity
For most of the 2000s, Cover 3 was something defenses played on early downs between the more fashionable calls. Then Pete Carroll’s Seattle Seahawks made it the most feared defense in football, mostly by showing one pre-snap picture, a single high safety and corners pressed on the receivers, and playing two coverages behind it: Cover 3 and its man twin, Cover 1 (“man free”).7 Coverage Fundamentals met this defense in its film room; here is why it worked as a scheme.
Carroll had spent decades as a defensive backs coach, coordinator and head coach before Seattle hired him in 2010; Gus Bradley ran the defense from 2009 to 2012 and Dan Quinn in 2013 and 2014.8 Carroll’s idea, laid out in his book Win Forever, was that a program needs one clearly defined philosophy and should try to do things “better than they have ever been done before.”9 On defense, that meant a 4-3 front with a one-high safety and five distinctive pieces:

A free safety with rare range. Earl Thomas, the 14th pick of the 2010 draft, covered the deep middle third alone, and fast enough to arrive at either seam. Cover 3 lives or dies with its post safety; Seattle’s could erase mistakes in front of him.
A strong safety built like a linebacker. Kam Chancellor, a fifth-round pick that same year, was the eighth man in the box: the sky or buzz player who came down at the snap, the force or alley defender against the run, and a seam-flat defender who could carry a tight end up the field.
Tall corners who pressed and carried. Richard Sherman and Brandon Browner (both 6 feet 3 or taller, a fifth-round pick and a Canadian Football League signing)10 lined up on receivers’ noses, jammed them inside the 5-yard limit with Carroll’s step-kick technique, and if the receiver went deep, ran with him into the corner’s own deep third. That press looked exactly like man coverage, which is the point: before the snap the quarterback couldn’t tell Cover 3 from Cover 1. The difference shows only after it, when a receiver breaks inside. In Cover 1 the corner follows him across the field; in Cover 3 he lets him go and sinks.
Match rules on the verticals. The corners carried #1’s vertical release like man defenders, the down safety matched a seam route from his underneath spot, and the free safety leaned toward the other seam (the “both versions” note in the match section), so four verticals met four defenders.11
Repetition. With few calls, the players practised the same reads thousands of times, and rarely blew an assignment. The scheme was simple enough to play fast.

The results were extraordinary. Seattle allowed the fewest points in the NFL four seasons running, 2012 to 2015, the first team to do so since the Cleveland Browns of the 1950s.12






NoteFilm room: Seattle Seahawks, Super Bowl XLVIII (Feb. 2, 2014) — one buzz snap



Early in the third quarter, Seattle leading Denver 29–0. Denver lines up in 11 personnel with twins to the right, Wes Welker in the slot; Kam Chancellor is on the other side, over the tight end. The call is buzz: Chancellor’s landing spot is the hook-curl on his side. Byron Maxwell, at corner, starts pressed on the line.
At the snap the tight end and the receiver on Chancellor’s side both run go routes. Chancellor, in his own words, “stayed with the tight end up the seam, keeping one eye on Peyton in the backfield”: the seam carry, from the buzz spot, exactly as the match table says. Then Welker comes underneath on a drag, into the zone Chancellor has just left. Chancellor can let the tight end go because Earl Thomas is in the post over the top, so he peels off, drives on Welker, and punches the ball away: pass broken up.13
What to notice: one defender doing three jobs in three seconds, in the order the chapter taught: buzz down inside, carry the seam while it’s a threat, come off it when the deep safety has it and the ball goes underneath. That’s Cover 3 match, and that’s why Seattle needed a strong safety who could run with a tight end and still hit like a linebacker.



The tree
Carroll’s assistants took the scheme with them, and for a while Seattle-style Cover 3 was the NFL’s fastest-spreading defense. Bradley went on to coach or coordinate four more defenses (Jacksonville, the Chargers, the Raiders and the Colts); Quinn took Atlanta to Super Bowl LI as head coach and is Washington’s head coach today.14 Robert Saleh, a junior quality-control assistant in Seattle (the entry-level staffer who breaks down film), built his first San Francisco defenses on the same eight-man-front Cover 3 before mixing in more coverages.15 The tree is still growing: Saleh, the Tennessee Titans’ head coach in 2026, hired Bradley as his defensive coordinator.
You can follow the coaches through the data. Bradley is the clearest case, because he moved three times in five years.


Show the Python

LEAGUE = COV["defense_coverage_type"].eq("COVER_3").mean()

    ax.set_xlim(2017.55, 2022.45)

axes[0].yaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}"))
axes[0].tick_params(axis="y", labelsize=7)

fig.legend(handles=handles, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 0.0), ncol=2, fontsize=7, frameon=False)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.8)
plt.show()








Figure 35.12: Follow the coach: the share of each defense’s charted dropbacks played in Cover 3, 2018–2022 (Next Gen Stats charting via nflverse). Orange points are seasons in which Gus Bradley, Seattle’s defensive coordinator from 2009 to 2012, ran that defense; grey points are seasons he didn’t. The dashed line is the league average (32 percent). Bradley’s 2019 and 2018 Chargers and his 2021 Raiders posted the three highest Cover 3 rates of any defense in this period (his 2020 Chargers were sixth), and the Raiders’ rate jumped from 18 to 65 percent the year he arrived and fell back to 27 percent the year he left.





The pattern is hard to miss. The 2019 Chargers played Cover 3 on 74 percent of their charted dropbacks, the highest rate of any defense from 2018 to 2022; the 2018 Chargers and the 2021 Raiders were second and third. When Bradley left Los Angeles the Chargers fell to the league average; when he arrived in Las Vegas the Raiders more than tripled their rate; when he left, it fell back. Coaches are their schemes, and a coverage this simple travels well. Indianapolis is the weaker case, and it’s worth saying why. The Colts’ rate rose from 29 to 41 percent in Bradley’s first year, a real jump but nothing like Las Vegas, partly because his predecessor, Matt Eberflus, had already played Cover 3 above the league average in two of his four seasons (38 percent in 2018), and partly because by 2022 the whole league was moving toward two-high shells.16 (The chart stops in 2022 because this charting source does.) (Not every member of the tree stayed with it: Quinn’s 2021 Cowboys played Cover 3 on about 27 percent of their dropbacks, below the league average, part of a broader shift you’ll see next.)






NoteFilm room: Los Angeles Chargers 2019 and Las Vegas Raiders 2021 — the coverage in the numbers



If you want to see Seattle’s Cover 3 without Seattle’s players, Bradley’s Chargers are the best library: a single-high safety, corners off and turned in, a safety rotating down to the strong side on nearly every early down (by the same nflverse count, Cover 3 on about 82 percent of their charted first- and second-down dropbacks in 2019), and the same handful of rotations week after week. The 2021 Raiders are the controlled experiment: a different roster, a new coordinator, and within one season their coverage mix looks like the Chargers’.
What to notice: how few different pictures the defense shows. That is the Carroll philosophy, and it has a modern cost: an offense that knows the coverage before the snap can call the concept that beats it. In the same years, Vic Fangio’s two-high defenses were showing quarterbacks a different picture on every snap (Coverage Fundamentals tells that story), and the league’s split-safety rate climbed every year. The fact that Cover 3 was still the most-charted single coverage in the NFL in 2025 says that the simple version keeps working;17 the fact that it’s now usually disguised says what changed. (The 2025 figure, about 28 percent, comes from a different charting service than this chapter’s 2018–2022 numbers, which label Cover 3 more often, so don’t read the gap as a decline of ten points.)


The coach who made it famous has moved on too. Carroll coached Seattle through the 2023 season and the Raiders in 2025, when they went 3–14 and dismissed him after one year. Seattle won Super Bowl LX in February 2026 under Mike Macdonald, with a split-safety defense from a different school (from Week 14 through the Super Bowl, two-high coverage on 54.8 percent of pass plays) (Fangio’s Two-High Revolution and Macdonald’s Answer).18 But nearly every NFL defense still plays Cover 3 on some early downs, usually as a match coverage, usually arrived at by one of the three rotations above. The Seattle version didn’t disappear; it became part of everyone’s playbook.

title: Cover 3: Sky, Buzz, Cloud, and Seattle’s Match Version
section: Recognising Cover 3: before and after the snap
text:
Recognising Cover 3: before and after the snap
Everything above adds up to a two-step read you can make from your couch: a hypothesis before the snap, a test one second after it. Here is the reasoning behind each check; the checklist at the end of the section is the short version.
Before the snap: the Cover 3 look.

One safety deep in the middle, 13 to 16 yards, roughly over the ball. Why it matters: the middle of the field is closed, which narrows the menu to the one-high coverages, Cover 3 and Cover 1.
Corners off and turned in, 7 to 9 yards from their receivers with outside leverage, shoulders angled toward the quarterback. Why: a corner who must stay deeper than everyone in his third starts deep and watches the ball; a man corner is more often pressed and square to his receiver. Seattle-style corners who press and then carry are the exception, and you check them after the snap.
A safety down near the box, 7 to 11 yards deep. Why: he is the fourth underneath defender and the eighth man against the run. Where he stands hints at the rotation: outside the slot or tight end suggests sky; inside, over the slot, with a nickel outside him, suggests buzz.
Underneath defenders in apex alignments, a few yards inside the slot receivers, not tight on them. Why: zone defenders split the difference between a run fit and a pass drop; man defenders line up on their man.
The cloud tell: a two-high look in which only one corner squats at 5 yards and the other is off, often with the free safety shaded toward the middle. Why: a real Cover 2 usually squats both corners; the off corner is already in a deep-third alignment. (Asymmetry is also how Cover 6 looks, so check after the snap.)
Motion. When a receiver motions across, watch the safeties. If they spin with him, one coming down on the new strong side and the other heading for the middle, the call is a single-high rotation tied to the strength; if a defender runs across with the motion man, think man coverage.

After the snap: count the deep defenders, at one second. About one second after the snap, look at the deep part of the field and count the defenders backpedalling or running away from the line, spread across the width. Three means a Cover 3 family call (Cover 3 or a three-deep fire zone); two means Cover 2 or a relative; four means quarters; one means Cover 1 (with or without a robber, it’s still Cover 1). Two refinements make the count reliable:

Count early. In Cover 3 match, the seam-flat defenders who carry slot receivers up the seams are 15 to 20 yards deep two seconds later and look like extra deep players (count the last panel of the match strip and you get five). The count means something only before the carries.
Check who the three are. In Cover 3, two of them are the corners, deep and wide. If the corners are sitting in the flats and the middle man is a linebacker running down the middle of the field, it’s Tampa 2, which also shows three deep at one second.

Then look underneath. Corners who keep their eyes inside and let a receiver who breaks short or across go are zone; corners who turn and follow him across the field are man. A safety into the flat is sky, a safety into the hook-curl is buzz, a corner sitting in the flat with a safety running over him is cloud. Slot defenders who run away from a vertical release to a spot are spot-drop; slot defenders who run with him up the seam are match. Four rushers and three deep is Cover 3; five rushers and three deep, with a defensive lineman dropping into coverage, is a fire zone (Zone Blitzes, Fire Zones, and Simulated Pressure). And for how often a one-high picture before the snap is honest, and how to keep score of a defense that lies, see Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage.






TipWatch for it on Sunday: count to three



For one quarter, on every passing down:

Before the snap: one high safety, corners off and turned in, a safety near the box? Say “Cover 3” and guess sky (safety outside) or buzz (safety inside, nickel outside). Two-high with one squatting corner? Say “cloud?”
Motion: do the safeties spin with it?
At one second, count deep defenders. Three, with the corners among them, is the Cover 3 family. Name the extra underneath player.
Watch one slot defender against a vertical release. Away to a spot (spot-drop) or up the seam with him (match)?
Find the ball. Hitch in front of a corner, seam between thirds, sail behind the curl-flat defender, or a check-down? On the replay, find the defender whose job that area was.
On early downs, count the box. Eight near the line against a two-back or two-tight-end set, with one safety deep, is Cover 3’s run defense. Watch for the play-action pass that punishes it.









NoteGo deeper: Cover 3 in real tracking data



The NFL’s Big Data Bowl files (no download is bundled with this book) label each play’s coverage, so you can find real Cover 3 plays and draw them with the same code. A sketch (the code is in the web version), assuming the 2025 edition’s plays.csv and tracking files in data/bdb/:


Show the Python (finding a real Cover 3 play in Big Data Bowl data)
from gridiron import bdb
plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")
trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_1.csv")
c3 = plays[plays["pff_passCoverage"].str.startswith("Cover-3", na=False)]   # Cover-3, Cover-3 Seam, ...
one = bdb.prepare(trk, plays, game_id=c3["gameId"].iloc[0], play_id=c3["playId"].iloc[0])
show_animation(one, times=[0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0])          # count the deep defenders at +1.0 s


The coverage labels come from PFF’s charting and split Cover 3 into variants whose names map onto this chapter: labels such as Cover-3 Seam (Cover 3 with the seams carried, roughly the match version) and Cover-3 Cloud left and right (the corner rotation), alongside plain Cover-3. Check the year’s data dictionary for the exact strings before filtering on them. The diagrams in this chapter are simulated in the same format (Play.to_tracking()), which is why the two draw identically.

Predict the play






TipPredict the play 1: first-and-10, two tight ends





Show the Python
off12 = offense("ace")
d12 = defense("4-3_over", "single_high", off12)
mv = {"SS": (8.0, 8.0), "FS": (15.0, 0.0), "LCB": (8.0, -16.2), "RCB": (8.0, 16.2)}
d12 = [q.moved(d=mv[q.key][0], w=mv[q.key][1], label="CB" if q.pos == "CB" else q.label)
       if q.key in mv else q for q in d12]
d12 = [q.moved(label="Sm") if q.key == "SAM" else q for q in d12]
pp1 = Play(off12, d12, los=LOS, to_go=10)
pp1.highlight("FS", "SS")
fld = draw(pp1, lateral=(-23, 23), window=(-9.0, 19.0))
plt.show()








Figure 35.13: First-and-10, ball in the middle, 12 personnel (two tight ends, Y and U, attached to the line; X and Z split wide). The defense is in its base 4-3: the Sam (Sm), Mike (M) and Will (W) linebackers behind four linemen. One safety (FS) is 15 yards deep in the middle; the strong safety (SS) is 8 yards deep, about 3 yards outside the right tight end; both corners (CB) are 8 yards off with outside leverage. The safeties are ringed; the orange line is the line to gain.





What coverage family is this, what will the strong safety do at the snap, and if the offense wants to throw, where should it aim?






TipAnswer





Cover 3 (or its man cousin, Cover 1), with the strong safety rotating down: a sky look. One safety deep in the middle closes the middle of the field; the corners off and outside say zone, deep thirds. The strong safety at 8 yards outside the tight end is the tell: he’s the eighth man in the box and the force player against a run to his side, and against a pass he’ll come down and out to the curl-flat area. The other three underneath jobs fall to the linebackers: the Sam takes the right hook-curl, the Mike the left hook, and the Will widens to the left curl-flat. Against 12 personnel on first down the defense is daring the offense to run into eight.
If the offense throws, the soft spots are the ones this chapter drew. Play-action first: the safety and linebackers are reading run, so a fake handoff followed by a tight end up the seam, or a deep crossing route behind the linebackers, attacks the exact space the eighth man left. Without a fake, the hitch in front of the bailing corners and the seam away from the safety’s lean are there. The defense accepts all of that in exchange for a run defense with a spare man.











TipPredict the play 2: two-high, but the corners don’t match





Show the Python
pp2 = Play(spread(), nickel({"MIKE": (4.5, 2.4), "WILL": (4.5, -2.2), "NB": (5.0, -7.0), "LCB": (8.0, -16.3),
                             "RCB": (5.0, 16.4), "FS": (13.0, -2.0), "SS": (12.0, 11.0)}), los=LOS, to_go=None)
pp2.highlight("FS", "SS", "LCB", "RCB")
fld = draw(pp2, lateral=(-23, 23), window=(-7.5, 18.5))
plt.show()








Figure 35.14: Second-and-7 against 11 personnel in a 2x2, ball in the middle. Two safeties deep: the free safety (FS) 13 yards deep, about 2 yards left of the ball, inside the left hash; the strong safety (SS) 12 yards deep, wide, between the right hash and the numbers. The right cornerback is squatting about 5 yards off Z with outside leverage; the left cornerback is 8 yards off X. The nickel ($) is in an apex over the left slot. Both corners and both safeties are ringed.





The shell says two-high. What else could it be, which corner gives it away, and what will you check one second after the snap?






TipAnswer





Probably Cover 3 cloud to the right, with Cover 6 as the other possibility. In a true Cover 2 both corners usually squat in the flats; here only the right one does, and the left one is off at 8 yards in a deep-third alignment. A squatting corner with a safety deep over him on one side and an off corner on the other is the cloud picture: at the snap, the right corner plays the flat, the strong safety runs to the deep right third behind him, and the free safety rotates to the middle. The free safety’s alignment helps: he’s inside the hash, almost over the ball, while the strong safety is wide over the squatting corner. Two Cover 2 safeties would be balanced, each on or outside his hash. A safety cheated toward the middle is already halfway to the deep middle third.
The same pre-snap picture also fits Cover 6, quarters on one half and Cover 2 on the other, which Quarters and the Two-High Match Family builds; its quarters side also has a corner off the ball, so here it would be quarters on the left and Cover 2 on the right. One second after the snap, look at the free safety. If he runs to the middle of the field, it’s three deep: cloud. If he stays on the left and reads the slot receiver, it’s two deep: Cover 6. Either way, the right side looks the same, which is the point of the disguise. Against cloud, the place to attack is the deep right third, where a safety has to run with Z.











TipPredict the play 3: two seconds after the snap





Show the Python
def flood_play():
    p = Play(spread(rb_w=1.5), nickel(C3_PRE | {"SS": (6.5, 7.5)}), los=LOS, to_go=10)
    protect(p)
    p.dropback(3.0)
    p.route("Z", [(-0.7, 15.0), (8.0, 15.8), (30.0, 17.0)], absolute=True)
    p.route("Y", [(-1.5, 9.0), (10.0, 9.8), (13.6, 15.2), (14.6, 20.5)], absolute=True)
    p.route("RB", [(-5.0, 1.5), (-3.4, 5.0), (1.6, 11.0), (3.0, 17.0)], absolute=True, speed=6.0)
    p.route("X", [(-0.7, -15.0), (12.0, -15.6), (10.6, -14.6)], absolute=True)
    p.route("H", [(-1.5, -9.0), (6.0, -8.0), (26.0, -6.6)], absolute=True)
    p.drop("RCB", (24.0, 17.4), speed=6.2)
    p.drop("LCB", (18.0, -16.8), speed=5.0)
    p.drop("FS", (18.0, 0.4), speed=3.0)
    p.drop("SS", (9.8, 13.0), speed=4.4)
    p.drop("NB", (10.5, -11.8), speed=4.4)
    p.drop("WILL", (9.0, -4.4), speed=4.0)
    p.drop("MIKE", (9.5, 7.5), speed=4.0)
    return p

fp = flood_play()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.6))
fld = moment(ax, fp, 2.25, (-24.5, 24.5), (-9.0, 26.0), rings=("SS",))
ruler(fld, fp)
plt.show()








Figure 35.15: A Cover 3 sky play against a flood to the right, 2.2 seconds after the snap (simulated). Faint lines are where each player has been. Z is running a go route with the right cornerback over him; Y, from the slot, has pushed upfield and is breaking toward the sideline at about 12 yards (a sail route); the back (R) is running to the right flat. The strong safety (SS, ringed) is the curl-flat defender on that side; the Mike (M) has widened from his hook toward the curl. On the left, X and H run to hold the nickel ($), the Will and the free safety.





Who’s the quarterback’s read, what has that defender done, and where does the ball go?






TipAnswer





The read is the strong safety, the curl-flat defender, and he has sunk under the sail route, so the ball goes to the back in the flat. This is the flood: three receivers at three depths on the right (the go, the sail, the flat) against two defenders, the corner and the curl-flat defender. The corner did his job, staying on top of Z’s go route, which leaves the safety alone with two receivers. He’s at about 10 yards, wide, in the window where the sail will arrive, so the back, running to the flat underneath him with nobody within 7 yards, is the throw. Had the safety jumped down toward the flat, the sail behind him would have been open instead. (Notice the Mike in the frame, too: with #2 going outside and the back heading for the flat, he has widened from his hook toward the curl, as he’s taught, and he still can’t reach the flat in time.)
If this were Cover 3 match, the picture would differ only a little: with #2 (Y) releasing vertically the safety would have carried him at first, and when Y broke out to the sail he’d stay with him, while the Mike, who matches the back (#3), would have a long way to run to the flat. The flat would still be the throw. Flood beats both versions for the same reason. There are only so many defenders on one side of the field.

title: Cover 3: Sky, Buzz, Cloud, and Seattle’s Match Version
text:
Takeaways

Cover 3 is three deep and four under. The corners take the outside thirds and a safety the middle; two curl-flat defenders and two hook defenders take the underneath areas; four rush. It guards the whole deep field with only three players, which is why it’s the NFL’s most common zone.
Its bargain is the eighth man. Bringing the second safety down gives the defense an extra run defender (and its force or alley player) while still playing three deep. The price is the seams, the soft spots in front of the corners, and an underneath defender with two zones.
Sky, buzz and cloud are three ways to arrive at the same coverage. Sky sends a safety to the curl-flat, buzz sends him inside to the hook-curl while an outside defender takes the flat, and cloud puts the corner in the flat with a safety over him. Each fits a different player to the job and leaks a different pre-snap tell.
The curl-flat defender is the key, and the match version changed his job. In spot-drop he guards a place and lets the seam go by; as a seam-flat defender in Cover 3 match he carries #2 up the seam first, which turns four verticals from an unsolvable count into four-on-four.
Seattle made it an identity. Carroll’s 2010s Seahawks showed one picture (a single high safety, pressed corners) and played Cover 3 or its man twin Cover 1 behind it, with a rangy free safety, a box strong safety and long corners who pressed and carried receivers into their thirds. They led the league in scoring defense four years running and sent coordinators across the league; Bradley’s defenses still topped the Cover 3 charts years later.
Recognise it by counting. One high safety, corners off and turned in, a safety near the box before the snap; three deep defenders one second after it, two of them the corners (count before the match carries, and don’t mistake Tampa 2’s running Mike for a third deep defender).

title: Cover 2 and Tampa 2
text:
Two deep, five under
Third-and-12 near midfield, a minute left in the first half. Both cornerbacks stand five yards off the wide receivers, a step outside them, flat-footed. Both safeties are deep, one on each side of the field. The quarterback throws a quick out to the sideline; the corner closes, tackles, gain of eight, and the offense punts. The analyst sounds almost pleased: “That’s Cover 2 doing its job. Keep everything in front, make the tackle.” Two series later the same corner stands in the same spot, the receiver runs straight past him, and the ball drops into his hands 22 yards downfield, between the corner and the safety, before the safety can get there. “And that’s the hole in Cover 2,” says the analyst. So which is it? Why would a defense build a coverage around a hole it knows is there, and why did one version of that coverage, Tampa 2, become the identity of a generation of NFL defenses and two Super Bowl champions? This chapter takes Cover 2 apart: who stands where, why, what it buys, where it bleeds, and what became of it.
You’ll be able to…
Reading the diagrams: offense is blue circles (X, Y, Z, H receivers; Q quarterback; R running back); defense is outlined squares (E and T ends and tackles; M the Mike, W the Will, $ the nickel back, CB corners, FS and SS safeties). Faint lines are 5 yards apart from the line of scrimmage (dark blue); small numbers on the edge give the depth; the orange line is the line to gain. Dashed arrows are defenders’ movements, solid arrows routes, dotted lines man assignments, shaded ovals zones.
Every coverage is an answer to the same arithmetic. The defense has eleven players. If four of them rush the passer, seven are left to cover. Those seven can be split between deep defenders, who stop the ball being thrown over everyone’s head, and underneath defenders, who stop the short and medium throws. Cover 3 splits them three deep and four under. Cover 2 splits them two deep and five under: two safeties each take a deep half of the field, and five defenders spread across the short zones in front of them.
Show the Python
off = offense("gun_2x2")
c2 = Play(off, c2_shell(off), los=35, to_go=10)
protect(c2)
for k, to in {"LCB": (8.5, -18.5), "RCB": (8.5, 18.5), "WILL": (10.0, -9.0), "NB": (10.0, 9.0),
              "MIKE": (10.5, 0.0), "FS": (18.5, -12.0), "SS": (18.5, 12.0)}.items():
    c2.drop(k, to)
ZONES = [((24.0, -13.3), (13.0, 25.5), "deep ½", (25.5, -13.3)), ((24.0, 13.3), (13.0, 25.5), "deep ½", (25.5, 13.3)),
         ((5.0, -21.5), (9.0, 9.5), "flat", (3.2, -22.0)), ((5.0, 21.5), (9.0, 9.5), "flat", (3.2, 22.0)),
         ((11.0, -11.0), (8.0, 9.0), "hook-curl", (8.3, -12.4)), ((11.0, 11.0), (8.0, 9.0), "hook-curl", (8.3, 12.4)),
         ((12.5, 0.0), (6.0, 8.0), "hole (M)", (14.0, 0.0))]
for c, sz, _, _ in ZONES:
    c2.zone(c, sz)
c2.highlight("FS", "SS", "LCB", "RCB")
fld = c2.draw(lateral="full", window=(-8, 32))
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, c2, widths=True)
for *_, lab, at in ZONES:
    zlabel(fld, c2, lab, at)
plt.show()








Figure 36.1: Cover 2 against a 2x2 formation (11 personnel, a nickel defense). Before the snap: two safeties 13 yards deep, between the hash and the numbers; both corners 5 or 6 yards off, a step outside the wide receivers. At the snap (dashed arrows) the four linemen rush and seven defenders drop to their landmarks: the safeties to the two deep halves, the corners to the flats, the Will (W) and the nickel ($) to the hook-curl zones on each side, and the Mike (M) to the hole, the defended zone in the middle. Five zones underneath, two deep: that is the whole coverage.
Here is each job, and the reason behind it.
Cover 2 also has a run-defense job built into it, and it explains the corners’ alignment as much as the passing game does. Against a run to his side, the Cover 2 corner is the force player: he comes up hard from the outside, meets the ball carrier at the edge and turns him back inside, toward the linebackers. The safety on that side becomes the alley player, filling the gap between the corner and the box. A corner standing five yards off, outside the receiver, with his eyes inside, is in exactly the right spot to force, which is one more reason he stands there.
Count the box against 11 personnel and you see the cost. The offense has six blockers: five linemen and the tight end. A nickel Cover 2 has six defenders in the box: four linemen, the Mike and the Will (the nickel is out over the slot). Six against six leaves no unblocked defender at the line, so the spare men are the two safeties, and they arrive as alley players from 12 or more yards away. A run that gets past the linebackers against Cover 2 tends to go for 8 or 10 yards, not 4. (Run Fits and Box Math builds the run fits and the counting.)

title: Cover 2 and Tampa 2
text:
The two safeties: a deep half each. Each safety owns everything deep on his side of the field, from the middle of the field to the sideline: about 27 yards of width. His rule, in its simplest form, is nothing gets behind me: as deep as the deepest receiver in his half, as wide as the widest. He reads the inside receiver (#2) first, because #2’s seam is the threat closest to the middle, then the outside one (#1), and breaks on the ball when it’s thrown. He lines up 12 to 14 yards deep, between the hash and the numbers, roughly 8 to 10 yards from the middle of the field, because from there he can reach both ends of his half; by the time the quarterback finishes his drop he has backpedalled to about 18 to 20 yards, near the top of the numbers. A quarters safety (Quarters and the Two-High Match Family) usually stands shallower and closer to the hash, because he has only a quarter of the field; being deeper and wider is the price of owning a half.
The two corners: the flats. A Cover 2 cornerback is not a deep defender at all. He lines up close, outside the wide receiver, and at the snap he jams or redirects him and then stays short, at the top of the flat (6 to 9 yards deep, a little deeper than the 0–6 of the textbook flat, so he can also slow down anything going deep). This is the hard corner, and the next section is about him.
The Will and the nickel: the hook-curl zones. Between the flat and the middle, each takes the curl and hook area on his side, 10 to 12 yards deep, under the inside receiver’s routes and in the lane of the outside receiver’s curls and digs. One more job matters a lot: if the slot receiver (#2) runs straight up the seam, the hook-curl defender gets in his way (coaches say he walls him) and rides him to 10 or 12 yards before letting the safety take over. Every step that costs the receiver is a step the safety gains. In a base 4-3 defense these two are the outside linebackers, the Sam and the Will; in nickel, the usual passing-down defense, the nickel back plays the Sam’s part.
The Mike: the hole. The middle linebacker drops straight back to the middle of the field, 10 to 12 yards deep, to take away throws over the ball: digs, crossing routes, a tight end sitting down in the middle. (Hold on to this job. Tampa 2 changes it.) A word trap: the hole is the name of this zone, a defended one, from Coverage Fundamentals. When announcers say “a hole in the coverage” they mean the opposite, an empty spot. This chapter calls those empty spots thin spots; the one exception is the name hole shot, which the whole league uses.
The four rushers. In a pure Cover 2 nobody else is spare. The coverage depends on four linemen getting to the quarterback without help, because seven defenders are all spoken for.







ImportantWhy it exists



What Cover 2 buys. Five underneath defenders is the most any common zone puts there, so every short throw has a defender within a few yards of it, and the quarterback has to fit the ball into small windows or settle for short gains. The corners in the flats take away the quick throws to the outside that beat off-coverage corners (quick outs, hitches, bubble screens), and they squeeze the outside receivers’ releases, which disrupts the timing of everything else. Two deep safeties mean no single deep defender is ever alone against two vertical routes in the middle of the field, as Cover 3’s lone safety can be. And the corners never have to run step for step with the fastest receivers on the field, which lets a defense survive with corners who are physical and smart rather than fast.
What it gives up. Only two defenders guard the whole deep field, so each safety has a huge area, and wherever two receivers go deep in one half, one safety is in a two-on-one. The corners stay short, so the sideline behind them is empty until a safety gets there. With both safeties deep, only six or seven defenders are near the line of scrimmage against the run (the box), one fewer than when a safety comes down. Cover 2 is a bet that the offense can’t complete enough of the hard throws to make up for all the easy ones it takes away.










NoteMadden vs. real life



On a video-game play-call screen, Cover 2 looks like one play: pick it and the same seven zones appear every time. On an NFL defense, “Cover 2” is a family with dozens of members. Some teams press the corners and some play them off; some spot-drop and some pattern-match; some play it with three linebackers and some with a nickel or dime; one coach’s safeties line up on the hashes and another’s on the numbers. Many staffs never call it “Cover 2” at all: the numbers on a call sheet are a team’s own dialect. What stays the same is the skeleton, two deep halves and five underneath, with the corners in the flats. That is what to look for.

title: Cover 2 and Tampa 2
text:
The hard corner
The single most distinctive player in Cover 2 is the cornerback who doesn’t go deep. A hard corner (also called a squat corner) lines up 5 to 7 yards off the outside receiver, or right on him in press, a step outside him with his shoulders turned slightly in so he can see through the receiver to the quarterback. At the snap he does three things in order:

Collision and redirect. He meets the receiver at the line or as he comes off it, gets his hands on him, and makes him release inside. A receiver who wants to run straight up the sideline gets pushed toward the middle of the field, where the safety is. Every step the receiver loses getting past the corner is a step the safety gains. All of this has to happen within five yards of the line of scrimmage: after that, contact before the ball is thrown is a foul, as long as the quarterback is still in the pocket with the ball.1
Read #2, and sink. Before the snap he looks at #1. At the snap his eyes go to the inside receiver (#2), because #2 is the one who can threaten his flat. If #2 goes straight up the field, or nobody comes toward the flat at all, he doesn’t stand still: he gives ground, backing up and widening under #1, often to 10 or 12 yards, to shrink the gap between himself and the safety. Coaches teach it as a rule: sink until something threatens the flat.
Squat. When #2 (or a running back) breaks toward the flat, or the quarterback’s eyes go there, he stops, plants and comes forward to make the tackle. He keeps outside leverage throughout, so anything that goes inside of him goes to the linebackers and the safety, and nothing escapes to the sideline.

“Squat” does double duty, and it’s worth saying once: a squat corner is the alignment (short and outside), and squatting on a route is step 3. Same idea both times: this corner lives low.
Set that next to the Cover 3 corner from the previous chapter, against the same receiver.


Show the Python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.9))
off = offense("gun_2x2")
# Cover 3: off corner bails to a deep third; the nickel is the curl-flat defender
right = [p for p in off if p.key in ("RT", "Y", "Z")]          # only the right side is drawn
c3_def = [p.moved(d=7.5, w=16.0, label="CB") if p.key == "RCB" else p.moved(d=5.0, w=7.0)
          for p in defense("nickel", "single_high", off) if p.key in ("RCB", "NB")]
a = Play(right, c3_def, los=35, to_go=None)
a.route("Z", r.go(19))
a.drop("RCB", (17.0, 17.0), speed=5.5)
a.drop("NB", (8.0, 13.5))
a.zone((19.0, 17.8), (12.0, 15.5), "deep third")
a.zone((4.5, 17.5), (6.5, 10.0), "flat")
a.highlight("RCB")
fa = a.draw(ax=axes[0], lateral=(1.5, HALF), window=(-3, 27.5), title=False)
no_numbers(fa.ax)
say(fa, a, "bail: open, run to\nhis third, eyes on Q", (13.5, 7.5), fs=6.5)
axes[0].set_title("Cover 3 corner: bail", fontsize=9, loc="left")
# Cover 2: hard corner jams, re-routes Z inside, sinks into the flat
b = Play(right, [p for p in c2_shell(off) if p.key in ("RCB", "NB", "SS")], los=35, to_go=None)
b.route("Z", r.path((3.0, -1.3), (19.0, -2.6)))
b.path("RCB", [(4.0, 15.4), (8.5, 18.3)], absolute=True, speed=3.0)
b.drop("SS", (18.0, 13.0))
b.zone((21.5, 13.3), (11.0, 22.0), "deep ½ (SS)")
b.zone((5.0, 20.5), (6.5, 10.0), "flat")
b.highlight("RCB")
fb = b.draw(ax=axes[1], lateral=(1.5, HALF), window=(-3, 27.5), title=False)
no_numbers(fb.ax)
say(fb, b, "jam, push him inside,\nsink, sit in the flat", (8.5, 7.5), fs=6.5)
pointer(fb, b, "jam", (1.0, 9.0), (2.2, 14.6), fs=6.5)
axes[1].set_title("Cover 2 corner: hard (squat)", fontsize=9, loc="left")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.8)
plt.show()








Figure 36.2: Two corners, one receiver (the offense’s right side only). Left, Cover 3: the corner lines up 7 or 8 yards off and bails at the snap, turning to run with Z into his deep third; the flat is the curl-flat defender’s ($). Right, Cover 2: the corner lines up 5 yards off, a step outside Z, jams him, forces his release inside toward the safety, then sinks under him and sits in the flat. Behind him, the strong safety (SS) has the whole deep half. Same receiver, opposite jobs: one corner is a deep defender who also helps in the flat, the other a flat defender who also slows down the deep ball.





Why build a corner this way? Three reasons, and each is about time.
The flats are where quick throws go. A corner 8 yards off and backing up concedes the 5-yard out and the hitch: by the time he plants and drives on the throw, the receiver has caught it and turned upfield. A squat corner is already there. Against offenses that live on quick timing throws to the outside (The Quick Game), that matters on every down.
The jam buys the safety time. The weakness of Cover 2 is the ground the safeties have to cover, so anything that delays the outside receiver helps. A receiver who has been knocked off his line and forced inside arrives at 15 yards a half-second late and closer to the middle, which is exactly where the safety is coming from.
Outside leverage turns the sideline into a defender. Because the corner refuses to let anything escape outside, every receiver on his side is funnelled toward the middle of the field, into the zones of the linebackers and the safety. The offense has to throw into the defense.
The price is plain from the picture: once the receiver is past him, the corner is no longer a deep defender. Everything behind him and outside the safety is grass, and it stays grass until the safety covers the 10 or 15 yards to get there.
Where else you’ll see him. The squat corner is not only a Cover 2 player. Many staffs call any side where the corner takes the flat a cloud side (C for corner) and a side where a safety comes down to the flat a sky side (S for safety): the same words as the Cover 3 rotations, because it’s the same job. The cloud corner in Cover 3 and the Cover 2 side of Cover 6 (Quarters and the Two-High Match Family) are both squat corners. And in today’s NFL the squat often comes after the snap: a corner lines up 7 or 8 yards off, looking like a deep defender, and drives down to the flat once the ball is snapped. Some defenses even flip the jobs, in what coaches call Cover 2 invert: the corners bail to the deep halves and the safeties come down to the flats.






NoteGo deeper: when the rules changed the corner’s job



Until the mid-1970s, defenders could keep chucking a receiver (hitting or shoving him with their hands as he ran his route) all the way down the field until the ball was in the air. The league chipped at that in 1974 and 1977, limiting how many times a defender could jam the same receiver. Pittsburgh’s Mel Blount, a 6-foot-3 cornerback on the Steelers defenses of the 1970s, was so good at manhandling receivers that the bigger 1978 change is still called the “Mel Blount rule”: from that season, defenders could make contact with a receiver only within 5 yards of the line of scrimmage.2 The Cover 2 corner’s jam survived because it happens inside those 5 yards. What disappeared was a defense’s ability to keep rerouting receivers with linebackers and safeties downfield. The full story of the chuck rule and its effect on passing is in 1978 and the Passing Revolution, and today’s contact rules are in Contact Rules and Penalties as Strategy.

title: Cover 2 and Tampa 2
text:
Where Cover 2 is thin
Every coverage has thin spots, because seven defenders can’t cover a field 53 yards wide and as deep as a quarterback can throw. Cover 2’s are unusually well known, because the coverage is so old and so common that every offense carries a list of its “Cover 2 beaters.” There are four classic attacks, aimed at three places: two of them, the hole shot and the smash corner, land in the same grass along the sideline, but they get there from different directions and put a different defender in a bind.


Show the Python
off = offense("gun_2x2")
land = {"LCB": (8.0, -18.0), "RCB": (8.0, 18.0), "WILL": (10.0, -9.0), "NB": (10.0, 9.0),
        "MIKE": (10.5, 0.0), "FS": (18.5, -12.0), "SS": (18.5, 12.0)}
dfn = [p.moved(d=land[p.key][0], w=land[p.key][1]) if p.key in land else p for p in c2_shell(off)]
keep = {"LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT", "QB", "Y", "Z"}
mp = Play([p.moved(d=-7.5) if p.key == "QB" else p for p in off if p.key in keep], dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
mp.route("Z", r.path((4.0, 0.6), (22.0, 6.2)))                 # go / fade, bending toward the sideline
mp.route("Y", r.path((10.0, 0.0), (19.5, 10.8)))               # corner route from the slot
fld = mp.draw(lateral="full", window=(-9, 31))
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, mp, widths=True)
hole(fld, mp, (21.5, 20.0), (8.0, 9.5), "")
pointer(fld, mp, "① hole shot:\nZ's go route", (27.0, 20.0), (17.0, 19.8), fs=7)
pointer(fld, mp, "② smash corner:\nY's corner route", (15.0, 3.5), (14.5, 14.8), fs=7)
hole(fld, mp, (24.0, 0.0), (8.0, 11.0), "③ deep middle")
hole(fld, mp, (15.0, -19.5), (5.5, 10.0), "④ sideline\nhole")
pointer(fld, mp, "one safety,\n27 yards of width", (28.0, 9.0), (18.5, 12.0), fs=7)
say(fld, mp, "corners sit\nat 8 yards", (4.0, -18.0), fs=6.5)
plt.show()








Figure 36.3: The Cover 2 map: the seven defenders at their landmarks about a second and a half after the snap, and the three thin places (green), attacked four ways. On the right, the deep sideline, behind the corner and in front of the safety, reached two ways: (1) the hole shot, Z’s go route straight up the sideline past the squatting corner (it tests the safety’s speed), and (2) the smash corner, Y breaking out to the same grass from inside, over the corner’s head (it tests the corner’s choice). (3) The deep middle, between the two safeties and behind the Mike. (4) On the left, the sideline hole: the intermediate band outside the hook-curl defender, above the corner and below the safety, where deep outs and comebacks land. Every thin place exists on both sides; each is marked once here. The receivers are drawn where they line up.





① The hole shot. The most famous one. The corner is sitting in the flat, 6 to 10 yards deep. The safety is on his half, starting 13 yards deep and 8 to 10 yards from the middle. Between them, along the sideline from about 15 to 25 yards deep, is a strip of grass that nobody is standing on at the snap. A hole shot is a ball thrown into that strip: usually the outside receiver’s go route or a fade (a go route that bends toward the sideline, away from the safety, and is thrown over the receiver’s outside shoulder; it gets its full treatment in the red-zone chapter), released past the squatting corner and thrown on time, before the safety can get across. The arithmetic is a race. From his alignment, the safety is roughly 14 yards from the spot where a fade is caught 20 or 22 yards downfield, 5 yards from the sideline. Opening and gaining depth while he reads, then running at 6 yards a second, he needs close to 3 seconds to get there. The throw leaves the quarterback’s hand a little after 2 seconds and hangs in the air for most of a second, so it lands at about the same moment. And a tie goes to the offense: to break up the pass the safety has to arrive a step before the ball, not with it. So anything that holds him for a beat (a second receiver running up the seam inside him, or the quarterback’s eyes looking that way) turns a tie into a completion. That is why offenses pair the outside go route with a seam inside it: two vertical routes in one half put one safety in a two-on-one. Four verticals does it on both sides at once.
② The smash corner. Smash reaches the same grass from the inside, and it tests a different defender. The outside receiver runs a hitch at 5 or 6 yards, which holds the hard corner in the flat: his rules tell him to sit on it. The inside receiver runs about 10 yards up the field and breaks toward the back corner of the field, over the corner’s head and under the safety. The corner can’t play both: if he sinks under the corner route, the hitch is open; if he squats on the hitch, the corner route is. It is a high-low read of one defender, and the next section plays it out frame by frame.
③ The deep middle. With two safeties each guarding a half, the line where the halves meet is the farthest point from both of them. Nobody is standing in the middle of the field 18 to 25 yards deep, and the Mike, who has the hole at 10 to 12 yards, can’t run with a receiver who goes past him. A seam route that splits the safeties, a post, or a tight end running straight up the middle puts both safeties in a bind: whichever one comes inside to help has left his own sideline. This is the hole Tampa 2 was built to close.
④ The sideline hole. Underneath the safety and above the corner there is also an intermediate gap, about 12 to 18 yards deep, outside the hook-curl defender. A deep out or a comeback from the outside receiver lands there; so does the middle route of a flood concept, which sends one receiver deep to hold the safety and one to the flat to hold the corner, then throws to the one in between. Coaches name these spots differently; some call the whole strip from 12 to 25 yards “the Cover 2 hole” (an empty spot, in the announcers’ sense) and some reserve the term for the deep end. The geometry is the same either way: the corner is low, the safety is high and wide, and the sideline between them is the offense’s.






CautionCommon misconception



“Cover 2 is soft.” It’s an easy thing to believe when a defense gives up 8-yard completions on third-and-12 and the announcer says the defense is “playing soft.” But Cover 2’s corners are the most aggressive in football against short throws, and five underneath defenders make the short middle crowded. What Cover 2 gives up is not the short ball but specific intermediate and deep windows, and a defense that plays it well makes the offense find those windows with a well-timed, accurate throw, over and over. A third-and-12 completion for 8 is the coverage working.



What the data say: quarterbacks throw deep middle against Cover 2
If the deep middle really is the weak spot, quarterbacks should aim there more often against Cover 2 than against other coverages. They do. The charting data in nflverse label the coverage on most dropbacks since 2018, and the play-by-play records whether each pass went to the left, middle or right of the field. (One limit: the labels have no separate code for Tampa 2, so “Cover 2” here and in the charts below is the whole Cover 2 family, Mike-runs-the-middle or not.)


Show the Python (nflverse coverage labels joined to play-by-play, 2018–2025)
from gridiron.data import nfl, pbp

SEASONS = list(range(2018, 2026))
PB_COLS = ["season", "season_type", "game_id", "play_id", "down", "ydstogo", "half_seconds_remaining",
           "qb_dropback", "pass_attempt", "air_yards", "pass_location", "epa"]
_pb = pbp(SEASONS, columns=PB_COLS)
_pb = _pb[_pb["season_type"] == "REG"]
_part = (nfl().load_participation(SEASONS).to_pandas()
         .rename(columns={"nflverse_game_id": "game_id"})[["game_id", "play_id", "defense_coverage_type"]])
CV = _pb.merge(_part, on=["game_id", "play_id"])
# charted dropbacks; blown coverages, 'combo' and prevent left out
CV = CV[(CV["qb_dropback"] == 1) & CV["defense_coverage_type"].notna()
        & ~CV["defense_coverage_type"].isin(["BLOWN", "COMBO", "PREVENT"])].copy()
ERAS = ["2018–2022 (NGS charting)", "2023–2025 (FTN charting)"]
CV["era"] = np.where(CV["season"] <= 2022, ERAS[0], ERAS[1])


def _dd(row):
    if pd.isna(row.down):        # two-point tries have no down (and ydstogo 2): keep them out of 3rd & short
        return "none"
    if row.down == 1:
        return "1st"
    if row.down == 2:
        return "2nd"
    for hi, lab in ((2, "3rd/4th & 1–2"), (6, "3rd/4th & 3–6"), (10, "3rd/4th & 7–10")):
        if row.ydstogo <= hi:
            return lab
    return "3rd/4th & 11+"


CV["dd"] = CV.apply(_dd, axis=1)
CV["c2"] = CV["defense_coverage_type"].eq("COVER_2")
CV["m2"] = CV["defense_coverage_type"].eq("2_MAN")
DEEP = CV[(CV["pass_attempt"] == 1) & (CV["air_yards"] >= 15) & CV["pass_location"].notna()].copy()
DEEP["middle"] = DEEP["pass_location"].eq("middle")




Show the Python

names = {"COVER_1": "Cover 1", "COVER_3": "Cover 3", "COVER_4": "Quarters\n(Cover 4)", "COVER_2": "Cover 2"}

                        rotation=90, fontweight="bold")
for ax, title, ylab in ((axes[0], "Share of deep passes thrown to the middle", "% of passes 15+ yards"),
                        (axes[1], "Value of a deep pass to the middle", "EPA per pass")):
    ax.set_xticks(x)
    ax.set_xticklabels([names[c] for c in order], fontsize=7.5)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=8.5)
    ax.set_ylabel(ylab, fontsize=7.5)
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)
    ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)

axes[1].set_ylim(0, 1.2)

           loc="upper center", ncol=2, fontsize=7.2, frameon=False, bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 1.02))
