Figure 36.4: Where deep passes go against each coverage. Left: of all passes thrown 15 or more yards past the line of scrimmage, the share the play-by-play records as thrown to the middle of the field (rather than left or right). Right: expected points added (EPA) per deep pass to the middle, with 95% intervals (thin lines). Against Cover 1 and Cover 3 a deep safety sits in the middle, and quarterbacks rarely throw there; against Cover 2 they throw there about one time in three, the most of these four in the Next Gen Stats seasons and level with quarters in the FTN seasons. The value of those throws is noisier: Cover 2 is at the top of the right panel, level with quarters in the FTN seasons, but the intervals overlap, so read it as ‘at least as valuable as anywhere else’, not ‘clearly the most’. Regular-season dropbacks with a charted coverage; the two charting sources are shown separately because they label coverages differently.





The pattern is the coverage’s geometry showing through the numbers. Against Cover 1, with a free safety parked in the middle, only about one deep pass in nine goes there. Against Cover 3 it is about one in five. Against Cover 2 it is about one in three in the Next Gen Stats seasons and a little under that in the FTN seasons, as high as against any coverage. A deep pass to the middle against Cover 2 has been worth about two-thirds to three-quarters of a point to the offense on average, at least as much as the same throw against Cover 1 or Cover 3, though with 500 to 800 such throws per charting era the gaps are inside the noise.3 Quarters, the other two-high family, is close behind or level on how often the middle is targeted, and in the FTN seasons a deep throw to the middle against it has been just as valuable; its safeties play narrower and help in the middle, which is part of why (that’s the next chapter).
Two cautions. The play-by-play’s “middle” is a scorer’s judgement, not a measured zone, so read the shares as rough. And these are results, which mix the coverage’s weakness with the offense’s choices: offenses that expect Cover 2 call plays that attack the middle. That is the point, though. The middle is where offenses go when they see two deep safeties, which is why defenses started looking for someone to put there.

title: Cover 2 and Tampa 2
section: Smash against Cover 2, move by move
text:
Smash against Cover 2, move by move
Dropback Concepts drew smash from the quarterback’s side, as a read. Here it is from the defense’s side, as a problem with a clock on it. Watch the right cornerback.


Show the Python
def smash_play():
    off = offense("gun_2x2")
    p = Play(off, c2_shell(off, corner_d=5.5), los=40, to_go=8)
    protect(p)
    p.dropback(2.0)
    p.route("Z", r.hitch(6.0))
    p.route("Y", r.path((10.0, 0.0), (20.0, 11.5)))
    p.route("X", r.hitch(6.0))
    p.route("H", r.path((19.0, 0.0)))                  # seam: holds the free safety on the other side
    p.route("RB", r.flat(1.5, 5.0), side=-1)
    p.pass_to("Y", t=1.85)
    # right corner: collision, sink a little, then drive on the hitch he sees in front of him
    p.drop("RCB", (5.8, 16.0), speed=1.2)
    p.drop("RCB", (7.6, 17.3), speed=2.4)
    p.path("RCB", [(6.4, 15.2)], absolute=True, speed=3.5)
    # strong safety: stays on top of Y's stem, breaks a beat after the ball is in the air
    p.drop("SS", (18.8, 12.3), speed=4.0)
    p.path("SS", [(17.8, 18.0)], absolute=True, speed=5.2, delay=0.75)
    p.drop("NB", (10.0, 9.5)); p.drop("MIKE", (10.5, 0.0)); p.drop("WILL", (9.5, -6.8))
    p.drop("LCB", (7.6, -17.3)); p.drop("FS", (18.8, -12.3))
    p.highlight("RCB")
    return p


smash = smash_play()
SMASH_T = [0.0, 0.9, 1.9, 3.7]
if PDF:
    strip(smash, SMASH_T, ["Snap · corner 5 yards off, outside Z", "+0.9 s · jam, Z turns for the hitch",
                           "+1.9 s · Y breaks to the corner: throw", "+3.7 s · over the corner, under the safety"],
          lateral=(-19.5, HALF), window=(-8.0, 23.5), ruler_side="right",
          notes_at={1: [("hitch", (3.0, 18.2))], 3: [("corner\nroute", (21.8, 21.0))]})
    plt.show()
else:
    show_animation(smash, times=SMASH_T)





  
  Your browser does not support the video tag.



Figure 36.5: Smash against Cover 2, the offense’s right side, simulated. Snap: the corner (ringed) is 5 or 6 yards off Z, a step outside him; the strong safety (SS) is 13 deep. +0.9 s: Z has pushed to 6 yards and is turning back for the hitch; the corner, doing his job, has jammed and is sitting in the flat. Y, the slot receiver, is running straight up the field past the nickel ($). +1.9 s: Y has broken toward the sideline at about 10 yards and the quarterback throws. The corner is driving on the hitch; the safety has backed up to 19 yards, on top of Y but 8 yards inside the spot Y is heading for, and is only now reacting. +3.7 s: the ball arrives about 18 yards downfield and 6 or 7 yards from the sideline, over the corner and under the safety, who is still a couple of steps away. On the left, X runs a hitch and H a seam, to keep the free safety (FS) busy on his own side.




Look at the corner across the panels and you see a player doing everything right and losing anyway. His rules say: jam the outside receiver, sink, and squat on anything short in the flat. The hitch is short and in the flat, so he squats on it. Meanwhile, the corner route breaks behind him into the strip of grass he just left. The safety’s rules say: stay deeper than anything in your half. He does: at 1.9 seconds he is 19 yards deep, deeper than Y, but 8 yards inside the spot the corner route is heading for, and he can’t start running at it until he’s sure that’s where the ball is going. By the time he is sure, the ball is in the air. The throw beats him by a step.
That is the general shape of beating any zone: find one defender with two jobs and make him choose. In smash the cornerback is that defender. And the quarterback’s read is mercifully simple: he watches only the corner. Corner sinks, throw the hitch. Corner squats, throw the corner route.
How does the defense fight back? Not by playing Cover 2 harder, but by changing what the corner and safety do when they see this route combination.

Wall the slot. Watch the nickel ($) in the figure: Y runs straight past him untouched. His rules say he should have got in Y’s way as Y released up the field and ridden him for a few yards. A collision at 6 yards delays the corner route by a beat, and a beat is all the safety needs. What the nickel can’t do is follow Y toward the sideline: that would empty the hook-curl zone behind him for the next route.
Teach the corner to sink further. This is the corner’s #2 key from the last section. When #2 goes vertical and #1 runs something short, many Cover 2 coaches tell the corner to keep sinking under the vertical instead of jumping the hitch: give up the 6-yard hitch, which the hook-curl defender can rally to, and take away the 18-yard corner route.
Widen the safety. A safety who aligns wider, or who reads the inside receiver’s release and goes straight to the corner route, gets there sooner, at the cost of the seam and the deep middle.
Change the coverage to that side. Against a team that loves smash, a defense can play Cover 2 to one side and quarters to the other (Cover 6), or play Palms (also called 2-Read), where the corner lines up off and stays on the outside receiver while the safety reads the slot and takes him when he goes vertical: the corner route runs into the safety and the hitch runs into the corner. Both are in Quarters and the Two-High Match Family. Or it can play 2-Man, where the corner ignores the zones and follows his man, and the corner route runs into a trailing slot defender and a safety over the top.

Smash also shows why play-calling is a guessing game. Smash is a great call against Cover 2 and a mediocre one against Cover 3, whose corners drop deep into the corner route’s path. Which is why defenses that play a lot of Cover 2 try hard to make it look like something else before the snap (Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage), and why What Beats What puts smash versus Cover 2 in the first row of its matrix.

title: Cover 2 and Tampa 2
section: Tampa 2: the Mike takes the middle
text:
Tampa 2: the Mike takes the middle
Go back to thin spot ③, the deep middle. Cover 2 has nobody there, and offenses learned to send a receiver straight up it: a tight end, a slot receiver, a running back out of the backfield. The Mike, sitting in the hole at 10 to 12 yards, watches him run past. Each safety is busy with his own half. The ball goes over the Mike and between the safeties.
Tampa 2 answers that with one change. At the snap, if it’s a pass, the Mike doesn’t stop at 10 yards. He opens (usually toward the side with more receivers), reads the quarterback’s eyes and whichever inside receiver goes vertical, and runs down the middle of the field to 15 or 20 yards. He stays on top of and inside that receiver and carries him, and he bumps anything crossing his path on the way. Coaches call his landing spot the “pipe” or the “middle of the field”: the space between the two deep safeties. Everything else is Cover 2: two safeties on the deep halves, squat corners in the flats, two outside linebackers (or a linebacker and the nickel) in the hook-curl zones.
How does he know it’s a pass in time? The same way every linebacker does: he reads the offensive linemen in front of him. Linemen who stand up and step back into pass protection (“high hats,” in coaching shorthand) mean pass; linemen firing forward mean run. He has to make that call in his first step.


Show the Python
def tampa_play():
    off = offense("gun_2x2")
    p = Play(off, c2_shell(off), los=40, to_go=10)
    protect(p)
    p.dropback(2.5)
    p.route("X", r.go(19)); p.route("Z", r.go(19))
    p.route("Y", r.path((10.0, 0.0), (20.0, -4.5)))
    p.route("H", r.curl(11.0))
    p.route("RB", r.path((3.0, 4.0), (6.5, 12.5)), side=-1)
    p.pass_to("RB", t=2.55)
    # Mike: open and run the middle, carrying the seam
    p.path("MIKE", [(9.0, 1.2), (16.0, 3.0), (19.5, 3.0)], absolute=True, speed=5.9, delay=0.15)
    # corners: collision, sink under the outside receivers; the left corner comes up on the flat throw
    p.drop("LCB", (6.0, -15.8), speed=1.3)
    p.drop("LCB", (9.5, -16.8), speed=2.8)
    p.path("LCB", [(2.9, -14.7)], absolute=True, speed=5.5, delay=0.15)
    p.drop("RCB", (6.0, 15.8), speed=1.3)
    p.drop("RCB", (9.5, 16.8), speed=2.8)
    # safeties widen over the outside verticals; underneath droppers to the hook-curl zones
    p.drop("FS", (22.5, -14.5), speed=4.8); p.drop("SS", (22.5, 14.0), speed=4.8)
    p.drop("WILL", (9.5, -10.0)); p.drop("NB", (9.5, 10.0))
    p.highlight("MIKE")
    return p


tampa = tampa_play()
TAMPA_T = [0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.4]
if PDF:
    strip(tampa, TAMPA_T, ["Snap · it looks like Cover 2", "+1.0 s · the Mike turns and runs",
                           "+2.0 s · the seam runs into him", "+3.4 s · checkdown; the corner rallies"],
          lateral=(-20.5, 20.5), window=(-8.5, 25.5),
          notes_at={2: [("Mike carries\nthe seam", (16.0, -4.5))]},
          extras={3: lambda f: hole(f, tampa, (12.5, -3.0), (5.0, 8.0), "empty now:\na dig sits here", fs=6.0)})
    plt.show()
else:
    show_animation(tampa, times=TAMPA_T)





  
  Your browser does not support the video tag.



Figure 36.6: Tampa 2 against a seam, simulated. Snap: a Cover 2 picture, Mike (M, ringed) 4.5 yards off the ball. +1.0 s: it’s a pass, so he turns and runs down the middle. The corners have jammed X and Z and sunk; the safeties are widening over them. +2.0 s: Y, the slot receiver, has bent his seam toward the middle, the throw Cover 2 hates, and runs into the Mike, now about 15 yards deep and still running, with the strong safety over the top. +3.4 s: nothing is open deep, so the quarterback checks the ball down to the running back in the left flat, and the left corner, who was sitting at the top of the flat, comes up to meet him. The green patch is the price: the middle at 10 to 15 yards, where the Mike used to be, is now empty, and a dig timed to sit there would be open. Five underneath at the snap; a second later, four underneath and three deep: that is the Tampa 2 bargain.




Look at the third panel and count the deep defenders: two safeties and the Mike. A coverage that started as two-high has become, by the time the seam gets to 15 yards, a three-deep coverage. The safeties are free to play wider, because the middle is covered, which also shrinks the thin spot along the sideline. Now do the arithmetic, because it is the whole point. At the snap there are five underneath defenders, as in any Cover 2, so the quick game still runs into a crowd. About a second later the Mike has run past the short routes, and the coverage is four underneath and three deep. Tampa 2 gives up its fifth underneath defender only once the throws he was there to stop have mostly come and gone.
What does it give up? The Mike’s departure opens a new thin spot of its own: the middle of the field at about 10 to 15 yards, in front of the running Mike and behind the hook-curl defenders (the green patch in the last panel). A dig or a curl by the inside receiver, timed to sit down where the Mike was, is the classic Tampa 2 answer, and offenses have named concepts built for it: dagger sends the slot up the seam to drag the Mike deep and throws a deep dig behind him, and levels and drive stack two in-breaking routes at two depths under him (Dropback Concepts). The Mike also has to make a decision on every snap: run, or stop because it’s a run play, a screen, or a draw. A Mike who runs on a draw has left the middle of the field to the ball carrier.






ImportantWhy it exists: Tampa 2



What it solves. Cover 2’s worst thin spot, the deep middle, without moving a safety. It keeps five defenders underneath against the quick game and gives one up only once the Mike has run past the short routes. It also turns a two-high picture into a three-deep coverage after the snap, so the quarterback who saw “middle of the field open” and decided to throw the seam finds it closed.
What it gives up. The intermediate middle behind the hook-curl defenders, and a lot of the Mike. He has to read run or pass instantly, then run 15 to 20 yards with a tight end or a slot receiver: a linebacker’s job and a safety’s job in one body.



Cover 2 against trips
Everything so far has been against two receivers on each side. Put three on one side (trips, or 3x1) and plain Cover 2’s rules leave a gap. On the trips side, the corner sits on #1’s flat, the nickel walls #2, and the safety has a whole half with three receivers in it. If #3, the innermost, runs straight up the middle, he is past the Mike at 12 yards and in the deep middle with nobody near him. Meanwhile, on the other side, the backside safety has a half with only one receiver in it, X, and the backside corner is already sitting short on X’s side.
Cover 2 teams don’t just accept that. Against 3x1 they adjust, and the common answers are:

Bring the backside safety’s eyes inside. He has only X, and the corner is already on X’s side, so he is told to help on #3 going up the middle and leave X to the corner and the sideline.
Give #3 to the Mike. This is the Tampa 2 rule exactly: the Mike carries #3 vertical up the pipe. Trips is the formation where the Tampa Mike earns his money.
Get out of Cover 2. Many defenses simply check to a different coverage against trips, one built for three receivers on a side; those 3x1 checks are in Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage.

Which answer a team uses is a big part of its identity, and the offense’s game plan is often built around finding out.


Why it existed: a defense for fast, smart, ordinary-sized players
The coverage didn’t come first. The players and the philosophy did.
Its roots are in Pittsburgh. Bud Carson, the Steelers’ defensive backs coach from 1972 and their defensive coordinator from 1973 to 1977, had started building a two-deep zone at Georgia Tech, and in Pittsburgh he refined it into the coverage behind the “Steel Curtain,” the nickname of the Steelers’ 1970s defense (and especially its four-man line). Its signature was a middle linebacker who dropped into coverage: when the Steelers got Jack Lambert, a rangy, fast middle linebacker, in 1974, Carson could ask him to run deep down the middle. The 1976 Steelers allowed 28 points in total during a nine-game winning streak at the end of the season.4 One of the safeties on the 1977 and 1978 Steelers was an undrafted rookie from Minnesota named Tony Dungy. After a season with the 49ers and a year coaching defensive backs at his old college, he returned to Pittsburgh as an assistant in the early 1980s and was its defensive coordinator from 1984 to 1988.5 Years later he described his whole approach in one sentence: “My philosophy is really out of the 1975 Pittsburgh Steelers playbook.”6
When Dungy became the Tampa Bay Buccaneers’ head coach in 1996, he brought that playbook and a defensive coordinator, Monte Kiffin, who had been on Dennis Green’s Minnesota Vikings staff with him in the early 1990s. Kiffin coordinated Tampa Bay’s defense for thirteen seasons, 1996 to 2008, and the two of them turned the old Steelers idea into an identity, so tightly linked to the franchise that the coverage took the city’s name.7
Their version was built on a few stubborn ideas:

Simplicity. A small number of calls, practised until every player could play them without thinking. Players who aren’t thinking play fast.
Speed over size. Lighter, faster players at every level: a quick, penetrating 3-technique defensive tackle (Warren Sapp) who penetrated rather than held his ground, linebackers who could run like safeties, and a 4-3 front in which every lineman attacked one gap (Even Fronts).
Four rushers, seven in coverage. No exotic blitzes. The four-man rush was expected to get home on its own, which is why the scheme prized pass-rushing linemen: if four can’t win, seven defenders can’t cover forever.
Everything in front, then tackle. Spot-drop zones, every underneath defender’s eyes on the quarterback, and a sprint to the ball the moment it’s thrown. Let the offense complete short passes, tackle immediately, and wait: a 12-play drive has a dozen chances for a penalty, a sack, a dropped pass or a turnover.

The Mike’s deep drop fits all four. It needs a fast linebacker rather than an extra safety, it uses no extra rusher, and it removes the one throw that turns a long drive into a short one.






NoteMadden vs. real life



In a video game you can call Tampa 2 with any eleven players and the Mike will run his drop. On a real field the coverage is only as good as the man running down the middle. Tampa 2 Mikes have to diagnose run or pass in a step, then turn and run 15 to 20 yards with a receiver while reading the quarterback. The players who made it famous were unusual athletes: Chicago’s Brian Urlacher, for example, had played a hybrid linebacker-safety position in college at New Mexico.8 A Tampa 2 with an ordinary middle linebacker is a Cover 2 with an extra hole.

title: Cover 2 and Tampa 2
text:
Film room






NoteFilm room: Pittsburgh Steelers 1974–1977 — Bud Carson’s two-deep zone



The Steelers won Super Bowls IX and X (the 1974 and 1975 seasons) with a defense that could play a two-deep zone with squeezing, physical corners and a middle linebacker who dropped into coverage. Jack Lambert, a rookie in 1974, was the prototype of the coverage linebacker; Mel Blount, the cornerback whose physical style later produced the 1978 contact rule, was the prototype of the corner who controlled a receiver’s release. In 1976 the defense was at its peak: during a nine-game winning streak to finish the season it allowed 28 points in total.
What to notice (on NFL Films footage of the era): the corners’ alignment, tight and outside, and how often the middle linebacker turns and runs down the middle of the field on passing plays. The defense is two-deep before the snap and, on those snaps, has a third player deep a second later. Carson’s Steelers mixed this with plenty of other coverages, but twenty years before it had a name, this is the seed of what became Tampa 2.








NoteFilm room: Tampa Bay Buccaneers 2002 — the scheme at its peak



The 2002 Buccaneers were coached by Jon Gruden, who replaced the fired Dungy before the season, but the defense was still Kiffin’s and still Dungy’s design. It led the NFL in fewest points allowed (196, 12.3 a game) and fewest yards allowed, and opponents had a 48.4 passer rating against it (passer rating is the league’s old one-number grade for passing efficiency; the league-wide figure that season was about 80). Derrick Brooks, the weak-side linebacker, was the AP Defensive Player of the Year and returned three interceptions for touchdowns in the regular season.9 In Super Bowl XXXVII, on January 26, 2003, Tampa Bay beat an Oakland offense led by the league MVP, Rich Gannon, 48–21. Gannon threw five interceptions, a Super Bowl record; three were returned for touchdowns (two by Dwight Smith, one by Brooks), and safety Dexter Jackson, with two interceptions, was the game’s MVP.10
What to notice: every underneath defender’s head. At the snap they turn to the quarterback, not to a receiver, and the instant he throws, all of them break toward the ball. Watch Brooks: he plays the hook-curl zone on his side and arrives at the ball at the same moment as the receiver. And watch the Mike (Shelton Quarles that year) run down the middle on passing downs, so that the seam throw the Raiders wanted was never there. Four of Tampa Bay’s starters from that defense, Sapp, Brooks, safety John Lynch and cornerback Ronde Barber, are in the Pro Football Hall of Fame.








NoteFilm room: Colts and Bears, 2006 season — one family, two head coaches, one Super Bowl



Super Bowl XLI, February 4, 2007, in the rain in Miami, was a Tampa 2 family reunion. Indianapolis was coached by Dungy, who had built the same defense there after Tampa Bay; Chicago by Lovie Smith, Dungy’s linebackers coach in Tampa from 1996 to 2000. They were the first two Black head coaches to reach a Super Bowl, and Dungy became the first to win one, 29–17.
The two defenses show how far one scheme can stretch. Chicago’s, coordinated by Ron Rivera and built around Brian Urlacher in the middle, was one of the best in the league: the Bears went 13–3, and the year before Urlacher had been the Defensive Player of the Year and the defense had allowed the fewest points in the NFL.11 Indianapolis’s, coordinated by Ron Meeks, was small and fast and, in the regular season, the worst run defense in the league, allowing 173 rushing yards a game: the light-box cost of a two-deep defense, paid in full. Then strong safety Bob Sanders, who had missed most of the season injured, came back for the playoffs. Sanders was a hard hitter who played close to the line, in effect an extra run defender in or near the box, and with him the Colts allowed about 73 rushing yards a game in the playoffs.12 In the Super Bowl he forced a fumble and intercepted a pass, and cornerback Kelvin Hayden returned an interception 56 yards for a fourth-quarter touchdown.
What to notice: in Chicago’s defense, Urlacher’s depth on passing downs: he routinely ends up 15 or more yards deep in the middle of the field. In Indianapolis’s, the corners: short, outside, and quick to the flat, with Dwight Freeney and Robert Mathis rushing from the ends. And watch the Colts’ offense against Chicago’s two deep safeties, because it is the best lesson in how to play against this family: patience. Indianapolis mostly took what was in front of it. Dominic Rhodes ran for 113 yards into the light box, Joseph Addai ran for 77 and caught 10 passes, and Peyton Manning completed 25 of 38 for 247 yards, a modest 6.5 a throw for the league’s most dangerous passer.13 Cover 2 bets that you won’t complete enough hard throws; the Colts declined the bet.

title: Cover 2 and Tampa 2
text:
2-Man: two deep, man underneath
Keep the two deep safeties, but change what the five underneath defenders do. Instead of dropping to zones, each one takes a receiver, man-to-man. That’s 2-Man, called Cover 5 in many playbooks and “Cover 2 Man” in video games and on many broadcasts. Don’t look for logic in the 5: unlike Cover 1, 2 and 3, it doesn’t count deep defenders. It is simply the number many systems gave this call, and some systems use 5 for something else entirely.


Show the Python
off = offense("gun_2x2")
mv = {"LCB": (1.5, -13.4), "RCB": (1.5, 13.4), "NB": (1.8, -7.5), "WILL": (4.5, 7.6), "MIKE": (4.5, -0.8)}
dfn = [p.moved(d=mv[p.key][0], w=mv[p.key][1]) if p.key in mv else p for p in c2_shell(off)]
m2 = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=8)
protect(m2)
for k, t in (("LCB", "X"), ("RCB", "Z"), ("NB", "H"), ("WILL", "Y"), ("MIKE", "RB")):
    m2.man(k, t)
m2.drop("FS", (18.5, -12.0)); m2.drop("SS", (18.5, 12.0))
m2.zone((24.0, -13.3), (13.0, 25.5), "deep ½")
m2.zone((24.0, 13.3), (13.0, 25.5), "deep ½")
m2.highlight("LCB", "RCB", "NB", "WILL", "MIKE")
fld = m2.draw(lateral="full", window=(-8, 32))
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, m2, widths=True)
pointer(fld, m2, "inside shoulder:\ntake away the inside,\nhelp is over the top", (10.5, -17.5), (1.5, -13.4), fs=7)
say(fld, m2, "man underneath, trail technique", (10.5, 3.5), fs=7)
plt.show()








Figure 36.7: 2-Man against a 2x2 formation. The safeties play exactly as in Cover 2, a deep half each. Underneath, five defenders play man (dotted lines): the corners on X and Z, the nickel ($) on the slot receiver H, the Will on the tight end Y and the Mike on the running back. (In man coverage the matchups decide where people line up, so the nickel and the Will have swapped sides from the Cover 2 figure: the defensive back takes the wide receiver, the linebacker the tight end.) The man defenders line up on the receiver’s inside shoulder (inside leverage), because the safety over the top has everything deep and outside; their job is to take away anything short and inside and to trail anything deep. Four rush.





The logic of 2-Man is a cleaner, more aggressive version of the logic of Cover 2. Each man defender knows that anything deep belongs to the safety over the top, so he can play underneath and inside his receiver, in trail technique: a step behind him, on his hip, ready to undercut any route that breaks inside or stops short. The receiver’s only open space is deep, and deep is where the safety is waiting. In effect every outside receiver is in a bracket: the man defender underneath, the safety on top.
When it’s called. 2-Man is a long-yardage and end-of-half coverage. On third-and-8 the offense has to throw past the line to gain, and it knows where: receivers run to 8 or 9 yards and sit down in the seams between zone defenders, right at the sticks. Against Cover 2 zone, a hook-curl defender may be 3 yards away when that ball arrives, close enough to tackle but not to stop the first down. In 2-Man the receiver at 8 yards has a defender on his hip, so he has to be beaten, not just found. 2-Man contests every short and medium throw with a defender on the receiver’s hip and still keeps two players deep, so the offense can’t throw over the top. The charting data show it:


Show the Python
dd_order = ["1st", "2nd", "3rd/4th & 1–2", "3rd/4th & 3–6", "3rd/4th & 7–10", "3rd/4th & 11+"]
ticks = ["1st", "2nd", "3rd/4th\n& 1–2", "& 3–6", "& 7–10", "& 11+"]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.1))
xs = np.arange(len(dd_order))
for ax, col, title, top in ((axes[0], "c2", "Cover 2", 30), (axes[1], "m2", "2-Man (Cover 5)", 12)):
    tab = (CV.groupby(["dd", "era"])[col].mean() * 100).unstack().reindex(dd_order)
    for i, e in enumerate(ERAS):
        ax.plot(xs, tab[e].values, marker="o", ms=4.5, lw=1.8, color=style.SERIES[i], label=e)
    ax.set_xticks(xs)
    ax.set_xticklabels(ticks, fontsize=7)
    ax.set_ylim(0, top)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=9)
    ax.set_ylabel("% of charted dropbacks", fontsize=7.5)
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)
axes[1].legend(fontsize=6.8, loc="upper left", frameon=False)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=1.5)
plt.show()








Figure 36.8: When NFL defenses call Cover 2 and 2-Man, by down and distance (share of charted regular-season dropbacks). Left, Cover 2 (zone): fairly steady on early downs and third-and-long, least common on third-and-short, where the offense needs only a yard or two and squat corners and deep safeties are the wrong tools. Right, 2-Man: rare on early downs and peaking on third-and-7 or more, where the defense must cover the receivers at the sticks and keep two safeties deep. The charting source changed after 2022 and FTN labels both coverages more often than Next Gen Stats did, so compare the shapes, not the levels.





In both charting eras, 2-Man is called on third-and-7 to 10 far more often than on first down (about 6 percent of charted dropbacks against about 1 in the Next Gen Stats seasons, and about 10 against 5 in the FTN seasons), and it rises again in the last two minutes of a half, when the offense has to move quickly and the defense can’t afford a long completion.14 It remains a specialist’s call: a few percent of all dropbacks. Cover 2 itself is a far bigger part of the menu, though how big depends on who is charting: about one dropback in seven by Next Gen Stats’ own count (13.9 percent in 2025), closer to one in five in the FTN labels in nflverse (23 percent in 2025), because the two charters draw the line between Cover 2 and its cousins differently. Either way it is least common on third-and-short, where an offense that needs two yards would love to face a defense with corners in the flats and two safeties 13 yards away.15
What 2-Man gives up. Everything man coverage gives up, plus the things two-deep gives up.

The quarterback’s legs. Five defenders have their backs turned to the quarterback, chasing receivers, and only four are rushing. If the pocket opens, there is nobody watching the quarterback, and a scramble up the middle can go for 15 yards. The usual counter uses the one defender who may be free: the man assigned to the running back. If the back stays in to block, that defender either rushes too (a “hug” or “green-dog” rule, from Man Coverage) or sits and mirrors the quarterback as a spy. Even so, 2-Man against a running quarterback is a risk every coordinator weighs.
The man-beaters. Rub routes and crossing routes like mesh make trailing defenders run through traffic, and routes that break outside (an out, a corner, a fade) go away from the defenders’ inside leverage (Man Coverage has the list).
The run. Two safeties deep and five defenders turned to their men: a draw on third-and-8 is a classic call against it.

Telling Cover 2 from 2-Man. Before the snap you can sometimes get a lean: corners pressed tight on the receivers’ inside shoulders, eyes on the receivers, on third-and-long, lean 2-Man; corners 5 yards off and a step outside, lean Cover 2. But it’s only a lean. Defenses know the tell, and plenty of 2-Man is played from the Cover 2 alignment, with corners off and outside until the snap. The answer comes after the snap, in the first second, and the cue is hips and eyes. A zone corner stays square or opens toward the quarterback, his eyes on the ball, while the receiver runs past him. A man corner turns his hips and runs with the receiver, on his inside hip, eyes on the receiver and back half-turned to the quarterback. (Depth alone can fool you: a Cover 2 corner who sinks because nobody threatens his flat can still be near the receiver at 12 yards, but he’ll be looking at the quarterback.)

title: Cover 2 and Tampa 2
section: Why classic Tampa 2 faded, and what survived
text:
Why classic Tampa 2 faded, and what survived
In 2005 the Buccaneers had the NFL’s best total defense and the Bears the second-best.16 By 2006 a long list of teams (Buffalo, Minnesota, Kansas City, Detroit and others) had imported the system, often by hiring coaches from Dungy’s and Kiffin’s staffs. A decade later almost none of them played it as a base defense. What happened?
The rules leaned against it. The coverage depended on squeezing receivers’ releases and on underneath defenders who could disrupt routes as they crossed their zones. After the 2003 AFC Championship Game, in which New England’s physical defensive backs (Ty Law above all) took apart Peyton Manning’s Colts, the league made downfield contact past 5 yards a “point of emphasis” for the 2004 season (a rule the league tells officials to enforce more strictly that year), and the flags for illegal contact more than doubled, from 79 in 2003 to 191 in 2004.17 Physical zone coverage became expensive. (There’s an irony in it: the Colts’ complaints drove the change, and Dungy was the Colts’ head coach.) Dynasties and Counterpunches tells the story of that rule and the passing boom that followed.
Offenses learned to live in the seam. A Tampa 2 Mike carrying a tight end up the middle was a fair fight in 1999. Against a 6-foot-6 tight end who ran like a receiver, or a slot receiver lined up as the inside man in a trips formation, it wasn’t. Offenses also learned to attack the hole the Mike vacates, with digs and curls that sit down 12 to 15 yards deep in front of him, and to flood the sideline holes the squat corners leave. Peyton Manning, who practised against Dungy’s Tampa 2 every day in Indianapolis, became one of the best at taking it apart (that, too, is in Dynasties and Counterpunches).
The Mikes were rare. A middle linebacker who can stop the run between the tackles and also run 20 yards with a receiver is one of the rarest athletes in the sport. Teams that copied the scheme without one found out quickly what Cover 2 without a deep middle defender looks like.
Light boxes met better run games. A two-deep, four-rush defense lives with six or seven defenders near the line. That was survivable when offenses lined up in two-back formations and ran into the teeth of it; it was less survivable against spread formations that thinned the box further and against run games designed to exploit it.
Then the league went one-high, and then two-high again, but differently. Through the early 2010s the fashionable answer to everything was Pete Carroll’s Seattle Cover 3, a single-high defense with press corners and an eighth defender near the line (The Cover 3 Family). (Gus Bradley, Seattle’s defensive coordinator from 2009 to 2012, had coached linebackers under Kiffin in Tampa.) When two-high defense came back after 2018, it came back as quarters and match coverage: two safeties who read the receivers in front of them and fit the run, not two safeties guarding halves while the Mike runs the middle (Quarters and the Two-High Match Family).

What survived
A great deal, just not under its old name.

Cover 2 itself. It never left. Next Gen Stats counted 13.9 percent of 2025 dropbacks as Cover 2 (the source is in the note on 2-Man’s situations), and the FTN charting in nflverse labels even more; it remains a standard call on long yardage, at the end of halves, and as a change-up for defenses whose base is something else.
The Mike who carries the seam. “The middle defender carries #3 vertical” (if the third receiver from the sideline runs straight up the field, the middle linebacker runs with him) is now a rule in Cover 3 match and quarters, the descendants of spot-drop zone. Any time you see a linebacker turn and run with a tight end up the middle of the field in a modern zone, that’s the Tampa 2 Mike’s job inside a newer coverage (Cover 3 match).
Two-high pictures that become three-deep. The Tampa 2’s real trick was showing two deep safeties and playing with three deep defenders after the snap. Modern defenses do the same thing by rotating a safety instead of running the Mike, and that is the whole subject of Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage.
Cover 2 as half a coverage. Cover 6 plays quarters to one side and Cover 2 to the other, squat corner and all; split-field defenses use the Cover 2 half to the short side of the field or against a formation’s lone receiver (Quarters and the Two-High Match Family).
2-Man on third down, as the chart above shows.
The people. The Tampa staffs of 1996–2008 seeded a generation of NFL coaches. Lovie Smith and Rod Marinelli took the system to Chicago and Detroit; Mike Tomlin, Tampa Bay’s defensive backs coach from 2001 to 2005, and Raheem Morris, who worked his way up the same secondary, became head coaches.18 The approach (simple calls, fast players, eyes on the quarterback, rally to the ball) outlived the coverage, and a branch of the tree, Matt Eberflus, ran some of the most Cover 2-heavy defenses of the charting era in Indianapolis and Chicago.19







TipWatch for it on Sunday: the squat-corner spotter



On every passing down for one quarter, look at the cornerbacks first.

Before the snap. Corners 5 to 7 yards off, a step outside the wide receiver, flat-footed, shoulders turned in toward the ball? Two safeties deep (12 to 14 yards) and wide (outside the hashes)? Think Cover 2. Corners pressed on the receiver’s inside shoulder on third-and-long? Lean 2-Man, but confirm it after the snap. Corners 7 or 8 off with two safeties deep? It may be quarters (Quarters and the Two-High Match Family), or a Cover 2 that squats only at the snap (Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage).
At the snap. Does the corner punch the receiver and then stop, hips square, eyes on the quarterback, while the receiver runs past? Cover 2. Does he turn his hips and run with him, eyes on the receiver? 2-Man (or a disguise into something else).
One second later. Find the Mike. Did he stop at 10 yards, eyes on the quarterback? Cover 2. Is he still running straight down the middle at 15? Tampa 2.
When the ball is thrown. Where did it go? A sideline throw between the corner and the safety, or a seam between the safeties, is the offense attacking exactly the holes this chapter mapped. A completed 6-yard out on third-and-12, followed by an immediate tackle, is the coverage winning.

title: Cover 2 and Tampa 2
text:
Predict the play






TipPredict the play 1: one squat corner





Show the Python
off = offense("gun_2x2")
dfn = [p.moved(d=8.0, w=15.4) if p.key == "RCB" else p
       for p in c2_shell(off, corner_d=5.0, safety_d=13.0, safety_w=10.0)]
pr1 = Play(off, dfn, los=60, to_go=10)
pr1.highlight("LCB", "RCB", "FS", "SS")
fld = pr1.draw(lateral="full", window=(-7.5, 17.5))
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, pr1, widths=True)
plt.show()








Figure 36.9: First-and-10 at midfield, ball in the middle of the field. Two safeties deep. The left corner is 5 yards off X, a step outside him; the right corner is 8 yards off Z, nearly head-up. The cornerbacks and safeties are ringed. Use the depth numbers on the left and the hash marks along the bottom.





The two corners disagree. Which coverages fit this picture, which side would you attack with smash or a hole shot, and what would you check in the first second after the snap?






TipAnswer





Several coverages fit; the left side means the same thing in all of them. A two-high shell with one squat corner could be plain Cover 2 (the right corner will squat at the snap), Cover 6 (Cover 2 on the left, quarters on the right; see Quarters and the Two-High Match Family), or Cover 3 with a cloud rotation to the left, where the left safety runs to the deep outside third and the other safety spins to the middle (The Cover 3 Family).
Attack the left. In every one of those, the left corner is a flat defender with a safety coming from inside and deep to cover the sideline behind him. Smash (hitch by X, corner route by H) or a go route by X with H up the seam attacks exactly that grass. Smash is a high-low on the squat corner whatever the coverage behind him; that’s why it’s a favourite call against a squat corner you can see.
Then check, in the first second: does one safety race to the middle of the field? Then it’s cloud Cover 3, the deep middle is closed, and the hole shot is against a safety running to his third. Do both safeties stay on their sides? Then it’s Cover 2 or Cover 6, and the right corner tells you which: squatting at the snap means Cover 2, backpedalling to a deep quarter means Cover 6.











TipPredict the play 2: the tight end up the middle





Show the Python
off = offense("gun_trips")
dfn = c2_shell(off, corner_d=5.5)
mv = {"NB": (5.0, 9.5), "MIKE": (4.5, 2.0), "WILL": (5.0, -4.0)}
dfn = [p.moved(d=mv[p.key][0], w=mv[p.key][1]) if p.key in mv else p for p in dfn]
pr2 = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=7)
pr2.route("Y", r.path((2.0, 0.6), (12.0, -3.5), (22.0, -4.0)))
pr2.highlight("MIKE", "Y")
fld = pr2.draw(lateral="full", window=(-7.5, 24))
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, pr2, widths=True)
plt.show()








Figure 36.10: Second-and-7. Trips to the offense’s right: Z (#1), H (#2) and the tight end Y (#3), in-line. The defense shows a two-high shell with squat corners. On this play Y will run straight up the middle of the field. The Mike (M) and Y are ringed.





(a) If this is plain Cover 2 played by the book, who has Y? (b) What would you watch in the first second to know whether it’s Tampa 2? (c) The defense has seen this formation all game. What might it have changed, and where would you look for it before the snap?






TipAnswer





(a) By the book, almost nobody. The Mike drops to the hole at 10 to 12 yards and watches Y run past him. The trips-side safety has three receivers in his half, and the outside two are running routes he can’t ignore; the far safety is guarding the left half and X. Y ends up in the deep middle, between the two safeties: thin spot ③. This is the classic way to attack Cover 2 from trips.
(b) The Mike. At one second, is he still running, opening toward the trips side and getting on top of Y? That is Tampa 2: the Mike carries #3 up the pipe, which is exactly the throw it was built to take away. Then the question becomes who is running up the middle. A big, slow tight end against a fast linebacker is a fair fight; a fast tight end or a slot receiver against a linebacker 15 yards downfield is not. And the dig by H, sitting down at 12 to 14 yards where the Mike used to be, is open underneath him.
(c) Look at the backside safety, the one on X’s side. He has only X in his half, and his corner is already sitting short on X’s side, so the most common adjustment is to give him #3: he cheats a couple of yards toward the middle before the snap, or he drifts there at the snap, and Y’s seam runs into him. Other defenses hand #3 to the Mike every snap, or check out of Cover 2 entirely against trips (Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage). A backside safety narrower than his partner is your pre-snap hint.











TipPredict the play 3: third-and-8, two-high, corners outside





Show the Python
off = offense("gun_2x2")
pr3 = Play(off, c2_shell(off, corner_d=5.0, safety_d=13.0), los=45, to_go=8)
pr3.highlight("LCB", "RCB", "NB", "WILL", "MIKE")
fld = pr3.draw(lateral="full", window=(-7.5, 17.5))
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, pr3, widths=True)
plt.show()








Figure 36.11: Third-and-8. Two safeties 13 yards deep. Both corners are 5 yards off, a step outside their receivers; the Will (W) is 5 yards off over the slot receiver H and the nickel ($) over the tight end Y. The ringed defenders are the five possible man defenders. The quarterback is a good runner.





Cover 2 or 2-Man? Which is more likely, what single thing would you watch in the first second, and how would you design the pass so the quarterback has an answer either way?






TipAnswer





You can’t be sure, and that is the point of the alignment. Third-and-8 is where 2-Man peaks, but even there Cover 2 is called about twice as often: on third or fourth and 7 to 10, the charting behind the down-and-distance chart has Cover 2 on roughly 12 to 17 percent of dropbacks and 2-Man on 6 to 10. And the corners are showing Cover 2’s alignment, off and outside, not the press-inside look of a 2-Man lean. So the base rate says Cover 2, with 2-Man very much alive.
Watch the corners’ hips and eyes. If a corner opens his hips and runs with his receiver, eyes on him, it’s 2-Man. If he stays square, eyes on the quarterback, and lets the receiver go, it’s Cover 2.
Design for both. Offenses facing this picture often put a zone-beater on one side and a man-beater on the other and let the quarterback pick after the snap: smash to one side (it beats the squat corner in zone), and a rub or an out-breaking route to the other (it beats a man defender playing inside leverage). And if it is 2-Man and nobody is open, the quarterback’s legs are the answer: five defenders have their backs to him, unless the one on the running back has been told to rush or spy. Throwing deep is the one thing not to do: two safeties are waiting there either way.

title: Cover 2 and Tampa 2
text:
Takeaways

Cover 2 is two deep and five under. The safeties each guard a deep half; the corners guard the flats; three linebackers (or two and a nickel) guard the hook-curl zones and the hole. It takes away the short throws and everything over the top, and it costs a defender in the box.
The hard (squat) corner is the tell. Five to seven yards off, outside leverage, eyes inside; at the snap he jams, sinks and sits in the flat. When you see two of them with two deep safeties, think Cover 2, then confirm it after the snap: a corner whose hips turn to run with the receiver is playing 2-Man.
Cover 2’s thin spots are known by heart: the hole shot along the sideline, the smash corner over the squat corner (the same grass, reached from inside), the deep middle between the safeties, and the intermediate sideline hole. Deep passes go to the middle against Cover 2 about one time in three, as often as or more often than against any other coverage in the charting data.
Tampa 2 sends the Mike down the middle: five underneath at the snap, then four under and three deep. It closes the deep middle, needs a rare linebacker, opens the intermediate middle (dagger and levels live there), and is Cover 2’s best answer to trips. It was the identity of Dungy and Kiffin’s Buccaneers, Dungy’s Colts and Lovie Smith’s Bears.
2-Man keeps the two deep safeties and plays man underneath, in trail technique with inside leverage. It’s a long-yardage and end-of-half call, vulnerable to scrambles, rubs and out-breaking routes.
Classic Tampa 2 faded (contact rules, seam-stretching offenses, rare Mikes, light boxes, the move to Cover 3 and then to quarters), but its pieces survive: Cover 2 as a call, the seam-carrying middle defender, two-high pictures that become three-deep, and a large coaching tree.

title: Cover 2 and Tampa 2
text:
Connections
Builds on: Coverage Fundamentals (zones, the shell read, press and off), Man Coverage (trail technique and inside help, for 2-Man), The Cover 3 Family (the three-deep alternative, and the cloud rotation that borrows the squat corner for one side), and Dropback Concepts (smash, flood and four verticals, the concepts built to beat this coverage).
Sets up: Quarters and the Two-High Match Family, the two-high coverage that replaced spot-drop Cover 2 as the NFL’s two-deep base, and Cover 6, which is half Cover 2; Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage, where Cover 2 is reached by rotating from a one-high picture; Zone Blitzes, Fire Zones, and Simulated Pressure; What Beats What, which recaps smash versus Cover 2 in its concept-by-coverage matrix; Third Down and Clock and Game Management, where 2-Man lives; and the history in From the Single Wing to the 1970s Scoring Drought (Carson’s Steelers) and Dynasties and Counterpunches (the Tampa 2 dynasty and how Manning and the seam-running tight ends beat it). The Coverage and Pressure Atlas has one-page cards for Cover 2, Tampa 2 and 2-Man, and a dialect table (Cover 5, Cover 2 Man, 2-Man).
If you want to go deeper: Tony Dungy’s memoir Quiet Strength (2007) for the coach and his Steelers education; Chris B. Brown’s The Art of Smart Football and his Smart Football essays on Cover 2 and Tampa 2; Cody Alexander’s MatchQuarters newsletter and his book Match Quarters for how two-high coverage evolved after Cover 2; and NFL Films’ footage of the 1976 Steelers and the 2002 Buccaneers, where you can watch the Mike run down the middle long before broadcasts showed you the All-22.

title: Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage
text:
Why a defense would lie
Third-and-7 from midfield. As the offense breaks the huddle, the broadcast’s high camera shows two safeties standing 13 yards deep, one on each side of the field, with a wide-open patch of grass between them. The quarterback sees it too. Two deep safeties usually mean the deep middle is empty, so he plans to throw a deep in-cut right into that patch. He takes the snap, sets his feet, and lets it go, and a safety who had been standing 13 yards deep and 7 yards to the side is suddenly sitting at 11 yards, right in the throwing lane. Interception. On the replay the analyst circles both safeties and says “the coverage rotated.” What does that mean? Why did one safety sprint to the middle while the other one came forward? And if defenses can do that, why does anyone bother to read the defense before the snap? This chapter is about the gap between what a defense shows and what it plays, and about the last half-second in which that gap closes.
You’ll be able to…
Start with what the quarterback is trying to do before the snap. In the 20 or so seconds he spends at the line, he decides a lot: which way his linemen slide in pass protection, which defender he must throw away from if that defender blitzes, which side of the field his progression starts on, and whether the called play is any good against what he sees. If it isn’t, he can change it (The Pre-Snap Phase). Almost all of that depends on one question: what coverage is this? If he knows the coverage before the snap, he knows roughly where the open grass will be before anyone has moved. Then the play is half over before it starts.
The defense, meanwhile, has to put eleven people somewhere. And where they stand leaks information, because of plain physics. A safety can only cover ground so fast. If he is going to guard the deep middle of the field, he has to stand somewhere from which he can get there before the ball does. If a cornerback is going to cover one receiver man-to-man, he tends to line up facing that receiver, close to him, on the side he wants to protect. A defense that simply lined up where its call works best would be handing the quarterback its call sheet.
Disguise is the answer: lining up in a way that hides or misrepresents the coverage the defense will actually play. It comes in three flavours, and good defenses use all of them:
There’s an asymmetry in the rules that makes this possible. The offense must be set: after a shift, all eleven players have to be still for a full second before the snap, and only one player may be in motion when the ball is snapped, and not toward the line. The defense has no such rule. Defenders may move, shift, walk up and back out as much as they like before the snap, as long as they stay out of the neutral zone (the strip, one ball long, between the two teams) and don’t use words or acts meant to disconcert the offense at the snap, such as imitating its snap count.1 The offense has to hold still and be read, while the defense can keep moving.

title: Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage
text:
Show one thing, play another. Line up in a two-high shell and play a one-high coverage, or the reverse. This is the dramatic kind, and the next three sections are about it.
Show the same thing every time. Line up in one shell for nearly everything, and play many coverages out of it. The quarterback isn’t fooled so much as left without information. This is the quieter kind, and it is how the two-high defenses that spread through the NFL after 2018 live. Case Study: Fangio’s Two-High Revolution and Macdonald’s Answer tells that story in full.
Move at the right moment. Hold a picture until the last instant and change it at the snap, so there’s no time to react. We’ll call that late rotation below.







ImportantWhy it exists



Disguise is about time. A quarterback who knows the coverage before the snap can decide where to throw before the pass rush has started. A quarterback who must work it out after the snap spends part of his roughly 2.5 to 3 seconds of protection just finding out what he is looking at. The defense isn’t trying to make the quarterback wrong so much as late. A late quarterback holds the ball, takes sacks, throws into windows that close, or settles for a short checkdown.




What disguise costs

The real job starts from the wrong spot. A safety who shows two-high but is really the robber has to travel to his real landmark; one who shows one-high in the box and is really a deep-half player has a long way to run. Every yard of travel is time out of position.
The run defense gets worse. A nickel defense usually has six or seven players near the line (four linemen, two linebackers, sometimes the nickel), the box. A safety who comes down makes it seven or eight, but a safety standing 13 yards deep who is supposed to be that extra run defender arrives late. A safety walked down to look like a run defender who is really bailing to a deep half has left the box one man short. Offenses that run the ball well punish disguise by simply handing it off (Run Fits and Box Math).
Communication and mistakes. Every rotation is a little play inside the play, with its own timing and its own way to go wrong. When one safety rotates and the other doesn’t, the defense ends up with two players in one zone and nobody in another: the “bust” you see when a receiver runs untouched through the middle of the field.
Practice time. A defense that can play five coverages from one look has to rehearse all five from that look, and every extra starting look multiplies the reps. Something has to give. Some defenses keep one look and many coverages (flavour 2 above); others keep a short list of coverages and practise reaching each one from several looks (flavours 1 and 3). Few can afford both.







NoteMadden vs. real life



In a video game the defense picks a play from a menu, and each defender walks to the spot that play’s diagram gives him. What you see is close to what was called. In the NFL, alignment is a separate decision from the call. Coordinators design their calls so that several coverages start from the same picture, and coach players to hold that picture until a set moment. Real quarterbacks are taught to treat the pre-snap shell as a hypothesis, a best guess they expect to confirm or overturn in the first second after the snap.

title: Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage
section: The physics of a disguise: what leaks before the snap
text:
The physics of a disguise: what leaks before the snap
If you can’t hide where you’re going, you can at least make it hard to see. But the distances involved put limits on what a defense can fake, and those limits are exactly what a good quarterback (and now you) can read.
Some rough numbers. A deep pass is usually released around 3 seconds after the snap (in 2025 the middle half of throws travelling 20 or more yards left between 2.6 and 3.6 seconds).2 But the safety’s real deadline is earlier: he has to be on top of the receiver before the receiver runs past him, and in this chapter’s simulated plays a slot receiver running up the seam is 15 yards downfield about two seconds after the snap. The safety also can’t sprint at the snap. His first step or two are a read (is it a pass? where are the quarterback’s eyes?), and a backpedal covers ground noticeably more slowly than turning and running. The fastest safeties top out around 22 miles an hour, roughly 10 yards a second, but a safety reading the quarterback is rarely anywhere near that.3
So give him a working speed of 5 to 6.5 yards a second once he goes (the figure the simulated plays use) and a few tenths of a second to read. That leaves about 1.6 seconds of running before the seam receiver arrives: roughly 8 to 10 yards. A safety 13 yards deep and 7.5 yards from the middle (a few yards outside the hash) is about 8 yards from the deep-middle landmark at 16 or 17 yards: inside the budget. One standing on the numbers, about 14 yards from the middle, is about 14 yards away: far outside it.
Each defender’s real job therefore draws a circle around his real landmark. He can line up anywhere inside it, and the disguise has to fit inside every defender’s circle at once. Within the circle there is still a trade. A safety who will really be a robber at 10 or 11 yards can line up at 13 and still get there, which keeps the two-high picture intact, but the trip costs him time. Lining up at 11 makes his job easy, and it is also a tell. Every disguise is that bargain, made defender by defender: the closer to the real job, the easier the job and the louder the tell. (These are model numbers for teaching the idea, not measurements; with the real tracking data in Tracking Data and the Big Data Bowl you can measure the circles.)
That is why disguises leak. Here is what to look at, and why each one tells you something. The figure shows the textbook two-high spots as faint outlines so you can see how far each defender has cheated from them.


Show the Python
off, dfn = nickel_vs_2x2()
tell_moves = {"SS": (10.0, 5.0), "FS": (13.5, -5.5), "LCB": (1.2, -15.8), "RCB": (1.2, 15.8),
              "NB": (1.5, -8.2), "WILL": (4.5, 7.0)}
textbook = {k: (pl.d, pl.w) for k, pl in ((q.key, q) for q in dfn) if k in ("SS", "FS", "LCB", "RCB")}
dfn = [p.moved(d=tell_moves[p.key][0], w=tell_moves[p.key][1]) if p.key in tell_moves else p for p in dfn]
tells = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=7)
tells.highlight("SS", "FS")
fld = tells.draw(lateral=(-22, 22), window=(-7.5, 18.5))
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, tells, widths=True)
ppy = fld.pts_per_yard()
for k, (d0, w0) in textbook.items():
    gx, gy = fld.xy(*tells.to_abs(d0, w0))
    ghost_marker(fld.ax, float(gx), float(gy), "", ppy, color=style.MUTED)
pointer(fld, tells, "shallower and narrower:\nhe can reach the box\nor the hole, not a deep half",
        (16.6, 13.0), (10.0, 5.0))
pointer(fld, tells, "narrower than usual:\nhe can reach the deep middle", (17.0, -12.0), (13.5, -5.5))
pointer(fld, tells, "press, eyes on the receiver,\noutside shade: man,\nexpecting help inside", (10.0, -11.0),
        (1.2, -15.8))
pointer(fld, tells, "nickel tight on the slot", (-4.6, -12.0), (1.5, -8.2))
fld.ax.legend(handles=[Patch(facecolor="none", edgecolor=style.MUTED, lw=1.2, ls=(0, (2, 1.2)),
                             label="textbook two-high spot")],
              loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 0.0), fontsize=7.5, frameon=False)
plt.show()








Figure 37.1: A two-high shell that isn’t going to stay two-high. The dashed outlines are the textbook two-high spots (safeties 13 deep, a few yards outside the hashes; corners 7 off). Against them, the right safety (SS) is three yards shallower and two and a half yards narrower, and the left safety (FS) is two yards narrower. The corners (CB) are pressed on the outside receivers, square to them, shading slightly outside (outside leverage): man technique, expecting help inside. The nickel ($) is tight on the left slot receiver, H; the slot to the right, Y, is the tight end, with the Will (W) over him. Each detail on its own means little. Together they suggest a rotation to one-high man at the snap: Cover 1, with the SS as a robber in the hole and the FS in the deep middle.






Safety depth. Deep-zone safeties in a two-high shell usually stand 12–14 yards off the ball. A safety at 8–10 yards is probably either coming down (into the box, the flat or the hole as a robber) or about to sprint backward, and the second is hard to do well. Why it tells: the deeper he is, the fewer underneath jobs he can reach in time; the shallower, the fewer deep ones.
Safety width. A safety within about 8 yards of the middle (on the hash or a few yards outside it) can reach the deep middle. One splitting the hash and the numbers, 9 to 11 yards out, is probably staying on his half of the field. When one safety pinches toward the middle and the other widens or creeps down, the shell is leaning toward one-high. Why: the deep middle is a destination, and the safety who will go there likes to start close to it.
Corner technique, then leverage. Two different questions. Technique (stance, eyes, depth) says man or zone: a man corner is square to his receiver with his eyes on him; a zone corner is turned toward the quarterback, seven or eight yards off and ready to backpedal or turn and run to a deep third, or five or six yards off and flat-footed (a squat Cover 2 corner). Leverage says where his help is. A corner who gives up the inside expects a safety or robber there (Cover 1, Cover 3). One who takes away the inside expects help over the top or has none (2-Man, Cover 0). Why it tells: the corner’s technique has to match his job, and technique is hard to fake. Corners can disguise too: a corner pressed in a two-high look who bails at the snap, one who shows deep-third depth and comes up into the flat (the cloud rotation), or a corner and safety who trade jobs (an invert: the safety comes down to the flat and the corner bails to the deep half, as Palms does on one side). They have less room to lie than safeties do, but an invert means the deep player can be a corner, so on the replay watch the two deepest defenders, whoever they are.
Eyes and weight. Zone defenders look at the quarterback. Man defenders look at their man. A safety leaning forward on his toes is thinking about coming downhill; one sitting on his heels is thinking about getting depth. This is the hardest tell to see on a broadcast, but the All-22 film coaches use (a high, wide camera showing all 22 players) shows it.
Timing. When does anyone move? A safety who drifts toward his real spot during the cadence (coaches say he creeps or walks down) is giving away his rotation; one who stands still until the ball moves is not. That discipline has a name, late rotation, and its own section below.
Situation and tendency. A defense that always rotates to the field on third-and-long has a habit opponents will have found on film (Tendencies). The best disguises also break the defense’s own patterns.







CautionCommon misconception



“Two high safeties means Cover 2.” It doesn’t. Two-high is a shell, a picture, not a coverage. From the same two-high look a defense can play Cover 2, 2-Man, quarters, Cover 6 or Palms, or rotate into Cover 3 or Cover 1 at the snap. What the shell tells you is which coverages are easy from here, and so which ones are likely. To name the coverage, look again one second after the snap.

title: Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage
section: Post-snap rotation, part 1: two-high becomes one-high
text:
Post-snap rotation, part 1: two-high becomes one-high
Post-snap rotation is defenders (almost always the safeties) moving at the snap from the shell they showed into a different one. The most common version starts two-high and ends one-high: one safety races to the deep middle and the other comes down. Where the down safety lands decides the coverage. If he goes to the flat, it’s a sky rotation into Cover 3. To the curl area, a buzz rotation. To the hole in the middle of the field at 10 or 11 yards, it’s Cover 3 or Cover 1 with a robber. In Cover 3 robber the robber is one of the four underneath defenders: the two curl-flat players and the hook player keep their zones and the robber takes the hole in front of the deep safety. (You’ll also hear rat: some staffs use it for any robber, others only for a linebacker sitting in the low hole at 5 to 8 yards, as in “Cover 1 rat”.) (Cover 3 built all three from a one-high start; here they start from two.)
Coaches describe all this movement with a pile of short verbs, and some of them mean different things in different mouths. This chapter uses them like this:







Word
What the defender does




rotate, spin
The whole shell turns: one safety goes to the post, the other comes down. “He spun down” and “he spun to the post” are both used; the verb names the rotation, not the direction.


come down, drop down
A deep safety moves toward the line, into the box, the flat, the curl or the hole.


bail
A defender who looked shallow turns and runs to a deep zone at the snap.


sink
A defender gives ground a few yards straight back, keeping his eyes forward.


creep, walk down, cheat
Small moves toward the real job before the snap; they are tells.


rob
Sit in a throwing lane (usually the hole) and jump in-breaking routes.


poach
A backside safety leaves his side to help on the trips side (see below).





Show the Python
def rob_play():
    off, dfn = nickel_vs_2x2()
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=55, to_go=7)
    # pre-snap: nobody in the secondary moves. The Mike's tiny shuffle only gives the play
    # pre-snap frames to draw (gridiron starts the clock at the first pre-snap movement).
    p.motion("MIKE", to=(4.5, 1.6), speed=0.12)
    # offense: dagger to the right (the seam clears out, the dig comes in behind it)
    p.route("Y", r.path((12, -1.0), (20, -2.0))); p.route("Z", r.dig(12, 11)); p.route("X", r.go(20))
    p.route("H", r.hitch(5)); p.route("RB", r.flat(1.5, 6), side=-1)
    p.dropback(2.5)
    p.pass_to("Z", t=1.7)
    protect(p)
    # defense: four rush; the rest rotate to Cover 3 with a robber
    p.drop("FS", (16.5, 0.0), speed=6.5)
    p.drop("SS", (11.0, 4.0), speed=4.5)
    # the boundary corner keeps his cushion on X's go route; the field corner squeezes over the dig
    p.drop("LCB", (20.5, -16.0), speed=5.5); p.drop("RCB", (15.0, 15.5))
    p.drop("NB", (6.5, 12.0)); p.drop("WILL", (6.5, -11.0)); p.drop("MIKE", (7.0, -2.0))
    p.highlight("FS", "SS")
    return p


rob = rob_play()
ROB_T = [-1.4, 0.0, 1.0, 2.6]
if PDF:
    strip(rob, ROB_T, ["−1.4 s · Two-high, as shown", "Snap · nothing has moved",
                       "+1.0 s · FS to the post, SS comes down", "+2.6 s · Cover 3 robber: the dig is thrown into him"],
          ghosts=("FS", "SS"), ghost_t=-1.4, window=(-8.5, 23.0),
          notes_at={3: [("robber", (13.4, 8.6)), ("deep middle", (20.2, -4.5))]})
    plt.show()
else:
    show_animation(rob, times=ROB_T)





  
  Your browser does not support the video tag.



Figure 37.2: Two-high rotates to Cover 3 with a robber. Before the snap (panel 1) both safeties sit 13 yards deep, one on each side: the deep middle looks open. Panels 1 and 2 are identical, and that is the point: no defensive back moves until the ball does. At the snap the free safety (FS) runs to the deep middle while the strong safety (SS) comes down and in to the hole at about 11 yards, right where Z’s dig is heading; the ball (panel 4) is thrown into him. The dashed outlines show where the safeties stood before the snap. The corners turn and run to deep thirds (the left one stays on top of X’s go route); underneath, the Will and the nickel ($) take the curl-flat zones, the Mike the hook and the SS the hole. In print, the four panels are four moments of one play.




Follow the play from the quarterback’s side. Before the snap he sees two-high and an empty deep middle. Against two-high, the space between the safeties and behind the linebackers is often where the ball should go, and dagger (a seam route that pulls the underneath and deep defenders away, with a deep dig coming in behind it; see Dropback Concepts) is built to hit it. Here Y’s seam bends slightly inside to push the middle open. At the snap, the defense changes the answer. The free safety’s sprint to the middle puts a defender over the top of the seam. The strong safety’s short trip down and in puts him exactly where the dig is going to arrive. The quarterback who decided before the snap, and throws on time without looking, throws it to the robber.
Notice the distances. The free safety travels about 8 yards to the deep middle, inside the 8-to-10 yard circle from the previous section. That’s possible only because he lined up 7 or 8 yards from the middle, not on the numbers. The strong safety travels about 4 yards. Neither had far to go, which is the whole design. The shell was two-high, but each safety was standing where his real job was still within reach.
The same rotation can land in man coverage instead: Cover 1 robber. The safeties move exactly as they do here, so the difference is in the corners. In Cover 3 they turn and run to deep thirds with their eyes on the quarterback; in Cover 1 they stay on their receivers, pressing or trailing them wherever they go. One second after the snap, the corners tell you which.
What beats the robber, once the quarterback sees him? The throws he left behind. He has come down from one side, so the seam and the curl on that side are thinner, and his spot in the hole is in front of the deep safety, so a route that gets behind him (a post or deep crosser) is open if the post safety is late. The rest of Cover 3’s weaknesses are still there too: the seams between the deep middle and each deep third, and four underneath defenders who can’t cover every short zone, so stress the curl-flat defender on the far side with a route in front of him and one behind. Concepts Versus Coverages builds the quarterback’s side of this.






ImportantWhy it exists: two-high to one-high



What it solves. It gets an extra defender near the line against the run, or a robber against in-breaking routes, without announcing either before the snap. Offenses facing two-high tend to run the ball, because with both safeties 12 or more yards deep only six or seven defenders are near the line to face the offense’s blockers, and to throw between the safeties. The rotation punishes both: the down safety adds a run defender or sits in the throwing lane.
What it gives up. The rotating safety starts late and from deep, so he arrives in the box after the run has started. The safety spinning to the middle has a long run, so a quick deep throw outside him (a post or a deep corner route released before he gets there) can beat it. And the robber looks only at the quarterback, so a quarterback who looks him off with his eyes and shoulders, then throws elsewhere, can move him out of the play (Concepts Versus Coverages).



Which safety comes down? A rule, not a whim
A defense doesn’t decide on the field which safety rotates. The call says so, usually by tying the rotation to something the offense shows: rotate to the passing strength (the side with more receivers), to the field (the wide side), toward motion, or the other way, weak or to the boundary. Staffs build names for these out of a direction and a landing spot (“sky strong,” “buzz weak” and the like); one of Nick Saban’s trips calls, for example, drops the safety down to the passing strength.4 Before the snap, then, your best guess about direction is:

Toward the strength or the motion is the default. That is where the extra receivers are, so that is where an extra underneath defender helps most. Quarterbacks are taught to expect it.
Away from the strength is itself a disguise. A defense that knows the quarterback expects the strong safety to come down can spin the weak safety down instead, so the robber appears on the side the quarterback thought was clean.
Look for the tells on one safety, not both. The safety who is shallower, narrower or leaning forward is the likely down safety; the other one is the likely post safety. Combine that with the strength of the formation and you can usually call the direction.

title: Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage
section: Post-snap rotation, part 2: one-high becomes two-high
text:
Post-snap rotation, part 2: one-high becomes two-high
The rotation can run the other way. Show one-high: a single safety deep in the middle, the other safety walked down near the box, corners off and ready to bail, the classic Cover 3 or Cover 1 picture. Then, at the snap, the deep safety bails to one deep half and the down safety bails to the other. The corners, instead of bailing to deep thirds, hold their depth and widen into the flats, the Cover 2 corner’s job. That is Cover 2 (or, with man coverage underneath, 2-Man), reached from a one-high start.


Show the Python
def spin_play():
    off, dfn = nickel_vs_2x2("single_high")
    dfn = [p.moved(d=13.5, w=0.0) if p.key == "FS" else p for p in dfn]
    dfn = [p.moved(d=9.0, w=6.0) if p.key == "SS" else p for p in dfn]
    dfn = [p.moved(d=8.0) if p.pos == "CB" else p for p in dfn]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=55, to_go=7)
    p.motion("MIKE", to=(4.5, 1.6), speed=0.12)      # pre-snap frames only; the secondary stays still
    # offense: outs outside (good against one-high with off corners), seams inside
    p.route("X", r.out(8, 5)); p.route("Z", r.out(8, 5)); p.route("H", r.seam(20))
    p.route("Y", r.path((10, 0.0), (19, -5.0)))            # a seam that bends into the open middle
    p.route("RB", r.flat(1.5, 6), side=-1)
    p.dropback(2.5)
    protect(p)
    p.drop("FS", (17.0, -9.5), speed=6.5)
    p.drop("SS", (17.0, 9.5), speed=6.5)
    p.drop("LCB", (8.5, -19.0), speed=2.5); p.drop("RCB", (8.5, 19.0), speed=2.5)   # sink and widen
    p.drop("NB", (8.0, 9.0)); p.drop("WILL", (8.0, -8.0)); p.drop("MIKE", (8.5, 1.0))
    p.highlight("FS", "SS")
    return p


spin = spin_play()
SPIN_T = [-1.4, 0.0, 1.0, 2.0]
if PDF:
    strip(spin, SPIN_T, ["−1.4 s · One-high, as shown", "Snap · nothing has moved", "+1.0 s · Both safeties bail",
                         "+2.0 s · Cover 2: halves, corners in the flats"],
          ghosts=("FS", "SS", "LCB", "RCB"), ghost_t=-1.4,
          notes_at={3: [("½", (18.4, -13.0)), ("½", (18.4, 13.0)), ("middle open", (17.0, 0.5))]})
    plt.show()
else:
    show_animation(spin, times=SPIN_T)





  
  Your browser does not support the video tag.



Figure 37.3: One-high bails to Cover 2. Before the snap the free safety (FS) is alone in the deep middle and the strong safety (SS) is down at 9 yards: middle of the field closed. Panels 1 and 2 are the same picture: no defensive back moves before the snap. At the snap both safeties bail to deep halves, landing between the hash and the numbers, and the corners (CB), who looked as though they would bail to deep thirds, hold their depth and widen three yards toward the sideline (compare each corner with his dashed outline). That puts them right where the outside receivers’ 8-yard outs are breaking. They play the flat from on top, at about 8 yards rather than the flat’s usual 0 to 6, because a corner who starts deep keeps the out in front of him. What opened is the deep middle between the two safeties: H’s seam holds the left safety, and Y bends his route inside into the open middle.




Why bother? One-high with off corners invites certain throws. With a safety in the deep middle and the corners backing off, the outside is where the quarterback looks: quick outs and hitches in front of the bailing corners, curls under them, back-shoulder throws to receivers facing one-on-one coverage. The bail to Cover 2 takes all of that away at once. The corners now sit exactly where the outs are going, and there’s a safety over the top on each side to take away the deep ball outside.
What opens instead is the deep middle, between the two safeties, which is exactly what the quarterback ruled out before the snap. A quarterback who reads the safeties after the snap sees them split and throws between them, up the seam or on a post (the throw that Cover 2 and Tampa 2 shows the Tampa 2 Mike running to carry). The other Cover 2 window is the sideline hole shot, the gap behind the corner and in front of the half-field safety, 18 to 22 yards deep. A quarterback who decided before the snap throws the out into a waiting corner.






ImportantWhy it exists: one-high to two-high



What it solves. It lets a defense look like it is loading up against the run, with the down safety near the box, and still play two deep defenders against the pass. Offenses that see one-high often check to throws outside or to deep shots against single (one-on-one) coverage. The bail punishes both.
What it gives up. The down safety was a run defender in the picture, and now he’s running away from the line, so a run against this look faces one fewer defender than it seemed to. He also has the longest trip on the field, 8 or more yards of depth plus width, so a fast vertical route outside can reach his area before he does.
